items.text: משנת ארבעה אבות נזיקין
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Four primary categories of damages
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the four 'fathers' (primary categories) of damages: the ox, the pit, the grazing animal, and the fire. It then explains that each has unique characteristics, but they share the common principle that they cause damage, their owner is responsible for guarding them, and the one who causes damage must pay compensation from the best land.
items.desc: המשנה מונה ארבעה אבות נזיקין: שור, בור, מבעה והבער. היא מבארת שאין דינם שווה זה לזה, אך כולם משותפים בכך שדרכם להזיק ושמירתם על המזיק, והמזיק משלם תשלומי נזק במיטב הארץ.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by listing the four primary categories (אבות) of damages: the ox, the pit, the grazing animal, and the fire.
sub.desc: המשנה פותחת במניית ארבעת אבות הנזיקין: שור, בור, מבעה והבער.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah explains that each category has unique characteristics that distinguish it from the others, such as the presence or absence of a living spirit (רוח חיים) and the tendency to move and cause damage.
sub.desc: המשנה מבארת שאין דין שור כדין מבעה, ואין דין מבעה כדין שור, ואין דין שניהם (שור ומבעה) שיש בהם רוח חיים כדין האש שאין בה רוח חיים.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah concludes by stating the common principle shared by all categories: they tend to cause damage, their owner is responsible for guarding them, and the one who causes damage must pay compensation from the best land (במיטב הארץ).
sub.desc: המשנה מסכמת את הצד השווה שבארבעת האבות: דרכן להזיק, שמירתן על המזיק, והמזיק משלם תשלומי נזק במיטב הארץ.

items.text: שאלת הגמרא על תולדות
items.text_en: Gemara's first question: Are subcategories like the primary ones?
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah uses the term 'fathers' (primary categories), implying there are subcategories. It asks whether these subcategories are analogous to the primary categories or not.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה: מדובר על 'אבות', משמע שיש תולדות. השאלה היא האם תולדותיהן דומות לאבותיהן או לא.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah's use of 'אבות' (primary categories) that there must be 'תולדות' (subcategories), and asks whether these subcategories are analogous to the primary categories or not.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: מדובר על 'אבות', משמע שיש תולדות. השאלה היא האם תולדותיהן דומות לאבותיהן או לא.

items.text: השוואה לשבת: תולדות דומות לאבות
items.text_en: Comparison to Shabbat laws
items.desc_en: The Gemara compares to Shabbat laws, where primary categories of labor and their subcategories are treated alike in terms of punishment (sin-offering or stoning). The difference between a primary category and its subcategory is only when one performs two primary categories or two subcategories together, he is liable for each, but a primary and its subcategory together incur only one liability. Rabbi Eliezer's opinion is cited, explaining that a primary category is one that was significant in the Tabernacle, while a subcategory was not.
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה ראיה ממסכת שבת: שם גם יש אבות ותולדות, והתולדות דומות לאבות לעניין חיוב חטאת וסקילה. ההבדל היחיד הוא שאם עשה שני אבות או שתי תולדות חייב על כל אחת, אבל אב ותולדה שלו חייב רק אחת. לרבי אליעזר שחייב גם על אב ותולדה, ההבחנה היא לפי חשיבות במשכן.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by comparing to Shabbat laws, where primary categories (אבות) and subcategories (תולדות) are treated alike in punishment: both incur a sin-offering or stoning.
sub.desc: הגמרא פותחת בהבאת ראיה ממסכת שבת, שם נשנה המושג 'אבות מלאכות', ומכאן שיש תולדות.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what difference exists between a primary category and its subcategory, and answers that performing two primary categories or two subcategories together incurs liability for each, but a primary and its subcategory together incur only one liability.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מה ההבדל בין אב לתולדה, ומשיבה: בעשיית שני אבות או שתי תולדות חייב על כל אחת, אבל אב ותולדה שלו חייב רק אחת.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer's opinion is cited, explaining that a primary category (אב) is one that was significant in the Tabernacle (משכן), while a subcategory (תולדה) was not, even though he holds one liable for a subcategory in place of a primary.
sub.desc: הגמרא מיישבת לשיטת רבי אליעזר, המחייב אף על אב ותולדה, שההבחנה בין אב לתולדה היא לפי חשיבות המלאכה במשכן.

items.text: השוואה לטומאות: אבות הטומאות
items.text_en: Comparison to impurity laws begins
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins a comparison to impurity laws, citing the Mishnah that lists primary categories of impurity such as the creeping animal and semen.
items.desc: הגמרא מתחילה להביא דוגמה נוספת ממסכת כלים, שם נמנים אבות הטומאות: שרץ, שכבת זרע ועוד.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens a comparison to impurity laws, citing the Mishnah that lists primary categories of impurity such as the creeping animal and semen.
sub.desc: הגמרא פותחת בהבאת דוגמה נוספת ממסכת כלים, שם נמנים אבות הטומאות: שרץ, שכבת זרע ועוד.

items.text: שאלת היחס בין אבות לתולדות בנזיקין
items.text_en: Introduction: Applying the אב/תולדה distinction to damages
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the subcategories (תולדות) of damages are like their primary categories (אבות) in all respects, drawing a parallel from the laws of impurity. Rav Pappa answers that some are like them and some are not.
items.desc: הגמרא מקבילה בין דיני נזיקין לדיני טומאה ושבת, ושואלת האם תולדות הנזיקין דומות לאבותיהן או לא. רב פפא עונה שיש תולדות שדומות ויש שאינן דומות.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question from the laws of impurity: just as the subcategories (תולדות) of impurity are not like their primary categories (אבות) in all respects, so too regarding damages—are the subcategories like the primary categories?
sub.desc: הגמרא פותחת בהשוואה בין דיני טומאה לנזיקין: תולדות הטומאה אינן דומות לאבותיהן.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa answers that some subcategories are like their primary categories and some are not.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מה הדין בנזיקין: האם תולדות דומות לאבותיהן?

items.text: ברייתא: שלושת אבות הנזיקין בשור ומקור קרן
items.text_en: Source for קרן as an אב
items.desc_en: The Tanna states that three primary categories (אבות) are stated regarding an ox: קרן, שן, and רגל. The Gemara derives קרן from the verse 'כי יגח', proving that נגיחה means with a horn, and addresses a potential objection that a horn attached to the animal might always be considered מועד.
items.desc: הברייתא מונה את שלושת אבות הנזיקין בשור: קרן, שן ורגל. הגמרא מבארת את מקור הקרן מפסוקי התורה והנביאים, ודנה בצורך בפסוק נוסף כדי ללמד שגם בקרן מחוברת יש חילוק בין תם למועד.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that three primary categories (אבות) are stated regarding an ox: קרן (horn), שן (tooth), and רגל (foot).
sub.desc: הברייתא פותחת ומציגה את שלושת אבות הנזיקין בשור: קרן, שן ורגל.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where do we derive that קרן (horn) is a primary category?
sub.desc: הברייתא מביאה את המקור לקרן מפסוקי התורה והנביאים, ומביאה פסוק נוסף כדי להראות שגם בקרן מחוברת יש חילוק בין תם למועד.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers by citing a baraita that derives קרן from the verse 'כי יגח' (when it gores), proving that נגיחה (goring) is done with a horn, and supports this with two biblical verses.
sub.desc: הברייתא מביאה את המקור לקרן מפסוקי התורה והנביאים, ומביאה פסוק נוסף כדי להראות שגם בקרן מחוברת יש חילוק בין תם למועד.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: why does the baraita add a second verse (ואומר)? It anticipates the objection that we do not derive Torah law from the words of the Prophets (דברי קבלה).
The Gemara resolves by saying: come and hear the second verse (בכור שורו), which is from the Torah itself, thus the derivation is valid.
The Gemara objects: this second verse is not a derivation at all, but merely a revelation that goring is done with a horn.

The Gemara reinterprets: rather, the verse is needed to counter a potential argument that the distinction between a tam (innocent) and a mu'ad (forewarned) ox applies only to a detached horn, but for an attached horn one might say it is always considered mu'ad.

The Gemara resolves: come and hear the verse 'בכור שורו הדר לו' (the firstborn of his ox, majesty is his), which teaches that even an attached horn is subject to the distinction between tam and mu'ad.

items.text: תולדות הקרן והבחנתן מאבות אחרים
items.text_en: Identifying the תולדה of קרן and distinguishing them from other אבות
items.desc_en: The Gemara lists the subcategories of קרן: נגיפה, נשיכה, רביצה, and בעיטה. It explains why נגיפה is not a separate אב, why נשיכה is not a תולדה of שן, and why רביצה and בעיטה are not תולדות of רגל, based on the criteria of intent, benefit, and frequency of damage.
items.desc: הברייתא מפרטת את תולדות הקרן: נגיפה, נשיכה, רביצה ובעיטה. הגמרא מבארת מדוע נגיפה אינה אב בפני עצמו, ומדוע נשיכה אינה תולדה של שן ורביצה ובעיטה אינן תולדות של רגל, תוך הבחנה בין כוונה להזיק, הנאה והיזק מצוי.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what are the תולדה (subcategories) of קרן (the goring ox), and lists four: נגיפה (pushing), נשיכה (biting), רביצה (lying down), and בעיטה (kicking).
sub.desc: הברייתא מונה את תולדות הקרן: נגיפה, נשיכה, רביצה ובעיטה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: why is נגיחה (goring) called an אב (primary category) since it is written 'כי יגח' (when he gores), while נגיפה (pushing) is also written 'כי יגף' (when he pushes)?
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה מדוע נגיפה אינה אב בפני עצמו, ומתרצת שהכתוב השווה נגיפה לנגיחה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that נגיפה (pushing) is actually the same as נגיחה (goring), as a baraita shows that the Torah opened with 'נגיפה' and concluded with 'נגיחה', teaching that they are identical.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה מדוע נגיפה אינה אב בפני עצמו, ומתרצת שהכתוב השווה נגיפה לנגיחה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara digresses to explain why the Torah uses 'כי יגח' (goring) for an ox that kills a person, but 'כי יגף' (pushing) for an ox that kills an animal, based on the presence or absence of a מזל (guardian angel).
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת על ההבדל הלשוני בין נגיחת אדם לנגיחת בהמה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that incidentally, the verse teaches that an ox declared מועד (forewarned) for goring a person is also מועד for goring an animal, but not vice versa.
sub.desc: הגמרא לומדת מכאן שמועד לאדם הוי מועד לבהמה, אבל לא להיפך.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that נשיכה (biting) should be a תולדה of שן (tooth), but rejects this because שן involves benefit from the damage (eating), while biting does not.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה שנשיכה ראויה להיות תולדה של שן, ודוחה משום שבנשיכה אין הנאה להזיקה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that רביצה (lying down) and בעיטה (kicking) should be תולדות of רגל (foot), but rejects this because רגל's damage is common (while walking), whereas these are uncommon.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה שרביצה ובעיטה ראויות להיות תולדות של רגל, ודוחה משום שהיזקן אינו מצוי.

items.text: בירור דברי רב פפא: תולדות הקרן דומות לאב
items.text_en: Clarifying Rav Pappa's statement: the תולדות of קרן are like קרן
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions which subcategories Rav Pappa referred to when he said some are like their אב and some are not. It concludes that the תולדות of קרן are like קרן, and Rav Pappa's statement applies to the תולדות of שן and רגל.
items.desc: הגמרא מבררת לאיזה אב התכוון רב פפא באומרו שיש תולדות שאינן דומות. היא דוחה את האפשרות שהתכוון לתולדות הקרן, שכן כולן דומות לאב בכוונה להזיק ובאחריות הבעלים, וקובעת שהתכוון לשן ורגל.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks to which subcategories Rav Pappa's statement about תולדות not being like their אב applies.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת: על איזה אב התכוון רב פפא באומרו שיש תולדות שאינן דומות לאב.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if Rav Pappa referred to the תולדות of קרן, they share the same characteristics (intent to harm and owner's responsibility) as the אב, so they should be like it, not unlike it.
sub.desc: הגמרא דוחה את האפשרות שהכוונה לתולדות הקרן, שכן גם תולדות הקרן דומות לאב בכוונה להזיק ובאחריות הבעלים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the תולדות of קרן are indeed like קרן, and Rav Pappa's statement applies to the תולדות of שן and רגל.
sub.desc: הגמרא קובעת שתולדות הקרן דומות לאב, ורב פפא התכוון לשן ורגל שתולדותיהן אינן דומות להן.

items.text: מקור שן ורגל מהתורה
items.text_en: Scriptural sources for שן and רגל
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to cite the verses for שן and רגל: 'ושלח' refers to רגל, and 'ובער' refers to שן, with supporting verses.
items.desc: הגמרא מבארת את מקור אבות השן והרגל מהפסוק 'ושילח' (רגל) ו'וביער' (שן), ומביאה פסוקים תומכים מהנביאים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks where in the Torah the categories of שן (tooth) and רגל (foot) are written.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת היכן כתובים אבות השן והרגל בתורה.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: 'ושלח' (and he sends) refers to רגל, with a supporting verse 'משלחי רגל השור והחמור' (those who send the foot of the ox and the donkey).
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת היכן כתובים אבות השן והרגל בתורה.

sub.desc_en: The baraita continues: 'ובער' (and he consumes) refers to שן, with a supporting verse 'כאשר יבער' (as when one consumes).

items.text: Conclusion of the Mishnah citation
items.text_en: Conclusion of the Mishnah citation
items.desc_en: The segment concludes the Mishnah's list of avot with the phrase 'the manure until it is finished'.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah concludes its list of avot with the phrase 'the manure until it is finished'.

items.text: Derivation of regel from the verse and its extension
items.text_en: Derivation of regel from the verse and its extension
items.desc_en: Mar explains that 'veshileiach' refers to regel, citing a prooftext. The Gemara questions why a separate verse is needed, and answers that it excludes a possible distinction between damaging with and without a horn. Then, having established regel, the Gemara derives shen's law by analogy to regel, showing that shen also pays full damages regardless of horn consumption.

sub.desc_en: Mar states that 'וְשִׁלַּח' (and sends) refers to the foot (רגל), citing a verse, and the Gemara questions how else the verse could be interpreted.
The Gemara objects that if the verse referred to קרן (horn) or שן (tooth), those categories are already written elsewhere.

The Gemara explains that the verse is necessary, lest one think both 'וְשִׁלַּח' and 'וּבִעֵר' refer to שן, distinguishing between cases where the horn is worn down and where it is not; the verse teaches otherwise.
Now that the verse is established as referring to רגל, the Gemara asks from where we derive that שן includes cases where the horn is not worn down.
The Gemara answers by analogy to רגל: just as רגל applies whether the horn is worn down or not, so too שן applies in both cases.

items.text: Derivation of shen from the verse and its extension
items.text_en: Derivation of shen from the verse and its extension
items.desc_en: Mar explains that 'uvi'eir' refers to shen, citing a prooftext. The Gemara questions why a separate verse is needed, and answers that it excludes a possible distinction between going on its own and being sent. Then, having established shen, the Gemara derives regel's law by analogy to shen, showing that regel pays full damages whether it goes on its own or is sent.

sub.desc_en: Mar states that 'וּבִעֵר' (and consumes) refers to the tooth (שן), citing a verse, and the Gemara questions how else the verse could be interpreted.
The Gemara objects that if the verse referred to קרן or רגל, those categories are already written elsewhere.

The Gemara explains that the verse is necessary, lest one think both verses refer to רגל, distinguishing between cases where the animal goes on its own and where it is sent; the verse teaches otherwise.
Now that the verse is established as referring to שן, the Gemara asks from where we derive that רגל includes cases where the animal goes on its own.
The Gemara answers by analogy to שן: just as שן applies whether the animal is sent or goes on its own, so too רגל applies in both cases.

items.text: Why both verses are necessary
items.text_en: Why both verses are necessary
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Torah needed both 'veshileiach' and 'uvi'eir', since each could imply both regel and shen. It answers that without the extra verse, one might think only one of the two is included, either regel because its damage is common, or shen because there is benefit from its damage. The extra verse teaches that both are included, and also that even when the animal goes on its own, it is still considered regel.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Torah needed both 'וְשִׁלַּח' and 'וּבִעֵר', since 'וְשִׁלַּח' alone could imply both רגל and שן through its dual meaning.
The Gemara answers that without the extra verse, one might think the Torah refers to either רגל (whose damage is common) or שן (whose damage provides benefit), but not both.
The Gemara objects that since both interpretations are equally plausible, one might still exclude the case where the animal goes on its own; the extra verse teaches that both cases are included.

items.text: Toladah of shen
items.text_en: Toladah of shen
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the toladah of shen, answering that it includes rubbing against a wall for benefit and soiling fruits for benefit. It explains that just as shen has benefit and the owner is responsible for guarding it, so too these toladot have benefit and the owner is responsible. Rav Pappa's statement is applied to the toladah of regel, not shen.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the תולדה (sub-category) of שן is, and answers: rubbing against a wall for benefit, or soiling fruits for benefit.

The Gemara objects that these sub-categories share the same rationale as שן (benefit from damage), so they should be considered the same; Rav Pappa's statement about תולדה actually refers to the sub-category of רגל.

The Gemara concludes that the toladah of shen is like shen itself, and Rav Pappa's statement about a toladah being unlike its av (primary category) applies to the toladah of regel (foot damage), not shen.

items.text: Toladah of regel
items.text_en: Toladah of regel
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the toladah of regel, answering that it includes damage caused by the animal's body, hair, load, bit, or bell while walking. It explains that just as regel's damage is common and the owner is responsible, so too these toladot have common damage and the owner is responsible. Rav Pappa's statement is applied to the toladah of a bee.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the תולדה of רגל is, and answers: damage caused by the animal's body, hair, pack, bit, or bell during its normal walking.

The Gemara objects that these sub-categories share the same rationale as רגל (common damage), so they should be considered the same; Rav Pappa's statement about תולדה actually refers to the sub-category of bee (דבור).

items.text: Toladah of bor and its identification
items.text_en: Toladah of bor and its identification
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the toladah of bor, initially suggesting a bee, but rejects that because the av of bor is ten and its toladah is nine, but neither ten nor nine are written. It resolves that the Rabbis know that ten cause death and nine cause damage. However, this is problematic because one is an av for death and the other for damage. Instead, the Gemara identifies the toladah of bor as stones, knife, and load placed in the public domain that cause damage. It then questions whether this is the same as bor itself if they are ownerless, concluding that it is indeed bor.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the toladah (derivative category) of bor (pit).

The Gemara initially suggests that the av (primary category) of bor causes death at ten handbreadths and its toladah causes damage at nine, but rejects this because neither nine nor ten are explicitly written in the Torah.

The Gemara rejects the objection, explaining that the Rabbis know through tradition that ten handbreadths cause death and nine cause damage, based on the verse 'וְהַמֵּת יִהְיֶה לוֹ' (and the dead shall be his).
The Gemara objects that even so, one is an av for death and the other is an av for damage, so they cannot be av and toladah of the same category.
The Gemara instead identifies the toladah of bor as stones, knife, and load placed in the public domain that cause damage.
The Gemara asks how this case is characterized.
The Gemara resolves that if the owner declared them ownerless (הפקר), then according to both Rav and Shmuel, this is exactly the category of bor.

items.text: Challenge to Rav Pappa's classification of toladot
items.text_en: Challenge to Rav Pappa's classification of toladot
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rav Pappa's earlier statement that toladot are not like their avot. It argues that if the toladot are not ownerless, then according to Shmuel they are like 'bor', and according to Rav they are like 'shor'. The Gemara then objects that these toladot share the same characteristics as 'bor' (initial creation for damage, responsibility for guarding), so they should be like 'bor'. The Gemara concludes that Rav Pappa's statement was about the toladah of 'mav'eh'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Pappa's classification of toladot, arguing that if they are not ownerless, they would be like 'bor' according to Shmuel or like 'shor' according to Rav.
The Gemara objects that these toladot share the same characteristics as 'bor' (initial creation for damage and responsibility for guarding), so they should be like 'bor'.
The Gemara resolves that Rav Pappa's statement was specifically about the toladah of 'mav'eh', not about all toladot.

items.text: Analysis of the toladah of mav'eh
items.text_en: Analysis of the toladah of mav'eh
items.desc_en: The Gemara tries to identify the toladah of mav'eh. According to Shmuel, mav'eh is 'shen', and its toladah is already established as like 'shen'. According to Rav, mav'eh is 'adam', so what are its avot and toladot? The Gemara suggests that the av is a waking person and the toladah is a sleeping person, but this is rejected because a person is always 'mu'ad', whether awake or asleep.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the toladah of mav'eh is, noting that according to Shmuel mav'eh is shen and its toladah is already established, but according to Rav mav'eh is adam, so what are its avot and toladot.
The Gemara rejects the suggestion that the av is a waking person and the toladah a sleeping person, citing the Mishnah that a person is always mu'ad (liable) whether awake or asleep.

items.text: Rejection and new proposal: toladah of mav'eh is kocho and nicho
items.text_en: Rejection and new proposal: toladah of mav'eh is kocho and nicho
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the previous suggestion and proposes that the toladah of mav'eh is 'kocho' (force) and 'nicho' (rest). It analyzes the case: if the damage occurs while the object is in motion, it is 'kocho'; if after it has come to rest, it is 'bor' according to both Rav and Shmuel. The Gemara concludes that the toladah of mav'eh is like mav'eh itself, and Rav Pappa's statement was about the toladah of 'esh'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the previous suggestion and proposes that the toladah of mav'eh is 'kocho' (force) and 'nicho' (rest), analyzing the case where damage occurs while the object is in motion.

The Gemara explains that if the damage occurs after the object has come to rest, it is classified as 'bor' (pit) according to both Rav and Shmuel, concluding that the toladah of mav'eh is like mav'eh itself.
The Gemara resolves that Rav Pappa's statement was actually about the toladah of 'esh' (fire), not about mav'eh.

items.text: Analysis of the toladah of esh
items.text_en: Analysis of the toladah of esh
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers the toladah of 'esh', such as stones, knife, or load placed on a roof that fall in a common wind and cause damage. It objects that if they cause damage while moving, they are like 'esh' itself, sharing the characteristics of 'esh' (another force involved, responsibility for guarding). The Gemara concludes that the toladah of 'esh' is like 'esh', and Rav Pappa's statement was about the toladah of 'regel'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what constitutes a toladah (subcategory) of 'esh' (fire), and suggests examples like stones, knife, or load placed on a roof that fall in a common wind and cause damage.
The Gemara objects that if the objects cause damage while still moving, they are identical to 'esh' (fire) itself.
The Gemara explains that 'esh' is characterized by another force being involved and the owner's responsibility to guard it, and the same applies to these objects.
The Gemara concludes that the toladah of 'esh' is like 'esh' itself, and that Rav Pappa's earlier statement actually referred to the toladah of 'regel' (foot).

items.text: Introduction of half-damage from pebbles (tzrorot)
items.text_en: Introduction of half-damage from pebbles (tzrorot)
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the toladah of 'regel', since it was already established that its toladah is like 'regel'. The answer is that Rav Pappa referred to the case of 'chatzi nezek tzrorot' (half-damage from pebbles), which is a halakha transmitted by tradition. The Gemara asks why it is called a toladah of 'regel', and answers: to teach that payment is made from the best quality (aliyah).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: why call it a toladah of 'regel' when we already established that a toladah of 'regel' is like 'regel' itself?
The Gemara answers: Rav Pappa referred to the case of half-damage from pebbles (צרורות), which is a halakha transmitted by tradition.
The Gemara asks: why is this case called a toladah of 'regel'?
The Gemara answers: to teach that payment is made from the best quality (עלייה).

items.text: Rava's question about payment for tzrorot
items.text_en: Rava's question about payment for tzrorot
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rava had a question about whether half-damage from pebbles is paid from the body (gufo) or from the best quality (aliyah). For Rava it is a question, but for Rav Pappa it is clear. The Gemara then asks: if for Rava it is a question, why did Rav Pappa call it a toladah of 'regel'? The answer: to exempt it in the public domain (reshut harabim).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rava had a question about whether half-damage from pebbles (צרורות) is paid from the body (גופו) or from the best quality (עלייה).
The Gemara clarifies that for Rava it is a question, but for Rav Pappa it is clear.
The Gemara resolves that even though Rava has a question, Rav Pappa called it a toladah of 'regel' to exempt it in the public domain (רשות הרבים).

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on the meaning of 'mav'eh'
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on the meaning of 'mav'eh'
items.desc_en: The Gemara returns to the Mishnah and explains the dispute: Rav says 'mav'eh' refers to 'adam' (person), citing a verse; Shmuel says it refers to 'shen' (tooth), citing a different verse. Each rejects the other's proof based on the precise wording of the Mishnah. Rav Yehuda explains that the Tanna listed 'shor' for its horn and 'mav'eh' for its tooth, and the Mishnah means that the horn is not like the tooth because there is no benefit from the damage of the horn, unlike the tooth.

sub.desc_en: The gemara asks what the Mishnah's term 'mav'eh' refers to.
Rav answers that 'mav'eh' refers to a person (אדם), citing a verse from Isaiah.
Shmuel answers that 'mav'eh' refers to the tooth (שן), citing a different verse from Obadiah, and Rav Yosef translates the verse to show the meaning of uncovering hidden things.
The gemara asks why Rav does not accept Shmuel's interpretation, and explains Rav's objection: the Mishnah uses the form 'מַבְעֶה', not 'נִבְעֶה'.
The gemara asks why Shmuel does not accept Rav's interpretation, and explains Shmuel's objection: the Mishnah uses 'מַבְעֶה', not 'בּוֹעֶה'.

sub.text: Gemara's rejection of the d'ikuy argument
sub.text_en: Gemara's rejection of the d'ikuy argument
sub.desc_en: The gemara rejects both d'ikuy arguments, noting that the verses are not decisive, and suggests a different basis: the Mishnah listed 'shor' to include all damages of the ox, so 'mav'eh' must be a separate category, not a person (which would already be covered).

Rav Yehuda resolves the dispute by explaining the Mishnah's formulation: 'shor' is listed for its horn (קרן), and 'mav'eh' for its tooth (שן), and the Mishnah means that the horn is not like the tooth because there is no benefit from the damage of the horn, unlike the tooth.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's comparison of tooth and horn
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's comparison of tooth and horn
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah needed to state that tooth is not like horn, since a fortiori reasoning would suggest that if tooth (which lacks intent to harm) is liable, then horn (which has intent) should certainly be liable. The Gemara explains that it was necessary because one might have thought that just as a Canaanite slave is exempt despite intent, so too horn might be exempt.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah needed to compare tooth and horn, since a קל וחומר (a fortiori) argument would make horn liable from tooth.
The Gemara answers that the comparison was necessary because one might have thought that horn is exempt like a Canaanite slave, who is exempt despite intent to harm.

items.text: Rav Ashi's objection to the slave analogy
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's objection to the slave analogy
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi objects that the case of a slave is different because there is a strong reason for exemption: the slave might be provoked by his master and set fire to another's stack, causing the master to be liable for a huge sum daily.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi objects that the slave's exemption has a strong reason — the master might be ruined by the slave's actions — so it cannot serve as a precedent for horn.

items.text: Revised comparison: horn is not like tooth, and tooth is not like horn
items.text_en: Revised comparison: horn is not like tooth, and tooth is not like horn
items.desc_en: The Gemara rephrases the Mishnah's comparison: horn is not like tooth because horn has intent to harm, and tooth is not like horn because tooth has benefit from the damage. It then asks about the missing category of foot (רגל) and explains that the phrase 'when it damages, the damager is liable' comes to include foot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rephrases the Mishnah's comparison: horn is not like tooth because horn has intent to harm, and tooth is not like horn because tooth has benefit from the damage.
The Gemara asks about the missing category of foot (רגל) in the comparison.
The Gemara explains that the phrase 'when it damages, the damager is liable' comes to include foot.

items.text: Objection: why not state foot explicitly?
items.text_en: Objection: why not state foot explicitly?
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the Mishnah should have stated foot explicitly rather than deriving it from a general phrase.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the Mishnah should have explicitly listed foot rather than relying on an inference.

items.text: Rava's alternative interpretation: the Mishnah discusses foot and tooth
items.text_en: Rava's alternative interpretation: the Mishnah discusses foot and tooth
items.desc_en: Rava explains that the Mishnah's 'ox' refers to its foot, and 'goring' refers to its tooth. The comparison is between foot (whose damage is common) and tooth (whose damage is uncommon), and between tooth (which has benefit) and foot (which has no benefit). The missing category of horn is derived from the general phrase. The Gemara objects again and answers that the Mishnah deals with mu'adim from the start, not with tamim that become mu'adim.

sub.desc_en: Rava reinterprets the Mishnah: 'ox' refers to its foot (רגל), and 'goring' (מבעה) refers to its tooth (שן), comparing foot (common damage) with tooth (uncommon damage) and tooth (benefit from damage) with foot (no benefit).
The Gemara objects that horn (קרן) is missing from the Mishnah's list, and Rava answers that it is derived from the general phrase 'כשהזיק חב המזיק' (when he caused damage, the damager is liable).

The Gemara objects that horn should have been explicitly listed, and the answer is that the Mishnah deals only with mu'adim (forewarned) from the start, not with tamim (innocuous) that become mu'adim.

items.text: Shmuel's and Rav's dispute regarding the inclusion of man
items.text_en: Shmuel's and Rav's dispute regarding the inclusion of man
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why Shmuel does not accept Rav's view: Shmuel argues that if man were included, the Mishnah's later mention of man would be redundant. Rav responds that the later mention is only to count man among the mu'adim. The Gemara then clarifies the meaning of the 'not like' formula.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Shmuel does not accept Rav's view regarding the inclusion of man among the אבות נזיקין (primary categories of damages).
Shmuel argues that if man were included in the opening list, the Mishnah's later mention of man in the seifa (second clause) would be redundant.
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah could have simply listed man in the opening reisha (first clause) instead.
Shmuel explains that the Mishnah's opening deals only with monetary damages (נזקי ממון), not with personal injury (נזקי גופו), so man is excluded from the initial list.
The Gemara asks how Rav, who includes man in the opening, accounts for the Mishnah's later mention of man in the seifa.
Rav responds that the seifa's mention of man is only to count him among the מועדים (forewarned categories), not to introduce him as a new category.

items.text: Explanation of the 'not like' formula regarding ox and man
items.text_en: Explanation of the 'not like' formula regarding ox and man
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the Mishnah's comparison: ox is not like man because ox pays atonement (כופר) while man does not, and man is not like ox because man is liable for four things (ארבעה דברים) while ox is not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah means by the formula 'not like' in comparing ox and man.

The Gemara explains the Mishnah's comparison: ox is not like man because ox pays atonement (כופר) while man does not, and man is not like ox because man is liable for four things (ארבעה דברים) while ox is not.

items.text: Discussion of the common denominator and the inclusion of man
items.text_en: Discussion of the common denominator and the inclusion of man
items.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes the common denominator that their way is to damage, explaining that a mu'ad ox has a way to damage, and a sleeping person has a way to damage. It then addresses the objection that man's guarding is upon himself, citing Karna's teaching that man is one of the four primary categories, and Rabbi Abahu's instruction to the Tanna to include man.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the common denominator that their way is to damage, explaining that a mu'ad ox has a way to damage, and a sleeping person has a way to damage.
The Gemara questions whether a sleeping person has a way to damage, and answers that since he stretches and contracts, it is his way.
The Gemara objects that man's guarding is upon himself, citing the verse 'and their guarding is upon you'.
The Gemara cites Karna's teaching that man is one of the four primary categories, and Rabbi Abahu's instruction to the Tanna to include man despite the objection.

items.text: Gemara's initial support for the Mishnah's categorization
items.text_en: Gemara's initial support for the Mishnah's categorization
items.desc_en: The Gemara supports the Mishnah's inclusion of 'Adam' (man) as a primary category by citing a baraita that man is responsible for his own body's damages.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara supports the Mishnah's inclusion of 'Adam' (man) as a primary category by citing a baraita that man is responsible for his own body's damages.

items.text: Challenges to the meaning of 'Mav'eh'
items.text_en: Challenges to the meaning of 'Mav'eh'
items.desc_en: Rav Mari and Rav Zevid challenge the identification of 'Mav'eh' with water or fire, using biblical verses and logical arguments about the number of categories.

sub.desc_en: Rav Mari objects that 'Mav'eh' might refer to water, citing the verse 'מים תבעה אש' (water is consumed by fire), but the Gemara rejects this because the verse writes 'תבעה אש' (fire consumes), not 'מים נבעו' (water is consumed).

Rav Zevid objects that 'Mav'eh' might refer to fire, since the verse uses 'תבעה' in connection with fire, but the Gemara counters that if so, the Mishnah's listing of 'המבעה וההבער' (the one who causes fire and the fire itself) would be redundant, reducing the four categories to three.

The Gemara raises additional objections: if one claims the Tanna listed 'שור' (ox) as a single category encompassing both its subcategories, then fire lacks 'רוח חיים' (a living spirit) unlike the other categories, and the Mishnah's phrase 'כהרי האש' (like the fire) is problematic.

items.text: Baraita of Rabbi Oshaya listing thirteen primary categories
items.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Oshaya listing thirteen primary categories
items.desc_en: Rabbi Oshaya's baraita enumerates thirteen primary categories of damages, including the four from the Mishnah and additional categories like watchmen and the five components of damages.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Oshaya teaches a baraita listing thirteen 'אבות נזיקין' (primary categories of damages): the four categories of the Mishnah plus the five types of payments (damage, pain, medical, lost time, shame) and the four categories of bailees (unpaid guardian, borrower, paid guardian, renter).

items.text: Why the Tanna of our Mishnah omitted those categories
items.text_en: Why the Tanna of our Mishnah omitted those categories
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that our Tanna only deals with damages to property, not bodily damages, and that Rabbi Oshaya includes two types of 'Adam' (damage to man and damage to ox).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Tanna of our Mishnah omitted the categories listed by Rabbi Oshaya, and notes that according to Shmuel, the Mishnah only deals with property damage, not bodily damage.

The Gemara objects that according to Rav, who includes bodily damage, the Tanna should have taught those categories, and answers that the Tanna taught the category of 'Adam' (man) which covers all matters of man.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Oshaya also includes two types of 'Adam' (man damaging man and man damaging ox), so the Tanna of our Mishnah covers the same categories.

items.text: Why not two types of 'Shor'?
items.text_en: Why not two types of 'Shor'?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Rabbi Oshaya does not list two types of 'Shor' (ox damaging ox and ox damaging man), and answers that in both cases only monetary damages are paid, unlike 'Adam' where bodily damages add extra payments.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rabbi Oshaya does not list two types of 'Shor' (ox damaging ox and ox damaging man), just as he listed two types of 'Adam'.
The Gemara answers that in the case of 'Adam', the two types differ in payments (monetary vs. four items), but for 'Shor', both cases only pay monetary damages, so no distinction is needed.

items.text: Addressing the inclusion of watchmen categories
items.text_en: Addressing the inclusion of watchmen categories
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that watchmen categories (shomer chinam, sho'el, etc.) are cases of man damaging an ox, yet Rabbi Oshaya includes them, and explains that he lists both direct damage (הזיקא דבידים) and indirect damage (הזיקא דממילא).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Rabbi Oshaya includes watchmen categories (שומר חנם, שואל, נושא שכר, שוכר) in his list of thirteen אבות נזיקין, since these are cases of a person (אדם) damaging an ox, not an ox damaging property.

The Gemara answers that Rabbi Oshaya's list includes both direct damage (הזיקא דבידים) — where a person actively causes harm — and indirect damage (הזיקא דממילא) — where damage occurs through the person's property or negligence, thus covering the watchmen categories as examples of direct damage.

items.text: Baraita of Rabbi Chiyya listing twenty-four primary categories
items.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Chiyya listing twenty-four primary categories
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya's baraita lists twenty-four primary categories, adding penalties (קנסות) and other categories like theft, rape, and seduction to the thirteen of Rabbi Oshaya.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya teaches a baraita listing twenty-four 'אבות נזיקין' (primary categories of damages), adding to Rabbi Oshaya's list: double payment, four/five-fold payment, thief, robber, conspiring witnesses, rapist, seducer, defamer, one who renders terumah impure, one who mixes terumah with hullin, and one who pours a libation for idolatry.

items.text: Why Rabbi Oshaya omitted Rabbi Chiyya's categories
items.text_en: Why Rabbi Oshaya omitted Rabbi Chiyya's categories
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Oshaya deals only with monetary damages (ממונא), not penalties (קנסא), and that categories like thief and robber are already covered by watchmen. Rabbi Chiyya distinguishes between property that came permissibly and that which came through transgression.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rabbi Oshaya did not include the categories listed by Rabbi Chiyya in his list of thirteen אבות נזיקין (primary categories of damages).
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Oshaya's list deals only with monetary damages (ממונא), not with penalties (קנסא), so he omits categories like thief and robber that involve penalties.
The Gemara objects that thief (גנב) and robber (גזלן) are monetary cases, so they should have been included in Rabbi Oshaya's list.
The Gemara answers that the categories of thief and robber are already covered by the watchmen categories (שומר חנם, שואל, נושא שכר, שוכר) in Rabbi Oshaya's list.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Chiyya also includes watchmen categories, so why does he need additional categories like thief and robber?
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Oshaya lists property that came to the owner permissibly (בהתירא), while Rabbi Chiyya adds property that came through transgression (באיסורא), such as stolen goods.

items.text: Opening Mishnah and initial debate on conspiring witnesses
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and initial debate on conspiring witnesses
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists 'Fathers of damages' but excludes conspiring witnesses (edim zomemin). The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Akiva's view that they pay from their own bodies (not from best property) justifies their exclusion, and compares with other cases like a goring ox that pays from best property.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why conspiring witnesses (עדים זוממין) are not listed among the primary categories of damage, since their payment is monetary.
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Oshaya follows Rabbi Akiva, who holds that conspiring witnesses do not pay on their own admission, so their payment is a fine, not monetary restitution.
The Gemara objects that if Rabbi Oshaya follows Rabbi Akiva, he should list two types of Ox: one that damages property and one that injures a person, since Rabbi Akiva distinguishes their liability.
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Akiva rules that an innocuous ox that injures a person pays full damages from the excess, unlike damage to property.
The Gemara rejects the objection, noting that Rabbi Akiva himself tempered his ruling: the owner pays only from the ox's body, not from his best-quality property.
A baraita is cited where Rabbi Akiva derives from the verse 'יֵעָשֶׂה לוֹ' that the owner pays only from the ox's body, not from his best-quality property, thus the case is not a primary category.
The Gemara asks why the rapist, seducer, and defamer are not listed, since they pay monetary restitution.
The Gemara answers that whichever component of damages is considered (damage, pain, humiliation, degradation), it is already covered by existing categories.
The Gemara concludes that these payments are fines (קנס), and Rabbi Oshaya does not deal with fines.

items.text: Debate on indirect damages (metame, medame, menasech)
items.text_en: Debate on indirect damages (metame, medame, menasech)
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers whether those who cause ritual impurity (metame), mix forbidden with permitted (medame), or pour libations to idols (menasech) are included. It argues that if the harm is unrecognizable (hezek she'eino nikar), it may be a penalty (kenas) not listed; or if it is recognizable, it is a direct damage (nezek) that should be listed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rabbi Oshaya did not include the cases of one who causes impurity (מטמא), one who mixes forbidden with permitted (מדמע), and one who pours libations to idols (מנסך) in his list of primary categories, since they involve monetary restitution.

The Gemara answers that whichever way one looks at it, these cases are not listed: if unrecognizable damage (היזק שאינו ניכר) is considered damage, then 'damage' (נזק) already covers them; if it is not considered damage, then it is a fine (קנס), and Rabbi Oshaya does not deal with fines.
The Gemara objects that if Rabbi Ḥiyya holds that unrecognizable damage is not considered damage, then why did he already list 'damage' (נזק)? This suggests he must consider it damage.

The Gemara rejects the objection, explaining that Rabbi Ḥiyya teaches both recognizable damage (היזקא דמינכרא) and unrecognizable damage (היזקא דלא מינכרא) as separate categories, so he does consider unrecognizable damage as a distinct type of damage.

The Gemara asks: Granted, the tanna of our mishna taught a number (4) to exclude Rabbi Oshaya's categories, and Rabbi Oshaya taught a number (13) to exclude Rabbi Ḥiyya's categories, but what does the number (24) of Rabbi Ḥiyya's list serve to exclude?

items.text: Exclusion of moser (informer) and mefagel (spoiler of sacrifices)
items.text_en: Exclusion of moser (informer) and mefagel (spoiler of sacrifices)
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Tanna of our Mishnah (Rabbi Oshaya) excludes moser (one who hands over Jewish property to gentiles) and mefagel (one who spoils sacrificial meat). It notes that mefagel involves sacred matters (kodashim) not monetary, and moser involves speech (dibbur) which may be excluded if it lacks a physical act. However, the case of motzi shem ra (defamation) involves speech but is included because it has an accompanying act (ma'aseh).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the number twenty-four excludes the cases of a מוסר (informer) and a מפגל (one who spoils sacrificial meat).

The Gemara asks why Rabbi Ḥiyya did not include these cases, and answers that regarding מפגל (spoiler of sacrifices) he does not deal with consecrated items, and regarding מוסר (informer) the damage is through speech, which he does not include.
The Gemara objects that the case of מוציא שם רע (defamer) is also speech, yet Rabbi Ḥiyya includes it, and answers that it involves an accompanying action.

The Gemara objects that the case of עדים זוממין (conspiring witnesses) involves speech without action, yet Rabbi Ḥiyya includes it, and answers that the Torah calls it an action, as written: 'ועשיתם לו כאשר זמם לעשות לאחיו' (and you shall do to him as he conspired to do to his brother).

items.text: Comparison of 'Avot' (fathers) and 'Toldot' (offspring) categories
items.text_en: Comparison of 'Avot' (fathers) and 'Toldot' (offspring) categories
items.desc_en: The Gemara examines whether the Mishnah's list of 'Avot' implies there are 'Toldot' (subcategories). For Rabbi Hiyya and Rabbi Oshaya, the term 'Avot' might not imply offspring; but Rabbi Abahu argues all are 'Avot' for payment from best property, deriving from verses using 'tachat', 'netinah', 'yeshalem', 'kesef'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the term 'Avot' (fathers) used by Rabbi Hiyya and Rabbi Oshaya implies there are 'Toldot' (subcategories), and asks what those subcategories would be.
Rabbi Abahu answers that all categories listed are considered 'Avot' in the sense that one must pay from the best-quality property.
The Gemara asks for the reason behind Rabbi Abahu's statement.

The Gemara explains that the requirement to pay from best-quality property is derived from the terms 'tachat' (in place of), 'netinah' (giving), 'yeshalem' (he shall pay), and 'kesef' (money) found in verses related to the categories.
The Mishna states that the category of Ox is not similar to the category of Maveh.
The Gemara asks what the Mishna means by this statement.

sub.text: Rav Zevid in the name of Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Zevid in the name of Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Zevid in the name of Rava explains that the Mishna means: let the Merciful One write one category and derive the other from it, but then it says that one cannot derive one category from another because each has unique characteristics.

items.text: Clarification of 'not this and that' phrase
items.text_en: Clarification of 'not this and that' phrase
items.desc_en: Rav Mesharshiya explains the phrase 'lo zeh vazeh sheyesh bahem ruach chayim' — it means that neither the ox nor the man (who cause damage) have 'ruach chayim' (living spirit) in the sense of being liable for full damages from best property, contrasting with other cases.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the mishna means by the phrase 'lo zeh vazeh sheyesh bahem ruach chayim'.

sub.text: Rav Mesharshiya in the name of Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Mesharshiya in the name of Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Mesharshiya in the name of Rava begins to explain the meaning of the mishna's phrase.

items.text: Initial question and rejection
items.text_en: Initial question and rejection
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Torah wrote two categories (קרן and שן/רגל) when one could be derived from the other, but then rejects the possibility of deriving one from the other.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Torah wrote two categories (קרן and שן/רגל) when one could be derived from the other.
The Gemara rejects the possibility of deriving one category from the other, stating that one cannot be learned from the other.

items.text: Rava's analysis and alternative view
items.text_en: Rava's analysis and alternative view
items.desc_en: Rava argues that if you compare all categories to בור, they could all be derived via a common element (מה הצד), except for קרן because it is מועד from the start. The Gemara then notes that according to the view that קרן is superior (since it intends to damage), even קרן could be derived.

sub.desc_en: Rava argues that if you compare all categories to בור (pit), they could all be derived via a common element (מה הצד), except for קרן (horn) because it is not מועד (forewarned) from the start.
The Gemara notes that according to the view that קרן (horn) is superior (since it intends to damage), even קרן could be derived via the common element.

items.text: Purpose of listing categories
items.text_en: Purpose of listing categories
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the Torah wrote each category not for derivation but to teach their specific halachot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: For what halachic purpose did the Torah write these categories?
The Gemara answers: They were written to teach their specific halachot (הלכות).

items.text: Specific halachot of each category
items.text_en: Specific halachot of each category
items.desc_en: The Gemara enumerates the unique halachic lessons: קרן teaches the distinction between תמה and מועדת; שן ורגל exempt in public domain; בור exempts vessels (or, according to Rabbi Yehuda who obligates vessels, exempts humans); אדם obligates four items; אש exempts טמוּן (or, according to Rabbi Yehuda who obligates טמוּן, the Gemara asks what it comes to include).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the category of קרן (goring) is written to teach the distinction between a תמה (innocent) and a מועדת (forewarned) ox.
The Gemara states that the categories of שן (tooth) and רגל (foot) are written to exempt them when damage occurs in the public domain.

sub.text: Gemara's enumeration with Rabbi Yehuda's alternative
sub.text_en: Gemara's enumeration with Rabbi Yehuda's alternative
sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the category of בור (pit) is written to exempt vessels from liability, but according to Rabbi Yehuda who obligates for vessel damage in a pit, it exempts humans instead.
The Gemara states that the category of אדם (a person) is written to obligate him in the four items of damages (nezek, tza'ar, ripui, shevet, and boshet).

sub.text: Gemara's enumeration with Rabbi Yehuda's alternative and question
sub.text_en: Gemara's enumeration with Rabbi Yehuda's alternative and question
sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the category of אש (fire) is written to exempt טמוּן (hidden items), but according to Rabbi Yehuda who obligates for hidden items in fire, the Gemara asks what this category comes to include.

items.text: Opening citation of the Tosefta
items.text_en: Opening citation of the Tosefta
items.desc_en: The Tosefta states that the common aspect of the four categories is used to include additional cases. The Gemara then asks what exactly is being included.

sub.desc_en: The Tosefta states that the common aspect of the four categories is used to include additional cases like a plowshare or a rolling stone.

items.text: Abaye's proposal and the ensuing dialectic
items.text_en: Abaye's proposal and the ensuing dialectic
items.desc_en: Abaye suggests that the common aspect includes stones, knife, and load placed on a roof that fall in a normal wind and cause damage. The Gemara challenges this: if they damage while moving, they are like Fire; if after settling and are ownerless, they are like Pit. The Gemara then constructs a formal argument (בנין אב) to distinguish them from both Fire and Pit, concluding that the case is unique.

sub.desc_en: Abaye proposes that the common aspect includes stones, knife, and load placed on a roof that fall in a normal wind and cause damage.
The Gemara asks: if the objects damage while moving, they are like Fire.
The Gemara objects: what distinguishes Fire is that another force is involved and your property and its guarding are upon you; these cases are similar.
The Gemara asks: if after they settle and are ownerless, they are like Pit.
The Gemara objects: what distinguishes Pit is that its initial creation is for damage and your property and its guarding are upon you; these cases are similar.
The Gemara asks: if they are not ownerless, according to Shmuel who derives all from his Pit, they are like Pit.
The Gemara answers: actually they are ownerless, but they are not like Pit because Pit has no other force involved, while these have another force involved.
The Gemara objects: Fire proves that another force is involved yet it is a separate category.
The Gemara answers: what distinguishes Fire is that its way is to go and damage.
The Gemara concludes: Pit proves the opposite, and the argument cycles back, establishing the unique status of the case.

items.text: Rava's proposal and the ensuing dialectic
items.text_en: Rava's proposal and the ensuing dialectic
items.desc_en: Rava suggests that the common aspect includes a pit that rolls due to the feet of people or animals. The Gemara again challenges: if ownerless, it is like Pit; if not ownerless, for Shmuel it is still Pit. The Gemara then constructs a formal argument distinguishing it from Pit (since his actions did not cause it) and from Ox, concluding with a dialectical standoff.

sub.desc_en: Rava proposes that the common aspect includes a pit that rolls due to the feet of people or animals.
The Gemara asks: if the items are ownerless, then according to both Rav and Shmuel this is simply Pit.
The Gemara objects: what distinguishes Pit is that its initial creation is for damage, and the same applies here.
The Gemara asks: if they are not ownerless, then for Shmuel who derives all from his Pit, this is still Pit.
The Gemara answers: actually they are ownerless, but they differ from Pit because his actions did not cause them.
The Gemara objects: let Ox prove the opposite, since Ox's actions cause damage.
The Gemara counters: what distinguishes Ox is that it naturally goes and damages; let Pit prove otherwise.
The Gemara concludes that the argument returns and the two cases are not analogous, leaving a dialectical standoff.

items.text: Rav Adda bar Ahava's proposal and the ensuing dialectic
items.text_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava's proposal and the ensuing dialectic
items.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava suggests that the common aspect includes a case from a baraita: people who open their drains or sweep their caves in summer without permission, but in winter with permission, yet if they cause damage they are liable. The Gemara challenges: if damage occurs while the water is flowing, it is his direct force; if after settling and ownerless, it is like Pit; if not ownerless, for Shmuel it is still Pit. The Gemara then distinguishes it from Pit because it was done with permission.

sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava proposes to include the case from a baraita where people open drains or sweep caves without permission in summer but with permission in winter, yet if they cause damage they are liable.
The Gemara asks: if the damage occurs while the water is flowing, it is his direct force (כוחו).
The Gemara asks: if after settling and the water is ownerless, it is like Pit (בור) for both Rav and Shmuel.
The Gemara asks: if the water is not ownerless, for Shmuel who derives all from Pit, it is still Pit.
The Gemara resolves: it is always ownerless, but it differs from Pit because Pit is dug without permission, whereas these actions were done with permission.

items.text: Return of the binyan av: 'Let the ox prove it' and 'Let the pit prove it'
items.text_en: Return of the binyan av: 'Let the ox prove it' and 'Let the pit prove it'
items.desc_en: The Gemara resumes the cyclical argument (binyan av) that attempts to derive a common principle for the four primary torts. It brings the ox as a counterexample to the pit, and then the pit as a counterexample to the ox, concluding that the argument returns to its starting point.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens the cyclical argument by proposing that the ox (שור) can prove a counterexample to the pit, and then the pit (בור) can prove a counterexample to the ox, concluding that the argument returns to its starting point.

items.text: Ravina's proposal: The case of a wall or tree that falls into the public domain
items.text_en: Ravina's proposal: The case of a wall or tree that falls into the public domain
items.desc_en: Ravina suggests that the binyan av is needed to include the case of a wall or tree that falls into the public domain and causes damage. The mishnah states that if the owner was given time to cut down the tree or demolish the wall, and it falls within that time, he is exempt; after the time, he is liable.

sub.desc_en: Ravina proposes that the binyan av (foundational case) is needed to include the case of a wall or tree that falls into the public domain and causes damage, citing the mishnah's ruling that the owner is exempt if it falls within the given time and liable afterward.

items.text: Analysis of Ravina's case: Is it like a pit or not?
items.text_en: Analysis of Ravina's case: Is it like a pit or not?
items.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes Ravina's case. If the wall or tree was declared ownerless, it resembles a pit (both Rav and Shmuel agree). If not ownerless, according to Shmuel who derives all from the pit, it is still like a pit. The Gemara then defends Ravina by distinguishing the case: unlike a pit, these objects were not initially created for damage.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if the wall or tree was declared ownerless, it is like a pit (בור) according to both Rav and Shmuel, because the damage is common and the owner is responsible for guarding it.
The Gemara asks: if the wall or tree was not declared ownerless, according to Shmuel who derives all damage categories from the pit, it is still like a pit.
The Gemara resolves: actually the wall or tree was declared ownerless, but it is not like a pit because a pit was initially created for damage, whereas these were not.

items.text: Return of the binyan av again: 'Let the ox prove it' and 'Let the pit prove it'
items.text_en: Return of the binyan av again: 'Let the ox prove it' and 'Let the pit prove it'
items.desc_en: The Gemara repeats the cyclical argument, bringing the ox and the pit as counterexamples to each other, concluding again that the argument returns to its starting point.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the ox can prove the case, as a counterexample to the wall and tree.
The Gemara objects that the ox is different because it naturally walks and causes damage, unlike the wall and tree.
The Gemara counters with the pit as a proof, and the argument returns to its starting point.

items.text: A linguistic note: 'חָב הַמַּזִּיק' vs. 'חַיָּיב הַמַּזִּיק'
items.text_en: A linguistic note: 'חָב הַמַּזִּיק' vs. 'חַיָּיב הַמַּזִּיק'
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a linguistic peculiarity in the mishnah: it says 'חָב הַמַּזִּיק' (the injurer is liable) instead of the expected 'חַיָּיב הַמַּזִּיק'. Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav explains that this tanna is from Jerusalem, who uses a lighter language.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah states that when the animal damages, the injurer is liable (חָב הַמַּזִּיק).
The Gemara questions why the mishnah uses the unusual phrase 'חָב הַמַּזִּיק' instead of the expected 'חַיָּיב הַמַּזִּיק'.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav explains that this tanna is from Jerusalem, who uses a lighter language (לִישָּׁנָא קַלִּילָא).

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva on payment from the best property
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva on payment from the best property
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a baraita: Rabbi Yishmael interprets 'מֵיטַב שָׂדֵהוּ וּמֵיטַב כַּרְמוֹ יְשַׁלֵּם' to mean the best of the injured party's field, while Rabbi Akiva says it comes only to collect for the injured party from the best (of the injurer's property), and a fortiori for the Temple treasury.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites the verse 'מֵיטַב שָׂדֵהוּ וּמֵיטַב כַּרְמוֹ יְשַׁלֵּם' and presents Rabbi Yishmael's position that payment is from the best of the injured party's field.
Rabbi Akiva argues that the verse comes only to collect for the injured party from the best property, and a fortiori for the Temple treasury.

items.text: First explanation of the dispute: Rava's objection and Rav Idi bar Avin's answer
items.text_en: First explanation of the dispute: Rava's objection and Rav Idi bar Avin's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Yishmael's position: if the animal ate a lean plant, does he pay for a fat one? Rav Idi bar Avin explains the case is where the animal ate from a bed between beds and we don't know if it was lean or fat, so he pays for the fat one. Rava objects: if we knew it was lean, he would pay lean; now that we don't know, he pays fat? The burden of proof is on the claimant.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Yishmael's position: if the animal ate a lean plant, does he still pay for a fat one?
Rav Idi bar Avin explains the case is where the animal ate from a bed between beds and we don't know if it was lean or fat, so he pays for the fat one.
Rava objects: if we knew it was lean he would pay lean, now that we don't know he pays fat? The burden of proof is on the claimant.

items.text: Second explanation of the dispute: Rav Acha bar Yaakov's resolution
items.text_en: Second explanation of the dispute: Rav Acha bar Yaakov's resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov explains the dispute differently: the case is where the injured party's best property is equivalent to the injurer's inferior property. Rabbi Yishmael holds we appraise based on the injured party's property, while Rabbi Akiva holds we appraise based on the injurer's property.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov introduces a new scenario: the injured party's best property is equivalent to the injurer's inferior property.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Yaakov's explanation of the dispute
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov's explanation of the dispute
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov explains the dispute: Rabbi Yishmael appraises based on the injured party's property, while Rabbi Akiva appraises based on the injurer's property.

items.text: Scriptural basis for Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva's positions
items.text_en: Scriptural basis for Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva's positions
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the scriptural derivations. Rabbi Yishmael uses a gezerah shavah (verbal analogy) from the word 'field' mentioned above and below. Rabbi Akiva interprets 'מֵיטַב שָׂדֵהוּ וּמֵיטַב כַּרְמוֹ יְשַׁלֵּם' to mean the best of the one who pays. The Gemara then explains how both the gezerah shavah and the verse are effective for Rabbi Yishmael.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the scriptural basis for Rabbi Yishmael's position.

The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yishmael derives his position from a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) between the word 'field' stated above (in the context of the injured party) and below (in the payment verse).
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Akiva interprets the verse 'מֵיטַב שָׂדֵהוּ וּמֵיטַב כַּרְמוֹ יְשַׁלֵּם' to mean the best of the one who pays (the injurer).

The Gemara resolves that for Rabbi Yishmael, both the גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) and the verse are effective: the גזירה שווה establishes the general principle, and the verse applies in a case where the injurer's inferior land is worth less than the injured party's superior land, so payment must be from the injurer's best land.

items.text: Explanation of the a fortiori argument for the Temple treasury
items.text_en: Explanation of the a fortiori argument for the Temple treasury
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies Rabbi Akiva's statement 'and a fortiori for the Temple treasury'. It rejects the possibility that it refers to an ox of ours goring an ox of the Temple (since the verse says 'the ox of his fellow', not of the Temple). Instead, it refers to one who says 'I pledge a maneh to the Temple maintenance', where the treasurer collects from the best property, and a fortiori from a regular creditor.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Rabbi Akiva's a fortiori argument for the Temple treasury refers to.
The Gemara rejects the possibility that the a fortiori argument refers to an ox of ours goring an ox of the Temple, because the verse says 'the ox of his fellow', not of the Temple.

The Gemara explains that the a fortiori argument refers to one who pledges a maneh to the Temple maintenance, where the treasurer collects from the best property, and a fortiori from a regular creditor.

items.text: Challenge to Rabbi Akiva's view on consecrated property
items.text_en: Challenge to Rabbi Akiva's view on consecrated property
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the assumption that Rabbi Akiva holds that a creditor collects from the best-quality land, by comparing a creditor to a tortfeasor and arguing that consecrated property, which has weaker rights in damages, should not be treated similarly.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Akiva's view by arguing that if a creditor collects from intermediate land, consecrated property, which has weaker rights in damages, should not be treated similarly.

items.text: Resolution: Rabbi Akiva follows Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya
items.text_en: Resolution: Rabbi Akiva follows Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Akiva's view on consecrated property is based on Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya's ruling that a consecrated ox that gores a common ox is exempt, while a common ox that gores a consecrated ox pays full damages, regardless of whether it is a tam or mu'ad.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Akiva's view on consecrated property is based on Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya's ruling.

sub.text: Supporting baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya
sub.desc_en: The baraita states Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya's ruling that a consecrated ox that gores a common ox is exempt, while a common ox that gores a consecrated ox pays full damages regardless of tam or mu'ad status.

items.text: Alternative interpretation: Dispute over Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya's ruling
items.text_en: Alternative interpretation: Dispute over Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the dispute between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva might not be about the quality of land but about whether to follow Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya or the Rabbis regarding consecrated property.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the dispute between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva is necessarily about the quality of land, suggesting it might instead be about whether to follow Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya or the Rabbis regarding consecrated property.
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Akiva follows Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya's ruling on consecrated property, while Rabbi Yishmael follows the Rabbis who disagree.

items.text: Refutation: Evidence from the verse and Rav Ashi's baraita
items.text_en: Refutation: Evidence from the verse and Rav Ashi's baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara refutes the alternative interpretation by pointing out that the verse 'לֹא בָּא הַכָּתוּב' and the kal vachomer for consecrated property would be meaningless, and cites Rav Ashi's explicit baraita where Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva dispute whether 'מֵיטַב שָׂדֵהוּ' refers to the victim's or the tortfeasor's land.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the alternative interpretation were correct, the verse's phrase 'לֹא בָּא הַכָּתוּב' and the kal vachomer for consecrated property would be meaningless.
Rav Ashi cites an explicit baraita where Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva dispute whether 'מֵיטַב שָׂדֵהוּ' refers to the victim's or the tortfeasor's land, confirming the original interpretation.

items.text: Abaye's contradiction and resolution regarding payment in kind
items.text_en: Abaye's contradiction and resolution regarding payment in kind
items.desc_en: Abaye raises a contradiction between the verse 'מֵיטַב שָׂדֵהוּ' implying only best land and a baraita that includes even bran as valid payment, and resolves it by distinguishing between voluntary payment (where any item of value suffices) and forced payment (where only best land is taken).

sub.desc_en: Abaye raises a contradiction: the verse 'מֵיטַב שָׂדֵהוּ וּמֵיטַב כַּרְמוֹ יְשַׁלֵּם' implies that only the best land is taken, not any other item.
A baraita teaches that the word 'יָשִׁיב' (he shall return) includes items of monetary value, even bran, as valid payment.
The gemara resolves the contradiction: the verse requiring best land applies when payment is forced (בעל כרחו), while the baraita allowing any item applies when payment is voluntary (מדעתו).

items.text: Ulla's support and Abaye's counterargument
items.text_en: Ulla's support and Abaye's counterargument
items.desc_en: Ulla supports the resolution by noting that the verse uses 'יְשַׁלֵּם' (active) implying forced payment, but Abaye counters that the active form 'יְשַׁלֵּם' actually implies voluntary payment, as the passive would be 'יְשׁוּלַּם'.

sub.desc_en: Ulla supports the resolution by noting that the verse uses 'יְשַׁלֵּם' (active) implying forced payment.
Abaye counters that the active form 'יְשַׁלֵּם' actually implies voluntary payment, as the passive would be 'יְשׁוּלַּם'.

items.text: Abaye's alternative resolution based on Mar's teaching
items.text_en: Abaye's alternative resolution based on Mar's teaching
items.desc_en: Abaye offers a different resolution based on a baraita about ma'aser ani, where Mar explains that if land prices drop generally, the debtor can sell at the lower price, but if only his land depreciates due to his dealings, he must sell at the higher market price.

sub.desc_en: Abaye introduces a different resolution based on a baraita about ma'aser ani, where a debtor with unsellable property is fed ma'aser ani up to half its value.
Mar asks a clarifying question about the baraita: if land prices drop generally, the debtor can sell at the lower price, so why limit to half?
Mar answers that the case is when land prices generally rise, but the debtor's own land depreciated due to his frequent dealings, so he must sell at the higher market price.

items.text: Gemara's initial ruling on discount for immediate payment
items.text_en: Gemara's initial ruling on discount for immediate payment
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that even a small discount should not be given to the creditor, because land prices fluctuate: in Nisan they are high, in Tishrei low. The debtor, needing cash, sells at the current low price, so the creditor cannot demand a discount for immediate payment.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that even a small discount should not be given to the creditor for immediate payment.
Mar explains that land prices fluctuate between Nisan and Tishrei, and the debtor sells at the current low price due to need, so the creditor cannot demand a discount.

items.text: Application to damages: the creditor can demand a discount
items.text_en: Application to damages: the creditor can demand a discount
items.desc_en: The Gemara applies the same logic to damages: the victim collects from the best land. If the victim says 'give me intermediate land with a small discount,' the debtor can respond: 'If you take according to your right, take at the current price; if not, take at the future high price.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by applying the previous logic to damages: the victim collects from the best land (עידית).
The Gemara presents the debtor's response: if the victim asks for intermediate land with a small discount, the debtor can offer either the current price or the future high price.

items.text: Rav Acha bar Yaakov's objection
items.text_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov's objection
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov objects: if so, you weaken the rights of victims regarding intermediate and inferior land, since the Torah says 'from the best' and you say they cannot even get intermediate or inferior land at a discount.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov objects that the proposed arrangement weakens the rights of victims regarding intermediate and inferior land, since the Torah says 'from the best' and the ruling would deny them even a discount on those lower grades.

items.text: Rav Acha bar Yaakov's alternative: compare to a creditor
items.text_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov's alternative: compare to a creditor
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov suggests comparing the case to that of a creditor, whose right is to intermediate land. If the creditor says 'give me inferior land with a small discount,' the debtor can offer the same deal: take at current price or future high price.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Yaakov's alternative proposal
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov's alternative proposal
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov proposes comparing the case to a creditor (בעל חוב), whose right is to intermediate land (בינונית), and if the creditor asks for inferior land (זיבורית) with a small discount, the debtor can offer the same deal: take at current price or future high price.

items.text: Rav Acha brei d'Rav Ika's objection
items.text_en: Rav Acha brei d'Rav Ika's objection
items.desc_en: Rav Acha brei d'Rav Ika objects: if so, you lock the door before borrowers, because the borrower can say 'If I had money, I would take at the current price; now that you have my money, I should take at the future high price?'

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha brei d'Rav Ika objects that the previous ruling would lock the door before borrowers, because a borrower could argue that if he had money he would buy at the current low price, but now that the lender holds his money he must pay the future high price.

items.text: Rav Acha brei d'Rav Ika's alternative: compare to a ketubah
items.text_en: Rav Acha brei d'Rav Ika's alternative: compare to a ketubah
items.desc_en: Rav Acha brei d'Rav Ika suggests comparing to a woman's ketubah, which is collected from inferior land. If she says 'give me intermediate land for a little less,' the husband can say: 'If you take according to your right, take at the current price; if not, take at the future high price.'

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha brei d'Rav Ika proposes comparing the case to a woman's ketubah, where if she requests intermediate land for a lower price, the husband can offer her the choice of taking the current price or the future high price.

items.text: Rava and the final resolution: 'from the best' applies to all property
items.text_en: Rava and the final resolution: 'from the best' applies to all property
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the difficulty remains. Rava initially says 'from the best' applies to all property, but the Gemara objects that the verse says 'from the best of his field.' Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Yehoshua explain: all movable property is considered 'best' because it can be sold elsewhere, but land must be given from the best so that buyers will jump to purchase it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara declares that the difficulty with the previous analogies remains unresolved.
Rava asserts that whatever property the tortfeasor gives to the victim must be from the best quality.
The Gemara objects that the verse explicitly says 'from the best of his field,' implying land only, not movable property.

sub.text: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Yehoshua
sub.text_en: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Yehoshua
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Yehoshua resolve the difficulty by explaining that all movable property is considered 'best' because it can be sold elsewhere, but land must be given from the best so that buyers will jump to purchase it.

items.text: Inquiry about appraisal: in whose land?
items.text_en: Inquiry about appraisal: in whose land?
items.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar Abba asks Rabbi Abba: when they appraise, do they appraise according to the debtor's land or the market? The question is only relevant according to Rabbi Akiva, who says we appraise in the damager's land. Rabbi Abba rejects the idea of market appraisal. The Gemara then cites a baraita detailing the order of collection from different types of land for different creditors.

sub.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar Abba asks Rabbi Abba whether the appraisal for collection is based on the debtor's land value or the market value.
The Gemara notes that according to Rabbi Yishmael, who appraises in the damaged party's land, the question is irrelevant.
The Gemara reframes the question according to Rabbi Akiva, who appraises in the damager's land, asking whether the verse 'מֵיטַב שָׂדֵהוּ' excludes only the damaged party's land or also the market.
Rabbi Abba rejects the market appraisal, arguing that the Torah's phrase 'מֵיטַב שָׂדֵהוּ' (the best of his field) implies the debtor's own land.
A baraita is cited that lists the order of collection from different land qualities for various creditors, supporting the principle of appraisal in the debtor's land.
The baraita details the specific allocation of land types for damages, debts, and marriage contracts, reinforcing the appraisal system based on the debtor's land.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a damaged party collects from עידית, while a creditor and a wife's ketubah collect from זיבורית.
