sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that a damaged party collects from עידית (prime-quality land), while a creditor and a wife's ketubah collect from זיבורית (inferior land).

items.text: Gemara's question and first answer
items.text_en: Gemara's question and first answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions a later clause: if a creditor collects from בינונית when the debtor has only בינונית and זיבורית, why doesn't the creditor's own בינונית become like עידית, pushing him to זיבורית? The Gemara answers that the case is where the debtor had עידית and sold it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why, if the creditor's own property is assessed, the creditor's בינונית (intermediate) should become like עידית (superior), pushing him to collect from זיבורית (inferior).
The Gemara answers that the case is where the debtor had עידית (superior) and sold it, so the creditor's own property is not compared to the debtor's former superior land.
Rav Chisda explicitly supports this answer, stating the same explanation.

items.text: Proof from a contradiction
items.text_en: Proof from a contradiction
items.desc_en: The Gemara proves the answer from a contradiction between two clauses: one implies the debtor had עידית and sold it, the other that he never had עידית.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asserts that the answer is supported by a contradiction between the two clauses of the Mishnah.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing: one clause refers to a case where the debtor had עידית and sold it, the other where he never had עידית.

items.text: Alternative answer: quality of בינונית
items.text_en: Alternative answer: quality of בינונית
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative: both cases are where he never had עידית, but one case his בינונית is like the market's עידית, the other not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative resolution: both cases are where he never had עידית (superior land), but one case his בינונית (intermediate land) is like the market's עידית, the other not.

items.text: Third answer: dispute over appraisal method
items.text_en: Third answer: dispute over appraisal method
items.desc_en: Another answer: both cases have בינונית equal to market בינונית, but they dispute whether we appraise by the debtor's own land or the market's.

sub.desc_en: The gemara offers a third answer: both cases involve a debtor whose בינונית (intermediate-quality land) equals the market's בינונית, but they dispute whether we appraise by the debtor's own land or the market's.

items.text: Ravina's answer: dispute over Ulla's enactment
items.text_en: Ravina's answer: dispute over Ulla's enactment
items.desc_en: Ravina says the dispute is about Ulla's enactment: by Torah law a creditor collects from זיבורית, but the Sages enacted בינונית to encourage lending; one opinion accepts this enactment, the other does not.

sub.desc_en: Ravina asserts that the dispute in the Mishnah is about Ulla's enactment, citing Ulla's statement that by Torah law a creditor collects from זיבורית (the poorest quality), but the Sages enacted בינונית (medium quality) to encourage lending.

Ulla explains the Torah law derivation from the verse 'בַּחוּץ תַּעֲמוֹד...' (stand outside) that a creditor takes the poorest item, and the rabbinic enactment of בינונית (medium quality) was to prevent locking the door before borrowers.
Ravina concludes that one opinion (Mar) accepts Ulla's enactment, while the other opinion (Mar) does not accept it, thus resolving the dispute in the Mishnah.

items.text: Baraita on sequential sales and Gemara's analysis
items.text_en: Baraita on sequential sales and Gemara's analysis
items.desc_en: A Baraita teaches that if one sold fields to multiple buyers simultaneously, all are equal; if sequentially, later buyers are collected from first. The Gemara questions the case of selling to one person sequentially, and resolves it by saying the last purchase was עידית, and the creditor can threaten to return the deed to force collection from זיבורית.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that if one sold fields to multiple buyers simultaneously, all are equal; if sequentially, later buyers are collected from the last buyer, and if that is insufficient, from the one before.
The Gemara asks: what is the case of 'sold them to one person' in the baraita?
The Gemara objects: if it were simultaneous, why mention 'to one' separately, since even for three simultaneously all are equal?
The Gemara concludes: it must be a case of sequential sales to one person.
The Gemara asks: why does the baraita distinguish between three buyers (where each can say 'you left me room') and one buyer sequentially?
The Gemara objects: in the case of one buyer sequentially, each purchase should also be able to claim 'you left me room'.

The Gemara resolves: the case is where the buyer purchased עידית (prime-quality land) last, so the earlier purchases are זיבורית (inferior land), and the creditor can threaten to return the deed to force collection from זיבורית.

items.text: Incomplete continuation
items.text_en: Incomplete continuation
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins a new line of questioning but the text is cut off.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara begins a new line of questioning with the phrase 'If so,' but the text is cut off.

items.text: Rejection of the initial comparison to damages
items.text_en: Rejection of the initial comparison to damages
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the idea that the same rule applies to damages, because here we are dealing with orphans who are not obligated to pay, and the lien is on the property itself. Therefore, the earlier reasoning does not apply.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: should we say the same regarding damages (that the creditor cannot collect from orphans)?
The Gemara answers: here we are dealing with orphans who are not obligated to pay, and the lien is on the property itself, so the earlier reasoning does not apply.

items.text: The creditor's refusal of the rabbinic ordinance
items.text_en: The creditor's refusal of the rabbinic ordinance
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the creditor can say: The reason the Sages said one cannot collect from liened property when there is free property is for my benefit, but I do not want this benefit. This follows Rava's principle that one may reject a rabbinic ordinance like this.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the creditor can reject the rabbinic ordinance by saying: The reason the Sages said one cannot collect from liened property when free property exists is for my benefit, but I do not want this benefit.
The Gemara cites Rava's principle that anyone who says 'I do not want the rabbinic ordinance' is listened to, supporting the creditor's rejection.

items.text: Clarification of 'like this' with Rav Huna's example
items.text_en: Clarification of 'like this' with Rav Huna's example
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'like this' means, and answers with Rav Huna's statement that a wife can say to her husband: I will not be supported and I will not work. This is another example of a rabbinic ordinance that can be rejected.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the phrase 'like this' refers to in Rava's statement.
The Gemara answers with Rav Huna's example: a wife can say to her husband 'I will not be supported and I will not work,' illustrating a rabbinic ordinance that can be rejected.

items.text: Case: buyer sold intermediate and poor land, kept superior
items.text_en: Case: buyer sold intermediate and poor land, kept superior
items.desc_en: The Gemara states a simple case: if the buyer sold the intermediate and poor land and kept the superior, all creditors can collect from the superior, since the other land is not available and the buyer cannot claim he wants the rabbinic ordinance.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states a simple case: if the buyer sold the intermediate and poor land and kept the superior, all creditors can collect from the superior, since the other land is not available and the buyer cannot claim he wants the rabbinic ordinance.

items.text: Dispute: buyer sold superior, kept intermediate and poor
items.text_en: Dispute: buyer sold superior, kept intermediate and poor
items.desc_en: Abaye thought all creditors could collect from the superior, but Rava disagreed. Rava explained that the first buyer sold all his rights to the second buyer, and since the first buyer could have told creditors to collect from the intermediate and poor (rejecting the ordinance), the second buyer can also say the same. Thus, they cannot collect from the superior.

sub.desc_en: The gemara asks: if the buyer sold the superior land and kept the intermediate and poor land, what is the law?
Abaye thought all creditors could collect from the superior land.

Rava objected: the first buyer sold all his rights to the second buyer, and since the first buyer could have told creditors to collect from the intermediate and poor (rejecting the ordinance), the second buyer can also say the same.
Rava concludes: the second buyer can also tell creditors to collect from the intermediate and poor, because when he bought, he bought with all the rights the first buyer had.

items.text: Rava's ruling: Reuven sold all fields to Shimon, Shimon sold one to Levi
items.text_en: Rava's ruling: Reuven sold all fields to Shimon, Shimon sold one to Levi
items.desc_en: Rava rules that a creditor of Reuven can collect from either Shimon or Levi if Shimon sold an intermediate field. But if Shimon sold superior and poor land, the creditor cannot collect from Levi because Levi can say he bought land unsuitable for you. Also, if Shimon kept an intermediate field of equal value, the creditor must collect from Shimon first.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that if Reuven sold all his fields to Shimon, and Shimon sold one field to Levi, a creditor of Reuven may collect from either Shimon or Levi.
Rava qualifies that this applies only if Shimon sold an intermediate field; if he sold superior and poor land, Levi can say he bought land unsuitable for the creditor.

Rava further qualifies that even if Shimon sold an intermediate field, the creditor cannot collect from Levi if Shimon kept an intermediate field of equal value, because Levi can say he left the creditor a place to collect from Shimon.

items.text: Abaye: Reuven sold with liability, creditor collects from Shimon
items.text_en: Abaye: Reuven sold with liability, creditor collects from Shimon
items.desc_en: Abaye rules that if Reuven sold a field to Shimon with liability, and a creditor of Reuven collects from Shimon, Reuven must litigate with the creditor. Reuven cannot say 'you are not my adversary' because Shimon can say 'if you extract from him, you will come back on me.' Some say even without liability, because Shimon would have a grievance against Reuven.

sub.desc_en: Abaye rules that if Reuven sold a field to Shimon with liability (אחריות), and a creditor of Reuven collects from Shimon, Reuven must litigate with the creditor because Shimon can say 'if you extract from him, you will come back on me.'
Some say that even without liability (אחריות), Reuven must litigate because Shimon would have a grievance (תרעומת) against Reuven.

items.text: Abaye's second statement: sale without liability
items.text_en: Abaye's second statement: sale without liability
items.desc_en: Abaye begins a new ruling about Reuven selling a field to Shimon without liability, but the segment is cut off.

sub.desc_en: Abaye begins a new ruling about Reuven selling a field to Shimon without liability (שלא באחריות), but the statement is cut off.

items.text: The point of no return in a sale
items.text_en: The point of no return in a sale
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses when a sale becomes final: before taking possession, one can retract; after taking possession, one cannot. The reason is that the seller can say 'you considered the knotty animal and accepted.' The Gemara then discusses the definition of possession and the difference between a sale with and without אחריות.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the rule: before taking possession of a field that had liens against it, the buyer can retract; after possession, he cannot.
The Gemara explains the reason: the seller can say 'you considered the knotty animal and accepted it.'
The Gemara asks from when possession is established, and answers: from when the buyer walks the boundaries.
The Gemara specifies that this rule applies only to a sale without אחריות (liability for liens), not with it.
Some say that even with אחריות the rule applies, because the seller can say 'show your seizure order and I will pay you.'

items.text: Rav Huna's ruling on paying with the best
items.text_en: Rav Huna's ruling on paying with the best
items.desc_en: Rav Huna says that one must pay either with silver or with the best-quality land. Rav Nachman objects from a baraita that includes even bran as 'equivalent to silver.' The Gemara resolves that the baraita deals with a case where the debtor has no land, and the teaching is that he must go to the trouble of selling and bringing silver.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that payment must be made either with silver or with the best-quality land.
Rav Nachman objects by citing a baraita that includes even bran as 'equivalent to silver' (שוה כסף), implying that any movable property suffices.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita deals with a debtor who has no land, and it teaches that he must go to the trouble of selling the bran and bringing silver.

items.text: Rav Asi's ruling: coins are like land
items.text_en: Rav Asi's ruling: coins are like land
items.desc_en: Rav Asi states that coins are like land. The Gemara initially thinks this refers to the law of paying with the best, but that is already Rav Huna's ruling. It then suggests it applies to brothers who divided an estate and a creditor seizes land from one brother. The Gemara discusses the dispute between Rav, Shmuel, and Rav Asi about whether the division is void or the brother forfeits. Finally, it concludes that Rav Asi's statement indeed refers to the law of the best, and the correct formulation is 'and so said Rav Asi.'

sub.desc_en: Rav Asi states that coins (כספים) are like land (קרקע) for the law of paying with the best.
The Gemara asks to what halachic context Rav Asi's statement applies, initially suggesting it refers to the law of paying with the best (מיטב), but objects that this is already Rav Huna's ruling.
The Gemara suggests Rav Asi's ruling applies to two brothers who divided an estate, one taking land and the other coins, and a creditor seizes the land from one brother.
The Gemara objects that this case is obvious, as one brother is a creditor and the other is not.
An alternative view reverses the case: the brother who took coins argues that he took coins to avoid loss from theft, while the brother who took land accepted the risk of seizure.
The Gemara shifts to a different case: two brothers who divided an estate, and a creditor seizes the portion of one of them.
The Gemara objects that Rav Asi already stated his position in a dispute with Rav and Shmuel about brothers who divided an estate and a creditor seizes one brother's portion.
Rav holds that the division is void (בטלה מחלוקת) because brothers who divided are considered like heirs (יורשים).
Shmuel holds that the brother forfeits (ויתר) because brothers who divided are considered like purchasers (לקוחות) without אחריות (guarantee).
Rav Asi holds that the brother takes a quarter in land and a quarter in money, because he is uncertain whether brothers are like heirs or like purchasers.
The Gemara concludes that Rav Asi's statement 'coins are like land' indeed refers to the law of paying with the best (מיטב).
The Gemara resolves the redundancy by stating that the correct formulation is 'and so said Rav Asi' (וכן אמר רב אסי), aligning him with Rav Huna.

items.text: The obligation to spend up to a third on a mitzvah
items.text_en: The obligation to spend up to a third on a mitzvah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira quotes Rav Huna: for a mitzvah, one should spend up to a third. The Gemara then asks: what does 'a third' mean?

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira quotes Rav Huna stating that for a mitzvah one should spend up to a third.
The Gemara asks what 'a third' refers to in Rav Huna's statement.

items.text: Limit of spending for beautifying a mitzvah
items.text_en: Limit of spending for beautifying a mitzvah
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the idea that 'third of one's wealth' refers to a third of one's entire estate, as that would be impractical. Rabbi Zeira explains it means up to a third of the cost of the mitzvah itself. Rav Ashi questions whether the third is calculated from within or without, left unresolved. In the West, they say up to a third is from one's own money, beyond that from God's.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the interpretation that 'third of one's wealth' means a third of one's entire estate, arguing that if three mitzvot came to a person, he would have to give all his money.
Rabbi Zeira explains that the limit of a third applies to beautifying a mitzvah (הידור מצוה), meaning up to a third of the cost of the mitzvah itself.
Rav Ashi questions whether the third is calculated from within (the cost of the mitzvah) or from without (the total expenditure), leaving the matter unresolved (תיקו).

sub.text: Sages of the West in the name of Rabbi Zeira
sub.text_en: Sages of the West in the name of Rabbi Zeira
sub.desc_en: The Sages of the West say in the name of Rabbi Zeira that up to a third is from one's own money, and beyond that is from God's (i.e., God provides the extra).

items.text: Mishnah: Principle of liability for damage
items.text_en: Mishnah: Principle of liability for damage
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one is liable for damage caused by an item they are responsible to guard, and the extent of liability is proportional to the degree of responsibility. It lists the types of property subject to this rule: items not subject to me'ilah, belonging to Jews, and designated. It also specifies that liability applies everywhere except in the domain of the damager or the shared domain of both parties. When damage occurs, the damager pays with the best land.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the principle that liability for guarding an item determines liability for its damage, and partial liability for guarding leads to proportional payment.
The Mishnah lists the types of property subject to this liability: items not subject to me'ilah (misuse of consecrated property), belonging to Jews (בני ברית), and designated (מיוחדים).
The Mishnah states that liability applies everywhere except in the exclusive domain of the damager or the shared domain of both parties.
The Mishnah concludes that when damage occurs, the damager pays with the best land (מיטב הארץ).

items.text: Gemara: Baraita on ox, pit, and fire
items.text_en: Gemara: Baraita on ox, pit, and fire
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita: one is liable for damage caused by an ox or pit entrusted to a deaf-mute, imbecile, or minor, but not for fire. The Gemara questions the scenario: if the ox is tied and pit covered, the parallel with fire (a coal) would also be liable; if the ox is loose and pit uncovered, the parallel with fire (a flame) would be exempt, contradicting Resh Lakish's ruling that a flame is liable. The Gemara resolves: with a tied ox and covered pit, the difference is that an ox tends to break loose and a pit tends to cave in, while a coal dies down. For Rabbi Yochanan, who exempts even a flame, the case is a loose ox and uncovered pit, where the deaf-mute's action (taking the coal) causes the fire, unlike the ox and pit.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states the principle: one is liable for damage from an ox or pit entrusted to a deaf-mute, imbecile, or minor, but not for fire.
The Gemara asks: what case is the baraita discussing? If it is a tied ox and covered pit, the parallel with a coal (גחלת) would also be liable — why the distinction?
Alternatively, if it is a loose ox and uncovered pit, the parallel with a flame (שלהבת) would be exempt — contradicting Resh Lakish's ruling that a flame is liable.
The Gemara resolves: it is a tied ox and covered pit; the difference is that an ox tends to break loose (נתוקי) and a pit tends to cave in (נתורי), while a coal dies down (מעמעם) on its own.
For Rabbi Yochanan, who exempts even a flame, the case is a loose ox and uncovered pit; the deaf-mute's action (taking the coal) causes the fire, unlike the ox and pit where the damage is inherent.

items.text: Baraita: Stringencies of ox and pit
items.text_en: Baraita: Stringencies of ox and pit
items.desc_en: A baraita lists the stringencies of an ox over a pit: the ox pays ransom, is liable for the thirty shekels of a slave, its carcass is forbidden after judgment, and it naturally goes and damages. The pit's stringencies over the ox: the pit is created for damage from the start and is forewarned from the beginning.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by listing the stringencies of an ox over a pit: the ox pays ransom, is liable for the thirty shekels of a slave, its carcass is forbidden after judgment, and it naturally goes and damages.
The baraita then lists the stringencies of a pit over an ox: the pit is created for damage from the start and is forewarned from the beginning.

items.text: Mishnah: Stringencies between ox and fire, and between fire and pit
items.text_en: Mishnah: Stringencies between ox and fire, and between fire and pit
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists stringencies of an ox over fire (e.g., ox pays atonement, is liable for the thirty of a slave, becomes forbidden after judgment, and liability when entrusted to a deaf-mute, imbecile, or minor) and stringencies of fire over ox (fire is forewarned from the start). It then lists stringencies of fire over pit (fire is forewarned from the start) and pit over fire (pit is made for damage from its inception, and liability when entrusted to a deaf-mute, imbecile, or minor).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by listing stringencies of an ox over fire: the ox pays atonement, is liable for the thirty of a slave, becomes forbidden after judgment, and is liable when entrusted to a deaf-mute, imbecile, or minor.
The Mishnah shifts to list stringencies of fire over ox: fire is forewarned from the start.
The Mishnah shifts to list stringencies of fire over pit: fire is forewarned from the start and its way is to go and damage, consuming both suitable and unsuitable items.
The Mishnah shifts to list stringencies of pit over fire: the pit is made for damage from its inception, and liability when entrusted to a deaf-mute, imbecile, or minor.

items.text: Gemara's question: Why not list stringency of ox over pit?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Why not list stringency of ox over pit?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah does not list a stringency of an ox over a pit: the ox is liable for damage to vessels, whereas the pit is not. It answers that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that a pit is liable for damage to vessels.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah does not list a stringency of an ox over a pit: the ox is liable for damage to vessels, whereas the pit is not.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that a pit is liable for damage to vessels.

items.text: Objection: If it is Rabbi Yehuda, the Mishnah's own statement contradicts him
items.text_en: Objection: If it is Rabbi Yehuda, the Mishnah's own statement contradicts him
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: If the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yehuda, then the later clause about fire's stringency over pit (that fire consumes both suitable and unsuitable items, unlike pit) contradicts him, because Rabbi Yehuda holds that a pit is liable for vessels (unsuitable items).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yehuda, the later clause about fire's stringency over pit (that fire consumes both suitable and unsuitable items) contradicts him, because Rabbi Yehuda holds that a pit is liable for vessels (unsuitable items).

items.text: First resolution: The Mishnah is actually the Rabbis, and it omitted the case of hidden items
items.text_en: First resolution: The Mishnah is actually the Rabbis, and it omitted the case of hidden items
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah is actually the Rabbis (who exempt the pit from vessels), and the Mishnah omitted the stringency of fire over pit regarding hidden items (which fire damages but pit does not).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah is actually the Rabbis (who exempt the pit from vessels), and the Mishnah omitted the stringency of fire over pit regarding hidden items (טָמוּן) which fire damages but pit does not.

items.text: Alternative resolution: The Mishnah is Rabbi Yehuda, and 'unsuitable' refers to licking and scraping
items.text_en: Alternative resolution: The Mishnah is Rabbi Yehuda, and 'unsuitable' refers to licking and scraping
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative: the Mishnah is indeed Rabbi Yehuda, and the phrase 'unsuitable for it' does not include vessels but rather refers to licking its plaster and scraping its stones (which fire does but pit does not).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative resolution: the Mishnah is indeed Rabbi Yehuda, and the phrase 'unsuitable for it' does not include vessels but rather refers to licking its plaster and scraping its stones.

items.text: Rav Ashi's challenge: Why not list stringency of ox over pit regarding disqualified consecrated animals?
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's challenge: Why not list stringency of ox over pit regarding disqualified consecrated animals?
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi challenges: Why does the Mishnah not list a stringency of an ox over a pit: the ox is liable for disqualified consecrated animals, whereas the pit is not? The Gemara analyzes: if the Mishnah is the Rabbis, it omitted this as well; if it is Rabbi Yehuda, what did it omit? It suggests it omitted the case of trampling with its plowing, but that is not an omission because fire's nature is to go and damage.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi challenges: why does the Mishnah not list a stringency of an ox over a pit — the ox is liable for disqualified consecrated animals, whereas the pit is not?
The Gemara analyzes: if the Mishnah follows the Rabbis, it omitted this stringency just as it omitted others; but if it follows Rabbi Yehuda, what else did it omit?
The Gemara suggests the Mishnah omitted the case of trampling with its plowing, but rejects this because fire's nature is to go and damage, so it is not a true omission.

items.text: Principle of 'preparing part of the damage' and the dispute about a pit dug by two
items.text_en: Principle of 'preparing part of the damage' and the dispute about a pit dug by two
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the principle: one who prepares part of the damage is liable for the entire damage. It cites a baraita: one who digs a pit of nine handbreadths and another completes it to ten – the last is liable. It notes this is not in accordance with Rabbi, who says the last is liable for death but both are liable for damages. Rav Pappa clarifies that for death, all agree the last is liable.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the principle: one who prepares part of the damage is liable for the entire damage.
The baraita cites a case: one who digs a pit of nine handbreadths and another completes it to ten – the last is liable.
The Gemara notes this baraita is not in accordance with Rabbi, who says the last is liable for death but both are liable for damages.
Rav Pappa clarifies that for death, all agree the last is liable.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's challenge: The case of entrusting an ox to five people
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's challenge: The case of entrusting an ox to five people
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira challenges: Is there no other omitted stringency? What about the case where one entrusts his ox to five people and one of them is negligent and it causes damage – the negligent one is liable. The Gemara analyzes: if without him it would not have been guarded, it is obvious; if without him it would have been guarded, what did he do?

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira challenges the Mishnah's list of stringencies, asking whether there is not another omitted stringency: the case where one entrusts his ox to five people and one of them is negligent and it causes damage – the negligent one is liable.

The Gemara analyzes the case: if without the negligent person the ox would not have been guarded, the liability is obvious; if without him it would have been guarded, what did he do to cause liability?

items.text: Rav Sheshet's challenge: The case of increasing the bundle
items.text_en: Rav Sheshet's challenge: The case of increasing the bundle
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet challenges: What about the case of increasing the bundle (where one adds to a pile of wood that later causes damage)? The Gemara asks: What are the circumstances?

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet objects: What about the case of increasing the bundle (where one adds to a pile of wood that later causes damage)?
The Gemara asks: What are the circumstances of this case?

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the case of five sitting on a bench
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the case of five sitting on a bench
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa challenges the earlier assumption about the last person being liable only if without him the bench would not have broken. The Gemara resolves that the last person is liable if he caused it to break sooner, and that his force is considered like his body.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa challenges the earlier assumption by citing a baraita about five sitting on a bench and the last one being liable, and he identifies himself as the example.
The Gemara asks how to understand the baraita: if without him it would not have broken, it is obvious; if it would have broken anyway, what did he do?
The Gemara asks how the Mishnah can be resolved in light of this difficulty.
The Gemara answers that the case is where without him it would have broken in two hours, but now it broke in one hour, so they say: without you we would have sat a bit longer and gotten up.
The Gemara objects: the last person could say to them, 'Without you, it would not have broken by me alone!'
The Gemara resolves that the case is where he leaned on them and broke the bench, so his force is combined with theirs.
The Gemara asks: this is obvious, why was it necessary to state it?
The Gemara resolves that one might have thought his force is not like his body, so it teaches that his force is like his body, and wherever his body would break, his force also breaks.

items.text: Distinction from the case of ten people hitting with sticks
items.text_en: Distinction from the case of ten people hitting with sticks
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a baraita where ten people hit one person and he dies; Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira holds the last liable. The Gemara deflects this as a case of killing, not damage, or as a dispute that is not used to resolve the current case.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether there is another case, citing a baraita where ten people hit one person with sticks and Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira holds the last liable.
The Gemara rejects the baraita, stating that the discussion does not deal with a case of killing.
The Gemara offers an alternative rejection: the baraita involves a dispute, and the Gemara does not establish the Mishnah according to Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira's minority opinion.

items.text: Introduction of the rule that the carcass belongs to the injured party
items.text_en: Introduction of the rule that the carcass belongs to the injured party
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states 'חַבְתִּי בְּתַשְׁלוּמֵי נִזְקוֹ' (I am liable for the payments of his damage), not just 'בְּנִזְקוֹ'. This teaches that the owners of the carcass must handle it, as the Sages taught: 'תַּשְׁלוּמֵי נֶזֶק' implies the owners deal with the carcass.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states 'I am liable for the payments of his damage' (חַבְתִּי בְּתַשְׁלוּמֵי נִזְקוֹ), not just 'for his damage', implying the carcass belongs to the injured party.
The Gemara cites a baraita that the phrase 'תַּשְׁלוּמֵי נֶזֶק' teaches that the owners (the injured party) must handle the carcass.

items.text: Derivations that the carcass belongs to the injured party
items.text_en: Derivations that the carcass belongs to the injured party
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ammi, Rav Kahana, and Chizkiyah each derive from verses that the carcass belongs to the injured party. Abaye explains that if the carcass were the injurer's, the Torah would not have needed to state 'וְהַמֵּת יִהְיֶה לוֹ'. The Gemara shows that all three derivations are necessary.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where are these matters (that the carcass belongs to the injured party) derived?

Rabbi Ammi answers by citing the verse 'מַכֵּה נֶפֶשׁ בְּהֵמָה יְשַׁלְּמֶנָּה' and reading it homiletically as 'יַשְׁלִימֶנָּה' (he shall make it whole), implying the carcass is returned to the injured party.
Rav Kahana derives from the verse 'אִם טָרֹף יִטָּרֵף... הַטְּרֵפָה לֹא יְשַׁלֵּם' that the carcass itself is not paid, implying it belongs to the injured party.
Chizkiyah derives from the verse 'וְהַמֵּת יִהְיֶה לוֹ' that the carcass belongs to the injured party.
The Tanna deVei Chizkiyah cites a baraita that also derives from 'וְהַמֵּת יִהְיֶה לוֹ' that the carcass is for the injured party, and rejects the possibility that it could be for the injurer.
The Gemara asks: What does 'לֹא כָּךְ הָיָה' (it was not so) mean in the baraita?

Abaye explains: If the carcass were the injurer's, the Torah would have written only 'שׁוֹר תַּחַת הַשּׁוֹר' and not 'וְהַמֵּת יִהְיֶה לוֹ'; the extra verse teaches that it belongs to the injured party.
The Gemara concludes that all three derivations are necessary, as each addresses a unique case where one might otherwise think the carcass belongs to the injurer.

items.text: Rav Kahana's question and the resolution regarding the carcass's value
items.text_en: Rav Kahana's question and the resolution regarding the carcass's value
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana asks Rav: without the verse, would we think the carcass belongs to the injurer? But then the injurer could pay with any worthless item, so why would he need his own carcass? The Gemara answers that the verse is needed for the case where the carcass's value is less than the damage, and this is a dispute among Tannaim.

sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana asks Rav: without the verse 'והמת יהיה לו', would we think the carcass belongs to the injurer? But then the injurer could pay with any worthless item, so why would he need his own carcass?
Rav Kahana objects: since the injurer can pay with any item of value, even bran, why would he specifically need his own carcass?
The Gemara answers: the verse is needed only for the case where the carcass's value has depreciated (פחת נבילה), so the injurer cannot simply give his own carcass at its current low value.
The Gemara resolves that the issue of depreciated carcass value is a dispute among Tannaim, citing a baraita that begins with the verse 'אם טרוף יטרף יביאהו עד'.

items.text: Dispute about who bears the loss of the carcass's value
items.text_en: Dispute about who bears the loss of the carcass's value
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if an animal was taken by force, the bailee brings witnesses and is exempt. Abba Shaul says he must bring the carcass to court. The Gemara asks if they argue over whether the loss of the carcass's value falls on the plaintiff or the defendant, but answers that all agree it falls on the plaintiff; they argue about who bears the burden of removing the carcass.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the Tanna Kamma's position that a bailee brings witnesses and is exempt, and Abba Shaul's position that he must bring the carcass to court.
The Gemara asks whether the dispute is about who bears the loss of the carcass's value — the plaintiff (ניזק) or the defendant (מזיק).
The Gemara answers that all agree the loss falls on the plaintiff; they argue about who bears the burden of removing the carcass (טורח נבילה).

items.text: Clarifying the burden of removing the carcass
items.text_en: Clarifying the burden of removing the carcass
items.desc_en: A baraita from others says the owner of the pit must raise the ox from his pit, based on the verse. Abaye asks Rava about the case: if the carcass is worth one zuz and the wood is worth four, the bailee benefits from his own effort; Rava explains it's when both are worth one zuz, and a folk saying supports that such a scenario exists.

sub.desc_en: A baraita from Others cites a verse to prove that the owner of the pit must raise the ox from his pit.

Abaye asks Rava about the case of טורח נבילה (the burden of the carcass): if the carcass is worth one zuz and the wood is worth four, the bailee benefits from his own effort, so why should the owner pay?
Rava explains that the case is when both the carcass and the wood are worth one zuz, so the bailee gains nothing from his effort.

sub.text: Gemara's confirmation with a folk saying
sub.text_en: Gemara's confirmation with a folk saying
sub.desc_en: The gemara confirms that such a scenario exists, citing a folk saying that a beam in the city costs a zuz and a beam in the field also costs a zuz.

items.text: Appraisal for thieves, robbers, and borrowers
items.text_en: Appraisal for thieves, robbers, and borrowers
items.desc_en: Shmuel says courts do not appraise for a thief or robber but do for a plaintiff. He adds that he says even for a borrower, and Abba agrees. The Gemara questions whether Shmuel means appraising or not appraising for a borrower. A story about a borrowed ax that broke is brought: Rav told the borrower to pay a good ax, implying no appraisal, but Rav Kahana and Rav Asi's objection and Rav's silence imply appraisal. Ulla says Rabbi Elazar rules appraisal for thieves and robbers, Rav Papi says no, and the halakha is no appraisal for thieves or robbers but appraisal for a borrower.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel states that courts do not appraise for a thief or robber, but do for a plaintiff; he adds that he says even for a borrower, and Abba agrees.
The Gemara questions whether Shmuel means that courts do appraise for a borrower or that they do not appraise for a borrower.

sub.text: Supporting story about a borrowed ax
sub.text_en: Supporting story about a borrowed ax
sub.desc_en: A story is brought about a borrowed ax that broke; Rav told the borrower to pay a good ax, implying no appraisal.

sub.text: Rav Kahana and Rav Asi's objection
sub.text_en: Rav Kahana and Rav Asi's objection
sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana and Rav Asi object to Rav's ruling, and Rav's silence implies that appraisal is required.

sub.text: Ulla, Rav Papi, and halakhic conclusion
sub.text_en: Ulla, Rav Papi, and halakhic conclusion
sub.desc_en: Ulla reports Rabbi Elazar's ruling that courts appraise for thieves and robbers, Rav Papi disagrees, and the halakha is that there is no appraisal for thieves or robbers but there is appraisal for a borrower, consistent with Rav Kahana and Rav Asi.

items.text: Counting impurity for a partially emerged afterbirth
items.text_en: Counting impurity for a partially emerged afterbirth
items.desc_en: Ulla says Rabbi Elazar rules that if an afterbirth partially emerged on the first day and the rest on the second, we count from the first. Rava objects that this is a stringency leading to leniency, as it purifies the woman from the first day. Rava says she is concerned but counts only from the second. The Gemara asks what this teaches, and cites a Mishnah that a partially emerged afterbirth is forbidden to eat, as it is a sign of a fetus.

sub.desc_en: Ulla reports Rabbi Elazar's ruling that if an afterbirth partially emerged on the first day and the rest on the second, the woman counts her impurity from the first day.
Rava objects that Rabbi Elazar's ruling, intended as a stringency (חומרא), actually leads to a leniency (קולא) by purifying the woman from the first day.
Rava rules instead that the woman is concerned (חוששת) but counts her impurity only from the second day.
The Gemara asks what Rava's ruling teaches, suggesting it may be that a partial afterbirth indicates a fetus.
The Gemara cites a Mishnah that a partially emerged afterbirth is forbidden to eat, as it is a sign of a fetus in both women and animals.

items.text: Conclusion of the previous sugya about the afterbirth
items.text_en: Conclusion of the previous sugya about the afterbirth
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the Mishnah's ruling about the afterbirth teaches that even a partial afterbirth without a fetus is considered impure, and this is a decree lest one come to treat the entire afterbirth leniently.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the Mishnah's ruling about the afterbirth teaches that even a partial afterbirth without a fetus is considered impure, and this is a decree lest one come to treat the entire afterbirth leniently.

items.text: Ulla's statement about a firstborn mauled within thirty days
items.text_en: Ulla's statement about a firstborn mauled within thirty days
items.desc_en: Ulla says in the name of Rabbi Elazar that a firstborn animal that was mauled within thirty days of birth is not redeemed. Rami bar Chama supports this with a baraita that derives from the word 'akh' that the redemption of a firstborn is divided, excluding such a case.

sub.desc_en: Ulla states in the name of Rabbi Elazar that a firstborn animal mauled within thirty days of birth is not redeemed.
Rami bar Chama supports Ulla's ruling by citing a baraita that derives from the word 'אך' (but) that the redemption of a firstborn is divided, excluding a case of mauling within thirty days.

items.text: Ulla's statement about acquisition of large animals
items.text_en: Ulla's statement about acquisition of large animals
items.desc_en: Ulla says in the name of Rabbi Elazar that a large animal is acquired through pulling (meshikhah). The Gemara questions this from the Mishnah which says it is acquired through delivery (mesirah). Ulla explains that he follows the opinion of the Sages who say both large and small animals are acquired through pulling, while Rabbi Shimon says through lifting.

sub.desc_en: Ulla states in the name of Rabbi Elazar that a large animal is acquired through pulling (משיכה).
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah states a large animal is acquired through delivery (מסירה), not pulling.
Ulla explains that he follows the opinion of the Sages who say both large and small animals are acquired through pulling, while Rabbi Shimon says through lifting.

items.text: Ulla's statement about brothers dividing an inheritance
items.text_en: Ulla's statement about brothers dividing an inheritance
items.desc_en: Ulla says in the name of Rabbi Elazar that when brothers divide an inheritance, the value of the clothes they are wearing is assessed, but the value of the clothes of their children is not assessed. Rav Pappa adds that sometimes even the clothes of the brothers themselves are not assessed, such as in the case of an older brother whose opinion the others respect.

sub.desc_en: Ulla states in the name of Rabbi Elazar that when brothers divide an inheritance, the value of the clothes they are wearing is assessed, but the value of the clothes of their children is not assessed.
Rav Pappa adds that sometimes even the clothes of the brothers themselves are not assessed, such as in the case of an older brother whose opinion the others respect.

items.text: Dispute about a bailee who entrusts to another bailee
items.text_en: Dispute about a bailee who entrusts to another bailee
items.desc_en: Ulla says in the name of Rabbi Elazar that a bailee who entrusts the deposit to another bailee is exempt, even if he gave it to a less reliable bailee, because he entrusted it to a competent person. Rava argues that he is liable, even if he gave it to a more reliable bailee, because the owner can say 'You are trustworthy to me with an oath, but he is not.'

sub.desc_en: Ulla in the name of Rabbi Elazar rules that a bailee who entrusts the deposit to another bailee is exempt, even if he gave it to a less reliable bailee, because he entrusted it to a competent person.
Rava argues that a bailee who entrusts to another bailee is liable, even if he gave it to a more reliable bailee, because the owner can say 'You are trustworthy to me with an oath, but he is not.'

items.text: Ulla's statement about collecting debts from slaves
items.text_en: Ulla's statement about collecting debts from slaves
items.desc_en: Ulla says in the name of Rabbi Elazar that the halakha is that debts are collected from slaves. Rav Nachman asks if this applies even from orphans, and Ulla clarifies it is from the debtor himself, even from the cloak on his shoulder. The Gemara explains that the case is where the debtor designated the slave as collateral (apoteiki), as per Rava's ruling that if one designates his slave as collateral and sells him, the creditor collects from him, but not if he designates his ox.

sub.desc_en: Ulla states in the name of Rabbi Elazar that the halakha is that debts are collected from slaves.
Rav Nachman asks Ulla whether Rabbi Elazar's ruling applies even to collecting from orphans.
Ulla clarifies that the collection is from the debtor himself, even from the cloak on his shoulder.
The Gemara explains that the case is where the debtor designated the slave as collateral (אפותיקי).
Rava rules that if one designates his slave as collateral and sells him, the creditor collects from him, but not if he designates his ox.
The Gemara explains the reason: a slave has a reputation (קול) when designated as collateral, but an ox does not.

items.text: Ulla's ruling and Rav Nachman's reaction
items.text_en: Ulla's ruling and Rav Nachman's reaction
items.desc_en: Ulla states that a prosbul can be collected even from orphans, citing Rabbi Elazar. Rav Nachman objects, saying Ulla slipped up. He recounts two precedents where courts collected from orphans and then reversed the collection, threatening to seize the judges' property if they don't return the money.

sub.desc_en: Ulla states that a prosbul can be collected even from orphans, citing Rabbi Elazar.
Rav Nachman objects, saying Ulla slipped up.
Rav Nachman recounts two precedents where courts collected from orphans and then reversed the collection, threatening to seize the judges' property if they don't return the money.

items.text: Rava asks Rav Nachman his opinion
items.text_en: Rava asks Rav Nachman his opinion
items.desc_en: Rava asks Rav Nachman which authority he follows, given the conflicting rulings of Ulla, Rabbi Elazar, the Nehardean judges, and Rav Chana bar Bizna. Rav Nachman responds by citing a baraita of Avimi: a prosbul applies to land but not to slaves, and movables are acquired with land but not with slaves.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks Rav Nachman which authority he follows, given the conflicting rulings of Ulla, Rabbi Elazar, the Nehardean judges, and Rav Chana bar Bizna.

sub.text: Rav Nachman's answer citing Avimi's baraita
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman's answer citing Avimi's baraita
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman responds by citing a baraita of Avimi: a prosbul applies to land but not to slaves, and movables are acquired with land but not with slaves.

items.text: Gemara suggests a Tannaitic dispute
items.text_en: Gemara suggests a Tannaitic dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the dispute about whether slaves are like land or movables underlies a Tannaitic disagreement. It cites a baraita where one who takes possession of slaves does not acquire land, and vice versa, and another baraita where taking possession of slaves does acquire movables. The Gemara suggests the dispute is whether slaves are like land or like movables.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the dispute about slaves is like a Tannaitic disagreement.
A baraita is cited: one who takes possession of slaves does not acquire land, and vice versa; slaves and movables are not acquired through each other's possession.
A contradictory baraita is cited: one who takes possession of slaves does acquire movables.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: the two baraitot reflect a dispute whether slaves are like land or like movables.

items.text: First version: Rav Ika bar Rav Ami's explanation
items.text_en: First version: Rav Ika bar Rav Ami's explanation
items.desc_en: Rav Ika bar Rav Ami explains that everyone agrees slaves are like land. The baraita that says 'acquired' is straightforward; the one that says 'did not acquire' requires that the land be like 'fortified cities in Judah' that are stationary. He cites a Mishnah that movables are acquired with land through money, document, or possession, and Hezekiah derives this from a verse about fortified cities.

sub.text: Rav Ika bar Rav Ami's explanation
sub.text_en: Rav Ika bar Rav Ami's explanation
sub.desc_en: Rav Ika bar Rav Ami asserts that all agree slaves are like land (קרקע).
Rav Ika bar Rav Ami cites a Mishnah that movables are acquired with land through money, document, or possession, and Hezekiah's derivation from the verse about fortified cities in Judah.

items.text: Second version: Rav Ika bar Rav Ami's alternative explanation
items.text_en: Second version: Rav Ika bar Rav Ami's alternative explanation
items.desc_en: An alternative version states that everyone agrees slaves are like movables. The baraita that says 'did not acquire' is straightforward; the one that says 'acquired' refers to when the slaves are still upon the land. The Gemara objects that a walking courtyard does not acquire, and Rava rules that if walking does not acquire, standing or sitting also does not acquire. The Gemara concludes that the case is where the slaves are tied up.

sub.text: Alternative version (איכא דאמרי) introducing Rav Ika bar Rav Ami's statement
sub.text_en: Alternative version (איכא דאמרי) introducing Rav Ika bar Rav Ami's statement
sub.desc_en: An alternative version states that Rav Ika bar Rav Ami said everyone agrees slaves are like movables.

sub.text: Rav Ika bar Rav Ami's resolution of the baraitot
sub.text_en: Rav Ika bar Rav Ami's resolution of the baraitot
sub.desc_en: Rav Ika bar Rav Ami explains that the baraita saying 'did not acquire' is straightforward, while the one saying 'acquired' refers to when the slaves are still upon the land.
The Gemara objects that even if the slaves are upon the land, the land is a walking courtyard (חצר מהלכת) which does not acquire.

sub.text: Gemara's rejection of a possible answer (standing)
sub.text_en: Gemara's rejection of a possible answer (standing)
sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the possibility that the slaves are standing, citing Rava's rule that if walking does not acquire, standing or sitting also does not acquire.
The Gemara concludes that the case is where the slaves are tied up (כפות), so the land functions as a stationary courtyard.

items.text: Final resolution: standing in the courtyard
items.text_en: Final resolution: standing in the courtyard
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that taking possession of land acquires slaves, and answers that this is when the slaves are standing inside the land. It infers that the earlier baraita that said 'did not acquire' refers to when they are not standing inside. This works for the version that slaves are like movables, but for the version that slaves are like land, the Gemara questions why standing inside is needed, citing Shmuel's rule that acquiring one field acquires ten. The Gemara then turns the question around for the other version.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the previous discussion by citing a baraita that states taking possession of land acquires slaves.
The Gemara answers that the baraita refers to slaves standing inside the land.
The Gemara infers that the earlier baraita stating 'did not acquire' refers to when the slaves are not standing inside the land.

sub.text: Gemara's analysis for the first version
sub.text_en: Gemara's analysis for the first version
sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that this works for the version where Rav Ika bar Rav Ami said slaves are like movables (מִטַּלְטְלִין), requiring standing inside for acquisition.

sub.text: Gemara's question for the second version
sub.text_en: Gemara's question for the second version
sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why standing inside is needed for the version that slaves are like land, citing Shmuel's rule that acquiring one field acquires ten.
The Gemara turns the question around for the version that slaves are like movables, asking why standing inside is needed.

items.text: Distinction between movable and immovable property
items.text_en: Distinction between movable and immovable property
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues that just as there is a distinction between movable items that are mobile and those that are not, so too with land: a slave is considered mobile land, while a millstone is considered one with the ground. This establishes a principle for categorizing property.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that we already know that we do not require the items to be piled up.
The Gemara explains that the distinction is between movable items that are mobile and those that are not.
The Gemara applies the same distinction to land: a slave is considered mobile land, while a millstone is considered one with the ground.

items.text: Introduction of the mishnah and identification of the tanna
items.text_en: Introduction of the mishnah and identification of the tanna
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that items without me'ilah are not subject to misuse, but they are still consecrated. Rabbi Yochanan identifies the tanna as Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, who holds that kodashim kalim are the owner's property (mamon ba'alim), as derived from a baraita.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah is cited: items without me'ilah (misuse) are not subject to misuse, but they are still consecrated.
The gemara infers from the mishnah that although there is no me'ilah (misuse), the items are still consecrated (קדשי).
Rabbi Yochanan identifies the tanna as Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, who holds that קדשים קלים (lesser sanctities) are the owner's property (ממון בעלים).
A baraita is cited: the verse 'וּמָעֲלָה מַעַל בַּה (and one commits a trespass against the Lord) includes קדשים קלים (lesser sanctities) as the owner's property, according to Rabbi Yosei HaGelili.

items.text: Challenge from the mishnah on consecrating with one's portion
items.text_en: Challenge from the mishnah on consecrating with one's portion
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's view with a mishnah stating that one who consecrates a woman with his portion of kodashim, whether kodshei kodashim or kodashim kalim, is not betrothed. The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yosei HaGelili only considers them the owner's property while alive, but after slaughter, even he agrees they are from the table of the Most High.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's view by citing a mishnah that one who consecrates a woman with his portion of kodashim is not betrothed, implying it contradicts his position.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yosei HaGelili only considers kodashim kalim the owner's property while alive, but after slaughter even he agrees they are from the table of the Most High.

items.text: Question on the status of a firstborn animal while alive
items.text_en: Question on the status of a firstborn animal while alive
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yosei HaGelili really holds that kodashim kalim are the owner's property while alive, citing a mishnah about a firstborn animal that can be sold and used to betroth a woman. Rav Nachman quotes Rabbah bar Avuh to distinguish between the present time (when the animal cannot be offered) and the time of the Temple (when it can).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's position by citing a mishnah that a firstborn animal can be sold alive and used to betroth a woman, implying it is the owner's property even while alive.

sub.text: Rav Nachman quoting Rabbah bar Avuh
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman quoting Rabbah bar Avuh
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avuh distinguishes between the present time when the firstborn cannot be offered (so priests have a share in it) and the time of the Temple when it can be offered (so it is not the owner's property).

items.text: Rava's objection and Ravina's resolution
items.text_en: Rava's objection and Ravina's resolution
items.desc_en: Rava objects to Rav Nachman's distinction by citing the baraita that includes kodashim kalim as the owner's property. Ravina resolves that the baraita refers to a firstborn outside the Land of Israel, according to Rabbi Shimon, who holds that if they come (perfect) they may be offered, but not ab initio.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects to Rav Nachman by citing the baraita that includes קדשים קלים (lesser sanctities) as the owner's property, per Rabbi Yosei HaGelili.
Ravina resolves that the baraita refers to a firstborn outside the Land of Israel, according to Rabbi Shimon, who holds that if they come (perfect) they may be offered, but not לכתחילה (ab initio).

items.text: Continuation of the discussion on Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's view
items.text_en: Continuation of the discussion on Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara continues to examine whether Rabbi Yosei HaGelili indeed holds that kodashim kalim are the owner's property while alive, setting up further analysis.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's ruling that קדשים קלים (lesser sanctities) are the owner's property applies only while the animal is alive.

items.text: Distinction between קדשים קלים and מתנות כהונה
items.text_en: Distinction between קדשים קלים and מתנות כהונה
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially suggests that the dispute between Rabbi Yosi HaGlili and the Rabbis can be resolved by distinguishing between קדשים קלים and מתנות כהונה. The response is that מתנות כהונה are different because they are acquired from the 'table of the Most High'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the dispute between Rabbi Yosi HaGlili and the Rabbis can be resolved by distinguishing between קדשים קלים (lesser sanctities) and מתנות כהונה (priestly gifts).
The response rejects the suggestion, arguing that priestly gifts are different because they are acquired from the 'table of the Most High' (i.e., they are not the owner's property).

items.text: The Baraita on מעילה in קדשים קלים
items.text_en: The Baraita on מעילה in קדשים קלים
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Baraita where Rabbi Yosi HaGlili interprets the verse 'וּמָעֲלָה מַעַל בַּה׳' to include קדשים קלים that are the owner's property. Ben Azzai says it includes שלמים, and Abba Yosi ben Dostai says Ben Azzai only meant בכור.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Baraita: Rabbi Yosi HaGlili interprets the verse 'וּמָעֲלָה מַעַל בַּה׳' to include קדשים קלים (lesser sanctified items) that are the owner's property; Ben Azzai says it includes שלמים (peace-offerings); Abba Yosi ben Dostai says Ben Azzai only meant בכור (firstborn animal).

items.text: Gemara's question on Ben Azzai: what does he exclude?
items.text_en: Gemara's question on Ben Azzai: what does he exclude?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Ben Azzai excludes when he says 'to include שלמים'. It considers excluding בכור but rejects it because שלמים are more stringent. Rabbi Yochanan answers that he excludes מעשר, citing a Baraita that distinguishes between בכור and מעשר in terms of sale.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Ben Azzai excludes when he says 'to include שלמים (peace offerings)'.
The Gemara rejects the possibility that Ben Azzai excludes בכור (firstborn), arguing that if even שלמים, which require more rituals, are considered the owner's property, then certainly בכור would be.
Rabbi Yochanan answers that Ben Azzai excludes מעשר (animal tithe).
A Baraita is cited to support Rabbi Yochanan's answer, distinguishing between בכור, which can be sold, and מעשר, which cannot be sold at all.

items.text: Gemara's question on Abba Yosi ben Dostai: what does he exclude?
items.text_en: Gemara's question on Abba Yosi ben Dostai: what does he exclude?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Abba Yosi ben Dostai excludes when he says Ben Azzai only meant בכור. It considers excluding שלמים but rejects it because בכור is more stringent. Rabbi Yochanan again answers that he excludes מעשר, citing the same Baraita. The Gemara notes a difficulty: Abba Yosi said 'only בכור', yet the Baraita discusses מעשר.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Abba Yosi ben Dostai excludes when he says Ben Azzai only meant בכור (firstborn).
The Gemara rejects the possibility that he excludes שלמים (peace offerings), arguing that if בכור (firstborn), which is more sacred, is considered the owner's property, then שלמים certainly would be.
Rabbi Yochanan answers that Abba Yosi excludes מעשר (tithe).
A baraita is cited to distinguish between בכור (firstborn), which can be sold, and מעשר (tithe), which cannot, supporting the exclusion.
The Gemara raises a difficulty: Abba Yosi said 'only בכור (firstborn),' yet the baraita discusses מעשר (tithe), creating a contradiction.

items.text: Rava's interpretation of 'נכסים שאין בהן מעילה'
items.text_en: Rava's interpretation of 'נכסים שאין בהן מעילה'
items.desc_en: Rava explains that 'נכסים שאין בהן מעילה' means property that has no law of מעילה, i.e., חולין. The Gemara objects that the Mishnah could have simply said 'חולין'.

sub.desc_en: Rava explains that the Mishnah's phrase 'נכסים שאין בהן מעילה' refers to property that has no law of מעילה, i.e., חולין (non-sacred property).
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah could have simply said 'חולין' instead of the longer phrase, leaving the difficulty unresolved.

items.text: Collection of damages from שלמים: from meat but not from sacrificial parts
items.text_en: Collection of damages from שלמים: from meat but not from sacrificial parts
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba states that if שלמים cause damage, the victim collects from their meat but not from their sacrificial parts (אימורים). The Gemara questions this, noting that אימורים go to the Most High. It then analyzes whether this ruling aligns with the Rabbis or Rabbi Natan, and offers two resolutions: according to the Rabbis, it applies when the meat and אימורים are considered one body; according to Rabbi Natan, it applies because the owner can claim from the one who caused the damage.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba states that if שלמים (peace offerings) cause damage, the victim collects from their meat but not from their sacrificial parts (אימורים).
The Gemara objects: it is obvious that one cannot collect from אימורים (sacrificial parts), since they ascend to the Most High.
The Gemara explains that the novel point is that one may collect from the meat even to offset the value of the אימורים (sacrificial parts).
The Gemara asks: according to which authority is this ruling stated?
The Gemara considers: if according to the Rabbis, it is obvious, since they hold that if one cannot collect from this body, one does not collect from that body.
The Gemara considers: if according to Rabbi Natan, he holds that if one cannot collect from this body, one does collect from that body, which would contradict Rabbi Abba's ruling.
The Gemara offers two alternative resolutions: either according to Rabbi Natan or according to the Rabbis.
According to the Rabbis, their principle applies only to two separate bodies, but within one body the owner can say 'I will collect from wherever I wish.'

According to Rabbi Natan, his principle applies only when the owner of the ox says to the owner of the pit 'I found my ox in your pit; what I cannot collect from you, I will collect from you' — but here the meat and אימורים are not separate owners.

items.text: Collection from a thanksgiving offering
items.text_en: Collection from a thanksgiving offering
items.desc_en: Rava rules that if a thanksgiving offering damages, the victim collects from its meat but not from its bread. The Gemara questions why this is not obvious, and explains that the novelty is that the victim eats the meat while the owner brings the bread for atonement, and that the bread is the owner's obligation, not just a prerequisite for the sacrifice.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the owner of a thanksgiving offering could claim that only the meat damaged, not the sacrificial portions (אימורין).
Rava rules that if a thanksgiving offering damages, the victim collects from its meat but not from its bread.
The Gemara objects that the ruling about the bread is obvious, since the bread is not part of the sacrificial animal's body.
The Gemara explains that the novelty is in the latter clause: the victim eats the meat while the owner brings the bread for atonement (כפרה).
The Gemara again objects that this too is obvious, because one might think the bread is merely a prerequisite (הכשר) for the sacrifice.
The Gemara resolves that the ruling teaches that the bread is the owner's obligation (חיובא דבעלים), not just a prerequisite, so the victim cannot be forced to bring it.

items.text: Exclusion of non-Jewish and disputed property
items.text_en: Exclusion of non-Jewish and disputed property
items.desc_en: The Mishnah excludes property of non-Jews and 'property that is not designated' (i.e., disputed). The Gemara notes that the exclusion of non-Jews is later taught explicitly, and Rav Yehuda explains that 'not designated' refers to a case where each claims the other's ox damaged his.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that damages are collected only from property belonging to Israelites (בני ברית).
The Gemara asks what this phrase excludes.
The Gemara considers whether it excludes a non-Jew's property, but notes that this is already taught later explicitly.
The Gemara explains that the Mishnah first states the rule and then later elaborates on it.

items.text: Exclusion of ownerless property and subsequent consecration
items.text_en: Exclusion of ownerless property and subsequent consecration
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that ownerless property is excluded. The Gemara questions how this applies, and Ravina explains it excludes cases where the ox gored and then was consecrated or declared ownerless. Rabbi Yehuda's baraita adds that even if goring preceded consecration or declaration of ownerless, the owner is exempt, requiring that death and standing in judgment be simultaneous.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that the verse excludes ownerless property, and the Gemara questions how this applies.
The Gemara answers that the case is where an ownerless ox gored a private ox, and the ownerless ox was later acquired by another person.
Ravina explains that the exclusion applies to cases where the ox gored and then was consecrated or declared ownerless.
A baraita supports this, quoting Rabbi Yehuda who exempts even if goring preceded consecration or declaration of ownerless, requiring that death and standing in judgment be simultaneous.

items.text: Liability in a shared courtyard: Rav Chisda vs. Rabbi Elazar
items.text_en: Liability in a shared courtyard: Rav Chisda vs. Rabbi Elazar
items.desc_en: The Mishnah exempts damage in the 'exclusive domain of the damager' and imposes liability in the 'domain of the victim and damager.' Rav Chisda explains that a shared courtyard is liable for Tooth and Foot, while Rabbi Elazar holds it is exempt for Tooth and Foot, and the phrase 'when he damages, the damager is liable' comes to include Kerren.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the principle of exemption in the exclusive domain of the damager and liability in the shared domain of victim and damager.
The Mishnah continues with the phrase 'domain of the victim and the damager.'

Rav Chisda in the name of Abimi explains that a shared courtyard (חצר השותפין) is liable for Tooth and Foot damage, interpreting the Mishnah's phrase 'when he damages, the damager is liable' as applying to this case.
Rabbi Elazar objects, holding that a shared courtyard is exempt for Tooth and Foot, and the phrase 'when he damages, the damager is liable' comes to include Kerren (Goring) damage.

items.text: The phrase 'when he damages, the damager is liable' includes bailees
items.text_en: The phrase 'when he damages, the damager is liable' includes bailees
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the phrase 'when he damages, the damager is liable' includes according to Rav, who already includes all ox-related matters. It answers that it includes a baraita about bailees (unpaid guardian, borrower, paid guardian, renter) who are liable for damage caused by the animal in their custody. The Gemara then analyzes the case, concluding that it involves a borrower who accepted responsibility for the animal's body.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the phrase 'וכשהזיק חב המזיק' (when he damages, the damager is liable) includes according to Rav, who already includes all ox-related matters.
The Gemara answers that it includes a baraita about bailees (שומר חנם, שואל, נושא שכר, שוכר) who are liable for damage caused by the animal in their custody.
Mar asks to clarify the specific case of the baraita: what scenario is being described?

The Gemara objects that if the case is the lender's ox goring the borrower's ox, the borrower could argue that he would have paid full damages if the ox had gored anyone else, so why should he pay only half now?

The Gemara objects alternatively that if the case is the borrower's ox goring the lender's ox, the borrower could argue that he would have paid full value if the ox had been injured by someone else, so why should he pay only half damages now?
The Gemara resolves that the case is indeed the lender's ox goring the borrower's ox, but the borrower accepted responsibility for the animal's body (שמירת גופו), making him liable for all damages.

items.text: Gemara's challenge to Rabbi Elazar
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge to Rabbi Elazar
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Elazar's ruling that a shared courtyard is exempt for tooth and foot damage, pointing out that the mishnah's case of a breached fence at night implies daytime liability even without accepting responsibility for damages.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Elazar's ruling by noting that the mishnah's case of a breached fence at night implies daytime liability even without accepting responsibility for damages.
The Gemara resolves the challenge by reinterpreting the mishnah: it means that if one accepted responsibility, he is liable; the breached fence case at night is an exception where he is exempt.

items.text: Baraita of Rav Yosef contradicts Rabbi Elazar
items.text_en: Baraita of Rav Yosef contradicts Rabbi Elazar
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef's baraita states that a shared courtyard and an inn are liable for tooth and foot damage, which directly contradicts Rabbi Elazar's position, leading to a refutation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rav Yosef's baraita explicitly states that a shared courtyard and an inn are liable for tooth and foot damage, which refutes Rabbi Elazar's position.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's response and the contradiction between baraitot
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's response and the contradiction between baraitot
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar deflects by noting that the mishnah itself is disputed, citing a baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar with four categories of damages. The Gemara then notes that this baraita itself contradicts Rav Yosef's baraita regarding a shared courtyard.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar deflects the challenge by asserting that the mishnah itself is disputed among Tannaim.

sub.text: Baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
sub.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar cites a baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar that lists four categories of damages, including a shared courtyard where one is exempt for tooth and foot.
The Gemara notes that this baraita explicitly states exemption for tooth and foot in a shared courtyard, creating a contradiction with Rav Yosef's baraita that imposes liability.
The Gemara declares the contradiction between the two baraitot as unresolved at this stage.

items.text: Resolution: distinguishing courtyard designation
items.text_en: Resolution: distinguishing courtyard designation
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by explaining that Rav Yosef's baraita refers to a courtyard designated for produce but not for animals, making it like the victim's domain for tooth damage, while Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's baraita refers to a courtyard designated for both produce and animals.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a courtyard designated for both produce and animals (where the baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar applies) and a courtyard designated only for produce (where Rav Yosef's baraita applies, making it like the victim's domain for tooth damage).

items.text: Objection by Rabbi Zeira and defense by Abaye
items.text_en: Objection by Rabbi Zeira and defense by Abaye
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira objects that if the courtyard is designated for produce, it lacks the requirement of 'field of another' for tooth damage. Abaye responds that since it is not designated for animals, it is considered 'another's field' regarding the animal. Rav Acha from Difti questions whether the amoraim dispute the tannaitic disagreement, and Ravina confirms they do not, or if they do, it is over Rabbi Zeira's question and Abaye's answer.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira objects that since the courtyard is designated for produce, it lacks the requirement of 'field of another' (שדה אחר) for tooth damage.
Abaye responds that since the courtyard is not designated for animals, it is considered 'another's field' (שדה אחר) regarding the animal.

sub.text: Rav Acha from Difti's question to Ravina
sub.text_en: Rav Acha from Difti's question to Ravina
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha from Difti asks Ravina whether the amoraim do not dispute the tannaitic disagreement, just as the mishnayot do not dispute.
Ravina confirms that the amoraim do not dispute, or if they do, it is over Rabbi Zeira's question and Abaye's answer.

items.text: Analysis of the four categories baraita: contradiction between Rabbi Tarfon and the Rabbis
items.text_en: Analysis of the four categories baraita: contradiction between Rabbi Tarfon and the Rabbis
items.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's baraita, noting that the first clause ('liable for all') aligns with Rabbi Tarfon's view that an unusual ox in the victim's domain pays full damages, while the last clause ('not for this nor that') implies a half-damage payment for tam, aligning with the Rabbis. This creates a contradiction within the baraita, resolved by Samuel's statement that the first part follows Rabbi Tarfon and the last part follows the Rabbis.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's four categories of damages, beginning with the first category where the domain belongs to the victim alone.
The Gemara identifies the first clause as following Rabbi Tarfon, who holds that an unusual ox in the victim's domain pays full damages.
The Gemara examines the last clause, clarifying that 'not for this nor for that' refers to a domain belonging to one person, and notes that it rules a tam pays half damages.
The Gemara identifies the last clause as aligning with the Rabbis, who hold that an unusual ox in the victim's domain pays only half damages.
The Gemara objects that the baraita appears self-contradictory, with the first clause following Rabbi Tarfon and the last clause following the Rabbis.
Samuel resolves the contradiction by telling Rav Yehuda that the first part follows Rabbi Tarfon and the last part follows the Rabbis.

items.text: Ravina's alternative resolution and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's objection
items.text_en: Ravina's alternative resolution and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's objection
items.desc_en: Ravina, citing Rava, argues that the entire baraita follows Rabbi Tarfon, interpreting 'not for this nor that' as not for produce but for one person, and for both for animals. This makes the courtyard the victim's domain for tooth and public domain for goring. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak objects that this would leave only three categories, not four.

sub.desc_en: Ravina, citing Rava, proposes that the entire baraita follows Rabbi Tarfon, interpreting 'not for this nor that' as not for produce but for one person, and 'for this and that' as for both for animals.
Ravina explains that regarding tooth, the courtyard is the victim's domain, and regarding goring, it is public domain.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak objects that if Ravina's interpretation is correct, there would be only three categories in the baraita, not four.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak begins his response to the objection.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states three general principles in four places: assessment must be in money, of equal value, before a court, based on witnesses who are free men and covenant members. Women are included in damages, and both the injured and injurer are liable for payment.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states three general principles in four places: assessment must be in money, of equal value, before a court, based on witnesses who are free men and covenant members; women are included in damages, and both the injured and injurer are liable for payment.

items.text: Gemara's first question and answer on 'shum kesef'
items.text_en: Gemara's first question and answer on 'shum kesef'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'shum kesef' means. Rav Yehuda answers that the assessment must be in money. This is supported by a baraita: if a cow damaged a cloak or vice versa, we do not exchange them but assess their value in money.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the phrase 'שום כסף' (assessment of money) in the Mishnah means.
Rav Yehuda answers that the assessment must be made specifically in money, not in kind.
A baraita is cited to support Rav Yehuda: when a cow damages a cloak or vice versa, we do not exchange the items but assess their value in money.

items.text: Analysis of 'shaveh kesef'
items.text_en: Analysis of 'shaveh kesef'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains 'shaveh kesef' from a baraita: courts only collect from property with lien (land), but if the victim seized movable property first, the court collects from it. The Gemara then questions the derivation, with Rabbah bar Ulla and Rav Ashi offering interpretations: it means something equivalent to money, not money itself, excluding items that are themselves money like slaves and documents.

sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches that 'shaveh kesef' means courts only collect from property with lien (land), but if the victim seized movable property first, the court collects from it.
The Gemara asks how the phrase 'shaveh kesef' implies that courts only collect from land.
Rabbah bar Ulla explains 'shaveh kesef' as something equivalent to all money, i.e., an item without price fraud (אונאה), but the Gemara objects that slaves and documents also lack price fraud.
Rabbah bar Ulla revises his explanation to 'something acquired with money', but the Gemara objects that slaves and documents are also acquired with money.
Rav Ashi resolves that 'shaveh kesef' means something equivalent to money, not money itself, thereby excluding slaves and documents which are themselves considered money.

items.text: Contradiction and resolution regarding movable property
