items.text_en: Contradiction and resolution regarding movable property
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda bar Chinana raises a contradiction: one baraita says courts only collect from land, but another says 'yashiv' includes even bran (movable property). The Gemara resolves that the first baraita deals with orphans. The objection that if the victim seized from orphans, why would the court collect? is answered by Rava citing Rav Nachman: the seizure was while the father was alive.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda bar Chinana raises a contradiction between two baraitot: one says courts only collect from land, another says 'יָשִׁיב' includes even bran (movable property).
The Gemara resolves that the first baraita deals with orphans, whose movable property is not subject to court collection.
The Gemara objects: if it deals with orphans, why does the baraita say that if the victim seized movable property, the court collects from it?
Rava answers in the name of Rav Nachman that the seizure occurred while the father was alive, so it is valid even for orphans.

items.text: Interpretation of 'before the court'
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'before the court'
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially suggests 'before the court' excludes one who sells his property and then goes to court, implying that if he borrowed and sold, the court does not collect. It then rejects this and explains it excludes informal courts (hedyotot).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the phrase 'בִּפְנֵי בֵּית דִּין' (before a court) and explains it excludes one who sells his property and then goes to court.
The Gemara infers that if one borrows and then sells his property, the court does not collect from those sold properties.
The Gemara corrects: 'בִּפְנֵי בֵּית דִּין' excludes informal courts (הדיוטות), not the case of selling property.

items.text: Interpretation of 'on the testimony of witnesses'
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'on the testimony of witnesses'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains 'on the testimony of witnesses' excludes one who admits to a fine and then witnesses come, as he is exempt. It then notes this depends on a dispute: for those who say he is liable, the phrase is needed for the latter part of the Mishnah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the phrase 'עַל פִּי עֵדִים' (based on witnesses) and explains it excludes one who admits to a fine (קנס) and then witnesses come, making him exempt.
The Gemara notes this works for the opinion that one who admits to a fine and then witnesses come is exempt, but asks what about the opinion that he is liable.
The Gemara answers that the phrase is needed for the latter part of the Mishnah (the continuation), not for the exclusion of the admitter.

items.text: Exclusion of slaves and gentiles from the law of the goring ox
items.text_en: Exclusion of slaves and gentiles from the law of the goring ox
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the law applies only to 'free men and members of the covenant,' excluding slaves and gentiles. The Gemara explains that both exclusions are necessary: a slave lacks lineage (חַיִיס) but is connected to mitzvot, while a gentile has lineage but is not connected to mitzvot.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the law of the goring ox applies only to 'free men and members of the covenant,' excluding slaves and gentiles.
The Gemara explains that both exclusions are necessary: a slave lacks lineage (חַיִיס) but is connected to mitzvot, while a gentile has lineage but is not connected to mitzvot.

items.text: Inclusion of women in all penalties and judgments
items.text_en: Inclusion of women in all penalties and judgments
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we know women are included in the law of damages. Three derivations are brought: from Rav Yehuda citing Rav and the school of Rabbi Yishmael (from the verse 'איש או אשה' for all punishments), from the school of Rabbi Elazar (from 'ואלה המשפטים' for all judgments), and from the school of Hezekiah and Rabbi Yosei HaGelili (from 'והמית איש או אשה' for all capital cases). The Gemara explains why all three are necessary, as each might otherwise be limited.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where do we derive that women are included in the law of damages?

sub.text: Rav Yehuda citing Rav and Tanna debei Rabbi Yishmael
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda citing Rav and Tanna debei Rabbi Yishmael
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav, and similarly the school of Rabbi Yishmael, derive from the verse 'איש או אשה כי יעשו מכל חטאת' that the Torah equates a woman to a man for all penalties.
The school of Rabbi Elazar teaches from the verse 'ואלה המשפטים' that the Torah equates a woman to a man for all judgments.

sub.text: Tanna debei Hezekiah and Rabbi Yosei HaGelili
sub.text_en: Tanna debei Hezekiah and Rabbi Yosei HaGelili
sub.desc_en: The school of Hezekiah and Rabbi Yosei HaGelili teach from the verse 'והמית איש או אשה' that the Torah equates a woman to a man for all capital cases.

The Gemara explains why all three derivations are necessary: each alone might be limited to its specific context (atonement, livelihood, or loss of life), so all three are required to establish the full inclusion of women.

items.text: Debate: Is half-damages for a tam ox monetary or a fine?
items.text_en: Debate: Is half-damages for a tam ox monetary or a fine?
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that both the injured party and the injuring party are involved in payment. Rav Pappa says half-damages are monetary (ממונא), because oxen are not presumed guarded and the Torah reduced the payment. Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua says it is a fine (קנסא), because oxen are presumed guarded and the Torah penalized the owner to ensure better watch.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that both the injured party and the injuring party are involved in payment.
The Gemara introduces a dispute: Rav Pappa says half-damages are monetary (ממונא), Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua says it is a fine (קנסא).
Rav Pappa argues that oxen are not presumed guarded, so the Torah reduced the payment from full to half as a mercy.

sub.text: Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua's reasoning
sub.text_en: Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua's reasoning
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua argues that oxen are presumed guarded, so the Torah imposed a fine (קנסא) to penalize the owner for negligence.

items.text: Challenge and resolution regarding the Mishnah's wording
items.text_en: Challenge and resolution regarding the Mishnah's wording
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: according to Rav Huna, if half-damages are a fine, how can the injured party be involved in payment? The Gemara answers that the Mishnah refers to the reduction in value of the carcass (פחת נבילה). It then notes that this was already taught earlier, and resolves that one case is for a tam ox and the other for a mu'ad ox, both necessary.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: according to the opinion that half-damages are a fine (קנס), how can the injured party be involved in payment, since the fine is not his?
The Gemara answers: the Mishnah's statement refers to the reduction in value of the carcass (פחת נבילה), which belongs to the injured party.
The Gemara objects: the reduction in value of the carcass was already taught earlier in the Mishnah regarding the owners' involvement with the carcass.
The Gemara resolves: one case refers to a tam ox and the other to a mu'ad ox, both necessary.
The Gemara explains why both cases are necessary: each addresses a unique concern that would otherwise be excluded.

items.text: Attempted proof from a baraita and its rejection
items.text_en: Attempted proof from a baraita and its rejection
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita listing differences between tam and mu'ad, and notes that it does not include the rule that a tam does not pay on his own admission while a mu'ad does. The Gemara suggests the baraita omitted this, but then rejects the proof because the baraita might follow Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, who holds that a tam pays half kofer, so the omission is not a problem.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita listing the differences between a tam and a mu'ad.
The Gemara objects that if the rule about payment on admission existed, the baraita should have listed it.
The Gemara suggests that the baraita omitted (שייר) the rule about half kofer.
The Gemara objects that half kofer is not a valid omission because it is not a difference between tam and mu'ad.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita follows Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, who holds that a tam pays half kofer, so the omission is not a problem.

items.text: Further attempted proof introduced
items.text_en: Further attempted proof introduced
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to bring another proof with the phrase 'תא שמע' (come and hear), but the daf ends before the proof is completed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a further attempted proof with the phrase 'תא שמע' (come and hear), but the daf ends before the proof is completed.

items.text: Question on payment by admission for tam vs. mu'ad
items.text_en: Question on payment by admission for tam vs. mu'ad
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah's case of one who says 'my ox killed so-and-so' and pays on his own admission refers to a tam (innocent) ox. It answers that it refers to a mu'ad (forewarned) ox, and questions why the Mishnah didn't distinguish between tam and mu'ad in the same clause. The conclusion is that the entire Mishnah deals with a mu'ad.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah's case of paying on one's own admission refers to a tam (innocent) ox.
The Gemara answers that the case refers to a mu'ad (forewarned) ox.
The Gemara objects that if the Mishnah only deals with a mu'ad, it should have distinguished between tam and mu'ad in the same clause, rather than teaching a separate case about a slave.
The Gemara proposes that the Mishnah could have distinguished by saying 'in what case are these words said? With a mu'ad, but with a tam he does not pay on his own admission.'
The Gemara concludes that the entire Mishnah deals with a mu'ad ox, so no distinction is needed.

items.text: Refutation from a baraita about the rule of paying more than damage
items.text_en: Refutation from a baraita about the rule of paying more than damage
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita stating that one who pays more than the damage does not pay on his own admission, implying that one who pays less does pay. It attempts to refute this, but the baraita is shown to be inconclusive because it could mean paying exactly the damage. The Gemara concludes with a refutation (תיוּבְתָּא) because the baraita should have stated the rule more broadly.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita stating that one who pays more than the damage does not pay on his own admission, and infers that one who pays less does pay.
The Gemara answers that the baraita means one who pays exactly the damage pays on his own admission, not less.
The Gemara objects that if so, the baraita should have stated the rule more broadly to include paying less, and concludes with a refutation (תיוּבְתָּא).

items.text: Resolution: half-damage is a fine, explaining the baraita
items.text_en: Resolution: half-damage is a fine, explaining the baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara states the halakha that half-damage (פַּלְגָא נִזְקָא) is a fine (קְנָסָא). It questions how there can be both a refutation and a halakha, and explains that the refutation stands because the baraita did not include the case of paying exactly the damage, but the halakha is not affected because there is the case of half-damage for pebbles (צְרוֹרוֹת) which is a halakha from tradition and is monetary, so the baraita's omission is justified.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the halakha that half-damage (פַּלְגָא נִזְקָא) is a fine (קְנָסָא).
The Gemara questions how there can be both a refutation (תְּיוּבְתָּא) and a halakha (הִלְכְתָא) regarding the same matter.
The Gemara answers that the refutation stands because the baraita did not include the case of paying exactly the damage.

The Gemara resolves that the halakha is not affected because there is the case of half-damage for pebbles (צְרוֹרוֹת), which is a halakha from tradition and is monetary, so the baraita's omission is justified.

items.text: Practical halakha for unusual animals in Babylonia
items.text_en: Practical halakha for unusual animals in Babylonia
items.desc_en: Given that half-damage is a fine, the Gemara rules that a dog that eats lambs or a cat that eats chickens is considered an unusual (מְשׁוּנֶּה) case, and such fines are not collected in Babylonia (outside of Israel). However, for small animals it is normal. If the plaintiff seizes property, we do not take it away. If the defendant asks for time to go to the Land of Israel for judgment, we set a time and excommunicate him if he doesn't go. In any case, we excommunicate him until he removes the damage, based on Rabbi Natan's teaching about not keeping a dangerous dog or a rickety ladder.

sub.desc_en: Given that half-damage is a fine, the Gemara rules that a dog that eats lambs or a cat that eats chickens is considered unusual and such fines are not collected in Babylonia.
The Gemara distinguishes that this applies only to large animals, but for small ones it is normal behavior.
If the plaintiff seizes property, we do not take it away.
If the defendant asks for time to go to the Land of Israel for judgment, we set a time and excommunicate him if he doesn't go.
In any case, we excommunicate him until he removes the damage, based on Rabbi Natan's teaching about not keeping a dangerous dog or a rickety ladder.

items.text: Mishnah: Five tam and five mu'ad categories
items.text_en: Mishnah: Five tam and five mu'ad categories
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists five tam (innocent) categories: an animal is not forewarned for goring, butting, biting, lying down, or kicking. Then it lists five mu'ad (forewarned) categories: the tooth (forewarned to eat what is suitable), the foot (forewarned to break while walking), a forewarned ox, an ox that damages in the plaintiff's domain, and a person. It also lists wild animals (wolf, lion, bear, leopard, bardelas, snake) as forewarned, with Rabbi Elazar saying that if they are domesticated they are not forewarned, and the snake is always forewarned.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that there are five tam (innocent) categories and five mu'ad (forewarned) categories.
The Mishnah lists the five tam categories: an animal is not forewarned for goring, butting, biting, lying down, or kicking.

The Mishnah lists the five mu'ad categories: the tooth (forewarned to eat what is suitable), the foot (forewarned to break while walking), a forewarned ox, an ox that damages in the plaintiff's domain, and a person.

The Mishnah lists wild animals (wolf, lion, bear, leopard, bardelas, snake) as forewarned, with Rabbi Elazar adding that if they are domesticated they are not forewarned, and the snake is always forewarned.

items.text: Gemara analysis of Mishnah's authorship
items.text_en: Gemara analysis of Mishnah's authorship
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's first clause (tooth and foot) implies we are dealing with the plaintiff's domain, and the statement that an animal is not forewarned to pay full damage implies it pays half-damage, which aligns with the Rabbis (who hold that an unusual goring in the plaintiff's domain pays half-damage). However, the later clause (forewarned ox, ox damaging in plaintiff's domain, and man) aligns with Rabbi Tarfon (who holds that an unusual goring in the plaintiff's domain pays full damage). The Gemara resolves this by citing Shmuel's instruction to Rav Yehuda: leave the Mishnah and follow me – the first part is the Rabbis and the latter part is Rabbi Tarfon. Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rav says something else.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah's wording that the first clause deals with the plaintiff's domain and that the animal pays half-damage.
The Gemara identifies the first clause as the Rabbis' position, who hold that an unusual goring in the plaintiff's domain pays only half-damage.

The Gemara notes that the latter clause (forewarned ox, ox damaging in plaintiff's domain, and man) aligns with Rabbi Tarfon, who holds that an unusual goring in the plaintiff's domain pays full damage.
The Gemara questions how the Mishnah can combine two conflicting opinions in one statement.
Shmuel instructs Rav Yehuda to leave the Mishnah and follow him, explaining that the first part is the Rabbis and the latter part is Rabbi Tarfon.

sub.text: Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar cites an alternative statement in the name of Rav, introducing a different perspective.

items.text: Initial explanation of the Mishnah as Rabbi Tarfon's view
items.text_en: Initial explanation of the Mishnah as Rabbi Tarfon's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the entire Mishnah is according to Rabbi Tarfon, explaining that the first clause refers to a courtyard designated for produce for one and for animals for another, making it a private domain for tooth damage but public for horn damage.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the entire Mishnah follows Rabbi Tarfon, explaining that the first clause refers to a courtyard designated for produce for one and for animals for another, making it a private domain for tooth damage but a public domain for horn damage.

items.text: Rav Kahana's report and Rav Zevid's objection
items.text_en: Rav Kahana's report and Rav Zevid's objection
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana reports this teaching to Rav Zevid, who objects: can you really establish the entire Mishnah as Rabbi Tarfon? The Mishnah states 'the tooth is mu'ad to eat what is fit for it,' implying only what is fit, but Rabbi Tarfon holds that a mu'ad animal pays full damages in the plaintiff's courtyard.

sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana reports that Rav Zevid objected: if the Mishnah is entirely Rabbi Tarfon, then the clause 'the tooth is forewarned to eat what is fit for it' would be redundant, since Rabbi Tarfon holds that even horn damage in the plaintiff's courtyard pays full damages.

Rav Zevid objects: the Mishnah states 'the tooth is mu'ad to eat what is fit for it,' implying only what is fit, but Rabbi Tarfon holds that a mu'ad animal pays full damages in the plaintiff's courtyard.

items.text: Revised explanation: the Mishnah is Rabbis, with a missing clause
items.text_en: Revised explanation: the Mishnah is Rabbis, with a missing clause
items.desc_en: The Gemara revises: the Mishnah is actually the Rabbis, and it is missing a clause. The correct text should be: 'Five are tam, and if they become mu'ad, all five are mu'ad. Tooth and foot are mu'ad from the beginning. Where is their evidence? In the plaintiff's courtyard.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah actually follows the Rabbis, and it is missing a clause: it should read 'Five innocents are they, and if they become forewarned, all five are forewarned; tooth and foot are forewarned from the outset, and their forewarning is in the plaintiff's courtyard.'

items.text: Ravina's objection from the phrase 'How so?'
items.text_en: Ravina's objection from the phrase 'How so?'
items.desc_en: Ravina objects: the Mishnah later teaches 'How does an ox that causes damage in the plaintiff's courtyard?' If the Mishnah did not discuss this case, why would it say 'How so?'

sub.desc_en: Ravina objects: if the Mishnah does not discuss the case of an ox damaging in the plaintiff's courtyard, why does it later ask 'How does an ox damaging in the plaintiff's courtyard?'

items.text: Ravina's alternative resolution with a different missing clause
items.text_en: Ravina's alternative resolution with a different missing clause
items.desc_en: Ravina proposes a different missing clause: the Mishnah should read: 'Five are tam, and if they become mu'ad, all five are mu'ad. Tooth and foot are mu'ad from the beginning. This is the mu'ad ox. The ox that causes damage in the plaintiff's courtyard is a dispute between Rabbi Tarfon and the Rabbis. And there are other mu'adim like these: the wolf, lion, bear, leopard, hyena, and snake.'

sub.desc_en: Ravina resolves that the Mishnah is indeed missing a clause: it should read 'Five innocents are they, and if they become forewarned, all five are forewarned; tooth and foot are forewarned from the outset; and this is the forewarned ox; and the ox damaging in the plaintiff's courtyard is a dispute between Rabbi Tarfon and the Rabbis; and there are other forewarned creatures like the wolf, lion, bear, leopard, panther, and snake.'

items.text: Support from a baraita
items.text_en: Support from a baraita
items.desc_en: A baraita supports Ravina's version, stating the same text: five tam, if mu'ad all five are mu'ad, tooth and foot are mu'ad from the beginning, this is the mu'ad ox, the ox in the plaintiff's courtyard is a dispute, and there are other mu'adim like these animals.

sub.desc_en: A baraita supports Ravina's version, listing the same five innocents, the forewarned ox, the dispute about the ox in the plaintiff's courtyard, and the additional forewarned creatures.

items.text: Contradiction between Mishnah and baraita resolved
items.text_en: Contradiction between Mishnah and baraita resolved
items.desc_en: Some raise a contradiction: the Mishnah says 'five tam and five mu'ad' and no more, but the baraita lists additional animals. Ravina resolves it by saying the Mishnah is missing a clause, repeating the same text as before.

sub.desc_en: Some raise a contradiction: the Mishnah says 'five innocents and five forewarned' and no more, yet the baraita lists additional forewarned creatures; Ravina resolves that the Mishnah is missing a clause, repeating the same emended version.
Ravina resolves the contradiction by asserting that the Mishnah is missing a clause, and he restates the full text including the additional animals.

items.text: Discussion on liability for lying down
items.text_en: Discussion on liability for lying down
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states an animal is not liable for lying down. Rabbi Elazar says this applies only to large jugs, but for small jugs, it is the animal's normal way and thus liable.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar explains that the Mishnah's rule 'and not to crouch' applies only to large jugs, but small jugs are within the animal's normal behavior.
Rabbi Elazar explains that the Mishnah's exemption applies only to large jugs, but for small jugs, lying down is the animal's normal way and thus it is liable.

items.text: Attempted support and rejection
items.text_en: Attempted support and rejection
items.desc_en: An attempt is made to support Rabbi Elazar from a baraita that says an animal is mu'ad to walk normally and crush people, animals, and vessels. The Gemara rejects this, saying perhaps it refers to crushing from the side.

sub.desc_en: An attempt to support Rabbi Elazar from a baraita that says an animal is forewarned to break and crush people, animals, and vessels, but the Gemara deflects: perhaps it refers to crushing from the side.
The Gemara rejects the support, suggesting the baraita may refer to crushing from the side, which is the animal's normal way, not directly underfoot.

items.text: Alternative version of Rabbi Elazar's statement
items.text_en: Alternative version of Rabbi Elazar's statement
items.desc_en: Some say Rabbi Elazar stated: do not say that only large jugs are not its normal way, but small jugs are; rather, even small jugs are not its normal way.

sub.desc_en: An alternate version of Rabbi Elazar's statement: even small jugs are not within the animal's normal behavior.

items.text: Objection and Rabbi Elazar's response
items.text_en: Objection and Rabbi Elazar's response
items.desc_en: An objection is raised from the baraita about crushing vessels. Rabbi Elazar answers that it refers to crushing from the side.

sub.desc_en: An objection is raised from the baraita that says the animal is forewarned to crush vessels; Rabbi Elazar deflects that it might be from the side.
Rabbi Elazar answers that the baraita refers to crushing from the side (מן הצד), which is the animal's normal way of walking, not deliberate crushing from above.

items.text: Contradiction between Mishnah and baraita resolved by Rabbi Elazar
items.text_en: Contradiction between Mishnah and baraita resolved by Rabbi Elazar
items.desc_en: Some raise a contradiction: the Mishnah says not liable for lying down, but a baraita says liable for crushing. Rabbi Elazar resolves: here (Mishnah) refers to large jugs, there (baraita) to small jugs.

sub.text: Some raise a contradiction and Rabbi Elazar resolves
sub.text_en: Some raise a contradiction and Rabbi Elazar resolves
sub.desc_en: Some raise a contradiction between the Mishnah 'and not to crouch' and the baraita about crushing vessels; Rabbi Elazar resolves: the Mishnah refers to large jugs, the baraita to small jugs.
Rabbi Elazar resolves: here (Mishnah) refers to large jugs, there (baraita) to small jugs.

items.text: Identification of 'bardelas'
items.text_en: Identification of 'bardelas'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'bardelas' means. Rav Yehuda says it is 'nafruza'. Rav Yosef says 'appa'.

sub.text: Gemara's question and Rav Yehuda and Rav Yosef
sub.text_en: Gemara's question and Rav Yehuda and Rav Yosef
sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'bardelas' means; Rav Yehuda says it is 'nafruza'; Rav Yosef explains that 'nafruza' is 'appa' (a leopard).
Rav Yehuda identifies 'bardelas' as 'nafruza' (a type of wild cat or hyena).
The Gemara asks what 'nafruza' means.
Rav Yosef explains that 'nafruza' is 'appa' (the Aramaic term for a hyena).

items.text: Contradiction regarding 'tzavua'
items.text_en: Contradiction regarding 'tzavua'
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited: Rabbi Meir includes the tzavua, Rabbi Elazar includes the snake. Rav Yosef says tzavua is 'appa'. This contradicts the earlier identification of 'appa' as bardelas.

sub.desc_en: An objection is raised from a baraita where Rabbi Meir adds 'the hyena' and Rabbi Elazar adds 'the snake'; Rav Yosef identifies 'hyena' as 'appa' (leopard), creating a contradiction with the earlier identification.
Rav Yosef identifies the tzavua as 'appa', which contradicts the earlier identification of 'appa' as bardelas.

items.text: Resolution: male vs. female tzavua
items.text_en: Resolution: male vs. female tzavua
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves: no contradiction; here (Rav Yosef) refers to a male tzavua, there (the baraita) to a female tzavua. A baraita describes the transformation of a male tzavua over seven-year cycles into various creatures, and a human spine that did not bow during 'Modim' becomes a snake after seven years.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction between Rav Yosef and the baraita by distinguishing between a male tzavua (צָבוֹעַ זָכָר) and a female tzavua (צָבוֹעַ נְקִיבָה).

A baraita describes the seven-year transformation cycle of a male tzavua into various creatures, and adds that a human spine that did not bow during the 'Modim' prayer becomes a snake after seven years.

items.text: Repetition of Rabbi Meir's statement
items.text_en: Repetition of Rabbi Meir's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara repeats that Rabbi Meir includes the tzavua.

sub.desc_en: Mar cites the baraita again: Rabbi Meir adds the hyena.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's ruling on the snake
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's ruling on the snake
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: Rabbi Elazar says a snake is not forewarned when it is a domesticated animal, yet the Mishnah states a snake is always forewarned. The resolution is that the Mishnah refers to a wild snake.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara points out a contradiction: Rabbi Elazar rules that a snake is not forewarned when domesticated, yet the Mishnah states a snake is always forewarned.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by explaining that the Mishnah refers to a wild snake, not a domesticated one.

items.text: Shmuel's distinction: trampling vs. tearing in the public domain
items.text_en: Shmuel's distinction: trampling vs. tearing in the public domain
items.desc_en: Shmuel rules that if a lion tramples and eats in the public domain, the owner is exempt, as trampling is its normal way of eating (like tooth in the public domain). But if it tears and eats, the owner is liable, as tearing is not its normal way.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel rules that a lion in the public domain is exempt for trampling and eating (as it is normal), but liable for tearing and eating (as it is abnormal).
The Gemara explains that trampling is the lion's normal mode (like tooth damage in public domain, exempt), while tearing is not its normal mode, so it is liable.

items.text: Challenge to Shmuel from verses about lions tearing
items.text_en: Challenge to Shmuel from verses about lions tearing
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Shmuel's claim that tearing is not a lion's normal way, citing verses that describe lions as tearing prey. The Gemara answers that those verses refer to tearing for their cubs or for their dens, not for eating.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: Is tearing really not the lion's normal mode? The verse says 'a lion tears prey for its cubs'.
The Gemara rejects the objection by explaining that the lion tears only for the sake of its cubs or lair, not as its normal eating behavior.

items.text: Challenge from a baraita and resolution
items.text_en: Challenge from a baraita and resolution
items.desc_en: A baraita states that if an animal enters the victim's courtyard and tears and eats, it pays full damages. The Gemara initially questions Shmuel, then resolves that the baraita refers to tearing to leave (not to eat), or that it lists alternatives: tearing to leave or trampling and eating.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Shmuel by citing a baraita that states a wild animal that enters the victim's courtyard, tears an animal and eats its meat, pays full damages.

The Gemara initially resolves that the baraita refers to a case where the animal tore to leave the meat, not to eat it, and then addresses the baraita's mention of eating by saying it means the animal later reconsidered and ate.
The Gemara objects that we cannot know the animal's intent, and further questions whether Shmuel's ruling might also be interpreted this way.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves that the baraita lists alternatives: either the animal tore to leave or it trampled and ate, both of which require full payment.

items.text: Ravina's alternative explanation and its difficulties
items.text_en: Ravina's alternative explanation and its difficulties
items.desc_en: Ravina suggests Shmuel's ruling applies to a domesticated lion according to Rabbi Elazar, who holds that tearing is not its normal way. The Gemara objects that then even trampling should be liable. It then says Ravina's statement was about the Mishnah, not Shmuel, but that leads to other difficulties, concluding with a קשיא.

sub.desc_en: Ravina explains that Shmuel's ruling applies to a domesticated lion, according to Rabbi Elazar who holds that tearing is not its normal way.
The Gemara objects that if tearing is not normal, then even trampling should be liable.
The Gemara rejects the objection by saying Ravina's statement was about the Mishnah, not about Shmuel.
The Gemara objects that if the lion is domesticated, it should pay only half damages as a תם (innocent ox).
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah's placement of this case among the תולדה (subcategories) of שן (tooth) is problematic, as it should be under קרן (horn), concluding with a קשיא (difficulty).

items.text: Mishnah: Difference between tam and mu'ad
items.text_en: Mishnah: Difference between tam and mu'ad
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states the difference between a tam (innocuous) and a mu'ad (forewarned) ox: the tam pays half damages from its body, while the mu'ad pays full damages from the best of its owner's property.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah asks: What is the difference between a tam (innocent ox) and a mu'ad (forewarned ox)? The tam pays half damages from its body, the mu'ad pays full damages from the best property.

items.text: Gemara on 'עלייה' and aggadic interpretations
items.text_en: Gemara on 'עלייה' and aggadic interpretations
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains 'עלייה' as the best of his property, citing verses about Hezekiah's burial. It then discusses various interpretations of verses about Hezekiah and Jeremiah's prayer, including a dispute about whether he was suspected of adultery or prostitution, and concludes with a teaching about charity and a dispute about the number of days of mourning.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah means by 'עלייה' (the best property).
Rabbi Elazar explains that 'עלייה' refers to the choicest (מעולה) of one's property.
Rabbi Elazar cites a verse about Hezekiah's burial to support that 'מעלה' means the choicest of the family.

sub.text: Gemara's digression on Hezekiah's burial spices
sub.text_en: Gemara's digression on Hezekiah's burial spices
sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks about the meaning of 'בשמים וזנים' in the verse, and Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani offer two interpretations.
The Gemara discusses a verse about Jeremiah, with Rabbi Elazar saying he was suspected of prostitution and Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani saying he was suspected of adultery.

sub.text: Gemara's objection to the prostitution interpretation
sub.text_en: Gemara's objection to the prostitution interpretation
sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection: for the one who says he was suspected of prostitution, the verse fits, but for the one who says adultery, why is the term 'שוחה' used, since an adulteress is also a type of prostitute?

sub.text: Gemara's objection to the adultery interpretation
sub.text_en: Gemara's objection to the adultery interpretation
sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises another objection: for the one who says adultery, the verse about death fits, but for the one who says prostitution, 'death' refers to being thrown into a pit of mud.
Rava interprets a verse from Jeremiah's prayer, explaining that Jeremiah asked God to cause the wicked to give charity through unworthy recipients so they receive no reward.
The Gemara interprets a verse about Hezekiah's honor at death, and Rabbi Natan and the Sages dispute the number of days of mourning.

items.text: The dispute about Hezekiah's funeral honors
items.text_en: The dispute about Hezekiah's funeral honors
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda says 36,000 shoulder-bared men went out before Hezekiah. Rabbi Nehemya objects that the same was done for Ahab, so the honor must be that they placed a Torah scroll on his bier and said 'this one fulfilled what is written in this.' The Gemara questions why this is unique, since we do the same today, and resolves that we take out a scroll but do not place it, or we place it but do not say 'fulfilled.'

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that the honor done to Hezekiah at his death was that 36,000 shoulder-bared men went out before him, according to Rabbi Yehuda.
Rabbi Nehemya objects that the same honor of shoulder-bared men was done for the wicked King Ahab, so this cannot be the unique honor.
The baraita resolves that the unique honor was placing a Torah scroll on Hezekiah's bier and declaring that he fulfilled what is written in it.
The Gemara questions why this is considered unique, since today we also place a Torah scroll on the bier of a deceased sage.
The Gemara answers that today we take out the scroll but do not place it on the bier, unlike the honor for Hezekiah.
Alternatively, the Gemara answers that we do place the scroll but do not say the declaration 'he fulfilled what is written in it.'

items.text: Rabbah bar bar Chanah's testimony about Rabbi Yochanan's practice
items.text_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah's testimony about Rabbi Yochanan's practice
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah relates that when he accompanied Rabbi Yochanan to ask a halakhic matter, Rabbi Yochanan would not answer until after using the restroom, washing hands, donning tefillin, and blessing. Then he would say 'fulfilled' (kiyeim) but not 'taught' (limmed). The Gemara questions this because Torah study leads to action, and resolves that 'to learn' (lemigmar) is different from 'to teach' (le'agmorei).

sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah testifies that Rabbi Yochanan, when asked a halakhic matter after using the restroom, would wash, don tefillin, bless, and then say 'fulfilled' (קִיֵּים) but not 'taught' (לִימֵּד).
The Gemara objects: the master said that Torah study is great because it leads to action, so why would Rabbi Yochanan not say 'taught' (לִימֵּד)?
The Gemara resolves: no difficulty — 'to learn' (לְמִיגְמַר) is different from 'to teach' (לְאַגְמוֹרֵי); Rabbi Yochanan's statement applies to teaching others, not to his own learning.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's homily on the reward for Torah and charity
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's homily on the reward for Torah and charity
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai expounds the verse 'Happy are you who sow by all waters, who send forth the foot of the ox and the donkey' to mean that one who engages in Torah and charity merits the inheritance of two tribes: Yosef (for strength and victory) and Yissachar (for wisdom). An alternative version says enemies fall before him like Yosef and he merits understanding like Yissachar.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan citing Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan citing Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai introduces a homily: one who engages in Torah and charity merits the inheritance of two tribes.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of the homily's prooftexts
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the homily's prooftexts
sub.desc_en: The gemara explains the verse's imagery: 'sowing' refers to charity (צדקה) and 'water' refers to Torah (תורה), citing supporting verses.
The gemara specifies the reward: one merits strength like Yosef (citing 'בן פורת יוסף') and the inheritance of Yissachar (citing 'יששכר חמור גרם').
An alternative version states that enemies fall before him like Yosef and he merits understanding like Yissachar, citing different verses.

items.text: Mishnah: The liability of regel (foot) for damage
items.text_en: Mishnah: The liability of regel (foot) for damage
items.desc_en: The Mishnah begins the fourth chapter, stating that an animal's foot is forewarned (mu'ad) to break things in its normal course of walking. If it kicks or sends pebbles flying and breaks vessels, half damages are paid. If it steps on a vessel and breaks it, and the vessel falls on another, full damages are paid for the first and half for the second. Chickens are similarly forewarned; if a string is tied to their leg or they hop and break vessels, half damages are paid.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens the chapter by defining the liability of an animal's foot (regel) as forewarned (mu'ad) to break things in its normal course of walking.
The Mishnah states that if the animal kicks or sends pebbles flying and breaks vessels, half damages are paid.
The Mishnah rules that if the animal steps on a vessel and it breaks, and the vessel falls on another, full damages are paid for the first and half for the second.
The Mishnah extends the rule to chickens, stating that if a string is tied to their leg or they hop and break vessels, half damages are paid.

items.text: Clarifying the relationship between 'regel' and 'behemah'
items.text_en: Clarifying the relationship between 'regel' and 'behemah'
items.desc_en: Ravina asks Rava why the Mishnah lists both 'regel' and 'behemah' as separate categories. Rava explains that the Tanna lists 'avot' (primary categories) and 'toladot' (subcategories). The Gemara questions this by pointing to the Mishnah's listing of 'shen' and 'behemah' as separate, and after a humorous exchange, Rav Ashi explains that 'shen' for a wild animal is taught to include it in the category of 'behemah' based on a scriptural derivation. The Gemara then resolves the order of the Mishnah by noting that the Tanna begins with 'regel' because he was just discussing it.

sub.desc_en: Ravina asks Rava why the Mishnah lists both 'regel' and 'behemah' as separate categories, since they seem identical.
Rava answers that the Tanna lists 'avot' (primary categories) and 'toladot' (subcategories), so 'behemah' is the primary category and 'regel' is its subcategory.
The Gemara objects that in the Mishnah's later clause, both 'shen' and 'behemah' are listed as 'mu'edet', so the avot/toladot distinction does not apply there.
Rava jokingly deflects the objection, saying each of them knows one thing (the other does not).

Rav Ashi explains that the Tanna lists 'shen' for a wild animal and 'shen' for a domestic animal, teaching that a wild animal is included in the category of 'behemah' based on a scriptural derivation.
The Gemara asks why the Tanna did not teach the case of 'shen' for a wild animal first, since it is derived from a verse.
The Gemara answers that the Tanna prefers to teach the case derived from a verse later because it is more beloved to him.
The Gemara objects that if so, the Tanna should have taught the primary category first, not the subcategory, and the answer distinguishes between the two cases.
The Gemara resolves that the Tanna began with 'regel' because he had just finished discussing it in the previous Mishnah.

items.text: Baraita on damages caused by an animal's normal movement
items.text_en: Baraita on damages caused by an animal's normal movement
items.desc_en: A baraita is taught listing cases where an animal is 'mu'ad' (forewarned) to damage through its normal movement, including damage caused by its body, hair, saddle, etc. The Gemara clarifies that the baraita refers to cases where the animal 'kicked and damaged' (hitiz ve'hizik). It then explains that the text of the baraita should be emended: for 'tsrorot' (pebbles) in the normal manner, the payment is half-damages, while Sumchos says full damages.

sub.desc_en: A baraita lists cases where an animal is forewarned for damage caused by its normal movement, including damage by its body, hair, saddle, and Sumchos adds pebbles kicked by a pig.
The Gemara objects that the baraita's phrase 'היזיק' (damaged) is obvious.
The Gemara emends the baraita: the case is when the animal 'kicked and damaged' (התיז והיזיק), and Sumchos rules full damages for such indirect damage.
The Gemara explains that the baraita is missing a phrase: for pebbles following normal movement, the Tanna Kamma rules half-damages, and Sumchos says full damages.

items.text: Baraitot on damages caused by chickens
items.text_en: Baraitot on damages caused by chickens
items.desc_en: Two additional baraitot are taught regarding damages caused by chickens. The first discusses chickens that fly from place to place and break vessels with their wings (full damages) or with the wind of their wings (half damages), with Sumchos arguing for full damages. The second baraita discusses chickens that tread on dough or fruits and soil or peck them (full damages), or raise dust or pebbles (half damages), again with Sumchos arguing for full damages. A third baraita teaches that if a chicken's wing-flapping causes wind to break vessels, the payment is half damages, which is a stam (anonymous) ruling in accordance with the Rabbis.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that chickens flying from place to place and breaking vessels with their wings pay full damages, with the wind of their wings half damages, and Sumchos argues for full damages.
Another baraita teaches that chickens treading on dough or fruits and soiling or pecking them pay full damages, while raising dust or pebbles pays half damages, with Sumchos arguing for full damages.
A third baraita teaches that if a chicken's wing-flapping causes wind to break vessels, the payment is half damages, and the anonymous ruling follows the Rabbis.

items.text: Rava's analysis of Sumchos and the Rabbis on 'kocho k'gufo dami'
items.text_en: Rava's analysis of Sumchos and the Rabbis on 'kocho k'gufo dami'
items.desc_en: Rava analyzes the dispute between Sumchos and the Rabbis. Sumchos holds that 'kocho k'gufo dami' (his force is considered like his body), so he requires full damages. The Rabbis, however, are inconsistent: if they consider force like the body, they should require full damages; if not, they should require no damages at all. Rava then retracts and explains that the Rabbis' ruling of half damages for 'tsrorot' is a halakha l'Moshe mi'Sinai (a tradition from Sinai).

sub.desc_en: Rava questions the Rabbis' position: if they hold that force is like the body, they should require full damages; if not, they should require no damages at all.
Rava retracts and resolves that the Rabbis indeed hold force is like the body, but the half-damages for צרורות (pebbles) is a halakha l'Moshe mi'Sinai (tradition from Sinai).

items.text: Rava's principle regarding zav and damages
items.text_en: Rava's principle regarding zav and damages
items.desc_en: Rava states a general principle: anything that is impure in the context of a zav (a person with a discharge) is subject to full damages in torts, while anything pure in that context is subject to half damages. The Gemara questions whether Rava is merely teaching about 'tsrorot', and explains that he is actually teaching about a 'calf pulling a wagon' (eglah moshechet bakaron), which is a new case.

sub.desc_en: Rava states a general principle linking zav impurity categories to tort damages.
The Gemara questions whether Rava's statement merely teaches about 'tsrorot' (pebbles), implying it is already known.
The Gemara answers that Rava is actually teaching a novel case: a calf-pulled wagon (עֶגְלָה מוֹשֶׁכֶת בַּקָּרוֹן), which is not about pebbles but a new application of the principle.

items.text: Baraita supporting Rava's ruling on a calf pulling a wagon
items.text_en: Baraita supporting Rava's ruling on a calf pulling a wagon
items.desc_en: A baraita is taught that supports Rava's ruling: an animal is 'mu'ad' to break things in its normal course of walking, and this includes a calf pulling a wagon, for which the owner pays full damages.

sub.desc_en: A baraita supports Rava, listing a calf pulling a wagon as paying full damages.

items.text: Rava's query on indirect damage and the dispute about 'hidus'
items.text_en: Rava's query on indirect damage and the dispute about 'hidus'
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that chickens that peck at a bucket rope, causing it to break and the bucket to shatter, pay full damages. Rava then raises a query: if an animal steps on a vessel without breaking it, and the vessel rolls to another place and breaks, do we follow the initial act (which is the animal's body, so full damages) or the breaking (which is like 'tsrorot', so half damages)? The Gemara attempts to resolve this from Rabba's ruling about a thrown vessel, but concludes that Rabba's case is clear to him while Rava is uncertain. The Gemara then cites a dispute about 'hidus' (treading) and suggests it may be about this very question, but ultimately rejects this interpretation.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that chickens pecking at a bucket rope, causing it to break and the bucket to shatter, pay full damages.
Rava raises a query: if an animal steps on a vessel without breaking it, and the vessel rolls to another place and breaks, do we follow the initial act (full damages) or the breaking (half damages)?
The Gemara attempts to resolve Rava's query from Rabba's ruling about a thrown vessel, but concludes that Rabba's case is clear to him while Rava remains uncertain.
The Gemara cites a dispute about 'הידוס' (treading): one opinion says it is not מועד (forewarned), another says it is מועד.

The Gemara questions whether the dispute about 'הידוס' (treading) actually refers to 'הידוס והתיז' (treading and causing to fly), and suggests it may be about Rava's very question: whether we follow the initial act or the breaking.
The Gemara rejects this interpretation, concluding that the dispute about 'הידוס' does not resolve Rava's query.

items.text: Introduction of the dispute between Sumchus and the Rabbis
items.text_en: Introduction of the dispute between Sumchus and the Rabbis
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that the dispute about pebbles (צרורות) is the same as the dispute between Sumchus and the Rabbis.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces that the dispute about pebbles (צרורות) is the same as the dispute between Sumchus and the Rabbis.

items.text: Attempt to prove liability follows the initial act
items.text_en: Attempt to prove liability follows the initial act
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about chickens that broke a bucket, suggesting that liability follows the initial act (בתר מעיקרא אזלינן). It is rejected and reinterpreted as referring to the rope, and then as the view of Sumchus.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about chickens pecking at a bucket rope, causing the bucket to break, and they pay full damages, suggesting liability follows the initial act (בתר מעיקרא אזלינן).
The Gemara infers from the baraita that liability follows the initial act (בתר מעיקרא אזלינן).
The Gemara reinterprets the baraita as referring to the rope, not the bucket.
The Gemara objects that the rope is a 'שינוי' (abnormal act), which should only incur half damages, not full.
The Gemara objects that the baraita explicitly states the bucket broke, not just the rope.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita follows Sumchus, who holds that צרורות (indirect damage from an animal's force) incurs full damages.

items.text: Challenge from the second clause of the baraita
items.text_en: Challenge from the second clause of the baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the attribution to Sumchus from the second clause, which mentions half-damages, which Sumchus does not hold. It then considers a distinction between direct force and indirect force, and a question of Rav Ashi is resolved.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the baraita is attributed to Sumchus, the second clause mentions half-damages (חצי נזק), which Sumchus does not hold.
The Gemara proposes a distinction for Sumchus between direct force (כחו) and indirect force (כח כחו), and cites Rav Ashi's unresolved question on this matter.
The Gemara resolves that Rav Ashi's question is answered: indirect force (כח כחו) is not considered like direct force (כחו) for Sumchus.

items.text: Reversion to the Rabbis' view
items.text_en: Reversion to the Rabbis' view
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the baraita must be according to the Rabbis, proving that liability follows the initial act.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the baraita must be according to the Rabbis, proving that liability follows the initial act (בתר מעיקרא אזלינן).

items.text: Rav Beivai bar Abaye's explanation
items.text_en: Rav Beivai bar Abaye's explanation
items.desc_en: Rav Beivai bar Abaye explains that the case is where the pebbles continue moving from the animal's force.

sub.desc_en: Rav Beivai bar Abaye explains that the case involves pebbles that continue moving from the animal's own force, thus the damage is considered direct.

items.text: Rava's question about payment source
items.text_en: Rava's question about payment source
items.desc_en: Rava asks whether half-damages for pebbles are paid from the animal's body or from the owner's pocket.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks whether half-damages for pebbles (צרורות) are paid from the animal's body (מגופו) or from the owner's pocket (מעלייה).

items.text: Attempt to resolve Rava's question from a baraita
items.text_en: Attempt to resolve Rava's question from a baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about 'hidus' (trampling) and 'hitiz' (kicking pebbles), suggesting that the dispute about being 'mu'ad' relates to payment from the body or from the pocket. It is rejected and reinterpreted as the dispute between Sumchus and the Rabbis.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about 'hidus' (trampling) being not mu'ad and 'yesh omrim' saying it is mu'ad, to resolve Rava's question.
The Gemara suggests that the dispute in the baraita is about whether payment is from the body (migufo) or from the pocket (me'aliyah), corresponding to Rava's question.
The Gemara rejects this interpretation and explains that the baraita actually reflects the dispute between Sumchus and the Rabbis regarding payment for pebbles (tzrorot).

items.text: Further attempt from a baraita about a dog and a loaf
items.text_en: Further attempt from a baraita about a dog and a loaf
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about a dog that took a coal and set fire to a stack, suggesting that half-damages for pebbles are paid from the body. This is analyzed and attributed to Rabbi Elazar, who follows Sumchus and Rabbi Yehuda.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about a dog taking a coal to a stack, and infers that half-damages for pebbles are paid from the body (מגופו).

The Gemara objects: according to Rabbi Elazar, who holds that a change in the animal's normal behavior (שינוי) in the plaintiff's domain pays full damages, how can the baraita mention full damages from the body?

The Gemara explains that the case involves a change (שינוי) with the coal, and Rabbi Elazar follows Rabbi Tarfon, who holds that a change in the animal's normal behavior (קרן) in the plaintiff's domain pays full damages.

The Gemara rejects the previous explanation and concludes that Rabbi Elazar actually follows Sumchus (who says pebbles pay full damages) and Rabbi Yehuda (who holds that the 'tam' aspect remains in place), so the baraita's 'from the body' refers to the tam aspect.

items.text: Rav Sama's question to Ravina
items.text_en: Rav Sama's question to Ravina
items.desc_en: Rav Sama bar Rav Ashi questions Ravina about Rabbi Yehuda's position, noting that he only spoke about a tam that becomes mu'ad, not a mu'ad from the start.

sub.text: Rav Sama bar Rav Ashi's question to Ravina
sub.text_en: Rav Sama bar Rav Ashi's question to Ravina
sub.desc_en: Rav Sama bar Rav Ashi questions Ravina about Rabbi Yehuda's position, noting that he only spoke about a tam that becomes mu'ad, not a mu'ad from the start.

items.text: Rava's question and the dispute between Rabbi Elazar and the Rabbis
items.text_en: Rava's question and the dispute between Rabbi Elazar and the Rabbis
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks who holds that there is forewarning for pebbles. It explains that Rabbi Elazar's ruling of full damages applies only when the animal is forewarned, and the dispute is about whether there is forewarning for pebbles.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who holds that there is forewarning for pebbles.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Elazar's ruling of full damages applies only when the animal is forewarned, and the dispute is about whether there is forewarning for pebbles.

items.text: Rava's clarification of his question
items.text_en: Rava's clarification of his question
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rava's question about forewarning for pebbles is already answered by the previous dispute. Rava responds that his question is according to the Rabbis who disagree with Sumchus, but here both sides follow Sumchus that pebbles require full damages.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rava's question about forewarning for pebbles is already answered by the previous dispute between Rabbi Elazar and the Rabbis.
Rava responds that his question is according to the Rabbis who disagree with Sumchus, but here both sides follow Sumchus that pebbles require full damages.

items.text: Reason for the Rabbis' half-damages
items.text_en: Reason for the Rabbis' half-damages
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Rabbis rule half-damages because the animal is not forewarned, and the dispute is between Rabbi Tarfon and the Rabbis.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Rabbis rule half-damages because the animal is not forewarned (שונה ולא אייעד).
The Gemara resolves that the dispute between Rabbi Tarfon and the Rabbis underlies the disagreement about whether the animal pays full or half damages.

items.text: Objection from Rabbi Tarfon's ruling and the 'dayo' principle
items.text_en: Objection from Rabbi Tarfon's ruling and the 'dayo' principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rabbi Tarfon only rules full damages for the body, not for pebbles. It is answered that Rabbi Tarfon derives it from a kal vachomer from 'keren' in the public domain, and he only rejects 'dayo' when the kal vachomer is refutable.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rabbi Tarfon's ruling of full damages applies only to the body of the animal, not to pebbles (צרורות).
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Tarfon derives the law for pebbles from a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument) from קרן (goring) in the public domain.
The Gemara objects that the principle of דיו (it is sufficient for the conclusion derived from a kal vachomer to be like the source) would limit the damages to half, not full.
The Gemara further objects that Rabbi Tarfon does not accept the principle of דיו (dayo) at all.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Tarfon rejects דיו only when the קל וחומר (kal vachomer) is refutable, but here it is not refutable, so he accepts it.

items.text: Rava's question: forewarning for pebbles
items.text_en: Rava's question: forewarning for pebbles
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents Rava's question: is there forewarning for pebbles? Do we compare it to 'keren' or is it a derivative of 'regel'?

sub.desc_en: Rava asks whether there is forewarning (העדאה) for pebbles (צרורות), comparing it to 'keren' or considering it a derivative of 'regel'.

items.text: First attempted proof from 'hidus'
items.text_en: First attempted proof from 'hidus'
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about 'hidus' (trampling) and 'hitiz' (kicking) where some say it is forewarned. It suggests this refers to three times, but is rejected as referring to one time, with the dispute being between Sumchus and the Rabbis.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about 'hidus' (trampling) and 'hitiz' (kicking) where some say it is forewarned, to test Rava's question about warning for pebbles.
The Gemara suggests that the dispute in the baraita refers to three occurrences, with one opinion holding that there is warning and the other that there is no warning.
The Gemara rejects this, explaining that the baraita refers to a single occurrence, and the dispute is actually between Sumchus and the Rabbis regarding liability for pebbles.

items.text: Second attempted proof from animal droppings
items.text_en: Second attempted proof from animal droppings
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a dispute between Rav Yehuda and Rabbi Elazar about an animal that dropped dung into dough. It suggests this refers to three times, but is rejected as one time, with the dispute being between Sumchus and the Rabbis. The Gemara explains why they didn't just state their ruling as halakha.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes a proof from a dispute between Rav Yehuda and Rabbi Elazar about an animal that dropped dung into dough, suggesting it involves the question of whether there is העדאה (forewarning) for pebbles.

The Gemara rejects the proof, explaining that the dispute is about a single occurrence and reflects the disagreement between Sumchus and the Rabbis, noting that the case is unusual because the animal was constipated.

The Gemara explains why Rav Yehuda and Rabbi Elazar did not simply state their ruling as הלכה (binding law): they needed to teach about droppings specifically, lest one think they are considered like the animal's body and require full damages.

items.text: Third attempted proof from a rooster and horse
items.text_en: Third attempted proof from a rooster and horse
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about a rooster that broke glass and a horse that neighed and broke vessels, with different damage payments. It suggests this refers to three times, implying a dispute about forewarning.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita of Rami bar Yechezkel about a rooster breaking glass and a horse neighing and breaking vessels, with different damage payments, to test whether forewarning applies to pebbles.
The Gemara asks whether the baraita refers to three occurrences, implying a dispute about the existence of forewarning (העדאה) for pebbles.

items.text: Dispute over ha'adah for tzrorot
items.text_en: Dispute over ha'adah for tzrorot
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the earlier dispute between Rav and Shmuel is not about ha'adah but about the opinion of Sumkhos and the Rabbis regarding tzrorot, which is a case of shinui (change) because the pebbles contain seeds.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the dispute between Rav and Shmuel is about the principle of ha'adah (propulsion) for tzrorot (pebbles).
The Gemara answers that the dispute is actually about the opinion of Sumkhos and the Rabbis regarding tzrorot, which is a case of shinui (change) because the pebbles contain seeds.

items.text: Rav Ashi's question on shinui for tzrorot
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's question on shinui for tzrorot
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi asks whether there is a shinui (change) for tzrorot regarding quarter-damage. The Gemara suggests resolving it from Rava's question about ha'adah for tzrorot, but concludes that Rava's question was conditional, leaving it unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi asks whether there is a shinui (change) for tzrorot regarding quarter-damage.
The Gemara suggests resolving Rav Ashi's question from Rava's question about ha'adah for tzrorot, implying there is no shinui.
The Gemara rejects the resolution, noting that Rava's question was conditional, leaving the matter unresolved (teiku).

items.text: Rav Ashi's question on ko'ach ko'cho for Sumkhos
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's question on ko'ach ko'cho for Sumkhos
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi asks whether indirect force (ko'ach ko'cho) is considered like direct force (ko'cho) according to Sumkhos, or whether Sumkhos did not learn the halakhah at all. The question remains unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi asks whether, according to Sumkhos, indirect force (ko'ach ko'cho) is considered like direct force (ko'cho) or not.

sub.text: Gemara's elaboration of Rav Ashi's question
sub.text_en: Gemara's elaboration of Rav Ashi's question
sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that Rav Ashi's question is whether Sumkhos learned the halakhah and applies it to ko'ach ko'cho, or whether he did not learn the halakhah at all.
The question remains unresolved (teiku).

items.text: Interpretation of the Mishnah about kicking and pebbles
items.text_en: Interpretation of the Mishnah about kicking and pebbles
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents an ambiguity in the Mishnah: whether it refers to damage from kicking itself or from pebbles dislodged by kicking, and whether the ruling of half-damage follows the Rabbis or Sumkhos.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the Mishnah's case of a kicking animal or pebbles dislodged, and raises an ambiguity about how to interpret the Mishnah's wording.

The Gemara poses two possible interpretations: either the Mishnah refers to damage from kicking itself or from pebbles in their normal course (Rabbis), or it refers to damage from kicking or from pebbles due to kicking (Sumkhos).

items.text: Proof from the Mishnah's seifa against Sumkhos
items.text_en: Proof from the Mishnah's seifa against Sumkhos
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove from the seifa (about a vessel broken by a shard) that the Mishnah cannot follow Sumkhos, since Sumkhos would not impose half-damage. Rav Ashi's question about ko'ach ko'cho is then resolved: it is not like direct force.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the seifa of the Mishnah about a hen that tramples a vessel and a shard breaks another, to prove that the Mishnah does not follow Sumkhos.
The Gemara raises a possible counterargument: Sumkhos might distinguish between direct force (כֹּחוֹ) and indirect force (כֹּחַ כֹּחוֹ), so the seifa could still align with Sumkhos.
The Gemara resolves Rav Ashi's question about Sumkhos's view on indirect force (כֹּחַ כֹּחוֹ) by concluding from the seifa that it is not considered like direct force.

items.text: Rav Ashi's interpretation according to the Rabbis
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's interpretation according to the Rabbis
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that the Mishnah follows the Rabbis, and his question is whether the Mishnah's case is about normal pebbles (half-damage) or pebbles from kicking (quarter-damage if there is shinui), leaving it unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that the Mishnah follows the Rabbis, and his question is whether the case of pebbles from kicking (מחמת ביעוט) is subject to a shinui (change) reducing liability to quarter-damage.
Rav Ashi raises the alternative possibility that the Mishnah's case is about normal pebbles (half-damage) and pebbles from kicking (also half-damage), meaning there is no shinui (change) for pebbles.
The Gemara leaves the question unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Rabbi Abba bar Memel's question about unavoidable pebbles
items.text_en: Rabbi Abba bar Memel's question about unavoidable pebbles
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba bar Memel asks Rabbi Ami (or Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba) about an animal walking where pebbles are unavoidable: is it considered normal gait (exempt) or due to kicking (liable)? The question remains unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba bar Memel asks whether an animal walking where pebbles are unavoidable is considered normal gait (exempt) or due to kicking (liable), and the question remains unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Rabbi Yirmeya's question about kicking in public domain
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's question about kicking in public domain
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Zeira whether kicking in the public domain is classified as keren (liable) or a toladah of regel (exempt). Rabbi Zeira rules it is a toladah of regel. A further question about lifting in public and damage in private leads to a retraction.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Zeira whether an animal that kicks in the public domain and damages is classified as קרן (liable for half damages) or a תולדה דרגל (exempt in the public domain).
Rabbi Zeira rules that the case is a תולדה דרגל (derivative of regel), thus the animal is exempt in the public domain.
Rabbi Yirmeya asks about a case where the animal kicks in the public domain but the damage occurs in the private domain.
Rabbi Zeira responds with a rhetorical question: since the lifting (עקירה) occurred in the public domain but the placement (הנחה) in the private domain, the animal should be liable.
The Gemara objects by citing a baraita that states the animal is liable whether the kicking occurs in the private or public domain, implying that Rabbi Zeira's distinction is contradicted.
Rabbi Zeira retracts his previous statement, admitting his error.

items.text: Further objection from the seifa about public domain
items.text_en: Further objection from the seifa about public domain
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings another objection from the seifa about a vessel broken by a shard, where the ruling differs in public domain. The Gemara again explains it as lifting in public and damage in private, leading to another retraction, ending with surprise.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects by citing a baraita about a chicken stepping on a vessel in public domain, where the ruling differs, challenging Rabbi Zeira's position.
Rabbi Zeira answers that the case involves lifting in public domain and damage in private domain, but then retracts his earlier position.
The Gemara expresses surprise at Rabbi Zeira's retraction.

items.text: Clarification of Rabbi Yochanan's statement on half-damage
items.text_en: Clarification of Rabbi Yochanan's statement on half-damage
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Yochanan's statement that half-damage is not divided between public and private domains, suggesting it refers to a case where the animal kicked in the public domain and damaged in the private domain. The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yochanan's statement applies to a horn (קרן) case.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Yochanan's statement that half-damage is not divided between public and private domains, interpreting it as referring to a case where the animal kicked in the public domain and damaged in the public domain.
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Yochanan's statement refers to a case where the animal kicked in the public domain but damaged in the private domain.
The Gemara objects that in a private domain there is no 'standing' (עקירה) but there is 'placement' (הנחה), which would make half-damage applicable, contradicting Rabbi Yochanan.
The Gemara resolves that the statement was retracted or that Rabbi Yochanan actually applied it to a horn (קרן) case, not a case of רגל (foot).

items.text: Discussion on an animal kicking with its tail
items.text_en: Discussion on an animal kicking with its tail
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda Nesia and Rabbi Oshaya debate whether an animal that kicks with its tail is liable for full or half damage. The Gemara distinguishes between normal behavior (kicking with the tail is normal) and abnormal behavior (kicking with the horn is not), and questions why the case is even in doubt, concluding that the doubt concerns excessive kicking.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda Nesia and Rabbi Oshaya were sitting in Rabbi Yehuda's court and a question emerged between them: if an animal kicked with its tail, what is the halacha?
Rabbi Oshaya objects: if tail-kicking is considered normal, then by analogy, horn-goring should also be considered normal, which is absurd.
The Gemara rejects the analogy: horn-goring is not normal behavior, but tail-kicking is normal.
The Gemara asks: since tail-kicking is normal, why was there any doubt about the halacha?
The Gemara resolves: the doubt was about excessive kicking (beyond normal tail-swishing), which is not normal.

items.text: Query about an animal kicking with its foreleg
items.text_en: Query about an animal kicking with its foreleg
items.desc_en: Rav Eina asks whether an animal that kicks with its foreleg is liable for full or half damage. The Gemara considers whether the foreleg is like a horn (intent to damage) or not, and leaves the question unresolved (תיקו).

sub.desc_en: Rav Eina asks whether an animal that kicks with its foreleg is liable for full or half damage, comparing it to goring with a horn (קרן) which has intent to damage, and the Gemara leaves the question unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Rav Huna's ruling on a rooster tied to a stick
items.text_en: Rav Huna's ruling on a rooster tied to a stick
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that roosters are forewarned to walk normally and break things. Rav Huna distinguishes between a stick that became tied on its own (owner of the stick is exempt) and one tied by a person (owner is liable). The Gemara clarifies that the Mishnah deals with a case where the rooster dragged the stick, and Rav Huna's statement applies to an ownerless stick.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that roosters are forewarned to walk normally and break things.
Rav Huna distinguishes: the Mishnah's exemption applies only when the stick became tied on its own, but if a person tied it, the owner is liable.

The Gemara asks: if the stick was tied on its own, who is liable? It rejects the owner of the stick, because if he hid it he is an אונס (forced circumstance), and if he did not hide it he is a פושע (negligent).
The Gemara asks: is the rooster's owner liable? It objects that the verse 'כי יפתח איש בור' (when a man opens a pit) excludes an animal from full damage, and also from half damage.
The Gemara resolves: the Mishnah deals with a case where the rooster dragged the stick, and Rav Huna's statement was said about an ownerless stick.

items.text: Reason for liability in the case of a tied stick
items.text_en: Reason for liability in the case of a tied stick
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Manoach explains that the person who tied the stick is liable because it is considered his pit (בור) that rolls around by the feet of people and animals.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the person who tied the stick is liable.
Rav Huna bar Manoach answers that it is considered his בור (pit) that rolls around by the feet of people and animals.

items.text: Mishnah: The tooth (שן) is forewarned
items.text_en: Mishnah: The tooth (שן) is forewarned
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that an animal is forewarned to eat what is suitable for it, paying full damage in the plaintiff's domain and half damage in the public domain. If it benefits, it pays only the benefit. Examples are given of eating from different locations.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by defining that the tooth (שן) is forewarned to eat what is suitable, and states the general rule of liability.

sub.text: Mishnah's distinction: public vs. private domain
sub.text_en: Mishnah's distinction: public vs. private domain
sub.desc_en: The Mishnah clarifies that the full damage applies in the plaintiff's domain, but in the public domain the owner is exempt.
The Mishnah gives examples: if the animal benefits from eating in the public domain or at the storefront, it pays only the benefit; if it enters the domain entirely, it pays full damage.

items.text: Gemara: Full damage for eating suitable food
items.text_en: Gemara: Full damage for eating suitable food
items.desc_en: The Gemara elaborates on the Mishnah, stating that an animal that enters the plaintiff's domain and eats suitable food pays full damage. Rav Pappa adds that even eating unusual food under duress is considered eating, so a cat eating dates or a donkey eating fish pays full damage.

sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches that an animal entering the plaintiff's domain and eating suitable food pays full damage, and similarly a wild animal that tears and eats meat pays full damage.
The baraita lists specific cases: a cow eating barley, a donkey eating vetch, a dog licking oil, and a pig eating meat — all pay full damage.
Rav Pappa rules that since eating unusual food under duress is still considered eating, a cat eating dates or a donkey eating fish pays full damage.

items.text: Case of a donkey eating bread and breaking a basket
items.text_en: Case of a donkey eating bread and breaking a basket
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda ruled that a donkey that ate bread and broke a basket pays full damage for the bread and half damage for the basket. The Gemara questions why the basket is not also full damage, since eating bread normally involves breaking the basket. The Gemara resolves that the donkey ate first and then broke the basket, and discusses whether bread is normal food for an animal, concluding with alternative explanations involving a wild animal or a goat.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda ruled that a donkey which ate bread and broke a basket pays full damage for the bread and half damage for the basket.
The Gemara questions why the basket is not also full damage, since eating bread normally involves breaking the basket.
The Gemara resolves that the donkey ate first and then broke the basket, so the breaking was not a normal consequence of eating.
The Gemara questions whether bread is normal food for a donkey, citing a baraita where an animal that ate bread pays only half damage.
The Gemara answers that the baraita refers to a wild animal (חיה), not a domesticated animal, so bread is normal for a donkey.
The Gemara objects that meat is normal food for a wild animal, so the baraita's mention of meat would still imply full damage.
The Gemara answers that the meat in the baraita was roasted, which is not normal for a wild animal, so the half-damage ruling stands.
The Gemara offers an alternative: the baraita refers to a goat (טביא), which does not normally eat bread or meat, so half damage applies.
The Gemara concludes that the baraita refers to a domesticated animal eating bread that was soaked in a dish (פתורא), which is not normal, so half damage applies.

items.text: Case of the goat that climbed and ate turnips
items.text_en: Case of the goat that climbed and ate turnips
items.desc_en: Rava rules that a goat which climbed and ate turnips from a barrel, breaking it, must pay full damages for both, because its nature includes climbing.

sub.desc_en: Presents the case: a goat saw turnips on a barrel opening, climbed, ate the turnips, and broke the barrel.
Rava rules that the goat pays full damages for both the turnips and the barrel, because climbing is part of its nature.

items.text: Ilfa's statement and the Gemara's support from Rava
items.text_en: Ilfa's statement and the Gemara's support from Rava
items.desc_en: Ilfa says an animal in the public domain that stretches its neck and eats from atop a fellow animal is liable, as the fellow animal is like the plaintiff's courtyard. The Gemara supports this with a case of a basket on one's back, but Rava qualifies it as a case where the animal jumps.

sub.desc_en: Ilfa states that an animal in the public domain that stretches its neck and eats from atop a fellow animal is liable, because the fellow animal is like the plaintiff's courtyard.
The Gemara suggests supporting Ilfa from a baraita about a basket on one's back, where the animal is liable.
Rava qualifies that the baraita applies only when the animal jumps, and Ilfa's case is likewise limited to a jumping animal.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's query about rolling produce
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's query about rolling produce
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira asks about a case where produce rolls from private to public domain. The Gemara attempts to resolve it from a baraita of Rabbi Chiya about a pile partly inside and outside, but concludes it refers to a wick of a basket.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira asks about the liability for produce that rolls from private to public domain.

sub.text: Gemara's attempt to resolve from a baraita
sub.text_en: Gemara's attempt to resolve from a baraita
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita of Rabbi Chiya about a pile partly inside and outside, suggesting it supports Rabbi Zeira's rolling case.
The Gemara rejects the proof, explaining that the baraita distinguishes between eating inside and outside, not rolling.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Chiya's baraita refers to a wick of a basket, not rolling produce.

items.text: Dispute about liability for eating clothing vs. produce
items.text_en: Dispute about liability for eating clothing vs. produce
items.desc_en: The Mishnah's case of an animal eating clothing or vessels is debated: Rav and Resh Lakish say it is exempt for all items, while Shmuel and Rabbi Yochanan say the exemption is only for produce, but for clothing it is liable. The Gemara explains Rabbi Yochanan's position does not contradict Resh Lakish's principle about two cows.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's case: an animal ate clothing or vessels.
The Gemara asks: to which part of the Mishnah does this refer?
Rav says the exemption applies to all items (clothing and produce), because the principle is: one who changes and another changes upon it is exempt.
Shmuel says the exemption was only stated for produce and vegetables, but for clothing and vessels one is liable.
Resh Lakish agrees with Rav that the exemption applies to all items, and the Gemara notes this aligns with his principle about two cows in the public domain.
Rabbi Yochanan agrees with Shmuel that the exemption is only for produce and vegetables, but for clothing and vessels one is liable.
