The Gemara objects: does Rabbi Yochanan disagree with Resh Lakish even regarding the two cows case?

The Gemara resolves: Rabbi Yochanan does accept Resh Lakish's principle; the difference is that people sometimes place cloaks and inflate them (making them unusual), but an animal's nature is not to eat clothing.

items.text: Dispute about payment when the animal benefits
items.text_en: Dispute about payment when the animal benefits
items.desc_en: Rabba and Rava dispute the measure of payment when the animal benefits: Rabba says the value of straw, Rava says the market price of barley. Both are supported by baraitot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: How much does the animal pay when it benefits from the food?
Rabba rules that the animal pays the value of straw (דְּמֵי עָמִיר).
Rava rules that the animal pays the market price of barley at a discount (דְּמֵי שְׂעוֹרִים בְּזוֹל).
A baraita supports Rabba: Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai says the animal pays only the value of straw (דְּמֵי עָמִיר).
A baraita supports Rava: the animal pays according to the benefit, assessed by what a person would pay to feed his animal suitable food, and if it ate harmful food it is exempt.

items.text: Question about a squatter in a courtyard
items.text_en: Question about a squatter in a courtyard
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda asks Rami bar Chama whether a squatter in another's courtyard must pay rent. The Gemara clarifies the scenario: a courtyard not for rent and a person who does not usually rent, or a courtyard for rent and a person who does rent, and then the intermediate case.

sub.text: Rav Chisda to Rami bar Chama
sub.text_en: Rav Chisda to Rami bar Chama
sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda asks Rami bar Chama whether a squatter in another's courtyard must pay rent.
The Gemara clarifies the two clear cases: a courtyard not for rent with a person who does not rent, and a courtyard for rent with a person who rents, where the answer is obvious.
The Gemara presents the intermediate case: a courtyard not for rent but a person who usually rents, and asks whether the squatter can say 'what did I take from you?' or the owner can demand payment.

items.text: Rava's observation on the dispute
items.text_en: Rava's observation on the dispute
items.desc_en: Rava comments on the earlier exchange between Rav Yehuda and Shmuel, noting that Shmuel accepted Rav Yehuda's ruling even though it did not match the Mishnah. Rava categorizes the case as 'zeh nehene ve-zeh haser' (one benefits and the other loses), not 'zeh nehene ve-zeh lo haser'.

sub.desc_en: Rava marvels at how Shmuel accepted Rav Yehuda's ruling even though it contradicted the Mishnah.
Rava categorizes the case as "zeh nehene ve-zeh haser" (one benefits and the other loses), not "zeh nehene ve-zeh lo haser" (one benefits and the other does not lose).

items.text: הסבר דעת רמי בר חמא
items.text_en: Rami bar Hama's challenge
items.desc_en: Rami bar Hama challenges the assumption that produce in the public domain is ownerless, questioning the application of the principle.
items.desc: הגמרא מסבירה שרמי בר חמא סובר שסתם פירות ברשות הרבים הם הפקר, ולכן במקרה של המשנה אין חסרון למזיק, מה שהופך את המקרה לדומה לשאלת הדיור.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Hama questions whether produce in the public domain is considered ownerless (הפקר), challenging the assumption that one who benefits without causing loss is exempt.

items.text: First attempted proof from the Mishnah of fencing
items.text_en: First attempted proof from the Mishnah of fencing
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove that 'zeh nehene ve-zeh lo haser' is liable from a Mishnah about fencing three sides of a field. The proof is rejected because the owner can claim the fencer caused extra enclosure.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah in which one who fences three sides of a neighbor's field is exempt, implying that fencing the fourth side obligates him, suggesting that 'zeh nehene ve-zeh lo haser' (one benefits and the other loses nothing) is liable.

The Gemara rejects the proof because the fencer caused an additional enclosure (הקפא יתירא) for the neighbor, so the case is 'zeh nehene ve-zeh haser' (one benefits and the other loses), not 'zeh nehene ve-zeh lo haser'.

items.text: Second attempted proof from Rabbi Yosei's statement
items.text_en: Second attempted proof from Rabbi Yosei's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara tries to prove that 'zeh nehene ve-zeh lo haser' is exempt from Rabbi Yosei's ruling about the one who fences the fourth side. The proof is rejected because the owner can say he was satisfied with minimal fencing.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Yosei's statement that if the enclosed party (ניקף) fences the fourth side, the encircler (מקיף) is exempt, attempting to prove that 'zeh nehene ve-zeh lo haser' is exempt.
The Gemara rejects the proof because the encircler can claim that the enclosed party was satisfied with minimal fencing (נטירא בר זוזא), so the case is not one of 'zeh nehene ve-zeh lo haser'.

items.text: Third attempted proof from the house and upper story
items.text_en: Third attempted proof from the house and upper story
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove exemption from the case of a collapsed house and upper story, where the upper story owner builds and lives there but only recovers expenses, not rent. The proof is rejected because the house is subservient to the upper story.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove exemption from the case of a collapsed house and upper story, where the upper story owner builds and lives there but only recovers expenses, not rent.
The Gemara rejects the proof because the house is subservient to the upper story, so the case is not analogous to the principle of 'one who benefits and the other does not lose'.

items.text: Fourth attempted proof from Rabbi Yehuda's ruling
items.text_en: Fourth attempted proof from Rabbi Yehuda's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara tries to prove liability from Rabbi Yehuda's statement that one who lives in another's courtyard without permission must pay rent. The proof is rejected because of the wear and tear on the walls.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings Rabbi Yehuda's ruling that a resident in another's courtyard without permission must pay rent, attempting to prove the principle of 'this one benefits and the other does not lose' (זה נהנה וזה לא חסר) is liable.
The Gemara rejects the proof, distinguishing that Rabbi Yehuda's case involves wear and tear (שחרוּריתא דאשייתא) to the walls, so the owner experiences a loss.

items.text: שליחת השאלה לרבי אמי ורבי חייא בר אבא
items.text_en: The inquiry to Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba
items.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Ami sent a question about the case, and Rabbi Ami responded that there is no loss. Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba initially agreed but later retracted, saying the question was trivial.
items.desc: שולחים את השאלה לרבי אמי, שאומר שאין לחייב כי אין חסרון. שולחים שוב לרבי חייא בר אבא, שמתוסכל שלא מצא תשובה.

sub.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Ami sends a question: what did the resident do to the owner, what loss or damage did he cause?
Rabbi Ami responds that the resident did nothing to the owner, causing no loss or damage.
Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba initially agrees with the response, settling on the matter.
Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba retracts, calling the question trivial and implying the answer was obvious.

items.text: The dispute between Rav Kahana and Rav Avahu
items.text_en: The dispute between Rav Kahana and Rav Avahu
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana and Rav Avahu report conflicting versions of Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on whether one must pay rent for living in another's courtyard without permission. Rav Pappa explains that Rav Avahu's version was inferred from a ruling about consecrated property. The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Yochanan's silence did not indicate agreement, following Rabba's principle that consecrated property without knowledge is not misused.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports a dispute: Rav Kahana says Rabbi Yochanan ruled one does not need to pay rent for living in another's courtyard without permission, while Rav Avahu says Rabbi Yochanan ruled one must pay.
Rav Pappa explains that Rav Avahu's version was not stated explicitly but inferred from a general principle.

The Gemara cites a Mishnah about misuse of consecrated property: one who takes a stone or beam from consecrated property has not misused it, but if he builds it into his house, he does not misuse until he dwells under it worth a perutah.
Shmuel qualifies that the Mishnah's ruling applies only when the beam was placed over an opening (so the dweller benefits from the consecrated item).

sub.text: Rav Avahu's inference before Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rav Avahu's inference before Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rav Avahu sat before Rabbi Yochanan and stated in Shmuel's name that this implies one who lives in another's courtyard without permission must pay rent, and Rabbi Yochanan was silent.

sub.text: Gemara's rejection of Rav Avahu's inference
sub.text_en: Gemara's rejection of Rav Avahu's inference
sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects Rav Avahu's assumption that Rabbi Yochanan's silence indicated agreement, explaining that Rabbi Yochanan simply did not pay attention to him.
The Gemara concludes with Rabba's principle that consecrated property used without knowledge does not constitute misuse, supporting the view that one need not pay rent.

items.text: השוואה לדין הקדש
items.text_en: Transition from previous daf
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the previous discussion about a cow eating in a public domain, stating that the cow is like a common person in terms of knowledge.
items.desc: הגמרא דוחה את ההוכחה מדין הקדש, שכן בהקדש שייך מעילה גם בלא ידיעת הבעלים, מה שאין כן בחצר חבירו.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the cow is like a common person in terms of knowledge, wrapping up the previous discussion.
sub.desc: הגמרא דוחה את ההוכחה מדין הקדש, שכן בהקדש שייך מעילה גם בלא ידיעת הבעלים, מה שאין כן בחצר חבירו.

items.text: The question of the unauthorized dweller
items.text_en: The question of the unauthorized dweller
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba bar Zavda sends a query to Marei bar Mar about whether an unauthorized dweller must pay rent. Rav Huna dies before answering, but his son Rabbah bar Rav Huna reports Rav's ruling: the dweller need not pay, but one who rents a house from Reuven must pay Shimon if the house is found to belong to Shimon. The Gemara resolves an apparent contradiction by distinguishing between a house that stands for rent and one that does not.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba bar Zavda sends a query to Marei bar Mar asking whether an unauthorized dweller must pay rent, but Rav Huna dies before answering.
Rabbah bar Rav Huna reports in the name of Rav that an unauthorized dweller need not pay rent, but one who rents from Reuven must pay Shimon if the house is found to belong to Shimon.
The Gemara objects that the two rulings appear contradictory, and resolves by distinguishing between a house that stands for rent and one that does not.

A parallel tradition from Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Avin in the name of Rav or Rav Huna states the same distinction: an unauthorized dweller need not pay rent, but one who rents from city residents must pay the owners if they are discovered.
The Gemara again notes the apparent contradiction and resolves it by the same distinction between a house that stands for rent and one that does not.

items.text: Rav's reason and a dispute about benefit
items.text_en: Rav's reason and a dispute about benefit
items.desc_en: Rav Savora quotes Rav Huna citing Rav that the dweller need not pay because of the verse 'and desolation shall be broken at the gate' (i.e., an empty house is beneficial to the owner). Mar bar Rav Ashi and Rav Yosef offer different interpretations of the benefit. The Gemara identifies a practical difference between them: whether the dweller uses the house for wood and straw.

sub.text: Rav Savora citing Rav Huna citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Savora citing Rav Huna citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Savora quotes Rav Huna citing Rav that one who resides in another's courtyard without knowledge need not pay rent, based on the verse 'וּשְׁאִיָּה יוּכַּת שַׁעַר' (and desolation shall be broken at the gate).
Mar bar Rav Ashi adds that he personally saw such a ruin and it 'gores like an ox,' emphasizing the benefit of occupation.
Rav Yosef states a similar idea: a lived-in house is settled and safeguarded, while an empty one is not.
The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the statements of Rav and Rav Yosef.
The Gemara answers that the difference lies in a case where the dweller uses the house for storing wood and straw.

items.text: מעשה באפדנא על קילקלתא של יתומים
items.text_en: A case of building on orphans' land
items.desc_en: A man built a palace on a garbage dump belonging to orphans. Rav Nachman seized the palace from him, seemingly implying that an unauthorized dweller must pay rent. The Gemara explains that the case is different because the orphans had previously received rent from tenants, and the builder refused to appease them.
items.desc: סיפור על אדם שבנה ארמון על קרקע של יתומים, ורב נחמן גבה ממנו את הארמון, לא משום דין הדר בחצר חבירו אלא משום שהקרקע הייתה מושכרת לאחרים והפסיד להם.

sub.text_en: Gemara's question about Rav Nachman's ruling
sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts a case where a man built a mansion on orphans' land, and Rav Nachman seized it, raising the question of whether Rav Nachman holds that a dweller must pay rent.
sub.desc: סיפור על אדם שבנה ארמון על מגרש של יתומים, ורב נחמן החרים את הארמון ממנו.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that originally, squatters (קַרְמְנָאֵי) lived there and paid the orphans a small amount; the man refused to appease them, so Rav Nachman seized the mansion as a penalty.
sub.desc: סיפור על אדם שבנה ארמון על מגרש של יתומים, ורב נחמן החרים את הארמון ממנו.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the case is different because the orphans had previously received rent from tenants, and the builder refused to appease them, so Rav Nachman seized the palace as a penalty.
sub.desc: סיפור על אדם שבנה ארמון על מגרש של יתומים, ורב נחמן החרים את הארמון ממנו.

items.text: Dispute about a cow eating in a public domain
items.text_en: Dispute about a cow eating in a public domain
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a cow pays for what it benefited. Rav says this applies only to a cow that is walking (מחזרת), while Shmuel says even a walking cow is exempt. The Gemara explains that for Shmuel, liability only applies if the cow left the public domain and stood at its side. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak raises an objection from the Mishnah, and resolves it by saying the cow was standing at a corner.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah is cited, stating that a cow pays for what it benefited.
Rav limits the Mishnah's liability to a cow that is walking (מחזרת) in the public domain.
Shmuel argues that even a walking cow is exempt from liability.
The Gemara asks how, according to Shmuel, a cow could ever be liable for eating in the public domain.
The Gemara explains that liability arises only if the cow left the public domain and stood at its side.
An alternative version of the dispute is presented, where Rav and Shmuel argue about a walking cow in the context of paying for damage, and the same resolution is given.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak objects from the Mishnah's phrase 'from the entrance of the store', arguing that it implies a walking cow pays only for benefit, not for damage.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves his own objection by explaining that the cow was standing at a corner (קרן זווית), which is like the side of the public domain.

items.text: Alternative version of the dispute
items.text_en: Alternative version of the dispute
items.desc_en: Some say that all agree a walking cow is liable; the dispute is about a cow that extends its head into the public domain. Rav says it is exempt, Shmuel says it is liable. The Gemara suggests this dispute reflects a deeper disagreement about a pit in one's own domain, but Rav rejects this interpretation.

sub.desc_en: Presents an alternative version of the dispute: all agree a walking cow is liable, and the dispute is about a cow that extends its head into the public domain.
Cites the explicit statements of Rav and Shmuel: Rav exempts the cow that extends its head, Shmuel holds it liable.
Suggests that the dispute reflects a deeper disagreement about a pit in one's own domain (בור ברשותו).
Rav rejects the proposed connection, asserting that his position can be explained differently.

items.text: Rav and Shmuel dispute liability for a pit in one's own property
items.text_en: Rav and Shmuel dispute liability for a pit in one's own property
items.desc_en: Rav holds that a pit in one's own property is exempt, but here the owner brought the animal to the public domain. Shmuel argues that a pit in one's own property is liable, because the animal's owner should have seen the fruits.

sub.desc_en: Rav states that generally a pit in one's own property is exempt, but here the owner is liable because he brought the fruits to the public domain, causing the animal to fall.
Shmuel argues that a pit in one's own property is always liable, because the animal's owner should have seen the fruits and avoided the pit.

items.text: Attempt to resolve via Tannaic dispute about a returning animal
items.text_en: Attempt to resolve via Tannaic dispute about a returning animal
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the dispute between Rav and Shmuel corresponds to a Tannaic dispute about an animal that eats from the side of a public area. Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda say it pays what it benefited, while Rabbi Yosei says it pays what it damaged. The Gemara clarifies that the difference is about a returning animal.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the dispute between Rav and Shmuel corresponds to a Tannaic dispute about an animal that eats from the side of a public area, citing a baraita where Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda say it pays what it benefited, while Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Elazar say it is not typical to eat there.
The Gemara clarifies that the difference between the Tannaim is about a returning animal: the first Tanna holds it pays what it benefited, while Rabbi Yosei holds it pays what it damaged.

items.text: Rejection: The dispute is about the verse 'and consumes in another's field'
items.text_en: Rejection: The dispute is about the verse 'and consumes in another's field'
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the previous suggestion, stating that all agree on the returning animal case, and the real dispute is about the interpretation of the verse 'וּבִעֵר בִּשְׂדֵה אַחֵר' – one says it excludes the public domain, the other says it excludes the domain of the one who causes damage.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the previous suggestion, stating that all agree on the returning animal case, and the real dispute is about the interpretation of the verse 'וּבִעֵר בִּשְׂדֵה אַחֵר' – one says it excludes the public domain, the other says it excludes the domain of the one who causes damage.

items.text: הבהרת מחלוקת התנאים
items.text_en: Further clarification: The dispute is between Ilfa and Rabbi Oshaya
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the phrase 'in the domain of the one who causes damage' would imply the animal's owner should not have brought it there, so the dispute is actually between Ilfa and Rabbi Oshaya.
items.desc: הגמרא דוחה את ההסבר הקודם ומסבירה שהמחלוקת בין התנאים אינה לגבי רשות הרבים, אלא לגבי מקרה שבו הבהמה אוכלת מגבו של חברו. רבי מאיר פוטר ורבי יוסי מחייב, והמחלוקת תלויה בשאלה האם נחשב הדבר כאילו הבהמה אוכלת ברשות הניזק.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the phrase 'in the domain of the one who causes damage' by asking why the animal's owner would bring his produce there.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: אם הפטור הוא על אכילה ברשות המזיק, הרי ברור שהניזק לא היה צריך להכניס פירותיו לרשות חברו, ולכן אין כאן חידוש.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the dispute is actually between Ilfa and Rabbi Oshaya, not about the domain itself.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: אם הפטור הוא על אכילה ברשות המזיק, הרי ברור שהניזק לא היה צריך להכניס פירותיו לרשות חברו, ולכן אין כאן חידוש.

items.text: משנת כלב וגדי שקפצו
items.text_en: Mishnah: Liability for jumping vs. falling from a roof
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a dog or goat that jumps from a roof and breaks vessels pays full damages, but if they fell they are exempt. It also discusses a case where a dog takes a coal and causes a fire.
items.desc: המשנה קובעת שכלב או גדי שקפצו מגג ושברו כלים, בעליהם משלמים נזק שלם, משום שהם מועדים לקפיצה. במקרה של כלב שנטל חררה והדליק גדיש, משלם על החררה נזק שלם ועל הגדיש חצי נזק.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a dog or goat that jumps from a roof and breaks vessels pays full damages, but if they fell they are exempt; it also discusses a case where a dog takes a coal and causes a fire.
sub.desc: המשנה פותחת בדין כלב או גדי שקפצו מראש הגג ושברו כלים: בעליהם משלמים נזק שלם, משום שהם מועדים לקפיצה.

items.text: דיוני הגמרא על קפיצה ונפילה
items.text_en: Gemara: The principle of initial negligence and final accident
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers that if they fell, they are exempt, implying that if the beginning was negligent and the end was accidental, one is exempt. A Tosefta supports this, but the Gemara questions how to reconcile with those who hold liable. It answers that the case involves vessels near the wall, so there is no negligence even at the start.
items.desc: הגמרא דנה במשנה ומסיקה שדווקא בקפיצה חייב, אבל בנפילה פטור, משום שתחילתו בפשיעה וסופו באונס פטור. הגמרא מביאה ברייתא התומכת בכך, ומסבירה שמדובר בכלים שהונחו סמוך לכותל, כך שגם אם נפלו לא היו שוברים אותם.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that if the animals fell (rather than jumped), the owner is exempt, implying the principle that if the beginning was negligent and the end was accidental, one is exempt.
sub.desc: הגמרא דנה במשנה: מדוע דווקא בקפיצה חייב? מכאן שאם נפלו פטור, כי תחילתו בפשיעה וסופו באונס פטור.

sub.desc_en: A Tosefta is cited that explicitly states: if the animals jumped, they pay full damages; if they fell, they are exempt, supporting the Gemara's inference.
sub.desc: ברייתא תומכת: אם קפצו חייבים, אם נפלו פטורים. מכאן שתחילתו בפשיעה וסופו באונס פטור.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the Tosefta can be reconciled with the opinion that holds one liable for initial negligence even if the end was accidental.
sub.desc: ברייתא תומכת: אם קפצו חייבים, אם נפלו פטורים. מכאן שתחילתו בפשיעה וסופו באונס פטור.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the case involves vessels placed near the wall, so even at the start there was no negligence, thus even those who hold liable in principle would agree to exemption here.
sub.desc: תירוץ: מדובר בכלים סמוך לכותל, כך שבקפיצה רגילה לא נופלים עליהם; לפיכך אין כאן אפילו תחילתו בפשיעה.

items.text: מקרה של כותל רעוע
items.text_en: Rav Zevid's qualification: Even falling can be liable with a weak wall
items.desc_en: Rav Zevid says in the name of Rava that sometimes even falling is liable, such as with a weak wall where one should have anticipated the fall. The Gemara questions this, but resolves it with a narrow wall where the fall is inevitable.
items.desc: רב זביד בשם רבא אומר שיש מקרים שבהם אפילו נפילה מחייבת, כמו בכותל רעוע, שבו הבעלים היה צריך לצפות שהחיות יפלו. הגמרא דוחה את ההסבר ומסבירה שמדובר בכותל צר, שבו הנפילה היא צפויה מראש.

sub.desc_en: Rav Zevid states in Rava's name that sometimes even falling animals are liable, specifically with a weak wall (כותל רעוע).
sub.desc: רב זביד בשם רבא מתרץ: מדובר בכותל צר, שבו הנפילה צפויה מראש, ולכן אפילו אם נפלו חייב.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions: What is the case? Should one have anticipated that passersby would fall? — implying the owner should have foreseen the danger.
sub.desc: רב זביד בשם רבא מתרץ: מדובר בכותל צר, שבו הנפילה צפויה מראש, ולכן אפילו אם נפלו חייב.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: Ultimately, passersby did not fall, but the animals did — this is still a case of initial negligence with an unavoidable end (תחילתו בפשיעה וסופו באונס), which should be exempt.
sub.desc: רב זביד בשם רבא מתרץ: מדובר בכותל צר, שבו הנפילה צפויה מראש, ולכן אפילו אם נפלו חייב.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves: The case is actually a narrow wall (כותל צר), where the fall is inevitable, making the owner fully liable even for falling animals.
sub.desc: רב זביד בשם רבא מתרץ: מדובר בכותל צר, שבו הנפילה צפויה מראש, ולכן אפילו אם נפלו חייב.

items.text: ברייתא על דילוגים
items.text_en: Baraita: Distinction between animals and humans in jumping
items.desc_en: A Baraita teaches that a dog or goat that jumps from below to above is exempt, but from above to below is liable. A person or rooster is liable in both directions.
items.desc: ברייתא קובעת שכלב וגדי שדילגו ממטה למעלה פטורים, אך ממעלה למטה חייבים. אדם ותרנגול שדילגו חייבים בכל מקרה, משום שדרכם לעשות כן.

sub.desc_en: Baraita: dog/goat jumping from below to above = exempt; from above to below = liable. Person/rooster jumping both directions = liable.
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת: הברייתא צריכה, כי המשנה לא פירטה את המקרה של דילוג ממטה למעלה, והברייתא מוסיפה חידוש.

items.text: ברייתא: כלב וגדי שדילגו
items.text_en: Challenge from a baraita about a dog and goat that jumped
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a baraita stating that a dog and goat that jump from above to below or vice versa are exempt. Rav Pappa explains the case involves a dog with a thorn and a goat with a rope, and clarifies they are exempt from full damages but liable for half damages.
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה ברייתא על כלב וגדי שדילגו, ומתרצת שר' פפא מפרש שמדובר בשינוי התנהגות (כלב בזקירה וגדי בסריכא), ולכן פטורים מנזק שלם אך חייבים בחצי נזק.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges with a baraita stating that a dog and goat that jump from above to below or vice versa are exempt from damages.
sub.desc: הגמרא מביאה ברייתא על כלב וגדי שדילגו, ומתרצת שר' פפא מפרש שמדובר בשינוי התנהגות (כלב בזקירה וגדי בסריכא), ולכן פטורים מנזק שלם אך חייבים בחצי נזק.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa explains the case involves a dog with a thorn and a goat with a rope, where they flipped over.
sub.desc: הגמרא מביאה ברייתא על כלב וגדי שדילגו, ומתרצת שר' פפא מפרש שמדובר בשינוי התנהגות (כלב בזקירה וגדי בסריכא), ולכן פטורים מנזק שלם אך חייבים בחצי נזק.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why they are exempt if the case is as Rav Pappa described.
sub.desc: הגמרא מביאה ברייתא על כלב וגדי שדילגו, ומתרצת שר' פפא מפרש שמדובר בשינוי התנהגות (כלב בזקירה וגדי בסריכא), ולכן פטורים מנזק שלם אך חייבים בחצי נזק.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that they are exempt from full damages (נזק שלם) but liable for half damages (חצי נזק).
sub.desc: הגמרא מביאה ברייתא על כלב וגדי שדילגו, ומתרצת שר' פפא מפרש שמדובר בשינוי התנהגות (כלב בזקירה וגדי בסריכא), ולכן פטורים מנזק שלם אך חייבים בחצי נזק.

items.text: Mishnah citation: The dog that took a coal
items.text_en: Mishnah citation: The dog that took a coal
items.desc_en: The Mishnah is cited: 'The dog that took a coal...' as the basis for the ensuing debate.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah is cited: 'The dog that took a coal' as the basis for the ensuing debate.

items.text: Debate between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish on the basis of fire liability
items.text_en: Debate between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish on the basis of fire liability
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan holds that fire liability is due to his arrows (direct force), while Reish Lakish holds it is due to his property (his chattel). Each explains why the other's reasoning fails: Reish Lakish argues fire does not travel by his force, and Rabbi Yochanan argues fire has no substance like property.

sub.desc_en: The gemara states the debate: Rabbi Yochanan holds that fire liability is due to his arrows (direct force), while Reish Lakish holds it is due to his property (his chattel).
The gemara asks why Reish Lakish does not accept Rabbi Yochanan's reasoning.
Reish Lakish argues that his arrows travel by his force, but fire does not travel by his force.
The gemara asks why Rabbi Yochanan does not accept Reish Lakish's reasoning.
Rabbi Yochanan argues that property has substance, but fire has no substance.

items.text: Challenge to Reish Lakish from the Mishnah of the dog with a coal
items.text_en: Challenge to Reish Lakish from the Mishnah of the dog with a coal
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Reish Lakish: according to Rabbi Yochanan, the fire is the dog's arrows, but according to Reish Lakish, the fire is not the dog owner's property, so how can the owner be liable?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Reish Lakish from the Mishnah of the dog with a coal: according to the view that fire is the dog's arrows, the dog owner is liable, but according to Reish Lakish's view that fire is the owner's property, the coal is not the dog owner's property, so how can he be liable?

items.text: Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan's resolutions for the dog case
items.text_en: Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan's resolutions for the dog case
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish explains the case involves the dog shaking the coal off, so the owner pays full damages for the coal, half for the place of the coal, and is exempt for the stack. Rabbi Yochanan explains the dog placed the coal down, so the owner pays full for the coal and its place, and half for the stack.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish resolves the dog case by explaining the dog shook the coal off, so the owner pays full damages for the coal, half for the place of the coal, and is exempt for the entire stack.
Rabbi Yochanan resolves the dog case by explaining the dog placed the coal down, so the owner pays full damages for the coal and its place, and half for the stack.

items.text: Baraita about a camel with flax and a shopkeeper's lamp
items.text_en: Baraita about a camel with flax and a shopkeeper's lamp
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited: a camel laden with flax passes through the public domain; its flax enters a shop and is ignited by the shopkeeper's lamp, causing a fire. The camel owner is liable. If the shopkeeper left his lamp outside, the shopkeeper is liable. Rabbi Yehuda exempts for a Chanukah lamp.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita: a camel laden with flax passes through the public domain, its flax enters a shop and is ignited by the shopkeeper's lamp, causing a fire; the camel owner is liable.
The baraita states: if the shopkeeper left his lamp outside, the shopkeeper is liable.
Rabbi Yehuda exempts the shopkeeper when the lamp was a Chanukah lamp.

items.text: Challenge to Reish Lakish from the camel case
items.text_en: Challenge to Reish Lakish from the camel case
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Reish Lakish: according to Rabbi Yochanan, the fire is the camel's arrows, but according to Reish Lakish, the fire is not the camel owner's property. Reish Lakish answers that the case involves the flax brushing against the lamp and igniting the entire building.

sub.desc_en: In peace for one who says the fire is because of his arrows – it is the camel's arrows. But for one who says because of his money – this fire is not the camel owner's money! Reish Lakish says: here we are dealing with a fire that spread throughout the entire building.

items.text: קושיית הגמרא על החנוני ותירוץ רב איקא
items.text_en: Refinement of the camel case: standing and brushing
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Reish Lakish's explanation: if the flax was brushing, why is the shopkeeper liable when he left the lamp outside? The Gemara suggests the camel stood still, then brushed. Rav Huna bar Manoach in the name of Rav Ika resolves that the camel stood to urinate, making the shopkeeper liable for the initial fire.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה: אם הגמל סיכך את כל הבירה, מדוע החנוני חייב כשהניח את נרו בחוץ? מתרצים שמדובר במקרה שבו הגמל עמד מלכת, ורב הונא בר מנוח בשם רב איקא מוסיף שמדובר בגמל שעמד להטיל מימיו, ולכן החנוני חייב.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Reish Lakish's explanation: if the flax was brushing (מסכסכת), why is the shopkeeper liable when he left the lamp outside?
The Gemara suggests the camel stood still, then brushed, which would make the shopkeeper liable.
The Gemara objects: if the camel stood and brushed, the shopkeeper should be exempt and the camel owner liable.

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Manoach in the name of Rav Ika
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Manoach in the name of Rav Ika
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Manoach in the name of Rav Ika resolves that the camel stood to urinate, making the shopkeeper liable for the initial fire.

items.text: Recap of the Mishnah's distinction
items.text_en: Recap of the Mishnah's distinction
items.desc_en: The Gemara restates the Mishnah's ruling: the camel owner is liable for overloading, and the shopkeeper is liable for not moving his lamp away from the camel.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara restates the Mishnah's ruling: the camel owner is liable for overloading, and the shopkeeper is liable for not moving his lamp away from the camel.

items.text: Challenge from a case of a bound slave
items.text_en: Challenge from a case of a bound slave
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita: one who sets fire to a stack with a bound goat and a nearby slave is liable; if the slave is bound and the goat nearby, he is exempt. This challenges the view that fire is considered one's property, since if his ox killed the slave he would be liable.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about a fire that burns a bound goat and a nearby slave, where liability depends on which is bound, to challenge the view that fire is considered one's property.
The Gemara objects: according to the view that fire is considered one's property (ממונו), why is one exempt when the slave is bound? If his ox killed the slave, he would be liable.

items.text: Resh Lakish's resolution
items.text_en: Resh Lakish's resolution
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish explains that the baraita deals with a case where the fire was lit on the slave's body, so the exemption is due to the principle of 'the one who is liable for a greater penalty' (i.e., capital punishment). The Gemara adds that this applies when the goat and slave belong to different owners.

sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish resolves the contradiction by explaining that the baraita deals with a case where the fire was lit on the slave's body, so the exemption is due to the principle of 'the one who is liable for a greater penalty' (i.e., capital punishment).
The Gemara clarifies that the novelty of the baraita is that the goat and slave belong to different owners, so the exemption applies only to the slave's owner, not the goat's owner.

items.text: Challenge from a case of a deaf agent
items.text_en: Challenge from a case of a deaf agent
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites another baraita: one who sends fire via a deaf-mute, imbecile, or minor is exempt from human court but liable in heavenly court. This challenges the property view, since if he sent his ox via such an agent he would be liable.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita: one who sends fire via a deaf-mute, imbecile, or minor is exempt from human court but liable in heavenly court.

The Gemara objects: according to the view that fire is his arrows, the exemption makes sense, but according to the property view, if he sent his ox via such an agent he would be liable, so why is fire different?

items.text: Resh Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan's dispute on the baraita
items.text_en: Resh Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan's dispute on the baraita
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish, citing Chizkiyah, limits the exemption to when one gave a coal and the agent fanned it; if one gave a flame, he is liable because the damage is certain. Rabbi Yochanan argues that even a flame exempts, since the deaf-mute's tongs cause the damage; liability only applies when one gives wood, kindling, and a lamp.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the dispute: Resh Lakish, citing Chizkiyah, limits the exemption to when one gave a coal and the agent fanned it, but if one gave a flame, he is liable because the damage is certain.
Rabbi Yochanan argues that even a flame exempts, since the deaf-mute's tongs cause the damage; liability only applies when one gives wood, kindling, and a lamp.

items.text: Rava's support for Rabbi Yochanan from Scripture and a baraita
items.text_en: Rava's support for Rabbi Yochanan from Scripture and a baraita
items.desc_en: Rava cites a verse: 'When a fire goes out' (by itself) and 'the one who kindled the fire shall pay' – implying fire is like one's arrows. He also cites a baraita where the verse begins with 'When a fire goes out', supporting the arrows view.

sub.desc_en: Rava announces that both Scripture and a baraita support Rabbi Yochanan's view that fire is classified as one's arrows (חִצָּיו).

Rava cites the verse 'כִּי תֵצֵא אֵשׁ' (when a fire goes out) implying it goes out by itself, and 'יְשַׁלֵּם הַמַּבְעִר' (the one who kindled shall pay), concluding that fire is treated as his arrows.
Rava introduces a baraita that begins with the same verse 'כִּי תֵצֵא אֵשׁ', further supporting the arrows view.

items.text: Opening statement: Fire as arrows
items.text_en: Opening statement: Fire as arrows
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah began with damage by one's property and concluded with damage by one's body, to teach that fire is considered like one's arrows (direct act).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by noting that the Mishnah begins with damage by one's property and concludes with damage by one's body, to teach that fire is considered like one's arrows (a direct act).

items.text: Rava's question and Abaye's resolution
items.text_en: Rava's question and Abaye's resolution
items.desc_en: Rava reports that Abaye was troubled: for one who holds fire is like arrows, how can there be a case of hidden items exempted by the Torah? The resolution is when a fire spreads to another courtyard after a fence fell not due to the fire, so his arrows are 'blocked'.

sub.desc_en: Rava reports that Abaye was troubled: for one who holds that fire is like arrows (משום חציו), how can the Torah's exemption for hidden items (טמוּן באֵש) ever apply?
The Gemara resolves: the case is when a fire spreads to another courtyard after a fence fell not due to the fire, so his 'arrows' are blocked (כלו לו חציו).

items.text: Objection and alternative explanation
items.text_en: Objection and alternative explanation
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if so, even for exposed items his arrows would be blocked. Rather, for one who holds fire is like arrows, he also holds it is like his property, e.g., when he could have fenced it but didn't; there it is his ox and he did not 'slap it in the face'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the previous explanation were correct, even for exposed items the fire's arrows would be blocked, making the exemption for hidden items illogical.

The Gemara resolves that one who holds fire is like arrows also holds it is like his property, applying the exemption for hidden items only when he could have fenced the fire but did not, making it his 'ox' that he failed to 'slap in the face'.

items.text: Practical difference between the views
items.text_en: Practical difference between the views
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: since one who holds fire is like arrows also holds it is like his property, what is the difference between the views? The difference is in liability for the four items (pain, medical, lost time, shame).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: since the one who holds fire is like arrows also holds it is like his property, what is the practical difference between the two views?
The Gemara answers: the difference lies in liability for the four items of damages (pain, medical, lost time, and shame).

items.text: Mishnah analysis: Dog carrying a coal
items.text_en: Mishnah analysis: Dog carrying a coal
items.desc_en: The Mishnah says: for the coal, the owner of the dog pays. The Gemara asks: why not also the owner of the coal? Answer: when he guarded his coal. But then why is the dog there? When it dug. Rav Mari bar Rav Kahana says: this teaches that doors are normally dug under by a dog.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's ruling that the owner of the dog pays for the coal (חררה), and asks who is liable.
The Gemara asks: why should the owner of the coal (גחלת) not also be liable?
The Gemara answers: the case is where the owner of the coal guarded his coal properly (שימר גחלתו), so he is exempt.
The Gemara asks: if the coal was guarded, why would a dog be present there at all?
The Gemara answers: the case is where the dog dug under the door (חתר) to reach the coal.
Rav Mari bar Rav Kahana deduces from this that doors are normally dug under (חתורות) by a dog, establishing a general principle.

items.text: Where did the dog eat the grain?
items.text_en: Where did the dog eat the grain?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: where did the dog eat the grain? If in a general heap, the verse requires 'and consumed in another's field' – not fulfilled. Rather, it ate in a heap belonging to the owner of the coal. This resolves the issue.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks where the dog ate the grain, proposing that if it ate from a general heap, the verse requirement of 'and consumed in another's field' is not fulfilled.
The Gemara resolves that the dog ate from a heap belonging to the owner of the coal, thereby satisfying the verse's condition.

items.text: Initial comparison of the animal's mouth to a courtyard
items.text_en: Initial comparison of the animal's mouth to a courtyard
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers whether the mouth of an animal is analogous to the victim's courtyard or the tortfeasor's courtyard, as this affects liability for damage caused by eating.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the animal's mouth is analogous to the victim's courtyard or the tortfeasor's courtyard, arguing that if it were the latter, the owner could claim the bread had no business being in the dog's mouth.

items.text: The dilemma of the cow's mouth and possible resolutions
items.text_en: The dilemma of the cow's mouth and possible resolutions
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises the specific dilemma about the cow's mouth and asks how the Torah's liability for tooth damage could be found if it is like the tortfeasor's courtyard. Rav Mari bar Kahana, Mar Zutra, Ravina, and Rav Ashi offer various scenarios to resolve the issue.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises the dilemma: is the cow's mouth (where it eats) considered like the victim's courtyard or the tortfeasor's courtyard for liability purposes?
The Gemara objects: if the mouth is like the tortfeasor's courtyard, how can the Torah's liability for tooth damage ever be found?
Rav Mari bar Kahana answers: the case is where the cow rubbed against a wall for its own pleasure and soiled produce for its own pleasure.
Mar Zutra objects: the verse requires 'as one clears away dung until it is gone' (complete consumption), but here the produce is only soiled, not consumed.
Ravina answers: the case is where the cow scraped off plaster figures (and ate them).
Rav Ashi answers: the case is where the cow stepped over (and ate produce from the other side).

items.text: Proof from inciting a dog or snake
items.text_en: Proof from inciting a dog or snake
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about inciting a dog or snake to bite, which seems to prove that the mouth is like the victim's courtyard. It then offers alternative interpretations to reconcile the text.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about inciting a dog or snake, where the inciter is exempt and the owner is liable, and argues that if the mouth were like the victim's courtyard, the inciter could not be exempt.
The Gemara offers a first answer: the baraita means that even the inciter is exempt, so the proof is neutralized.
The Gemara offers an alternative answer: the case is where the dog extended its fangs and scratched the victim, so the damage was not purely from the mouth.

items.text: Proof from a snake bite and distinction for capital cases
items.text_en: Proof from a snake bite and distinction for capital cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages about liability for a snake bite, and Rav Acha bar Yaakov explains their positions. The Gemara then argues that in capital cases, the principle of 'what were you doing in my domain' does not apply.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda holds the inciter liable for a snake bite and the Sages exempt him.

Rav Acha bar Yaakov explains the dispute: Rabbi Yehuda holds the snake's venom is stored in its fangs, so the snake is exempt and the inciter is liable; the Sages hold the venom is self-ejected, so the snake is stoned and the inciter is exempt.

The Gemara resolves that the principle of 'what were you doing in my domain' does not apply in capital cases, so the snake-bite baraita does not disprove the view that the cow's mouth is like the domain of the damager.

items.text: Support from the case of an intruder gored by an ox
items.text_en: Support from the case of an intruder gored by an ox
items.desc_en: A baraita about an intruder killed by the owner's ox shows that in capital cases, the owner is exempt from ransom because the victim was trespassing, but the ox is stoned. This supports the distinction that the 'what were you doing' argument applies only for monetary damages, not for capital liability.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where do we derive this principle (that the 'what were you doing' argument applies only to monetary damages, not capital cases)?
A baraita is cited: an intruder who enters a homeowner's courtyard without permission and is gored to death by the owner's ox — the ox is stoned, but the owners are exempt from ransom.

The Gemara explains: the owners are exempt from ransom because they can say 'what were you doing in my domain?', but regarding the ox's liability for killing, we do not apply the 'what were you doing' argument — thus supporting the distinction between monetary and capital cases.

items.text: Practical case of goats damaging property and Rav Yosef's ruling
items.text_en: Practical case of goats damaging property and Rav Yosef's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts an incident where goats from the house of Tarbu damaged Rav Yosef's property. Rav Yosef instructs Abaye to warn the owners, and Abaye objects. The Gemara discusses scenarios where tooth damage is still possible, and Rav Yosef (or Rava) establishes a procedure for warning owners of stray goats.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that goats from the house of Tarbu damaged Rav Yosef's property; Rav Yosef tells Abaye to warn the owners, but Abaye objects that the owners could say Rav Yosef should have fenced his own land.
The Gemara asks: if the owner fences his land, how can the Torah's liability for tooth damage ever apply?
The Gemara answers: tooth damage can still occur when the animal digs under the fence, or when the fence collapses at night.

Rav Yosef (or Rabbah) establishes a procedure: for stray goats that damage, the court warns the owners two or three times; if they do not heed, the court tells them to sit and collect their payment (i.e., they must bear the loss).

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara on the definitions of tam and mu'ad
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on the definitions of tam and mu'ad
items.desc_en: The Mishnah defines a tam and mu'ad according to Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Meir. The Gemara explains the scriptural basis for Rabbi Yehuda's view (Abaye and Rava) and begins to explain Rabbi Meir's reasoning.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by defining tam and mu'ad according to Rabbi Yehuda: a mu'ad is one warned for three days, and a tam is one that returns to tam status after three days without goring.
Rabbi Meir gives an alternative definition: a mu'ad is one warned three times (not necessarily on three consecutive days), and a tam is one that children can poke without it goring.
The Gemara asks: what is the scriptural basis for Rabbi Yehuda's view?
Abaye explains that the verse uses three terms (תמול, מתמול, שלשום) to indicate three days of warning, and the phrase 'ולא ישמרנו' introduces liability for a fourth goring.
Rava offers an alternative interpretation: the combined phrase 'תמול–מתמול' counts as one day, 'שלשום' as a second, and the current warning ('ולא ישמרנו') makes the ox liable.
The Gemara asks: what is the scriptural basis for Rabbi Meir's view?
The Gemara introduces a baraita that will explain Rabbi Meir's reasoning, but the text cuts off at the end of the section.

items.text: Gemara's challenge to the Mishnah's logic using the zavah analogy
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge to the Mishnah's logic using the zavah analogy
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's distinction between distancing and approaching goring incidents, arguing that if distancing incurs liability, approaching should certainly incur liability. The Sages counter with the zavah analogy, where distancing sightings makes her impure but approaching makes her pure. Rabbi Yehuda responds by citing a verse that distinguishes the zav from the zavah, and the Gemara analyzes the derivation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the Mishnah's logic: if distancing goring incurs liability, then approaching goring should certainly incur liability; the Sages counter with the zavah analogy, where distancing sightings makes her impure but approaching makes her pure.
Rabbi Yehuda cites the verse 'וְזֹאת תִּהְיֶה טֻמְאָתוֹ בְּזוֹבוֹ' to argue that the Torah links the zav to sightings and the zavah to days, thereby distinguishing the two cases.

The Gemara objects: how do we know that 'וְזֹאת' excludes the zavah from sightings, rather than excluding the zav from days? It then answers by citing the verse 'וְהַזָּב אֶת זוֹבוֹ לַזָּכָר וְלַנְּקֵבָה', which juxtaposes male and female, teaching that the male is also governed by days.
The Gemara objects further: why not juxtapose female to male, so that the female is also governed by sightings? It answers that the Merciful One excluded this with 'וְזֹאת'.
The Gemara resolves: what did you see? It is logical that since the verse stands in the context of sightings, it excludes sightings (from the zavah), not days.

items.text: Baraita defining mu'ad and tam
items.text_en: Baraita defining mu'ad and tam
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited defining a mu'ad as an ox that has been testified against for three days, and a tam as one that children can touch without it goring. Rabbi Yosi states this, while Rabbi Shimon says mu'ad is defined by three incidents, and the mention of three days is only for the return to tam status.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with the Tanna Kamma's definition of mu'ad (an ox testified against for three days) and tam (one that children can touch without goring), attributed to Rabbi Yosi.
Rabbi Shimon defines mu'ad by three incidents of goring, and explains that the mention of three days is only for the return to tam status.

items.text: Rav Nachman's ruling and Rava's challenge
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's ruling and Rava's challenge
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules that the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda regarding mu'ad (since Rabbi Yosi agrees with him) and Rabbi Meir regarding tam (since Rabbi Yosi agrees with him). Rava challenges this, suggesting alternative pairings based on Rabbi Shimon's agreement, but Rav Nachman defends his position by stating he holds like Rabbi Yosi because his reasoning is compelling.

sub.text: Rav Nachman citing Rav Adda bar Ahavah
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman citing Rav Adda bar Ahavah
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules that the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda regarding mu'ad and Rabbi Meir regarding tam, because Rabbi Yosi agrees with each respectively.
Rava challenges Rav Nachman, suggesting alternative pairings based on Rabbi Shimon's agreement.
Rav Nachman defends his position by stating he holds like Rabbi Yosi because his reasoning is compelling.

items.text: Inquiry: Does 'three days' refer to the ox or the owner?
items.text_en: Inquiry: Does 'three days' refer to the ox or the owner?
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: does the requirement of three days of testimony serve to establish the ox as mu'ad or to establish the owner's liability? The practical difference is if three sets of witnesses testify on a single day. The Gemara leaves the question unresolved.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an unresolved inquiry: does the phrase 'three days' in the Mishnah refer to establishing the ox as mu'ad (forewarned) or to establishing the owner's liability?

The Gemara explains the practical difference: if three sets of witnesses testify on a single day, the ox becomes mu'ad only if the requirement is to establish the ox, but not if it is to establish the owner, since the owner can claim the witnesses are testifying about him only now.
The Gemara leaves the inquiry unresolved with the word 'מַאי' (what is the answer?).

items.text: Resolution from a baraita about testimony
items.text_en: Resolution from a baraita about testimony
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to resolve the inquiry by citing a baraita that details the requirements for making an ox mu'ad, including testimony before the owners and the court. The baraita discusses cases of multiple sets of witnesses and the consequences of their being found conspiring. The Gemara concludes that if the purpose is to establish the ox as mu'ad, the baraita works well.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that states an ox is not made mu'ad unless witnesses testify before the owners and the court.
The baraita details that if two witnesses testify on each of three days, they constitute three testimonies but one unit for the purpose of being found conspiring (הזמה).
The baraita explains that if the first or second set of witnesses is found conspiring, the ox owner is exempt and the witnesses are exempt from paying.
The baraita concludes that if the third set is found conspiring, all witnesses are liable, citing the verse 'and you shall do to him as he conspired'.
The Gemara concludes that if the purpose of the three days is to establish the ox as mu'ad (לְיַיעוֹדֵי תּוֹרָא), the baraita works well as a resolution.

items.text: Resolving the difficulty of establishing a mu'ad
items.text_en: Resolving the difficulty of establishing a mu'ad
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the earlier difficulty about witnesses who saw the ox gore but did not know it was a mu'ad. Rav Ashi and Ravina offer different solutions: either the witnesses hinted, or they came in a continuous stream, or they recognized the owner but not the ox. The final solution is that the court says: 'You have a goring ox in your herd, you should have guarded all your cattle.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how witnesses who saw the goring but did not know the ox was a mu'ad could establish it as a mu'ad, since the first witnesses could claim ignorance of the later goring.

Rav Ashi reports Rav Kahana's objection: later witnesses cannot know if earlier witnesses came to testify about the ox or to obligate the owner for half damages, so establishing a mu'ad is impossible.
The Gemara first suggests the witnesses hinted, then Rav Ashi says they came in a continuous stream so the court knew they were testifying about the same ox.
Ravina offers an alternative solution: the witnesses recognized the owner but not the specific ox, so the court could establish the owner as a mu'ad.
The Gemara resolves the difficulty by stating that the court says: 'You have a goring ox in your herd, you should have guarded all your cattle.'

items.text: The dilemma of inciting a dog
items.text_en: The dilemma of inciting a dog
items.desc_en: A dilemma is raised: if one incites another's dog against a third party, what is the liability? The inciter is certainly exempt (since he did not own the dog), but is the owner liable? The question is whether the owner can claim he did nothing, or whether he should have known his dog's nature and not kept it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a dilemma: if one incites another's dog against a third party, the inciter is certainly exempt, but is the owner liable because he should have known his dog's nature and not kept it?

items.text: Attempted proof from a Mishnah about a tam ox
items.text_en: Attempted proof from a Mishnah about a tam ox
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira attempts to prove the owner's liability from a Mishnah: a tam ox is one that children touch and it does not gore. If it does gore, it is liable. Abaye deflects: the Mishnah means if it gores it is not a tam, but it is not liable for that goring.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira attempts to prove the owner's liability from a Mishnah: a tam ox is one that children touch and it does not gore; if it does gore, it is liable.
Abaye deflects: the Mishnah means if it gores it is not a tam, but it is not liable for that goring.

items.text: Another attempted proof from a baraita
items.text_en: Another attempted proof from a baraita
items.desc_en: Another attempt: a baraita states that if one incites a dog or snake against another, he is exempt. The Gemara wonders if this means the inciter is exempt but the owner is liable. It concludes: no, it means even the inciter is exempt.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove from a baraita that if one incites a dog against another, the inciter is exempt but the owner is liable.
The Gemara rejects the proof, explaining that the baraita means even the inciter is exempt, not that the owner is liable.

items.text: Rava's ruling and Reish Lakish's support
items.text_en: Rava's ruling and Reish Lakish's support
items.desc_en: Rava rules: if one incites another's dog, the inciter is liable; if he incites his own dog, he is exempt (since the dog changed its nature). Rav Pappa reports that Reish Lakish agrees with Rava, citing a case of two cows in the public domain. Rava clarifies that in that case he would hold the walking cow liable for kicking the resting one.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that if one incites another's dog against the owner, the inciter is liable; if he incites his own dog, he is exempt, because one who changes (the dog's nature) and another comes and changes through it is exempt.

sub.text: Rav Pappa's report of Reish Lakish's support
sub.text_en: Rav Pappa's report of Reish Lakish's support
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa reports that Reish Lakish agrees with Rava, citing a case of two cows in the public domain: a walking cow that kicks a resting one is exempt, but a resting cow that kicks a walking one is liable.
Rava clarifies that in that case he would hold the walking cow liable for kicking the resting one, because the walking cow has permission to walk but not to kick.

items.text: Mishnah: Damage in the plaintiff's domain
items.text_en: Mishnah: Damage in the plaintiff's domain
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the case of an ox damaging in the plaintiff's domain. For keren damage in the public domain, the owner pays half damages. In the plaintiff's domain, Rabbi Tarfon says full damages, while the Sages say half damages. Rabbi Tarfon argues a kal vachomer from the leniency of tooth and foot, but the Sages respond that the deduction is limited to the same liability as the original case.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the case of an ox damaging in the plaintiff's domain, listing the actions and stating that in the public domain the owner pays half damages, while in the plaintiff's domain Rabbi Tarfon says full damages and the Sages say half damages.

Rabbi Tarfon argues a kal vachomer (a fortiori) from the leniency of tooth and foot in the public domain to the stringency of keren in the plaintiff's domain, concluding that keren should also require full damages.
The Sages reject Rabbi Tarfon's kal vachomer by applying the principle of דיו (sufficiency), limiting the deduction to the same liability as the original case — half damages.
Rabbi Tarfon begins his rejoinder, saying 'אף אני' (I too), but the Mishnah cuts off, leaving the argument incomplete.

items.text: Rabbi Tarfon's kal vachomer and the Sages' dayo objection
items.text_en: Rabbi Tarfon's kal vachomer and the Sages' dayo objection
items.desc_en: Rabbi Tarfon argues from horn in the public domain (half damages) to horn in the plaintiff's domain (full damages) using a kal vachomer from tooth and foot. The Sages respond with the principle of dayo, limiting the conclusion to half damages.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Tarfon proposes a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument) from horn in the public domain (half damages) to horn in the plaintiff's domain (full damages), based on the leniency of tooth and foot in the public domain.
The Sages object with the principle of דיו (dayo), arguing that the conclusion of a kal vachomer cannot exceed the source, so horn in the plaintiff's domain still yields only half damages.

items.text: Gemara's question: Does Rabbi Tarfon reject dayo?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Does Rabbi Tarfon reject dayo?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Rabbi Tarfon can reject dayo, which is Torah-derived from Miriam's example. It answers that he only rejects dayo when the kal vachomer would otherwise be refuted; here, half-damages are already written, so applying dayo would break the kal vachomer.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Does Rabbi Tarfon not accept the principle of דיו (dayo), which is Torah-based, as shown from the kal vachomer of Miriam's isolation?

The Gemara answers: Rabbi Tarfon rejects דיו only where applying it would undermine the kal vachomer itself, as in the case of Miriam where the kal vachomer would bring 14 days but דיו reduces it to 7, which is already written.
The Gemara resolves: Here, half damages are already written, and the kal vachomer would add another half to make full damages; applying דיו would destroy the kal vachomer, so Rabbi Tarfon rejects it.
The Gemara explains that in Miriam's case, the seven days of isolation were not explicitly written, so the קל וחומר (kal vachomer) brought fourteen, and דיו (dayo) removed seven, leaving seven.

The Gemara contrasts: here, half-damages are already written, so the קל וחומר (kal vachomer) would bring another half to make full damages; applying דיו (dayo) would refute the קל וחומר (kal vachomer).

items.text: Dispute over the source of dayo
items.text_en: Dispute over the source of dayo
items.desc_en: The Rabbis argue that the verse 'תִּסָּגֵר שִׁבְעַת יָמִים' provides the source for dayo, while Rabbi Tarfon holds that verse itself teaches dayo. The Rabbis then cite another verse 'וַתִּסָּגֵר מִרְיָם' to prove dayo applies generally, not just for Moses' honor.

sub.desc_en: The Rabbis argue that the seven days for the Shechinah are already written in the verse 'תִּסָּגֵר שִׁבְעַת יָמִים', so the kal vachomer is not undermined.

Rabbi Tarfon responds that the verse 'תִּסָּגֵר' itself is the source for the principle of דיו, and the additional verse 'וַתִּסָּגֵר מִרְיָם' teaches that דיו applies universally, not just out of respect for Moses.
The Rabbis cite another verse 'וַתִּסָּגֵר מִרְיָם' to prove that dayo applies generally, not just for Moses' honor.

items.text: Rav Pappa's challenge: a Tanna who rejects dayo even when kal vachomer is not refuted
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's challenge: a Tanna who rejects dayo even when kal vachomer is not refuted
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa challenges Abaye with a baraita where a Tanna derives that a zav's semen imparts impurity both by touch and by carrying via kal vachomer, without applying dayo to exclude carrying. The Gemara explains that the kal vachomer was needed for touch because otherwise one might think the zav's semen is not impure by touch.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa challenges Abaye by citing a baraita where a Tanna derives that a zav's semen (קֶרִי) imparts impurity both by touch and by carrying via a kal vachomer (קל וחומר), without applying the principle of דיו (enough) to exclude carrying.
Rav Pappa objects: why does the baraita apply the kal vachomer (קל וחומר) to both touch and carrying? The principle of דיו should limit the derivation to touch alone, excluding carrying.

The Gemara answers that the kal vachomer (קל וחומר) was necessary for touch because one might have thought that the zav's semen is not impure by touch, since the verse 'מקרה לילה' (a nocturnal emission) implies only one whose emission is caused by a natural event, excluding the zav whose emission is caused by something else.

items.text: Identifying the Tanna who holds semen of a zav imparts impurity by carrying
items.text_en: Identifying the Tanna who holds semen of a zav imparts impurity by carrying
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the baraita's premise, noting that neither Rabbi Eliezer nor Rabbi Yehoshua hold that view. Rabbi Eliezer says it does not impart impurity by carrying, and Rabbi Yehoshua says it does only because it inevitably contains traces of zivah. The Gemara concludes the Tanna must be from a different source.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the baraita's reasoning by asking whether the verse explicitly says 'and not another thing' to exclude the case of a zav's seminal emission.
The Gemara asks which Tanna holds that a zav's semen imparts impurity by carrying, noting that neither Rabbi Eliezer nor Rabbi Yehoshua holds that view.

The Gemara cites a Mishnah where Rabbi Eliezer rules that a zav's semen imparts impurity only by contact, not by carrying, and Rabbi Yehoshua rules it imparts impurity by carrying only because it inevitably contains traces of zivah.
The Gemara concludes that the Tanna of the baraita must be from a different source, since Rabbi Yehoshua's ruling is conditional on the presence of zivah traces.

items.text: Opening Mishnah citation
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah citation
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the fluids of a zav and a menstruating woman that transmit impurity through both contact and carrying.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the fluids of a zav and a menstruating woman that transmit impurity through both contact and carrying.

items.text: Gemara's question and resolution about the Mishnah's listing
items.text_en: Gemara's question and resolution about the Mishnah's listing
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah lists certain items separately, suggesting that one might be included in another, and resolves that the listing is due to a specific source.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah lists 'מימי רגליו' (his urine) separately, since it is impossible without traces of זיבה (gonorrhea discharge), and asks why it is listed with רוק (spit) rather than with זוב (gonorrhea discharge).
The Gemara answers that the urine is listed with the spit because it derives from the spit (i.e., the source of its impurity is the same as that of spit).

items.text: Discussion of the principle of dayo and the derivation of mat (מפץ) impurity
items.text_en: Discussion of the principle of dayo and the derivation of mat (מפץ) impurity
items.desc_en: Rav Acha from Difti challenges Ravina with a baraita that seems to ignore the principle of dayo (דיו) in a kal vachomer argument about a mat (מפץ) and corpse impurity. The Gemara then presents a resolution by Abaye, who reinterprets the baraita as referring to a creeping sheretz (שרץ) rather than a corpse.

sub.text: Rav Acha from Difti's challenge to Ravina
sub.text_en: Rav Acha from Difti's challenge to Ravina
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha from Difti challenges Ravina by citing a baraita about a mat (מפץ) that seems to ignore the principle of dayo (דיו) in a kal vachomer argument, even though the kal vachomer is not refuted.

The baraita derives the impurity of a mat (מפץ) for a corpse via a kal vachomer from small vessels, and then applies it to both evening impurity and seven-day impurity, ignoring the principle of dayo (דיו).
Abaye resolves the difficulty by reinterpreting the baraita: the kal vachomer is actually about a creeping sheretz (שרץ), not a corpse, so the principle of dayo (דיו) does not apply.

items.text: Derivation of mat impurity for a corpse through a gezerah shavah
items.text_en: Derivation of mat impurity for a corpse through a gezerah shavah
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives the impurity of a mat (מפץ) for a corpse using a gezerah shavah from the word pair 'beged va'or' (בגד ועור) mentioned both by a sheretz and by a corpse. It then addresses the need for the gezerah shavah to be 'mufneh' (free for derivation) and demonstrates that it is indeed mufneh.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of a mat's impurity for a corpse, and answers with a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the shared phrase 'בגד ועור' (garment and skin) used for both a sheretz and a corpse.

The Gemara objects that the גזירה שווה must be מופנה (free for derivation), otherwise a refutation could be raised based on the difference in the minimum size of impurity (a lentil for a sheretz vs. an olive for a corpse).

The Gemara demonstrates that the phrase 'בגד ועור' in the context of a sheretz is indeed מופנה (free), because it is redundant given the juxtaposition of sheretz to seminal emission, which already includes the phrase; thus the derivation is valid.

items.text: Challenge regarding a one-sided mufneh and resolution with a two-sided mufneh
items.text_en: Challenge regarding a one-sided mufneh and resolution with a two-sided mufneh
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the gezerah shavah is valid if it is only mufneh from one side (מופנה מצד אחד), and resolves that it is actually mufneh from both sides, as the word pair 'beged va'or' is also superfluous in the context of a corpse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that the gezerah shavah is only מופנה מצד אחד (free from one side) and questions how it holds for the opinion that such a gezerah shavah is rebuttable.
The Gemara resolves that the word pair 'בגד ועור' (garment and skin) is also superfluous in the context of a corpse, making the gezerah shavah מופנה משני צדדין (free from both sides).

items.text: Further challenge and resolution regarding the principle of 'don minah'
items.text_en: Further challenge and resolution regarding the principle of 'don minah'
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a challenge based on the dispute about whether one can derive a law from a gezerah shavah and then apply it to the original context ('דון מינה ואוקי באתרא' vs 'דון מינה ומינה'). Rava resolves by citing a verse that all corpse impurities require seven days of purification.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a challenge: the previous resolution works for the opinion that one derives from a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) and applies it to the original context ('דון מינה ואוקי באתרא'), but for the opinion that one derives from it and applies it fully ('דון מינה ומינה'), what can be said?
Rava resolves by citing a verse ('וכבסתם בגדיכם ביום השביעי') that all corpse impurities require seven days of purification, thus establishing the rule from the Torah itself.

items.text: Proposed kal vachomer for tooth and foot damage in public domain and its rejection
items.text_en: Proposed kal vachomer for tooth and foot damage in public domain and its rejection
items.desc_en: The Gemara proposes a kal vachomer that tooth and foot (שן ורגל) should be liable in the public domain, but rejects it with a biblical verse limiting liability to 'in the field of another' (ובשדה אחר).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument) that tooth and foot (שן ורגל) should be liable in the public domain, reasoning from the case of horn (קרן) which is less severe in the private domain yet liable in the public domain.

The Gemara rejects the kal vachomer by citing the biblical verse 'וּבִעֵר בִּשְׂדֵה אַחֵר' (and it consumes in the field of another), which limits liability for tooth and foot to the private domain of the injured party, excluding the public domain.

items.text: Gemara's rhetorical question on the Mishnah's wording
items.text_en: Gemara's rhetorical question on the Mishnah's wording
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's phrase 'all of it' regarding payment, clarifying that it means half.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rhetorically questions the Mishnah's phrase 'all of it' regarding payment, clarifying that it means half.

items.text: Derivations for keren and shen/regel via kal vachomer and verses
items.text_en: Derivations for keren and shen/regel via kal vachomer and verses
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives that keren pays half damage in the plaintiff's domain from a verse, and then uses a kal vachomer to argue that shen and regel should also pay half in the plaintiff's domain, but a verse requires full payment. Another kal vachomer attempts to exempt keren in public domain, but Rabbi Yochanan cites a verse that half damage is uniform.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a verse that keren (goring) pays half damage only from the plaintiff's property, not from another's.

The Gemara proposes a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument) that shen and regel (tooth and foot) should pay only half damage in the plaintiff's domain, since keren pays half there despite being liable in public domain.
The Gemara rejects the kal vachomer by citing a verse that requires full payment for shen and regel.
The Gemara proposes another kal vachomer that keren should be exempt in public domain, since shen and regel are exempt there despite paying full damage in the plaintiff's domain.
Rabbi Yochanan cites a verse that half damage for keren is uniform, whether in public or private domain, rejecting the second kal vachomer.

items.text: Kal vachomer for kofer on a person and four items on an ox
items.text_en: Kal vachomer for kofer on a person and four items on an ox
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to impose kofer on a person via kal vachomer from an ox, but a verse exempts him. Conversely, it tries to impose the four items on an ox via kal vachomer from a person, but a verse excludes it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument) to impose kofer (ransom) on a person who kills, based on an ox which pays kofer despite not paying the four items.
The Gemara rejects the kal vachomer by citing a verse that limits kofer to an ox, excluding a person.
The Gemara proposes a reverse kal vachomer to impose the four items (arba'ah devarim) on an ox, based on a person who pays them despite not paying kofer.
The Gemara rejects the second kal vachomer by citing a verse that limits the four items to a person, excluding an ox.

items.text: Inquiry about regel trampling a child and kofer
items.text_en: Inquiry about regel trampling a child and kofer
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: if an animal's foot (regel) tramples a child in the plaintiff's domain, does it pay kofer? The doubt is whether regel, which is not inherently intended to damage like keren, still incurs kofer.

items.text: Proof from Rabbi Tarfon's ruling and subsequent discussion
items.text_en: Proof from Rabbi Tarfon's ruling and subsequent discussion
items.desc_en: A baraita with Rabbi Tarfon's ruling that a tam ox pays full kofer in the plaintiff's domain is brought as proof that regel pays kofer. The Gemara analyzes the source, initially suggesting it comes from regel's damages, but after a series of refutations, concludes it must come from regel's kofer, proving that regel pays kofer.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: Rabbi Tarfon rules that an ox (whether tam or mu'ad) that entered the plaintiff's courtyard without permission and gored the owner to death pays full kofer (ransom).

The Gemara asks: For Rabbi Tarfon, what is the source that a tam ox pays full kofer? It suggests that Rabbi Tarfon follows Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, who derives tam's half-kofer in the public domain via a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument) from regel (foot-damage), implying that regel itself pays kofer.
Rav Shimi miNeharde'a objects: The Tanna derives the tam's full kofer from the damages (נזקין) of regel, not from regel's kofer.

sub.text: Gemara's rejection of Rav Shimi's view
sub.text_en: Gemara's rejection of Rav Shimi's view
sub.desc_en: The Gemara refutes Rav Shimi's suggestion by showing that the קל וחומר (a fortiori argument) from regel's damages would be vulnerable to a series of counter-arguments (פירכא) based on fire, pit, and hidden vessels, which are not applicable to kofer.
The Gemara concludes: Therefore, the derivation must be from regel's kofer, proving that regel pays kofer.

items.text: Rav Acha's support for the conclusion
items.text_en: Rav Acha's support for the conclusion
items.desc_en: Rav Acha miDifti supports the conclusion that regel pays kofer by arguing that if it did not, the baraita's kal vachomer would be flawed.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha miDifti argues to Ravina that the conclusion that regel pays kofer is logically necessary, because if it did not, the baraita's kal vachomer would be flawed.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara on a person's perpetual liability
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on a person's perpetual liability
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a person is always liable for damages, even when asleep. The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's examples of blinding and breaking vessels are parallel, implying only payment for damage, not the four additional payments.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a person is always liable for damages, whether awake or asleep, and gives examples of blinding a fellow's eye and breaking vessels, for which he pays full damages.
The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's examples of blinding and breaking vessels are parallel, implying only payment for damage (נזק) and not the four additional payments (ארבעה דברים).

items.text: Derivation of liability for negligence from 'wound for wound'
items.text_en: Derivation of liability for negligence from 'wound for wound'
items.desc_en: Ḥizkiyah and the Tanna of the school of Ḥizkiyah derive from the verse 'wound for wound' that one is liable for an unwitting act like a deliberate act, and for an unavoidable accident like a willing act. The Gemara questions this, noting the verse is needed to teach that pain is compensated even where there is no injury, but resolves that the extra word 'under' implies both.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where are these matters (that one is liable for damages even when acting unintentionally) derived?

sub.text: Chizkiya and the Tanna of the school of Chizkiya
sub.text_en: Chizkiya and the Tanna of the school of Chizkiya
sub.desc_en: Chizkiya and the Tanna of the school of Chizkiya answer: The verse 'פֶּצַע תַּחַת פָּצַע' (wound for wound) teaches that one is liable for an unintentional act as for an intentional one, and for an act under duress as for a willing one.
The Gemara objects: This verse is needed to teach that pain (צער) is compensated even where there is no permanent damage (נזק)!
The Gemara resolves: If that were the only intent, the verse would have said 'פֶּצַע בְּפָצַע' (wound for wound); the extra word 'תַּחַת' (under) teaches both lessons.

items.text: Rabbah's first case: stone in bosom, unknown
items.text_en: Rabbah's first case: stone in bosom, unknown
items.desc_en: Rabbah presents a case where a stone was placed in one's bosom and he was unaware of it, then stood and it fell. He rules: liable for damages, but exempt from the four additional payments; for Shabbat, exempt because a prohibited labor requires intent; for exile, exempt; for a Canaanite slave, it is a dispute between Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and the Rabbis, as cited in a baraita about a slave who injures his master.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah states a case: A stone was placed in one's lap without his knowledge, and when he stood up it fell; for damages (נזקין) he is liable, for the four additional payments (ארבעה דברים) he is exempt, for Shabbat liability he is exempt (since מלאכת מחשבת is required), and for exile (גלות) he is exempt.
