Rabbah adds: Regarding a slave (עבד), the ruling depends on a dispute between Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and the Rabbis, as cited in a baraita about a master who is a physician and instructs the slave to injure him.

The baraita teaches: If a master who is a physician told his slave 'gouge my eye' and he blinded it, or 'knock out my tooth' and he did so, the slave is considered to have 'played with the master' and goes free.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says: The verse 'וְשִׁחֲתָהּ' (and he destroyed it) implies that the slave is only freed if he intended to destroy (i.e., the injury was intentional).

items.text: Rabbah's second case: stone known but forgotten
items.text_en: Rabbah's second case: stone known but forgotten
items.desc_en: Rabbah presents a case where one knew of the stone but forgot it, then stood and it fell. He rules: liable for damages; exempt from the four additional payments; liable for exile because the verse 'unwittingly' implies prior knowledge; exempt for Shabbat; for a slave, it is the same dispute between Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and the Rabbis.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah states a second case: He knew about the stone but forgot it, then stood up and it fell; for damages he is liable.

Rabbah continues: For the four additional payments he is exempt; for exile he is liable because the verse 'בִּשְׁגָגָה' (unintentionally) implies prior knowledge, which existed; for Shabbat he is exempt.
Rabbah concludes: Regarding a slave, the ruling again depends on the dispute between Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and the Rabbis.

items.text: Rabbah's third case: intended to throw two, threw four
items.text_en: Rabbah's third case: intended to throw two, threw four
items.desc_en: Rabbah presents a case where one intended to throw two cubits but threw four. He rules: liable for damages; exempt from the four additional payments; for Shabbat, exempt because a prohibited labor requires intent; for exile, exempt because the verse 'who did not lie in wait' excludes this case; for a slave, the same dispute.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah states a third case: He intended to throw two (cubits) but threw four; for damages he is liable.

Rabbah continues: For the four additional payments he is exempt; for Shabbat, intent (מלאכת מחשבת) is required; for exile, the verse 'אֲשֶׁר לֹא צָדָה' (who did not lie in wait) excludes one who intended to throw two but threw four.
Rabbah concludes: Regarding a slave, the ruling again depends on the dispute between Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and the Rabbis.

items.text: Rabbah's fourth case: intended to throw four, threw eight
items.text_en: Rabbah's fourth case: intended to throw four, threw eight
items.desc_en: Rabbah presents a case where one intended to throw four cubits but threw eight. He rules: liable for damages; exempt from the four additional payments; for Shabbat, liable only if he said 'wherever it will rest'; for exile, exempt; for a slave, the same dispute.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah states a fourth case: He intended to throw four (cubits) but threw eight; for damages he is liable.

Rabbah continues: For the four additional payments he is exempt; for Shabbat, liability depends on whether he said 'let it rest wherever it will' (כׇּל מָקוֹם שֶׁתִּרְצֶה תָּנוּחַ); for exile, the verse 'אֲשֶׁר לֹא צָדָה' excludes this case.
Rabbah concludes: Regarding a slave, the ruling again depends on the dispute between Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and the Rabbis.

items.text: Rabbah's fifth case: throwing a vessel, another breaks it
items.text_en: Rabbah's fifth case: throwing a vessel, another breaks it
items.desc_en: Rabbah rules that if one threw a vessel from a roof and another came and broke it with a stick, the latter is exempt, because he broke a broken vessel.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah states: If one threw a vessel from the roof and another came and broke it with a stick, the second person is exempt.
Rabbah explains the reason: He broke a vessel that was already broken (i.e., destined to break anyway).

items.text: Rabbah's sixth case: throwing a vessel onto cushions, another removes them
items.text_en: Rabbah's sixth case: throwing a vessel onto cushions, another removes them
items.desc_en: Rabbah rules that if one threw a vessel from a roof and there were cushions or blankets underneath, and another removed them or the thrower removed them beforehand, the remover is exempt, because at the time of throwing the arrows were already stopped.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah states: If one threw a vessel from the roof and there were cushions or blankets underneath, and another person removed them, or the thrower himself removed them, the remover is exempt.
Rabbah explains: At the time he threw it, his 'arrows' (i.e., the force of the throw) had already ceased (since the cushions would have stopped it).

items.text: Rabbah's seventh case: throwing a child, another catches with a sword
items.text_en: Rabbah's seventh case: throwing a child, another catches with a sword
items.desc_en: Rabbah presents a case where one threw a child from a roof and another caught him with a sword, and notes it is a dispute between Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira and the Rabbis, citing a baraita about ten people hitting one person with ten sticks.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah states: If one threw a child from the roof and another caught him with a sword (killing him), the ruling depends on a dispute between Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira and the Rabbis.
The baraita teaches: If ten people struck him with ten sticks (whether simultaneously or sequentially), all of them...

items.text: Continuation of Mishnah: liability when one ox gores another
items.text_en: Continuation of Mishnah: liability when one ox gores another
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one ox gores another and the second ox dies, the owner of the first ox is exempt. Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira says that if the goring happened one after the other, the last ox is liable because it hastened the death.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one ox gores another and the second ox dies, the owner of the first ox is exempt. Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira says that if the goring happened one after the other, the last ox is liable because it hastened the death.

items.text: Dispute about the valuation of a gored ox
items.text_en: Dispute about the valuation of a gored ox
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that if an ox came and received the goring with its horns, there is a dispute between Rabbi Yishmael ben Yochanan ben Beroka and the Rabbis regarding the interpretation of 'and he shall give the ransom of his soul' – whether it means the value of the injured party or the value of the injurer.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the dispute between Rabbi Yishmael ben Yochanan ben Beroka and the Rabbis over the interpretation of 'and he shall give the ransom of his soul' as referring to the value of the injured party.

sub.text: Rabbi Yishmael ben Yochanan ben Beroka
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yishmael ben Yochanan ben Beroka
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael ben Yochanan ben Beroka argues that the ransom is the value of the one responsible for the damage, i.e., the owner of the ox.

items.text: Rabbah's rulings on falling from a roof and liability for boshet
items.text_en: Rabbah's rulings on falling from a roof and liability for boshet
items.desc_en: Rabbah rules that if one falls from a roof and becomes lodged in a woman, he is liable for four items (nezek, tza'ar, ripui, shevet) but not for boshet because boshet requires intent. He further distinguishes between a common wind (liable for four items but not boshet) and an uncommon wind (liable only for nezek). The Gemara supports this with a brayta about the verse 'and she put forth her hand' teaching that if one intends to damage, he is liable even if he did not intend to embarrass.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah rules that if one falls from a roof and is inserted into a woman, he is liable for the four types of indemnity, but if she is his yevama, he does not acquire her.
The Gemara explains that the four types are damage, pain, medical costs, and loss of livelihood, but not humiliation, because one is not liable for humiliation unless he intended to humiliate.

Rabbah distinguishes between falling due to an atypical wind (liable only for damage) and a typical wind (liable for four types but not humiliation), and if he tumbled, he is liable even for humiliation.
The Gemara cites a baraita from the verse 'and she put forth her hand' to support that one who intends to damage is liable even if he did not intend to humiliate.

items.text: Rabbah and Rava on placing a coal on someone's heart or garment
items.text_en: Rabbah and Rava on placing a coal on someone's heart or garment
items.desc_en: Rabbah rules that if one places a coal on another's heart and he dies, he is exempt; if on his garment and it burns, he is liable. Rava notes that both cases are taught in a Mishnah: pressing someone into fire or water from which he cannot escape makes one liable, while pushing him into fire or water from which he can escape makes one exempt; and the case of the garment is like the Mishnah about tearing a garment or breaking a jug where one is liable unless done with intent to be exempt.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah rules that placing a coal on another's heart, causing death, exempts the one who placed it; but placing it on his garment, causing it to burn, makes him liable.

Rava notes that both of Rabbah's rulings are taught in a Mishnah: pressing someone into fire or water from which he cannot escape makes one liable, while pushing him into fire or water from which he can escape makes one exempt.
Rava cites the Mishnah about tearing a garment or breaking a jug, where one is liable unless the owner explicitly says 'on condition that you are exempt'.

items.text: Rabbah's query about placing a coal on a slave's heart
items.text_en: Rabbah's query about placing a coal on a slave's heart
items.desc_en: Rabbah asks: if one places a coal on his slave's heart, is the slave considered like his body (so he is exempt) or like his property (so he is liable)? He then resolves that a slave is like his body, but his ox is like his property.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah asks whether placing a coal on a slave's heart is treated like his body (exempt) or like his property (liable).
Rabbah raises a conditional follow-up: if a slave is like his body, what is the ruling for his ox?
Rabbah resolves the dilemma: a slave is like his body, but an ox is like his property.

items.text: Conclusion of the previous chapter
items.text_en: Conclusion of the previous chapter
items.desc_en: The Gemara marks the end of the chapter 'Keitzad haRegel'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara marks the end of the chapter 'Keitzad haRegel'.

items.text: Opening Mishnah of the new chapter: leaving a jug in the public domain
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah of the new chapter: leaving a jug in the public domain
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states: If one leaves a jug in the public domain and another comes and stumbles on it and breaks it, the latter is exempt. But if he is injured by it, the owner of the jug is liable for his damage.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the case of one who leaves a jug in the public domain: if another stumbles and breaks it, he is exempt; but if he is injured, the owner is liable for his damage.

items.text: Gemara's question about the interchangeability of 'kad' and 'chavit'
items.text_en: Gemara's question about the interchangeability of 'kad' and 'chavit'
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah begins with 'kad' (jug) and ends with 'chavit' (barrel), and cites other Mishnayot with similar inconsistencies. Rav Papa explains that 'kad' and 'chavit' are the same vessel, and the practical difference is for buying and selling. The Gemara clarifies that in a place where most people call a 'kad' a 'kad' and a 'chavit' a 'chavit', but some call a 'chavit' a 'kad', we follow the majority.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes the inconsistency in the Mishnah, which begins with 'kad' (jug) and ends with 'chavit' (barrel).
The Gemara cites another Mishnah (31b) that also switches between 'chavit' and 'kad', showing the inconsistency is common.
The Gemara cites yet another Mishnah (115a) with the same interchange, reinforcing the pattern.
Rav Papa explains that 'kad' and 'chavit' are the same vessel, and the practical difference is for buying and selling.
The Gemara asks in what circumstances this matters, and rejects the case where the terms are completely distinct.
The Gemara clarifies that the case is where most people use distinct terms but some interchange them, and we follow the majority.

items.text: Gemara's inference from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's inference from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah teaches that in monetary cases we do not follow the majority, as the first passerby is not liable despite the statistical likelihood of stumbling.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that in monetary matters the court does not follow the majority principle.

items.text: Question and three Amoraic answers
items.text_en: Question and three Amoraic answers
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the second person who stumbles is exempt, since he should have watched his step. Three Amoraim offer different scenarios: Rav says the street was filled with barrels, Shmuel says it was dark, and Rabbi Yochanan says it was a corner.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the second person who stumbles and breaks the barrel is exempt, since he should have examined the road.
Rav explains that the mishna deals with a case where the owner filled the entire public domain with barrels, blocking the path.
Shmuel explains that the mishna was taught regarding a case where it was dark, so the pedestrian could not see the barrel.
Rabbi Yochanan explains that the mishna deals with a case where the barrel was placed at a corner, so the pedestrian could not see it in advance.

items.text: Rav Pappa's challenge and Rav Zevid's resolution
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's challenge and Rav Zevid's resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa argues that the Mishnah does not align with Rav's view, as it specifically says 'stumbled' implying only stumbling, not breaking. Rav Zevid explains that the Mishnah uses 'stumbled' in the first clause to parallel the second clause where only stumbling matters.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa objects that the Mishnah is precise only according to Shmuel or Rabbi Yochanan, because if it followed Rav, why specify 'stumbled' when even intentional breaking would be exempt.

sub.text: Rav Zevid in the name of Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Zevid in the name of Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Zevid resolves that the same law applies even if he broke it intentionally; the Mishnah uses 'stumbled' in the first clause to parallel the second clause where only stumbling matters, since if he broke it intentionally he damaged himself.

items.text: Rabbi Abba's alternative explanation
items.text_en: Rabbi Abba's alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba reports in the name of Rabbi Ulla that the exemption is because people are not accustomed to watch their steps carefully in the roads.

sub.text: Rabbi Abba in the name of Rabbi Ulla
sub.text_en: Rabbi Abba in the name of Rabbi Ulla
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba reports in the name of Rabbi Ulla that the exemption is because people are not accustomed to watch their steps carefully in the roads.

items.text: Incidents in Nehardea and Pumbedita
items.text_en: Incidents in Nehardea and Pumbedita
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that Shmuel in Nehardea and Rava in Pumbedita both held someone liable for stumbling. Rav Pappa explains that Rava's case involved a narrow alley where one should have watched his step.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports two incidents: in נהרדעא (Nehardea) שמואל (Shmuel) held the pedestrian liable, and in פומבדיתא (Pumbedita) רבא (Rava) also held the pedestrian liable.
The Gemara questions: Granted, שמואל (Shmuel) ruled according to his own opinion, but does רבא (Rava) also hold like שמואל (Shmuel)?

רב פפא (Rav Pappa) explains that the incident in פומבדיתא (Pumbedita) occurred at a narrow alley near an olive press, where people placed jugs with permission, so the pedestrian should have watched his step.

items.text: Rav Chisda's query and Rav Nachman's response on self-help
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's query and Rav Nachman's response on self-help
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda asks Rav Nachman about the penalty for using a shovel or basket to strike someone. Rav Nachman rebukes him for imposing fines in Babylonia and asks for the facts. Rav Chisda describes a case where one person took water on another's day, and the victim struck him with a shovel. Rav Nachman rules that even those who prohibit self-help allow it where there is potential loss.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda (רב חסדא) asks Rav Nachman (רב נחמן) about the penalty for striking with a shovel or basket, given the known penalties for kneeing, kicking, and punching.
Rav Nachman (רב נחמן) rebukes Rav Chisda (רב חסדא) for imposing fines in Babylonia and demands the facts of the incident.
Rav Chisda (רב חסדא) describes the incident: a shared cistern where one person drew water on the other's day, and the victim struck him with a shovel.
Rav Nachman (רב נחמן) rules that even those who prohibit self-help allow it where there is potential loss, so the striker was justified.

items.text: Dispute between Rav Yehuda and Rav Nachman on self-help
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav Yehuda and Rav Nachman on self-help
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a dispute: Rav Yehuda says one may not take the law into his own hands, while Rav Nachman says he may. They agree that where there is potential loss, one may act; the dispute is only where there is no loss, with Rav Yehuda requiring going to court and Rav Nachman allowing self-help since it is just.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a dispute: Rav Yehuda says a person may not take justice into his own hands, while Rav Nachman says he may.

The Gemara clarifies that where there is potential loss, all agree one may act; the dispute is only where there is no loss, with Rav Yehuda requiring going to court and Rav Nachman allowing self-help since it is just.

items.text: Rav Kahana's objection and incomplete response
items.text_en: Rav Kahana's objection and incomplete response
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana cites a baraita where Ben Bag Bag says one should break the other's teeth and take his own, implying self-help is allowed even without loss. The Gemara begins a response but is cut off.

sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana raises an objection by citing a baraita from Ben Bag Bag, who says one should break the other's teeth and take his own, implying self-help is permitted even without loss.
The Gemara begins a response to Rav Kahana's objection but the text is cut off, leaving the response incomplete.

items.text: Rejection of Ben Bag Bag's view and Rabbi Yannai's interpretation
items.text_en: Rejection of Ben Bag Bag's view and Rabbi Yannai's interpretation
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the earlier proof from Ben Bag Bag, noting he is an individual against the Sages. Rabbi Yannai explains the phrase 'break his teeth' refers to a court case, but the Gemara raises textual difficulties with this reading.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the proof from Ben Bag Bag, noting he is an individual opinion against the Sages.
Rabbi Yannai explains that 'break his teeth' means to sue in court.
The Gemara raises textual difficulties with Rabbi Yannai's interpretation, noting the baraita's wording is inconsistent with a court proceeding.

items.text: First baraita: ox climbing on another
items.text_en: First baraita: ox climbing on another
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about an ox climbing on another to kill it, where the lower owner is exempt if he dislodges his ox. The Gemara initially assumes this supports self-help when there is no loss, but then distinguishes between a tam and a mu'ad, and adds a condition about opportunity to dislodge.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about an ox climbing on another, where the lower owner is exempt if he dislodges his ox, and asks if this supports self-help when there is no loss.
The Gemara rejects the proof, explaining that the baraita deals with a tam (innocuous ox) where there is a loss.
The Gemara objects that the latter clause says if he pushed the upper ox and it died, he is liable, which would be inconsistent with a tam.
The Gemara answers that he is liable because he could have dislodged his own ox but instead pushed the other, so self-help is limited.

items.text: Second baraita: filling a courtyard with jugs
items.text_en: Second baraita: filling a courtyard with jugs
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita where a person fills another's courtyard with jugs and the owner breaks them to exit. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains this refers to breaking to go to court, not self-help.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita where a person fills another's courtyard with jugs and the owner breaks them to exit, suggesting self-help is permitted.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that the owner breaks the jugs only to go to court or bring proof, not as outright self-help.

items.text: Third baraita: the bored slave whose term ended
items.text_en: Third baraita: the bored slave whose term ended
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about a bored slave whose master delays his release; the slave is exempt for injuring the master. The Gemara initially questions this, then explains it refers to a thieving slave or one given a Canaanite maidservant, where the master's authority changes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about a bored slave whose master delays his release, deriving from a verse that the master is exempt for injuring the slave, suggesting one may take justice into his own hands.
The Gemara explains the baraita deals with a thieving slave, where the master has a financial loss, so he may act.
The Gemara objects: if he didn't steal before, why would he start now? It answers that the slave's fear of his master is gone after freedom.

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's alternative explanation
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's alternative explanation
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak offers an alternative: the slave was given a Canaanite maidservant, and now staying would be prohibited, so the master acts as a court agent.

items.text: Fourth baraita: jug in public domain
items.text_en: Fourth baraita: jug in public domain
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about one who leaves a jug in the public domain and another trips and breaks it; the latter is exempt. The Gemara infers that if he broke it intentionally he would be liable, but Rav Zevid in the name of Rava says the same applies even if he broke it, and the wording is due to the latter clause.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about one who leaves a jug in the public domain and another trips and breaks it; the latter is exempt, implying that if he broke it intentionally he would be liable.

sub.text: Rav Zevid in the name of Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Zevid in the name of Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Zevid in the name of Rava rejects the proof, stating that the same ruling applies even if he broke it intentionally, and the wording is due to the latter clause.

items.text: Fifth baraita: the woman who cuts off her hand
items.text_en: Fifth baraita: the woman who cuts off her hand
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita interpreting 'you shall cut off her hand' as monetary compensation, initially assuming it applies when she cannot save herself otherwise. The Gemara then clarifies that when she cannot save herself, she is like a court agent and exempt.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita interpreting 'you shall cut off her hand' as monetary compensation, and asks whether it applies when she cannot save herself otherwise, then answers that it is when she can save herself by other means.

The Gemara objects: if she cannot save herself by other means, is she exempt? If so, the baraita should have distinguished within the case itself rather than teaching a separate exclusion for a court agent.
The Gemara resolves: the baraita indeed means that when she cannot save herself by other means, her hand is like a court agent and she is exempt.

items.text: Sixth baraita: public path through a field
items.text_en: Sixth baraita: public path through a field
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about a public path through one's field; if the owner moves it to the side, his gift is void. The Gemara questions why he cannot take the law into his own hands, and answers with a decree against giving a crooked path, citing Rav Yehudah's principle that a path held by the public cannot be disturbed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about a public path through a field, where the owner's alternative route is void, to challenge the principle of taking justice into one's own hands.
The Gemara objects: if one may take justice into his own hands, why can't the owner block the original path with a stick?

sub.text: Rav Zevid in the name of Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Zevid in the name of Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Zevid answers that it is a rabbinic decree, lest the owner give them a circuitous route.
Rav Mesharshiya says the baraita refers to a case where he actually gave them a circuitous route.
Rav Ashi says any side route is inherently circuitous, being close for some and far for others.
The Gemara objects: if the side route is invalid, why can't the owner reclaim his original path?
The Gemara answers that a path held by the public cannot be disturbed, citing Rav Yehudah's principle.

items.text: Seventh baraita: pe'ah from one side, poor take from another
items.text_en: Seventh baraita: pe'ah from one side, poor take from another
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about a homeowner who leaves pe'ah on one side and poor people take from another; both are considered pe'ah. The Gemara questions why the owner cannot take the law into his own hands, and Rava explains that 'both are pe'ah' means only to exempt from tithes, citing a related baraita.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about a homeowner who leaves pe'ah on one side and poor people take from another; both are considered pe'ah, and questions why the owner cannot take the law into his own hands.
Rava explains that 'both are pe'ah' means only to exempt from tithes, not that the owner cannot prevent them.
A baraita is cited to support Rava's explanation, showing that ownerless produce is exempt from tithes.

items.text: Mishnah and beginning of Gemara: broken jug in public domain
items.text_en: Mishnah and beginning of Gemara: broken jug in public domain
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one's jug breaks in the public domain and another is injured by the water or shards, the owner is liable; Rabbi Yehudah distinguishes between intentional and unintentional. The Gemara begins with Rav Yehudah citing Rav, limiting the case to when the water soiled the other's vessels.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one's jug breaks in the public domain and another is injured by the water or shards, the owner is liable; Rabbi Yehudah distinguishes between intentional and unintentional.

sub.text: Rav Yehudah in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehudah in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehudah citing Rav limits the Mishnah's liability to cases where the water soiled the other's vessels.

items.text: Rav and Shmuel's dispute on liability for one's stones, knife, and load
items.text_en: Rav and Shmuel's dispute on liability for one's stones, knife, and load
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites Shmuel's view that one's stones, knife, and load are exempt for killing a person or damaging vessels, but liable for injuring a person. Rav distinguishes between cases where the objects were declared ownerless (exempt) and where they were not (liable).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Shmuel's ruling that one's stones, knife, and load are exempt for killing a person or damaging vessels, but liable for injuring a person.
Rav distinguishes between cases where the objects were declared ownerless (exempt) and where they were not (liable).

items.text: Rav Oshaya's objection from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Rav Oshaya's objection from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rav Oshaya cites the Mishnah that exempts vessels damaged by a pit, comparing it to one's stones, knife, and load. The Gemara corrects the Mishnah's wording to align with the comparison.

sub.desc_en: Rav Oshaya cites the Mishnah that exempts vessels damaged by a pit, comparing it to one's stones, knife, and load.
The Gemara corrects the Mishnah's wording from 'דומה לזה' (resembles this) to 'דומה לזה' (this resembles), aligning the comparison with the stones, knife, and load.

items.text: Contradiction between the Mishnah's beginning and end
items.text_en: Contradiction between the Mishnah's beginning and end
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's beginning (exempt for vessels) contradicts Rav, and its end (liable if one smashed a flask against a stone) contradicts Shmuel. It then points out an internal contradiction within the Mishnah itself.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one smashed his flask against a stone, he is liable.
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah's beginning contradicts Rav's position and its end contradicts Shmuel's position.
The Gemara further objects that the Mishnah itself is internally contradictory, as its beginning exempts and its end imposes liability.

items.text: Rav and Shmuel resolve the contradiction according to their views
items.text_en: Rav and Shmuel resolve the contradiction according to their views
items.desc_en: Rav explains the Mishnah as referring to ownerless objects (exempt) but not ownerless (liable), so the end case is liable. Shmuel explains that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yehuda, who holds one liable for vessel damage in a pit, so the end case is liable.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that Rav and Shmuel each resolve the contradiction in the baraita according to their own reasoning.

Rav resolves the contradiction by explaining that the baraita's ruling of exemption applies only when the objects were renounced (הפקר), but if not renounced, the owner is liable, so the end case where one drops a flask on a stone is liable.

Shmuel resolves the contradiction by explaining that since the cases of stone, knife, and load are analogous to a pit, and according to Rabbi Yehuda one is liable for vessel damage in a pit, the end case where one drops a flask on a stone is liable.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's distinction and dispute with Rabbi Natan
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's distinction and dispute with Rabbi Natan
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar limits liability to when one tripped over the stone and was scratched by it, but exempts if tripped on the ground and scratched by the stone. The Gemara notes this aligns with Rabbi Natan's view, and an alternative version holds Rabbi Elazar liable even in the latter case, aligning with Rabbi Natan.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar states that liability applies only when one tripped over the stone and was scratched by it, but if he tripped on the ground and was scratched by the stone, the owner is exempt.
The Gemara notes that this ruling is not in accordance with Rabbi Natan's opinion.
An alternative version holds that Rabbi Elazar deems the owner liable even if one tripped on the ground and was scratched by the stone, aligning with Rabbi Natan's view.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's opinion on intentional dropping and Rabbi Meir's liability for an unavoidable accident
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's opinion on intentional dropping and Rabbi Meir's liability for an unavoidable accident
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains Rabbi Yehuda's case of intentional dropping (lowering from the shoulder). Abaye questions whether Rabbi Meir would hold liable even if the jug slipped, and Rava confirms yes. The Gemara objects that an unavoidable accident is exempt by Torah law, but distinguishes between killing and damages, citing a baraita where Rabbi Meir holds liable for damages even in such cases.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Yehuda's statement that one is liable for intentional dropping, and asks what constitutes 'intentional'.
Rabbah defines intentional dropping as intending to lower the jug from below the shoulder.
Abaye asks whether Rabbi Meir would hold liable even if the jug slipped unintentionally.
Rava confirms that Rabbi Meir would hold liable even if the handle was in his hand and the jug slipped.
The Gemara objects that an unavoidable accident (אונס) is exempt by Torah law, citing the verse 'to the girl you shall do nothing'.

The Gemara resolves that the exemption applies only to capital cases, but for damages Rabbi Meir holds liable, citing a baraita where Rabbi Meir obligates one for damages even in cases of unavoidable accident.

items.text: Opening Mishnah and initial clarification
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and initial clarification
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who stumbles and falls is exempt from human court but liable in heavenly court. The Gemara then notes that the Sages agree with Rabbi Meir in certain cases of damage caused by objects placed on a roof, and Rabbi Meir agrees with the Sages in other cases, establishing a partial consensus.

items.text: Abaye's explanation of the dispute
items.text_en: Abaye's explanation of the dispute
items.desc_en: Abaye explains that the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages involves two separate issues: first, whether stumbling constitutes negligence (during the fall), and second, whether one who abandons his damaging property is liable (after the fall). Each side holds different positions on these two matters.

items.text: Proof from the Mishnah and Baraita
items.text_en: Proof from the Mishnah and Baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara provides proof for Abaye's interpretation by analyzing the Mishnah's phrasing, which mentions two separate cases: slipping in water (during the fall) and being struck by a potsherd (after the fall). It then argues that the Baraita similarly addresses both scenarios.

items.text: Clarifying the case of a camel falling into water
items.text_en: Clarifying the case of a camel falling into water
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a camel can be damaged during the fall, since if there is an alternative path, the owner is negligent, and if not, it is unavoidable. Rav Acha suggests a case where the camel crosses a narrow river path and stumbles, causing damage. The Gemara then refines this to a scenario where the camel stumbles and falls onto another object.

items.text: Intent in abandoning damages
items.text_en: Intent in abandoning damages
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what intent could be involved in the case of abandoning one's damaging property. Rav Yosef and Rav Ashi explain that the owner intends to claim the broken pottery (the remnants of the damaged item), which constitutes a deliberate act.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's alternative view
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's alternative view
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar argues that the dispute is only during the fall, implying that after the fall all agree. The Gemara challenges this, noting that Rabbi Meir and the Sages disagree on both points. It concludes that Rabbi Elazar means 'even during the fall,' aligning with Abaye's position.

items.text: Clarifying Rabbi Yochanan's position on the dispute's timing
items.text_en: Clarifying Rabbi Yochanan's position on the dispute's timing
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Yochanan's statement that the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis is only after the fall, but during the fall all agree. It infers from his later comment that Rabbi Meir would hold liable, implying the Rabbis would exempt, but then reinterprets that the Rabbis exempt only in this case of an unavoidable accident, but elsewhere they would hold liable for abandoning damaging property.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Yochanan's statement that the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis is only after the fall.

The Gemara infers from Rabbi Yochanan's later comment that Rabbi Meir would hold liable, implying that during the fall all agree he is exempt, but this contradicts the inference that Rabbi Meir holds liable.
The Gemara alternatively infers that during the fall all agree he is liable, but this contradicts the inference that the Rabbis would exempt.
The Gemara resolves that the Rabbis exempt only in this case of an unavoidable accident (אונס), but elsewhere they would hold liable for abandoning damaging property.

items.text: The dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar on מפקיר נזקיו
items.text_en: The dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar on מפקיר נזקיו
items.desc_en: It is stated that Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar disagree about one who abandons his damaging property: one says liable, one says exempt. The Gemara suggests that the one who says liable follows Rabbi Meir, and the one who says exempt follows the Rabbis. It then clarifies that all agree regarding Rabbi Meir's view, and the dispute is only according to the Rabbis: the one who exempts follows the Rabbis, while the one who says liable argues that the Rabbis only exempt in this case of an unavoidable accident, but elsewhere they would hold liable.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar disagree about one who abandons his damaging property: one says liable, one says exempt.
The Gemara suggests that the one who says liable follows Rabbi Meir, and the one who says exempt follows the Rabbis.

The Gemara clarifies that all agree regarding Rabbi Meir's view, and the dispute is only according to the Rabbis: the one who exempts follows the Rabbis, while the one who says liable argues that the Rabbis only exempt in this case of an unavoidable accident, but elsewhere they would hold liable.

items.text: Proof that Rabbi Elazar holds liable from a principle of Rabbi Yishmael
items.text_en: Proof that Rabbi Elazar holds liable from a principle of Rabbi Yishmael
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Elazar is the one who says liable, citing a statement from Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Yishmael: two things are not in a person's control, yet the Torah treats them as if they are in his control—a pit in the public domain and leaven after the sixth hour. This supports liability for abandoning damaging property.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Elazar is the one who holds liable, citing a statement from Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Yishmael that two things not in a person's control—a pit in the public domain and leaven after the sixth hour—are treated by the Torah as if they are in his control.

items.text: Contradiction from a mishna and resolution by Rava and Rav Ashi
items.text_en: Contradiction from a mishna and resolution by Rava and Rav Ashi
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that Rabbi Elazar said the opposite in a mishna about one who overturns dung in the public domain: if he intended to acquire it he is liable, but if not, he is exempt, implying that one who abandons his damaging property is exempt. Rav Adda bar Ahavah and Ravina offer a parable of a covered pit that was uncovered again, but Mar Zutra rejects it. Rav Ashi resolves that the mishna refers to overturning less than three handbreadths, and Rava explains that the mishna's language 'overturned' implies less than three handbreadths, so the exemption only applies when he did not intend to acquire, but otherwise he is liable.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that Rabbi Elazar said the opposite in a mishna about overturning dung in the public domain, implying that one who abandons his damaging property is exempt.
Rav Adda bar Ahavah answers that the mishna refers to one who returned the dung to its place, and Ravina illustrates this with a parable of a covered pit that was uncovered again.

Mar Zutra objects that the parable is not analogous because in the pit case the first action is not nullified, whereas here it is, and proposes a different analogy of a pit that was filled and then re-dug.
Rav Ashi resolves that the mishna refers to overturning the dung less than three handbreadths high.

sub.text: Gemara's question on Rav Ashi's resolution
sub.text_en: Gemara's question on Rav Ashi's resolution
sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Rabbi Elazar was forced to interpret the mishna as less than three handbreadths, rather than above three handbreadths where one would be liable even without intent to acquire.
Rava explains that the mishna's language 'overturned' implies less than three handbreadths, so the exemption only applies when he did not intend to acquire, but otherwise he is liable.

items.text: Contradiction from Rabbi Yochanan's own statements and resolution
items.text_en: Contradiction from Rabbi Yochanan's own statements and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that from the previous conclusion, Rabbi Elazar says liable and Rabbi Yochanan says exempt. But it brings a mishna where Rabbi Yochanan said that one who places thorns or glass in the public domain is liable only if they protrude, but if they are flush with the wall he is exempt, implying that abandoning damaging property is liable. The Gemara initially deflects by saying the exemption is because people don't rub against walls. Then it brings another contradiction: Rabbi Yochanan said the halakha follows an anonymous mishna that one who digs a pit in the public domain is liable. The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Yochanan actually holds liable, reversing the earlier assignment.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the conclusion from the previous discussion: Rabbi Elazar holds liable, Rabbi Yochanan holds exempt.

The Gemara objects by citing a mishna where one who places thorns or glass in the public domain is liable, and Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that only protruding items are liable, implying that abandoning damaging property (מפקיר נזקיו) is liable, contradicting the earlier assignment of Rabbi Yochanan as exempt.

The Gemara deflects by citing Rav Acha bar Rav Ika's explanation that the exemption for flush items is because people do not rub against walls, not because of the principle of abandoning damaging property.

The Gemara raises another contradiction: Rabbi Yochanan ruled that the halakha follows an anonymous mishna stating that one who digs a pit in the public domain is liable, implying that abandoning damaging property is liable.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yochanan actually holds liable, reversing the earlier assignment and concluding that Rabbi Yochanan holds liable for abandoning damaging property.

items.text: Final reversal: Rabbi Elazar says exempt
items.text_en: Final reversal: Rabbi Elazar says exempt
items.desc_en: The Gemara now infers that if Rabbi Yochanan says liable, then Rabbi Elazar must say exempt. It cites a statement from Rabbi Elazar that supports exemption, but the text is cut off.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers that since Rabbi Yochanan holds liable, Rabbi Elazar must hold exempt, and begins to cite a statement from Rabbi Elazar that would support exemption.

items.text: Resolution of contradiction regarding Rabbi Yishmael
items.text_en: Resolution of contradiction regarding Rabbi Yishmael
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves a contradiction between two statements attributed to Rabbi Yishmael by distinguishing between his own opinion and that of his teacher.

items.text: Mishnah: Liability for damage in public domain
items.text_en: Mishnah: Liability for damage in public domain
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists cases where one is liable for damage caused by objects placed or fallen in the public domain, such as pouring water, hiding thorns, or a fallen fence.

items.text: Gemara on pouring water: Rav's distinction and Rav Huna's challenge
items.text_en: Gemara on pouring water: Rav's distinction and Rav Huna's challenge
items.desc_en: Rav limits liability to cases where one's vessels were soiled, but exempts the person himself because the ground caused the damage. Rav Huna challenges this, and the Gemara explains the distinction between dry and wet seasons, citing a baraita about permission to drain water.

items.text: Gemara on hiding thorns: Rabbi Yochanan's distinction
items.text_en: Gemara on hiding thorns: Rabbi Yochanan's distinction
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan distinguishes between projecting thorns (liable) and flush ones (exempt), because people do not normally rub against walls.

items.text: Baraita on hiding thorns in a friend's wall and Ravina's ruling
items.text_en: Baraita on hiding thorns in a friend's wall and Ravina's ruling
items.desc_en: A baraita discusses liability when one hides thorns in a friend's wall and the owner demolishes it, causing damage. Rabbi Yochanan distinguishes between a weak wall (hider liable) and a strong wall (owner liable). Ravina derives a principle about covering a pit with another's lid.

items.text: Practices of the early pious and definitions of piety
items.text_en: Practices of the early pious and definitions of piety
items.desc_en: The early pious would bury thorns deep in their fields to avoid plowing obstruction. Rav Sheshet and Rava disposed of thorns in fire and river. Rav Yehuda and Rava define piety as fulfilling laws of damages, Avot, or blessings.

items.text: Mishnah: Liability for straw and manure in public domain
items.text_en: Mishnah: Liability for straw and manure in public domain
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who puts out straw or manure for fertilizer is liable for damage, and anyone who takes them acquires them. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds that anyone who damages in public domain must pay. The Mishnah also discusses liability for turning over dung.

items.text: Gemara: Reconciling Mishnah with Rabbi Yehuda's opinion
items.text_en: Gemara: Reconciling Mishnah with Rabbi Yehuda's opinion
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah aligns with Rabbi Yehuda, who permits storing manure for 30 days. It resolves that Rabbi Yehuda agrees one must pay for damage caused. A baraita shows Rabbi Yehuda exempts for Chanukah lights due to mitzvah permission. Rav Nachman explains the Mishnah refers to a time other than manure season, and it follows Rabbi Yehuda. Rav Ashi offers an alternative resolution.

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Ze'iri
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Ze'iri
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who puts out straw or dung in the public domain is liable for damages, and whoever takes them first acquires them. Rav holds that both the body and its appreciation are acquired, while Ze'iri holds only the appreciation but not the body. The Gemara explains their disagreement: Rav holds that the Sages penalized the body because of the appreciation, while Ze'iri holds they did not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's rule that one who puts out straw or dung in the public domain is liable for damages, and whoever takes them first acquires them.
The Gemara presents the dispute: Rav holds that both the body and its appreciation are acquired, while Ze'iri holds only the appreciation but not the body.
The Gemara explains their disagreement: Rav holds that the Sages penalized the body because of the appreciation, while Ze'iri holds they did not.

items.text: Challenge from the Mishnah of overturning dung
items.text_en: Challenge from the Mishnah of overturning dung
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav and Ze'iri from a Mishnah about one who overturns dung in the public domain: it states liability but does not say 'whoever takes first acquires it'. The Gemara initially suggests that the first clause implies the latter, but then notes that the Mishnah says 'forbidden because of theft', which seems to contradict the idea of acquisition. The Gemara resolves that the prohibition applies to the one who took first and acquired it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav and Ze'iri from a Mishnah about one who overturns dung in the public domain: it states liability but does not say 'whoever takes first acquires it'.
The Gemara initially suggests that the first clause implies the latter, i.e., the same rule applies to the second case.
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah says 'forbidden because of theft', which seems to contradict the idea of acquisition.
The Gemara resolves that the prohibition applies to the one who took first and acquired it, i.e., the prohibition is against taking from the one who already acquired it.

items.text: Resolution by Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak
items.text_en: Resolution by Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a full baraita that distinguishes between straw/dung (which has appreciation) and dung (which does not). Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains: for an item that has appreciation, the Sages penalized its body because of the appreciation; for an item without appreciation, they did not penalize the body.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a full baraita that distinguishes between straw/dung (which has appreciation) and dung (which does not), showing the missing clause.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains: for an item that has appreciation, the Sages penalized its body because of the appreciation; for an item without appreciation, they did not penalize the body.

items.text: Question about timing of the penalty
items.text_en: Question about timing of the penalty
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: according to the one who says the body is penalized because of the appreciation, is the penalty immediate or only when the appreciation materializes? The Gemara attempts to answer from the case of dung, but rejects it because Rav Nachman's distinction was introduced later.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: according to the one who says the body is penalized because of the appreciation, is the penalty immediate or only when the appreciation materializes?
The Gemara attempts to answer from the case of dung, which implies the penalty is immediate.
The Gemara rejects the answer because Rav Nachman's distinction was introduced later, so the case of dung is no longer relevant.

items.text: Comparison with Tannaim about usurious documents
items.text_en: Comparison with Tannaim about usurious documents
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to align Rav and Ze'iri with a tannaitic dispute about a document with interest: Rabbi Meir penalizes both principal and interest, while the Sages allow collecting principal. Rav could be like Rabbi Meir, and Ze'iri like the Sages. However, Rav and Ze'iri each argue that their position is consistent even with the opposing Tanna's reasoning.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes aligning Rav and Ze'iri with a tannaitic dispute about a usurious document: Rabbi Meir penalizes both principal and interest, while the Sages allow collecting principal.
Rav argues that his position is consistent even with the Sages, because there the principal was permitted, but here the principal itself causes damage.
Ze'iri argues that his position is consistent even with Rabbi Meir, because there the damage was certain from the time of writing, but here it is uncertain whether the item will cause damage.

items.text: Dispute between Tanna Kamma and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
items.text_en: Dispute between Tanna Kamma and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Tanna Kamma says the body is forbidden due to theft, while Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel permits even the body. The Gemara explains that for Ze'iri, this is a clear tannaitic dispute. For Rav, the Gemara suggests that all agree the body is penalized, but they dispute whether to instruct the public accordingly (halacha ve'ein morin ken vs. halacha u'morin ken).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes to resolve the dispute between Rav and Ze'iri by citing a baraita where Tanna Kamma forbids the body due to theft.
The Gemara notes an internal contradiction in the baraita: it says both 'whoever takes them acquires' and 'they are forbidden due to theft'.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: Tanna Kamma means the improvement is acquired but the body is forbidden, while Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel permits even the body.
The Gemara states that for Ze'iri this is clearly a tannaitic dispute, but questions whether for Rav it is also a tannaitic dispute.
Rav explains that all agree the body is penalized due to its improvement, but they dispute whether to instruct the public accordingly (הלכה ואין מורין כן vs. הלכה ומורין כן).

items.text: Evidence from practice
items.text_en: Evidence from practice
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rav Huna and Rav Adda bar Ahava actually acted by declaring property ownerless, implying that the halacha is to permit taking the body, but the text is cut off.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the distinction between halacha and practice by noting that Rav Huna and Rav Adda bar Ahava actually declared property ownerless, implying the halacha permits taking the body.

items.text: Clarification of Rav Huna's ruling
items.text_en: Clarification of Rav Huna's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rav Huna's earlier ruling about stumbling, noting that Rav Adda bar Ahava's practice aligns with his own view, but Rav Huna's ruling seems contradictory. It resolves that the cases involved were permitted (i.e., the stumbling was not negligent).

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case: two potters walking one after another; the first stumbles and falls, and the second trips over him. The first is liable for the second's damages.

items.text: Gemara's analysis: Rabbi Yochanan and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis: Rabbi Yochanan and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that the Mishnah's ruling applies even to the Rabbis who consider a stumbler compelled (and thus exempt), because here the first should have stopped. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak adds that even if he need not stop, he should have warned. Rabbi Yochanan counters that if he need not stop, he is preoccupied and need not warn.

items.text: Proof from a baraita about a beam and a barrel
items.text_en: Proof from a baraita about a beam and a barrel
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita: if a beam-owner walks first and a barrel-owner behind, and the barrel breaks on the beam, the beam-owner is exempt unless he stopped. The Gemara initially assumes 'stopped' means to rest (which is normal), implying liability for not warning. It is rejected: the case is when he stopped to rest, but if he stopped to adjust his load, he is exempt. The baraita's extra clause teaches that even when stopping to rest, if he warned, he is exempt.

items.text: Proof from a baraita about potters and glassmakers
items.text_en: Proof from a baraita about potters and glassmakers
items.desc_en: Another baraita: potters walking in a line; if the first stumbles, he is liable to the second, and the second to the third. If they warned each other, they are exempt. The Gemara initially assumes this shows they need not stop, but it is rejected: they must stop. The baraita's extra clause teaches that even when they must stop, warning exempts.

items.text: Rava's distinction and the Gemara's challenge
items.text_en: Rava's distinction and the Gemara's challenge
items.desc_en: Rava rules: the first is liable for the second's bodily and property damages, but the second is liable only for the third's bodily damages, not property. The Gemara challenges: if a stumbler is negligent, the second should also be liable for property; if not negligent, even the first should be exempt.

items.text: Initial ruling on first and second fallers
items.text_en: Initial ruling on first and second fallers
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that the first person to fall into a pit is certainly negligent, while the second is liable for bodily injury but not for property damage, since he can claim he did not dig the pit.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rules that the first person to fall into a pit is certainly negligent, while the second is liable for bodily injury but exempt for property damage because he can claim he did not dig the pit.

items.text: Challenge from the baraita and resolution by Rav Adda bar Ahavah
items.text_en: Challenge from the baraita and resolution by Rav Adda bar Ahavah
items.desc_en: A baraita states that all are liable for bodily injury but exempt for property damage, implying even the first. Rav Adda bar Ahavah explains that 'all' refers to the injured parties, excluding the first. The Gemara questions why the baraita would use 'all' if it excludes the first.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the previous ruling by citing a baraita that states all are liable for bodily injury and exempt for property damage, asking if this includes even the first person.
Rav Adda bar Ahavah answers that the baraita excludes the first person, and 'all' refers to the injured parties, not the ones who caused the pit.
The Gemara objects that if the baraita excludes the first person, it should have said 'the injured parties' rather than 'all', which implies inclusion.

items.text: Rava's alternative ruling
items.text_en: Rava's alternative ruling
items.desc_en: Rava rules that the first is liable for both bodily injury and property damage of the second, while the second is liable only for bodily injury of the third, because the second is like a pit, and a pit does not render vessels liable.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that the first person is liable for both bodily injury and property damage of the second, while the second is liable only for bodily injury of the third, because the second is like a pit (בור), and a pit does not render vessels liable.

items.text: Challenge from Shmuel and Rav's dispute
items.text_en: Challenge from Shmuel and Rav's dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rava's reasoning works for Shmuel, who considers any obstacle a pit, but not for Rav, who requires the pit to be ownerless. The Gemara asks what can be said according to Rav.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rava's reasoning works for Shmuel, who considers any obstacle a pit, but asks what can be said according to Rav, who requires the pit to be ownerless.

items.text: Resolution by Rav Adda bar Minyomi
items.text_en: Resolution by Rav Adda bar Minyomi
items.desc_en: The Gemara returns to the original explanation and resolves the difficulty with the baraita by interpreting that it refers to cases where vessels were damaged by other vessels.

sub.text: Gemara's resolution via Rav Adda bar Minyomi
sub.text_en: Gemara's resolution via Rav Adda bar Minyomi
sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the difficulty by reverting to the original explanation, interpreting the baraita as referring to cases where vessels were damaged by other vessels.

items.text: Discussion of how the first causes the fall
items.text_en: Discussion of how the first causes the fall
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that if the fall was caused by the first person, he is liable for all damages. Rav Pappa and Rav Zevid offer analogies for how the first could cause the fall: like a ship's mast or a blind person's staff.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the principle: if the fall was caused by the first person, he is liable for all damages.
The Gemara asks: how could the first person cause the fall?
Rav Pappa answers: like a ship's mast that blocks the path, causing the second to fall.
Rav Zevid answers: like a blind person's staff that causes the second to trip.

items.text: Mishnah: Two people with a barrel and a beam
items.text_en: Mishnah: Two people with a barrel and a beam
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where one carries a barrel and another a beam; if the barrel breaks on the beam, both are exempt because each has the right to walk. If the beam carrier is first and the barrel carrier is second, the beam carrier is exempt.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the general case: two people carrying a barrel and a beam respectively, and if the barrel breaks on the beam, both are exempt because each has the right to walk.
The Mishnah adds a sub-case: if the beam carrier is first and the barrel carrier is second, the beam carrier is exempt from liability for the broken barrel.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Liability for collision between a beam and a barrel
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Liability for collision between a beam and a barrel
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents cases where a beam-carrier and a barrel-carrier collide in the public domain. If the beam-carrier was first and the barrel-carrier later, the beam-carrier is liable; if the beam-carrier stood still, he is exempt; if he told the barrel-carrier to stop, he is liable. The reverse scenario is also given, and a parallel case with fire and flax is mentioned.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the first case: if the beam-carrier stood still, he is liable; if he told the barrel-carrier to stop, he is exempt.
The Mishnah presents the reverse scenario and a parallel case with fire and flax.

items.text: Gemara: Question about harming one's wife during marital relations
items.text_en: Gemara: Question about harming one's wife during marital relations
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar Natan asks Rav Huna whether a husband who harms his wife during marital relations is liable, since he acts with permission. Rav Huna cites the Mishnah's principle that both have permission to walk. Rava argues a fortiori from the case of a forest, but the Gemara objects that the Mishnah explicitly says both have permission. The Gemara distinguishes: there both act equally, here the husband performs the active deed. A further objection from a verse is resolved by noting that both derive benefit, but the husband performs the act.

sub.text: Rabbah bar Natan's question to Rav Huna
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar Natan's question to Rav Huna
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar Natan asks Rav Huna whether a husband who harms his wife during marital relations is liable, given that he acts with permission, or whether he must be careful.
Rav Huna answers by citing the Mishnah's principle that when both have permission to walk, neither is liable for damage caused.
Rava argues a fortiori: if in a forest where both enter with permission, one who damages is liable, then here where the husband enters his wife's domain, he is certainly liable.
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah explicitly states both have permission, implying no liability.
The Gemara distinguishes: in the Mishnah both act equally, but here the husband performs the active deed.

sub.text: Gemara's further objection from a verse
sub.text_en: Gemara's further objection from a verse
sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the wife also performs an act, citing the verse 'the souls that do shall be cut off'.
The Gemara resolves: both derive benefit, but the husband performs the active deed, so he is liable.

items.text: Reish Lakish's ruling on two cows and support from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Reish Lakish's ruling on two cows and support from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish rules that if a walking cow kicks a lying cow, it is exempt; if a lying cow kicks a walking cow, it is liable. The Gemara attempts to support this from the Mishnah's case of the beam-carrier and barrel-carrier, but initially finds a contradiction. It resolves by distinguishing: the Mishnah deals with blocking the path like a skeleton, while Reish Lakish's case involves lying on one side. The Gemara then finds support from the reverse case in the Mishnah, and distinguishes again: the Mishnah involves normal walking, while Reish Lakish's case involves the lying cow having no right to kick.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish rules that if a walking cow kicks a lying cow, it is exempt; if a lying cow kicks a walking cow, it is liable.

The Gemara attempts to support Reish Lakish from the Mishnah's case of the beam-carrier and barrel-carrier, but finds a contradiction: the Mishnah rules liable in a case that seems analogous to the lying cow kicking the walking cow.

The Gemara objects that the attempted support actually poses a difficulty: the Mishnah rules liable for accidental damage, while Reish Lakish exempts the walking cow that kicks, implying a contradiction.
The Gemara resolves: the Mishnah deals with blocking the path entirely like a skeleton, while Reish Lakish's case involves the cow lying on one side, leaving room to pass on the other.

The Gemara finds support from the reverse case in the Mishnah: when the barrel-carrier is first and the beam-carrier is last, the beam-carrier is exempt, matching Reish Lakish's ruling for the walking cow kicking the lying cow.
The Gemara distinguishes: the Mishnah involves normal walking, while Reish Lakish's case involves the lying cow having no right to kick, even though the walking cow has the right to walk over her.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara: Two runners in the public domain and the dispute with Isi ben Yehudah
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara: Two runners in the public domain and the dispute with Isi ben Yehudah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if two people are walking in the public domain, one running and one walking, or both running, and they damage each other, both are exempt. The Gemara notes this contradicts Isi ben Yehudah, who holds a runner is liable because he is unusual, except on Shabbat eve at twilight when running is permitted. Rabbi Yochanan rules like Isi ben Yehudah, but the Gemara questions this given his own principle of ruling like an anonymous Mishnah. The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah refers specifically to Shabbat eve at twilight, as inferred from its redundant language. The Gemara then asks what permission exists on Shabbat eve, and cites Rabbi Chanina.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if two people are walking in the public domain, one running and one walking, or both running, and they damage each other, both are exempt.
The Gemara notes that the Mishnah contradicts Isi ben Yehudah, who holds a runner is liable because he is unusual, except on Shabbat eve at twilight when running is permitted.
Rabbi Yochanan rules like Isi ben Yehudah, but the Gemara questions this given his own principle of ruling like an anonymous Mishnah.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah refers specifically to Shabbat eve at twilight, as inferred from its redundant language.
Mar asks what permission exists on Shabbat eve for running.
The Gemara cites Rabbi Chanina to explain the permission for running on Shabbat eve.

items.text: Opening anecdote about greeting Shabbat
items.text_en: Opening anecdote about greeting Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a story about Rabbi Yannai wrapping himself and greeting Shabbat as a bride, establishing the theme of entering a domain.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a story about Rabbi Yannai wrapping himself and greeting Shabbat as a bride, establishing the theme of entering a domain.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara on liability for splitting wood in different domains
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on liability for splitting wood in different domains
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who splits wood in a public domain and damages in a private domain, or vice versa, or in one private domain and damages in another, is liable. The Gemara explains why all three cases are necessary, addressing concerns about frequency of people and permission.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who splits wood in a public domain and damages in a private domain, or vice versa, or in one private domain and damages in another, is liable.

The Gemara asks why all three cases are necessary, suggesting that if only the first case (private to public) were taught, one might think liability is only because many people are present, but not for the reverse.

The Gemara explains that if only the second case (public to private) were taught, one might think liability is because the act was done without permission, but not for the reverse where permission is granted.
The Gemara concludes that if only the first two cases were taught, one might think the third case (private to another private) is exempt, so all three are necessary.

items.text: Baraita on entering a carpenter's shop without permission
items.text_en: Baraita on entering a carpenter's shop without permission
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches: one who enters a carpenter's shop without permission and is struck by a flying splinter and dies – the carpenter is exempt; if he entered with permission, he is liable. Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina explains he is liable for four things but exempt from exile, because this case is unlike the forest where both enter with permission.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states the basic ruling: one who enters a carpenter's shop without permission and is killed by a flying splinter is exempt; if he entered with permission, the carpenter is liable.
The gemara asks what 'liable' means in this context.
Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina explains that the carpenter is liable for four types of payment but exempt from exile, because this case differs from the forest where both parties entered with permission.

items.text: Rava's kal vachomer and reinterpretation of exemption from exile
items.text_en: Rava's kal vachomer and reinterpretation of exemption from exile
items.desc_en: Rava initially argues a kal vachomer that one who enters with permission should be exiled, but then reinterprets: the exemption from exile is because it is a case of shogeg karov l'mezid (negligence close to intentional).

sub.desc_en: Rava proposes a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument): if in the forest, where both enter with permission, the killer is exiled, then here, where the victim entered with permission, the killer should certainly be exiled.
Rava reinterprets: the exemption from exile is not because of permission but because the case is considered שוגג קרוב למזיד (negligence close to intentional), which does not qualify for exile.

items.text: Objection from the case of an extra lash and resolution
items.text_en: Objection from the case of an extra lash and resolution
items.desc_en: Rava raises an objection from a baraita where a judge who adds an extra lash and kills is exiled, even though it is shogeg karov l'mezid. Rav Shimi of Nehardea answers that the judge erred in counting, and Rava slaps him with a sandal, but then Rav Shimi revises: the judge himself erred.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects from a baraita: a judge who adds one extra lash and the convict dies is exiled, even though this is shogeg karov l'mezid (negligence close to intent).

sub.text: Rav Shimi of Nehardea's first answer
sub.text_en: Rav Shimi of Nehardea's first answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Shimi of Nehardea answers that the judge erred in counting the lashes.

sub.text: Rava's rejection with a sandal slap
sub.text_en: Rava's rejection with a sandal slap
sub.desc_en: Rava slaps Rav Shimi with a sandal, objecting that the judge does not count the lashes himself; the second judge counts.

sub.text: Rav Shimi of Nehardea's revised answer
sub.text_en: Rav Shimi of Nehardea's revised answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Shimi revises his answer: the judge himself erred in some other way, not in counting.

items.text: Objection from throwing a stone into the public domain and resolution
items.text_en: Objection from throwing a stone into the public domain and resolution
items.desc_en: Another objection is raised: one who throws a stone into the public domain and kills is exiled, even though it is shogeg karov l'mezid. Rav Shmuel bar Yitzchak answers that it is a case of demolishing his wall at night to a garbage dump. Rav Pappa clarifies the scenario: a dump used at night but not by day, where someone might occasionally sit.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita: one who throws a stone into the public domain and kills is exiled, even though it is a case of shogeg karov l'mezid (negligence close to intent).
Rav Shmuel bar Yitzchak answers that the case involves one who is demolishing his wall, so he is not fully negligent.
The Gemara objects that even when demolishing a wall, one should have looked carefully; Rav Shmuel bar Yitzchak clarifies it is at night.
The Gemara objects that even at night one should have looked; Rav Shmuel bar Yitzchak specifies it is demolishing his wall by day into a garbage dump.
The Gemara questions the nature of the dump: if people are commonly there, it is intentional; if not, it is accidental.
Rav Pappa resolves the difficulty: the dump is used at night but not by day, so it is neither fully intentional nor fully accidental, and exile applies.

items.text: Debate on applying Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's statement to the beginning or end of the baraita
items.text_en: Debate on applying Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's statement to the beginning or end of the baraita
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa cites Rava: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's statement applies to the beginning of the baraita (entering without permission). The Gemara discusses who teaches it on the beginning versus the end, and raises an objection from a case of a blacksmith's shop where even with permission one is exempt. The resolution involves a blacksmith's bellows and a scenario where the master hurries the worker to leave.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa cites Rava that Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's statement applies to the beginning of the baraita (entering without permission).
The Gemara explains the logical relationship between teaching the statement on the end versus the beginning of the baraita.
The Gemara objects: Is one really liable for exile? A baraita about a blacksmith's shop says one is exempt even when entering with permission.
The Gemara answers: The case involves a blacksmith's bellows, where the master hurries the worker to leave but he does not leave.

The Gemara objects: Because the master hurries him to leave, does that make him liable to be killed? The resolution is that the worker thought the master had already left, but then the Gemara asks: If so, the same would apply to any other person.

items.text: Distinction between one who brings injury upon himself and one who does not
items.text_en: Distinction between one who brings injury upon himself and one who does not
items.desc_en: The Gemara contrasts two versions of a teaching: one who brings himself into danger (e.g., by putting his head under a falling stone) is exempt from exile but liable for the four payments, while one who does not is fully exempt. The discussion clarifies which version applies to which case.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a distinction: one person lacks fear of his master, while another has it.

sub.text: Rav Zevid in the name of Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Zevid in the name of Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Zevid cites Rava's version of the teaching, applied to the case of one who brings injury upon himself, quoting Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov that such a person is exempt.
Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina clarifies that such a person is exempt from exile but liable for the four payments.

The Gemara resolves the relationship between the two versions: one who applies the teaching to the latter case applies it all the more to the former, but one who applies it to the former holds that the latter is completely exempt.

items.text: Workers entering to claim wages: liability for damage by the homeowner's ox or dog
items.text_en: Workers entering to claim wages: liability for damage by the homeowner's ox or dog
items.desc_en: A baraita discusses workers who come to claim wages from the homeowner and are gored or bitten by his animals. The Tanna Kamma exempts the homeowner, while Acherim holds the workers permitted to enter. The Gemara analyzes the circumstances: if the homeowner is usually home or not, and whether his response 'yes' means 'come in' or 'stay where you are'. A supporting baraita is cited.

sub.desc_en: A baraita presents a dispute: the Tanna Kamma exempts the homeowner when workers coming to claim wages are gored or bitten by his animals, while Acherim holds the workers are permitted to enter.
The Gemara asks: under what circumstances does this dispute apply? If the homeowner is usually in town, why do Acherim exempt? If he is usually home, why does the Tanna Kamma exempt?

The Gemara resolves: the case involves a man who is sometimes home and sometimes not; when the workers call and he says 'אין (yes)', one opinion interprets this as 'come in' and the other as 'stay where you are'.
A supporting baraita is cited, which rules that a worker entering to claim wages is exempt even if he entered with permission, implying that 'אין (yes)' means 'stay where you are'.

items.text: Mishnah: Mutual damage between two oxen or between an ox and a person
items.text_en: Mishnah: Mutual damage between two oxen or between an ox and a person
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the rules for when two tam oxen gore each other, or two mu'adim, or one tam and one mu'ad. It then extends to two people who injure each other, and to cases of a person and an ox (tam or mu'ad). Rabbi Akiva adds that a tam that injures a person pays full damages.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the rule for two tam oxen that gore each other: they pay half damages on the excess.
The Mishnah states the rule for one tam and one mu'ad: the mu'ad pays full damages on the excess, the tam pays half damages on the excess.
The Mishnah extends the rule to two people who injure each other: they pay full damages on the excess.
The Mishnah gives the rules for a person and an ox (mu'ad or tam), and Rabbi Akiva adds that a tam that injures a person pays full damages on the excess.

items.text: Gemara: Derivation of tam and mu'ad liability for goring a person, and exemption from four payments
items.text_en: Gemara: Derivation of tam and mu'ad liability for goring a person, and exemption from four payments
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita deriving from the verse 'as this judgment is done to him' that an ox that gores a person follows the same rules as an ox goring an ox: tam pays half, mu'ad full. Rabbi Akiva interprets the verse differently, focusing on 'this' to exclude payment from the owner's property. The Rabbis use 'this' to exempt the ox from the four payments (e.g., pain, healing, lost wages). Rabbi Akiva derives this exemption from another verse. The Rabbis explain that without this, one might think only pain is exempt, but not healing and lost wages.

sub.desc_en: The baraita derives from the verse 'as this judgment is done to him' that an ox goring a person follows the same rules as an ox goring an ox: tam pays half, mu'ad full.
Rabbi Akiva interprets the verse differently, focusing on 'this' to exclude payment from the owner's property (the 'upper story').
The Gemara explains that the Rabbis use the word 'this' to exempt the ox from the four payments (pain, healing, lost wages, etc.).
The Gemara asks: from where does Rabbi Akiva derive the exemption from the four payments?
Rabbi Akiva derives the exemption from the verse 'If a man gives a blemish in his fellow' — 'a man in his fellow' excludes an ox in his fellow.
The Gemara explains that without the word 'this', the Rabbis might have thought only pain is exempt, but not healing and lost wages; therefore the verse teaches otherwise.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara: Valuation of the ox when the carcass is worthless, and dispute between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara: Valuation of the ox when the carcass is worthless, and dispute between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a ox worth 100 zuz gores an ox worth 200 and the carcass is worthless, the victim takes the live ox.
