The Gemara identifies this as Rabbi Akiva's view, citing a dispute: Rabbi Yishmael holds the ox is appraised in court (the victim is a creditor), while Rabbi Akiva holds the ox is 'consecrated' (they are partners). The difference is whether the victim can consecrate the ox. Rava asks Rav Nachman about the status if the damaging ox was sold by the owner.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if an ox worth 100 zuz gores an ox worth 200 and the carcass is worthless, the victim takes the live ox.
The Gemara identifies the Mishnah as following Rabbi Akiva's view.
A baraita cites the dispute: Rabbi Yishmael holds the ox is appraised in court, while Rabbi Akiva holds the ox is 'consecrated' (they are partners).
The Gemara asks what is the fundamental dispute between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva.
The Gemara explains: Rabbi Yishmael holds the victim is a creditor, while Rabbi Akiva holds they are partners.

The Gemara cites the verse 'וּמָכְרוּ אֶת הַשּׁוֹר הַחַי וְחָצוּ אֶת כַּסְפּוֹ' (they shall sell the live ox and divide its money) to show the dispute: Rabbi Yishmael says the verse commands the court, while Rabbi Akiva says it commands the victim and the damager.
The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the two views.
The Gemara answers: the difference is whether the victim can consecrate the ox.
Rava asks Rav Nachman: according to Rabbi Yishmael, if the damager sold the ox, what is the status?
Rava reasons: since Rabbi Yishmael holds the victim is a creditor, perhaps the ox is sold; or perhaps not.

items.text: Gemara's question on sale of the ox after liability
items.text_en: Gemara's question on sale of the ox after liability
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the earlier ruling that the ox is not sold after liability, citing a baraita that says it is sold but the creditor can reclaim it. It explains that the sale is valid only for plowing (לרידיא).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the owner can sell the ox after it has been pledged to the injured party, and receives the answer that it is not sold.
The Gemara objects by citing a baraita that says the ox is sold, and explains that the sale is valid only for plowing (לרידיא).

items.text: Comparison to a debtor selling movable property and Rava's distinction
items.text_en: Comparison to a debtor selling movable property and Rava's distinction
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers whether a debtor who sells movable property can have it seized by the court, and distinguishes using Rava's rule: a slave made an אפותיקי is recoverable by the creditor after sale, but an ox is not, because the ox has a reputation as a gorer.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a debtor who sells movable property can have it seized by the court, inferring from the earlier case.
The Gemara answers that the case is different because the ox was effectively made an אפותיקי (designated collateral) for the damage.
The Gemara objects by citing Rava's rule: a slave made an אפותיקי is recoverable by the creditor after sale, but an ox is not.
The Gemara resolves that the ox has a reputation as a gorer (תורא נגחנא), so it is like a slave with public notoriety, allowing the creditor to recover it.

items.text: Baraita of Rav Tachlifa and resolution of the contradiction
items.text_en: Baraita of Rav Tachlifa and resolution of the contradiction
items.desc_en: Rav Tachlifa's baraita states that the ox is not sold but is consecrated. The Gemara tries to attribute this to different Tannaim (Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yishmael), but ultimately resolves it as the view of all, explaining that sale is invalid due to the lien, while consecration is valid due to Rabbi Avahu's decree against saying consecration goes out without redemption.

sub.desc_en: Rav Tachlifa bar Ma'arva cites a baraita before Rabbi Avahu stating that if the ox was sold it is not sold, but if consecrated it is consecrated.

The Gemara asks who the subject of the baraita is: if it is the damaging owner, then the 'not sold' part follows Rabbi Akiva (who holds the ox is finally condemned), but the 'consecrated' part follows Rabbi Yishmael (who holds the ox is appraised in court).
Alternatively, if the subject is the injured party, then the 'not sold' part follows Rabbi Yishmael, but the 'consecrated' part follows Rabbi Akiva — again a contradiction.

The Gemara resolves that the baraita always refers to the damaging owner and reflects the view of all Tannaim: sale is invalid because the ox is already liened to the injured party, while consecration is valid due to Rabbi Avahu's decree against saying that consecration goes out without redemption.

items.text: Tannaic baraita on the laws of a tam ox before and after judgment
items.text_en: Tannaic baraita on the laws of a tam ox before and after judgment
items.desc_en: A baraita details the laws for a tam ox: before judgment, sale and consecration are valid; after judgment, they are not. Creditors who seize it before judgment (whether the debt preceded the damage or vice versa) get nothing, because payment is only from the body. For a mu'ad, sale and consecration are always valid, and creditors can collect because payment is from the superior property.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating the law for a tam ox before judgment: sale, consecration, slaughter, or gift are all valid.
The baraita contrasts the law after judgment: sale, consecration, slaughter, or gift are all void.
The baraita rules that creditors who seize a tam ox before judgment get nothing, because payment is only from the body.
The baraita concludes with the law for a mu'ad ox: sale, consecration, slaughter, or gift are always valid, and creditors can collect because payment is from the superior property.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the baraita's details
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the baraita's details
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains each clause: sale is valid only for plowing; consecration is valid due to Rabbi Avahu's decree; slaughter is valid because the verse 'and they shall sell the ox' includes any disposition. Rav Sheizvi limits this to a defective slaughter (פחת שחיטה).

sub.desc_en: Mar explains that the baraita's statement 'sold it, it is sold' applies only for plowing (לְרִדְיָא).
The Gemara explains that the consecration is valid due to Rabbi Avahu's decree (גְּזֵירָה שֶׁמָּא יֹאמְרוּ הֶקְדֵּשׁ יוֹצֵא בְּלֹא פִּדְיוֹן).
The Gemara questions why slaughter is valid: the gift can be explained for plowing, but slaughter should allow the victim to collect from the meat.
A baraita is cited: the verse 'and they shall sell the ox' includes any disposition, even after slaughter.
Rav Sheizvi resolves that the baraita's ruling applies only to a defective slaughter (פחת שחיטה), where the meat is not fit for collection.

items.text: Rav Huna's principle and Rabba's parallel
items.text_en: Rav Huna's principle and Rabba's parallel
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua derives that one who damages another's lien is exempt. The Gemara initially finds this obvious, but clarifies it teaches that even though the damage is like digging pits (which would normally be liable), here it is exempt. Rabba's similar ruling about burning documents is cited.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua states that one who damages another's lien is exempt from payment.
The Gemara objects that Rav Huna's ruling is obvious, since the lien is intangible.
The Gemara explains that the ruling is not obvious: one might have thought that damaging a lien is like digging pits (which is actionable), but Rav Huna teaches that even so, the damager is exempt.
The Gemara cites Rabba's similar ruling that one who burns another's documents (destroying the evidence of a debt) is exempt.
The Gemara resolves that even though damaging a lien is like digging pits (which normally incurs liability), Rabba's case shows that here too the act is considered done and the damager is exempt.

items.text: Clarification of the creditor's priority
items.text_en: Clarification of the creditor's priority
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the baraita's ruling that creditors who seize the ox get nothing, asking: if the debt preceded the damage, the creditor should have priority. The Gemara implies a difficulty but does not resolve it here.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the baraita's ruling that creditors who seize the ox get nothing, regardless of the order of events.
The Gemara objects that if the debt preceded the damage, the creditor should have priority over the ox.

items.text: Gemara's question and answer about the creditor's priority
items.text_en: Gemara's question and answer about the creditor's priority
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a creditor who collected after the debtor damaged the ox can keep the proceeds, suggesting that if the damage occurred before the debt was due, the creditor's claim is prior. It answers that the creditor's collection stands, because the debtor can argue that the ox that caused the damage is the one from which he will be paid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a creditor who collected after the debtor damaged the ox can keep the proceeds, suggesting that if the damage occurred before the debt was due, the creditor's claim is prior.
The Gemara answers that the creditor's collection stands, because the debtor can argue that the ox that caused the damage is the one from which he will be paid.

items.text: Baraita on appreciation and depreciation of the damaged ox
items.text_en: Baraita on appreciation and depreciation of the damaged ox
items.desc_en: A baraita presents a case where an ox worth 200 zuz gored another ox worth 200 zuz, causing a 50 zuz injury, and then the damaged ox appreciated to 400 zuz (or would have been 800 without the injury). The rule is: if the ox appreciated, payment is at the time of damage; if it depreciated, payment is at the time of judgment. The same applies if the damaging ox appreciated or depreciated.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with a case: an ox worth 200 zuz gored another ox worth 200 zuz, causing a 50 zuz injury, and the damaged ox appreciated to 400 zuz (or would have been 800 without the injury); the rule is that payment is at the time of damage.
The baraita adds the converse rule: if the damaged ox depreciated, payment is at the time of judgment.
The baraita extends the same rule to the damaging ox: if it appreciated, payment is at the time of damage; if it depreciated, at the time of judgment.

items.text: Gemara's analysis: contradiction between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis: contradiction between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the first clause of the baraita (appreciation of the damaging ox) follows Rabbi Yishmael, who views the injured party as a creditor, while the second clause (depreciation) follows Rabbi Akiva, who views them as partners. This would be a contradiction within one baraita.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the baraita's ruling that if the damaging ox appreciated, payment is at the time of damage.
The Gemara identifies the first clause as following Rabbi Yishmael, who views the injured party as a creditor.
The Gemara objects that the second clause follows Rabbi Akiva, who views them as partners, creating a contradiction within one baraita.

items.text: Resolution: the baraita is entirely Rabbi Akiva, dealing with a fattened ox
items.text_en: Resolution: the baraita is entirely Rabbi Akiva, dealing with a fattened ox
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the entire baraita is Rabbi Akiva, and it deals with a case where the damaging ox was fattened by the injured party. Rav Papa explains that the first clause applies whether the ox fattened itself or was fattened, while the second clause only applies when the injured party fattened it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the entire baraita is Rabbi Akiva's view, and it deals with a case where the injured party fattened the ox.
The Gemara objects: if the ox was fattened by the injured party, why would the first clause need to state that the payment is at the time of damage?
Rav Papa explains that the first clause applies whether the ox fattened itself or was fattened, while the second clause only applies when the injured party fattened it.

items.text: Clarification of depreciation: due to the wound, not work
items.text_en: Clarification of depreciation: due to the wound, not work
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the depreciating ox is valued at the time of judgment, and explains that it is depreciation from the wound, not from work. Rav Ashi says the injured party can claim that the horn of the goring ox is embedded in the wound, causing the depreciation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the depreciation is assessed at the time of judgment, and questions whether the depreciation is due to work (which the injured party would not pay for).
Rav Ashi answers that the depreciation is due to the wound itself, as the injured party can claim that the horn of the goring ox is embedded in the wound, causing the loss.

items.text: Mishnah: dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda on division
items.text_en: Mishnah: dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda on division
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where an ox worth 200 zuz gored another ox worth 200 zuz, and the carcass is worthless. Rabbi Meir says this is the case of 'they shall sell the live ox and divide its money.' Rabbi Yehuda says that is not the correct application; rather, the verse 'and also the dead they shall divide' applies when the carcass is worth 50 zuz, and each takes half the live and half the dead.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where an ox worth 200 zuz gored another ox worth 200 zuz, and the carcass is worthless; Rabbi Meir says this is the case of 'they shall sell the live ox and divide its money.'

Rabbi Yehuda objects that Rabbi Meir's case fulfills only one verse but not 'and also the dead they shall divide,' and explains that the correct case is when the carcass is worth 50 zuz, and each takes half the live and half the dead.

items.text: Gemara: baraita elaborating the dispute
items.text_en: Gemara: baraita elaborating the dispute
items.desc_en: A baraita repeats the dispute: Rabbi Yehuda says the case with a 50-zuz carcass is the ox of the Torah, while Rabbi Meir insists the case with a worthless carcass is the one, and explains that 'and also the dead they shall divide' refers to the depreciation caused by death being divided in the live ox.

sub.desc_en: A baraita presents Rabbi Yehuda's position: the case of a 200-zuz ox that gored another 200-zuz ox with a 50-zuz carcass is the ox of the Torah, and each takes half the live ox and half the dead.

The baraita continues with Rabbi Meir's position: the Torah's ox is the case with a worthless carcass, and the verse 'וגם את המת יחצון' (and also the dead they shall divide) refers to the depreciation caused by death being divided in the live ox.

items.text: Gemara's question: what is the practical difference?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: what is the practical difference?
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that in both cases each party receives 125 zuz, and asks what is the difference between them. Rava answers: the depreciation of the carcass is the point – Rabbi Meir holds the depreciation belongs to the injured party, while Rabbi Yehuda holds it is split. Abaye challenges this, but the text is cut off.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the practical difference is between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda, since in both cases each party receives 125 zuz.
Rava answers that the difference lies in the depreciation of the carcass: Rabbi Meir holds it belongs to the injured party, while Rabbi Yehuda holds it is split.
Abaye challenges Rava's answer, but the text is cut off before the full objection is recorded.

items.text: Gemara's challenge: Tam more stringent than Mu'ad?
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge: Tam more stringent than Mu'ad?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the earlier claim that a tam can be more stringent than a mu'ad, citing Rabbi Yehuda's view that a tam pays while a mu'ad is exempt. It argues that Rabbi Yehuda only holds this for guarding, not for payment, and brings a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda suggests a tam pays half damages even when the carcass is valuable, concluding that a mu'ad is stricter.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the earlier claim that a tam (תם) can be more stringent than a mu'ad (מועד).
The Gemara proposes that Rabbi Yehuda's view (תם חייב, מועד פטור) applies only to guarding (שמירה), not to payment (תשלומין).
A baraita is cited where Rabbi Yehuda suggests that a tam pays half damages even when the carcass is valuable, implying a tam can be more stringent.
The Gemara resolves that a mu'ad (מועד) is inherently more stringent, and if a mu'ad pays only for actual damage, a tam (תם) certainly pays no more.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's resolution: Appreciation of the carcass
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's resolution: Appreciation of the carcass
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages concerns the appreciation of the carcass: one holds it belongs to the injured party, the other that it is split.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan resolves the dispute by explaining that the point of contention is the appreciation of the carcass (שבח נבילה): one opinion holds it belongs to the injured party, the other that it is split.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's difficulty and resolution
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's difficulty and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara elaborates on Rabbi Yehuda's difficulty: if the Torah is lenient with the injurer by giving him a share in the carcass's appreciation, then in a case where the injured ox is worth more, the injurer might profit. The Gemara resolves that the verse 'shall surely pay' teaches that only owners pay, not receive.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yehuda's difficulty
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yehuda's difficulty
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains Rabbi Yehuda's difficulty: if the Torah is lenient with the injurer by giving him a share in the carcass's appreciation, then in a case where the injured ox is worth more, the injurer might profit.
The Gemara resolves that the verse 'שַׁלֵּם יְשַׁלֵּם' (shall surely pay) teaches that only owners pay, not receive.

items.text: Rav Acha bar Tachlifa's objection and resolution
items.text_en: Rav Acha bar Tachlifa's objection and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Tachlifa objects to Rava that Rabbi Yehuda's view would make a tam pay more than half damages, contradicting the verse 'they shall sell the live ox and divide its money'. The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yehuda holds that the depreciation from death is divided in the live ox, derived from the extra word 've-gam' in the verse.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Tachlifa's objection to Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Tachlifa's objection to Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Tachlifa objects to Rava that according to Rabbi Yehuda's view, a tam would pay more than half damages, contradicting the verse 'וּמָכְרוּ אֶת הַשּׁוֹר הַחַי וְחָצוּ אֶת כַּסְפּוֹ' (they shall sell the live ox and divide its money).
Rava answers that Rabbi Yehuda holds that the depreciation from death (פחת שפחתה מיתה) is divided in the live ox, so the tam does not pay more than half damages.

The Gemara asks from where Rabbi Yehuda derives this, noting that the verse 'וְגַם אֶת הַמֵּת יֶחֱצוּן' (and also the dead ox they shall divide) was already used by Rabbi Yehuda for the rule that each takes half the live and half the dead.

The Gemara resolves that if the verse only intended the division of the dead, it would have said 'וְאֶת הַמֵּת' (and the dead); the extra word 'וְגַם' (and also) teaches two things: the division of the dead and the division of the depreciation.

items.text: Mishnah: Liability for one's ox versus oneself
items.text_en: Mishnah: Liability for one's ox versus oneself
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists cases where one is liable for one's ox but exempt for oneself, and vice versa, including embarrassment, injuring a slave, honoring parents, and setting a fire on Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating the general principle that there are cases where one is liable for one's ox but exempt for oneself, and vice versa.
The Mishnah gives examples: one is exempt for one's ox that caused embarrassment or blinded a slave, but liable for oneself doing so.

The Mishnah continues with examples: one is liable for one's ox that injured parents but exempt for oneself, and liable for one's ox that set a fire on Shabbat but exempt for oneself because one is liable for capital punishment.

items.text: Gemara: Rabbi Avahu's teaching and clarification
items.text_en: Gemara: Rabbi Avahu's teaching and clarification
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu teaches before Rabbi Yochanan that all who cause damage are exempt except for one who wounds and one who sets a fire. Rabbi Yochanan rejects this, saying it is not a Mishnah, and if it were, it applies only when the wounder needs the dog or the fire-setter needs the ashes. The Gemara then notes that the Mishnah's case of setting a fire on Shabbat parallels the ox, where the ox is not designated for a specific purpose.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu teaches before Rabbi Yochanan that all who cause damage are exempt except for one who wounds and one who sets a fire.
Rabbi Yochanan rejects the teaching, saying it is not a Mishnah, and if it were, it applies only when the wounder needs the dog or the fire-setter needs the ashes.
The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's case of setting a fire on Shabbat parallels the ox, where the ox is not designated for a specific purpose.

items.text: Gemara's objection and resolution regarding the ox's similarity to its owner
items.text_en: Gemara's objection and resolution regarding the ox's similarity to its owner
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the Mishnah's case (where the ox is exempt) cannot be compared to the owner's case because the ox does not have a fixed court (to determine its liability). It then resolves that the ox is analogous to its owner: just as the owner has a fixed court, so too the ox has a fixed court.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the ox cannot be compared to its owner because the ox lacks a fixed court to determine its liability, yet the Mishnah rules it exempt.
The Gemara resolves that the ox is analogous to its owner: just as the owner has a fixed court, so too the ox has a fixed court.

items.text: Rav Avya's explanation and supporting story
items.text_en: Rav Avya's explanation and supporting story
items.desc_en: Rav Avya explains the case: a sensible ox that had a bite on its back and needed to be roasted, and it fell into the fire. The Gemara questions whether such a scenario exists, and provides a story from Rav Papa's house where an ox with a toothache drank beer and was healed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how one can find a case where the ox is analogous to the owner in terms of intent.
Rav Avya explains the case: a sensible ox with a bite on its back that needed roasting fell into the fire.

sub.text: Supporting story from Rav Papa's house
sub.text_en: Supporting story from Rav Papa's house
sub.desc_en: The Gemara provides a supporting story from Rav Papa's house where an ox with a toothache drank beer and was healed.

items.text: Rabbis' challenge and resolution regarding intent to shame
items.text_en: Rabbis' challenge and resolution regarding intent to shame
items.desc_en: The rabbis challenge Rav Avya's analogy: the Mishnah states that an ox that shames is exempt, while the owner who shames is liable. How can the ox be analogous to the owner? The Gemara resolves that the case is where the owner intended to damage (even if not to shame), as the principle states: intent to damage suffices even without intent to shame.

sub.desc_en: The rabbis challenge Rav Avya's analogy: the Mishnah states that an ox that shames is exempt while the owner who shames is liable, so how can the ox be analogous to the owner if the ox cannot intend to shame?
The Gemara resolves that the case is where the owner intended to damage, even if not to shame, as the principle states that intent to damage suffices without intent to shame.

items.text: Rava's alternative explanation: the Mishnah deals with an unintentional act
items.text_en: Rava's alternative explanation: the Mishnah deals with an unintentional act
items.desc_en: Rava argues that the Mishnah deals with an unintentional case, citing the Tanna of the school of Chizkiyah who derives a comparison between striking a person and striking an animal: just as with an animal there is no distinction between intentional and unintentional for monetary liability, so too with a person. The rabbis object that the Mishnah says 'because he is judged by his own life' (implying intentional). Rava explains that the Mishnah means: since in an intentional case he is judged by his own life (e.g., he intended to roast the ox), therefore in an unintentional case he is exempt.

sub.desc_en: Rava opens by asserting that the Mishnah deals with an unintentional (שוגג) case.

sub.text: Tanna of the school of Chizkiyah
sub.text_en: Tanna of the school of Chizkiyah
sub.desc_en: Rava cites the Tanna of the school of Chizkiyah, who derives a comparison between striking a person and striking an animal: just as with an animal there is no distinction between intentional and unintentional for monetary liability, so too with a person.
The rabbis object to Rava, arguing that the Mishnah says 'because he is judged by his own life' (implying intentional), so it cannot be an unintentional case.

Rava resolves the objection by explaining that the Mishnah means: since in an intentional case he is judged by his own life (e.g., he intended to roast the ox), therefore in an unintentional case he is exempt.

items.text: Mishnah: dispute over a pursuing ox that is injured
items.text_en: Mishnah: dispute over a pursuing ox that is injured
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where one ox pursues another and is injured. One claims the other's ox caused the damage, the other claims it was injured by a rock. The burden of proof is on the claimant. It then presents a case of two oxen pursuing one, where each owner claims the other's ox caused the damage.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with a case of one ox pursuing another and being injured, where each owner disputes the cause, and the burden of proof is on the claimant.
The Mishnah presents a second case of two oxen pursuing one, where each owner claims the other's ox caused the damage.

items.text: Mishnah: Disputes about which ox gored
items.text_en: Mishnah: Disputes about which ox gored
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents cases where two oxen (one large and one small, or one tam and one mu'ad) gored, and the parties disagree about which ox caused the damage. The ruling is that the burden of proof is on the claimant (המוציא מחבירו עליו הראיה).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the rule: if two oxen gored and both are ownerless, both owners are exempt; if both belong to one person, both are liable.

The Mishnah presents the case of one large and one small ox, or one tam and one mu'ad, where the parties disagree; the ruling is that the burden of proof is on the claimant (המוציא מחבירו עליו הראיה).

items.text: Gemara: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba infers that Sumchus disagrees
items.text_en: Gemara: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba infers that Sumchus disagrees
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba states that the Mishnah shows that Sumchus's colleagues disagree with him, because Sumchus says that when money is in doubt, they divide. Rabbi Abba bar Memel asks whether Sumchus applies this even when both parties are certain (ברי וברי), and Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba confirms that he does.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba infers from the Mishnah that Sumchus's colleagues disagree with him, because Sumchus holds that money in doubt is divided.
Rabbi Abba bar Memel asks Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba whether Sumchus applies his principle even when both parties are certain (ברי וברי).
Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba confirms that Sumchus indeed applies his rule even when both parties are certain.

items.text: Proof that the Mishnah is a case of certain claims
items.text_en: Proof that the Mishnah is a case of certain claims
items.desc_en: The Gemara proves that the Mishnah deals with a case where both parties are certain (ברי וברי), because it says 'this one says your ox gored, and that one says no.' Rav Pappa objects that if the first clause is certain, the latter clause is also certain.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we know the Mishnah deals with certain claims (ברי וברי), citing the Mishnah's language 'this one says your ox gored, and that one says no.'
Rav Pappa objects that if the first clause is certain, the latter clause must also be certain, implying a contradiction.

items.text: Challenge from the latter clause against Rabbah bar Natan
items.text_en: Challenge from the latter clause against Rabbah bar Natan
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the latter clause of the Mishnah where the claimant says 'large ox gored' and the defendant says 'small ox gored,' and the ruling is that the burden of proof is on the claimant. If he does not bring proof, he takes only what the defendant admits. This challenges Rabbah bar Natan, who says that if one claims wheat and the other admits barley, he is exempt entirely.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the latter clause of the Mishnah where the claimant says 'large ox gored' and the defendant says 'small ox gored,' and the ruling is that the burden of proof is on the claimant.
The Gemara infers that if the claimant does not bring proof, he takes only what the defendant admits.

sub.text: Gemara's challenge against Rabbah bar Natan
sub.text_en: Gemara's challenge against Rabbah bar Natan
sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbah bar Natan, who says that if one claims wheat and the other admits barley, he is exempt entirely.

items.text: Resolution: The case is one certain and one uncertain
items.text_en: Resolution: The case is one certain and one uncertain
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah's latter clause is a case of certain and uncertain (ברי ושמא), where the claimant is uncertain and the defendant is certain. The Gemara then considers whether Sumchus would apply even in such a case, and concludes that the first clause is certain-claimant and uncertain-defendant, while the latter clause is uncertain-claimant and certain-defendant.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah's latter clause deals with a case of certain (ברי) and uncertain (שמא), not both certain.
The Gemara asks who is the certain party and who is uncertain, and considers whether the claimant is certain and the defendant uncertain, which would still pose a difficulty for Rabbah bar Natan.
The Gemara answers that in the latter clause the claimant (ניזק) is uncertain (שמא) and the defendant (מזיק) is certain (ברי).

The Gemara objects that if the latter clause is claimant-uncertain and defendant-certain, then the first clause would also be so, and Sumchus would still apply even there, which seems unnecessary to teach.

items.text: Distinction between certain-uncertain and certain-certain
items.text_en: Distinction between certain-uncertain and certain-certain
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the first clause is certain-claimant and uncertain-defendant, while the latter clause is uncertain-claimant and certain-defendant. The Gemara notes that these are two different categories: certain-uncertain and uncertain-certain are the same, but certain-certain and uncertain-certain are different.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the latter clause involves an uncertain claimant and a certain defendant, while the first clause involves a certain claimant and an uncertain defendant.
The Gemara objects that the first clause and the latter clause are not comparable, since one is certain-uncertain and the other uncertain-certain.
The Gemara resolves that certain-uncertain and uncertain-certain are the same category, but certain-certain and uncertain-certain are different categories.

items.text: Rabbah bar Natan's ruling on wheat and barley
items.text_en: Rabbah bar Natan's ruling on wheat and barley
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses Rabbah bar Natan's ruling that if one claims wheat and the other admits barley, he is completely exempt. This is not obvious from the Mishnah, which might have implied he is exempt from wheat but liable for barley; Rabbah bar Natan teaches that he is entirely exempt.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar Natan rules that if one claims wheat and the other admits barley, he is completely exempt, and the Gemara questions what novel point this teaches since the Mishnah already states this.
The Gemara explains that without Rabbah bar Natan's ruling, one might have thought the exemption is only from the wheat payment but liable for barley; he teaches that he is entirely exempt.

items.text: Challenges from the Mishnah against Rabbah bar Natan
items.text_en: Challenges from the Mishnah against Rabbah bar Natan
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbah bar Natan from the Mishnah's cases of two oxen (large and small, tam and mu'ad). In those cases, if the claimant does not bring proof, he takes only what the defendant admits, which seems to contradict Rabbah bar Natan's principle. The Gemara answers that he is 'fit to take' but does not actually take, and cites a baraita that he is paid from the small for the large and vice versa, but only if he seized (תפס) the property.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbah bar Natan from the Mishnah's case of two injured parties (one large, one small) and two oxen (one large, one small), where the claimant without proof takes only what the defendant admits, asking why this does not contradict Rabbah bar Natan's ruling that admitting to barley when sued for wheat exempts entirely.

The Gemara answers that the claimant is 'fit to take' (רָאוּי לִיטּוֹל) but does not actually take, meaning the Mishnah only describes what he would be entitled to if he brought proof, not that he takes without proof.

The Gemara objects by citing a baraita that explicitly states the claimant is paid from the small for the large and from the large for the small, implying actual payment, not just theoretical entitlement.
The Gemara resolves the objection by explaining that the baraita applies only when the claimant has already seized (תפס) the property, thereby acquiring it before the dispute.
The Gemara cites a parallel Mishnah case (one tam and one mu'ad) to reinforce the same challenge against Rabbah bar Natan, showing the pattern holds across different scenarios.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's ruling about a minor and adult ox
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's ruling about a minor and adult ox
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's statement that a minor ox is 'fit to take' but does not receive payment, citing a baraita that says payment is made from the mu'ad for the minor and from the tam for the adult, and resolves that it refers to a case where the plaintiff seized property.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling that a minor ox is 'fit to take' but does not receive payment, citing a contradictory baraita.
The baraita states that payment is made from the mu'ad (forewarned ox) for the minor and from the tam (innocent ox) for the adult.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by explaining that the Mishnah refers to a case where the plaintiff seized property (תפס).

items.text: Rava's inference about two tam oxen belonging to one owner
items.text_en: Rava's inference about two tam oxen belonging to one owner
items.desc_en: Rava from Parzika infers from the Mishnah's statement that if both oxen belong to one owner, both are liable, that when two tam oxen gore, the plaintiff can collect from whichever he chooses.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if both oxen belong to one owner, both are liable.
Rava mi-Parzika infers to Rav Ashi that when two tam oxen gore, the plaintiff can collect from whichever he chooses.

items.text: Gemara's objection: the case involves mu'ad oxen
items.text_en: Gemara's objection: the case involves mu'ad oxen
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the Mishnah's case is actually about mu'ad oxen, not tam oxen, so Rava's inference is unfounded.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the Mishnah's case is actually about mu'ad oxen (מועדים), not tam oxen, so Rava's inference is unfounded.

items.text: Gemara's challenge from the seifa about a large and small ox
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge from the seifa about a large and small ox
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that if the case is about mu'ad oxen, the seifa's dispute about which ox gored is pointless, since the mu'ad pays full damages regardless of size.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that if the case is about mu'ad oxen, the seifa's dispute about which ox gored is pointless, since the mu'ad pays full damages regardless of size.

items.text: Rav Ashi's answer: seifa in tam, reisha in mu'ad
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's answer: seifa in tam, reisha in mu'ad
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi answers that the seifa deals with tam oxen while the reisha deals with mu'ad oxen, resolving the contradiction.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi answers that the seifa deals with tam oxen while the reisha deals with mu'ad oxen, resolving the contradiction.

items.text: Rav Acha Saba's objection to Rav Ashi's answer
items.text_en: Rav Acha Saba's objection to Rav Ashi's answer
items.desc_en: Rav Acha Saba objects that if the reisha is about mu'ad oxen, the Mishnah should say 'the man is liable' not 'both are liable', and the word 'both' is problematic.

sub.text: Rav Acha Saba's objection to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Rav Acha Saba's objection to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha Saba objects to Rav Ashi's answer: if the reisha deals with mu'ad oxen, the Mishnah should say 'the man is liable' (חייב גברא) not 'both are liable' (שניהם חייבים), and the word 'both' (שניהם) is problematic.

items.text: Gemara's resolution: the Mishnah follows Rabbi Akiva
items.text_en: Gemara's resolution: the Mishnah follows Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the Mishnah always deals with tam oxen and follows Rabbi Akiva, who holds they are partners; the plaintiff can only collect from both if both are available, otherwise he must bring proof.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah always deals with tam oxen and follows Rabbi Akiva, who holds they are partners; the plaintiff can only collect from both if both are available, otherwise he must bring proof.

items.text: Mishnah: distribution of damages for successive gorings
items.text_en: Mishnah: distribution of damages for successive gorings
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents Rabbi Meir's and Rabbi Shimon's rules for distributing payment when an ox gores multiple oxen in sequence, with the last victim collecting first and any surplus going to previous victims.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents Rabbi Meir's rule: when an ox gores multiple oxen in sequence, the last victim collects first, and any surplus goes to the previous victims in reverse order.
Rabbi Shimon presents his first case: an ox worth 200 that gores another ox worth 200 with no carcass value, each owner takes 100.
Rabbi Shimon presents his second case: after goring a second ox worth 200, the last victim takes 100, and the previous victim takes 50 while the first owner takes 50.
Rabbi Shimon presents his third case: after goring a third ox worth 200, the last victim takes 100, the previous victim takes 50, and the first two victims each take a gold dinar.

items.text: Gemara's analysis: the Mishnah contradicts both Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis: the Mishnah contradicts both Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whose opinion the Mishnah follows, arguing that it aligns with neither Rabbi Yishmael (who would prioritize the first creditor) nor Rabbi Akiva (who would see the ox as shared property).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whose view the Mishnah follows, noting it aligns with neither Rabbi Yishmael nor Rabbi Akiva.

The Gemara objects: if it followed Rabbi Yishmael (who views them as creditors), the last should not be preferred; if it followed Rabbi Akiva (who views them as partners), the surplus distribution is problematic.
The Gemara objects that if the Mishnah followed Rabbi Akiva, who views the ox as shared property (תורא דשותפי), the phrase 'if there is surplus' would be problematic.

items.text: Gemara's initial objection
items.text_en: Gemara's initial objection
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's phrasing, asking why it says 'returns to the one before him' instead of 'to all of them'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects to the Mishnah's phrase 'returns to the one before him', arguing it should say 'to all of them'.

items.text: Rava's resolution
items.text_en: Rava's resolution
items.desc_en: Rava explains that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yishmael, who holds that the injured parties are creditors, and the case involves the injured party seizing the ox, becoming a paid guardian for damages.

sub.desc_en: Rava explains that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yishmael, who treats the oxen as debtors, and the case involves the victim seizing the ox, making him a paid guardian for subsequent damages.

items.text: Second objection
items.text_en: Second objection
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects again: if so, why does the Mishnah say 'returns to the one before him' instead of 'returns to the owners'?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if so, the Mishnah should say 'returns to the owners' instead of 'returns to the one before him'.

items.text: Ravina's and Rabbi Yochanan's explanation
items.text_en: Ravina's and Rabbi Yochanan's explanation
items.desc_en: Ravina clarifies the Mishnah's wording: 'if there is a surplus in his damages, he returns to the one before him.' Rabbi Yochanan adds that the case involves negligence of the guardians.

sub.desc_en: Ravina explains that the Mishnah's wording means: 'if there is a surplus in his damages, he returns to the one before him.'
Rabbi Yochanan adds that the case involves negligence of the guardians, supporting Ravina's interpretation.

items.text: Challenge from the Mishnah's latter clause
items.text_en: Challenge from the Mishnah's latter clause
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rava's interpretation by citing the latter part of the Mishnah (Rabbi Shimon's case) and the distribution of damages among multiple injured oxen.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rava's interpretation by citing the Mishnah's latter clause (Rabbi Shimon's case) and asking how it fits with Rava's view.
The Gemara cites the full text of Rabbi Shimon's case in the Mishnah, detailing the distribution of damages among multiple injured oxen.

items.text: Reconciliation: Reisha and Seifa follow different Tannaim
items.text_en: Reconciliation: Reisha and Seifa follow different Tannaim
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the first part of the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yishmael, while the latter part follows Rabbi Akiva, as stated by Shmuel to Rav Yehuda.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the first clause of the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yishmael and the latter clause follows Rabbi Akiva, given the apparent inconsistency.
The Sages answer that yes, this is the case, citing Shmuel's instruction to Rav Yehuda that the first clause follows Rabbi Yishmael and the latter clause follows Rabbi Akiva.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's additional distinction
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's additional distinction
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that the dispute between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva is whether the injured party can consecrate the ox.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports that Rabbi Yochanan (רבי יוחנן) states that the practical difference between the opinions of Rabbi Yishmael (רבי ישמעאל) and Rabbi Akiva (רבי עקיבא) is whether the injured party can consecrate the ox.

items.text: Case of a slap and coin values
items.text_en: Case of a slap and coin values
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses a case of one who slaps another, the value of a sela, and resolves that Torah coins are Tyrian while rabbinic coins are provincial, concluding with a story about a litigant and charity.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah is cited: one who slaps another pays a sela; Rabbi Yehuda in the name of Rabbi Yosei HaGelili says a maneh.

sub.text: Rav Toviyya bar Matna's question to Rav Yosef
sub.text_en: Rav Toviyya bar Matna's question to Rav Yosef
sub.desc_en: Rav Toviyya bar Matna asks Rav Yosef whether the sela mentioned is a Tyrian sela or a provincial sela.
Rav Yosef answers by citing the Mishnah's mention of a gold dinar, arguing that if it were a provincial sela, the Mishnah would have listed up to twelve and a sela.
Rav Toviyya bar Matna objects that the Tanna does not need to list all values like a peddler.

sub.text: Gemara's resolution via Rav Yehuda citing Rav
sub.text_en: Gemara's resolution via Rav Yehuda citing Rav
sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the question by citing Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav: all silver mentioned in the Torah is Tyrian silver, while rabbinic silver is provincial.

sub.text: Story of the litigant and charity
sub.text_en: Story of the litigant and charity
sub.desc_en: The litigant, noting the half-zuz difference, first says he does not want it and suggests giving it to the poor, then changes his mind and asks to keep it for his own sustenance.

sub.text: Rav Yosef's ruling and supporting citation
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef's ruling and supporting citation
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef rules that the poor have already acquired the half-zuz, and even though there are no poor here, the court acts as their agents, citing Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel regarding orphans.

items.text: Opening baraita on orphans and prosbul
items.text_en: Opening baraita on orphans and prosbul
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita stating that orphans do not need a prosbul, because Rabban Gamliel and his court are considered their fathers. This is a tangential halakhic statement before the main Mishnah.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that orphans do not require a prosbul (a document circumventing the sabbatical year's cancellation of debts).
Rami bar Chama teaches the same rule, explaining that Rabban Gamliel and his court are considered the father of orphans, thus their property is protected without a prosbul.

items.text: Story of Chanan Bisha and Rav Huna
items.text_en: Story of Chanan Bisha and Rav Huna
items.desc_en: A brief anecdote about Chanan Bisha who struck a man and was ordered by Rav Huna to pay half a zuz, but the man could not extract the coin, so Chanan struck him again and gave him the full zuz.

sub.desc_en: The gemara recounts that Chanan Bisha struck a man, and Rav Huna ordered him to pay half a zuz; when the man could not extract the coin, Chanan struck him again and gave him the full zuz.

items.text: Mishnah: Categories of mu'ad for specific types
items.text_en: Mishnah: Categories of mu'ad for specific types
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that an ox can be mu'ad for its own species but not for others, for people but not animals, for small ones but not large ones. It pays full damage for what it is mu'ad and half for what it is not. Rabbi Yehuda adds the case of Shabbatot vs. weekdays, and defines when it becomes tam again.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by listing categories of mu'ad: an ox can be mu'ad for its own species but not others, for people but not animals, for small but not large, and pays full damage for what it is mu'ad and half for what it is not.
Rabbi Yehuda adds the case of Shabbatot vs. weekdays, ruling that the ox pays full damage for Shabbatot and half for weekdays.
The Mishnah concludes by defining when the ox becomes tam again: after it refrains for three Shabbatot.

items.text: Gemara: Debate between Rav Zevid and Rav Pappa on the Mishnah's wording
items.text_en: Gemara: Debate between Rav Zevid and Rav Pappa on the Mishnah's wording
items.desc_en: Rav Zevid and Rav Pappa argue whether the Mishnah reads 'וְאֵינוֹ מוּעָד' (implying a default of mu'ad) or 'אֵינוֹ מוּעָד' (implying a default of tam). Each deduces his position from different parts of the Mishnah, with Rav Zevid citing the seifa and Rav Pappa the reisha, and they respond to each other's challenges.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute: Rav Zevid claims the Mishnah reads 'וְאֵינוֹ מוּעָד' (implying a default of mu'ad), while Rav Pappa claims it reads 'אֵינוֹ מוּעָד' (implying a default of tam).
The Gemara explains: Rav Zevid's reading implies that the default status of an ox is mu'ad, while Rav Pappa's reading implies that the default is tam.
The Gemara notes that each Amora derives his position from a different part of the Mishnah: Rav Zevid from the seifa (later clause) and Rav Pappa from the reisha (first clause).

sub.text: Rav Zevid's proof from the seifa
sub.text_en: Rav Zevid's proof from the seifa
sub.desc_en: Rav Zevid argues that the seifa's phrase 'וְאֵינוֹ מוּעָד' (with a vav) implies a default of mu'ad, because otherwise the statement that an ox is not mu'ad from small to large animals would be superfluous.

sub.text: Rav Pappa's response to Rav Zevid
sub.text_en: Rav Pappa's response to Rav Zevid
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa counters that the seifa is necessary even on his reading, because one might have thought that goring small animals makes the ox mu'ad for large animals of the same species, so the Mishnah teaches that it does not.

sub.text: Rav Pappa's proof from the reisha
sub.text_en: Rav Pappa's proof from the reisha
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa argues that the reisha's phrase 'אֵינוֹ מוּעָד' (without a vav) implies a default of tam, because otherwise the statement that an ox is not mu'ad from humans to animals would be superfluous.

sub.text: Rav Zevid's response to Rav Pappa
sub.text_en: Rav Zevid's response to Rav Pappa
sub.desc_en: Rav Zevid counters that the reisha deals with a case of return (חזרה) from being mu'ad, teaching that even if the ox stopped goring animals but not humans, the return regarding animals is valid.

items.text: Challenge from Sumchos and Rav Zevid's response
items.text_en: Challenge from Sumchos and Rav Zevid's response
items.desc_en: An objection is raised from Sumchos who says 'mu'ad for people is mu'ad for animals' by a kal vachomer, implying the first tanna said 'אֵינוֹ מוּעָד'. Rav Zevid explains that Sumchos is actually discussing the case of חזרה (retraction from being mu'ad), arguing that retraction from animals is not valid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from Sumchos, who says 'mu'ad for people is mu'ad for animals' by a kal vachomer, implying the first tanna said 'אֵינוֹ מוּעָד'.
Rav Zevid explains that Sumchos is actually discussing the case of חזרה (retraction from being mu'ad), arguing that retraction from animals is not valid.

items.text: Proof from Rabbi Yehuda's statement and Rav Yannai's support
items.text_en: Proof from Rabbi Yehuda's statement and Rav Yannai's support
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi brings a proof from the Mishnah's dialogue with Rabbi Yehuda, where the phrasing 'וְאֵינוֹ מוּעָד' is used, indicating a question. Rav Yannai adds that the reisha also supports this reading, as it explains the distinction rather than stating a new rule.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi brings a proof from the Mishnah's dialogue with Rabbi Yehuda, citing the case of a mu'ad for Shabbatot but not for weekdays.

The Gemara argues that if the Mishnah read 'וְאֵינוֹ מוּעָד' (and it is not mu'ad), the sages' statement would be a question, and Rabbi Yehuda's response would be an answer; but if it read 'אֵינוֹ מוּעָד' (it is not mu'ad), the sages would be teaching a rule, and Rabbi Yehuda's response would be redundant.
Rav Yannai adds that the reisha of the Mishnah also supports the reading 'וְאֵינוֹ מוּעָד', as it explains the distinction between mu'ad and tam.
The Gemara argues that if the Mishnah read 'וְאֵינוֹ מוּעָד', the reisha would be explaining the rule; but if it read 'אֵינוֹ מוּעָד', the reisha would be stating a new rule that is already obvious.
The Gemara concludes that even according to Rav Pappa's reading, there is a case where an ox that gored a donkey and a camel becomes mu'ad for all.

items.text: Baraitot on becoming mu'ad through serugin (intermittent goring)
items.text_en: Baraitot on becoming mu'ad through serugin (intermittent goring)
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites baraitot: if an ox gores intermittently (e.g., gored an ox, then did not, then gored again), it becomes mu'ad for that species through serugin. Similarly, if it gores different species intermittently, it becomes mu'ad for all through serugin.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a hypothetical scenario: if an ox gores a cow, a donkey, and a camel, it becomes mu'ad for all species.
A baraita teaches: if an ox gores intermittently (e.g., gored, did not gore, gored again), it becomes mu'ad for that species through serugin (intermittent goring).
A second baraita teaches: if an ox gores different species intermittently (e.g., gored a cow, did not gore a donkey, gored a horse), it becomes mu'ad for all species through serugin.

items.text: Unfinished query about goring pattern
items.text_en: Unfinished query about goring pattern
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins a new inquiry: if an ox gored... but the text cuts off, leaving the question incomplete.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an incomplete query about an ox that gored, but the text cuts off before specifying the scenario.

items.text: Gemara's questions about sequential gorings
items.text_en: Gemara's questions about sequential gorings
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises several cases of an ox goring multiple times in different sequences (e.g., ox, ox and donkey, camel) and questions whether the later gorings establish mu'ad status for all types or only for the specific pattern. Each case presents two possibilities: either the later goring follows the earlier ones of the same type or the mixed set. The section ends with 'תיקו' (let it stand unresolved).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks about the status of an ox that gored in the sequence ox, ox, ox, donkey, camel: does the last ox goring follow the earlier ox gorings (making it mu'ad only for oxen) or the mixed set (making it mu'ad for all types)?
The Gemara elaborates the two possibilities for the sequence: either the last ox is grouped with the previous ox gorings (mu'ad only for oxen) or with the donkey and camel (mu'ad for all species).
The Gemara asks a second case: donkey, camel, ox, ox, ox — does the first ox follow the donkey and camel (mu'ad for all) or the later ox gorings (mu'ad only for oxen)?

The Gemara asks about gorings on Shabbat, Shabbat, Shabbat, Sunday, Monday — does the last Shabbat goring follow the earlier Shabbat gorings (mu'ad only for Shabbat) or the weekday gorings (mu'ad for all days)?

The Gemara asks about gorings on Thursday, Friday, Shabbat, Shabbat, Shabbat — does the first Shabbat follow the weekday gorings (mu'ad for all days) or the later Shabbat gorings (mu'ad only for Shabbat)?
The Gemara concludes that all these questions remain unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on establishing a pattern
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on establishing a pattern
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a dispute between Rav and Shmuel regarding a case where an ox gored on the 15th, 16th, and 17th of a month. Rav holds that this establishes a fixed pattern (mu'ad), while Shmuel requires three occurrences with a gap (dilug) to establish a pattern. This is analogous to a woman seeing menstrual blood on those dates.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a case of an ox goring on the 15th, 16th, and 17th of consecutive months and notes that this is a dispute between Rav and Shmuel.

The Gemara cites a parallel dispute between Rav and Shmuel regarding a woman who sees menstrual blood on the 15th, 16th, and 17th of consecutive months: Rav says she establishes a fixed cycle (וסת), while Shmuel says she must see three times with a skipped pattern (בדילוג).

items.text: Rava's ruling on shofar sounds
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on shofar sounds
items.desc_en: Rava states that if an ox gored upon hearing a shofar blast three times, it becomes a mu'ad for shofar sounds. The Gemara notes this is obvious but clarifies that one might think the first blast was just a fright, so Rava teaches that it establishes mu'ad status.

sub.desc_en: Rava states that if an ox heard a shofar blast and gored, then heard another shofar blast and gored, and then a third shofar blast and gored, it becomes mu'ad for shofar blasts.
The Gemara objects that this is obvious, but explains that Rava's statement is necessary to counter the possible claim that the first shofar blast was merely a momentary frenzy (סיוטא בעלמא).
The Gemara explains that Rava's teaching is necessary to counter the possible assumption that the first shofar blast was merely a fright, not establishing mu'ad status.

items.text: Mishnah: Goring involving consecrated property and gentiles
items.text_en: Mishnah: Goring involving consecrated property and gentiles
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that an ox of an Israelite that gores an ox of consecrated property is exempt, as is an ox of consecrated property that gores a common ox, based on the verse 'ox of his fellow' excluding consecrated property. An Israelite's ox goring a gentile's ox is exempt, but a gentile's ox goring an Israelite's ox pays full damages whether tam or mu'ad.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that an ox of an Israelite that gored an ox of Temple property (הקדש) is exempt, and an ox of Temple property that gored a commoner's ox is also exempt, based on the verse 'שור רעהו' (the ox of his fellow) — excluding Temple property.
The Mishnah continues: an Israelite's ox that gored a gentile's ox is exempt, but a gentile's ox that gored an Israelite's ox — whether tam (תם) or mu'ad (מועד) — pays full damages (נזק שלם).

items.text: Gemara: Dispute with Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya and resolution
items.text_en: Gemara: Dispute with Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah disagrees with Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya, who holds that a common ox goring consecrated property pays full damages. The Gemara questions his reasoning, considering whether 'fellow' is precise. Resh Lakish resolves that all oxen were initially liable for full damages, but the verse 'fellow' by a tam exempts consecrated property from half damages, implying consecrated property pays full damages whether tam or mu'ad.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah disagrees with Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya, citing a baraita that exempts both a common ox goring consecrated property and a consecrated ox goring a common ox.
Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya states that a consecrated ox goring a common ox is exempt, but a common ox goring a consecrated ox pays full damages whether tam or mu'ad.

The Gemara questions Rabbi Shimon's reasoning: if 'רֵעֵהוּ' (fellow) is precise, even a common ox goring consecrated property should be exempt; if not precise, a consecrated ox goring a common ox should be liable.

The Gemara suggests that Rabbi Shimon might hold 'רֵעֵהוּ' is precise, but derives liability for a common ox goring consecrated property via a קל וחומר (a fortiori) from a common ox goring another common ox.
The Gemara objects that the קל וחומר (a fortiori) inference should yield only half damages for a tam, not full damages, as the source case of a tam goring another common ox pays only half.

Resh Lakish resolves that all oxen were initially liable for full damages; the verse 'רֵעֵהוּ' by a tam exempts consecrated property from half damages, implying consecrated property pays full damages whether tam or mu'ad.

items.text: Opening question on the law of a Jew's ox goring a gentile's ox
items.text_en: Opening question on the law of a Jew's ox goring a gentile's ox
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a dilemma: if the word 'רֵעֵהוּ' (his fellow) in the verse is precise, then even a gentile's ox that gored a Jew's ox should be exempt; if not precise, then even a Jew's ox that gored a gentile's ox should be liable. This sets up the need for a scriptural derivation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a dilemma: if the word 'רֵעֵהוּ' (his fellow) in the verse is precise, then even a gentile's ox that gored a Jew's ox should be exempt; if not precise, then even a Jew's ox that gored a gentile's ox should be liable.

items.text: Derivation from verses: Rabbi Avahu and Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Derivation from verses: Rabbi Avahu and Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu and Rabbi Yochanan each cite a verse to justify the law. Rabbi Avahu says the verse 'עָמַד וַיְמֹדֶד אֶרֶץ' teaches that God permitted the property of gentiles to Israel because they did not keep the seven Noahide laws. Rabbi Yochanan says the verse 'הוֹפִיעַ מֵהַר פָּארָן' teaches that from Paran God made their property permitted to Israel.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu cites the verse 'עָמַד וַיְמֹדֶד אֶרֶץ' to teach that God permitted the property of gentiles to Israel because they did not keep the seven Noahide laws.
Rabbi Yochanan cites the verse 'הוֹפִיעַ מֵהַר פָּארָן' to teach that from Paran God made the property of gentiles permitted to Israel.

items.text: Supporting baraita
items.text_en: Supporting baraita
items.desc_en: A baraita explicitly states the law: a Jew's ox that gored a gentile's ox is exempt; a gentile's ox that gored a Jew's ox pays full damages whether tam or mu'ad, citing the same verses.

sub.desc_en: A baraita supports the ruling: a Jew's ox that gored a gentile's ox is exempt, while a gentile's ox that gored a Jew's ox pays full damages, citing both verses.

items.text: Explanation of 'וְאוֹמֵר' and the expositions of Rav Mattana and Rav Yosef
items.text_en: Explanation of 'וְאוֹמֵר' and the expositions of Rav Mattana and Rav Yosef
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the baraita adds 'וְאוֹמֵר' (and it says). It explains that if one might think the verse 'עָמַד וַיְמֹדֶד' is needed for the expositions of Rav Mattana and Rav Yosef, then the additional verse 'הוֹפִיעַ מֵהַר פָּארָן' teaches the permission of property. Rav Mattana expounds that God saw the seven Noahide laws were not kept and exiled them; Rav Yosef expounds that God permitted their property. The Gemara also proves that 'וַיַּתֵּר' means 'permitted' from a parallel usage.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the baraita adds the word 'וְאוֹמֵר' (and it says) before the second verse.

The Gemara explains that the second verse 'הוֹפִיעַ מֵהַר פָּארָן' is needed to teach that property was permitted, because the first verse 'עָמַד וַיְמֹדֶד' might otherwise be taken for the expositions of Rav Mattana and Rav Yosef.
Rav Mattana expounds that God saw the seven Noahide laws were not kept and therefore exiled the nations from their land.
The Gemara proves that 'וַיַּתֵּר' means 'permitted' by comparing it to the verse 'לְנַתֵּר בָּהֵן עַל הָאָרֶץ' which is translated as 'to jump' (קַפָּצָא), showing the root implies release.
Rav Yosef expounds that God saw the seven Noahide laws were not kept and therefore permitted their property to Israel.

items.text: Objection and resolution regarding reward for gentiles
items.text_en: Objection and resolution regarding reward for gentiles
items.desc_en: An objection is raised: if gentiles' property is permitted because they did not keep the seven laws, then they would be rewarded for sinning. Mar bar Ravana answers that even if they keep them, they do not receive reward. A further objection from Rabbi Meir's teaching that a gentile who studies Torah is like a High Priest is resolved: they do not receive reward like one who is commanded and does, but like one who is not commanded and does, as Rabbi Chanina says the commanded person is greater.

sub.desc_en: The gemara objects: if gentiles' property is permitted because they violated the seven Noahide laws, then they would be rewarded for sinning.
Mar bar Ravana answers that even if gentiles keep the seven laws, they do not receive reward.
The gemara objects from Rabbi Meir's teaching that a gentile who studies Torah is like a High Priest, implying reward.
The gemara resolves: gentiles do receive reward, but not like one who is commanded and does, rather like one who is not commanded and does, as Rabbi Chanina says the commanded person is greater.

items.text: Story of Roman soldiers questioning the law
items.text_en: Story of Roman soldiers questioning the law
items.desc_en: The rabbis taught that the Roman government once sent two soldiers to learn Torah. After studying, they acknowledged its truth except for this law about the ox. They raised the same dilemma as before and said they would not report this to the government.

sub.desc_en: A baraita recounts that Roman officials studied Torah and found it true except for the law exempting a Jew's ox that gored a gentile's ox, which they refused to report to the kingdom.

The soldiers raise the same logical dilemma: if 'רֵעֵהוּ' (his fellow) is precise, then a gentile's ox goring a Jew's should also be exempt; if not precise, then a Jew's ox goring a gentile's should also be liable.
The soldiers decide not to report this inconsistent law to the Roman government.

items.text: Story of consolation and a kal vachomer from Moses
items.text_en: Story of consolation and a kal vachomer from Moses
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that when Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda's daughter died, the rabbis asked Ulla to go console him. Ulla initially declined, but later went alone and consoled him with a kal vachomer from Moses: if Midianites who only came to help Moab were to be attacked, certainly Moab itself should be attacked, but God said not to distress Moab, teaching that one should not cause distress even to those who are not obligated in commandments.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that when Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda's daughter died, the rabbis asked Ulla to go console him, but Ulla initially declined, criticizing Babylonian consolation as mere blasphemy.

Ulla went alone and consoled Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda with a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument) from Moses: if Midianites who only came to help Moab were to be attacked, certainly Moab itself should be attacked, but God said not to distress Moab, teaching that one should not cause distress even to those who are not obligated in commandments.

items.text: The Gemara's argument about Moabites and Ammonites
items.text_en: The Gemara's argument about Moabites and Ammonites
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why God did not destroy Moab and Ammon despite their harsh treatment of Israel, and answers that two good 'branches' (Ruth and Naamah) would emerge from them. It then applies a kal vachomer argument to the daughter of Rabbi.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: If the Moabite women were spared, should not the Moabite men themselves certainly have been spared?
God answers that His plan differed from human understanding: two good 'branches'—Ruth the Moabite and Naamah the Ammonite—would emerge from these nations.

The Gemara applies a kal vachomer (a fortiori) argument: if God spared two great nations for two good branches, how much more should Rabbi's daughter live if she is worthy and will produce something good.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's principle about reward
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's principle about reward
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that God does not withhold reward from any creature, even for a pleasant conversation.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that God does not withhold reward from any creature, even for a pleasant conversation.

items.text: Proof from the daughters of Lot
items.text_en: Proof from the daughters of Lot
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the reward for the pleasant speech of the older daughter (Moab) and the younger daughter (Ammon), showing how their words led to different divine commands to Moses.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of the older daughter's speech
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the older daughter's speech
sub.desc_en: The Gemara shows that the older daughter's pleasant speech (saying 'Moab') led God to command Moses not to wage war against Moab, but permitted conscription (אנגריא).

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of the younger daughter's speech
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the younger daughter's speech
sub.desc_en: The Gemara shows that the younger daughter's even more pleasant speech (saying 'ben ami') led God to command Moses a total prohibition against Ammon, including conscription.

items.text: Reward for precedence in mitzvah
items.text_en: Reward for precedence in mitzvah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha teaches that one should always be early to perform a mitzvah, as the older daughter's precedence over the younger led to four generations of kings for Israel.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha teaches that one should always be early to perform a mitzvah, as the older daughter's precedence over the younger led to four generations of kings for Israel.

items.text: Mishnah about an ox of an Israelite and a Kutite
items.text_en: Mishnah about an ox of an Israelite and a Kutite
items.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Meir dispute the liability when an ox of an Israelite or a Kutite (Samaritan) gores the other's ox. Rabbi Meir holds that a Kutite always pays full damages.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma states the basic law: an Israelite's ox that gores a Kutite's ox is exempt, while a Kutite's ox that gores an Israelite's ox pays half damages for a tam and full damages for a mu'ad.
Rabbi Meir adds that a Kutite's ox that gores an Israelite's ox always pays full damages, whether tam or mu'ad.

items.text: Contradiction about the status of Kutim
items.text_en: Contradiction about the status of Kutim
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Meir considers Kutim as true converts or lion converts, citing a contradiction from a baraita about stains where Rabbi Meir treats them as true converts.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Rabbi Meir's ruling in the baraita implies that he considers Kutim to be lion converts (גרי אריות), i.e., insincere converts.
The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita about stains (כתמים), where Rabbi Meir rules that stains from Kutim are impure, treating them as true converts (גרי אמת).
The Gemara concludes that the contradiction shows Rabbi Meir indeed considers Kutim to be true converts (גרי אמת), not lion converts.

items.text: Resolution: Rabbi Meir's penalty
items.text_en: Resolution: Rabbi Meir's penalty
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu explains that Rabbi Meir's ruling is a penalty on Kutim's property to prevent intermarriage. Rabbi Zeira objects from a mishnah about fines for relations with Kutite women, and Abaye responds.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu explains that Rabbi Meir's ruling is a penalty (קנס) on Kutim's property to prevent intermarriage.

Rabbi Zeira objects from a mishnah listing Kutite women among those for whom there is a fine (קנס) for relations, arguing that if Rabbi Meir penalizes their property, he should also penalize here to prevent intermarriage.
Abaye begins to respond to Rabbi Zeira's objection, but the text cuts off at the end of the section.

items.text: Conclusion of previous discussion: payment to the poor
items.text_en: Conclusion of previous discussion: payment to the poor
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the payment for the goring ox cannot be given to the poor because it is money without claimants.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the payment for the goring ox cannot be given to the poor, invoking the principle that a sinner should not profit.
The Gemara asks why the payment cannot be given to the poor.
Rav Mari answers that it is money without claimants, so it cannot be given to the poor.

items.text: Mishnah: Ox of a deaf-mute, imbecile, or minor
items.text_en: Mishnah: Ox of a deaf-mute, imbecile, or minor
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the laws of an ox belonging to a deaf-mute, imbecile, or minor: if it gores an ox of a competent person, the owner is exempt; if it is gored, the competent owner is liable. A guardian is appointed for such owners, and the ox's status changes upon the owner's recovery.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the basic rule: a competent person's ox that gores the ox of a deaf-mute, imbecile, or minor is liable, but the reverse case is exempt.
The Mishnah adds that for an ox of such owners that gores, a court appoints a guardian and testimony is given in the guardian's presence.
Rabbi Meir rules that when the owner recovers, the ox returns to its status of a תם (innocent ox).
Rabbi Yosei disagrees, holding that the ox remains in its previous status (presumably as a מועד).
The Mishnah concludes that an ox goaded to gore (שור האצטדין) is not liable to death, citing the verse 'כי יגח' (when it gores) — not when it is made to gore.

items.text: Gemara's contradiction within the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's contradiction within the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara points out an internal contradiction: the first clause implies no guardian is appointed for a tam ox, while the later clause implies a guardian is appointed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara points out an internal contradiction in the Mishnah: the first clause implies no guardian is appointed for a tam ox, while the later clause implies a guardian is appointed.

items.text: Rava's resolution: the Mishnah refers to a mu'ad
items.text_en: Rava's resolution: the Mishnah refers to a mu'ad
items.desc_en: Rava resolves the contradiction by explaining that the Mishnah's later clause refers to an ox that has been established as a gorer, for which a guardian is appointed to make it a mu'ad and collect from the best property.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves the contradiction by explaining that the Mishnah's later clause refers to an ox that has been established as a gorer, for which a guardian is appointed to make it a mu'ad and collect from the best property.

items.text: Dispute: whose property pays?
items.text_en: Dispute: whose property pays?
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina dispute whether the payment comes from the orphans' property or the guardian's property.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks from whose property the payment is made after the ox is declared a mu'ad.
Rabbi Yochanan rules that the payment comes from the orphans' property.
Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina rules that the payment comes from the guardian's property.

items.text: Challenge from Rabbi Yochanan's own ruling
items.text_en: Challenge from Rabbi Yochanan's own ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Yochanan's position by citing his own statement that courts do not involve themselves with orphans' property except for usury or a wife's ketubah, suggesting he would not allow collection from orphans' property.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Yochanan's position by citing Rav Yehuda's statement in Rav Asi's name that courts do not involve themselves with orphans' property unless usury is consuming it.
The Gemara adds that Rabbi Yochanan himself ruled that courts only intervene for orphans' property in cases of a usurious loan or a wife's ketubah due to her sustenance needs.
The Gemara proposes reversing the attributions: Rabbi Yochanan said collection is from the guardian's property, and Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina said from the orphans' property.

items.text: Rava's objection and final resolution
items.text_en: Rava's objection and final resolution
items.desc_en: Rava objects to reversing the opinions, arguing that Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina is a deep judge. He concludes that the cases are different because a damaging ox is a special case, and Rabbi Yochanan's original position stands: payment from orphans' property.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects to reversing the opinions, arguing that doing so would make Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina, a deep judge, appear mistaken.
Rava resolves that the opinions should not be reversed; a damaging ox (מזיק) is a special case, so Rabbi Yochanan's original position stands: payment from orphans' property (מעליית יתומים).

items.text: Opening statement: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's view on guardians
items.text_en: Opening statement: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's view on guardians
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina states that the court appoints a guardian for the ox, and later collects from the orphans when they grow up. This sets up the debate about whether guardians are appointed for a tam ox.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina states that the court appoints a guardian for the ox and later collects from the orphans when they grow up.

items.text: Tannaitic dispute: Sumchos vs. Sages on appointing guardians
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute: Sumchos vs. Sages on appointing guardians
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies a tannaitic source for the dispute: Sumchos (in the name of Yehuda ben Nekosa) holds that an ox remains in its tam status until witnesses testify before the owners, implying no guardian is appointed; the Sages hold that guardians are appointed and testimony is given before them. The baraita also discusses cases where the owners recover, with Sumchos and Rabbi Yosei disagreeing on whether the ox returns to its tam status.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a tannaitic dispute underlying the question of appointing guardians for a tam ox.

sub.text: Baraita: Sumchos (in name of Yehuda ben Nekosa)
sub.text_en: Baraita: Sumchos (in name of Yehuda ben Nekosa)
sub.desc_en: Sumchos holds that an ox remains in its tam status until witnesses testify before the owners, implying no guardian is appointed.
The Sages hold that guardians are appointed and testimony is given before them.
Sumchos holds that when the owners recover, the ox returns to its tam status until testimony is given before them.
Rabbi Yosei holds that the ox remains in its established status (presumably mu'ad) even after the owners recover.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of Sumchos's statement
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of Sumchos's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions what Sumchos means by 'it remains in its tam status.' It concludes that he means the ox is not diminished (i.e., no guardian is appointed), while the Sages hold that a guardian is appointed. This clarifies the dispute: Sumchos says no guardian for a tam, the Sages say yes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Sumchos means by 'it remains in its tam status,' and rejects the possibility that it means the ox was never warned at all, since the later clause 'returns to its tam status' implies it had been warned.
The Gemara answers that Sumchos means the ox is not diminished (no guardian is appointed), while the Sages hold that a guardian is appointed for a tam to collect from its body.

items.text: Dispute in the seifa: Sumchos vs. Rabbi Yosei on reshut meshaneh
items.text_en: Dispute in the seifa: Sumchos vs. Rabbi Yosei on reshut meshaneh
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the dispute in the latter part of the baraita: Sumchos holds that 'reshut meshaneh' (the owner's status changes), so the ox returns to tam status; Rabbi Yosei holds that 'reshut eina meshaneh' (the owner's status does not change), so the ox remains in its previous status.
