sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: On what basis do Sumchos and Rabbi Yosei dispute in the latter part of the baraita?

The Gemara explains: The dispute is about whether the owner's status changes (reshut meshaneh) — Sumchos holds that it does, so the ox reverts to tam status; Rabbi Yosei holds that it does not, so the ox remains in its previous status.

items.text: Baraita: Rabbi Yaakov's ruling on deaf, insane, minor's ox
items.text_en: Baraita: Rabbi Yaakov's ruling on deaf, insane, minor's ox
items.desc_en: A baraita states that Rabbi Yaakov says the owner pays half damages for a goring ox belonging to a deaf, insane, or minor person. The Gemara questions this: if it's a tam, half damages is obvious; if it's a mu'ad, either no payment (if guarded) or full payment (if not guarded).

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that Rabbi Yaakov rules the owner pays half damages for a goring ox belonging to a deaf, insane, or minor person.
The Gemara corrects the baraita's phrasing, noting that Rabbi Yaakov himself states the ruling rather than being cited as a passive subject.
The Gemara questions the baraita's context: if the ox is a tam (תם), half damages is obvious; if a mu'ad (מועד), either no payment (if guarded) or full payment (if not guarded) applies.

items.text: Rava's resolution: mu'ad with substandard guarding
items.text_en: Rava's resolution: mu'ad with substandard guarding
items.desc_en: Rava explains that the case is a mu'ad with substandard guarding (not proper guarding). Rabbi Yaakov holds like Rabbi Yehuda that the tam aspect remains in place, and like Rabbi Yehuda that a mu'ad requires only substandard guarding, and like the Rabbis that a guardian is appointed for a tam to collect from its body.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves the difficulty by explaining that the case involves a mu'ad (forewarned ox) with substandard guarding (שמירה פחותה), not proper guarding.

sub.text: Rava's explanation of Rabbi Yaakov's position
sub.text_en: Rava's explanation of Rabbi Yaakov's position
sub.desc_en: Rava explains that Rabbi Yaakov holds like Rabbi Yehuda in two respects: that the tam aspect remains in place (צד תמות במקומה עומדת) and that a mu'ad requires only substandard guarding (מועד סגי ליה בשמירה פחותה).

sub.text: Rava's explanation of Rabbi Yaakov's position (continued)
sub.text_en: Rava's explanation of Rabbi Yaakov's position (continued)
sub.desc_en: Rava adds that Rabbi Yaakov also holds like the Rabbis that a guardian is appointed for a tam to collect from its body (מעמידין אפוטרופוס לתם לגבות מגופו).

items.text: Abaye's objection and alternative explanation
items.text_en: Abaye's objection and alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Abaye objects that Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yaakov do disagree, citing a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda obligates full payment and Rabbi Yaakov only half. Rabba bar Ulla explains that Rabbi Yaakov merely explains Rabbi Yehuda's view. For Abaye, the dispute is about a mu'ad with no guarding: Rabbi Yaakov holds like Rabbi Yehuda on the tam aspect but disagrees on appointing a guardian, so he pays only half of the mu'ad damages.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects that Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yaakov do disagree, citing a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda obligates full payment and Rabbi Yaakov only half.
Rabba bar Ulla explains that Rabbi Yaakov merely explains Rabbi Yehuda's view, not disagrees.
The gemara asks Abaye: if they disagree, on what point do they disagree?
Abaye answers that the case is a mu'ad with no guarding at all.
Abaye explains that Rabbi Yaakov agrees with Rabbi Yehuda on the tam aspect but disagrees on appointing a guardian, so he pays only half of the mu'ad damages.

items.text: Rav Acha bar Avye's challenge to Rava
items.text_en: Rav Acha bar Avye's challenge to Rava
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Avye challenges Rava: according to Abaye the dispute is clear, but according to Rava who says they don't disagree, why not explain the baraita as referring to a tam rather than a mu'ad? This question remains unresolved.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Avye's challenge to Ravina
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Avye's challenge to Ravina
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Avye challenges Ravina: according to Abaye the dispute is clear, but according to Rava who says they don't disagree, why not explain the baraita as referring to a tam rather than a mu'ad?

items.text: Appointing guardians for a tam ox
items.text_en: Appointing guardians for a tam ox
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yaakov's statement teaches that guardians are appointed for a tam ox to collect damages from its body, contrasting with Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov who hold that reduced or no guardianship suffices.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that according to Rabbi Yehuda, a tam ox requires reduced guardianship (שמירה פחותה), not full guardianship.
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov holds that both a tam and a mu'ad ox given reduced guardianship are exempt, implying no guardianship is needed for a tam.
The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Yaakov's statement teaches that guardians are appointed for a tam ox to collect damages from its body.

items.text: Two reasons in one statement
items.text_en: Two reasons in one statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara responds that Rabbi Yaakov's statement contains two reasons in one.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that Rabbi Yaakov's statement contains two reasons in one.

items.text: Dispute about changed status
items.text_en: Dispute about changed status
items.desc_en: Ravina explains that the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yaakov is about a case where the ox's status changed, e.g., a mu'ad that became tam, and whether the original status remains.

sub.desc_en: Ravina introduces the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yaakov as revolving around a change in the ox's legal status (רשות משנה).
Ravina gives an example: a mu'ad (forewarned) ox whose owner became sane, or a minor who matured, illustrating a change in the owner's legal capacity.
Ravina concludes: Rabbi Yehuda holds the original status remains in force (חזקה), while Rabbi Yaakov holds that the status changes (רשות משנה).

items.text: Guardians do not pay kofer
items.text_en: Guardians do not pay kofer
items.desc_en: A baraita states that guardians pay from the upper story but do not pay kofer. The Gemara questions whether kofer is atonement, and orphans cannot atone. Rav Chisda identifies the baraita with Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka, who holds kofer is atonement. Rav Papa explains the dispute is about whether valuation is based on the victim or the injurer.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that guardians pay from the upper story but do not pay kofer.
The Gemara questions whether kofer is atonement, and orphans cannot atone.
Rav Chisda identifies the baraita with Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka, who holds that kofer is atonement.
The Gemara infers that the dispute is whether kofer is monetary compensation or atonement.
Rav Papa explains that all agree kofer is atonement, but they dispute whether valuation is based on the victim or the injurer.

items.text: Kofer for a jointly owned ox
items.text_en: Kofer for a jointly owned ox
items.desc_en: Rava praises Rav Acha bar Yaakov, who asks Rava about how partners pay kofer for their ox. The Gemara raises a dilemma about whether kofer is like a sin-offering (atonement) or monetary, and whether the owner needs to be distrained.

sub.desc_en: Rava praises Rav Acha bar Yaakov to Rav Nachman and asks to bring him.
Rav Acha bar Yaakov asks Rava how partners pay kofer for their jointly owned ox.
Rav Acha bar Yaakov raises the dilemma: each partner cannot pay a full kofer (kofer is one), nor half a kofer (kofer must be complete).
While pondering, Rava asks a related question: whether those liable for kofer are distrained like those liable for valuations or not like those liable for sin-offerings.

The Gemara presents the dilemma: since kofer is atonement (כפרה), it may be like a sin-offering (חטאת) and not require distraint, or since it is paid to the victim, it may be monetary and require distraint.
Alternatively, since the owner did not sin and only his property caused damage, the matter is not stringent and distraint is needed.
Rava tells Rav Acha bar Yaakov to leave him alone so he can focus on the first question.

items.text: Borrower's liability for a mu'ad ox
items.text_en: Borrower's liability for a mu'ad ox
items.desc_en: A baraita discusses a borrower who borrowed an ox presumed tam but found to be mu'ad, and the borrower's liability. The Gemara questions why the borrower pays half damages, and Rav explains that the borrower knew the ox was a gorer. The Gemara further discusses the borrower's claim that he borrowed a tam, not a mu'ad.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that if one borrowed an ox presumed tam and it was found to be mu'ad, both the owner and the borrower pay half damages.
The baraita adds that if the ox was warned in the borrower's domain and then returned, the owner pays half damages and the borrower is exempt.
The Gemara questions why the borrower pays half damages, arguing he could claim he borrowed an ox (תּוֹרָא), not a lion (אַרְיָא).
Rav answers that the case is where the borrower knew the ox was a gorer (נַגְחָן).
The Gemara objects that the borrower could still claim he borrowed a tam, not a mu'ad.
The Gemara rejects the objection, explaining the owner can say: ultimately, even if it were a tam, you would owe half damages, so now too pay half.
The borrower objects that if it were a tam, payment would come from the ox's body (not from the borrower's pocket).
The Gemara rejects this, explaining the owner can say: ultimately, you owe me an ox (the value of the animal).
The Gemara begins another objection, but the text cuts off, indicating an incomplete argument.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the borrower's claim
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the borrower's claim
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the borrower cannot claim that if the ox were a tam he would admit liability or flee, and resolves that the court seized the ox. It then addresses the owner's counter-argument that the borrower could have returned the ox and the borrower's response that he would have fled, concluding with the owner's retort that payment would come from his property anyway.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises the borrower's hypothetical claim: if the ox were a tam (innocent), he would admit liability and be exempt.
The Gemara adds that even according to the view that half-damages are monetary, the borrower could claim he would have fled with the ox to the marsh.
The Gemara resolves that the case involves a situation where the court seized the ox first, preventing the borrower's flight.
The owner objects that if the court seized the ox, why should he pay half-damages, and argues the borrower could have returned the ox to him.
The borrower retorts that even if he returned the ox, he would have fled, but the owner counters that ultimately payment would come from the borrower's property anyway.

items.text: The case of the borrower without assets and Rabbi Natan's principle
items.text_en: The case of the borrower without assets and Rabbi Natan's principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what happens if the borrower has no assets, and answers that the owner can collect from the borrower's debtor based on Rabbi Natan's principle, which derives from the verse 'and he shall give to whom he is indebted'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: granted, the previous argument works when the borrower has assets, but what if he has no assets?
The Gemara answers that the owner can collect from the borrower's debtor based on Rabbi Natan's principle, derived from the verse 'and he shall give to whom he is indebted'.

items.text: Contradiction in the Mishnah regarding the borrower's liability
items.text_en: Contradiction in the Mishnah regarding the borrower's liability
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if an ox was warned in the borrower's domain and returned, the borrower is exempt, but the earlier part of the Mishnah implies the borrower is liable. The Gemara notes the contradiction between the end (borrower exempt) and the beginning (borrower liable).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if an ox was warned in the borrower's domain and returned, the borrower is exempt and the owners pay half damages.
The Gemara points out a contradiction: the end of the Mishnah implies that a change of domain changes liability, while the beginning implies it does not.

items.text: Three resolutions to the Mishnah's contradiction
items.text_en: Three resolutions to the Mishnah's contradiction
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan says the Mishnah is a broken teaching from two different Tannaim. Rabbah says the end also means the domain does not change liability, but the borrower is exempt because the owner could not have warned the ox. Rav Pappa says the beginning also means the domain changes liability, but the ox is considered under the owner's name wherever it goes.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan resolves the contradiction by asserting that the Mishnah is a broken teaching (תִּבְרַהּ) from two different Tannaim.
Rabbah resolves the contradiction by explaining that the end of the Mishnah also means the domain does not change liability, but the borrower is exempt because the owner could not have warned the ox.
Rav Pappa resolves the contradiction by asserting that the beginning of the Mishnah also means the domain changes liability, but the ox is considered under the owner's name wherever it goes.

items.text: Debate about the arena ox's fitness for sacrifice
items.text_en: Debate about the arena ox's fitness for sacrifice
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that an ox used for arena combat is not liable to death. The Gemara asks whether it is fit for the altar. Rav says it is fit because it was forced, while Shmuel says it is unfit because a transgression was performed with it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether an arena ox, which the Mishnah exempts from death, is fit for the altar.
Rav rules the ox is fit for the altar because it was forced (אָנוּס) and not acting willingly.
Shmuel rules the ox is unfit for the altar because a transgression (עֲבֵירָה) was performed with it.

items.text: Baraita excluding unfit animals from sacrifice and Rabbi Shimon's explanation
items.text_en: Baraita excluding unfit animals from sacrifice and Rabbi Shimon's explanation
items.desc_en: A baraita lists animals excluded from sacrifice: a rove'a (one that copulated with a human), a nirba (one that was copulated with), a ne'evad (one worshipped), a muktzah (set aside for idolatry), and a nogeach (a goring ox). Rabbi Shimon explains why both rove'a and nogeach are needed, as each has a unique stringency.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited, deriving from the verse 'מן הבהמה' (from the animal) to exclude a rove'a (one that copulated with a human) and a nirba (one that was copulated with), 'מן הבקר' (from the cattle) to exclude a ne'evad (one worshipped), 'מן הצאן' (from the flock) to exclude a muktzah (set aside for idolatry), and 'ומן הצאן' (and from the flock) to exclude a nogeach (a goring ox).
Rabbi Shimon asks why both rove'a and nogeach are needed, since each alone might seem sufficient.

Rabbi Shimon explains that each has a unique stringency: rove'a treats coercion like willingness (אונס כרצון), while nogeach does not; nogeach pays kofer (ransom), while rove'a does not, so both are necessary.

items.text: Determining the halakha of the baraita's distinction
items.text_en: Determining the halakha of the baraita's distinction
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the distinction between rove'a (where coercion equals willingness) and nogeach (where coercion does not equal willingness) applies to sacrifice or to capital punishment. It concludes it applies to capital punishment, as for sacrifice the distinction would be irrelevant since the animal's own coercion is not written.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the baraita's distinction between rove'a (where coercion equals willingness) and nogeach (where coercion does not equal willingness) applies to sacrifice (קרבן) or to capital punishment.
The Gemara answers that the distinction applies to capital punishment (לקטלא), not to sacrifice.

The Gemara provides supporting reasoning: if the distinction were for sacrifice, the phrase 'נוגח לא עשה בו אונס כרצון' would be irrelevant since the animal's own coercion is not written in the Torah, so it must be for capital punishment.

items.text: Analysis of the kofer payment distinction between nogeach and rove'a
items.text_en: Analysis of the kofer payment distinction between nogeach and rove'a
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the baraita's statement that a nogeach pays kofer while a rove'a does not. It considers cases where the animal killed or did not kill, and Abaye resolves that the rove'a was brought to court and killed, so one might think the owner should pay kofer, but the baraita teaches otherwise.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the baraita's ruling that a goring ox (נוגח) pays kofer, but a bestiality ox (רובע) does not.
The Gemara asks: in what case does this apply? If the ox raped and killed, why should the mode of killing matter for kofer?
Alternatively, if the ox raped but did not kill, then the reason it does not pay kofer is simply that it did not kill, not because of the halacha of rove'a.
Abaye resolves: it is a case where the ox raped but did not kill, yet it was brought to court and killed; one might think the owner should pay kofer, but the baraita teaches otherwise.

items.text: Abaye and Rava dispute the case of an ox that copulated with and killed a person
items.text_en: Abaye and Rava dispute the case of an ox that copulated with and killed a person
items.desc_en: Abaye and Rava argue about whether an ox that copulates with a person and kills him is considered a mu'ad for kofer. Abaye holds that it is like killing with a horn, while Rava distinguishes that the intention is for self-gratification, not to harm. The dispute is applied to a case where an ox tramples a child in the victim's courtyard.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the dispute by stating that Abaye considers the ox that copulated with and killed a person as equivalent to one that killed with a horn.
Rava argues that the ox's intention is for self-gratification, not to harm, so it is not considered a mu'ad for kofer.
The Gemara asks what practical case the dispute applies to, and answers that it concerns an ox that tramples a child in the victim's courtyard.
A baraita is cited supporting Rava's view that an ox used in the arena is not liable to death and is fit for the altar, because it is like one forced.

items.text: Mishnah: Laws of kofer and death penalty for a goring ox
items.text_en: Mishnah: Laws of kofer and death penalty for a goring ox
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a mu'ad ox that kills a person pays kofer, while a tam is exempt from kofer, but both are put to death. The same applies for killing a son or daughter. For a slave, the owner pays thirty sela'im regardless of the slave's value.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the laws of kofer and death penalty for a goring ox, including distinctions between mu'ad and tam, and the fixed payment for a slave.

items.text: Gemara: How can a tam be a mu'ad for kofer?
items.text_en: Gemara: How can a tam be a mu'ad for kofer?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a tam ox can be put to death yet still be considered a mu'ad for kofer. Various Amoraim offer scenarios: the ox was assessed for three people (Rabbah), endangered three people (Rav Ashi), killed three animals (Rav Zevid), killed three gentiles (Rav Shimi), killed three treifa people (Reish Lakish), killed and fled to a marsh (Rav Pappa), or the witnesses were disqualified (Rav Acha). The Gemara concludes with a case where the owner is known but the ox is not, and the owner is liable for not guarding his ox.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: since a tam ox is put to death, how can it ever become a mu'ad for kofer?
Rabbah answers: the case is where the ox was assessed for three people (i.e., it gored three people but was not yet sentenced).
Rav Ashi rejects assessment as insufficient and says the ox endangered three people (but did not kill them).
Rav Zevid answers: the ox killed three animals.
The Gemara objects: does being a mu'ad for animals make it a mu'ad for humans?
Rav Shimi answers: the ox killed three gentiles.
The Gemara objects: does being a mu'ad for gentiles make it a mu'ad for Jews?
Reish Lakish answers: the ox killed three treifa (terminally ill) people.
The Gemara objects: does being a mu'ad for treifa people make it a mu'ad for healthy people?
Rav Pappa answers: the ox killed and fled to a marsh (so it was not sentenced).

sub.text: Rav Acha brei d'Rav Ika's answer
sub.text_en: Rav Acha brei d'Rav Ika's answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha answers: the witnesses were disqualified through zomem (false witness) testimony.
The Gemara objects: if we need to establish the ox as mu'ad, this works; but if we need to establish the owner as warned, the owner can claim ignorance.

sub.text: Gemara's resolution to Rav Acha's case
sub.text_en: Gemara's resolution to Rav Acha's case
sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves: the case is where witnesses say the owner was present every time his ox killed.
Ravina answers: the case is where the owner is known but the ox is not (so the ox cannot be sentenced).
The Gemara concludes: the owner is liable because he should have guarded all his cattle.

items.text: Derivation of prohibition against benefit from a stoned ox
items.text_en: Derivation of prohibition against benefit from a stoned ox
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from the verse 'lo ye'achel et besaro' that an ox slaughtered after its verdict is forbidden for consumption. It then asks about benefit, citing Shimon ben Zoma's analogy. A challenge is raised that the verse might only prohibit benefit from the stoned ox itself, but the Gemara concludes that it also applies to slaughter, based on Rabbi Avahu's principle that 'lo ye'achel' includes both eating and benefit unless specified otherwise. Mar Zutra objects.

sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches that from the verse 'סָקֹל יִסָּקֵל הַשּׁוֹר' (the ox shall be stoned) one might think it is a neveila (carcass) forbidden for eating, so the verse 'לֹא יֵאָכֵל אֶת בְּשָׂרוֹ' (do not eat its flesh) teaches that if one slaughtered the ox after its verdict, it is forbidden for consumption.

The Gemara asks how we know that benefit (הנאה) from the ox is also forbidden, and cites Shimon ben Zoma's analogy that 'וּבַעַל הַשּׁוֹר נָקִי' (the owner of the ox is clear) means the owner is cleared of any benefit from the ox.

The Gemara challenges that perhaps the verse 'לֹא יֵאָכֵל' (do not eat) refers only to the stoned ox itself, forbidding benefit, and that slaughter after the verdict would be permitted; it then invokes Rabbi Avahu's principle that wherever 'לֹא יֹאכַל' (do not eat) is stated, it includes both eating and benefit unless the verse specifies otherwise, as it does with neveila (carcass) permitting giving to a ger (convert) or selling to a gentile.

The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Avahu's principle applies only when both prohibitions derive from 'לֹא יֹאכַל' (do not eat), but here the prohibition of eating comes from 'סָקֹל יִסָּקֵל' (shall be stoned), so the extra phrase 'אֶת בְּשָׂרוֹ' (its flesh) teaches that even if one slaughtered it, it remains forbidden.
Mar Zutra objects to the resolution, suggesting an alternative interpretation.

items.text: Gemara's initial objection to the distinction between stoning and slaughter
items.text_en: Gemara's initial objection to the distinction between stoning and slaughter
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the earlier assumption that slaughtering with a knife is different from stoning, arguing that the Torah does not specify a knife and any valid slaughtering method is permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the distinction between stoning and slaughter is based on using a rock versus a knife, but the Torah does not specify a knife.
The Gemara cites a baraita that slaughter with a sickle, rock, or reed is valid, proving the Torah does not require a knife.
The Gemara resolves that since the prohibition of eating and benefit derives from 'לֹא יֵאָכֵל', the phrase 'בַּעַל הַשּׁוֹר נָקִי' teaches that the hide is also forbidden for benefit.
The Gemara asks how the Tannaim who interpret 'בַּעַל הַשּׁוֹר נָקִי' for another derivation learn the prohibition of the hide.
The Gemara answers that they derive it from 'אֶת בְּשָׂרוֹ', interpreting 'אֶת' to include the hide as secondary to the flesh.
The Gemara notes that the first Tanna does not expound the word 'אֶת'.

A baraita recounts that Shimon HaAmsoni (or Nechemya HaAmsoni) used to expound every 'אֶת' in the Torah until he reached 'אֶת ה׳ אֱלֹהֶיךָ תִּירָא' and stopped, saying he received reward for both the exposition and the withdrawal.
Rabbi Akiva taught that 'אֶת ה׳ אֱלֹהֶיךָ תִּירָא' includes Torah scholars, resolving the difficulty.
A baraita states that Rabbi Eliezer interprets 'וּבַעַל הַשּׁוֹר נָקִי' as meaning the owner is exempt from half the ransom.
Rabbi Akiva objects that the ox itself is not subject to payment except from its body, citing the verse 'הֲבִיאֵהוּ לְבֵית דִּין, וִישַׁלֶּם לָךְ'.
Rabbi Eliezer responds that his ruling applies only when the ox killed based on one witness or the owners themselves.
The Gemara objects that if the owners testify, they are admitting to a penalty (קנס), which is invalid.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Eliezer considers the ransom (כופר) as atonement (כפרה), not a penalty, so admission is valid.

Another baraita records Rabbi Eliezer's alternative response: his ruling applies only when the ox intended to kill an animal but killed a person, or intended to kill a gentile but killed a Jew, or intended to kill a non-viable fetus but killed a viable child.
The Gemara asks which of the two responses Rabbi Eliezer said first.

sub.text: Rav Kahana in the name of Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Kahana in the name of Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana in the name of Rava says that Rabbi Eliezer first said the response about intention (מתכוון), and provides a parable of a fisherman.

sub.text: Rav Tavyomi in the name of Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Tavyomi in the name of Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Tavyomi in the name of Rava says that Rabbi Eliezer first said the response about killing (המית).

items.text: Gemara's counter-question about the knife requirement
items.text_en: Gemara's counter-question about the knife requirement
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the previous statement by noting that the Torah does not explicitly require a knife, citing a mishnah that allows slaughter with various implements.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the requirement for a knife by noting that the Torah does not explicitly mention a knife, citing a mishnah that permits slaughter with various implements like a hand sickle, stone, or reed.

items.text: Derivation of the prohibition of the hide from 'Ba'al HaShor Naki'
items.text_en: Derivation of the prohibition of the hide from 'Ba'al HaShor Naki'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that since the prohibition of eating and deriving benefit from the flesh is derived from 'lo ye'achel', the phrase 'Ba'al HaShor Naki' teaches that the hide is also forbidden for benefit.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that since the prohibition of eating and deriving benefit from the flesh is derived from 'לֹא יֵאָכֵל' (it shall not be eaten), the phrase 'בַּעַל הַשּׁוֹר נָקִי' (the owner of the ox is clear) teaches that the hide is also forbidden for benefit.

items.text: Alternative derivation for the prohibition of the hide
items.text_en: Alternative derivation for the prohibition of the hide
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how those Tannaim who use 'Ba'al HaShor Naki' for another derivation learn the prohibition of the hide)Skip. It answers that they derive it from 'et besaro', including that which is secondary to the flesh, i.e., the hide. However, the Tanna who does not expound 'et' cannot use this method.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how those Tannaim who use the phrase 'Ba'al HaShor Naki' for another derivation learn the prohibition of benefiting from the hide.
The Gemara answers that they derive it from 'et besaro', including that which is secondary to the flesh, i.e., the hide.
The Gemara notes that the Tanna who does not expound 'et' cannot use this method.

items.text: The story of Shimon HaAmsoni and Rabbi Akiva's teaching
items.text_en: The story of Shimon HaAmsoni and Rabbi Akiva's teaching
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that Shimon HaAmsoni (or Nechemya HaAmsoni) used to expound every 'et' in the Torah until he reached 'et Hashem Elokecha tira', where he stopped. His students asked what would become of the other expositions, and he said he received reward for both the exposition and the withdrawal. Rabbi Akiva later taught that 'et' includes talmidei chachamim.

sub.desc_en: The baraita introduces Shimon HaAmsoni (or Nechemya HaAmsoni) who used to expound every 'et' in the Torah until he reached 'et Hashem Elokecha tira' and stopped.
The students ask what will become of all the previous expositions of 'et' that he had taught.
He answers that he received reward both for the exposition and for the withdrawal.
Rabbi Akiva later taught that 'et' in 'et Hashem Elokecha tira' includes talmidei chachamim, resolving the difficulty.

items.text: Debate between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva about 'Ba'al HaShor Naki'
items.text_en: Debate between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva about 'Ba'al HaShor Naki'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer says 'Ba'al HaShor Naki' teaches that the owner is exempt from half-kofér. Rabbi Akiva objects, arguing that the owner is only liable from the body of the ox. Rabbi Eliezer clarifies that his ruling applies only when the ox killed based on a single witness or the owner's own admission. The Gemara questions how the owner's admission can be valid, since he is a confessor to a fine, and answers that Rabbi Eliezer holds that kofér is atonement, not a fine.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites Rabbi Eliezer's position that the phrase 'Ba'al HaShor Naki' teaches the owner is exempt from half-kofér.
Rabbi Akiva objects, arguing that the owner is only liable from the body of the ox, as implied by the verse 'bring it to court and it shall pay you'.
Rabbi Eliezer clarifies that his ruling applies only when the ox killed based on a single witness or the owner's own admission.
The Gemara questions how the owner's admission can be valid, since he is a confessor to a fine (מודה בקנס) and thus exempt.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Eliezer holds that kofér is atonement (כפרה), not a fine, so the owner's admission is valid.

items.text: Alternative version of Rabbi Eliezer's ruling and the dispute about which version was first
items.text_en: Alternative version of Rabbi Eliezer's ruling and the dispute about which version was first
items.desc_en: A baraita presents another version where Rabbi Eliezer says his ruling applies only when one intended to kill the animal but killed a person, or intended to kill a gentile but killed a Jew, or intended to kill a non-viable fetus but killed a viable child. The Gemara then debates which version Rabbi Eliezer stated first: Rav Kahana in the name of Rava says he stated the 'intended' version first, while Rav Tavyomei in the name of Rava says he stated the 'killed' version first. Rav Kahana illustrates with a parable of a fisherman.

sub.desc_en: A baraita presents Rabbi Eliezer's alternative version: his ruling applies only when one intended to kill the animal but killed a person, intended to kill a gentile but killed a Jew, or intended to kill a non-viable fetus but killed a viable child.
The Gemara asks which version Rabbi Eliezer stated first.

sub.text: Rav Kahana in the name of Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Kahana in the name of Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana in the name of Rava says Rabbi Eliezer stated the 'intended' version first, while Rav Tavyomei in the name of Rava says he stated the 'killed' version first.

sub.text: Rav Tavyomei in the name of Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Tavyomei in the name of Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Tavyomei in the name of Rava says Rabbi Eliezer stated the 'killed' version first.
Rav Kahana illustrates his position with a parable of a fisherman who catches fish from the sea.

items.text: Opening statement about the ox's owner
items.text_en: Opening statement about the ox's owner
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a statement about an ox that kills a woman: if it finds large (fetuses) it takes them, if small it takes them, implying liability for the fetuses.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a general statement about an ox that kills a pregnant woman: whether it finds large fetuses or small ones, it takes them, implying liability for the fetuses.

items.text: Rav Tavyomei's explanation of the opening statement
items.text_en: Rav Tavyomei's explanation of the opening statement
items.desc_en: Rav Tavyomei in the name of Rava explains the statement with a parable of a fisherman who takes small fish when he finds them, but throws them away when he finds large ones, indicating that the ox takes both large and small fetuses.

sub.text: Rav Tavyomei in the name of Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Tavyomei in the name of Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Tavyomei explains the opening statement by a parable of a fisherman who takes small fish when he finds them, but throws them away when he finds large ones, indicating that the ox takes both large and small fetuses.

items.text: Rabbi Yosei HaGlili and Rabbi Akiva on "ba'al hashor naki"
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei HaGlili and Rabbi Akiva on "ba'al hashor naki"
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that Rabbi Yosei HaGlili interprets "ba'al hashor naki" as exempt from payment for the fetuses. Rabbi Akiva objects, citing the verse about men who fight and strike a pregnant woman, which implies liability only for men, not oxen. The Gemara affirms Rabbi Akiva's statement.

sub.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi Yosei HaGlili's interpretation of the verse 'ba'al hashor naki' as exempting the ox owner from payment for the fetuses.
Rabbi Akiva objects, citing the verse 'כי ינצו אנשים' (when men fight) to argue that liability for striking a pregnant woman applies only to men, not to oxen.
The Gemara affirms that Rabbi Akiva's statement is well-said.

items.text: Rav Ulla's initial explanation of the necessity of the verse
items.text_en: Rav Ulla's initial explanation of the necessity of the verse
items.desc_en: Rav Ulla bar Rav Idi suggests that the verse "ba'al hashor naki" is necessary to teach that a tam ox is exempt, because one might have thought that since men are forewarned, oxen that are like men (mu'ad) are also forewarned, and a tam would be liable; the verse exempts the tam.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ulla bar Rav Idi explains that the verse "ba'al hashor naki" is necessary to teach that a tam ox is exempt, because one might have thought that since men are forewarned (מועדין), oxen that are like men (mu'ad) are also forewarned, and a tam would be liable; the verse exempts the tam.

items.text: Rava's objection to Rav Ulla's explanation
items.text_en: Rava's objection to Rav Ulla's explanation
items.desc_en: Rava objects strongly, asking if this is established in the earth and a convert in the heavens, implying the explanation is absurd.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects to Rav Ulla's explanation, rhetorically asking if the ox is established in the earth and the convert in the heavens, implying the explanation is absurd.

items.text: Rava's corrected explanation
items.text_en: Rava's corrected explanation
items.desc_en: Rava explains that the verse is necessary because one might have thought that since men are forewarned, oxen that are like men are forewarned, and a kal vachomer would exempt a tam; the verse teaches that a tam is exempt and a mu'ad is liable.

sub.desc_en: Rava explains that the verse is necessary because one might have thought that since men are forewarned, oxen that are like men are forewarned, and a kal vachomer would exempt a tam; the verse teaches that a tam is exempt and a mu'ad is liable.

items.text: Abaye's challenge and the Gemara's response
items.text_en: Abaye's challenge and the Gemara's response
items.desc_en: Abaye challenges Rava's explanation, arguing that the same logic would apply to boshet (shame), and the verse should then exempt from boshet as well. The Gemara responds that if so, the baraita should have mentioned boshet.

sub.desc_en: Abaye challenges Rava's explanation by arguing that the same logic applied to boshet (shame) would lead to the verse exempting a tam ox from shame damages, which is not the case.
The Gemara objects that if Abaye's logic were correct, the baraita should have explicitly mentioned that Rabbi Yose HaGelili exempts from boshet as well, which it does not.

items.text: Abaye and Rava's joint explanation
items.text_en: Abaye and Rava's joint explanation
items.desc_en: Abaye and Rava together explain that the verse about men teaches that if there is no misfortune to the woman, they are punished; if there is misfortune, they are not. For oxen, even if there is misfortune, they are punished. The verse "ba'al hashor naki" exempts the ox.

sub.desc_en: Abaye and Rava together resolve the difficulty by explaining that the verse 'אנשים' teaches that for men, if there is no misfortune to the woman they are punished, but if there is misfortune they are not; for oxen, even if there is misfortune they are punished, and the verse 'בעל השור נקי' exempts the ox.

items.text: Rav Adda bar Ahava's objection and alternative explanation
items.text_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava's objection and alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava objects that the matter depends on intent, not misfortune. He explains that for men, if they intended for each other, they are punished even if there is misfortune; if they intended for the woman, they are not. For oxen, even if they intended for the woman, they are punished. The verse exempts them.

sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava objects that the matter depends on intent, not on the presence of misfortune (אסון).

sub.text: Rav Adda bar Ahava's alternative explanation
sub.text_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava's alternative explanation
sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava explains that for men, if they intended for each other they are punished even with misfortune; if they intended for the woman they are not. For oxen, even if they intended for the woman they are punished, and the verse 'בַּעַל הַשּׁוֹר נָקִי' exempts them.

items.text: Support for Rav Adda bar Ahava from Rav Chaggai
items.text_en: Support for Rav Adda bar Ahava from Rav Chaggai
items.desc_en: When Rav Chaggai came from the south, he brought a baraita that supports Rav Adda bar Ahava's explanation.

sub.desc_en: The gemara reports that when Rav Chaggai came from the south, he brought a baraita (מתניתא) that supports Rav Adda bar Ahava's explanation.

items.text: Another baraita: Rabbi Akiva on "ba'al hashor naki"
items.text_en: Another baraita: Rabbi Akiva on "ba'al hashor naki"
items.desc_en: Another baraita teaches that Rabbi Akiva interprets "ba'al hashor naki" as exempt from payment for a slave.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that Rabbi Akiva interprets 'בַּעַל הַשּׁוֹר נָקִי' (the owner of the ox is clear) as exempting the owner from payment for a slave.

items.text: Gemara's question and Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak's answer
items.text_en: Gemara's question and Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rabbi Akiva does not simply argue that the ox should pay from its own body, since it is liable to be stoned. Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak answers that the case is where the owner slaughtered the ox first, so one might think it can still be used for payment, but the verse teaches that since it was condemned to death, even after slaughter it cannot be used.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rabbi Akiva does not simply argue that the ox should pay from its own body, since it is liable to be stoned.

sub.text: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak's answer
sub.text_en: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak's answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak answers that the case is where the owner slaughtered the ox first, so one might think it can still be used for payment, but the verse teaches that since it was condemned to death, even after slaughter it cannot be used.

items.text: Applying the same logic to Rabbi Eliezer
items.text_en: Applying the same logic to Rabbi Eliezer
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the same reasoning applies to Rabbi Eliezer, and answers that it does, but Rabbi Eliezer has a stronger reason. The Gemara then questions why Rabbi Eliezer doesn't use this argument, and explains that in his case the ox was not condemned to death because it intended to kill an animal but killed a person, so a verse is needed to exempt it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the same logic of prior slaughter applies to Rabbi Eliezer's case.
The Gemara answers that the same applies, but Rabbi Eliezer has a stronger reason and would not use this argument.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Eliezer could have used the same prior-slaughter argument.
The Gemara resolves that in Rabbi Eliezer's case the ox was not condemned to death because it intended to kill an animal, so a verse is needed to exempt it, unlike the case of a condemned ox.

items.text: Rejection of the previous answer for Rabbi Akiva
items.text_en: Rejection of the previous answer for Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that according to Rabbi Akiva, the same reasoning should apply, implying the previous answer is insufficient.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that according to Rabbi Akiva, the same reasoning should apply, implying the previous answer is insufficient.

items.text: Rav Asi's explanation in the name of Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina
items.text_en: Rav Asi's explanation in the name of Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina
items.desc_en: Rav Asi reports a tradition from Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina: one might think that since Rabbi Akiva rules that a tam that injures a person pays full damages from the best property, the slave's value should also be paid from the best property; therefore the verse says 'the owner of the ox is clear' to exempt him.

sub.text: Rav Asi in the name of Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina
sub.text_en: Rav Asi in the name of Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina
sub.desc_en: Rav Asi resolves the difficulty by citing a tradition from Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina: one might think that since Rabbi Akiva rules that a tam that injures a person pays full damages from the best property, the slave's value should also be paid from the best property; therefore the verse says 'the owner of the ox is clear' to exempt him.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's objection to Rav Asi
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's objection to Rav Asi
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira objects that Rabbi Akiva himself already refuted this reasoning, citing a baraita where Rabbi Akiva says the verse 'according to this judgment shall be done to him' teaches that payment is from the body, not from the best property.

sub.text: Rabbi Zeira's objection to Rav Asi
sub.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's objection to Rav Asi
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira objects that Rabbi Akiva himself already refuted the reasoning that payment could come from the best property, citing a baraita where Rabbi Akiva derives from the verse 'כמשפט הזה יעשה לו' (according to this judgment shall be done to him) that payment is from the body of the ox, not from the best property.

items.text: Rava's alternative explanation
items.text_en: Rava's alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Rava explains that the verse is needed because one might think that since we are stricter with a slave than a free person (a slave worth one sela pays thirty), the slave's value should be paid from the best property; therefore the verse says 'the owner of the ox is clear'.

sub.desc_en: Rava explains that the verse is needed because one might think that since we are stricter with a slave than a free person (a slave worth one sela pays thirty), the slave's value should be paid from the best property; therefore the verse says 'the owner of the ox is clear'.

items.text: Baraita supporting Rava and the logical argument
items.text_en: Baraita supporting Rava and the logical argument
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Rava, stating that Rabbi Akiva says 'the owner of the ox is clear' means clear from paying for a slave. The Gemara then presents a logical argument: since one might think that just as with a free person we distinguish between tam and mu'ad, so too with a slave, but the verse teaches that because of the stringency of a slave, he is exempt.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Rava, stating that Rabbi Akiva interprets 'the owner of the ox is clear' as clear from paying for a slave.

The Gemara raises a logical argument: since one is liable for both a slave and a free person, just as one distinguishes between tam and mu'ad for a free person, so too should one distinguish for a slave.

The Gemara adds an a fortiori argument: if for a free person, who pays full value, one distinguishes between tam and mu'ad, then for a slave, who pays only thirty, it is all the more fitting to distinguish.

The baraita rejects the argument, explaining that because the slave is more stringent (paying thirty even if worth only a sela), one might think he is liable, but the verse 'the owner of the ox is clear' teaches that he is clear from paying for a slave.

items.text: Rabbi Akiva's teaching on the verse 'if it kills a man or a woman'
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's teaching on the verse 'if it kills a man or a woman'
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses Rabbi Akiva's interpretation of the verse 'and it kills a man or a woman', which he says comes to teach that a woman's damages go to her heirs, just as a man's go to his. The Gemara questions this, noting that Rabbi Akiva holds that a husband inherits his wife. Resh Lakish answers that this applies only to kofer, which is paid after death and is considered 'ראוי' (not yet possessed), and a husband does not inherit such property.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites Rabbi Akiva's question: why is the verse 'and it kills a man or a woman' needed, since the obligation to include a woman is already stated earlier?
Rabbi Akiva answers that the verse comes to equate a woman to a man: just as a man's damages go to his heirs, so too a woman's damages go to her heirs.
The Gemara objects: does Rabbi Akiva really hold that a husband does not inherit his wife? But a baraita states that Rabbi Akiva derives from a verse that a husband inherits his wife.
Resh Lakish resolves: Rabbi Akiva's statement applies only to kofer (ransom), which is paid after death and is considered 'ראוי' (not yet possessed), and a husband does not inherit such property.

items.text: Proof from the verse and extension to damages
items.text_en: Proof from the verse and extension to damages
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse to support Resh Lakish, then asks whether Rabbi Akiva holds this only for kofer but not for damages. It brings a baraita about a man who strikes a woman causing miscarriage, where the damages go to the woman's heirs if she has no husband, implying that for damages the husband does inherit, contradicting the earlier teaching.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse to support Resh Lakish's distinction that kofer is paid after death and thus the husband does not inherit.
The Gemara asks whether Rabbi Akiva holds this distinction only for kofer but not for damages.

The Gemara brings a baraita about a man who strikes a woman causing miscarriage, where the damages go to the woman's heirs if she has no husband, implying that for damages the husband does inherit, contradicting the earlier teaching.

items.text: Opening statement: the divorcee acquires fetal damages
items.text_en: Opening statement: the divorcee acquires fetal damages
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that if a pregnant divorcee is injured, the husband does not receive the fetal damages; rather, she acquires them herself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that a pregnant divorcee acquires the fetal damages herself, not the husband.

items.text: Rabbah and Rav Nachman: the case of a divorcee
items.text_en: Rabbah and Rav Nachman: the case of a divorcee
items.desc_en: Rabbah and Rav Nachman explain that the ruling applies specifically to a divorcee. The Gemara questions why a divorcee should not also share in the fetal damages. Rav Pappa answers that the Torah grants fetal damages to the husband even if he had relations with her illicitly, citing the verse 'as the husband of the woman shall lay upon him'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah and Rav Nachman state that the ruling applies specifically to a divorcee (גרושה).
The Gemara questions why a divorcee should not also share in the fetal damages (דמי ולדות).

Rav Pappa answers that the Torah grants fetal damages to the husband even if he had relations with her illicitly, citing the verse 'as the husband of the woman shall lay upon him' (כאשר ישית עליו בעל האשה).

items.text: Distinction between collecting land and money
items.text_en: Distinction between collecting land and money
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the positions of Rabbah and Rav Nachman by distinguishing whether the damages were collected as land or money. Rabbah holds that if land was collected, the husband has a share; if money, he does not. Rav Nachman holds the opposite.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the dispute between Rabbah and Rav Nachman by distinguishing whether the damages were collected as money or land.
The Gemara cites the explicit positions of Rabbah and Rav Nachman on the rule: if land was collected the husband has a share, if money he does not, and vice versa.

items.text: Attribution to the Westerners and Rabbi
items.text_en: Attribution to the Westerners and Rabbi
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the previous distinction applies according to the Westerners (the sages of Eretz Yisrael) who follow the Rabbis, but here they speak according to Rabbi's opinion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the earlier distinction applies according to the Westerners who follow the Rabbis, but here the statement is made according to Rabbi's opinion.

items.text: Reish Lakish: unintentional killing of a slave exempts from thirty shekels
items.text_en: Reish Lakish: unintentional killing of a slave exempts from thirty shekels
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish states that if an ox kills a slave unintentionally, the owner is exempt from the thirty-shekel fine, as the verse links the payment to the ox being stoned.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish rules that an ox that kills a slave unintentionally is exempt from the thirty-shekel fine, based on the verse linking payment to the ox's stoning.

items.text: Rabbah: unintentional killing of a free person exempts from kofer
items.text_en: Rabbah: unintentional killing of a free person exempts from kofer
items.desc_en: Rabbah extends the principle to a free person: if an ox kills a free person unintentionally, the owner is exempt from kofer (ransom), based on the same scriptural link.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah rules that an ox that kills a free man unintentionally is exempt from the ransom (כופר), based on the same scriptural logic linking payment to the ox's stoning.

items.text: Abaye's objection and resolution
items.text_en: Abaye's objection and resolution
items.desc_en: Abaye challenges Rabbah from a mishnah where one who admits 'my ox killed so-and-so' pays on his own admission. The Gemara initially suggests this refers to kofer, but then distinguishes: the first clause refers to damages (dammim), the latter to a fine (kenas). However, the Gemara rejects this forced distinction and concludes both clauses refer to damages.

sub.desc_en: Abaye challenges Rabbah by citing a mishnah where one who admits 'my ox killed so-and-so' pays on his own admission, and asks whether this refers to kofer (ransom).
The Gemara initially answers that the mishnah refers to damages (דמים), not kofer.
The Gemara objects: if the first clause is about damages, why does the latter clause say one does not pay on his own admission for killing a slave? If it's damages, he should pay.
The Gemara initially suggests a forced distinction that the first clause is damages and the latter a fine, but then rejects this and concludes both clauses refer to damages.

items.text: Distinction between a free man and a slave regarding self-incrimination
items.text_en: Distinction between a free man and a slave regarding self-incrimination
items.desc_en: The Gemara sets up a contrast: a free man's ox can pay kofer on his own admission when there are witnesses but uncertainty about the ox's status, while a slave's owner cannot pay the fine (knas) on his own admission; without witnesses, the free man pays damages but the slave owner pays nothing.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara establishes a distinction: a free man's ox pays kofer on his own admission when witnesses exist but the ox's status is uncertain, while a slave's owner cannot pay the fine (knas) on his own admission, and without witnesses the free man pays damages but the slave owner pays nothing.

items.text: Objection from a baraita and resolution
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak objects with a baraita that equates liability for a free man and a slave, implying a slave also pays kofer. The Gemara clarifies that the baraita refers to damages (damim) for a free man and a fine (knas) for a slave, or alternatively, it distinguishes between intentional and unintentional killing with witnesses.

sub.text: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak's objection
sub.text_en: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak's objection
sub.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak objects by citing a baraita that states whatever a free man is liable for, a slave is also liable, both for kofer and for death.
The Gemara questions how kofer can apply to a slave, concluding the baraita must refer to damages (damim) instead.

Some say Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak himself resolves the objection: the baraita means that for a free man, intentional killing with witnesses requires kofer, and for a slave, the equivalent is a fine (knas); for unintentional killing with witnesses, both pay damages (damim).

Others say Rabbah resolved it: the baraita teaches that whatever a free man is liable for intentionally with witnesses (kofer), a slave is liable for a fine (knas); and whatever a free man is liable for unintentionally with witnesses (damim), a slave is liable for damages (damim).

items.text: Rava's challenge and the Gemara's inquiry
items.text_en: Rava's challenge and the Gemara's inquiry
items.desc_en: Rava challenges Rabbah's explanation: if unintentional killing with witnesses requires damages for a slave, then an unintentional fire that kills a slave should also require damages. The Gemara asks how Rava knows that such a fire does not pay damages.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects to Rabbah's explanation: if unintentional killing with witnesses requires damages for a slave, then an unintentional fire that kills a slave should also require damages.
The Gemara asks how Rava knows that such a fire does not pay damages.

items.text: Attempted proofs and dismissal
items.text_en: Attempted proofs and dismissal
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers two possible proofs for Rava's position: a mishna about a tied slave and a baraita comparing fire and a pit. Both are rejected—the first because of Reish Lakish's interpretation, the second because the baraita might have omitted details.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes a proof from a mishna: if a tied slave is burned with the fire, the owner is exempt, implying no payment of דמים (compensation) for an unintentional act.
Reish Lakish explains that the mishna's exemption applies only when the fire was set directly on the slave's body, which is a case of intentional killing, not an unintentional act.

The Gemara offers another proof from a baraita comparing fire and a pit: the baraita lists fire's stringencies but does not include that fire pays דמים (compensation) for unintentional acts, implying it does not.
The Gemara dismisses the baraita proof by suggesting the Tanna might have omitted details, so the absence of a clause is not conclusive.

items.text: Rava's own dilemma and teiku
items.text_en: Rava's own dilemma and teiku
items.desc_en: The Gemara reveals that Rava himself was uncertain whether an unintentional fire pays damages for a slave. It presents the logical arguments on both sides and concludes with teiku (the question remains unresolved).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reveals that Rava himself was uncertain whether an unintentional fire pays damages for a slave, and presents the dilemma.

The Gemara presents the logical arguments on both sides: whether the rule of an ox (intentional pays atonement, unintentional pays damages) applies to fire, or whether fire, which never pays atonement, also exempts damages for a slave.
The Gemara concludes that the question remains unresolved, marking it with תֵּיקוּ (let it stand).

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's derivation for unintentional kofer and Abaye's objection
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's derivation for unintentional kofer and Abaye's objection
items.desc_en: Rav Dimi reports that Rabbi Yochanan derives from the word

sub.desc_en: Rav Dimi reports that Rabbi Yochanan derives from the word 'אִם כֹּפֶר' (if a ransom) that unintentional kofer is included like intentional kofer.

Abaye objects that by the same logic, the word 'אִם עֶבֶד' (if a slave) should include unintentional killing of a slave, but Reish Lakish ruled that an ox that kills a slave unintentionally is exempt from the thirty-shekel fine.
Rabbi Yochanan rejects Abaye's objection, saying that one cannot compare the opinion of one sage (Reish Lakish) to another (Rabbi Yochanan).

items.text: Resolution of the dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish
items.text_en: Resolution of the dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish
items.desc_en: Abaye's objection is dismissed because Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish disagree. Ravin reports that Rabbi Yochanan derives the same for a slave from

sub.desc_en: Abaye dismisses the objection by saying one cannot compare one authority (Rabbi Yochanan) to another (Reish Lakish).
Ravin reports that Rabbi Yochanan derives from the extra word 'אִם עֶבֶד' (if a slave) to include an unintentional goring of a slave as subject to the thirty-shekel penalty.
The Gemara questions whether Reish Lakish, who does not expound the extra word 'עֶבֶד' (slave), would also not expound the extra word 'כֹּפֶר' (ransom).
The Gemara answers that Reish Lakish does not expound the extra word regarding a slave but does expound the extra word regarding ransom.
The Gemara explains the distinction: the extra word regarding a slave is not written in the context of payment, whereas the extra word regarding ransom is written in the context of payment.

items.text: Derivation for minors from the verse
items.text_en: Derivation for minors from the verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that derives from

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites the verse 'אוֹ בֵן יִגָּח אוֹ בַת יִגָּח' to teach that liability applies for minors as for adults.

The baraita presents a logical inference: just as when a person kills another person there is no distinction between minors and adults, so too when an ox kills a person there should be no distinction.

The baraita adds a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument): if a person who kills another person, where the Torah did not treat minors like adults in all respects, is nevertheless liable for minors as for adults, then certainly an ox that kills a person should be liable for minors as for adults.

items.text: Deriving liability for minors from the verse
items.text_en: Deriving liability for minors from the verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues that just as an ox that kills an adult is liable, so too for minors, using a kal vachomer from 'man against man'. It then refutes the kal vachomer by noting that man is liable for four things, unlike an ox, and concludes with a verse: 'or a son or daughter it shall gore' to include minors.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument): if an ox goring a person is liable for minors as for adults, then a person killing another should certainly be liable for minors as for adults.
The Gemara refutes the kal vachomer: a person is liable for four types of damages (nezek, tza'ar, ripui, shevet), unlike an ox, so the comparison fails.
The Gemara resolves the issue by citing the verse 'אוֹ בֵן יִגָּח אוֹ בַת יִגָּח' (or a son or daughter it shall gore) to include minors as liable like adults.

items.text: Extending liability to a tam ox
items.text_en: Extending liability to a tam ox
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we know that this liability applies to a tam ox as well as a mu'ad. It offers a logical argument: just as for adults you did not distinguish between tam and mu'ad, so too for minors. It then presents a kal vachomer and addresses objections, concluding with a verse that equates goring in tam and mu'ad, and for death and damages.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we know that the liability for goring minors applies to a tam ox as well as a mu'ad.
The Gemara offers a logical argument: just as for adults (איש ואשה) the law did not distinguish between tam and mu'ad, so too for minors (בן ובת) the law should not distinguish.

The Gemara adds a kal vachomer (a fortiori) argument: if for adults, whose power is weaker in damages, you did not distinguish between tam and mu'ad, then for minors, whose power is stronger in damages, certainly you should not distinguish.
An objection is raised: can we derive a leniency for the kal (tam) from the chamur (mu'ad) when the kal vachomer would actually impose a stringency on the kal?
A second objection is raised: the analogy to adults fails because adults are חייב במצות (obligated in commandments) while minors are פטורין מן המצות (exempt from commandments).
The Gemara resolves with a verse: 'אוֹ בֵן יִגָּח אוֹ בַת יִגָּח' teaches that goring by a tam is like goring by a mu'ad, and goring to death is like goring for damages.

items.text: Mishnah: Cases where the ox is exempt
items.text_en: Mishnah: Cases where the ox is exempt
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists cases where an ox that rubs against a wall and falls on a person, or intends to kill an animal but kills a person, or intends to kill a gentile but kills a Jew, or intends to kill a non-viable fetus but kills a viable child, is exempt from liability.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists cases where an ox that rubs against a wall and falls on a person, or intends to kill an animal but kills a person, or intends to kill a gentile but kills a Jew, or intends to kill a non-viable fetus but kills a viable child, is exempt from liability.

items.text: Dispute between Shmuel and Rav on liability
items.text_en: Dispute between Shmuel and Rav on liability
items.desc_en: Shmuel rules that the ox is exempt from the death penalty but liable for ransom, while Rav says it is exempt from both. The Gemara questions why, given that the ox is a tam, and explains that Rav's case involves a mu'ad for rubbing against people on walls. It then addresses the objection that such an ox should be liable for death, explaining that it rubs for its own pleasure, and we know this because it continues rubbing after falling.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel rules the ox is exempt from death but liable for ransom; Rav rules it is exempt from both.
The Gemara questions why the ox is exempt, noting it is a tam, and Rav explains it is a mu'ad for rubbing against people on walls.
An objection is raised: if the ox is a mu'ad, it should be liable for death, unlike the case of falling into a pit where the ox sees greenery.
The Gemara answers that the ox rubs for its own pleasure, as evidenced by its continuing to rub after falling, so it is not liable for death.

items.text: Gemara's question on the earlier dispute about tzrorot
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the earlier dispute about tzrorot
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the earlier explanation of tzrorot (pebbles) and Rav Mari bar Rav Kahana clarifies that the ox is liable because the pebbles are thrown from the ox's movement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks about the status of tzrorot (pebbles) and Rav Mari bar Rav Kahana answers that the ox is liable because the pebbles are thrown from the ox's own movement.

items.text: Baraita supporting Shmuel's view on kofer and death
items.text_en: Baraita supporting Shmuel's view on kofer and death
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Shmuel's position, distinguishing four cases: a mu'ad with intent (liable for death and kofer), a mu'ad without intent (liable for kofer but not death), a tam with intent (liable for death but not kofer), and a tam without intent (exempt from both).

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited in support of Shmuel and as a refutation of Rav, listing four categories of liability for an ox: mu'ad with intent, mu'ad without intent, tam with intent, and tam without intent.

A baraita is cited that supports Shmuel's position, distinguishing four cases: a mu'ad with intent (liable for death and kofer), a mu'ad without intent (liable for kofer but not death), a tam with intent (liable for death but not kofer), and a tam without intent (exempt from both).

items.text: Debate between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon on damages without intent
items.text_en: Debate between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon on damages without intent
items.desc_en: The baraita continues with a dispute: Rabbi Yehuda holds that the ox is liable for damages even without intent, learning from kofer, while Rabbi Shimon exempts, learning from the ox's killing. The Gemara explains their reasoning and the logical distinctions between the cases.

sub.desc_en: The baraita presents the four categories of ox goring: mu'ad with intent, mu'ad without intent, tam with intent, and tam without intent, specifying liability for death penalty and kofer.
The baraita introduces the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon regarding liability for damages caused without intent.
The Gemara explains Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning: he derives liability for damages without intent from kofer, which is also paid without intent.
The Gemara explains Rabbi Shimon's reasoning: he derives exemption for damages without intent from the ox's killing, which requires intent for the death penalty.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yehuda should also derive from the ox's killing, and answers that damages (תשלומין) are derived from damages (kofer), not from the death penalty.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Shimon should derive from kofer, and answers that one derives the ox's liability from the ox's liability, excluding kofer which is the owner's liability.

items.text: Mishnah's case of intent to kill an animal vs. a person, and Rabbi Shimon's view
items.text_en: Mishnah's case of intent to kill an animal vs. a person, and Rabbi Shimon's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's ruling (liable if one intended to kill this person and killed another) contradicts Rabbi Shimon, who exempts even in that case. Rabbi Shimon derives from the verse that the ox's death must be like the owner's death, requiring intent toward the victim.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's ruling (liable if one intended to kill this person and killed another) contradicts Rabbi Shimon's position.
A baraita cites Rabbi Shimon's explicit ruling that even if one intended to kill this person and killed another, he is exempt.

The Gemara asks for Rabbi Shimon's reasoning and derives it from the verse 'השור יסקל וגם בעליו יומת' (the ox shall be stoned and its owner shall be put to death), requiring intent toward the victim for both the owner and the ox.

items.text: Rabbis' interpretation of 've'arab lo' and the case of a fixed majority
items.text_en: Rabbis' interpretation of 've'arab lo' and the case of a fixed majority
items.desc_en: The Rabbis interpret the verse 've'arab lo' as excluding one who throws a stone into a group. The Gemara clarifies the scenario: nine Jews and one gentile, where the gentile creates a fixed (kavua) situation, treated as half-and-half, and a doubt about capital cases is resolved leniently.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the Rabbis interpret the verse 'וְאָרַב לוֹ' (and he lay in wait for him), since they do not use it to require intent for capital liability.
Bei Rabbi Yannai answers that the verse excludes one who throws a stone into a group (where the victim is not specifically targeted).

The Gemara questions the scenario: if there are nine gentiles and one Jew among them, the majority is gentiles, or if it is half-and-half, a doubt about capital cases is resolved leniently, so why would the verse be needed?

The Gemara resolves that the case is where there are nine Jews and one gentile; since the gentile creates a fixed (קָבוּעַ) situation, it is treated as half-and-half, and a doubt about capital cases is resolved leniently, so the verse excludes liability.

items.text: Mishnah: oxen liable to stoning despite lacking owners
items.text_en: Mishnah: oxen liable to stoning despite lacking owners
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists oxen that are liable to stoning even without conventional owners: the ox of a woman, orphans, a guardian, the desert, consecrated property, and a convert who died without heirs. Rabbi Yehuda exempts the desert ox, consecrated ox, and the convert's ox because they have no owners.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists oxen that are liable to death: the ox of a woman, orphans, a guardian, the desert, the Temple, and a convert who died without heirs; Rabbi Yehuda exempts the last three because they have no owners.

items.text: Gemara on the Mishnah: derivation and Rabbi Yehuda's extension
items.text_en: Gemara on the Mishnah: derivation and Rabbi Yehuda's extension
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that derives the seven cases from the repeated word 'shor'. Rav Huna explains that Rabbi Yehuda exempts even if the ox gored and was later consecrated or abandoned. A baraita supports this, requiring that the ox's death, court hearing, and verdict all occur simultaneously.

sub.desc_en: A baraita cites the seven repetitions of 'שׁוֹר' to include the listed oxen, with Rabbi Yehuda exempting those without owners.
Rav Huna explains that Rabbi Yehuda exempts even if the ox gored and was later consecrated or abandoned.
The Gemara asks how Rav Huna derives this, noting the redundancy of 'ox of the desert' and 'ox of a convert', and concludes it teaches the extension.
A baraita supports Rav Huna, stating Rabbi Yehuda exempts even if the ox gored and was later consecrated or abandoned, requiring death and court hearing to be simultaneous.
The Gemara objects that the baraita omitted the final verdict, and corrects it to require death, court hearing, and verdict all to be simultaneous.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara: status of an ox after goring and before verdict
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara: status of an ox after goring and before verdict
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if an ox is already sentenced to stoning, consecrating it is ineffective; if before the verdict, it is consecrated. The Gemara begins to discuss the case of selling the ox before the verdict.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if an ox is already sentenced to stoning, consecrating it is ineffective and its meat is forbidden; if before the verdict, it is consecrated and its meat is permitted.
The Mishnah adds that if the owner entrusts the ox to a bailee, the bailee assumes the owner's liability: a mu'ad pays full damage, a tam pays half damage.
The Gemara cites a baraita that begins to discuss the case of selling an ox that killed before its verdict was finalized.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Status of a condemned ox before and after verdict
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Status of a condemned ox before and after verdict
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that before the verdict, a condemned ox can be sold, consecrated, its meat is permitted, and if a shomer returns it, it is considered returned. After the verdict, none of these apply, except Rabbi Yaakov holds that the shomer's return is valid even after the verdict.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that before the verdict, a condemned ox can be sold, consecrated, its meat is permitted, and if a shomer returns it, it is considered returned.

The Mishnah states that after the verdict, the ox cannot be sold, consecrated, its meat is forbidden, and the shomer's return is invalid, except Rabbi Yaakov holds the shomer's return is valid even after the verdict.

items.text: Gemara's initial suggestion: dispute over 'harei shelcha lefanecha'
items.text_en: Gemara's initial suggestion: dispute over 'harei shelcha lefanecha'
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the dispute is about whether the principle of 'harei shelcha lefanecha' applies to forbidden benefit items. The Rabbis reject it, while Rabbi Yaakov accepts it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the dispute is about whether the principle of 'הרי שלך לפניך' (here is yours before you) applies to forbidden items of benefit.

items.text: Rabbah's rejection: all agree on 'harei shelcha lefanecha'
items.text_en: Rabbah's rejection: all agree on 'harei shelcha lefanecha'
items.desc_en: Rabbah argues that everyone agrees on the principle, as otherwise they would have disputed regarding chametz on Pesach. Therefore, the real dispute must be elsewhere.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah rejects the suggestion, arguing that all agree the principle applies, otherwise the dispute would appear in the case of חמץ בפסח (leaven on Passover).

items.text: Rabbah's explanation: dispute over judging the ox in its absence
items.text_en: Rabbah's explanation: dispute over judging the ox in its absence
items.desc_en: Rabbah explains that the dispute is about whether the court can finalize the verdict of an ox in its absence. The Rabbis require the ox's presence, as the owner could argue that if he had the ox, he would have fled to the marsh. Rabbi Yaakov holds that the verdict can be finalized without the ox, since the court would eventually judge it anyway.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah explains that the dispute is about whether the court can finalize the verdict of an ox in its absence, with the Rabbis requiring the ox's presence because the owner could claim he would have fled to the marsh.
Rabbi Yaakov holds that the verdict can be finalized without the ox, since the court would eventually judge it anyway.

items.text: Scriptural basis for the Rabbis and Rabbi Yaakov's rebuttal
items.text_en: Scriptural basis for the Rabbis and Rabbi Yaakov's rebuttal
items.desc_en: The Rabbis derive from the verse 'the ox shall be stoned and also its owners shall die' that the ox's death must be like the owner's death—in their presence. Rabbi Yaakov counters that owners can argue, but an ox cannot, so the comparison fails.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the scriptural basis for the Rabbis' position that the ox's death must be in its presence.
The Gemara explains that the Rabbis derive from the verse 'the ox shall be stoned and also its owners shall die' that the ox's death must be like the owner's death—in their presence.
Rabbi Yaakov objects that the comparison fails because owners can argue their case, but an ox cannot.

items.text: Baraita: Four bailees and their liability when their animal kills
items.text_en: Baraita: Four bailees and their liability when their animal kills
items.desc_en: A baraita lists four bailees (shomer chinam, sho'el, nosei sachar, socher) who are liable when their animal kills. For tam animals, they are executed but exempt from kofer; for mu'ad animals, they are executed and pay kofer. They must return the value of the ox to the owner, except for shomer chinam.

sub.desc_en: A baraita lists the four types of shomrim (guardians) and their liability: if the ox kills, they are executed and pay kofer, except a shomer chinam who is exempt from returning the ox's value.

items.text: Gemara's question and answer: distinction between inferior and superior guardianship
items.text_en: Gemara's question and answer: distinction between inferior and superior guardianship
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the bailees can be liable if they guarded the animal, and exempt if they didn't. It answers that they guarded with inferior guardianship but not superior guardianship. For shomer chinam, inferior guardianship suffices, but for the others, it does not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the baraita's distinction between shomer chinam and the other bailees can be consistent: if the bailee guarded the animal, all should be exempt; if not, even shomer chinam should be liable.

The Gemara answers that the case involves inferior guardianship (שמירה פחותה) but not superior guardianship (שמירה מעולה); for shomer chinam, inferior guardianship suffices, but for the other bailees, it does not.

items.text: Gemara's inquiry: whose opinion does this follow?
items.text_en: Gemara's inquiry: whose opinion does this follow?
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to ask which Tanna's view this baraita aligns with, starting with Rabbi Meir.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whose opinion this baraita follows, suggesting it might be Rabbi Meir's.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's omission
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's omission
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah did not include a paid guardian (שוכר) in the list of those exempt from paying kofer for a mu'ad, based on the assumption that a paid guardian is like an unpaid guardian (שומר חנם) according to Rabbi Meir, or like a paid bailee (נושא שכר) according to Rabbi Yehuda.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah omitted a paid guardian (שוכר) from the list of those exempt from kofer, considering both Rabbi Meir's view that a paid guardian is like an unpaid guardian and Rabbi Yehuda's view that he is like a paid bailee.

items.text: Rav Huna bar Chinana's answer
items.text_en: Rav Huna bar Chinana's answer
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Chinana explains that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Eliezer, who holds that only a knife (i.e., locking the animal in a pen) constitutes proper guarding, and regarding a paid guardian, he agrees with Rabbi Yehuda that a paid guardian is like a paid bailee.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Chinana resolves the contradiction by identifying the Mishnah as following Rabbi Eliezer on guarding and Rabbi Yehuda on the paid guardian's status.

items.text: Abaye's alternative answer
items.text_en: Abaye's alternative answer
items.desc_en: Abaye argues that the Mishnah can still follow Rabbi Meir, but with the version of Rabba bar Avuh who taught that Rabbi Meir actually says a paid guardian is like a paid bailee, and Rabbi Yehuda says it is like an unpaid guardian.

sub.desc_en: Abaye answers that the Mishnah can still follow Rabbi Meir, but according to the version of Rabba bar Avuh who taught that Rabbi Meir considers a paid guardian like a paid bailee and Rabbi Yehuda considers it like an unpaid guardian.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's ruling on a bailee's liability
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's ruling on a bailee's liability
