items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar states that if one gives his ox to an unpaid guardian and the ox damages, the guardian is liable; if the ox is damaged, the guardian is exempt. The Gemara questions this distinction, and Rava resolves it by explaining that the guardian accepted responsibility for the ox's damage (since it was known to gore) but not for damage to the ox from others.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar rules that if one gives his ox to an unpaid guardian (שומר חנם) and the ox damages, the guardian is liable; if the ox is damaged, the guardian is exempt.

The Gemara questions the distinction: if the guardian accepted responsibility for the ox's damage, he should also be liable for damage to the ox; if he did not accept such responsibility, he should be exempt even for damage caused by the ox.

Rava resolves: the guardian accepted responsibility for the ox's damage because the ox was known to gore, but he did not anticipate that others would damage the ox, so he is exempt for damage to the ox.

items.text: Mishnah: Dispute on guarding a tam and mu'ad
items.text_en: Mishnah: Dispute on guarding a tam and mu'ad
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute: if the owner tied the ox with a halter and locked the door properly, but the ox escaped and damaged, Rabbi Meir holds both a tam and mu'ad liable; Rabbi Yehuda holds a tam liable but a mu'ad exempt because it is considered guarded; Rabbi Eliezer holds that only a knife (locking in a pen) suffices.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with Rabbi Meir's position that if the owner tied the ox with a halter and locked the door properly, but the ox escaped and damaged, both a tam and a mu'ad are liable.
Rabbi Yehuda states that a tam is liable but a mu'ad is exempt, citing the verse 'וְלֹא יִשְׁמְרֶנּוּ' (and its owner did not guard it) — implying that this one is considered guarded.
Rabbi Eliezer rules that the only effective guarding for a mu'ad is a knife (locking it in a pen).

items.text: Gemara: Reasoning of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Gemara: Reasoning of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains Rabbi Meir's view: oxen are not presumed guarded, so a tam requires lesser guarding and a mu'ad requires superior guarding, derived from the verse. Rabbi Yehuda holds oxen are presumed guarded, so a tam requires superior guarding, and the verse's repetition for a mu'ad is a limitation, excluding the mu'ad from liability when given superior guarding. The Gemara then addresses a potential derivation from the verse and explains the extra word 'וְלֹא יִשְׁמְרֶנּוּ' teaches that the guarding is for this ox, not another.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the reasoning behind Rabbi Meir's position and explains that oxen are not presumed guarded, so the Torah requires lesser guarding for a tam and superior guarding for a mu'ad, derived from the verse.

The Gemara explains Rabbi Yehuda's view: oxen are presumed guarded, so a tam requires superior guarding, and the repetition of the verse for a mu'ad is a limitation (ריבוי אחר ריבוי) that excludes the mu'ad from liability when given superior guarding.

The Gemara raises a potential objection: if one derives the mu'ad's liability from the tam via a verbal analogy, the limitation of 'וְלֹא יִשְׁמְרֶנּוּ' would exclude the mu'ad only from liability for another ox, not from liability entirely.
The Gemara resolves the objection by noting that the extra word 'וְלֹא יִשְׁמְרֶנּוּ' (rather than 'וְלֹא יִשְׁמוֹר') teaches that the guarding is for this ox, not another.

items.text: Tosefta: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's view
items.text_en: Tosefta: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's view
items.desc_en: A Tosefta cites Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov who says both a tam and mu'ad are exempt if given inferior guarding. The Gemara explains he agrees with Rabbi Yehuda that a mu'ad can be guarded with inferior guarding, and he derives the tam from the mu'ad via a verbal analogy.

sub.desc_en: A Tosefta cites Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov who rules that both a tam and a mu'ad are exempt if given inferior guarding.

The Gemara explains that Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov agrees with Rabbi Yehuda that a mu'ad can be guarded with inferior guarding, and he derives the tam from the mu'ad via a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) of 'נגיחה' (goring).

items.text: Rav Adda bar Ahava and Rav on partial mu'ad status
items.text_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava and Rav on partial mu'ad status
items.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava says Rabbi Yehuda only exempts the mu'ad aspect, but the tam aspect remains. Rav states a mu'ad for goring with the right horn is not a mu'ad for the left. The Gemara questions this according to Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda, and resolves that it follows Rabbi Yehuda but rejects Rav Adda bar Ahava's view, explaining that such a case involves both tam and mu'ad aspects.

sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava states that Rabbi Yehuda only exempts the mu'ad aspect of the ox, but the tam aspect remains fully liable.
Rav rules that an ox declared mu'ad for goring with the right horn is not automatically mu'ad for goring with the left horn.

The Gemara questions which Tanna's view Rav follows, noting that according to Rabbi Meir both tam and mu'ad require superior guarding, and according to Rabbi Yehuda even the right horn has both tam and mu'ad aspects.
The Gemara resolves that Rav follows Rabbi Yehuda but rejects Rav Adda bar Ahava's view, explaining that the case involves both tam and mu'ad aspects.

items.text: Conclusion of previous sugya: mu'ad has no aspect of tam
items.text_en: Conclusion of previous sugya: mu'ad has no aspect of tam
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that a mu'ad ox has no aspect of tam whatsoever, meaning it is always fully liable.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that a mu'ad ox has no aspect of tam whatsoever, meaning it is always fully liable.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's opinion on guarding a mu'ad and Abaye's explanation
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's opinion on guarding a mu'ad and Abaye's explanation
items.desc_en: Rabba explains Rabbi Eliezer's view that a mu'ad has no guarding except a knife, based on the verse 'and he did not guard him.' Abaye objects that the same logic would apply to covering a pit, which is not the case. Abaye then provides a different source: Rabbi Nathan's teaching that one must not keep a dangerous dog or a rickety ladder, derived from 'Do not place blood in your house.'

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer states that a mu'ad ox has no effective guarding except a knife (i.e., it must be killed), and Rabba explains the scriptural basis: the verse 'וְלֹא יִשְׁמְרֶנּוּ' (and he did not guard it) implies that once it gored, it can no longer be guarded.
Abaye objects: if the same logic were applied to the verse 'וְלֹא יְכַסֶּנּוּ' (and he did not cover it), it would absurdly imply that a pit once uncovered can never be covered again.

The Gemara rejects the objection: if one were to say that indeed the pit cannot be covered, the Mishnah explicitly rules that if one covered it properly and an animal fell in and died, he is exempt, showing that covering is possible.

Abaye provides an alternative explanation: Rabbi Eliezer's ruling is based on a baraita where Rabbi Natan derives from the verse 'וְלֹא תָשִׂים דָּמִים בְּבֵיתֶךָ' (and you shall not put blood in your house) that one must not keep a dangerous dog or a rickety ladder in one's home, so a mu'ad ox must be killed.

Abaye provides a different source for Rabbi Eliezer's view: Rabbi Nathan's teaching that one must not keep a dangerous dog or a rickety ladder, derived from the verse 'וְלֹא תָשִׂים דָּמִים בְּבֵיתֶךָ' (Do not place blood in your house).

items.text: Return to the chapter: 'An ox that gored four or five'
items.text_en: Return to the chapter: 'An ox that gored four or five'
items.desc_en: The Gemara signals the end of the previous chapter and the beginning of a new one with the phrase 'We return to you, an ox that gored four or five.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara signals the end of the previous chapter and the beginning of a new one: 'We return to you, ox that gored four and five.'

items.text: Mishnah: Ox that gored a cow and the fetus is found alongside
items.text_en: Mishnah: Ox that gored a cow and the fetus is found alongside
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case of uncertainty: an ox gored a cow and a fetus is found beside it, but it is unknown whether the cow gave birth before or after the goring. The ruling is that the owner pays half-damages for the cow and quarter-damages for the fetus. The same applies if a cow gored an ox.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case: an ox gored a cow and a fetus was found beside it; if it is uncertain whether the cow gave birth before or after the goring, the owner pays half-damages for the cow and quarter-damages for the calf.
The Mishnah presents a parallel case: a cow gored an ox and a fetus was found beside it; the same uncertainty applies, and the payment is half-damages from the cow and quarter-damages from the calf.

items.text: Gemara: Attribution to Sumchus and the principle of uncertainty
items.text_en: Gemara: Attribution to Sumchus and the principle of uncertainty
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel states that the Mishnah follows Sumchus, who holds that uncertain monetary matters are divided. The Sages, however, rule that the burden of proof is on the claimant. The Gemara explains that the phrase 'a great principle in law' teaches that even when the plaintiff is certain and the defendant is uncertain, the burden remains on the plaintiff.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel attributes the Mishnah's ruling to Sumchus, who holds that uncertain monetary matters are divided between the parties.
The Sages reject Sumchus's view and state the principle that the burden of proof rests on the claimant.
The Gemara asks why the Sages needed to add the phrase 'a great principle in law' instead of simply stating the rule.
The Gemara explains that the phrase was necessary to teach that even when the plaintiff is certain and the defendant is uncertain, the burden of proof remains on the plaintiff.

items.text: Application of the principle to a case of selling a goring ox
items.text_en: Application of the principle to a case of selling a goring ox
items.desc_en: The Gemara applies the principle to a case where one sells an ox that turns out to be a gorer. Rav says it is a mistaken transaction, while Shmuel says the seller can claim he sold it for slaughter. The Gemara questions how to determine the buyer's intent and the market price, concluding that the case is when the buyer could use it for either plowing or slaughter, and the price of meat is high, making the price ambiguous.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute: Rav says selling a goring ox is a mistaken transaction, while Shmuel says the seller can claim he sold it for slaughter.
The Gemara questions why the dispute is needed: one could simply check if the buyer buys for plowing or slaughter, and answers that the case is when the buyer buys for both purposes.
The Gemara further questions: one could check the price paid, and answers that the case is when meat prices rose, making the price ambiguous.
The Gemara resolves that the dispute applies when meat prices are high and the ox stands at the price of a plowing ox, making the buyer's intent unclear.

items.text: Transition: 'They said'
items.text_en: Transition: 'They said'
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins a new discussion with the word 'They said,' indicating a continuation or a new point.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara begins a new discussion with the word 'אָמְרִי' (they said), indicating a continuation.

items.text: Rejection of the proposed solution
items.text_en: Rejection of the proposed solution
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the suggestion that if the owner cannot pay, the ox should be taken for its value, citing a folk saying. It clarifies that the case is where the owner can pay.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why, if the owner cannot pay, the ox should not be taken for its value, citing a folk saying about collecting from the debtor's best assets.
The Gemara clarifies that the case is unnecessary because the owner can pay, so the question does not arise.

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on following the majority
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on following the majority
items.desc_en: Rav holds that the sale of an ox is a mistaken transaction because most people buy oxen for plowing, so the buyer can claim fraud. Shmuel argues the seller can say he sold it for slaughter, and in monetary cases we do not follow the majority; the burden of proof is on the claimant.

sub.desc_en: Rav rules that the sale is a mistaken transaction because we follow the majority, and most people buy oxen for plowing.
Shmuel argues that the seller can claim he sold it for slaughter, and in monetary cases we do not follow the majority; the burden of proof is on the claimant.

items.text: Supporting baraita and scriptural source
items.text_en: Supporting baraita and scriptural source
items.desc_en: A baraita supports Shmuel's view: in a case of a goring ox and a pregnant cow, Sumchos says the owner pays half-damages for the cow and quarter-damages for the calf, but the Sages say the burden of proof is on the claimant. Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani derives this principle from a verse.

sub.desc_en: A baraita supports Shmuel's principle: in a case of a goring ox and a pregnant cow, Sumchos says the owner pays half-damages for the cow and quarter-damages for the calf, but the Sages say the burden of proof is on the claimant.

Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani derives the principle that the burden of proof is on the claimant from the verse 'מִי בַעַל דְּבָרִים יִגַּשׁ אֲלֵהֶם' (whoever has a claim shall present his evidence to them).

items.text: Rav Ashi's objection and alternative derivation
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's objection and alternative derivation
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi objects that the principle is logical and does not need a verse. The Gemara explains that the verse is actually needed for Rav Nachman's teaching that the court only attends to the plaintiff first.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi objects that the principle 'the burden of proof is on the claimant' is logical and does not require a biblical verse, since one who is injured naturally seeks a doctor.

The Gemara resolves that the verse is actually needed for Rav Nachman's teaching that the court only attends to the plaintiff first, as derived from the verse 'יַגִּישׁ דְּבָרָיו אֲלֵיהֶם' (he shall present his words to them).

items.text: Exception from Nehardeans
items.text_en: Exception from Nehardeans
items.desc_en: The Nehardeans say that sometimes the court attends to the defendant first, specifically when his property is being depreciated.

sub.desc_en: The Nehardeans state that sometimes the court attends to the defendant first, specifically when his property is being depreciated.

items.text: Question on the baraita's damages and Abaye's explanation
items.text_en: Question on the baraita's damages and Abaye's explanation
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the baraita's mention of half-damages and quarter-damages, since the ox only pays half-damages. Abaye explains that 'half-damages' means one-fourth of the total damage, and 'quarter-damages' means one-eighth.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the baraita's mention of 'half-damages' and 'quarter-damages' for the calf, since the ox only pays half-damages, asking what the calculation of 'total damage minus a quarter' means.
Abaye explains that 'half-damages' means one-fourth of the total damage, and 'quarter-damages' means one-eighth, resolving the apparent inconsistency.

items.text: Analysis of the baraita's scenario
items.text_en: Analysis of the baraita's scenario
items.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes the baraita, considering cases where the cow and calf belong to different owners, and whether the plaintiff first sued the cow's owner or the calf's owner. It presents two versions of the analysis.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions: if the cow and calf belong to the same owner, why wouldn't the plaintiff simply demand half-damages from the cow's owner?
The Gemara answers: the baraita is necessary only when the cow and calf belong to different owners.
The Gemara asks: if the plaintiff first sued the cow's owner, why wouldn't the cow's owner be liable for the full half-damages?
The Gemara answers: the baraita refers to a case where the plaintiff first sued the calf's owner, revealing that he knows there is a partner.
An alternative version states that even if the plaintiff first sued the cow's owner, the cow's owner can deflect by claiming he knows there is a partner.

items.text: Rava's objection and resolution
items.text_en: Rava's objection and resolution
items.desc_en: Rava objects that the baraita says 'half-damages' and 'quarter-damages', not fractions of the total damage. He explains that the case is where the cow and calf belong to the same owner, and the plaintiff collects half-damages from the cow.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects that the baraita explicitly says 'half-damages' and 'quarter-damages', not fractions of the total damage.
Rava resolves that the case involves a cow and calf belonging to the same owner, so the plaintiff collects half-damages from the cow.

items.text: Liability from the calf when the cow's pregnancy is uncertain
items.text_en: Liability from the calf when the cow's pregnancy is uncertain
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that if we do not know whether the cow was pregnant when it gored, only a quarter of the damage is collected from the calf. But if it is certain that the cow was pregnant, the full half-damage is collected from the calf.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that when the cow's pregnancy at the time of goring is unknown, only a quarter of the damage is collected from the calf, but if the pregnancy is certain, the full half-damage is collected from the calf.

items.text: Rava's principle: cow's calf is part of its body
items.text_en: Rava's principle: cow's calf is part of its body
items.desc_en: Rava states that if a cow damages, the victim collects from its calf because the calf is considered part of the cow's body. In contrast, if a hen damages, one does not collect from its eggs because eggs are mere excrement.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces Rava's consistent principle: if a cow damages, the victim collects from its calf.
Rava explains that the calf is considered part of the cow's body (גופה), so it can be seized for damages.
Rava contrasts with a hen: one does not collect damages from its eggs because eggs are mere excrement (פירשא בעלמא), not part of the hen's body.

items.text: Rava's ruling: appraise the calf together with the cow
items.text_en: Rava's ruling: appraise the calf together with the cow
items.desc_en: Rava further rules that the cow and calf are not appraised separately; rather, the calf is appraised together with the cow. Otherwise, the assessment would disadvantage the damager. This principle is applied to cutting a slave's hand or damaging another's field.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that the cow and calf are not appraised separately; rather, the calf is appraised together with the cow, otherwise the assessment would disadvantage the damager.
The Gemara extends Rava's principle to analogous cases: cutting a slave's hand or damaging another's field.

items.text: Objection and resolution: why not disadvantage the damager?
items.text_en: Objection and resolution: why not disadvantage the damager?
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rava asks Rav Ashi: if this is the law, why not disadvantage the damager? Rav Ashi answers that the damager is told: you damaged a pregnant cow, so I will appraise a pregnant cow for you.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rava asks Rav Ashi: if the law is as stated, why not disadvantage the damager (by appraising the cow without the fetus)?
Rav Ashi answers that the damager is told: you damaged a pregnant cow, so I will appraise a pregnant cow for you (thus no disadvantage).

items.text: Dispute: who gets the placenta?
items.text_en: Dispute: who gets the placenta?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if the cow belongs to one person and the calf to another, who gets the placenta? Rav Pappa says the owner of the cow; Rav Acha bar Rav Ika says they divide it. The halakha is that they divide it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the obvious case: if the cow belongs to one person and the calf to another, the placenta goes to the cow's owner.
The Gemara asks: what about the afterbirth (נִפְחָא)?
Rav Pappa rules that the afterbirth belongs to the cow's owner.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika's answer
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika's answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika rules that the cow's owner and the calf's owner divide the afterbirth.
The Gemara concludes that the halakha follows Rav Acha bar Rav Ika: they divide the afterbirth.

items.text: Mishnah: potter enters courtyard without permission
items.text_en: Mishnah: potter enters courtyard without permission
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states: if a potter brings his pots into a homeowner's courtyard without permission and the homeowner's animal breaks them, the homeowner is exempt. If the animal is injured by the pots, the potter is liable. If he entered with permission, the homeowner is liable. The same applies to produce and to an ox.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the case of a potter who enters a homeowner's courtyard without permission, stating that if the homeowner's animal breaks the pots, the homeowner is exempt; if the animal is injured by the pots, the potter is liable; and if the potter entered with permission, the homeowner is liable.

The Mishnah extends the same rule to produce: if a person brings produce into a homeowner's courtyard without permission and the homeowner's animal eats it, the homeowner is exempt; if the animal is injured by the produce, the produce owner is liable; and if entered with permission, the homeowner is liable.
The Mishnah extends the same rule to an ox: if a person brings his ox into a homeowner's courtyard without permission, the same liability rules apply.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one enters a courtyard without permission and his ox gores the homeowner's ox, or his dog bites, he is exempt; but if his ox is gored, he is liable. If he falls into a well and fouls the water, he is liable. If his father or son is inside, he pays kofer. If he entered with permission, the homeowner is liable. Rabbi says: In all cases he is not liable unless the homeowner accepted to guard.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the basic liability rules for entering a courtyard without permission: if the entrant's ox gores the homeowner's ox or his dog bites, he is exempt; if his ox is gored, he is liable; if he falls into a well and fouls the water, he is liable; if his father or son is inside, he pays kofer; if he entered with permission, the homeowner is liable.
Rabbi adds a dissenting opinion: in all these cases the entrant is not liable unless the homeowner accepted to guard.

items.text: Rabbi's statement
items.text_en: Rabbi's statement
items.desc_en: Rabbi says that in all these cases the homeowner is not liable unless he explicitly accepted to guard the entrant's property.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi states that in all these cases the homeowner is not liable unless he explicitly accepted to guard the entrant's property.

items.text: Gemara's contradiction between Mishnah's parts
items.text_en: Gemara's contradiction between Mishnah's parts
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's first clause (without permission, the entrant is exempt from damages by the homeowner's animal) implies that with permission the homeowner is liable, which matches Rabbi's view that without explicit acceptance there is no liability. But the last clause (with permission, the homeowner is liable) matches the Rabbis who hold that even without explicit acceptance, the homeowner accepts liability. This creates a contradiction: the beginning and end follow Rabbi, but the middle follows the Rabbis.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah's first clause that without permission the entrant is exempt, implying that with permission the homeowner would be liable, contradicting Rabbi's view that without explicit acceptance there is no liability.
The Gemara identifies that the first clause follows Rabbi, who holds that without explicit acceptance one does not assume guardianship.
The Gemara notes that the last clause (with permission, the homeowner is liable) follows the Rabbis, who hold that even without explicit acceptance the homeowner accepts liability.
The Gemara objects that the beginning and end of the Mishnah follow Rabbi, but the middle follows the Rabbis, creating an internal contradiction.

items.text: Resolutions by Rabbi Zeira and Rava
items.text_en: Resolutions by Rabbi Zeira and Rava
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira says the Mishnah is a broken teaching from two different sources. Rava says the entire Mishnah follows the Rabbis: when it says 'with permission' the homeowner is liable, it means he accepted to guard the pots, even if they break in the wind.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira resolves the contradiction by declaring the Mishnah a broken teaching (תִּבְרַהּ) from two different sources.
Rava resolves the contradiction by asserting the entire Mishnah follows the Rabbis, and the phrase 'with permission' means the homeowner accepted to guard the pots, even if they break in the wind.

items.text: Rav's distinction and the baraita about poison
items.text_en: Rav's distinction and the baraita about poison
items.desc_en: Rav says the Mishnah's case of 'if she was injured by them' refers only to stumbling over them, but if the animal ate them, the homeowner is exempt because the animal should not have eaten. Rav Sheshet questions this from a baraita about giving poison to an animal, which exempts from human court but liable in heavenly court. The Gemara resolves that the baraita teaches that even poison, which is not normally eaten, is liable in heavenly court; or alternatively, the poison was in fruit form.

sub.desc_en: Rav distinguishes the Mishnah's case: the homeowner is liable only if the animal stumbled over the produce, but if it ate them, he is exempt because the animal should not have eaten.

Rav Sheshet objects from a baraita about giving poison to an animal: if poison exempts from human court because it is not normally eaten, then produce, which is normally eaten, should be liable in human court — contradicting Rav's exemption.

The Gemara answers that the baraita's principle applies even to produce: one is exempt from human court, and the baraita's novelty is that even poison, which is not normally eaten, is liable in heavenly court.
Alternatively, the poison case in the baraita involved poison in fruit form (אפרזתא), which is normally eaten, so the exemption from human court still applies.

items.text: Challenge from a baraita about a woman grinding wheat
items.text_en: Challenge from a baraita about a woman grinding wheat
items.desc_en: A baraita states: A woman who entered a homeowner's premises without permission to grind wheat, and the homeowner's animal ate them, the homeowner is exempt; if she was injured, she is liable. The Gemara questions why the homeowner is not liable for the eating, since the animal should not have eaten. The answer distinguishes the Mishnah (which says 'if she was injured by them' implying stumbling) from the baraita (which says 'if she was injured' without 'by them', implying eating). Another opinion says there is no difference.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav's ruling by citing a baraita where a woman entered without permission to grind wheat, the homeowner's animal ate them, and the homeowner is exempt; the Gemara asks why the homeowner is not liable, since the animal should not have eaten.
The Gemara answers that the baraita is no stronger than the Mishnah, which was already interpreted as referring to stumbling (הוּחְלְקָה) rather than eating.
The Gemara objects that the baraita's wording differs: it says 'if she was injured' without 'by them', implying the injury was from eating, not stumbling.
Another opinion rejects the distinction, asserting that there is no difference between the Mishnah and the baraita.

items.text: Challenge from a baraita about an ox eating wheat
items.text_en: Challenge from a baraita about an ox eating wheat
items.desc_en: A baraita: If one brought his ox into a courtyard without permission and it ate wheat and died, the homeowner is exempt; if with permission, the homeowner is liable. The Gemara questions why the homeowner is liable for the ox's death, since the ox should not have eaten. Rava answers that with permission, the homeowner accepted to guard the ox, even if it chokes itself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rava's position by citing a baraita where a homeowner is liable for an ox that died after eating wheat in his courtyard with permission, questioning why the ox's owner is not at fault since the ox should not have eaten.
Rava responds that the baraita is not a challenge because when entry is with permission, the homeowner accepted full responsibility for the ox's safety, even if the ox chokes itself.

items.text: Inquiry about the scope of acceptance of guarding
items.text_en: Inquiry about the scope of acceptance of guarding
items.desc_en: The Gemara inquires: If one accepted to guard, does he accept only guarding his own property, or even guarding against external damages? A baraita from Rav Yehuda bar Simon is cited: If one brought fruits into a courtyard with permission and another ox ate them, the homeowner is liable. The Gemara clarifies that the liability is on the owner of the ox, not the homeowner, and the discussion continues.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara inquires whether one who accepted to guard accepts only guarding his own property or also guarding against external damages.

sub.text: Baraita of Rav Yehuda bar Simon
sub.text_en: Baraita of Rav Yehuda bar Simon
sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: if one brought fruits into a courtyard without permission and an ox from elsewhere ate them, the homeowner is exempt; if with permission, liable.
The Gemara asks: who is exempt and who is liable — is it the homeowner in both cases?
The Gemara answers: no, the exemption and liability refer to the owner of the ox, not the homeowner.
The Gemara begins to analyze the implications of the baraita regarding the owner of the ox.

items.text: Initial question on the meaning of 'with permission' and 'without permission'
items.text_en: Initial question on the meaning of 'with permission' and 'without permission'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is meant by 'with permission' and 'without permission' in the context of the Mishnah. It answers that 'with permission' refers to the tooth damage in the domain of the injured party, which is liable, while 'without permission' refers to tooth damage in the public domain, which is exempt.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is meant by 'with permission' and 'without permission' in the context of the Mishnah.

The Gemara answers that 'with permission' refers to tooth damage in the domain of the injured party, which is liable, while 'without permission' refers to tooth damage in the public domain, which is exempt.

items.text: Challenge from a baraita about an ox entering a courtyard
items.text_en: Challenge from a baraita about an ox entering a courtyard
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about an ox entering a courtyard without permission and being gored by another ox. It initially suggests that the owner of the courtyard is exempt when the ox entered without permission and liable when it entered with permission, but the Gemara rejects this, explaining that the baraita refers to the owner of the ox, not the courtyard owner.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about an ox entering a courtyard without permission and being gored, and asks whether the courtyard owner is exempt or liable.
The Gemara rejects the initial understanding, explaining that the baraita refers to the owner of the ox, not the courtyard owner, and questions the relevance of permission.

items.text: Resolution: The baraita follows Rabbi Tarfon
items.text_en: Resolution: The baraita follows Rabbi Tarfon
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the difficulty by stating that the baraita follows Rabbi Tarfon, who holds that a goring ox in the injured party's domain pays full damages. Thus, 'with permission' means the ox is in the injured party's domain and pays full damages, while 'without permission' means it is in the public domain and pays only half damages.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the difficulty by stating that the baraita follows Rabbi Tarfon, who holds that a goring ox in the injured party's domain pays full damages, so 'with permission' means the ox is in the injured party's domain and pays full damages, while 'without permission' means it is in the public domain and pays only half damages.

items.text: Case of a woman entering a house to bake
items.text_en: Case of a woman entering a house to bake
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses a case where a woman entered a house to bake with permission, and the owner's dog ate the dough and died. Rava ruled that she must pay for the dog. The Gemara questions whether this contradicts Rav's principle that an animal entering without permission is exempt, but distinguishes that here she entered with permission and thus accepted responsibility for guarding.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara relates a case where a woman entered a house to bake with permission, the owner's dog ate the dough and died, and Rava ruled she must pay for the dog.
The Gemara questions whether Rava's ruling contradicts Rav's principle that an animal entering without permission is exempt from liability for eating.

The Gemara distinguishes that in Rav's case the animal entered without permission and the owner did not accept responsibility, whereas here she entered with permission and thus accepted responsibility for guarding.

items.text: Distinction between grinding wheat and baking
items.text_en: Distinction between grinding wheat and baking
items.desc_en: The Gemara contrasts this with a case where a woman entered to grind wheat without permission and the owner's animal ate the wheat: the owner is exempt. The Gemara explains that grinding does not require privacy, so the owners do not remove themselves and the responsibility is on them, but baking requires privacy, so the owners remove themselves and the responsibility falls on the woman.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the case of baking differs from the case of a woman who entered to grind wheat without permission, where the owner is exempt, implying that with permission she would be exempt.

The Gemara answers that grinding wheat does not require privacy, so the owners do not remove themselves and the responsibility is on them, but baking requires privacy, so the owners remove themselves and the responsibility falls on the woman.

items.text: Rava's ruling on an ox that digs pits in a courtyard
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on an ox that digs pits in a courtyard
items.desc_en: Rava rules that if one brings his ox into a courtyard without permission and the ox digs pits, the ox's owner is liable for damage to the courtyard, and the courtyard owner is liable for damage caused by the pit. Even though the Torah says 'when a man digs a pit' and not an ox, since the courtyard owner could have filled the pit but did not, he is considered as if he dug it.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that if one brings his ox into a courtyard without permission and the ox digs pits, the ox's owner is liable for damage to the courtyard, and the courtyard owner is liable for damage caused by the pit.
The Gemara explains that even though the Torah says 'when a man digs a pit' and not an ox, since the courtyard owner could have filled the pit but did not, he is considered as if he dug it.

items.text: Rava's ruling on an ox that damages or lies down
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on an ox that damages or lies down
items.desc_en: Rava rules that if an ox enters a courtyard without permission and damages the owner or the owner is damaged by it, the ox's owner is liable. However, if the ox lies down, the owner is exempt. Rav Pappa explains that 'lies down' refers to the ox depositing dung, which soils the owner's vessels, and this is considered a pit, and we do not find a pit liable for vessels. The Gemara then addresses a difficulty with Rav's view that the pit must be abandoned, and answers that dung is typically abandoned.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that if an ox enters a courtyard without permission and damages the owner or the owner is damaged by it, the ox's owner is liable, but if the ox lies down, the owner is exempt.
The Gemara questions why lying down should exempt the owner.
Rav Pappa explains that 'lies down' refers to the ox depositing dung, which soils the owner's vessels, and this is considered a pit, and we do not find a pit liable for vessels.
The Gemara notes that this explanation works for Shmuel, who considers any obstacle a pit, but raises a difficulty for Rav, who requires the pit to be abandoned.
The Gemara answers that typical dung is abandoned, satisfying Rav's requirement.

items.text: Rava's ruling on a person entering a courtyard without permission
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on a person entering a courtyard without permission
items.desc_en: Rava rules that if a person enters a courtyard without permission and damages the owner or the owner is damaged by him, the entrant is liable. But if the owner damages the entrant, the owner is exempt. Rav Pappa qualifies that this is only if the owner did not know the entrant was there; if he knew, the owner is liable because he has permission to expel but not to damage. The Gemara notes that Rava and Rav Pappa follow their own reasoning.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that if a person enters a courtyard without permission and damages the owner or is damaged by the owner, the entrant is liable, but if the owner damages the entrant, the owner is exempt.
Rav Pappa qualifies Rava's ruling: the owner is exempt only if he did not know the entrant was there; if he knew, the owner is liable because he has permission to expel but not to damage.
The Gemara notes that Rava and Rav Pappa follow their own reasoning, citing a prior statement attributed to either Rava or Rav Pappa.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Mutual damage in shared or private domains
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Mutual damage in shared or private domains
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that when both parties are in a shared domain or both in a private domain without permission, they are liable for damage but exempt for injury. The Gemara infers that if one is in a permitted domain and the other is not, the permitted one is exempt and the other is liable.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule for mutual damage in shared or private domains: both are liable for damage but exempt for injury.
The Gemara infers that if one party is in a permitted domain and the other is not, the permitted one is exempt and the other is liable.

items.text: Rava's two versions on an ox that fouls a pit's water
items.text_en: Rava's two versions on an ox that fouls a pit's water
items.desc_en: Rava initially says the ox owner is liable only if the ox fouls the water at the moment of falling, because after falling it becomes a 'pit' and water is 'vessels', and a pit is not liable for vessels. The Gemara questions this according to Rav, who requires the pit to be ownerless. Rava then revises: the liability is only if the ox fouls the water from its body, not from its smell, as that is merely indirect causation.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if an ox fell into a pit and fouled its water, the owner is liable.
Rava limits the liability to when the ox fouls the water at the moment of falling, because after falling the ox becomes a 'pit' and the water 'vessels', and a pit is not liable for vessels.
The Gemara objects that Rava's reasoning works for Shmuel, who considers any obstacle a pit, but not for Rav, who requires the pit to be ownerless.
Rava revises his statement: the liability is only when the ox fouls the water from its body, not from its smell, which is merely indirect causation (גרמא).

items.text: Kofer for a tam ox that kills a relative in a pit
items.text_en: Kofer for a tam ox that kills a relative in a pit
items.desc_en: The Mishnah says if the victim is the owner's father or son, he pays kofer. The Gemara asks why, since the ox is tam. Rav answers that we deal with a mu'ad for falling on people in pits. Rav Yosef explains it saw green and fell. Shmuel says it follows Rabbi Yose HaGelili, who holds a tam pays half kofer. Ulla says it follows Rabbi Yose HaGelili who agrees with Rabbi Tarfon that in the victim's domain, full payment is made. The Gemara questions Shmuel's view, as the Mishnah specifies father or son, but Shmuel would apply to anyone; the Gemara answers it's just the typical case.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if the owner's father or son falls into the pit, the owner pays kofer (ransom).
The Gemara asks why kofer is paid, since the ox is a tam (not forewarned) and a tam does not pay kofer.
Rav answers that the case deals with an ox that is a mu'ad (forewarned) for falling on people in pits.
The Gemara objects that if the ox is a mu'ad, it should be liable for capital punishment, not just kofer.
Rav Yosef explains that the ox saw something green and fell, so it was not deliberate and not subject to capital punishment.
Shmuel answers that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yose HaGelili, who holds that a tam pays half kofer.
Ulla answers that Rabbi Yose HaGelili agrees with Rabbi Tarfon that in the victim's domain, full payment is made, so here full kofer is paid.
The Gemara questions Shmuel's view: why does the Mishnah specify father or son, if according to Shmuel it should apply to anyone?
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah merely mentions the typical case (father or son) but the law applies to all.

items.text: Rav and Shmuel on the halakha of the Mishnah's dispute
items.text_en: Rav and Shmuel on the halakha of the Mishnah's dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara reports that Rav rules like the first Tanna, and Shmuel rules like Rabbi, regarding the liability of the courtyard owner when the ox was brought in with permission.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports that Rav rules like the first Tanna and Shmuel rules like Rabbi regarding the liability of the courtyard owner when the ox was brought in with permission.

items.text: Braita on accepting responsibility and the debate over its consistency
items.text_en: Braita on accepting responsibility and the debate over its consistency
items.desc_en: A braita states that if the owner says 'keep your ox and guard it', the ox owner is liable for damage and the courtyard owner is exempt for injury; if the owner says 'keep your ox and I will guard it', the courtyard owner is liable for injury and exempt for damage. The Gemara notes a contradiction: the first clause implies that without explicit acceptance, the courtyard owner accepts responsibility, while the second clause implies the opposite. Rabbi Elazar says the braita is a broken teaching. Rava says both clauses follow the Rabbis, but the wording differs. Rav Pappa says both follow Rabbi, who holds like Rabbi Tarfon that in the victim's domain full damage is paid. The Gemara explains that saying 'guard it' does not grant a place in the courtyard, so it is like the victim's domain; not saying 'guard it' grants a place, making it a shared domain where only half damage is paid.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited presenting two cases: if the owner says 'keep your ox and guard it', the ox owner is liable for damage and the courtyard owner is exempt for injury; if the owner says 'keep your ox and I will guard it', the courtyard owner is liable for injury and exempt for damage.

The Gemara points out an internal contradiction in the baraita: the first clause implies that without explicit acceptance, the courtyard owner accepts responsibility, while the second clause implies the opposite, leading to a conflict between the positions of the Rabbis and Rabbi.
Rabbi Elazar resolves the contradiction by declaring the baraita a broken teaching (תַּבְרָא), meaning it was taught by two different Tannaim with conflicting views.

Rava offers an alternative resolution: the entire baraita follows the Rabbis, but the wording of the first clause ('guard it') led the Tanna to formulate the second clause with 'I will guard it' for stylistic consistency, not to indicate a different halacha.
Rav Pappa provides a third resolution: the entire baraita follows Rabbi, who holds like Rabbi Tarfon that damage in the victim's domain (חצר הניזק) requires full payment.

The Gemara explains the underlying logic: saying 'guard it' does not grant a place in the courtyard, making it like the victim's domain where full damage is paid; not saying 'guard it' grants a place, making it a shared domain where only half damage is paid.

items.text: Mishnah: Liability for causing miscarriage
items.text_en: Mishnah: Liability for causing miscarriage
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that if an ox intended to gore a person but struck a woman and caused a miscarriage, the ox owner is exempt from paying for the offspring. But if a person intended to strike another and struck a woman causing miscarriage, he pays for the offspring. The valuation is done by assessing the woman's worth before and after childbirth.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the basic rule: an ox that intended to gore another and caused a miscarriage is exempt from paying for the offspring, but a person who intended to strike another and caused a miscarriage pays for the offspring.
The Mishnah explains the valuation method: assess the woman's worth before and after childbirth to determine the payment for the offspring.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel is introduced as the next speaker, likely offering an alternative opinion on the valuation.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Payment for offspring and exemptions
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Payment for offspring and exemptions
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a goring ox intended to gore another ox but gored a woman and caused miscarriage, the owner pays the value of the offspring to the husband. If the woman was a freed slavewoman or convert, the owner is exempt.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a goring ox intended to gore another ox but gored a woman and caused miscarriage, the owner pays the value of the offspring to the husband; if the woman was a freed slavewoman or convert, the owner is exempt.

items.text: Gemara's challenge to Rav Adda bar Ahavah
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge to Rav Adda bar Ahavah
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that if the ox intended to gore the woman, the owner pays for offspring. This challenges Rav Adda bar Ahavah, who said oxen that intended to gore a woman are exempt from paying for offspring. Rav Adda bar Ahavah responds that the Mishnah's wording is due to the parallel case of a man, not to indicate a distinction.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that if the ox intended to gore a person, the owner pays for offspring, but if it intended to gore the woman, he is exempt, challenging Rav Adda bar Ahavah's ruling that oxen intending to gore a woman are exempt from paying for offspring.
Rav Adda bar Ahavah responds that the same law applies even if the ox intended to gore the woman, and the Mishnah's wording is only to parallel the case of a man mentioned in the verse.

items.text: Rav Pappa: Goring a slavewoman
items.text_en: Rav Pappa: Goring a slavewoman
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa rules that if an ox gored a slavewoman and she miscarried, the owner pays for offspring because a slavewoman is like a donkey, as per the verse 'with the donkey' referring to those similar to a donkey.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa rules that if an ox gored a slavewoman and caused miscarriage, the owner pays for offspring, because a slavewoman is considered merely a donkey-like entity, as per the verse comparing slaves to donkeys.
Rav Pappa explains his reasoning: the slavewoman is like a donkey, as per the verse 'with the donkey' referring to those similar to a donkey.

items.text: Clarification: Payment includes appreciation of offspring
items.text_en: Clarification: Payment includes appreciation of offspring
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's phrase 'pays the value of offspring' and explains it means the value of offspring and the appreciation of offspring. The method is to appraise the woman's value before and after childbirth.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's phrase 'pays the value of offspring' and clarifies that it means both the value and the enhancement (שבח ולדות), assessed by comparing the woman's value before and after childbirth.
The Gemara explains that the Mishnah means 'the value of offspring and the appreciation of offspring', and the method is to appraise the woman's value before and after childbirth.

items.text: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's objection and resolution
items.text_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's objection and resolution
items.desc_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel objects that a woman's value increases after childbirth, so the appraisal method is flawed. He proposes appraising the offspring separately and giving them to the husband. A baraita supports this interpretation.

sub.desc_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel objects that a woman actually increases in value after childbirth, so the assessment method is flawed; instead, the offspring themselves are appraised and given to the husband.
Rabbah clarifies that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's objection is rhetorical: a woman's value increases after childbirth, so the Tanna Kamma's method is indeed flawed.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel proposes appraising the offspring separately and giving their value to the husband, resolving the flaw in the Tanna Kamma's method.

items.text: Rava's alternative interpretation: Sharing the appreciation
items.text_en: Rava's alternative interpretation: Sharing the appreciation
items.desc_en: Rava interprets Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's statement differently: the woman does not benefit from the appreciation of offspring, so the offspring are given to the husband, and the appreciation is shared. A baraita supports this, adding that separate payments are made for damage and pain.

sub.desc_en: Rava introduces his alternative interpretation of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's statement, arguing that the woman does not benefit from the appreciation of offspring.
Rava concludes that the offspring are valued and given to the husband, while the appreciation of the offspring is shared between the husband and the woman.

items.text: Reconciling the two versions of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
items.text_en: Reconciling the two versions of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction between the two versions of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's statement. It resolves that one refers to a firstborn (where the woman's value increases) and the other to a non-firstborn (where it decreases).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction between the two versions of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's statement.
The Gemara resolves that one version refers to a firstborn (מבכרת, where the woman's value increases) and the other to a non-firstborn (שאינה מבכרת, where it decreases).

items.text: Rabbis' reasoning and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's use of the verse
items.text_en: Rabbis' reasoning and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's use of the verse
items.desc_en: The Rabbis who say the appreciation goes to the husband derive it from the verse 'pregnant' teaching that the benefit of pregnancy belongs to the husband. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel uses the same word to teach that one is liable only if he strikes the womb area, as per Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, excluding limbs.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the reasoning of the Rabbis who hold that the appreciation of the offspring also belongs to the husband.
The Gemara answers by citing a baraita that derives from the verse 'הָרָה' (pregnant) that the benefit of pregnancy belongs to the husband.
The Gemara asks how Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel interprets the same word 'הָרָה' (pregnant).

sub.text: Gemara's answer (citing Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov)
sub.text_en: Gemara's answer (citing Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov)
sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel uses the word to teach, as per Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, that one is liable only if he strikes the womb area.
Rav Pappa clarifies that the liability is not limited to a direct strike on the womb, but applies wherever the blow reaches the fetus, excluding limbs.

items.text: Exemption for freed slavewoman or convert: Rabbah and Rav Chisda's debate
items.text_en: Exemption for freed slavewoman or convert: Rabbah and Rav Chisda's debate
items.desc_en: Rabbah explains the Mishnah's exemption applies only if the injury occurred during the convert's lifetime and the convert died, so the convert acquired the offspring and they pass to heirs. Rav Chisda objects that offspring are not like bundles to be acquired. A baraita contradicts the Mishnah, and the Gemara resolves it by applying Rabbah's distinction or positing the injury occurred after the convert's death.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a woman was a freed slavewoman or a convert, the injurer is exempt from paying for the offspring.

Rabbah explains that the exemption applies only if the injury occurred during the convert's lifetime and the convert died, so the convert acquired the offspring and they pass to heirs; but if the injury occurred after the convert's death, the woman acquires the offspring and the injurer must pay her.
Rav Chisda objects that offspring are not like bundles to be acquired; rather, if there is a husband, the Torah grants him rights, but if there is no husband, the woman does not acquire them.
A baraita is cited that contradicts the Mishnah, stating that for a freed slavewoman or convert, the injurer does pay (זָכָה).

The Gemara resolves the contradiction by applying Rabbah's distinction: the baraita also refers to injury during the convert's lifetime and the convert's death, or alternatively, it refers to injury after the convert's death.

items.text: Citation of the Mishnah's phrase
items.text_en: Citation of the Mishnah's phrase
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's phrase 'זָכְתָה' (she acquires) as a starting point for the discussion about a woman's rights to the value of offspring after her convert husband dies.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's phrase 'זָכְתָה' (she acquires) as a starting point for the discussion about a woman's rights to the value of offspring after her convert husband dies.

items.text: The dispute about a convert's wife and offspring
items.text_en: The dispute about a convert's wife and offspring
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a baraita about a Jewish woman married to a convert who becomes pregnant and is injured. If the convert is alive, the assailant pays the value of the offspring to the convert. After the convert dies, there is a dispute: one Tanna says the assailant is liable (to pay the woman), another says he is exempt. The Gemara asks whether this dispute aligns with the views of Rabba and Rav Chisda.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a baraita about a Jewish woman married to a convert who is injured while pregnant, and the dispute over liability after the convert's death.
The Gemara asks whether this dispute corresponds to the views of Rabba and Rav Chisda.

items.text: First resolution: the dispute is between the Rabbis and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
items.text_en: First resolution: the dispute is between the Rabbis and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the dispute is not difficult: one opinion follows the Rabbis, the other follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel. This resolves the apparent contradiction.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by attributing one opinion to the Rabbis and the other to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.

items.text: Objection to the first resolution
items.text_en: Objection to the first resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if the dispute is between Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and the Rabbis, why does the baraita only mention a difference after the convert's death? According to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, the woman should receive a half share even during the convert's lifetime. The Gemara explains that during his lifetime she gets half, but after his death she gets the entire amount.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if the dispute is between Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and the Rabbis, why does the baraita only mention a difference after the convert's death? According to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, the woman should receive a half share even during the convert's lifetime.
The Gemara explains that during his lifetime she gets half, but after his death she gets the entire amount.

items.text: Alternative resolution: both opinions are Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, distinguishing between enhancement and value
items.text_en: Alternative resolution: both opinions are Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, distinguishing between enhancement and value
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative: both opinions are Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, but they differ in context: one case deals with the enhancement of the offspring (שבח ולדות), where the woman acquires a share, and the other deals with the value of the offspring (דמי ולדות), where she does not acquire anything.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative resolution: both opinions are Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, but one case deals with the enhancement of the offspring (שבח ולדות) and the other with the value of the offspring (דמי ולדות).

items.text: Challenge to the alternative resolution
items.text_en: Challenge to the alternative resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the alternative: one might infer from the term 'שבח ולדות' (enhancement of offspring) that it includes 'דמי ולדות' (value of offspring), and from Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's opinion one might infer the Rabbis' opinion. This suggests the distinction is not clear.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the alternative resolution: from the term 'שבח ולדות' (enhancement of offspring) one might infer 'דמי ולדות' (value of offspring), and from Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's opinion one might infer the Rabbis' opinion, undermining the distinction.

items.text: Resolution of the challenge
items.text_en: Resolution of the challenge
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the challenge: enhancement of offspring (שבח ולדות) is different because the woman has a hand in them (she is pregnant), so she acquires all of them; value of offspring (דמי ולדות) is different because she has no hand in them, so she acquires nothing.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the challenge: enhancement of offspring (שבח ולדות) is different because the woman has a hand in them (she is pregnant), so she acquires all of them; value of offspring (דמי ולדות) is different because she has no hand in them, so she acquires nothing.

items.text: Rav Yeiva Sava's question about holding a convert's documents
items.text_en: Rav Yeiva Sava's question about holding a convert's documents
items.desc_en: Rav Yeiva Sava asks Rav Nachman: if someone takes possession of a convert's documents (shtarot) after the convert dies without heirs, does he acquire them? The question is whether the person intends to acquire the land (which he did not take possession of) or the document itself. Rav Nachman responds with a cryptic answer: 'עֲנַי מוֹרִי, וְכִי לָצוֹר עַל פִּי צְלוֹחִיתוֹ הוּא צָרִיךְ?' (Does he need it to seal his flask?), implying the document is only valuable for the land. Rav Yeiva Sava insists: 'לָצוֹר וְלָצוֹר' (he needs it to seal, and to seal).

sub.desc_en: Rav Yeiva Sava asks Rav Nachman whether one who takes possession of a convert's documents after the convert's death acquires them, given the ambiguity of intent regarding the land versus the document itself.
Rav Nachman responds cryptically, asking if the person needs the document to seal his flask, implying the document's only value is for the land; Rav Yeiva Sava insists he needs it for sealing.

items.text: Rabba's ruling on a Jew's pledge in a convert's hand
items.text_en: Rabba's ruling on a Jew's pledge in a convert's hand
items.desc_en: Rabba rules: if a Jew's pledge (mashkon) is in the hand of a convert, and the convert dies, and another Jew takes possession of it, the pledge is taken from him because the convert's lien is void. But if the convert's pledge is in the hand of a Jew, and the convert dies, and another Jew takes possession, the first Jew acquires the pledge up to the value of his debt, and the second Jew acquires the remainder.

sub.desc_en: Rabba rules that if a Jew's pledge is in a convert's hand and the convert dies, another Jew who takes it must surrender it because the convert's lien is void.
Rabba rules that if a convert's pledge is in a Jew's hand and the convert dies, the first Jew acquires it up to the value of his debt, and a second Jew who takes it acquires the remainder.

items.text: Question about the pledge and the courtyard principle
items.text_en: Question about the pledge and the courtyard principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: why does the second Jew acquire the remainder? Shouldn't the first Jew's courtyard acquire it for him, as per Rabbi Yossi bar Chanina's principle that a person's courtyard acquires for him without his knowledge? The Gemara answers: we are dealing with a case where the first Jew is not present (ליתיה). If he were present and could acquire, his courtyard would acquire for him; but if he is not present and cannot acquire, his courtyard does not acquire.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the second Jew acquires the remainder, invoking Rabbi Yossi bar Chanina's principle that a person's courtyard acquires for him without his knowledge.
The Gemara answers that the case involves a first Jew who is not present (ליתיה), so his courtyard cannot acquire for him, unlike when he is present and could acquire himself.

items.text: Halakhic conclusion
items.text_en: Halakhic conclusion
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the halakha: if the first Jew is not present in his courtyard, he does not acquire the pledge.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara issues a final halakhic ruling: if the first Jew is not present in his courtyard, he does not acquire the pledge.

items.text: Mishnah: liability for digging a bor in various locations
items.text_en: Mishnah: liability for digging a bor in various locations
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states: one who digs a bor in private property and opens it to the public domain, or in the public domain and opens it to private property, or in private property and opens it to another's private property, is liable.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who digs a bor (pit) in private property and opens it to the public domain, or in the public domain and opens it to private property, or in private property and opens it to another's private property, is liable.

items.text: Gemara: dispute between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva about the definition of 'bor'
items.text_en: Gemara: dispute between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva about the definition of 'bor'
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita: Rabbi Yishmael says the bor mentioned in the Torah is one dug in private property and opened to the public domain, or in the public domain and opened to private property. Rabbi Akiva says: if one abandoned his property but not his bor, that is the bor mentioned in the Torah. Rabba explains that all agree one is liable for a bor in the public domain, as the verse 'כי יפתח' and 'כי יכרה' implies liability for opening, and certainly for digging. The dispute is only about a bor in private property.

sub.desc_en: The baraita presents Rabbi Yishmael's definition of the Torah's 'bor' as a pit dug in private property and opened to the public domain, or vice versa, and Rabbi Akiva's definition as one who abandoned his property but not his pit.

Rabba explains that all agree on liability for a bor in the public domain, citing the verse 'כי יפתח' and 'כי יכרה' to show that opening implies liability, and digging certainly does; the dispute is only about a bor in private property.

items.text: Initial dispute: Rabbi Akiva vs. Rabbi Yishmael on a pit in one's own domain
items.text_en: Initial dispute: Rabbi Akiva vs. Rabbi Yishmael on a pit in one's own domain
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents the core disagreement: Rabbi Akiva holds that one is liable for a pit in his own domain, deriving from the phrase 'ba'al ha-bor' (owner of the pit) which implies any pit with an owner. Rabbi Yishmael holds that the Torah speaks of the 'ba'al ha-takalah' (the one who caused the damage), implying liability only for a pit in the public domain.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the dispute: Rabbi Akiva holds one liable for a pit in his own domain, deriving from 'בַּעַל הַבּוֹר' (owner of the pit), while Rabbi Yishmael holds the Torah speaks of 'בַּעַל הַתַּקָּלָה' (the one who caused the damage), implying liability only for a public-domain pit.

items.text: Clarification of Rabbi Akiva's statement
items.text_en: Clarification of Rabbi Akiva's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Rabbi Akiva means by 'this is the pit mentioned in the Torah' – it refers to the pit that the Torah first opened with for payment (i.e., the pit in the public domain).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Rabbi Akiva means by 'this is the pit mentioned in the Torah'.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Akiva's phrase refers to the pit that the Torah first opened with for payment (i.e., the pit in the public domain).

items.text: Rav Yosef's alternative framing of the dispute
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's alternative framing of the dispute
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef argues that everyone agrees one is liable for a pit in one's own domain, as the verse 'ba'al ha-bor' refers to a pit with an owner. The dispute is only about a pit in the public domain: Rabbi Yishmael holds one is liable, deriving from the verses 'ki yiftach' and 'ki yichreh', while Rabbi Akiva holds those verses are necessary to teach that both opening and digging require covering.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef asserts that regarding a pit in one's own domain, all agree one is liable, because the verse 'ba'al ha-bor' speaks of a pit with an owner.
Rav Yosef explains that the dispute is only about a pit in the public domain, with Rabbi Yishmael holding one liable from the verses 'ki yiftach' and 'ki yichreh'.
Rabbi Akiva holds that both verses are necessary to teach that both opening and digging require covering, each addressing a different potential leniency.

items.text: Clarification of Rabbi Yishmael's statement
items.text_en: Clarification of Rabbi Yishmael's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains what Rabbi Yishmael means by 'this is the pit mentioned in the Torah' – it refers to the pit that the Torah first opened with for damages (i.e., the pit in the public domain).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Rabbi Yishmael means by 'this is the pit mentioned in the Torah'.
Rabbi Yishmael explains that it refers to the pit with which the Torah first opened for damages (i.e., the pit in the public domain).

items.text: First baraita challenge and resolution
items.text_en: First baraita challenge and resolution
items.desc_en: A baraita is brought about digging a pit in the public domain and opening it into private domain (exempt), and digging in private domain and opening into public domain (liable), with exceptions for pits dug for 'ushin' (foundations). The Gemara analyzes this baraita according to Rabbah and Rav Yosef: Rabbah can explain the first clause as Rabbi Yishmael and the latter as Rabbi Akiva, but Rav Yosef struggles until he explains the first clause as a case where one did not relinquish his domain or his pit.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: digging a pit in the public domain and opening it into private domain is exempt; digging in private domain and opening into public domain is liable; digging for 'ushin' (foundations) near public domain is exempt, with Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda requiring a partition or distance.
The Gemara infers from the baraita that only digging for 'ushin' (foundations) is exempt, but otherwise one is liable.
The Gemara asks whose opinion the baraita follows: for Rabbah, the first clause fits Rabbi Yishmael and the latter fits Rabbi Akiva.
The Gemara asks: for Rav Yosef, the latter clause is unanimous, but the first clause fits neither Rabbi Yishmael nor Rabbi Akiva.
Rav Yosef answers that the entire baraita is unanimous, and the first clause refers to a case where one did not relinquish his domain or his pit.

items.text: Rav Ashi's alternative resolution for Rabbah
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's alternative resolution for Rabbah
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi suggests that since Rav Yosef's interpretation makes the baraita unanimous, Rabbah can also interpret it as Rabbi Yishmael throughout, explaining the exemption for 'ushin' as a case where one widened the pit into the public domain.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi proposes that since Rav Yosef interprets the baraita as unanimous, Rabbah can also interpret it consistently as Rabbi Yishmael, explaining the exemption for 'ushin' as a case where one widened the pit into the public domain.

items.text: Second baraita challenge and resolution
items.text_en: Second baraita challenge and resolution
items.desc_en: Another baraita is brought that seems to contradict Rav Yosef, but he explains it as referring to digging for 'ushin', and it is unanimous.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Yosef by citing a baraita that seems to contradict his position, showing that neither Rabbi Yishmael nor Rabbi Akiva can explain the baraita's ruling.
Rav Yosef resolves the challenge by explaining that the baraita refers to digging for 'ushin' (foundations), and that all agree on this ruling.

items.text: Baraita about Nechunya the pit-digger
items.text_en: Baraita about Nechunya the pit-digger
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches: if one dug, opened, and handed over to the public, he is exempt; if he dug and opened but did not hand over, he is liable. This was the practice of Nechunya the pit-digger, who would dig and hand over to the public, and the Sages praised him.

sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches that one who dug, opened, and handed over a pit to the public is exempt, while one who dug and opened but did not hand over is liable, and this was the practice of Nechunya the pit-digger, who was praised by the Sages.

items.text: Story of Nechunya's daughter and the principle of divine exactitude
items.text_en: Story of Nechunya's daughter and the principle of divine exactitude
items.desc_en: A story is told about Nechunya's daughter falling into a large pit; Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa prophesied her safety. She was saved by a ram led by an old man. The Sages marveled, but Rabbi Acha notes that despite this, Nechunya's son died of thirst, teaching that God is exacting with the righteous even to a hair's breadth.

sub.desc_en: The baraita introduces the story of Nechunya's daughter falling into a large pit and Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa's initial prophecy of peace.
Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa prophesies that she has emerged safely, and the people ask her how she was saved.
The daughter explains that a ram led by an old man appeared and saved her.
The people ask Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa if he is a prophet.
Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa explains that he reasoned that a righteous person's children would not suffer from the very thing that causes the righteous distress.
Rabbi Acha notes that despite the miracle, Nechunya's son died of thirst, teaching that God is exacting with the righteous even to a hair's breadth.
Rabbi Nechunya cites a different verse to support the same principle of divine exactitude with the righteous.

items.text: Rabbi Chanina's principle: God is not indulgent
items.text_en: Rabbi Chanina's principle: God is not indulgent
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina states that anyone who says God is indulgent will have his life cut short, as the verse says 'The Rock, His work is perfect, for all His ways are justice.' Rabbi Chana (or Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani) then begins a new exposition.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina declares that anyone who says God is indulgent (ותרן) will have his life cut short, citing the verse 'The Rock, His work is perfect, for all His ways are justice.'

sub.text: Rabbi Chana (or Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani)
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chana (or Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani)
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chana (or alternatively Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani) begins a new exposition, asking 'What is written?' to introduce a further interpretation.

items.text: Opening story: clearing stones into the public domain
items.text_en: Opening story: clearing stones into the public domain
items.desc_en: The daf begins with a discussion of the verse 'ארך אפים' (slow to anger) for both righteous and wicked. Then a baraita recounts a story of a man who cleared stones from his property into the public domain; a pious man rebuked him, and later the man needed to sell his field and stumbled on those stones, realizing the pious man was right.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the verse uses the plural 'ארך אפים' (slow to anger) instead of the singular 'ארך אף'.
The Gemara answers that the plural form indicates God is slow to anger toward both the righteous and the wicked.
A baraita is cited, teaching that one should not clear stones from his property into the public domain, and recounts a story of a pious man who rebuked someone for doing so.
The story concludes that later the man needed to sell his field, stumbled on those stones in the public domain, and acknowledged the pious man was correct.

items.text: Mishnah: laws of a pit in the public domain
items.text_en: Mishnah: laws of a pit in the public domain
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who digs a pit in the public domain is liable for any ox or donkey that falls into it. It specifies that the pit must be ten handbreadths deep to be lethal, and if less than ten, the digger is exempt for death but liable for damages.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the liability of one who digs a pit in the public domain, including the depth requirement of ten handbreadths for death liability and exemption for death but liability for damage if less.

items.text: Rav and Shmuel debate: liability for heat vs. impact
items.text_en: Rav and Shmuel debate: liability for heat vs. impact
items.desc_en: Rav holds that Torah liability for a pit is only for its lethal heat (הבלא), not for the impact of the fall (חבטה). Shmuel argues liability includes both heat and impact, and if the Torah only meant impact, it would apply even to a pit filled with sponges. The practical difference between them is a raised area in the public domain: Rav exempts, Shmuel obligates. Rav derives his view from the word 'ונפל' (and falls) implying a normal fall, while Shmuel says 'ונפל' means any fall.

sub.desc_en: Rav states that Torah liability for a pit is only for its lethal heat (הבלא), not for the impact of the fall (חבטה), because the ground itself causes the impact damage.
Shmuel argues that liability includes both heat and impact, and if the Torah only meant impact, it would apply even to a pit filled with sponges.
The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between Rav and Shmuel, and answers that it concerns a raised area in the public domain: Rav exempts, Shmuel obligates.
The Gemara explains Rav's reasoning from the word 'ונפל' (and falls) implying a normal fall, while Shmuel interprets 'ונפל' to mean any fall.

items.text: Gemara questions the Mishnah's 'אף כל' for Rav
items.text_en: Gemara questions the Mishnah's 'אף כל' for Rav
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: according to Shmuel, the Mishnah's 'אף כל' (so too anything) includes a raised area. But for Rav, what does 'אף כל' include? The answer: it includes pits and trenches (חריצין ונעיצין), even though they are explicitly listed; the Tanna lists them and then explains.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: according to Shmuel, the Mishnah's 'אף כל' (so too anything) includes a raised area; but for Rav, what does 'אף כל' include?
The Gemara answers: it includes pits and trenches (חריצין ונעיצין), even though they are explicitly listed; the Tanna lists them and then explains.

items.text: Why all four types of excavations are listed
items.text_en: Why all four types of excavations are listed
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the Mishnah lists all four types (pit, cistern, cave, trenches): each teaches that even in a narrow or wide excavation, ten handbreadths suffice for lethal heat, countering potential assumptions that only a specific shape would have heat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah lists all four types of excavations (pit, cistern, cave, trenches) if the principle of ten handbreadths applies to all.
The Gemara answers that all are necessary to counter potential assumptions about shape and heat.
The Gemara explains that if only 'pit' (בור) were taught, one might think only a narrow, round pit has lethal heat at ten handbreadths, but not a long cistern (שיח).
The Gemara explains that if only 'cistern' (שיח) were taught, one might think only a narrow cistern has heat, but not a square cave (מערה).
The Gemara explains that if only 'cave' (מערה) were taught, one might think only a covered cave has heat, but not open trenches (חריצין).
The Gemara explains that if only 'trenches' (חריצין) were taught, one might think only narrow-bottomed trenches have heat, but not wide-mouthed ditches (נעיצין); thus all are needed.

items.text: Gemara questions the Mishnah's exemption for less than ten handbreadths
items.text_en: Gemara questions the Mishnah's exemption for less than ten handbreadths
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: the Mishnah exempts for death in a pit less than ten handbreadths; is this because there is no impact (חבטה)? It answers: no, it is because there is no lethal heat (הבלא). But then why is one liable for damages? Because there is heat for injury but not for death.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah's exemption for death in a pit less than ten handbreadths is due to the absence of impact (חבטה).
The Gemara answers that the exemption is due to the absence of lethal heat (הבלא), not lack of impact, and explains that there is heat sufficient for injury but not for death.

items.text: Rav Nachman's ruling: impact exists in less than ten handbreadths
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's ruling: impact exists in less than ten handbreadths
items.desc_en: A case: an ox fell into a date-palm pit and was slaughtered. Rav Nachman ruled the owner was negligent, arguing that if the owner had spent a small amount to check the law, he would have known that an animal that waited overnight is kosher, and he would not have lost the ox. This shows Rav Nachman holds there is impact (חבטה) even in less than ten handbreadths. Rava challenges him from the Mishnah.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a case: an ox fell into a date-palm pit and its owner slaughtered it; Rav Nachman ruled the owner liable.
Rav Nachman explains his ruling: if the owner had spent a small amount to learn the law that an animal that waited overnight is kosher, he would not have lost the ox.
