The gemara infers from Rav Nachman's ruling that he holds there is impact (חבטה) even in a pit less than ten handbreadths deep.
Rava challenges Rav Nachman from the Mishnah: for a pit less than ten handbreadths, the owner is exempt from death — is that not because there is no impact (חבטה)?

items.text: Gemara's question on the necessity of ten handbreadths for death
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the necessity of ten handbreadths for death
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a fall from less than ten handbreadths can cause death through impact (חבטה). It argues that if there is no heat (הבלא) in a shallow pit, then a fall into it would not be lethal, but the Gemara objects that if so, why would one be liable for damage? The answer distinguishes between the heat of death and the heat of injury.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why a pit less than ten handbreadths deep cannot cause death, and the answer distinguishes between the heat (הבלא) needed for death versus injury.

items.text: Challenge from the height of the stoning platform
items.text_en: Challenge from the height of the stoning platform
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the idea that impact (חבטה) can occur at less than ten handbreadths by citing the Mishnah that the stoning platform was two stories high, and the condemned man's height adds another, totaling three stories. If impact could occur at less than ten, why such height? The Gemara answers that the height is for a beautiful death, as per Rav Nachman's teaching, and not to increase impact.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the idea that impact (חבטה) can occur at less than ten handbreadths by citing the Mishnah that the stoning platform was two stories high, plus the condemned man's height, totaling three stories, and asks why such height is needed if impact occurs at less than ten.

The Gemara answers that the height is not for impact but for a beautiful death, as per Rav Nachman's teaching from the verse 'ואהבת לרעך כמוך' (love your neighbor as yourself) to choose a dignified death.
The Gemara objects that if the height is for a beautiful death, why not make it even higher, and answers that excessive height would cause disfigurement (ניוול).

items.text: Challenge from the verse 'כי יפול הנופל ממנו'
items.text_en: Challenge from the verse 'כי יפול הנופל ממנו'
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita that discusses a pit in the public domain: if the public domain is ten handbreadths higher than the pit, one who falls from the public domain into the pit is exempt, but if the pit is ten handbreadths deeper, one is liable. This implies that a ten-handbreadth difference is necessary for liability, contradicting the idea of impact at less than ten. The answer distinguishes a pit from a house, as a pit less than ten handbreadths is not considered a pit.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects with a baraita that explicitly requires a ten-handbreadth difference for liability in a pit, implying that less than ten handbreadths cannot cause death.

The answer distinguishes between a pit and a house: a structure less than ten handbreadths is not considered a house (בית), so the baraita's requirement is about the definition of a house, not about lethality.
The Gemara asks: if impact is possible at less than ten handbreadths, why require specifically ten handbreadths for liability?
The answer distinguishes a pit from a house, as a pit less than ten handbreadths is not considered a pit (בור) for liability purposes.

items.text: Objection regarding internal vs. external height
items.text_en: Objection regarding internal vs. external height
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that even if the external height is ten handbreadths, the internal height might be less due to the roof and plaster. The answer is that the case is where the interior is compressed to ten handbreadths. The Gemara then counters that if so, even when the external height is less than ten, one could find a case where the interior is ten handbreadths by compressing more.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that even if the external height is ten handbreadths, the interior height is less due to the roof and plaster, so it is not a valid house.
The answer is that the case is where the interior is compressed to ten handbreadths.
The Gemara counters that if so, even when the external height is less than ten, one could find a case where the interior is ten handbreadths by compressing more.

items.text: Rav Nachman's explanation of the ten-handbreadth measure
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's explanation of the ten-handbreadth measure
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman explains that the ten-handbreadth measure is derived from the height of a cow's belly (four handbreadths) plus the height of a palm branch (six handbreadths), totaling ten. Thus, the impact occurs from ten handbreadths. The Gemara then questions the Mishnah that states a pit must be ten handbreadths to kill, asking why six handbreadths would not suffice. The answer is that the Mishnah refers to a case where one falls into the pit (איגנדר לבור), not where one falls from a height into it.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman explains that the ten-handbreadth measure is derived from the height of a cow's belly (four handbreadths) plus the height of a palm branch (six handbreadths), totaling ten, so the impact occurs from ten handbreadths.
The Gemara questions the Mishnah that states a pit must be ten handbreadths to kill, asking why six handbreadths would not suffice.
The answer is that the Mishnah refers to a case where one falls into the pit (איגנדר לבור), not where one falls from a height into it.

items.text: Mishnah: Pit of two partners
items.text_en: Mishnah: Pit of two partners
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a pit belongs to two partners, and the first passed by without covering it, and the second also passed by without covering it, the second is liable.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a pit belongs to two partners and the first fails to cover it, then the second also fails, the second is liable.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's scenario
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's scenario
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a pit of two partners can be found liable. If we follow Rabbi Akiva, who holds that a pit in one's own property is liable, it can be found in a jointly owned courtyard where they renounced ownership of the courtyard but not the pit. If we follow the view that a pit in one's own property is exempt, it must be in the public domain. The Gemara then discusses how two partners can dig a pit in the public domain, rejecting the possibility of an agent (since there is no agency for sin) and the possibility of each digging five handbreadths (since the first act is nullified). Rabbi Yochanan resolves that they both removed a clod simultaneously, completing ten handbreadths.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how a pit belonging to two partners can be found liable.

The Gemara explains that according to Rabbi Akiva, who holds a pit in one's own property is liable, the case is found in a jointly owned courtyard where they renounced ownership of the courtyard but not the pit.
The Gemara asks how, according to the view that a pit in one's own property is exempt, a pit of two partners in the public domain can be found liable.
The Gemara rejects the possibilities of both partners appointing an agent (since there is no agency for sin) and each digging five handbreadths (since the first act is nullified).
Rabbi Yochanan resolves that both partners removed a clod simultaneously, completing ten handbreadths.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi and the Rabbis regarding a digger who completes a pit
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi and the Rabbis regarding a digger who completes a pit
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the dispute: if one digs a pit of nine handbreadths and another completes it to ten, the Rabbis hold the last one liable for both death and damage, while Rabbi holds the last liable for death but both liable for damage. The Gemara analyzes the scriptural sources for their positions, including the verses 'כי יפתח' and 'כי יכרה', and the principle that the one who causes death is liable. It also discusses a baraita about digging to twenty and thirty handbreadths, and a contradiction regarding plastering and cementing.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the dispute between Rabbi and the Rabbis, citing a baraita where one digs nine handbreadths and another completes to ten: the last is liable for death, and both for damages according to Rabbi.
The Gemara cites a baraita: one who digs a pit of nine handbreadths and another completes it to ten — the last is liable; Rabbi says: the last is liable for death, both for damage.

sub.text: Gemara's analysis of the Rabbis' position
sub.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the Rabbis' position
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains the Rabbis' reasoning: the verses 'כי יפתח' and 'כי יכרה' imply that one who digs after another has nullified the first's action, making the last liable.
The Gemara states that Rabbi holds the verses are necessary for their own exegesis, and the Rabbis also need them.

sub.text: Gemara's alternative explanation of the Rabbis' position
sub.text_en: Gemara's alternative explanation of the Rabbis' position
sub.desc_en: The Gemara gives an alternative reason for the Rabbis: the verse 'כי יכרה איש בור' implies one digger, not two, so the last is liable.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi's alternative derivation
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi's alternative derivation
sub.desc_en: Rabbi uses the verse 'כי יכרה איש בור' to exclude an ox that digs a pit, not to limit liability to one digger.

sub.text: Gemara's response to the Rabbis' counter-argument
sub.text_en: Gemara's response to the Rabbis' counter-argument
sub.desc_en: The Rabbis respond that the phrase 'איש בור' appears twice in the verse, allowing both exclusions.
Rabbi argues that the second 'איש בור' is merely a stylistic repetition, not an additional exclusion.
The Gemara objects: how do we know the verse intends to hold the last digger liable? Perhaps it holds the first liable.
The Gemara rejects this: the verse 'והמת יהיה לו' indicates that the one who causes death is liable, which is the last digger who completes the pit to ten handbreadths.

The Gemara objects: the verse 'והמת יהיה לו' is needed for Rava's teaching that an animal of disqualified consecrated property that falls into a pit is exempt, because the dead animal belongs to the Temple treasury.
The Gemara rejects this: from Rava's teaching itself we infer that the verse deals with the one who causes death, so it still supports the last digger's liability.

The Gemara cites a baraita: one who digs a pit of ten handbreadths, another completes it to twenty, and another to thirty — all are liable; but a contradiction is raised regarding plastering and cementing where only the last is liable.

items.text: Resolving the contradiction between the Mishnah and the Baraita
items.text_en: Resolving the contradiction between the Mishnah and the Baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially questions whether the Mishnah (all liable) follows Rabbi and the Baraita (last liable) follows the Rabbis. Rav Zevid explains both follow the Rabbis: they only exempt the first if his action alone did not create lethal heat; but if it did, all agree all are liable. The case of plastering and painting (סייד וכייד) is then addressed, where the first did create lethal heat yet the Baraita says only the last is liable; the answer is that the first's heat was insufficient for death, and the last added the necessary heat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah (all liable) follows Rabbi and the Baraita (last liable) follows the Rabbis.
Rav Zevid explains that both sources follow the Rabbis: they only exempt the first if his action alone did not create lethal heat; but if it did, all agree all are liable.
The Gemara objects: the case of plastering and painting (סייד וכייד) has the first creating lethal heat, yet the Baraita says only the last is liable.
The anonymous answer resolves that the first's heat was insufficient for death, and the last added the necessary heat.

items.text: Alternative version of Rav Zevid's explanation
items.text_en: Alternative version of Rav Zevid's explanation
items.desc_en: An alternative version states that both the Mishnah and Baraita follow Rabbi: the Baraita's case (last liable) is where the first's heat was insufficient for either death or injury, and the last added heat sufficient for both.

sub.desc_en: An alternative version presents Rav Zevid's explanation that both the Mishnah and Baraita follow Rabbi, with the Baraita's case being where the first person's heat was insufficient for either death or injury, and the last person added heat sufficient for both.

items.text: Rava's case: placing a stone on the pit's mouth
items.text_en: Rava's case: placing a stone on the pit's mouth
items.desc_en: Rava states that if one placed a stone on the pit's mouth, completing it to a depth of ten handbreadths, the liability depends on the dispute between Rabbi and the Rabbis. The Gemara notes this is obvious, but clarifies that one might think only below (where the heat kills) is disputed, but above (where the stone kills) all agree; the statement teaches that even above is disputed.

sub.desc_en: Rava states that if one placed a stone on the pit's mouth, completing it to a depth of ten handbreadths, the liability depends on the dispute between Rabbi and the Rabbis.
Rava states that if one placed a stone on the pit opening and completed it to ten handbreadths, the case falls into the dispute between Rabbi and the Sages.
The Gemara objects that Rava's statement is obvious.
The Gemara asks: is this obvious? One might think that only below the stone the heat kills, but above it the heat does not kill, so perhaps the later person is not liable.

The Gemara explains that Rava's statement is not obvious: one might think the dispute applies only below (where the heat kills), but Rava teaches that even above (where the stone kills) the dispute applies.
The Gemara concludes that Rava's statement teaches us that even above the stone, the heat is considered lethal.

items.text: Rava's query: filling a handbreadth and removing stones
items.text_en: Rava's query: filling a handbreadth and removing stones
items.desc_en: Rava asks: if one filled a handbreadth of the pit and then removed its stones, is it considered that he merely removed his action, or that the original action is nullified and the entire pit is now under his responsibility? The question remains unresolved (תיקו).

sub.desc_en: Rava asks whether filling a handbreadth of the pit and then removing its stones constitutes merely removing his action or nullifying the original action, making the entire pit his responsibility.
Rava asks: if one filled a handbreadth and then removed the stones, do we say he has undone his action?
The question remains unresolved (תיקו).
Rava asks alternatively: perhaps the first action is nullified and the entire pit is now under his responsibility? The question remains unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Liability for a pit with water
items.text_en: Liability for a pit with water
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah quotes Shmuel bar Marta: a pit of eight handbreadths, with two of water, is liable because each handbreadth of water counts as two of dry land. The Gemara then raises unresolved queries: a pit of nine with one handbreadth of water (is there heat?), and a pit of seven with three handbreadths of water (is there heat?). Both remain unanswered (תיקו).

sub.text: Rabbah bar bar Chanah quoting Shmuel bar Marta
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah quoting Shmuel bar Marta
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah states in the name of Shmuel bar Marta that a pit eight handbreadths deep with two handbreadths of water is liable, because each handbreadth of water counts as two of dry land.
The Gemara raises an unresolved query: if a pit is nine handbreadths deep with only one handbreadth of water, does it have lethal heat or not?
The Gemara raises another unresolved query: if a pit is seven handbreadths deep with three handbreadths of water, does it have lethal heat or not, and both queries remain unanswered (תיקו).

items.text: Rav Sheizvi's query about widening the pit
items.text_en: Rav Sheizvi's query about widening the pit
items.desc_en: Rav Sheizvi asks Rabbah: if one widened the pit, what is the law? Rabbah says it reduces the heat, but Rav Sheizvi counters that it brings the danger closer. Rav Ashi then resolves: if the victim died from heat, widening reduces heat; if from impact, widening brings danger closer. An alternative version distinguishes which side the victim fell from.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheizvi asks Rabbah: if one widened the pit, what is the law regarding liability?
Rav Sheizvi asks Rabbah: if one widened the pit, what is the law? Rabbah answers: he has reduced the heat.
Rabbah answers that widening reduces the heat (הבלא) of the pit.
Rav Sheizvi objects: on the contrary, he has brought the danger closer!
Rav Sheizvi objects: on the contrary, widening brings the danger closer.
Rav Ashi resolves: we look at the cause of death — if by heat, widening reduced heat; if by impact, widening brought danger closer.
Rav Ashi resolves: if the victim died from heat, widening reduces heat; if from impact, widening brings danger closer.
An alternative version: Rav Ashi says we look at which side the victim fell from — if from the widened side, danger is closer; if from the other side, heat is reduced.
An alternative version distinguishes which side the victim fell from: if from one side, danger is closer; if from the other, heat is reduced.

items.text: Dispute about a pit whose depth equals its width
items.text_en: Dispute about a pit whose depth equals its width
items.desc_en: Rabbah and Rav Yosef report in the name of Rabbah bar bar Chanah, who cites Rabbi Mani: one says a pit always has heat until its width exceeds its depth; another says it never has heat until its depth exceeds its width.

sub.desc_en: The gemara reports a dispute between two opinions transmitted by Rabbah and Rav Yosef in the name of Rabbah bar bar Chanah, who cites Rabbi Mani: one says a pit always has heat (הבל) until its width exceeds its depth; the other says it never has heat until its depth exceeds its width.
Another authority says there is never heat until the depth exceeds the width.

items.text: When does the first passerby become exempt?
items.text_en: When does the first passerby become exempt?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: when does the first person who passed over the pit without covering it become exempt? Rabbah and Rav Yosef report a dispute: one says from when he leaves it usable (משמניחו משתמש), another says from when he hands over his bucket (משימסור לו דליו). This is then shown to correspond to a Tannaitic dispute between Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov and the Rabbis.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from what point does the first passerby who passed over the pit without covering it become exempt from liability?

sub.text: Rabbah and Rav Yosef citing Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Mani
sub.text_en: Rabbah and Rav Yosef citing Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Mani
sub.desc_en: Rabbah and Rav Yosef report a dispute in the name of Rabbi Mani: one says the first passerby is exempt from when he leaves the pit usable (משמניחו משתמש), and another says from when he hands over his bucket (משימסור לו דליו).
A baraita is cited that parallels the dispute: the Tanna Kamma says the first person is exempt from when he leaves it usable, while Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says from when he hands over his bucket.

items.text: The dispute explained by the principle of ברירה
items.text_en: The dispute explained by the principle of ברירה
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the Tannaitic dispute: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov holds that there is retroactive clarification (יש ברירה), so each draws from his own portion; the Rabbis hold there is no retroactive clarification (אין ברירה). Ravina notes this aligns with their dispute in a Mishnah about partners who vowed not to benefit from each other.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the basis of the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov and the Rabbis.

The Gemara explains that Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov holds the principle of יש ברירה (retroactive clarification), so each draws from his own portion, while the Rabbis hold אין ברירה (no retroactive clarification).

items.text: Acquisition of a pit by handing over the bucket
items.text_en: Acquisition of a pit by handing over the bucket
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar states that when one sells a pit to another, once he hands over the bucket (דלי), the buyer acquires it. The Gemara questions why not use money or a formal act of possession (חזקה). It answers that the case is one of possession, and handing over the bucket is like saying 'go, take possession and acquire' (לך חזק וקני).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar states that when one sells a pit to another, once he hands over the bucket (דלי), the buyer acquires it.
Rabbi Elazar states that one who sells a pit to another acquires it once he hands over his bucket. The Gemara questions: why not acquire by money or by chazakah (presumption of ownership)?
The Gemara questions why the buyer does not acquire through money (כסף) or a formal act of possession (חזקה) instead of handing over the bucket.
The Gemara answers: it is indeed by chazakah, and handing over the bucket is like saying 'go, take possession and acquire'.
The Gemara answers that the case involves possession (חזקה), and handing over the bucket is like saying 'go, take possession and acquire' (לך חזק וקני).

items.text: Beginning of a new topic: selling a house
items.text_en: Beginning of a new topic: selling a house
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi begins a new discussion about selling a house, which is cut off at the end of the daf.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi begins a new discussion about selling a house, which is cut off at the end of the daf.

items.text: Acquisition by handing over the key
items.text_en: Acquisition by handing over the key
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how handing over the key can effect acquisition, and explains that it is considered like saying 'go and take possession' in the context of a חזקה acquisition.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that once one hands over the key, the buyer acquires the property.
The Gemara questions how handing over the key alone can effect acquisition, since acquisition is normally done by money or by a formal act of possession (חזקה).
The Gemara answers that the acquisition is indeed by a formal act of possession (חזקה), and handing over the key is considered equivalent to saying 'go and take possession and acquire'.

items.text: Acquisition by handing over the lead animal
items.text_en: Acquisition by handing over the lead animal
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish in the name of Rabbi Yannai teaches that one who sells a herd acquires it by handing over the lead animal (משכוכית). The Gemara explains that this is like saying 'go and pull and acquire', and defines משכוכית as a bellwether or a goat that leads the herd.

sub.text: Reish Lakish in the name of Rabbi Yannai
sub.text_en: Reish Lakish in the name of Rabbi Yannai
sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish in the name of Rabbi Yannai rules that one who sells a herd acquires it by handing over the lead animal (משכוכית).
The Gemara questions the ruling: if the acquisition is by pulling (משיכה) or by handing over (מסירה), why is the lead animal needed?
The Gemara answers that the acquisition is always by pulling (משיכה), and handing over the lead animal is like saying 'go and pull and acquire'.
The Gemara asks: what is a משכוכית (lead animal)?
In the local tradition (in Eretz Yisrael), they translate it as קרקשתא (a bellwether).
Rabbi Yaakov defines it as a goat that goes at the head of the herd, citing a Galilean's homily before Rav Chisda: when the shepherd is angry with the flock, he makes the lead goat blind.

items.text: Mishnah: Liability for an uncovered pit
items.text_en: Mishnah: Liability for an uncovered pit
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents cases of liability for a pit: if the first person covered it and the second found it uncovered and did not cover it, the second is liable. If covered properly, the owner is exempt; if not, liable. Additional cases include falling due to digging noise, and damage to animals and vessels.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the case: if the first covered the pit and the second found it uncovered and did not cover it, the second is liable.
The Mishnah states that if covered properly, the owner is exempt; if not covered properly, he is liable.
The Mishnah adds that falling due to the noise of digging in front of the pit incurs liability, but behind it does not.
The Mishnah rules that for an animal falling with vessels, the owner is liable for the animal but exempt for the vessels.
The Mishnah concludes that for a deaf, insane, or minor animal falling in, the owner is liable; for a son, daughter, slave, or maidservant, he is exempt.

items.text: Gemara: How long is the first person exempt?
items.text_en: Gemara: How long is the first person exempt?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks until when the first person is exempt from covering the pit. Rav says until he knows, Shmuel says until they inform him, and Rabbi Yochanan says until they inform him and he hires workers and cuts cedars to cover it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks until when the first person is exempt from covering the pit.
Rav answers that the first person is exempt until he knows about the pit.
Shmuel answers that the first person is exempt until others inform him about the pit.
Rabbi Yochanan answers that the first person is exempt until they inform him and he hires workers and cuts cedars to cover it.

items.text: Gemara: How can an animal fall into a properly covered pit?
items.text_en: Gemara: How can an animal fall into a properly covered pit?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how an animal can fall into a pit that was covered properly. Rabbi Yitzchak bar bar Chanah answers that the pit rotted from within.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how an animal could fall into a pit that was covered properly (כיסהו כראוי).

sub.text: Rabbi Yitzchak bar bar Chanah's answer
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar bar Chanah's answer
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar bar Chanah answers that the pit rotted from within (התליע מתוכו), causing the cover to collapse.

items.text: Gemara: Partial coverage – can withstand oxen but not camels
items.text_en: Gemara: Partial coverage – can withstand oxen but not camels
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question about a pit covered to withstand oxen but not camels, where camels come and break the cover, and then oxen fall in. The Gemara considers whether the owner is negligent or forced, and attempts to resolve it from the Mishnah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question about a pit covered to withstand oxen but not camels, where camels break the cover and then oxen fall in, asking what the liability is.
The Gemara objects that if camels are common the owner is negligent, and if not he is forced, so the question seems resolved.
The Gemara refines the case to camels that come only intermittently, and questions whether the owner is negligent for anticipating them or forced since they are not currently present.
The Gemara attempts to resolve the question by citing the Mishnah's case of covering 'properly' and deducing that it means only for oxen, implying liability for intermittent camel damage.

items.text: First challenge to the Mishnah's ruling
items.text_en: First challenge to the Mishnah's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's case where one covers a pit adequately for oxen but not for camels, and camels come periodically and weaken the covering, then oxen fall in and die. The Mishnah says he is exempt, implying that since camels are not currently present, he is considered an innocent victim (anus).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the Mishnah's ruling: if camels are present, why is he exempt (he is negligent); if not, it is obvious he is an innocent victim (אנוס); the only plausible scenario is camels that come periodically, yet the Mishnah still says exempt, implying that since camels are not currently present, he is considered an innocent victim (אנוס).

items.text: First answer: worm-eaten from within
items.text_en: First answer: worm-eaten from within
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the case is where the covering was adequate for both oxen and camels, but it became worm-eaten from within, so the owner is not negligent.

sub.text: Gemara's answer via Rabbi Yitzchak bar bar Chanah
sub.text_en: Gemara's answer via Rabbi Yitzchak bar bar Chanah
sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the covering was adequate for both oxen and camels, but it became worm-eaten from within, so the owner is not negligent.

items.text: Second challenge from a baraita: liability for inadequate covering
items.text_en: Second challenge from a baraita: liability for inadequate covering
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita that if one did not cover the pit adequately and an animal falls in and dies, he is liable. The Gemara analyzes the case: if it is inadequate for both oxen and camels, liability is obvious. If it is adequate for oxen but not for camels, and camels are not common, he is an innocent victim. The only plausible case is where camels come periodically, and the baraita rules him liable, implying that since camels come periodically, he is negligent because he should have anticipated them.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about inadequate covering and questions which case it refers to, rejecting obvious scenarios.
The Gemara concludes that the baraita refers to camels that come periodically, making the owner negligent for not anticipating them, thus liable.

items.text: Second answer: the baraita is a stylistic pairing
items.text_en: Second answer: the baraita is a stylistic pairing
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the baraita is discussing a case where the covering is adequate for oxen but not for camels, and camels are common. The reason he is liable is simply because he is negligent, and the baraita's wording is just a stylistic parallel to the first clause.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the baraita is discussing a case where the covering is adequate for oxen but not for camels, and camels are common; the reason he is liable is simply because he is negligent, and the baraita's wording is just a stylistic parallel to the first clause.

items.text: The real question: the principle of 'since' (מיגו)
items.text_en: The real question: the principle of 'since' (מיגו)
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the real question is about a case where the covering is adequate for oxen but not for camels, camels are common, and the covering becomes worm-eaten from within. Does the principle of 'since he is negligent regarding camels, he is also negligent regarding worm-eaten coverings' apply?

sub.desc_en: The alternative formulation states that the previous question is unnecessary because when camels come periodically, the owner is negligent and must anticipate them.

The Gemara poses the real question: if the covering is adequate for oxen but not for camels, camels are common, and the covering becomes worm-eaten from within, does the principle of מיגו (since) apply to deem him negligent regarding the worm-eaten covering?

items.text: Attempt to resolve from the first Mishnah: exempt
items.text_en: Attempt to resolve from the first Mishnah: exempt
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings the Mishnah's case where one covered adequately and an animal falls in and dies – he is exempt. Rabbi Yitzchak bar bar Chanah said this is because it became worm-eaten from within. The Gemara analyzes: if the covering was adequate for both, exemption is obvious. So it must be that it was adequate for oxen but not for camels, and camels are common, yet he is exempt – proving that the 'since' principle does not apply. The Gemara deflects: perhaps the covering was adequate for both, and the teaching is that he is not required to tap on it to check for worms.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings the Mishnah's case where one covered adequately and an animal falls in and dies – he is exempt, and questions: if the covering was adequate for both oxen and camels, why is the exemption not obvious?
The Gemara reinterprets: the covering was adequate for oxen but not for camels, and camels are common, yet the Mishnah rules exempt – implying that the 'since' principle does not apply.
The Gemara deflects: perhaps the covering was adequate for both, and the teaching is that he is not required to tap on it to check for worms.

items.text: Attempt to resolve from the baraita: liable
items.text_en: Attempt to resolve from the baraita: liable
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings the baraita that if one did not cover adequately and an animal falls in and dies, he is liable. The analysis suggests the case is where the covering is adequate for oxen but not for camels, camels are common, and it became worm-eaten – and he is liable, proving that the 'since' principle does apply. The Gemara deflects: the case is where camels actually came and weakened the covering, so he is simply negligent, and the baraita's wording is stylistic.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita stating that if one did not cover adequately and an animal falls in and dies, he is liable, and questions the obviousness of the case.

The Gemara proposes that the case is where the covering is adequate for oxen but not for camels, camels are common, and it became worm-eaten, yet the baraita says liable, suggesting the 'since' principle applies.
The Gemara deflects by explaining that the case is where camels actually came and weakened the covering, so he is simply negligent, and the baraita's wording is stylistic.

items.text: Resolution from a baraita about a deaf, insane, or minor ox
items.text_en: Resolution from a baraita about a deaf, insane, or minor ox
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita: if a deaf, insane, or minor ox falls into a pit, the owner is liable; if a sighted ox falls in during the day, he is exempt. The Gemara argues: why not say that since he is negligent regarding the deaf ox, he is also negligent regarding the sighted ox? This proves that the 'since' principle is not applied. The Gemara concludes: indeed, learn from this that it is not applied.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about a deaf, insane, or minor ox falling into a pit to challenge the application of the 'since' principle.
The Gemara questions why the owner is not liable for the sighted ox as well, since he is negligent regarding the deaf ox, applying the 'since' principle.
The Gemara concludes that the baraita proves the 'since' principle is not applied, as the owner is exempt for the sighted ox despite negligence for the deaf ox.

items.text: Rav's interpretation of 'before him' and 'behind him'
items.text_en: Rav's interpretation of 'before him' and 'behind him'
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rav's statement that in the Mishnah's phrase 'fell before him' means literally before him, and 'behind him' means literally behind him.

sub.desc_en: Rav states that the Mishnah's terms 'before him' and 'behind him' are to be understood literally.

items.text: Opening Mishnah citation
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah citation
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that both cases (falling in front or behind) are under the category of pit.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that both cases (falling in front or behind) are under the category of pit.

items.text: Rav and Shmuel's positions on liability
items.text_en: Rav and Shmuel's positions on liability
items.desc_en: Rav holds that Torah liability for a pit is only for its 'breath' (the pit's air) not for its 'striking' (the fall), so falling behind the pit due to the sound of digging is exempt. Shmuel holds that both front and back are liable, and explains that the exempt case is when one tripped in the pit and fell outside it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that Rav holds Torah liability for a pit is only for its 'breath' (הבל) and not for its 'striking' (חבט).
Shmuel states that for a pit, whether one falls in front or behind, the pit owner is liable.
The Gemara explains that Shmuel holds liability for the 'breath' (הבל) and all the more so for 'striking' (חבט), and the exempt case is when one tripped in the pit and fell outside it.

items.text: Objection against Rav
items.text_en: Objection against Rav
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that states liability for both front and back, which is a refutation of Rav's position.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection against Rav from a baraita that states liability for both front and back falls, declaring it a refutation of Rav.

items.text: Three resolutions for Rav
items.text_en: Three resolutions for Rav
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda, Rabbah, and Rav Yosef each offer a resolution to defend Rav. Rav Chisda says Rav admits liability when the pit is in his own property. Rabbah says the case is where the animal flipped over. Rav Yosef says the case is about damage from the pit's water becoming foul.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda resolves the contradiction by stating that Rav admits liability when the pit is in his own property, because regardless of whether the animal died from the pit's heat or impact, the damage is attributable to the pit owner.
Rabbah resolves the contradiction by explaining that the case involves an animal that flipped over, so the pit's heat affected it regardless of whether it fell forward or backward.
Rav Yosef resolves the contradiction by stating that the case involves damage from the pit's water becoming foul, which applies equally whether the animal fell in front or behind.

items.text: Baraita supporting Rav
items.text_en: Baraita supporting Rav
items.desc_en: A baraita taught by Rav Chananya supports Rav, stating that 'and he falls' implies a normal fall, exempting falling behind due to the sound of digging.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chananya teaches a baraita supporting Rav, stating that liability requires a normal fall, exempting a fall behind from the digging noise.

items.text: Analysis of Rabbi Nathan's principle
items.text_en: Analysis of Rabbi Nathan's principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why falling in front is liable, and Rav Shimi bar Ashi explains it follows Rabbi Nathan's view that the pit owner is a tortfeasor, and payment can be collected from either tortfeasor. The Gemara then discusses a contradiction in Rabbi Nathan's statements about division of liability between a goring ox and a pit, and Rava resolves it by explaining Rabbi Nathan's reasoning.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why falling in front of the pit is liable, since the digger (כּוֹרֶה) caused the fall.
Rav Shimi bar Ashi explains that the ruling follows Rabbi Nathan, who holds the pit owner is a tortfeasor and payment can be collected from either party.
A baraita is cited showing Rabbi Nathan's principle: when an ox pushes another into a pit, both owners share liability.
The Gemara objects with another baraita where Rabbi Nathan assigns three-quarters to the pit owner and one-quarter to the ox owner.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: the first baraita deals with a tam (innocent ox), the second with a mu'ad (forewarned ox).
The Gemara questions Rabbi Nathan's reasoning regarding a tam: if each caused the full damage, why not split equally?

Rava explains that Rabbi Nathan is a deep jurist; in the tam case, the ox owner argues that his partnership didn't benefit him, so the pit owner pays more; alternatively, the ox owner argues he found his ox in the pit and the pit owner killed it, so he collects from whichever party can pay.

items.text: Case of a stone placed at the pit's mouth
items.text_en: Case of a stone placed at the pit's mouth
items.desc_en: Rava presents a case where a stone was placed at the pit's mouth and an animal tripped and fell, which is a dispute between Rabbi Nathan and the Rabbis. The Gemara clarifies that the stone owner cannot claim the pit caused the damage, as the pit was necessary for the fall.

sub.desc_en: Rava presents a case where a stone was placed at the pit's mouth)Skip, an animal tripped and fell into the pit, and he declares this falls under the dispute between Rabbi Nathan and the Rabbis.
The Gemara objects that this case is obvious and does not need to be stated.

The Gemara explains that the novelty is that one might have thought the stone owner could argue that without the pit the stone would have caused no harm, but Rava teaches that the pit owner can counter that without the stone the animal would not have fallen into the pit.

items.text: Transition marker
items.text_en: Transition marker
items.desc_en: The Gemara signals that a new discussion is about to begin.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara signals a transition to a new discussion with the word 'איתמר' (it was stated).

items.text: Dispute between Abaye and Ravina regarding a consecrated ox that gored
items.text_en: Dispute between Abaye and Ravina regarding a consecrated ox that gored
items.desc_en: Abaye and Ravina debate the payment for damage caused by a consecrated ox (a firstborn ox that cannot be redeemed). Abaye says half-damages, Ravina says quarter-damages.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces the case of a consecrated ox that gored, identifying it as a firstborn ox that cannot be redeemed.
Abaye rules that the owner pays half-damages (חצי נזק).
Ravina rules that the owner pays only quarter-damages (רביע נזק).

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the dispute
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers two alternative explanations for the dispute: either both are speaking of a tam ox but disagree on the halakha (Rabbis vs. Rabbi Natan), or one is tam and one is mu'ad. A second version of the dispute is also presented, where Ravina demands full damages, and the Gemara again offers two resolutions.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that both Abaye and Ravina speak of a tam ox, but they disagree on the halakha: Abaye follows the Rabbis (half damages), Ravina follows Rabbi Natan (quarter damages).
Alternatively, the Gemara suggests that both follow the Rabbis, but one case is a tam ox and the other a mu'ad ox.
An alternative version of the dispute is presented: Abaye says half damages, Ravina says full damages, and both speak of a mu'ad ox, disagreeing between the Rabbis and Rabbi Natan.
Alternatively, both follow Rabbi Natan, but one case is a mu'ad ox and the other a tam ox.

items.text: Rava's ruling on an ox, person, and pit pushing into a pit
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on an ox, person, and pit pushing into a pit
items.desc_en: Rava rules that when an ox, a person, and a pit jointly push someone into a pit, liability varies: for damages, all are liable; for the four items and offspring value, only the person is liable; for ransom and the thirty shekels of a slave, only the ox is liable; for vessels and a consecrated ox, the person and ox are liable, but the pit is exempt.

sub.desc_en: Rava opens with a ruling that when an ox and a person push someone into a pit, liability for damages falls on all three (ox, person, pit), but for the four items and offspring value only the person is liable.
Rava continues: for ransom and the thirty shekels of a slave, only the ox is liable; for vessels and a consecrated ox, the person and ox are liable, but the pit is exempt.

Rava explains the rationale: the verse 'וְהַמֵּת יִהְיֶה לוֹ' (and the dead animal shall be his) applies only to one for whom the dead animal belongs, excluding cases where the dead animal does not belong to the pit owner.

The Gemara objects: is this ruling so obvious to Rava? He himself raised a question about a consecrated ox falling into a pit, debating whether the verse excludes the owner or merely requires the owner to handle the carcass.
The Gemara resolves: after Rava raised the question, he later resolved it, so his ruling here is consistent.

The Gemara questions: if the verse is used for the exclusion, from where does Rava derive the rule that owners handle the carcass? It could be reversed, applying the exclusion to the ox and the handling to the pit.

The Gemara answers: it is logical to assign the exclusion to the pit because the Torah already exempts vessels there, whereas the ox is not fully exempt (only half damages), so the exclusion fits the pit better.

items.text: Reason for the pit's exemption regarding consecrated ox
items.text_en: Reason for the pit's exemption regarding consecrated ox
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the pit's exemption for a consecrated ox based on the verse 'and the dead shall be his' – it applies only to one who owns the carcass, excluding consecrated property.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains the pit's exemption for a consecrated ox based on the verse 'and the dead shall be his' – it applies only to one who owns the carcass, excluding consecrated property.

items.text: Rava's own question about a consecrated ox falling into a pit
items.text_en: Rava's own question about a consecrated ox falling into a pit
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rava himself was uncertain about this very case: does the verse exclude consecrated oxen, or does it only teach that owners must tend to the carcass? After raising the question, Rava resolved it. The Gemara then debates which application of the verse is more plausible, concluding that the pit's exemption for vessels supports the exclusion of consecrated oxen.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rava's ruling in the previous section indicates that the matter was obvious to him.

The Gemara objects that Rava actually raised a question about a consecrated ox falling into a pit, debating whether the verse excludes such an ox or merely teaches that owners must tend to the carcass.
The Gemara notes that after raising the question, Rava resolved it himself.
The Gemara asks: if the verse is used to exclude consecrated oxen, from where does Rava derive the rule that owners must tend to the carcass?
The Gemara answers that the rule about owners tending to the carcass is derived from the same verse in the context of the ox.
The Gemara objects: why assume the verse about the ox teaches the owner's duty to tend the carcass, while the verse about the pit excludes consecrated oxen? One could reverse the interpretations.
The Gemara concludes that it is more reasonable to apply the exclusion to the pit, since the pit already exempts vessels, whereas the ox's exemption of half-damage is not a full exemption.

items.text: Mishnah on an ox and vessels falling into a pit, and the dispute with Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Mishnah on an ox and vessels falling into a pit, and the dispute with Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if an ox and its vessels fall into a pit and break, only the ox is compensated. The Gemara notes this contradicts Rabbi Yehuda, who holds the pit liable for vessels. The Gemara explains the reasoning: the Rabbis derive from 'ox or donkey' that only animals are included, while Rabbi Yehuda uses the word 'or' to include vessels.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the case of an ox and its vessels falling into a pit and breaking, implying only the ox is compensated.
The Gemara notes that the Mishnah contradicts Rabbi Yehuda, who holds the pit liable for vessels, as cited in a baraita.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of the Rabbis' reasoning
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the Rabbis' reasoning
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Rabbis derive from the verse 'שׁוֹר אוֹ חֲמוֹר' (ox or donkey) that only animals are included, excluding vessels.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yehuda uses the word 'אוֹ' (or) to include vessels in the pit's liability.

sub.text: Incomplete statement of the Rabbis' position
sub.text_en: Incomplete statement of the Rabbis' position
sub.desc_en: The Gemara begins to state the Rabbis' counter-position but cuts off, leaving the argument incomplete.

items.text: Opening dispute: the word 'or' and the derivation of liability for partial damage
items.text_en: Opening dispute: the word 'or' and the derivation of liability for partial damage
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the word 'or' is needed to teach liability for partial damage. Rabbi Yehuda derives this from 'and falls', while the Rabbis interpret 'and falls' as implying multiple items.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that the word 'or' is needed to teach liability for partial damage, and notes that Rabbi Yehuda derives this from 'and falls'.
The Rabbis respond that 'and falls' implies multiple items, not partial damage.

items.text: Hermeneutic challenge: Klal u'Prat and Klal u'Prat u'Chlal
items.text_en: Hermeneutic challenge: Klal u'Prat and Klal u'Prat u'Chlal
items.desc_en: A challenge is raised: if 'and falls' is a general term and 'ox and donkey' is a specific term, then only ox and donkey are included. The Gemara responds that 'the owner of the pit shall pay' is a second general term, forming a klal u'prat u'chlal, which includes only items similar to the specific case—living creatures.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: if 'and falls' is a general term (כלל) and 'ox and donkey' is a specific term (פרט), then by the rule of כלל ופרט (general and specific), only ox and donkey are included, excluding all other items.

The Gemara responds that 'the owner of the pit shall pay' is a second general term, forming a כלל ופרט וכלל (general, specific, general), which includes only items similar to the specific case—living creatures.

items.text: Refining the comparison: items whose carcasses convey impurity
items.text_en: Refining the comparison: items whose carcasses convey impurity
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the specific case might be limited to items whose carcasses convey impurity through touch and carrying, excluding birds. It then argues that if so, the Torah could have written only one specific term, but it wrote two to exclude animals that are fit for the altar or sanctified for the firstborn.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the specific items in the פרט (detail) might be limited to those whose carcasses convey impurity through touch and carrying, excluding birds.

The Gemara objects that if the limitation were only to impure animals, the Torah could have written only one specific term, but it wrote two to exclude animals fit for the altar or sanctified for the firstborn.

items.text: Alternative derivation: 'and the dead shall be his'
items.text_en: Alternative derivation: 'and the dead shall be his'
items.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the verse 'and the dead shall be his' includes anything that can die, broadening liability beyond the specific list.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the derivation by citing the verse 'והמת יהיה לו' (and the dead shall be his) to include anything that can die, broadening liability beyond the specific list of ox and donkey.

items.text: Objection: vessels and the nature of death
items.text_en: Objection: vessels and the nature of death
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that vessels are not subject to death, but both the Rabbis and Rabbi Yehuda include or exclude vessels. The answer is that their breakage is their death. A further objection from Rav's distinction between 'its heat' and 'its impact' is answered by referring to new vessels that burst from the heat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that vessels are not subject to death, yet both the Rabbis and Rabbi Yehuda include or exclude them.
The answer is given that the breakage of vessels is their death.
A further objection is raised from Rav's distinction that the Torah's liability for a pit applies to its heat (הבל) and not its impact (חבטו), questioning whether vessels are subject to heat.
The answer is given that the case involves new vessels that burst from the heat.

items.text: דרשת 'והמת יהיה לו' לפטור שור פסולי מוקדשין
items.text_en: Rava's derivation: 'and the dead shall be his' excludes consecrated animals
items.desc_en: Rava uses the verse 'and the dead shall be his' to exclude animals that are not the owner's property, such as disqualified consecrated animals, from liability.
items.desc: רבא דורש את הפסוק 'והמת יהיה לו' לפטור שור פסולי מוקדשין שנפל לבור, משום שהמת אינו שייך לבעל הבור. דרשה זו סותרת את האפשרות להשתמש באותו פסוק להרחבת החיוב.

sub.desc_en: Rava derives from the verse 'וְהַמֵּת יִהְיֶה לוֹ' (and the dead shall be his) that a disqualified consecrated animal (פסולי המוקדשין) that falls into a pit is exempt from liability, because the dead animal does not belong to the owner.
sub.desc: רבא דורש את הפסוק 'והמת יהיה לו' לפטור שור פסולי מוקדשין שנפל לבור, משום שהמת אינו שייך לבעל הבור.

items.text: דרשת 'כסף ישיב לבעליו' – הכללת בעלים ומיעוט אדם וכלים
items.text_en: Alternative derivation: 'silver shall he return' and the exclusion of humans and vessels
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that 'silver shall he return to its owners' includes anything with owners, but this would include vessels and humans. The verse 'ox' excludes humans, and 'donkey' excludes vessels. For Rabbi Yehuda, who includes vessels, the exclusion of 'donkey' is problematic. Rava notes a difficulty with 'donkey' in the pit for Rabbi Yehuda and 'sheep' in the lost property context.
items.desc: הגמרא מציעה דרשה מהפסוק 'כסף ישיב לבעליו' המרחיבה לכל דבר שיש לו בעלים. נשאלת קושיה: אם כן, גם כלים ואדם צריכים להיכלל. התשובה היא שהפסוק ממעט אדם ('שור' ולא אדם) וכלים ('חמור' ולא כלים). לרבי יהודה, שמרחיב לכלים, קשה מה ממעט 'חמור'. רבא מעיר שקושיה זו קשה גם לגבי 'שה' באבידה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the verse 'silver shall he return to its owners' includes anything with owners, but this would absurdly include vessels and humans.
sub.desc: הגמרא מציעה דרשה מהפסוק 'כסף ישיב לבעליו' המרחיבה לכל דבר שיש לו בעלים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the verse 'ox' excludes humans and 'donkey' excludes vessels, but for Rabbi Yehuda who includes vessels, the exclusion of 'donkey' is problematic.
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת שהפסוק ממעט אדם ('שור' ולא אדם) וכלים ('חמור' ולא כלים).

sub.desc_en: Rava notes that the difficulty with 'donkey' in the pit for Rabbi Yehuda and 'sheep' in the lost property context remains unresolved.
sub.desc: רבא מעיר שקושיה זו קשה גם לגבי 'שה' באבידה.

items.text: פירוש 'שור חרש שוטה וקטן'
items.text_en: Clarification: a deaf, insane, or minor ox
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a deaf, insane, or minor ox falls into a pit, the owner is liable. The Gemara questions whether this refers to an ox belonging to such a person, which would imply that an ox of a competent person is exempt. Rabbi Yochanan explains it means an ox that is itself deaf, insane, or minor.
items.desc: הגמרא מבררת את משנת 'שור חרש שוטה וקטן' שבמשנה. רבי יוחנן מפרש שמדובר בשור שהוא עצמו חרש, שוטה או קטן, ולא בשור השייך לאנשים אלו. פירוש זה מונע את המסקנה ששור של פיקח פטור.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a deaf, insane, or minor ox falls into a pit, the owner is liable.
sub.desc: המשנה קובעת שאם שור חרש, שוטה או קטן נפל לבור, בעל הבור חייב.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah means by 'a deaf, insane, or minor ox' — if it means an ox belonging to such a person, then an ox of a competent person would be exempt, which is problematic.
sub.desc: המשנה קובעת שאם שור חרש, שוטה או קטן נפל לבור, בעל הבור חייב.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that the Mishnah refers to an ox that is itself deaf, insane, or minor, not an ox belonging to such a person.
sub.desc: רבי יוחנן מפרש שהכוונה לשור שהוא עצמו חרש, שוטה או קטן, ולא לשור השייך לאנשים אלו, ובכך מונע את המסקנה ששור של פיקח פטור.

items.text: Clarifying the Mishnah's intent regarding a sighted ox
items.text_en: Clarifying the Mishnah's intent regarding a sighted ox
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya explains that the Mishnah's statement about a sighted ox being exempt is not meant literally; rather, it is a 'it goes without saying' argument: a sighted ox is certainly liable, but one might think a deaf, insane, or minor ox is exempt because its disability caused the fall, so the Mishnah teaches that it is still liable.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's statement that a sighted ox is exempt from liability for falling into a pit.

Rabbi Yirmeya explains that the Mishnah is using a 'it goes without saying' (לא מיבעיא) formulation: a sighted ox is certainly liable, but one might think a deaf, insane, or minor ox is exempt because its disability caused the fall, so the Mishnah teaches that it is still liable.

items.text: Challenge from a baraita about a 'sentient being'
items.text_en: Challenge from a baraita about a 'sentient being'
items.desc_en: Rav Acha challenges Ravina with a baraita stating that if a 'sentient being' falls into a pit, the owner is exempt. Ravina initially interprets this as a sentient ox, but Rav Acha argues it refers to a human. Ravina then counters that if a human is exempt, a non-sentient human would be liable, contradicting the verse 'ox and not man'. Rav Acha then clarifies that 'sentient being' means a species with intelligence, and cites another baraita explicitly stating a sentient ox is exempt.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha challenges Ravina by citing a baraita that exempts a 'sentient being' (בר דעת) that falls into a pit, and asks whether this refers to a sentient ox.
Ravina answers that the baraita refers to a human, not an ox.
Rav Acha objects that if a sentient human is exempt, a non-sentient human would be liable, contradicting the verse 'ox and not man'.
Rav Acha clarifies that 'sentient being' means a species with intelligence, not an individual sentient ox.
Rav Acha cites another baraita that explicitly states a sentient ox is exempt, supporting his interpretation.

items.text: Rava's resolution and a supporting baraita
items.text_en: Rava's resolution and a supporting baraita
items.desc_en: Rava resolves the contradiction by stating that the Mishnah's exemption applies specifically to a deaf, insane, or minor ox, but a sighted ox is exempt because it should have looked where it was going. A baraita supports this, listing cases where the owner is liable (deaf, insane, minor, blind, or night-walking ox) and exempt (sighted ox walking by day).

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves the contradiction: the Mishnah's exemption for a sighted ox is literal, because a sighted ox can look out for itself, while a deaf, insane, or minor ox is liable.
A baraita supports Rava's ruling: a deaf, insane, minor, blind, or night-walking ox is liable, but a sighted ox walking by day is exempt.

items.text: Mishnah: Equating all animals for various laws
items.text_en: Mishnah: Equating all animals for various laws
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the laws of a pit, Mount Sinai, double payment, returning lost property, unloading, muzzling, kilayim, and Shabbat apply equally to an ox and all other domesticated animals, and similarly to undomesticated animals and birds. The verse specifying 'ox or donkey' is merely speaking in the common manner.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the same laws apply to all animals as to an ox in various contexts, and explains that the Torah's specific mention of 'ox or donkey' is because it speaks in common terms.

items.text: Gemara: Deriving the inclusion of all animals for each law
items.text_en: Gemara: Deriving the inclusion of all animals for each law
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the scriptural basis for each law: for the pit, the verse 'he shall pay money to its owner' includes anything with owners; for Mount Sinai, 'if a beast or a man shall not live' includes undomesticated animals and birds; for double payment, 'concerning any matter of trespass' includes all trespass; for returning lost property, 'for any lost thing of your brother'; for unloading, a verbal analogy from 'donkey' to Shabbat; for muzzling, a verbal analogy from 'ox' to Shabbat; for kilayim of plowing, a verbal analogy from 'ox' to Shabbat; for kilayim of breeding, a verbal analogy from 'your animal' to Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by explaining that the inclusion of all animals for the pit law is derived from the verse 'he shall pay money to its owner', which includes anything with owners, as previously stated.
The Gemara explains that for Mount Sinai, the verse 'if a beast or a man shall not live' includes undomesticated animals (חיה) within the category of בהמה, and the word 'אם' (if) includes birds.

The Gemara explains that for double payment, the phrase 'על כל דבר פשע' (concerning any matter of trespass) includes all trespass, and for returning lost property, the phrase 'לכל אבדת אחיך' (for any lost thing of your brother) includes all lost items.
The Gemara explains that for unloading, a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) is derived from the word 'חמור' (donkey) used in the context of Shabbat.

The Gemara explains that for muzzling, a verbal analogy is derived from the word 'שור' (ox) used in Shabbat; for kilayim of plowing, from 'שור' again; and for kilayim of breeding, from 'בהמתך' (your animal) used in Shabbat.

items.text: Derivation from the Decalogue and the hermeneutical debate
items.text_en: Derivation from the Decalogue and the hermeneutical debate
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives the inclusion of undomesticated animals and birds for Shabbat from the Decalogue: the first version says 'your animal', the second says 'your ox and your donkey and all your animal'. A baraita of Rabbi Yosei in the name of Rabbi Yishmael uses this to teach that just as ox and donkey are specified, so too any similar undomesticated animal or bird. The Gemara then debates whether this is a 'general and specific' or 'general, specific, and general' hermeneutic, and whether the word 'all' is a generalization or a amplification. It concludes that 'all' here is an amplification, and the specific terms 'ox', 'donkey', and 'your animal' are needed for verbal analogies for muzzling, unloading, and kilayim respectively.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where do we derive the inclusion of undomesticated animals and birds for Shabbat?
A baraita of Rabbi Yosei in the name of Rabbi Yishmael derives the inclusion from the Decalogue: just as ox and donkey are specified, so too any similar undomesticated animal or bird.
An objection argues that the verses form a 'general and specific' pattern, limiting the inclusion to only ox and donkey.
The Gemara answers that the word 'all' in the later Decalogue creates a 'general, specific, and general' pattern, including all living creatures.
A second objection argues that the specific terms might limit the inclusion to animals whose carcasses convey ritual impurity by touch and carrying, excluding birds.
The Gemara rejects the objection: if only one specific term were needed, the Torah would have written only one; the fact that it wrote both 'ox' and 'donkey' shows they serve other purposes.
The Gemara concludes that 'all your animal' is an amplification, not a generalization, thus including all undomesticated animals and birds.

items.text: Challenge from ma'aser and resolution regarding 'all'
items.text_en: Challenge from ma'aser and resolution regarding 'all'
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the claim that 'all' always indicates an amplification, citing the case of ma'aser where 'all' is used in a 'general, specific, and general' pattern. The Gemara resolves that 'all' can be a generalization, but here it is an amplification because the verse could have written 'your animal' as in the first version but instead wrote 'and all your animal'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the principle that 'all' always indicates an amplification, citing the case of ma'aser where 'all' is interpreted through a 'general, specific, and general' pattern.
The Gemara cites a baraita that interprets the ma'aser verse using a 'general, specific, and general' pattern, showing that 'all' can be a generalization.
The Gemara initially answers that 'בכל' (with a prefix) is a generalization, while 'כל' (without a prefix) is an amplification.
The Gemara resolves that even if 'כל' can be a generalization, here it is an amplification because the verse could have written 'ובהמתך' as in the first version but instead wrote 'וכל בהמתך'.

items.text: Purpose of the specific terms and the exclusion of humans
items.text_en: Purpose of the specific terms and the exclusion of humans
items.desc_en: The Gemara now asks why the specific terms 'ox', 'donkey', and 'your animal' are needed if 'all' is an amplification. It answers that they are for verbal analogies: 'ox' for muzzling, 'donkey' for unloading, and 'your animal' for kilayim. A challenge is raised: if so, humans should also be prohibited from plowing with animals, but the Mishnah permits it. Rav Pappa cites Rav Acha bar Yaakov who answers with a verse: 'so that your male and female servant may rest like you' – the comparison is only for rest, not for other matters.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: now that we established that 'כל' (all) is an amplification, why are the specific terms 'בהמתך' (your animal), 'שור' (ox), and 'חמור' (donkey) needed?
The Gemara answers: 'שור' (ox) is for a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) for muzzling, 'חמור' (donkey) for unloading, and 'בהמתך' (your animal) for kilayim.
The Gemara objects: if so, humans should also be prohibited from plowing with animals, but the Mishnah permits it.

sub.text: Rav Pappa citing Rav Acha bar Yaakov
sub.text_en: Rav Pappa citing Rav Acha bar Yaakov
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa cites Rav Acha bar Yaakov who resolves the objection with a verse: 'למען ינוח עבדך ואמתך כמוך' (so that your male and female servant may rest like you) – the comparison is only for rest, not for other matters.

items.text: Question about 'good' in the Decalogue
items.text_en: Question about 'good' in the Decalogue
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina ben Agil asks Rabbi Chiya bar Abba why the word 'good' is not mentioned in the first version of the Decalogue but is mentioned in the second version. The segment cuts off mid-sentence.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina ben Agil asks Rabbi Chiya bar Abba: why is the word 'טוב' (good) not stated in the first tablets but is stated in the later tablets?

items.text: מדוע לא נאמר 'טוב' בלוחות הראשונים?
items.text_en: Why 'good' is said of them
items.desc_en: Rabbi Tanchum bar Chanilai explains that the word 'good' is said of certain things because they are destined to be broken, and Rav Ashi clarifies that this does not mean goodness has ceased from Israel.
items.desc: רבי חנינא בר אגיל שואל מדוע המילה 'טוב' לא נאמרה בלוחות הראשונים. רבי תנחום בר חנילאי משיב בשם שמואל בר נחום שהסיבה היא שהלוחות נועדו להישבר. רב אשי מוסיף שאם הייתה נאמרת, הטובה הייתה פוסקת מישראל.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the word 'good' is said of certain things, and the interlocutor admits ignorance, directing the question to Rabbi Tanchum bar Chanilai.
sub.desc: רבי חנינא בר אגיל שואל מדוע המילה 'טוב' לא נאמרה בלוחות הראשונים, ורבי חייא בר אבא מפנה אותו לרבי תנחום בר חנילאי.

sub.text_en: Rabbi Tanchum bar Chanilai (via Samuel bar Nachum)
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Tanchum bar Chanilai, citing Samuel bar Nachum, explains that the word 'good' is said because these things are destined to be broken.
sub.desc: רבי תנחום בר חנילאי משיב בשם שמואל בר נחום שהסיבה היא שהלוחות נועדו להישבר.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: what difference does it make that they are destined to be broken?
sub.desc: רב אשי מוסיף שאם המילה 'טוב' הייתה נאמרת בלוחות הראשונים, הטובה הייתה פוסקת מישראל לאחר שבירתם.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi resolves that this does not mean goodness has ceased from Israel, but rather that the word 'good' is said of them despite their eventual breaking.
sub.desc: רב אשי מוסיף שאם המילה 'טוב' הייתה נאמרת בלוחות הראשונים, הטובה הייתה פוסקת מישראל לאחר שבירתם.

items.text: פירוש חלום על האות טי"ת
items.text_en: Seeing tet in a dream
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua says seeing the letter tet in a dream is a good sign, because it is the first letter of 'tov' (good) and appears first in the Torah at 'Vayar Elohim et ha'or' (and God saw the light).
items.desc: רבי יהושע אומר שהרואה טי"ת בחלום סימן יפה לו. הגמרא דוחה הסברים שונים ומסבירה שהסיבה היא שהאות טי"ת נפתחה בתורה לראשונה במילה 'טוב', בפסוק 'וירא אלהים את האור כי טוב'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua states that seeing the letter tet in a dream is a good sign.
sub.desc: רבי יהושע פותח ואומר שהרואה טי"ת בחלום סימן יפה לו.

sub.desc_en: The gemara asks for the reason behind Rabbi Yehoshua's statement.
sub.desc: רבי יהושע פותח ואומר שהרואה טי"ת בחלום סימן יפה לו.

sub.desc_en: The gemara proposes and immediately rejects the idea that the sign is because tet begins the word 'tov' (good), noting that tet also begins negative words like 'וְטֵאטֵאתִיהָ' (I will sweep it away).
sub.desc: רבי יהושע פותח ואומר שהרואה טי"ת בחלום סימן יפה לו.

sub.desc_en: The gemara proposes and rejects another possibility that tet appears in the word 'טֻמְאָתָהּ' (her impurity), noting that the dream is about a single tet, not a tet-beit combination.
sub.desc: הגמרא מציעה הסבר שני: שמדובר בצירוף טי"ת-בי"ת כמו במילה 'טוב', אך דוחה אותו משום שגם הפסוק 'טומאתה בשוליה' פותח בטי"ת-בי"ת.

sub.desc_en: The gemara proposes and rejects a third possibility that tet appears in the word 'טָבְעוּ' (they sank), which is also negative.
sub.desc: הגמרא מציעה הסבר שני: שמדובר בצירוף טי"ת-בי"ת כמו במילה 'טוב', אך דוחה אותו משום שגם הפסוק 'טומאתה בשוליה' פותח בטי"ת-בי"ת.

sub.desc_en: The gemara concludes that the sign is good because the letter tet first appears in the Torah in a positive context — from 'בראשית' (In the beginning) until 'וַיַּרְא אֱלֹהִים אֶת הָאוֹר' (And God saw the light), the letter tet is not written, implying its first appearance is with the good light.
sub.desc: הגמרא מיישבת: הטעם הוא שהאות טי"ת נפתחה בתורה לראשונה במילה 'טוב' בפסוק 'וירא אלהים את האור כי טוב', ומבריאת העולם ועד אותו פסוק לא נכתבה טי"ת.

items.text: פירוש חלום על הספד
items.text_en: Seeing a eulogy in a dream
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says that seeing a eulogy in a dream indicates that Heaven has had mercy on the dreamer and redeemed him, but only if the eulogy is written.
items.desc: רבי יהושע בן לוי אומר שהרואה הספד בחלום סימן שחסו עליו מן השמים ופדאוהו. הגמרא מציינת שדין זה נאמר דווקא כשרואה את המילה 'הספד' בכתב.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi states that seeing a eulogy in a dream indicates that Heaven has had mercy and redeemed the dreamer.
sub.desc: רבי יהושע בן לוי אומר שהרואה הספד בחלום סימן שחסו עליו מן השמים ופדאוהו.

sub.desc_en: The gemara qualifies that this applies only when the eulogy is written (in the dream).
sub.desc: רבי יהושע בן לוי אומר שהרואה הספד בחלום סימן שחסו עליו מן השמים ופדאוהו.

items.text: כלאיים בעופות: תרנגול, טווס ופסיוני
items.text_en: Kilayim among fowl: chicken, peacock, and pheasant
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish states that a chicken, peacock, and pheasant are kilayim with each other. Rav Chaviva explains that this is necessary because they might be thought to be the same species since they breed together.
items.desc: המשנה קובעת שחיה ועוף דינם כבהמה לעניין כלאיים. ריש לקיש מביא ברייתא שתרנגול, טווס ופסיוני הם כלאיים זה בזה. רב חביבא מסביר שהחידוש הוא שלמרות שהם גדלים יחד, הם מינים שונים.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah is cited, stating that the same law of kilayim applies to animals and fowl.
sub.desc: ריש לקיש מביא ברייתא ששנה רבי, הקובעת שתרנגול, טווס ופסיוני הם כלאיים זה בזה.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish reports that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi taught: a chicken, peacock, and pheasant are kilayim with each other.
sub.desc: ריש לקיש מביא ברייתא ששנה רבי, הקובעת שתרנגול, טווס ופסיוני הם כלאיים זה בזה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: this is obvious, why was it necessary to state it?
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: הרי הדבר פשוט, מה החידוש?

sub.desc_en: Rav Chaviva explains: because they breed together, one might think they are the same species; the Mishnah teaches that they are not.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: הרי הדבר פשוט, מה החידוש?

items.text: כלאיים באווז הבר ואווז הבית
items.text_en: Kilayim between domestic goose and wild goose
items.desc_en: Shmuel says a domestic goose and a wild goose are kilayim. Rava bar Rav Chanan objects based on neck length, but Abaye and Rav Pappa give different reasons: one has external testicles and the other internal, or one lays one egg at a time and the other many.
items.desc: שמואל קובע שאווז הבית ואווז הבר כלאיים זה בזה. רבא בר רב חנן מקשה על הסברו של שמואל. אביי ורב פפא מציעים הבדלים פיזיולוגיים בין המינים: מיקום האשכים ומספר הביצים בשחלה.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel rules that a domestic goose and a wild goose are kilayim (forbidden to crossbreed).
sub.desc: שמואל פוסק שאווז הבית ואווז הבר הם כלאיים זה בזה.

sub.desc_en: Rava bar Rav Chanan objects: if the reason is neck length, then a Persian camel and an Arabian camel would also be kilayim, which is absurd.
sub.desc: שמואל פוסק שאווז הבית ואווז הבר הם כלאיים זה בזה.

sub.desc_en: Abaye explains the difference: one species has external testicles and the other internal.
sub.desc: אביי מציע הבחנה פיזיולוגית: באווז הבר האשכים מבחוץ, ובאווז הבית מבפנים.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa gives an alternative reason: one species lays one egg at a time and the other lays many eggs in a single laying cycle.
sub.desc: אביי מציע הבחנה פיזיולוגית: באווז הבר האשכים מבחוץ, ובאווז הבית מבפנים.

items.text: Kilayim for sea creatures
items.text_en: Kilayim for sea creatures
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya quoting Reish Lakish says that one who crossbreeds two species of sea creatures is liable, derived from a verbal analogy of 'leminehu' from land creatures.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya quotes Reish Lakish stating that one who crossbreeds two species of sea creatures is lashed.
The gemara asks for the reason behind this liability.

sub.text: Rav Adda bar Ahavah in the name of Ulla
sub.text_en: Rav Adda bar Ahavah in the name of Ulla
sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahavah in the name of Ulla explains that the liability is derived from a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) of the word 'למינהו' (to its kind) used for sea creatures from the same word used for land creatures.

items.text: Leading a goat and a fish together
items.text_en: Leading a goat and a fish together
items.desc_en: Rachava asks whether leading a goat and a fish (shibuta) together is prohibited, since the goat does not go into the sea and the fish does not come onto land. Ravina objects by comparing to planting wheat and barley partly in the ground, but the Gemara distinguishes because both the sea and land are places of liability.

sub.desc_en: Rachava asks whether leading a goat and a shibuta fish together constitutes prohibited leading, given that the goat does not go into the sea and the fish does not come onto land.
Ravina objects by comparing to planting wheat and barley partly in the ground and partly outside, suggesting that if the goat-fish case is liable, then that case should also be liable.
The Gemara distinguishes: in Ravina's case, the ground is a place of liability and outside is not, but here both sea and land are places of liability, so the goat-fish case is prohibited.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Liability for enclosing sheep
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Liability for enclosing sheep
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one encloses sheep properly and they escape and cause damage, the owner is exempt; if not properly enclosed, he is liable. It also covers cases of a fence breached at night, or by thieves, and the liability of a shepherd or a deaf-mute, minor, or insane person. Finally, it discusses payment for grazing damage and the method of assessment.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the basic rule: if one encloses sheep properly and they escape and cause damage, the owner is exempt; if not properly enclosed, he is liable.
The Mishnah adds that if the fence was breached at night or by thieves, the owner is exempt; if thieves took the sheep out, the thieves are liable.
The Mishnah rules that if one left the sheep in the sun or entrusted them to a deaf-mute, minor, or insane person, the owner is liable.
The Mishnah states that if one entrusted the sheep to a shepherd, the shepherd assumes liability.

The Mishnah explains payment for grazing damage: if the sheep fell and benefited, it pays the benefit; if it entered normally and damaged, it pays the damage, assessed by the field's value before and after.
Rabbi Shimon says that if the sheep ate fully ripe produce, it pays the value of the produce consumed, measured by the quantity eaten.

items.text: Gemara: Definition of 'proper' enclosure
items.text_en: Gemara: Definition of 'proper' enclosure
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita defining 'proper' enclosure as a door that can withstand a normal wind, and 'improper' as one that cannot.

sub.desc_en: The baraita defines 'proper' enclosure as a door that can withstand a normal wind, and 'improper' as one that cannot.

items.text: Rabbi Mani bar Pattish: Identifying the Tanna of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Rabbi Mani bar Pattish: Identifying the Tanna of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Mani bar Pattish suggests that the Mishnah's ruling that a mu'ad requires only minimal guarding follows Rabbi Yehuda's view, as opposed to Rabbi Meir who holds that both a tam and a mu'ad require proper guarding. Rabbi Yehuda exempts a mu'ad if it is properly guarded, citing the verse 'and he did not guard him'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Mani bar Pattish asks which Tanna holds that a mu'ad requires only minimal guarding, and answers that it is Rabbi Yehuda.
The gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Meir holds both tam and mu'ad liable, Rabbi Yehuda exempts a mu'ad if properly guarded, and Rabbi Eliezer says a mu'ad has no guarding except a knife.

items.text: Even according to Rabbi Meir: Tooth and foot are different
items.text_en: Even according to Rabbi Meir: Tooth and foot are different
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that even according to Rabbi Meir, the Mishnah's leniency for tooth and foot is because the Torah reduced their required standard of guarding. Rabbi Elazar (or a baraita) lists four categories where the Torah reduced guarding: pit, fire, tooth, and foot, each derived from a biblical verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by asserting that even according to Rabbi Meir, tooth and foot are different because the Torah reduced their required standard of guarding.
Rabbi Elazar (or a baraita) lists four categories where the Torah reduced guarding: pit, fire, tooth, and foot.
The Gemara derives the reduced guarding for pit from the verse 'כִּי יִפְתַּח אִישׁ בּוֹר... וְלֹא יְכַסֶּנּוּ', implying that covering exempts.
The Gemara derives the reduced guarding for fire from the verse 'שַׁלֵּם יְשַׁלֵּם הַמַּבְעִר', requiring an act akin to kindling.
The Gemara derives the reduced guarding for tooth from the verse 'וּבִעֵר בִּשְׂדֵה אַחֵר', requiring an act akin to 'וּבִעֵר' (grazing).
The Gemara derives the reduced guarding for foot from the verse 'וְשִׁלַּח', requiring an act akin to 'וְשִׁלַּח' (sending forth).
A baraita supports the derivations by identifying 'וְשִׁלַּח' with foot and 'וּבִעֵר' with tooth, citing biblical parallels.
The Gemara concludes that only when the animal acts in a manner akin to 'וְשִׁלַּח' or 'וּבִעֵר' is the owner liable; otherwise, he is exempt.

items.text: Rabbah: Proof from the Mishnah's wording
items.text_en: Rabbah: Proof from the Mishnah's wording
