The Gemara clarifies that according to the view that courts do not adjudicate cases of indirect damage (gramei), the question does not arise, as informers are also not adjudicated.
Amemar refines the question: according to the view that courts do adjudicate indirect damage, does the remedy apply to an informer, so that he swears and collects?
The Gemara concludes that the question remains unresolved (teiku).

items.text: Case of a purse thrown into a river: Rav Ashi's deliberation and the Mishnah's parallel
items.text_en: Case of a purse thrown into a river: Rav Ashi's deliberation and the Mishnah's parallel
items.desc_en: A man threw his friend's purse into a river. The owner claims it contained valuables. Rav Ashi deliberates. Ravina suggests it is similar to the Mishnah about one who sets fire to a building, where the owner is believed to swear and collect. Rav Ashi distinguishes: if the owner claims coins, it is like the Mishnah; but here the owner claims a pearl, and the question is whether people keep pearls in purses. The issue remains unresolved.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a case where a man threw his friend's purse into a river, the owner claims it contained valuables, and Rav Ashi deliberates on the halacha.

sub.text: Ravina (or Rav Acha bar Rava) to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Ravina (or Rav Acha bar Rava) to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Ravina (or Rav Acha bar Rava) suggests to Rav Ashi that this case is parallel to the Mishnah about one who sets fire to a building, where the owner is believed to swear and collect all contents.
Rav Ashi distinguishes: if the owner claims coins, it is like the Mishnah; but here the owner claims a pearl, and the question is whether people keep pearls in purses.
The gemara concludes that the issue remains unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Rav Yemar's inquiry about a silver cup in a building
items.text_en: Rav Yemar's inquiry about a silver cup in a building
items.desc_en: Rav Yemar asks Rav Ashi about a case where one claims a silver cup was in a building that was burned. Rav Ashi responds that we assess whether the claimant is a person of means or trustworthy; if so, he swears and collects. Otherwise, he is not believed.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yemar asks Rav Ashi about a case where one claims a silver cup was in a building that was burned.
Rav Ashi responds that we assess whether the claimant is a person of means or trustworthy; if so, he swears and collects; otherwise, he is not believed.

items.text: Distinction between a robber (gazlan) and an extortionist (chamsan)
items.text_en: Distinction between a robber (gazlan) and an extortionist (chamsan)
items.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Rav Avya asks Rav Ashi the difference between a robber and an extortionist. Rav Ashi answers that an extortionist pays money, while a robber does not. Rav Adda objects, citing Rav Huna that a forced sale is valid. Rav Ashi resolves: if the victim says 'I am willing,' it is a sale; if not, it is extortion.

sub.text: Rav Adda bar Rav Avya's question
sub.text_en: Rav Adda bar Rav Avya's question
sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Rav Avya asks Rav Ashi to explain the difference between a robber (גזלן) and an extortionist (חמסן).
Rav Ashi answers that an extortionist (חמסן) pays money for what he takes, while a robber (גזלן) does not.

sub.text: Rav Adda bar Rav Avya's objection
sub.text_en: Rav Adda bar Rav Avya's objection
sub.desc_en: Rav Adda objects: if the extortionist pays money, why call him an extortionist? He cites Rav Huna that a forced sale (תלויה וזבין) is a valid sale.
Rav Ashi resolves: if the victim says 'I am willing' (רוצה אני), it is a valid sale; if not, it is extortion (חמסן).

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Liability for Fire and Indirect Damage
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Liability for Fire and Indirect Damage
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents cases of liability: a spark from a hammer that causes damage obligates the blacksmith; a camel carrying flax that enters a shop and ignites from the shopkeeper's candle obligates the camel owner, but if the shopkeeper left his candle outside, he is liable. Rabbi Yehuda exempts for a Hanukkah candle.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the case of a spark from a blacksmith's hammer that causes damage, establishing liability.
The Mishnah presents a second case: a camel laden with flax enters a shop and ignites from the shopkeeper's candle, holding the camel owner liable.
The Mishnah shifts to a variant: if the shopkeeper left his candle outside, he is liable.
Rabbi Yehuda states an exception: for a Hanukkah candle, the shopkeeper is exempt.

items.text: Gemara's Inference from Rabbi Yehuda's Ruling
items.text_en: Gemara's Inference from Rabbi Yehuda's Ruling
items.desc_en: Ravina in the name of Rava infers from Rabbi Yehuda's exemption that a Hanukkah candle must be placed within ten handbreadths, otherwise the shopkeeper could have placed it above the camel and rider.

sub.text: Ravina in the name of Rava
sub.text_en: Ravina in the name of Rava
sub.desc_en: Ravina in the name of Rava infers from Rabbi Yehuda's exemption that a Hanukkah candle must be placed within ten handbreadths, otherwise the shopkeeper could have placed it above the camel and rider.

items.text: Rejection of the Inference
items.text_en: Rejection of the Inference
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the proof, arguing that even if placed above ten handbreadths, the Sages did not burden one engaged in a mitzvah to place it above the camel and rider.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the proof, arguing that even if the Hanukkah lamp could be placed above ten handbreadths, the Sages did not burden one engaged in a mitzvah to place it above the camel and rider.

items.text: Rav Kahana's Teaching on Hanukkah Candle Height
items.text_en: Rav Kahana's Teaching on Hanukkah Candle Height
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana cites Rav Nathan bar Minyomi in the name of Rabbi Tanchum that a Hanukkah candle placed above twenty cubits is invalid, analogous to a sukka and an alleyway.

sub.text: Rav Kahana citing Rav Nathan bar Minyomi in the name of Rabbi Tanchum
sub.text_en: Rav Kahana citing Rav Nathan bar Minyomi in the name of Rabbi Tanchum
sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana transmits a tradition that a Hanukkah candle placed above twenty cubits is invalid, analogous to the laws of a sukka (סוכה) and an alleyway (מבוי).

items.text: Conclusion of the Chapter
items.text_en: Conclusion of the Chapter
items.desc_en: The standard concluding formula for the chapter is stated.

sub.desc_en: The standard concluding formula for the chapter is recited.

items.text: New Mishnah: Double Payment vs. Four/Five-Fold Payment
items.text_en: New Mishnah: Double Payment vs. Four/Five-Fold Payment
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that double payment applies to both animate and inanimate objects, while four/five-fold payment applies only to ox or sheep, as per the verse. It also rules that a thief who steals from a thief does not pay double, and one who slaughters or sells after a thief does not pay four/five-fold.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that the double-payment rule applies broadly to both animate and inanimate objects, while the four/five-fold payment applies only to an ox or sheep, as derived from the verse.
The Mishnah adds that a thief who steals from a thief does not pay double payment, and one who slaughters or sells after the thief does not pay four/five-fold payment.

items.text: Gemara: Omission of the Case of One Who Falsely Claims Theft
items.text_en: Gemara: Omission of the Case of One Who Falsely Claims Theft
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah omitted the case of one who falsely claims theft (טוען טענת גנב) from the list of those liable for double payment. It cites Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that such a person pays double, and if he then slaughters or sells, pays four/five-fold. The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah's phrase 'מרובה' implies it listed only some differences, not all.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah omitted the case of one who falsely claims theft (טוען טענת גנב) from the list of those liable for double payment.

sub.text: Supporting baraita via Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita via Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that one who falsely claims theft pays double, and if he then slaughters or sells, pays four/five-fold.
An alternative version questions whether the Mishnah's omission actually supports Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba's position.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah's phrase 'מרובה' (greater) implies it listed only some differences, not all, so the omission is not problematic.

items.text: Derivation of the Scope of Double Payment
items.text_en: Derivation of the Scope of Double Payment
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from the verse 'על כל דבר פשע' using a כלל ופרט וכלל that double payment applies to movable property with intrinsic value, excluding land, slaves, documents, and consecrated property. It then considers an alternative derivation based on ritual impurity of carcasses, but rejects it because 'שלמה' (a garment) is included, which is not a living creature.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural source of the Mishnah's rule that double payment applies broadly, and cites the baraita's use of the verse 'על כל דבר פשע' with a כלל ופרט וכלל (general-further general) hermeneutic pattern.
The Gemara applies the rule of כלל ופרט וכלל (general-particular-general), concluding that double payment applies only to movable property whose body has monetary value, like the enumerated items.

The Gemara derives the exclusions: land (קרקעות), slaves (עבדים) equated to land, documents (שטרות) lacking intrinsic value, and consecrated property (הקדש) excluded by the word 'רֵעֵהוּ' (his fellow).

The Gemara raises an alternative possible derivation: the particular items are living creatures whose carcasses transmit טומאה (ritual impurity) by touch and carrying, which would exclude birds (עופות) that do not transmit such impurity.

The Gemara rejects the alternative derivation because 'שַׂלְמָה' (a garment) is included in the particular list, and a garment is not a living creature; it then refines the derivation to apply only to living creatures, excluding those whose carcasses do not transmit impurity.

items.text: Initial objection: birds excluded from the oath
items.text_en: Initial objection: birds excluded from the oath
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that if each animal term (שור, חמור, שה) is interpreted individually as a כלל ופרט, then birds would not be included in the oath.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if each animal term (שור, חמור, שה) is interpreted individually as a כלל ופרט (general followed by specific), then birds would not be included in the oath.

items.text: Gemara's question and hypothetical reasoning
items.text_en: Gemara's question and hypothetical reasoning
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Torah wrote multiple specific animals; if only one were written, we might mistakenly limit the oath to animals that are offered on the altar or sanctified as firstborn.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if the Torah's intention is to exclude certain items, why not write just one specific animal (a single פרט) rather than multiple?

The Gemara reasons: if only 'שׁוֹר' (ox) were written, we would limit the oath to animals offered on the altar; if only 'חֲמוֹר' (donkey), we would limit it to animals sanctified as firstborn — so multiple animals are needed to teach that the oath applies to all animals.

items.text: Conclusion: "שה" comes to include birds
items.text_en: Conclusion: "שה" comes to include birds
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that since the Torah wrote both "שור" and "חמור", the additional term "שה" must come to include birds in the oath.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that since the Torah wrote both 'שור' and 'חמור', the additional term 'שה' must come to include birds in the oath.

items.text: Challenge: only pure birds?
items.text_en: Challenge: only pure birds?
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a possibility that only pure birds (which can become impure via the gullet) are included, but the word "כֹל" amplifies to include all birds.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that perhaps the word 'שֶׂה' only includes pure birds (עופות טהורים) which are similar to a sheep in that they impart impurity to garments at the point of swallowing, but not impure birds which lack such impurity.
The Gemara answers that the word 'כֹל' (all) in the verse is an amplification (ריבוי), including even impure birds.

items.text: Counterexample: "כֹל" in ma'aser is a כלל
items.text_en: Counterexample: "כֹל" in ma'aser is a כלל
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that in the context of ma'aser, "כֹל" is treated as a כלל in a כלל ופרט וכלל pattern, not as a ריבוי.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the claim 'כֹל' always indicates a ריבוי (amplification) is contradicted by the case of ma'aser, where 'כֹל' is interpreted through a כלל ופרט (general-particular) pattern.
A baraita is cited showing that in the ma'aser context, 'כֹל' is part of a כלל ופרט וכלל (general-particular-general) pattern, limiting the scope to fruit and produce of the land.

items.text: Resolution: "בכל" vs. "כל"
items.text_en: Resolution: "בכל" vs. "כל"
items.desc_en: The Gemara distinguishes: "בכל" is a כלל, but "כֹל" alone is a ריבוי; alternatively, "כֹל" can be a כלל, but here it is a ריבוי.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers a resolution: the term 'בכל' (in all) functions as a כלל (generalization), while 'כל' (all) alone functions as a ריבוי (amplification).
An alternative resolution is offered: 'כל' can be a כלל (generalization), but in this specific context it functions as a ריבוי (amplification).

items.text: Proof from the structure of the watchman's oath
items.text_en: Proof from the structure of the watchman's oath
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues that the verse already has a כלל ופרט וכלל pattern ("כי יתן... כסף או כלים... לשמור"), so the additional phrase "על כל דבר פשע" must be a ריבוי, not another כלל.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara establishes that the verse already contains a כלל ופרט וכלל pattern from the phrase 'כי יתן... כסף או כלים... לשמור'.
The Gemara questions why the phrase 'על כל דבר פשע' would be needed if it were merely another כלל, since the specific items could have been written alongside the existing pattern.
The Gemara concludes that 'על כל דבר פשע' must be a ריבוי (amplification) rather than another כלל, because otherwise it would be superfluous.

items.text: Application: purpose of each פרט
items.text_en: Application: purpose of each פרט
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that each specific term in the verse serves to exclude land, slaves, documents, and unspecific items, and the phrase "על כל אבדה" is for Rabbi Chiya bar Abba's teaching.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: now that we have established that 'כל' (all) is a ריבוי (amplification), what is the purpose of each specific term (פרט) in the verse?
The Gemara answers: each specific term serves to exclude land, slaves, documents, and unspecific items (דבר שאינו מסוים).

sub.text: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: The Gemara adds that the phrase 'על כל אבדה' (concerning any lost item) serves for the teaching of Rabbi Chiya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan regarding one who claims a thief's claim.

items.text: Opening Mishnah citation
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah citation
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that a bailee who claims the deposit was lost pays only the principal, but if he claims it was stolen and is convicted by witnesses, he pays double; if he admits on his own, he pays principal, fifth, and a guilt-offering.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that a bailee who claims the deposit was lost pays only the principal, but if he claims it was stolen and is convicted by witnesses, he pays double; if he admits on his own, he pays principal, fifth, and a guilt-offering.

items.text: Gemara's inference from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's inference from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers that double payment applies only to a claim of theft, not loss, and only when an oath is taken.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where are these matters (the source for double payment on a theft claim) derived?
The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that double payment applies only to a claim of theft, not loss, and only when an oath is taken.

items.text: Derivation from verses: dispute on the referent of 'if the thief is found'
items.text_en: Derivation from verses: dispute on the referent of 'if the thief is found'
items.desc_en: Two baraitot debate whether the verse 'if the thief is found' speaks of the actual thief or the bailee who claims theft; both agree that 'if the thief is not found' refers to the bailee claiming theft.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where are these matters (that a bailee who claims theft pays double payment only upon oath) derived? It cites a baraita.
The first baraita states that the verse 'if the thief is found' speaks of a bailee who claims theft, not the actual thief.
The baraita raises an alternative: perhaps the verse speaks of the actual thief, not the bailee.
The baraita resolves: since the verse 'if the thief is not found' already speaks of the bailee, the earlier verse 'if the thief is found' must refer to the bailee as well.
A second baraita states that the verse 'if the thief is found' speaks of the actual thief himself.
The second baraita raises an alternative: perhaps the verse speaks of the bailee, not the actual thief.
The second baraita resolves: since the verse 'if the thief is not found' already speaks of the bailee, the earlier verse 'if the thief is found' must refer to the actual thief.

items.text: Rava's explanation of the verse
items.text_en: Rava's explanation of the verse
items.desc_en: Rava explains that 'if it is not found' means the bailee himself stole it, so he pays double.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where is it derived that double payment applies only when an oath was taken?
Rava explains that 'if it is not found' means the bailee himself stole it, so he pays double.

items.text: Derivation that double payment requires an oath
items.text_en: Derivation that double payment requires an oath
items.desc_en: A baraita derives from the verse 'and the master of the house shall approach God' that it refers to an oath, using a verbal analogy of 'sending a hand'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where do we derive that the double payment is specifically through an oath?
A baraita derives from the verse 'and the master of the house shall approach God' that it refers to an oath, using a verbal analogy of 'sending a hand' (שליחות יד).

items.text: Dispute over the two verses: excluding loss claim
items.text_en: Dispute over the two verses: excluding loss claim
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why two verses are needed; one opinion says one for the thief and one for the bailee, the other says both for the bailee, with one excluding the loss claim. The latter derives the exclusion from 'gannav-hagannav'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: according to the opinion that both verses refer to the bailee who claims theft, why are two verses needed?
The Gemara answers: one verse excludes the loss claim from the double payment.
The Gemara asks: according to the opinion that one verse refers to the thief and one to the bailee, from where does he derive the exclusion of the loss claim?

items.text: Use of 'gannav-hagannav' for Rabbi Yochanan's law
items.text_en: Use of 'gannav-hagannav' for Rabbi Yochanan's law
items.desc_en: The opinion that both verses refer to the bailee uses 'gannav-hagannav' for Rabbi Yochanan's teaching that a bailee who claims theft and then slaughters or sells pays four or five; the other opinion derives this from a hekesh.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: according to the opinion that both verses refer to the bailee who claims theft, what does he derive from the extra word 'גנב-הגנב' (the thief-the thief)?

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the extra word is needed for Rabbi Yochanan's teaching: a bailee who claims theft pays double payment, and if he slaughters or sells, he pays four or five.

The Gemara asks: according to the opinion that one verse refers to the actual thief and one to the bailee, who used 'גנב-הגנב' to exclude the claim of loss, from where does Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba derive his law?
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba derives the law from a הֶקֵּשׁ (verbal analogy), and one does not raise objections against a הֶקֵּשׁ.

items.text: Derivation of the actual thief's liability
items.text_en: Derivation of the actual thief's liability
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the opinion that both verses refer to the bailee derives the actual thief's liability; after rejecting a kal vachomer, it cites the baraita of Chizkiyah's school that includes all in the general rule.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: for the opinion that both verses refer to the bailee, from where does he derive the actual thief's liability?

The Gemara rejects a possible kal vachomer (a fortiori) derivation because the conclusion would be limited by the principle of דיו (sufficiency), requiring an oath, which is not the case for the actual thief.

sub.text: Baraita of the school of Chizkiyah
sub.text_en: Baraita of the school of Chizkiyah
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the baraita of the school of Chizkiyah (תנא דבי חזקיה) that includes the actual thief in the general rule through the terms 'שור' (ox) and 'גניבה' (theft).

The Gemara clarifies the baraita's method: just as the specified details (פרט) refer to animals fit for the altar, so too the general rule includes only such animals, concluding with 'what can you bring? — a sheep (שה).'

items.text: Initial derivation: why the Torah adds 'גניבה' after listing specific animals
items.text_en: Initial derivation: why the Torah adds 'גניבה' after listing specific animals
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins by questioning why the Torah writes 'גניבה' after specifying 'שור' and 'שה'. It argues that without 'גניבה', one might think only items sanctified for the firstborn are included. The same logic is applied to 'חמור' and 'חיים', showing that each additional term serves to broaden the category.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Torah adds 'גניבה' after specifying 'שה', and answers that it comes to include all items.

items.text: Objection: the order of 'גניבה' and 'שור' changes the interpretive rule
items.text_en: Objection: the order of 'גניבה' and 'שור' changes the interpretive rule
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the previous analysis assumed the order 'שור וגניבה', but the verse actually writes 'גניבה ושור'. If the order were reversed, the interpretation would follow כלל ופרט, limiting liability to only a שור. This challenges the earlier derivation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the verse actually writes 'גניבה' before 'שור', not the reverse order assumed in the earlier analysis.

The Gemara considers the possibility that the earlier statement was hypothetical ('if it were written'), but then shows that the order 'שור וגניבה' would create a פרט וכלל (specific then general) pattern, which would include everything — contradicting the intended limitation.

The Gemara resolves that the Tanna is actually referring to the verse as written ('גניבה ושור'), which creates a כלל ופרט (general then specific) pattern, limiting liability to only a שור (ox) and excluding other items.
Rava explains that the Tanna is actually relying on the word 'חיים' (living creatures) and is employing a כלל ופרט וכלל (general-specific-general) interpretive pattern.

The Gemara objects that the final general term does not match the initial general term, and resolves that the Tanna follows the school of Rabbi Yishmael, who interprets general and specific terms in this manner.

The Gemara asks why the verse needs the phrase 'אם המצא תמצא' (if the stolen item is found), since one could have derived everything from the words 'שור', 'גניבה', and 'חיים' using a general-inclusive pattern.
The Gemara shows that without the extra phrase, one might have limited liability to items fit for the altar, so the verse adds 'שה' (sheep) to include that, and then 'גניבה' to include everything.

The Gemara continues the hypothetical: if the verse listed 'גניבה', 'שור', 'שה', and 'חיים', one might limit liability to items consecrated for the firstborn, so the verse adds 'חמור' (donkey) to include that, and then 'גניבה' to include everything.

The Gemara concludes the hypothetical: if the verse listed all five terms, one might limit liability to living creatures, so the verse adds 'חיים' to include that, and then 'גניבה' to include everything — yet the phrase 'אם המצא תמצא' remains unexplained, prompting the original question.

items.text: Rava's resolution: the Tanna relies on 'חיים' and uses כלל ופרט וכלל
items.text_en: Rava's resolution: the Tanna relies on 'חיים' and uses כלל ופרט וכלל
items.desc_en: Rava explains that the Tanna is actually relying on the word 'חיים' and applying the method of כלל ופרט וכלל (general, particular, general). Although the first and last general terms are not identical, this is consistent with the school of Rabbi Yishmael, which interprets such patterns broadly.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves the difficulty by asserting that the Tanna relies on the word 'חַיִּים' (living things) and employs the hermeneutical method of כלל ופרט וכלל (general, particular, general).
The Gemara objects that the final general term does not match the initial general term, and answers that the Tanna follows the school of Rabbi Yishmael, which interprets such patterns broadly.

items.text: Reconstructed derivation: the necessity of 'אם המצא תמצא'
items.text_en: Reconstructed derivation: the necessity of 'אם המצא תמצא'
items.desc_en: The Gemara reconstructs the Tanna's reasoning: without the phrase 'אם המצא תמצא', one might think only items fit for the altar are included. The Torah therefore adds 'שה', 'חמור', and 'חיים' to expand liability, but ultimately the phrase 'אם המצא תמצא' is needed to include all items, as the final general term 'גניבה' alone would not suffice.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the phrase 'אם המצא תמצא' is necessary, given that the terms 'שור', 'גניבה', and 'חיים' already form a general-inclusive pattern that would include everything.

The Gemara explains that without 'אם המצא תמצא', one might mistakenly limit liability to items fit for the altar; the phrase 'שה' is therefore added to expand the category, but ultimately 'גניבה' includes everything.

The Gemara continues: even with 'שור', 'שה', and 'חיים', one might mistakenly limit liability to items sanctified as firstborn; the phrase 'חמור' is therefore added, but 'גניבה' still includes everything.
The Gemara adds that 'חמור' is introduced to counter the limitation to firstborn-sanctified items, but 'גניבה' still includes everything.
The Gemara notes that even with all listed items, one might limit liability to living creatures; the phrase 'חיים' is added, but 'גניבה' still includes everything.

The Gemara concludes that 'חיים' is added to include other living creatures, but ultimately the phrase 'אם המצא תמצא' is necessary because without it, the general term 'גניבה' alone would not suffice to include all items; the question is thus resolved.

items.text: Challenge to the previous interpretation
items.text_en: Challenge to the previous interpretation
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a difficulty: if the double expression is interpreted as a כלל ופרט וכלל, the word "חַיִּים" already limits the inclusion to living things, so the extra phrase "אִם הִמָּצֵא" is necessary to include other items.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a difficulty: if the double expression is interpreted as a כלל ופרט וכלל, the word 'חַיִּים' already limits the inclusion to living things, so the extra phrase 'אִם הִמָּצֵא' seems unnecessary.
The Gemara answers that the phrase 'אִם הִמָּצֵא' is necessary to include items that are not living beings, which the word 'חַיִּים' would exclude.

items.text: Ravina's resolution: two adjacent generalities
items.text_en: Ravina's resolution: two adjacent generalities
items.desc_en: Ravina explains that since the two generalities are adjacent, we insert the specific term between them and treat it as a כלל ופרט.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the two generalities are adjacent, which undermines the standard כלל ופרט (general and specific) interpretation.

Ravina resolves the difficulty by citing the Western practice: when two generalities are adjacent, insert the specific term between them and treat the whole as a כלל ופרט (general and specific) structure.

items.text: Deriving movable property and distinctive items
items.text_en: Deriving movable property and distinctive items
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the word "שׁוֹר" is inserted to include movable property with monetary value, and "חֲמוֹר" is inserted to include distinctive items, as each specific term adds something not already covered.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the word 'שׁוֹר' (ox) inserted between 'הִמָּצֵא' and 'תִמָּצֵא' comes to include, since living beings are already derived from 'חַיִּים' (living things).
The Gemara answers that 'שׁוֹר' comes to include movable property that is not a living being, applying the principle that the specific term (פרט) indicates movable property with monetary value.
The Gemara asks what the word 'חֲמוֹר' (donkey) inserted between 'הִמָּצֵא' and 'תִמָּצֵא' comes to include, since non-living movable property is already derived from 'שׁוֹר'.
The Gemara answers that 'חֲמוֹר' comes to include distinctive items (דָּבָר מְסוּיָּים) that are individually identifiable.

items.text: Reinterpretation as ריבה ומיעט וריבה
items.text_en: Reinterpretation as ריבה ומיעט וריבה
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the need for "שֶׂה" and concludes that the proper hermeneutic is ריבה ומיעט וריבה, as taught by the school of Rabbi Yishmael, which includes everything and then excludes land, slaves, and documents, with additional derivations for the principle of Rav.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if the previous derivation is correct, why is the word 'שֶׂה' (sheep) needed in the verse?
The Gemara answers that the proper hermeneutic is ריבה ומיעט וריבה (inclusion, exclusion, inclusion), as taught by the school of Rabbi Yishmael.
The baraita of the school of Rabbi Yishmael teaches that the double occurrence of 'בַּמַּיִם' (in water) indicates a pattern of inclusion and exclusion, not a general and specific.
The Gemara asks: what does the inclusion include — everything? If so, why are all these specific exclusions needed?

The Gemara answers: one exclusion removes land, one removes slaves, one removes documents, and the words 'גְּנֵיבָה' and 'חַיִּים' are used for Rav's principle that the principal is restored as it was stolen.

items.text: Debate on the derivation of the self-incrimination exemption
items.text_en: Debate on the derivation of the self-incrimination exemption
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses different views on whether the double expression "אִם הִמָּצֵא תִמָּצֵא" is used for the thief or for the one who falsely claims theft, and whether the exemption for one who incriminates himself is derived from this verse or from "אֲשֶׁר יַרְשִׁיעֻן אֱלֹהִים".

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: according to the view that one occurrence of 'הִמָּצֵא' refers to the thief and the other to the one who falsely claims theft, and the thief himself is derived from 'אִם יִמָּצֵא הַגַּנָּב', what does the double expression 'אִם הִמָּצֵא תִמָּצֵא' teach?

The Gemara answers: it is needed for the teaching of Rava bar Ahilai, who derives from 'אִם הִמָּצֵא תִמָּצֵא' that one who incriminates himself is exempt from the penalty, as the verse implies discovery by witnesses and judgment by judges, excluding one who incriminates himself.

items.text: The purpose of the repeated specifics
items.text_en: The purpose of the repeated specifics
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why all the specific terms are needed if the thief is derived from elsewhere, and answers with the principle of the school of Rabbi Yishmael that a repeated passage comes only for something new.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: according to the view that one specific is for the thief and one for the bailee who claims theft, and the thief himself is derived from elsewhere, why are all the specific terms needed?

sub.text: Gemara's answer via the school of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.text_en: Gemara's answer via the school of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers with the principle of the school of Rabbi Yishmael that any passage that is stated and repeated is repeated only for something new that is innovated in it.

items.text: Rejecting the possibility of an oath for the thief
items.text_en: Rejecting the possibility of an oath for the thief
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the idea that the thief pays double only after an oath, citing a baraita of Rabbi Yaakov and Abaye's explanation that the Torah wrote "שְׁנַיִם יְשַׁלֵּם" for the thief himself to teach that it applies even without an oath.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: perhaps the thief himself pays double only after taking an oath.
The Gemara rejects this possibility, stating it is inconceivable.
A baraita is cited where Rabbi Yaakov states that the verse 'שְׁנַיִם יְשַׁלֵּם' teaches that the thief pays double without an oath.

Abaye explains that the Torah wrote 'שְׁנַיִם יְשַׁלֵּם' for the thief himself to teach that the double payment applies even without an oath, as otherwise it could have been derived by a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument) from the one who falsely claims theft.

items.text: Alternative use of the verse
items.text_en: Alternative use of the verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to suggest that the verse "אִם הִמָּצֵא" is needed for another teaching, as in a baraita, but the segment is cut off.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the verse 'אִם הִמָּצֵא' is needed for another teaching from a baraita, but the segment is cut off.

items.text: Derivation of liability for theft from one's property
items.text_en: Derivation of liability for theft from one's property
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from the double expression 'הִמָּצֵא תִמָּצֵא' that liability for theft applies not only to the thief's hand but also to his roof, courtyard, and enclosed field. The redundancy of the phrase teaches two laws.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from the verse we only derive liability for theft by the thief's hand; how do we include his roof, courtyard, and enclosed field? It answers: the verse says 'אִם הִמָּצֵא תִמָּצֵא' (if the stolen item is found) to include any location.

The Gemara explains: if the verse intended only one law, it would have used a single expression; the doubled form 'הִמָּצֵא תִמָּצֵא' teaches two laws — liability for the thief's hand and for his property.

items.text: Rav's distinction between principal and additional payments
items.text_en: Rav's distinction between principal and additional payments
items.desc_en: Rav states that the principal (keren) is assessed as it was at the time of theft, while the double payment and four/five-fold payment are assessed at the time of standing in court. He derives this from the juxtaposition of 'גְּנֵיבָה' and 'חַיִּים' in the verse.

sub.desc_en: Rav states that the principal (קרן) is assessed as at the time of theft, while the double and four/five-fold payments are assessed at the time of standing in court.
The Gemara explains Rav's derivation from the juxtaposition of 'גְּנֵיבָה' (theft) and 'חַיִּים' (life) in the verse, indicating that the Torah preserved the principal as at the time of theft.

items.text: Rav Sheshet's challenge from a baraita
items.text_en: Rav Sheshet's challenge from a baraita
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet challenges Rav with a baraita stating that if an animal was lean and then fattened, the thief pays the additional payments as it was at the time of theft. The Gemara explains that this is because the owner can claim 'I fattened it, and you took it?'

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet challenges Rav's ruling by citing a baraita that when an animal was lean and then fattened, the thief pays the additional payments (כפל, ארבעה וחמישה) as it was at the time of theft, contradicting Rav's principle that these payments are assessed at the time of standing in court.

The Gemara resolves the challenge by explaining that the baraita's case is different: the owner can claim 'I fattened it, and you took it,' so the thief pays according to the value at theft because the increase is attributed to the owner's effort, not to the thief's liability.

items.text: Second challenge: fattened then lean animal
items.text_en: Second challenge: fattened then lean animal
items.desc_en: A baraita states that if an animal was fat and then became lean, the thief pays additional payments as at the time of theft. The Gemara explains this is because we say to him: 'What difference is it to me if he killed it entirely or half?' Rav's statement applies only to changes in market value.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita as a challenge to Rav: if an animal was fattened and then became lean, the thief pays the additional payments as at the time of theft, contradicting Rav's rule that only the principal is assessed at the time of theft.

The Gemara resolves the challenge: the baraita's case is different because the thief is told 'what difference is it to me if he killed it entirely or half?' — the animal's physical change is not a change in market value, so Rav's statement applies only to fluctuations in market price (יוקרא וזולא).

items.text: Clarification of Rav's case: increase in value
items.text_en: Clarification of Rav's case: increase in value
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers a case where the animal was worth one zuz initially and later four zuzim. It questions whether Rav's ruling conflicts with Rabbah's ruling that if one stole a barrel of wine worth one zuz and broke or drank it when it was worth four, he pays four. The Gemara distinguishes between theft and damage.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks about the case: if the animal was worth one zuz initially and later four zuzim, does Rav's ruling that the principal is paid as at the time of theft conflict with Rabbah's ruling that a thief who broke or drank a barrel of wine pays four?

The Gemara objects that Rav's ruling would contradict Rabbah's ruling, since Rabbah says that if the barrel broke on its own the thief pays only one zuz, implying the principal is paid as at the time of theft.

The Gemara resolves that Rav's case is where the animal was worth four zuzim initially and later one zuz, so the principal is paid as at the time of theft and the penalties as at the time of judgment.

items.text: Resolution: Rav's case is decrease in value
items.text_en: Resolution: Rav's case is decrease in value
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that Rav's statement applies to a case where the animal was worth four zuzim initially and later one zuz. The principal is assessed at the time of theft, while the additional payments are assessed at the time of standing in court.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that Rav's statement applies to a case where the animal was worth four zuzim initially and later one zuz, with the principal assessed at the time of theft and the additional payments at the time of standing in court.

items.text: Supporting baraita from Rabbi Chanina
items.text_en: Supporting baraita from Rabbi Chanina
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina teaches a baraita supporting Rav: a bailee who falsely claimed theft, swore, and then confessed before witnesses came pays principal, fifth, and guilt-offering; if after witnesses came, he pays double payment and guilt-offering, with the fifth included in the double payment. This shows that the double payment is assessed at the time of standing in court.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina teaches a baraita supporting Rav: a bailee who falsely claimed theft, swore, and confessed before witnesses came pays principal, fifth, and guilt-offering.

The baraita concludes: if the bailee confessed after witnesses came, he pays double payment and guilt-offering, with the fifth included in the double payment, showing that the double payment is assessed at the time of standing in court.

items.text: Opening Mishnah citation and dispute
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah citation and dispute
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the added fifth applies only to the principal, not to the double payment. Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai says that neither the fifth nor the guilt-offering are paid where there is a double payment.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the Sages' position that the added fifth applies only to the principal, and Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's position that neither the fifth nor the guilt-offering are paid where there is a double payment.

items.text: Gemara's question on Rabbi Yaakov's statement
items.text_en: Gemara's question on Rabbi Yaakov's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the fifth can be included in the double payment, as stated by Rabbi Yaakov. It analyzes a case where the value changes, concluding that the principal is paid as at the time of theft, while the double and four/five payments are assessed at the time of standing in court.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's statement that the fifth is included in the double payment according to Rabbi Yaakov.
The Gemara asks how the fifth can be included in the double payment, considering a case where the value changes.
The Gemara suggests that the case involves a decrease in value, so the double payment is one zuz and the fifth is also one zuz, making them equal.
The Gemara concludes that the principal is assessed at the time of theft, while the double and four/five payments are assessed at the time of standing in court.

items.text: Rava's resolution of the difficulty
items.text_en: Rava's resolution of the difficulty
items.desc_en: Rava explains that the case involves multiple oaths and confessions, where the Torah adds many fifths to one principal. The difficulty is resolved by understanding that the fifth is multiplied, not included in the double payment.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves the difficulty by explaining that the case involves multiple oaths and confessions, where the Torah adds many fifths (חמישיות) to one principal, so the fifth is multiplied and not included in the double payment.

items.text: Debate on the guilt-offering and the added fifth
items.text_en: Debate on the guilt-offering and the added fifth
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses why the guilt-offering is not paid along with the fifth, based on the verse. The Sages and Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai argue over the interpretation of the word 'אֶת' and the conjunction 'וָיו', with Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai holding that the 'וָיו' connects the guilt-offering to the principal.

sub.desc_en: Mar cites the Sages' position that only property paid with the principal adds a fifth, while property not paid with the principal does not.
The Gemara questions why the guilt-offering is brought but not paid with the fifth, given the verse includes both 'בראשו' and 'ואת אשמו'.
The Rabbis answer that the word 'אֶת' separates the guilt-offering from the fifth, so the guilt-offering is not included.
Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai objects that the conjunction 'וְאֶת' connects the guilt-offering to the principal, implying it should be included.
The Rabbis reject this, arguing that the Torah could have omitted both the 'וָיו' and 'אֶת' if they were meant to connect.
Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai resolves that 'אֶת' is necessary to separate sacred from common property, so the 'וָיו' comes to connect the guilt-offering.

items.text: Rabbi Ila'a's statement on change and acquisition
items.text_en: Rabbi Ila'a's statement on change and acquisition
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ila'a says that if a stolen lamb becomes a ram, the change effects acquisition, so the thief owns it. Rabbi Chanina objects with a baraita that requires payment as at the time of theft, leading to a debate about whether change acquires or not.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ila'a states that if a stolen lamb becomes a ram or a calf becomes an ox, the change (שינוי) effects acquisition, and the thief owns it, so subsequent slaughter or sale is his own.
Rabbi Chanina objects by citing a baraita that requires payment of double or four/five times the value as at the time of theft, arguing that if change acquires, why would the thief pay at all?
Rabbi Ila'a counters that if change does not acquire, the thief should pay the current value, not the value at the time of theft.

Rabbi Chanina retorts that the reason for not paying current value is that the victim can say 'Did I steal an ox from you? Did I steal a ram from you?', and then both exchange exclamations of 'May Heaven save us from your opinion!'

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's challenge and Rava's proof
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's challenge and Rava's proof
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira asks why the change of name does not effect acquisition. Rava proves that a day-old animal is still called by its name, so there is no change of name. Rav Sheshet attributes the baraita to Beit Shammai, who hold that change does not acquire.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira challenges the baraita's ruling that the thief pays according to the value at the time of theft, asking why the change of name (from lamb to ram) does not effect acquisition (קניין) through שינוי השם (change of name).

Rava answers that a day-old animal is still called by its name (e.g., 'שור' for an ox, 'איל' for a ram), citing verses to prove that the name does not change with age, so there is no שינוי השם (change of name) to effect acquisition.
Rav Sheshet resolves the difficulty by attributing the baraita to Beit Shammai, who hold that שינוי (change) does not effect acquisition (קניין) and the object remains in its original status.

items.text: Support from a baraita on change in consecrated items
items.text_en: Support from a baraita on change in consecrated items
items.desc_en: A baraita discusses whether a change in the form of an item given as a harlot's hire is permitted or forbidden. Rav Yosef reports that Beit Shammai forbid it, while Beit Hillel permit it, based on the interpretation of the word 'גַּם' and 'הֵם'.

sub.desc_en: A baraita presents a dispute about whether a change in the form of an item given as a harlot's hire renders it permitted or forbidden.
Rav Yosef reports that the dispute in the baraita aligns with Beit Shammai forbidding and Beit Hillel permitting.

The Gemara explains the scriptural basis for the dispute: Beit Shammai derive from the word 'גַּם' that the changed item is still forbidden, while Beit Hillel derive from 'הֵם' that only the original form is forbidden.

items.text: Beit Hillel's dual derivation from 'hem'
items.text_en: Beit Hillel's dual derivation from 'hem'
items.desc_en: Beit Hillel derives both that shinui does not exempt from the law of theft and that offspring are not included, from the word 'hem'. The difficulty of the word 'gam' for Beit Hillel is raised.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Beit Hillel derives two laws from the word 'hem' (they): that shinui (change) does not exempt from the law of theft, and that offspring are not included; it then raises the difficulty of the word 'gam' (also) for Beit Hillel.

items.text: Agreement on restitution value
items.text_en: Agreement on restitution value
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that until now, the dispute is only whether shinui acquires, but all agree that the thief pays restitution as at the time of theft, as taught in the Mishnah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the dispute between the schools is only about whether shinui (change) acquires ownership, but all agree that the thief pays restitution as at the time of theft, as taught in the Mishnah.

items.text: Challenge to Rav and Rava's resolution
items.text_en: Challenge to Rav and Rava's resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a challenge to Rav's view that the principal is paid as at the time of theft but the double payment is at the time of judgment. Rava resolves that for live animals it is as at the time of theft, for monetary value it is as at present.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a challenge to Rav's view that the principal is paid as at the time of theft but the double payment is at the time of judgment.
Rava resolves that for live animals the payment is as at the time of theft, but for monetary value it is as at present.

items.text: Proofs that shinui acquires
items.text_en: Proofs that shinui acquires
items.desc_en: Rabba cites a biblical verse and a Mishnah to prove that shinui acquires. The verse implies that if the object is unchanged it is returned, otherwise money is paid. The Mishnah states that if one stole wood and made vessels, he pays as at the time of theft; if he dyed it before returning, he is exempt, indicating shinui acquires.

sub.desc_en: Rabba opens by asserting that shinui (change) acquires, citing both a biblical verse and a Mishnah as proof.
Rabba cites a Mishnah: one who steals wood and makes vessels pays as at the time of theft, implying shinui does not acquire.
Rabba cites the Mishnah's second clause: if one dyed the stolen object before returning it, he is exempt, proving that shinui acquires.

items.text: Uncertainty about ye'ush: biblical or rabbinic?
items.text_en: Uncertainty about ye'ush: biblical or rabbinic?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether ye'ush (despair) effects acquisition by Torah law or rabbinic law. It compares to a found object, which is permitted when it comes to hand, but here it came through transgression, so it may be only rabbinic, as a takanah for returnees.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an uncertainty whether ye'ush (despair) effects acquisition by Torah law or rabbinic law.
The Gemara suggests that if ye'ush is biblical, it parallels a found object, where despair before acquisition grants ownership, so here too the thief acquires.
The Gemara objects that a found object comes permissibly, but here the object came through transgression, so ye'ush may be only rabbinic.
The Gemara resolves that the rabbis instituted acquisition through ye'ush as a takanah (enactment) for returnees, implying it is rabbinic.

items.text: Rav Yosef: ye'ush does not acquire even rabbinically
items.text_en: Rav Yosef: ye'ush does not acquire even rabbinically
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef states that ye'ush does not acquire, even by rabbinic law.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef asserts that ye'ush (despair of recovery) does not effect acquisition of stolen property, even by rabbinic law.

items.text: Rav Yosef's challenge to Rabba
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's challenge to Rabba
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef challenges Rabba with a case of stolen chametz that Passover passed over it.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef challenges Rabba by citing a case of stolen חמץ (leaven) that Passover passed over it, implying a question about the effect of יאוש (despair) and שינוי (change) on the obligation to return the original item.

items.text: Gemara's challenge from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the view that despair acquires, citing the Mishnah's case where a thief returns the object saying 'here is yours before you' after the time of prohibition, implying despair does not effect acquisition; otherwise, why would he need to return the object? He should pay its value.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the view that יאוש (despair) acquires, citing the Mishnah where a thief returns the object after the time of prohibition, implying despair does not effect acquisition; otherwise, he would only need to pay its value.

items.text: Rabbah's distinction
items.text_en: Rabbah's distinction
items.desc_en: Rabbah responds by distinguishing between a case where the owner despairs and the thief wants to acquire (where despair acquires) and the Mishnah's case where the owner despairs but the thief does not want to acquire (so despair does not acquire).

sub.desc_en: Rabbah distinguishes between the case where the owner despairs and the thief wants to acquire (despair acquires) and the Mishnah's case where the owner despairs but the thief does not want to acquire (so despair does not acquire).

items.text: Abaye's objection from the verse 'his offering'
items.text_en: Abaye's objection from the verse 'his offering'
items.desc_en: Abaye objects to Rabbah from a baraita that interprets 'his offering' (קרבנו) as excluding a stolen animal, implying that even after despair the stolen animal cannot be offered. This suggests despair does not acquire, otherwise the animal would be his.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects to Rabbah by citing a baraita that interprets 'his offering' (קרבנו) as excluding a stolen animal, and argues that if the case is before despair, the verse is unnecessary.
Abaye concludes that the baraita must refer to after despair, proving that despair does not acquire.

items.text: Rava's counter-objection from 'his bed'
items.text_en: Rava's counter-objection from 'his bed'
items.desc_en: Rava deflects Abaye's proof by drawing an analogy to a baraita about 'his bed' (משכבו) excluding a stolen bed. Just as that baraita refers to a bed stolen from another (not made by the thief), so too the verse about 'his offering' refers to an animal stolen from another, not one changed by the thief. Thus no proof about despair.

sub.desc_en: Rava deflects Abaye's proof by drawing an analogy to a baraita about 'his bed' (משכבו) excluding a stolen bed, arguing that just as that baraita refers to a bed stolen from another (not made by the thief), so too the verse about 'his offering' refers to an animal stolen from another, not one changed by the thief.

Rava concludes that the verse about 'his offering' (קרבנו) excludes a stolen animal that was taken from another person, not one that underwent a change by the thief, thus no proof about despair (יאוש).

items.text: Abaye's objection from the baraita on hides
items.text_en: Abaye's objection from the baraita on hides
items.desc_en: Abaye challenges Rav Yosef with a baraita about hides: a householder's hides are susceptible to impurity through intention, a thief's hides are susceptible, but a robber's hides are not. Rabbi Shimon reverses the ruling, explaining that the owners have not despaired. This implies that despair effects acquisition (making the robber the owner), so his hides become susceptible. Rav Yosef answers that the case is where the robber cut the hides (a change of deed), which itself effects acquisition.

sub.desc_en: Abaye cites the beginning of the baraita to Rav Yosef: hides of a householder are susceptible to impurity through intention.
The baraita continues: hides of a craftsman (עבדן) are not susceptible to impurity through intention.
The baraita states: a thief's hides are susceptible, but a robber's hides are not.
Rabbi Shimon reverses the ruling: a robber's hides are susceptible because the owners have not despaired, implying that despair effects acquisition.
Rav Yosef answers that the case is where the robber cut the hides (a change of deed), which itself effects acquisition, so the baraita does not prove that despair alone acquires.

items.text: Rabbah bar Rav Chanan's objection about the 'itzba'
items.text_en: Rabbah bar Rav Chanan's objection about the 'itzba'
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Chanan objects that the baraita mentions 'itzba' (a type of hide) which does not require cutting, so the answer of 'cutting' is insufficient. He cites a mishnah that for items lacking a missing craft, intention alone imparts impurity, except for the 'itzba'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Chanan objects that the baraita mentions 'עיצבא' (a type of hide) which does not require cutting, so the answer of cutting is insufficient.
Rabbah bar Rav Chanan cites a mishnah that for items lacking a missing craft, intention alone imparts impurity, except for the 'עיצבא' (itzba).

items.text: Rava's resolution: change of name is like change of deed
items.text_en: Rava's resolution: change of name is like change of deed
items.desc_en: Rava reports that Rabbah challenged Rav Yosef with this difficulty for 22 years until Rav Yosef became head and resolved it: a change of name (שינוי השם) is equivalent to a change of deed (שינוי מעשה). Just as a change of deed (e.g., wood into vessels) effects acquisition, so too a change of name (e.g., 'skin' to 'parchment') effects acquisition, explaining the baraita.

sub.desc_en: Rava reports that Rabbah challenged Rav Yosef with this difficulty for 22 years until Rav Yosef became head and resolved it: a change of name (שינוי השם) is equivalent to a change of deed (שינוי מעשה), just as wood becomes vessels, so 'skin' becomes 'parchment' (אברזין).

items.text: Objection from the case of a stolen beam
items.text_en: Objection from the case of a stolen beam
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: consider a stolen beam (מריש) which undergoes a change of name (from 'beam' to 'roof'), yet the mishnah rules that the thief only pays its value due to the ordinance of the penitents, implying the beam is not acquired by the thief. This contradicts the principle that a change of name effects acquisition.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: consider a stolen beam (מריש) which undergoes a change of name (from 'beam' to 'roof'), yet the mishnah rules that the thief only pays its value due to the ordinance of the penitents, implying the beam is not acquired by the thief. This contradicts the principle that a change of name effects acquisition.
The Gemara emphasizes that the mishnah's ruling is only due to the ordinance of the penitents, implying that without this ordinance the thief would not acquire the beam despite the change of name.

items.text: Rav Yosef's definition of 'marish'
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's definition of 'marish'
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef clarifies that 'marish' (beam) is a name change, citing a baraita that identifies 'marish' as the beams of a house.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef defines 'marish' as a name change, citing a baraita that identifies 'marish' as the beams of a house.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's principle and the pipe (צינור) objection
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's principle and the pipe (צינור) objection
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira states that a change that reverts to its original state is not a change regarding a name change. The Gemara objects with the case of a pipe (צינור) that changes name from 'קציצתא' to 'צינורא', yet the halakha depends on whether it was carved before or after being fixed. The Gemara resolves that the pipe's disqualification is rabbinic, distinguishing between a detached object with 'תורת כלי' and one without.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira states that a change which reverts to its original state does not constitute a change regarding a name change.
The Gemara objects with the case of a pipe (צינור) that changes name from 'קציצתא' to 'צינורא', yet the halakha depends on whether it was carved before or after being fixed.
The baraita specifies that if the pipe was fixed and then carved, it does not disqualify the mikveh.
The Gemara argues that if a name change is significant, even the fixed-then-carved pipe should disqualify the mikveh.
The Gemara resolves that the disqualification of the pipe is rabbinic, distinguishing between a detached object with 'תורת כלי' (status of a vessel) and one without.

items.text: Objection from the baraita on consecration of stolen items
items.text_en: Objection from the baraita on consecration of stolen items
items.desc_en: A baraita states that a thief's consecration is valid, implying that a name change (from חולין to הקדש) effects acquisition. The Gemara explains that this is indeed a name change, so it is a valid change.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita stating that a thief's consecration is valid, implying that a name change effects acquisition.
The Gemara answers that the baraita involves a name change (from חולין to הקדש), which is a valid change, so the objection is resolved.

items.text: Rav Chisda citing Rabbi Yonatan: change acquires
items.text_en: Rav Chisda citing Rabbi Yonatan: change acquires
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda in the name of Rabbi Yonatan derives from the verse 'והשיב את הגזלה' that a change in the stolen object effects acquisition, requiring return of value if the object is not as stolen. The Gemara deflects a challenge that the verse teaches about adding a fifth for a father's theft, concluding that both lessons are derived.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda in the name of Rabbi Yonatan derives from the verse 'וְהֵשִׁיב אֶת הַגְּזֵלָה' that a change in the stolen object effects acquisition, requiring return of value if the object is not as stolen.
The Gemara objects that the word 'אֲשֶׁר גָּזָל' is needed to exclude a father's theft from the requirement to add a fifth.
The Gemara resolves that the verse could have said 'גְּזֵילוֹ' instead, so the extra word 'אֲשֶׁר גָּזָל' teaches both lessons: change acquires and the exclusion of a father's theft.

items.text: Alternative version: change does not acquire
items.text_en: Alternative version: change does not acquire
items.desc_en: An alternative version states that Rav Chisda in the name of Rabbi Yonatan derives that change does not acquire, interpreting 'והשיב את הגזלה' to mean return the object itself. The verse 'אשר גזל' is needed to limit the addition of a fifth to the father's theft.

sub.desc_en: An alternative version states that Rav Chisda in the name of Rabbi Yonatan derives that change does not acquire, interpreting 'והשיב את הגזלה' to mean return the object itself.
The gemara objects that the verse also says 'אשר גזל' (which he stole), implying the object itself must be returned.
The gemara answers that the word 'אשר גזל' is needed to limit the addition of a fifth to the father's theft, not to require return of the object itself.

items.text: Ulla: despair does not acquire
items.text_en: Ulla: despair does not acquire
items.desc_en: Ulla derives from the verse 'והבאתם גזול את הפסח ואת החולה' that despair (יאוש) does not effect acquisition, comparing the stolen item to a lame animal which has no remedy.

sub.desc_en: Ulla derives from the verse 'והבאתם גזול את הפסח ואת החולה' that יאוש (despair) does not effect acquisition, comparing the stolen item to a lame animal which has no remedy.

items.text: Rava's proof that despair does not acquire
items.text_en: Rava's proof that despair does not acquire
items.desc_en: Rava brings a proof from the verse 'קרבנו' that a stolen offering is invalid even after despair, concluding that יאוש does not acquire. The Gemara notes that Rava himself said otherwise, and resolves the contradiction by suggesting he retracted or that Rav Pappa said it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that a stolen offering has no remedy, whether before or after despair (יאוש).
Rava proves from the verse 'קרבנו' (his offering) that a stolen animal is invalid even after יאוש (despair), concluding that יאוש does not acquire.
The Gemara objects that Rava himself elsewhere said that a stolen offering is valid after יאוש, contradicting his own proof.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by suggesting either that Rava retracted his earlier statement or that one of the two statements was actually said by Rav Pappa.

items.text: Mishnah citation: the measure of fourfold/fivefold payment
items.text_en: Mishnah citation: the measure of fourfold/fivefold payment
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the law of fourfold/fivefold payment applies only to an ox or a sheep, not to other animals.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the law of fourfold/fivefold payment applies only to an ox or a sheep, not to other animals.

items.text: Gemara's question and Rava's answer from the verse
items.text_en: Gemara's question and Rava's answer from the verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why we don't learn from the analogy of 'שור-שור' from Shabbat to include wild animals and birds. Rava answers that the repetition of 'שור ושה' twice excludes anything else.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why we should not learn a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the word 'שור' (ox) in Shabbat to include wild animals and birds in the law of תשלומי ארבעה וחמישה (fourfold and fivefold payment).
Rava answers that the Torah's repetition of 'שור ושה' (ox and sheep) twice excludes any other animal, so wild animals and birds are not included.

items.text: Analysis of which verse is superfluous
items.text_en: Analysis of which verse is superfluous
items.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes which occurrence of 'שור ושה' is superfluous. It rejects the possibility that the second one is extra, because it is needed for a different drasha about payment value. It then considers the first one, but shows that without it we might think the thief must steal two animals. Finally, it concludes that the 'שור' of the latter clause and the 'שה' of the first clause are superfluous, proving the exclusion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which occurrence of 'שור ושה' is superfluous.
The Gemara suggests that the second 'שור ושה' is superfluous, but shows that without it one might think the thief must pay nine animals for each.
The Gemara objects that the extra 'תחתיו' could be used to derive the payment value, not the superfluity of 'שור ושה'.
The Gemara cites a baraita showing that the extra 'תחתיו' is needed for a different drasha about payment value.
The Gemara suggests that the first 'שור ושה' is superfluous, proposing an alternative verse without it.
The Gemara objects that without the first 'שור ושה', one might think the thief must steal two animals and slaughter both, but the verse says 'וּטְבָחוֹ' (singular).
The Gemara further objects that one might think the thief must steal both and sell both, but the verse says 'וּמְכָרוֹ' (singular).
The Gemara objects that one might think the thief must steal two, slaughter one and sell one, but the verse says 'אוֹ מְכָרוֹ' (or sell it).
The Gemara concludes that the 'שור' of the latter clause and the 'שה' of the first clause are superfluous, proving that only a שור or שה is included, not other animals.

items.text: The law of a thief after a thief and Rav's statement
items.text_en: The law of a thief after a thief and Rav's statement
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who steals from a thief does not pay double payment. Rav says this is only before despair, but after despair the first thief acquires it and the second thief pays double to the first. Rav Sheishet expresses astonishment, citing a baraita where Rabbi Akiva explains the reason for fourfold/fivefold payment.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who steals from a thief does not pay double payment.
Rav qualifies the Mishnah: the exemption applies only before despair (יאוש), but after despair the first thief acquires the object and the second thief pays double payment to the first thief.

Rav Sheishet expresses astonishment at Rav's statement, citing a baraita where Rabbi Akiva explains that the reason for fourfold/fivefold payment is that the thief has become entrenched in sin, and questions whether this applies before or after despair.

items.text: First objection from the baraita of 'nichtaresh'
items.text_en: First objection from the baraita of 'nichtaresh'
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a baraita that implies the thief pays the fourfold or fivefold penalty only after יאוש, questioning whether יאוש acquires ownership. If it does, why should the thief pay? The answer is given like Rava: because he repeated the sin.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a baraita about 'nichtaresh' (despaired) and questions: if יאוש (despair) acquires ownership, why should the thief pay the fourfold or fivefold penalty for slaughtering or selling his own property?
The Gemara answers like Rava: the thief pays because he repeated the sin (שנה בחטא), not because he acquired ownership.

items.text: Second objection from the verse 'וּטְבָחוֹ אוֹ מְכָרוֹ'
items.text_en: Second objection from the verse 'וּטְבָחוֹ אוֹ מְכָרוֹ'
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a derivation that sale must be irreversible like slaughter, implying it occurs after יאוש. If יאוש acquires, why pay? Rav Nachman answers: it excludes a sale for thirty days.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that compares slaughter and sale, both being irreversible, to imply the sale occurs after יאוש.
The Gemara asks: if the sale is after יאוש and יאוש acquires, why should the thief pay the penalty for selling his own property?
The Gemara answers like Rav Nachman: the baraita excludes a sale where the thief granted ownership for thirty days, which is not a full acquisition, so the penalty applies.

items.text: Challenge from the baraita of successive thefts
items.text_en: Challenge from the baraita of successive thefts
items.desc_en: A baraita describes cases of multiple thefts. The Gemara analyzes the middle case: if the first thief sold after יאוש, why does he pay the fourfold or fivefold? And why does the second thief pay double? This seems to prove that יאוש does not acquire, contradicting Rav.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that presents three cases of successive thefts, establishing the payment rules for each.
The baraita states the second case: if the first thief stole and sold, and a second thief stole from him, the first pays fourfold or fivefold and the second pays double.
The Gemara focuses on the middle case and asks: when did the sale occur — before or after יאוש (despair of the owners)?
The Gemara objects: if the sale was before יאוש, why does the second thief pay double? No one holds that a change of possession without יאוש acquires.
The Gemara assumes the sale was after יאוש and asks: if יאוש acquires, why does the first thief pay fourfold or fivefold? He is selling his own property.
The Gemara further asks: in the first case, if the sale was after יאוש, why does the second thief pay only the principal and not double?
The Gemara concludes that the baraita proves יאוש does not acquire, posing a difficulty for Rav's position.

items.text: Rava's resolution by flipping the baraita
items.text_en: Rava's resolution by flipping the baraita
items.desc_en: Rava argues the baraita is not straightforward; he suggests flipping the middle and last cases. The middle case (sale) then has the second thief paying only principal because change of possession without יאוש does not acquire; the last case (slaughter) has the second thief paying double because the change of act (slaughter) acquires.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects that the baraita cannot be read straightforwardly, pointing out that the last case (slaughter then theft) would contradict the view that a change of act (שינוי מעשה) does not acquire.

Rava resolves by flipping the middle and last cases of the baraita: the middle case (sale) now has the second thief paying only principal because a change of possession without יאוש (despair) does not acquire.
Rava continues: the last case (slaughter then theft) now has the second thief paying double because the change of act (שינוי מעשה) acquires the animal.

items.text: Rav Pappa and Rav Zevid's alternative explanations
items.text_en: Rav Pappa and Rav Zevid's alternative explanations
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa says the baraita is not flipped; the last case follows Beit Shammai who hold that change of place does not acquire. Rav Zevid explains all cases are before יאוש, but the owners despaired only after the sale, creating יאוש with change of possession. He adds that יאוש alone also acquires for the thief, but the baraita's details require this specific scenario.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa says not to flip; the last case follows Beit Shammai, who hold that a change in place does not acquire.
The Gemara objects: if so, the first and middle cases still contradict Rav's view that יאוש does not acquire.
Rav Zevid resolves: the baraita is before יאוש, but the owners despaired only regarding the buyer, not the thief, creating יאוש and change of possession together, which acquires.
Rav Zevid adds that יאוש (despair) alone would also acquire for the thief, but the baraita's details require this specific scenario.
Rav Zevid concludes that only in this scenario—where the owners despair after the sale—do both the first and second thief pay the full penalties.

items.text: Dispute between Rav Nachman and Rav Sheshet on selling before יאוש
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav Nachman and Rav Sheshet on selling before יאוש
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman holds the thief is liable even if he sold before יאוש, while Rav Sheshet holds he is exempt because the sale is ineffective. Rav Sheshet supports his view with Rabbi Akiva's statement and the verse 'וּטְבָחוֹ אוֹ מְכָרוֹ', which Rav Nachman explains as excluding a thirty-day sale. Rabbi Elazar agrees with Rav Sheshet.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a dispute: Rav Nachman holds a thief who sells before יאוש (despair of the owners) is liable for the fourfold/fivefold payment, while Rav Sheshet holds he is exempt.
Rav Nachman argues that the Torah's term 'וּמְכָרוֹ' (and sold it) applies regardless of timing, so selling before יאוש also triggers liability.
Rav Sheshet argues that liability applies only after יאוש, when the sale is effective, paralleling the requirement that the slaughter (טביחה) be effective.

sub.text: Rav Sheshet's citation of Rabbi Akiva
sub.text_en: Rav Sheshet's citation of Rabbi Akiva
sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet cites a baraita where Rabbi Akiva states that the fourfold/fivefold payment applies because the thief became 'rooted in sin' (נשתרש בחטא), implying the sale must be effective.

sub.text: Gemara's question on Rabbi Akiva's statement
sub.text_en: Gemara's question on Rabbi Akiva's statement
sub.desc_en: The gemara asks: when does Rabbi Akiva's statement apply? If before יאוש, how is he 'rooted in sin'? It must be after יאוש, supporting Rav Sheshet.
Rava rejects the inference, explaining that Rabbi Akiva's phrase 'נשתרש בחטא' means 'because he repeated the sin' (שנה בחטא), not that the sale was effective, so it can apply even before יאוש.

sub.text: Rav Sheshet's second proof from the verse
sub.text_en: Rav Sheshet's second proof from the verse
sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet brings a second proof: the verse 'וּטְבָחוֹ וּמְכָרוֹ' (and slaughtered it or sold it) requires the sale to be irreversible like slaughter, which only applies after יאוש.

sub.text: Rav Nachman's resolution of the verse
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman's resolution of the verse
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman explains the verse as excluding a sale that is limited to thirty days, which is reversible, not as requiring the sale to be after יאוש.

sub.text: Rabbi Elazar's agreement with Rav Sheshet
sub.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's agreement with Rav Sheshet
sub.desc_en: The gemara notes that Rabbi Elazar also holds that liability applies only after יאוש, as he states in a following statement.

items.text: Proof that standard theft involves ye'ush
items.text_en: Proof that standard theft involves ye'ush
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues that the Torah's mention of slaughter or sale implies the owner has despaired, otherwise the thief would not benefit from the sale. It rejects the possibility that the owner did not despair.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asserts that standard theft involves יאוש בעלים (the owner's despair), as proven by the Torah's mention of slaughter or sale.
The Gemara objects: perhaps the owner did not despair even after the theft.
The Gemara rejects the objection: slaughter and sale both require the thief's benefit, which is impossible before יאוש (despair).
The Gemara objects: perhaps we heard that the owner explicitly despaired.
The Gemara rejects the objection: the sale must be immediate like the slaughter, implying יאוש (despair) at the time of theft.

items.text: Refining the proof: immediate benefit and immediate despair
items.text_en: Refining the proof: immediate benefit and immediate despair
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers the possibility that the owner did not despair, but rejects it by comparing sale to slaughter: both must provide immediate benefit. It also rejects the idea that we heard the owner despair, as slaughter is immediate.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the proof from the Torah's juxtaposition of slaughter and sale is valid, suggesting that perhaps the owner had not yet despaired.

The Gemara rejects the question by comparing sale to slaughter: just as slaughter provides immediate benefit (eating), so too sale must provide immediate benefit (money), which would not be the case if the sale occurred before despair, when the thief has no ownership.
The Gemara raises a further objection: perhaps the owner's despair was actually heard, so the sale could still be after despair.

The Gemara resolves the objection by comparing sale to slaughter: just as slaughter is immediate (the animal is killed right away), so too the sale must be immediate (occurring right after the theft), before any despair could be heard.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's counterexample: kidnapping
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's counterexample: kidnapping
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan argues that kidnapping (theft of a person) proves that not all theft involves despair, as the kidnapper is liable even without despair. This implies Rabbi Yochanan holds that before despair the thief is liable.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan argues that kidnapping (theft of a person) proves that not all theft involves יאוש (despair), as the kidnapper is liable even without despair, implying that before יאוש the thief is liable.

items.text: Dispute after ye'ush: Rabbi Yochanan vs. Resh Lakish
items.text_en: Dispute after ye'ush: Rabbi Yochanan vs. Resh Lakish
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents the dispute: Rabbi Yochanan holds the thief is liable even after ye'ush, while Resh Lakish holds he is exempt because the thief acquires the object and it is his own.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the law is after ye'ush (the owners' despair) regarding the thief's liability for the fourfold or fivefold payment.
Rabbi Yochanan rules that the thief is liable even after ye'ush.
Resh Lakish rules that the thief is exempt after ye'ush because he acquires the object.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yochanan's reasoning
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yochanan's reasoning
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yochanan holds the thief liable both before and after ye'ush.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Resh Lakish's reasoning
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Resh Lakish's reasoning
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Resh Lakish holds the thief liable only before ye'ush, but after ye'ush the thief acquires the object and it is his own that he slaughters or sells.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's challenge: consecration after ye'ush
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's challenge: consecration after ye'ush
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan cites a case where a thief consecrates the stolen animal after ye'ush and then slaughters it; he pays double but not four or five. If ye'ush acquires, why is he liable at all? The implication is that ye'ush does not acquire.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan's challenge to Resh Lakish
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's challenge to Resh Lakish
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan cites a baraita: a thief who consecrates a stolen animal and then slaughters it pays double payment but not four or five payment.
