Rabbi Yochanan argues that if the consecration occurred before יאוש (despair), the animal cannot be consecrated because it is not the thief's property.
Rabbi Yochanan concludes that the case must be after יאוש, and if יאוש (despair) acquires, why should the thief be liable at all for slaughtering his own property?

items.text: Resh Lakish's answer: consecration by owners in the thief's hand
items.text_en: Resh Lakish's answer: consecration by owners in the thief's hand
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish explains the case as one where the owners consecrated the animal while it was in the thief's possession, relying on the practice of the modest ones who can consecrate even without physical possession.

sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish answers that the case involves owners consecrating the animal while it is in the thief's hand.
The Gemara objects that according to Rabbi Yochanan, neither the thief nor the owner can consecrate the animal when the owner has not despaired.
The Gemara answers that Resh Lakish follows the practice of the modest ones (צנועין) who can consecrate even without physical possession.

items.text: Refining the case: after judgment and the rule of Rava
items.text_en: Refining the case: after judgment and the rule of Rava
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the principal has returned to the owners, and resolves that the case is after the court has ruled 'go and give', which makes the thief a robber, and a robber does not pay the four- or five-fold penalty.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: but the principal has returned to the owners (so why is the thief exempt from the four- or five-fold penalty?).
The Gemara answers: the case is when the thief stood in court (after judgment).
The Gemara questions: if the court said 'go and give him', why mention consecration? Even without consecration he should be exempt.
Rava's principle is cited: after the court rules 'go and give', the thief becomes a robber (גזלן), and a robber does not pay the four- or five-fold penalty.

items.text: Court order and the thief's liability
items.text_en: Court order and the thief's liability
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why a thief who has been told by the court 'You are obligated to give it to him' and then slaughters or sells the animal still pays the fourfold or fivefold penalty. It explains that since the matter is not yet settled (the thief hasn't actually returned it), he is still considered a thief.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why a thief who has been told by the court 'You are obligated to give it to him' and then slaughters or sells the animal still pays the fourfold or fivefold penalty, and answers that since the matter is not yet settled (the thief hasn't actually returned it), he is still considered a thief.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan on consecration of stolen property
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan on consecration of stolen property
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that if someone stole an object and the owners have not despaired, neither the thief nor the owner can consecrate it: the thief because it is not his, and the owner because it is not in his possession.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that if someone stole an object and the owners have not despaired, neither the thief nor the owner can consecrate it: the thief because it is not his, and the owner because it is not in his possession.

items.text: Challenge from the Mishnah of Fourth-Year Vineyard
items.text_en: Challenge from the Mishnah of Fourth-Year Vineyard
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Yochanan's statement by citing a Mishnah that discusses marking a fourth-year vineyard with clods of earth, orlah with potsherds, and graves with lime. It then quotes Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's distinction between the Sabbatical year (where produce is ownerless) and other years (where one should feed the wicked and let him die), and the practice of the pious who leave money and declare that whatever is gathered from the vineyard is redeemed onto that money.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah is cited, stating that a fourth-year vineyard (כרם רבעי) was marked with clods of earth, and the Gemara explains the symbolism: just as earth is beneficial, so too the produce is permitted for benefit after redemption.
The Mishnah continues: an orlah vineyard was marked with potsherds, symbolizing that just as potsherds have no benefit, so too orlah produce is forbidden for benefit.
The Mishnah concludes: graves were marked with lime, symbolizing whiteness like bones, and the lime was mixed and poured to make it especially white.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel states that the Mishnah's marking applies only in the Sabbatical year (שביעית), when the produce is ownerless (הפקר).
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds that in other years of the Sabbatical cycle, one should feed the wicked person and let him die (i.e., not mark the vineyard).
The pious (צנועין) would leave money and declare that whatever is gathered from the vineyard is redeemed (מחולל) onto that money.

items.text: Attempt to reconcile Rabbi Yochanan with the Mishnah
items.text_en: Attempt to reconcile Rabbi Yochanan with the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the Mishnah's 'pious' might be the view of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, and Rabbi Yochanan does not rule like a lone individual. However, it notes that Rabbi Yochanan himself said that wherever Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel teaches in our Mishnah, the law follows him except in three cases.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the Mishnah's 'pious' (צנועין) is the view of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, and Rabbi Yochanan does not rule like a lone individual.

sub.text: Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yochanan himself said that wherever Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel teaches in our Mishnah, the law follows him except in three cases, contradicting the suggestion that he would dismiss his view.

items.text: Textual emendation of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Textual emendation of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the Mishnah should be read as 'all that is gathered' (מִתְלַקֵּט) rather than 'all that is picked' (נִלְקָט), to align with Rabbi Yochanan's view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes emending the Mishnah's wording from 'נִלְקָט' (picked) to 'מִתְלַקֵּט' (gathered) to align with Rabbi Yochanan's view.

items.text: Challenge from Rabbi Dosa's statement
items.text_en: Challenge from Rabbi Dosa's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the emendation by noting that Rabbi Yochanan himself said that the pious and Rabbi Dosa said the same thing, and Rabbi Dosa uses the term 'נִלְקָט' (picked). It cites a baraita where Rabbi Dosa says that at evening the owner declares 'whatever the poor have picked (לָקְטוּ) shall be ownerless.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the emendation by noting that Rabbi Yochanan himself said that the pious and Rabbi Dosa said the same thing, and Rabbi Dosa uses the term 'נִלְקָט' (picked).
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Dosa says that at evening the owner declares 'whatever the poor have picked (לָקְטוּ) shall be ownerless.'

items.text: Resolution: switching the opinions
items.text_en: Resolution: switching the opinions
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the baraita should be reversed: Rabbi Yehuda's statement should be attributed to Rabbi Dosa and vice versa. It then questions why not simply switch Rabbi Yochanan's statement to say 'the pious and Rabbi Yehuda said the same thing.' The Gemara answers that the baraita must be reversed because Rabbi Yehuda elsewhere holds that there is no retroactive clarification (ברירה), while the Mishnah's pious implies retroactive clarification.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes to reverse the attributions in the baraita: Rabbi Yehuda's statement becomes Rabbi Dosa's and vice versa.
The Gemara objects: why reverse the baraita? Instead, reverse Rabbi Yochanan's statement to say 'the pious and Rabbi Yehuda said the same thing.'

The Gemara answers that the baraita must be reversed because Rabbi Yehuda elsewhere holds that there is no retroactive clarification (ברירה), while the Mishnah's pious implies retroactive clarification.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Dispute on separating tithes from purchased wine
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Dispute on separating tithes from purchased wine
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where one buys wine from Kutim and designates future separations as terumah and tithes, allowing immediate drinking. Rabbi Meir permits this, while Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Yosei, and Rabbi Shimon forbid it.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents Rabbi Meir's position permitting one who buys wine from Kutim to designate future separations as תרומה (priestly portion) and tithes and drink immediately.
The Mishnah presents the opposing position of Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Yosei, and Rabbi Shimon, who forbid this practice.

items.text: Gemara's question: Contradiction in Rabbi Yochanan's view on bereirah
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Contradiction in Rabbi Yochanan's view on bereirah
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: Rabbi Yochanan's statement about 'all that is gathered' implies he accepts bereirah, but another statement by him (via Rav Asi) about brothers dividing inheritance suggests he rejects bereirah, as they must return property in the Jubilee.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah was reversed, noting that the contradiction in Rabbi Yochanan's views is now the real issue.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yochanan's statement 'all that is gathered' implies he accepts בְּרֵירָה (retroactive designation).
The Gemara cites Rav Asi's report that Rabbi Yochanan said brothers who divide inheritance are considered purchasers and must return property in the Jubilee, showing he rejects בְּרֵירָה.

items.text: Resolution: Rabbi Yochanan follows a different anonymous Mishnah
items.text_en: Resolution: Rabbi Yochanan follows a different anonymous Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yochanan's statement 'all that is gathered' is maintained, and he follows a different anonymous Mishnah (about a thief not paying double to subsequent thieves) which teaches that one cannot consecrate or renounce ownership of what is not in one's domain, supported by a verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yochanan's statement 'all that is gathered' is maintained as originally stated.

sub.text: Gemara's citation of a different anonymous Mishnah
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of a different anonymous Mishnah
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yochanan follows a different anonymous Mishnah (about a thief not paying double to subsequent thieves) and questions why the thief does not pay double to the original owners.
The Gemara infers that the Mishnah teaches that one cannot consecrate or renounce ownership of what is not in one's domain, because the thief does not own the stolen item and it is not in his domain.
The Gemara objects: why does Rabbi Yochanan follow that anonymous Mishnah rather than the anonymous Mishnah of the pious ones (צְנוּעִין)?

The Gemara answers that Rabbi Yochanan follows that Mishnah because a verse supports it: 'And if a man consecrates his house' — just as his house is in his domain, so too everything must be in his domain.

items.text: Abaye's analysis: Distinguishing between the discreet ones and Rabbi Dosa
items.text_en: Abaye's analysis: Distinguishing between the discreet ones and Rabbi Dosa
items.desc_en: Abaye notes that Rabbi Yochanan equates the discreet ones (Tz'nu'im) with Rabbi Dosa, but without that, he would have thought the discreet ones follow Rabbi Dosa's leniency for thieves, while Rabbi Dosa does not extend it to the poor.

sub.desc_en: Abaye states that without Rabbi Yochanan's equation of the discreet ones (Tz'nu'im) with Rabbi Dosa, he would have thought the discreet ones follow Rabbi Dosa's view for thieves, but Rabbi Dosa does not extend it to the poor.

Abaye explains that the discreet ones would apply Rabbi Dosa's leniency to thieves because the Sages instituted a remedy for thieves, but Rabbi Dosa would not apply it to the poor because the Sages only instituted a remedy for the poor.

items.text: Rava's analysis: The discreet ones follow Rabbi Meir's logic
items.text_en: Rava's analysis: The discreet ones follow Rabbi Meir's logic
items.desc_en: Rava suggests that the discreet ones follow Rabbi Meir, who holds that ma'aser is sacred property, yet the Torah allows redemption with a surcharge while it is in one's domain. This is extended to kerem revai via a gezeirah shavah, but for leket, since it is one's own money, renunciation is only possible when in one's domain.

sub.desc_en: Rava opens by stating that were it not for Rabbi Yochanan's statement linking the discreet ones and Rabbi Dosa, he would have thought the Tanna of the discreet ones is Rabbi Meir.

Rava cites Rabbi Meir's view that ma'aser is sacred property, yet the Torah allows redemption with a surcharge while it is in one's domain, as per the verse 'וְאִם גָּאֹל יִגְאַל אִישׁ מִמַּעַשְׂרוֹ, חֲמִשִׁתוֹ יֹסֵף עָלָיו'.

Rava extends the same logic to kerem revai via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the word 'קדש' (sacred), showing that even though it is not one's own property, the Torah placed it in one's domain for the purpose of renunciation.
Rava concludes that for leket, since it is one's own money, renunciation is only possible when it is in one's domain, not when it is outside.

items.text: Ravina's alternative: The discreet ones are Rabbi Dosa
items.text_en: Ravina's alternative: The discreet ones are Rabbi Dosa
items.desc_en: Ravina suggests that without Rabbi Yochanan's statement, he would have said the discreet ones are Rabbi Dosa himself, to avoid a contradiction between the anonymous Mishnah and Rabbi Yochanan.

sub.desc_en: Ravina proposes that without Rabbi Yochanan's statement, he would have identified the discreet ones as Rabbi Dosa himself, to avoid a contradiction between the anonymous Mishnah and Rabbi Yochanan.

items.text: Opening statement: Stam rejects the view of the individual
items.text_en: Opening statement: Stam rejects the view of the individual
items.desc_en: The anonymous voice (Stam) states that the individual (Rabbi Eliezer) does not say his opinion as a settled matter, implying it is not accepted.

sub.desc_en: The anonymous voice (Stam) states that the individual (Rabbi Eliezer) does not state his opinion as a settled matter, implying it is not accepted.

items.text: Nehardeans' ruling on powers of attorney for movables, citing Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Nehardeans' ruling on powers of attorney for movables, citing Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: The Nehardeans state that they do not write a power of attorney for movable property. Rav Ashi asks for the reason, and Amemar explains it is due to Rabbi Yochanan's principle that a robber and the victim cannot consecrate the stolen object because neither fully owns it.

sub.desc_en: The Nehardeans state that they do not write a power of attorney (אורכתא) for movable property.
Rav Ashi asks Amemar for the reason behind the Nehardeans' practice.

Amemar explains that the reason is Rabbi Yochanan's principle: when a robber steals and the owners have not despaired, neither the robber nor the victim can consecrate the object, because the robber lacks ownership and the victim lacks possession.

items.text: Alternative version: Nehardeans' ruling only when the debtor denies the debt
items.text_en: Alternative version: Nehardeans' ruling only when the debtor denies the debt
items.desc_en: There is a version where the Nehardeans say they do not write a power of attorney for movable property only when the debtor denies the debt, because it would appear false; but if he does not deny, they do write it.

sub.desc_en: An alternative version states that the Nehardeans only refuse to write a power of attorney for movable property when the debtor denies the debt, because it would appear false; but if he does not deny, they do write it.

items.text: Nehardeans: Power of attorney must include specific empowerment clause
items.text_en: Nehardeans: Power of attorney must include specific empowerment clause
items.desc_en: The Nehardeans further state that a power of attorney without the phrase 'Go, judge, acquire, and take for yourself' is invalid, because the defendant can claim the agent is not his adversary.

sub.desc_en: The Nehardeans rule that a power of attorney lacking the clause 'Go, judge, acquire, and take for yourself' is invalid, because the defendant can claim the agent is not his adversary.

items.text: Abaye: If the power of attorney includes a share, it covers the whole
items.text_en: Abaye: If the power of attorney includes a share, it covers the whole
items.desc_en: Abaye rules that if the power of attorney grants a half, third, or quarter share, then since the agent can litigate over the share, he can litigate over the entire claim.

sub.desc_en: Abaye rules that if the power of attorney grants a half, third, or quarter share, then since the agent can litigate over the share, he can litigate over the entire claim.

items.text: Amemar and Rav Ashi: If the agent seized property, we do not take it; he is a messenger or partner
items.text_en: Amemar and Rav Ashi: If the agent seized property, we do not take it; he is a messenger or partner
items.desc_en: Amemar says if the agent seized property, we do not take it from him. Rav Ashi says that since the principal wrote 'I accept upon myself whatever is decreed from the court,' the agent is made a messenger. There is a version that he is made a partner; the practical difference is whether he can seize half. The halakha is that he is a messenger.

sub.desc_en: Amemar rules that if the agent seized property, we do not take it from him.
Rav Ashi explains that since the principal wrote 'I accept upon myself whatever is decreed from the court,' the agent is made a messenger (שליח).
An alternative version states that the agent is made a partner (שותף), not a messenger.
The gemara asks what practical difference arises between the two versions.
The gemara answers that the difference is whether the agent can seize half the property.
The gemara concludes that the halakha follows the version that the agent is a messenger (שליח).

items.text: Mishnah: Cases of theft and slaughter requiring fourfold or fivefold payment
items.text_en: Mishnah: Cases of theft and slaughter requiring fourfold or fivefold payment
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists cases where a thief who steals on the testimony of two witnesses and then slaughters or sells on their testimony or on that of two others pays the fourfold or fivefold penalty. It includes cases of slaughter on Shabbat, for idolatry, on Yom Kippur, after the father's death, after consecration, for medicine or dogs, a terefah, or slaughtering non-sacred animals in the Temple courtyard. Rabbi Shimon exempts in the last two cases.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the general rule: a thief who steals on the testimony of two witnesses and then slaughters or sells on their testimony or that of two others pays the fourfold or fivefold penalty.
The Mishnah lists cases where the thief still pays the penalty: slaughter on Shabbat, for idolatry, on Yom Kippur, after the father's death, or after consecration.
The Mishnah adds cases where the penalty applies: slaughter for medicine or dogs, a terefah, or slaughtering non-sacred animals in the Temple courtyard.
Rabbi Shimon exempts the thief in the last two cases (terefah and slaughter of non-sacred animals in the Temple courtyard).

items.text: Gemara: Does the Mishnah contradict Rabbi Akiva's view on partial testimony?
items.text_en: Gemara: Does the Mishnah contradict Rabbi Akiva's view on partial testimony?
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the Mishnah might not follow Rabbi Akiva, who holds that 'a matter' excludes half a matter (partial testimony is invalid). It cites a baraita where Rabbi Yose recounts that Abba Chalaphta went to Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri to learn Torah, implying a dispute about partial testimony.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah contradicts Rabbi Akiva's view.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Akiva holds the principle 'דבר' (a matter) excludes 'חצי דבר' (half a matter), meaning partial testimony is invalid.
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Yose recounts that Abba Chalaphta went to Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri to learn Torah, implying a dispute about partial testimony.

items.text: Question about chazaka with different witnesses each year
items.text_en: Question about chazaka with different witnesses each year
items.desc_en: Chalafta asks whether eating the fruit in the first year before two witnesses, second year before two, and third year before two constitutes a chazaka. Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri affirms it is a chazaka, but notes that Rabbi Akiva disagrees, citing the verse 'davar' (a matter) and not half a matter.

sub.desc_en: Chalafta asks whether eating the fruit in three consecutive years, each year before a different pair of witnesses, constitutes a chazaka (presumption of ownership).
Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri affirms that this is indeed a valid chazaka.
Chalafta agrees but notes that Rabbi Akiva disputes this, citing the verse 'דבר' (a matter) to require a unified testimony, not half a matter.

items.text: Abaye's defense of Rabbi Akiva's position
items.text_en: Abaye's defense of Rabbi Akiva's position
items.desc_en: Abaye argues that even Rabbi Akiva would agree in a case where two witnesses say 'he betrothed' and two say 'he had intercourse', because although the witnesses of intercourse need witnesses of betrothal, the witnesses of betrothal do not need witnesses of intercourse, so it is considered a 'davar'. Similarly here, witnesses of slaughter need witnesses of theft, but witnesses of theft do not need witnesses of slaughter, so it is a 'davar'.

sub.desc_en: Abaye opens by asserting that even Rabbi Akiva would agree in the case of two witnesses saying 'he betrothed' and two saying 'he had intercourse', because the witnesses of betrothal do not need the witnesses of intercourse, making it a 'דבר' (complete matter).

Abaye applies the same logic to the case of theft and slaughter: witnesses of slaughter need witnesses of theft, but witnesses of theft do not need witnesses of slaughter, so it is considered a 'דבר' (complete matter).

items.text: Rabbis' interpretation of 'davar ve-lo chatzi davar'
items.text_en: Rabbis' interpretation of 'davar ve-lo chatzi davar'
items.desc_en: The Rabbis ask what the verse 'davar ve-lo chatzi davar' excludes. They initially suggest it excludes one witness saying one lobe and another saying one lobe, but reject that as half a matter and half testimony. Instead, they say it excludes two witnesses saying one lobe and two saying one lobe, where each pair says the animal is small.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Rabbis exclude with the verse 'דבר' (a matter) and not half a matter.
The Gemara initially suggests the verse excludes one witness saying one lobe on the back and another saying one lobe on the belly.
The Gemara objects that this is half a matter and half testimony, not a proper exclusion.
The Gemara resolves that the verse excludes two witnesses saying one lobe on the back and two saying one lobe on the belly, where each pair claims the animal is small.

items.text: Contradiction from a baraita about Shabbat
items.text_en: Contradiction from a baraita about Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: the Mishnah says one who steals and sells on Shabbat is liable, but a baraita says he is exempt.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: the Mishnah holds one who steals and sells on Shabbat liable, but a baraita explicitly says he is exempt.

items.text: Rami bar Chama's resolution
items.text_en: Rami bar Chama's resolution
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama resolves that the baraita refers to a case where the seller said 'Pick a fig from my fig tree and acquire the theft for me', so the sale is not valid because the seller is liable for capital punishment.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama resolves that the baraita's exemption applies when the seller said 'Pick a fig from my fig tree and acquire the theft for me', so the sale is invalid because the seller is liable for capital punishment.

items.text: Objection to Rami bar Chama
items.text_en: Objection to Rami bar Chama
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if the seller is not forced to pay in court because he is liable for capital punishment, then the sale itself is invalid, so how can the buyer acquire?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects to Rami bar Chama: since the seller cannot be forced to pay in court because he is liable for capital punishment, the sale itself is invalid, so the buyer cannot acquire.

items.text: Rav Papa's alternative resolution
items.text_en: Rav Papa's alternative resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Papa resolves that the baraita refers to a case where the seller said 'Throw your theft into my courtyard and acquire the theft for me'. This follows Rabbi Akiva, who holds that 'klutah' (a thrown object) is considered as if it were placed. If it followed the Rabbis, the buyer would acquire upon entering the courtyard, but for Shabbat liability, it requires reaching the ground. So the seller says 'Do not acquire until it rests'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Papa resolves the contradiction by positing that the seller said 'Throw your theft into my courtyard and acquire the theft for me'.
The Gemara identifies that this follows Rabbi Akiva, who holds that קלוטה (a thrown object caught in midair) is considered as if it were placed.
The Gemara objects that if the case followed the Rabbis, the buyer would acquire upon entering the courtyard, but for Shabbat liability, liability requires reaching the ground, creating a mismatch.
Rav Papa refines that the seller said 'Do not acquire my theft for me until it rests', thereby aligning acquisition with Shabbat liability.

items.text: Rava's defense of Rami bar Chama
items.text_en: Rava's defense of Rami bar Chama
items.desc_en: Rava defends Rami bar Chama by comparing to the case of a harlot's hire: the Torah forbids it even if one had intercourse with his mother, and if she sues in court, we do not tell him to pay, yet if he pays, it is still considered a harlot's hire. Similarly here, even though the court does not force payment, the sale is valid.

sub.desc_en: Rava defends Rami bar Chama by asserting that the case of a harlot's hire (אתנן) is analogous: even if one had intercourse with his mother, the Torah forbids it, yet the court does not compel payment.
Rava concludes that just as the harlot's hire is valid if paid voluntarily despite no court coercion, so too the sale here is valid even though the court does not force the thief to pay.

items.text: Continuation of previous discussion on acquisition
items.text_en: Continuation of previous discussion on acquisition
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that even in the case where the owner transfers ownership through such a statement, it is considered a sale.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that even if the owner transfers ownership through such a statement, it is considered a sale.

items.text: Question on slaughter on Yom Kippur and answer
items.text_en: Question on slaughter on Yom Kippur and answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah lists Yom Kippur as a case where one pays, since one is also liable to lashes, and the principle is that one does not both receive lashes and pay. It answers that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Meir, who holds that one does receive lashes and pay.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah lists Yom Kippur as a case where one pays, since one is also liable to lashes, and the principle is that one does not both receive lashes and pay.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Meir, who holds that one does receive lashes and pay.

items.text: Challenge from slaughter on Shabbat
items.text_en: Challenge from slaughter on Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that if the Mishnah follows Rabbi Meir, then slaughter on Shabbat should also be included, but a baraita shows that Rabbi Meir distinguishes between lashes and payment (where he holds one pays) and death and payment (where he does not). The baraita states that Rabbi Meir obligates payment for slaughter on Shabbat, for idolatry, and for a gored ox, while the Sages exempt.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that if the Mishnah follows Rabbi Meir, then slaughter on Shabbat should also be included, but suggests that Rabbi Meir distinguishes between lashes and payment (where he holds one pays) and death and payment (where he does not).
The Gemara objects by citing a baraita that shows Rabbi Meir obligates payment for slaughter on Shabbat, for idolatry, and for a gored ox, while the Sages exempt.

items.text: Resolution via slaughter by an agent
items.text_en: Resolution via slaughter by an agent
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by citing Rabbi Yochanan and others who explain that the baraita deals with slaughter through an agent. Rava derives this from a biblical verse, and the schools of Rabbi Yishmael and Hezekiah also derive the inclusion of an agent from the verses.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by citing Rabbi Yochanan and others who explain that the baraita deals with slaughter through an agent (טוֹבֵחַ עַל יְדֵי אַחֵר).
The Gemara objects: how can one person sin (the agent) and another (the principal) become liable?

Rava answers that the case is different because the verse 'וּטְבָחוֹ וּמְכָרוֹ' (and he slaughtered it and sold it) draws an analogy: just as sale can be through an agent, so too slaughter can be through an agent.

sub.text: Supporting baraita from schools of Rabbi Yishmael and Hezekiah
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita from schools of Rabbi Yishmael and Hezekiah
sub.desc_en: The schools of Rabbi Yishmael and Hezekiah each derive from a different word in the verse ('אוֹ' and 'תַּחַת') that the law includes an agent.

items.text: Objection by Mar Zutra and response
items.text_en: Objection by Mar Zutra and response
items.desc_en: Mar Zutra objects: can there be a case where if the person himself does it he is exempt, but if he does it through an agent he is liable? Rav Ashi responds that the person himself is not exempt, but rather he is subject to a more severe penalty (death) that exempts him from payment.

sub.desc_en: Mar Zutra objects: can there be a case where if the person himself does it he is exempt, but if he does it through an agent he is liable?
Rav Ashi responds that the person himself is not exempt, but rather he is subject to a more severe penalty (death) that exempts him from payment.

items.text: Reason for the Sages' exemption
items.text_en: Reason for the Sages' exemption
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if the case is slaughter by an agent, why do the Sages exempt? It answers that the Sages in the baraita are Rabbi Shimon, who holds that an improper slaughter is not considered slaughter.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if the case is slaughter by an agent, why do the Sages exempt?
The Gemara answers that the Sages in the baraita are Rabbi Shimon, who holds that an improper slaughter is not considered slaughter.

items.text: Distinction between Shabbat and other cases
items.text_en: Distinction between Shabbat and other cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Shabbat is different from idolatry and a gored ox, since slaughter on Shabbat is valid. It answers that the Sages follow Rabbi Yochanan HaSandlar, who holds that Shabbat labor is forbidden in benefit, making the slaughter improper. The Gemara then cites the Tosefta and the derivation from verses.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Shabbat is different from idolatry and a gored ox, since slaughter on Shabbat is valid according to the Mishnah.
The Gemara answers that the Sages follow Rabbi Yochanan HaSandlar, who holds that Shabbat labor is forbidden in benefit.

The Gemara cites a Tosefta where Rabbi Yochanan HaSandlar rules that food cooked on Shabbat by an intentional violator is forbidden forever, supporting the view that Shabbat labor renders the product forbidden in benefit.
The Gemara asks for the scriptural basis of Rabbi Yochanan HaSandlar's position.

Rabbi Chiyya derives from the verse 'ושמרתם את השבת כי קדש היא לכם' (keep the Shabbat for it is holy to you) that Shabbat labor products are forbidden in benefit like קדש (sacred items), but the word 'לכם' (to you) permits benefit for the person, and the death penalty for intentional violation excludes the unwitting violator.

items.text: Dispute on the status of Shabbat labor
items.text_en: Dispute on the status of Shabbat labor
items.desc_en: The Gemara records a dispute between Rav Acha and Ravina: one says the prohibition of Shabbat labor is biblical, the other says it is rabbinic. It explains the scriptural basis for each view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute between Rav Acha and Ravina regarding whether the prohibition of Shabbat labor (מעשה שבת) is biblical (דאורייתא) or rabbinic (דרבנן).
The first opinion holds that the prohibition is biblical, citing the earlier derivation from the verse 'קדש הוא' (it is holy).
The second opinion holds that the prohibition is rabbinic, interpreting the verse 'קדש הוא' (it is holy) to mean that only the day itself is holy, not its products.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Rabbis' exemption for slaughtering an ox that was gored or for idolatry
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Rabbis' exemption for slaughtering an ox that was gored or for idolatry
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Rabbis exempt one who slaughters an ox that was gored or for idolatry from the fourfold or fivefold penalty, given that these items are forbidden for benefit. Rabbi Meir, who holds one liable, is questioned: since slaughtering for idolatry renders the animal forbidden immediately, the slaughterer is not slaughtering his own property. The Gemara explains that Rabbi Meir's view applies when one worships the animal through the act of slaughter itself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Rabbis exempt one who slaughters an ox that was gored or for idolatry from the fourfold or fivefold penalty, given that these items are forbidden for benefit, and questions Rabbi Meir's view since slaughtering for idolatry renders the animal forbidden immediately, so the slaughterer is not slaughtering his own property.
Rava answers that Rabbi Meir's case is where one worships the animal through the act of slaughter itself, so the animal is not forbidden until the end of the slaughter.
The Gemara asks the same question regarding the ox that was gored, which is also forbidden for benefit, so the slaughterer is not slaughtering his own property.

Rava answers that the case involves a bailee who was guarding the ox when it gored and was sentenced, and Rabbi Meir follows Rabbi Yaakov (who holds that returning the ox to the owner after sentencing restores ownership) and Rabbi Shimon (who holds that a cause of money is like money).

Rav Kahana objects that the mishna's latter clause (Rabbi Shimon exempts in these two cases) implies Rabbi Shimon agrees with the Rabbis in the rest of the mishna, so the mishna cannot be entirely according to Rabbi Meir; Rav Zevid responds that the agreement is only regarding slaughter for medicine or dogs.

items.text: Rava's answer regarding slaughter for idolatry
items.text_en: Rava's answer regarding slaughter for idolatry
items.desc_en: Rava explains that Rabbi Meir's liability applies when the slaughterer worships the animal through the act of slaughter itself, meaning the animal is not yet forbidden until the act is complete, so it is still his property at the moment of slaughter.

sub.desc_en: Rava answers that Rabbi Meir's liability applies when the slaughterer worships the animal at the moment of completing the slaughter, so the animal is still the owner's property at the time of slaughter.

items.text: Rava's resolution for the ox that was gored and Rabbi Meir's position
items.text_en: Rava's resolution for the ox that was gored and Rabbi Meir's position
items.desc_en: Rava explains that the case of the ox that was gored involves a scenario where the ox was given to a guardian, gored in the guardian's domain, was warned there, and its trial concluded there. Rabbi Meir holds like Rabbi Yaakov, who says that if the guardian returned the ox to the owner after the trial, it reverts to the owner's liability, and like Rabbi Shimon, who considers a cause of money as money itself, citing a Mishnah where Rabbi Shimon holds one liable for consecrated animals for which he is responsible.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Rabbi Meir can hold the slaughterer liable for an ox that was stoned, since it is forbidden for benefit and thus not the owner's property.
Rava explains that the case involves an ox given to a guardian, which gored, was warned, and had its trial concluded in the guardian's domain.
Rava notes that Rabbi Meir holds like Rabbi Yaakov, who says that if the guardian returned the ox to the owner after the trial, liability reverts to the owner.

Rava adds that Rabbi Meir also holds like Rabbi Shimon, who considers a cause of money (דבר הגורם לממון) as money itself, citing a Mishnah where Rabbi Shimon holds one liable for consecrated animals for which he is responsible.

items.text: Rav Kahana's challenge and Rav Zevid's response
items.text_en: Rav Kahana's challenge and Rav Zevid's response
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana challenges Rava's explanation, noting that the Mishnah's latter clause states Rabbi Shimon exempts in these two cases, implying he agrees with the rest of the Mishnah. Rav Zevid responds that Rabbi Shimon only agrees with the case of slaughtering for medicine or for dogs, not the entire Mishnah.

sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana challenges Rav Zevid's explanation, arguing that the Mishnah's latter clause stating Rabbi Shimon exempts in two cases implies he agrees with the entire Mishnah.
Rav Zevid responds that Rabbi Shimon only agrees with the case of slaughtering for medicine or for dogs, not the entire Mishnah.

items.text: Rava's question to Rav Nachman about a stolen ox belonging to partners
items.text_en: Rava's question to Rav Nachman about a stolen ox belonging to partners
items.desc_en: Rava asks Rav Nachman: if one steals an ox belonging to two partners, slaughters it, and confesses to one of them, what is the law? Does the Torah's phrase 'five oxen' exclude half-oxen, or does it include even half-oxen? Rav Nachman answers that 'five oxen' means five whole oxen, not five half-oxen.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks Rav Nachman whether one who steals an ox belonging to two partners and slaughters it, then confesses to one partner, pays the full fivefold penalty or only half; Rav Nachman answers that the Torah said 'five oxen' and not 'five half-oxen', so he pays only half.

The Gemara objects from a baraita where one who steals from his father and slaughters after the father's death pays the full penalty, which is analogous to confessing to one partner, yet the baraita requires full payment.
Rav Nachman answers that the baraita deals with a case where the father had already stood trial, so the son's liability is established before the father's death.
The Gemara objects that if the father did not stand trial, the baraita should have distinguished within the same case rather than teaching a separate case.
Rav Nachman concedes that the baraita indeed teaches both cases, with the first case implying the father stood trial and the second case where the father died before trial.
The next morning, Rav Nachman retracts his earlier ruling and says that 'five oxen' includes even five half-oxen, explaining that he did not say so the night before because he was distracted.

items.text: Objection from the Mishnah and resolution
items.text_en: Objection from the Mishnah and resolution
items.desc_en: An objection is raised from the Mishnah: if one steals from his father, slaughters and sells, and then his father dies, he pays the fourfold or fivefold penalty. This seems analogous to confessing to one partner, yet the Mishnah requires payment. Rav Nachman answers that the case is where the father stood in judgment. The Gemara then questions why the Mishnah didn't distinguish this in the same clause, and Rav Nachman explains that the Mishnah's structure naturally pairs the two cases: one where the father dies after slaughter, and one where the father dies before slaughter.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from the Mishnah: one who steals from his father, slaughters and sells, and then the father dies, pays the fourfold or fivefold penalty, which seems analogous to confessing to one partner, yet the Mishnah requires payment.
Rav Nachman answers that the case is where the father stood in judgment before his death.
The Gemara questions why the Mishnah did not distinguish this condition in the same clause, since if the father did not stand in judgment, the thief would not pay.

Rav Nachman explains that the Mishnah's structure naturally pairs the two cases: one where the father dies after slaughter, and one where the father dies before slaughter, so the condition is implicit in the contrast.

items.text: Rav Nachman's retraction
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's retraction
items.desc_en: In the morning, Rav Nachman tells Rava that 'five oxen' includes even five half-oxen, explaining that he did not say so the previous night for a reason.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman retracts his previous ruling, stating that the Torah's phrase 'חמשה בקר' (five oxen) includes even five half-oxen, and explains why he withheld this the previous night.

items.text: Gemara's question and answer on the Mishnah's distinction
items.text_en: Gemara's question and answer on the Mishnah's distinction
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah distinguishes between the first clause (treifa found after slaughter) and the second clause (slaughtering a non-consecrated animal in the courtyard). Rav answers that in the first case, the entire animal is forbidden because it was slaughtered in a prohibited state, while in the second, only part is forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah distinguishes between the first clause (treifa found after slaughter) and the second clause (slaughtering a non-consecrated animal in the courtyard).
Rav answers that in the first case, the entire animal is forbidden because it was slaughtered in a prohibited state, while in the second, only part is forbidden.

items.text: Rav Chavivi's inference: slaughter is only at the end
items.text_en: Rav Chavivi's inference: slaughter is only at the end
items.desc_en: Rav Chavivi of Mechoza infers from the Mishnah that slaughter is valid only at the end. If slaughter were valid from beginning to end, then once a small amount was slaughtered, the animal would be forbidden, and the rest would not be considered slaughtering one's own animal.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chavivi infers from the Mishnah that slaughter (שחיטה) is valid only at the end (לבסוף), not from beginning to end.

Rav Chavivi argues that if slaughter were valid from beginning to end, once a small amount was slaughtered the animal would be forbidden, and the rest would not be considered slaughtering one's own animal.

items.text: Rav Huna's objection and Rav Ashi's rejection
items.text_en: Rav Huna's objection and Rav Ashi's rejection
items.desc_en: Rav Huna the son of Rava objects that the liability could be for the small amount slaughtered. Rav Ashi rejects this, arguing that the verse requires slaughtering the entire animal, which is not the case.

sub.text: Rav Huna the son of Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Huna the son of Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna the son of Rava objects that the liability could be for the small amount slaughtered (the portion done outside).
Rav Ashi rejects the objection, arguing that the verse requires slaughtering the entire animal (כולו), which is not the case here.

items.text: Rav Gamda's resolution: partial slaughter outside, completion inside
items.text_en: Rav Gamda's resolution: partial slaughter outside, completion inside
items.desc_en: Rav Gamda in the name of Rava resolves the difficulty by explaining the case as one where the animal was partially slaughtered outside the courtyard and completed inside, thus avoiding the problem.

sub.text: Rav Gamda in the name of Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Gamda in the name of Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Gamda resolves the difficulty by explaining that the case involves an animal partially slaughtered outside the courtyard and completed inside, so the slaughter is not entirely forbidden.

items.text: Alternate version: dispute between Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Alternate version: dispute between Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: An alternate version presents the dispute directly: Rabbi Shimon citing Rabbi Levi Saba holds slaughter is only at the end, while Rabbi Yochanan holds it is from beginning to end. Rav Chavivi then asks Rav Ashi whether Rabbi Yochanan holds that non-consecrated animals slaughtered in the Temple courtyard are not biblically prohibited.

sub.desc_en: The stam introduces an alternate version of the dispute: Rabbi Shimon citing Rabbi Levi Saba holds slaughter is only at the end, while Rabbi Yochanan holds it exists from beginning to end.

sub.text: Rav Chavivi of Mechoza to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Rav Chavivi of Mechoza to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rav Chavivi asks Rav Ashi whether Rabbi Yochanan's position implies that non-consecrated animals slaughtered in the Temple courtyard are not biblically prohibited.

items.text: Resolving the contradiction about slaughter for idolatry
items.text_en: Resolving the contradiction about slaughter for idolatry
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves a contradiction: if slaughter for idolatry is Torah-prohibited, the first cut would forbid the animal, so the second slaughterer wouldn't be liable. Rav Acha bar Rava suggests liability for the first cut, but Rav Ashi rejects this because 'and slaughtered' requires the whole animal. Rav Gamda cites Rava: liability applies when one cuts some simanim outside and completes them inside.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: if slaughter for idolatry is Torah-prohibited, the first cut would forbid the animal, so the second slaughterer wouldn't be liable for slaughtering his master's animal.
Rav Acha bar Rava answers that the liability applies to the first cut itself.
Rav Ashi rejects this, arguing that the verse 'וּטְבָחוֹ' (and they slaughtered) requires slaughter of the entire animal, which is absent here.
Rav Gamda cites Rava's resolution: liability applies when one cuts some simanim outside and completes them inside.

items.text: Mishnah: Divided testimony for theft and slaughter
items.text_en: Mishnah: Divided testimony for theft and slaughter
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents cases where witnesses testify about theft and slaughter. If both sets are found conspiring, the first pay double, the second pay four or five. If only the second are conspiring, the thief pays double and they pay four or five. If one of the second is conspiring, the second testimony is void; if one of the first is conspiring, all testimony is void because without theft there is no slaughter or sale.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the case where both theft and slaughter are testified by the same two witnesses who are found conspiring: they pay the full penalty (double for theft plus four/five for slaughter).

The Mishnah presents a second case: theft by one pair, slaughter/sale by another pair; if both pairs are found conspiring, the first pay double and the second pay threefold (four/five minus the double already paid).
The Mishnah states: if only the second pair are found conspiring, the thief pays double and the conspiring witnesses pay threefold.

The Mishnah concludes: if one of the second pair is conspiring, the second testimony is void; if one of the first pair is conspiring, all testimony is void because without theft there is no slaughter or sale.

items.text: Debate: Retroactive vs. future disqualification of conspiring witnesses
items.text_en: Debate: Retroactive vs. future disqualification of conspiring witnesses
items.desc_en: Abaye and Rava debate whether a conspiring witness is disqualified retroactively (from the time of testimony) or only from now on. Abaye argues retroactive disqualification because he was a wicked person from that moment. Rava argues it is a novelty, since both sets of witnesses are equal, so we only apply the penalty from the time of the novelty. An alternative version says Rava agrees with Abaye on retroactive disqualification, and the dispute is about something else.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a dispute between Abaye and Rava regarding whether a conspiring witness (עד זומם) is disqualified retroactively (למפרע) or only from now onward (מכאן ולהבא).

Abaye argues for retroactive disqualification because from the moment he testified, the witness became a wicked person (רשע), and the Torah says 'do not place a wicked person as a witness' (אל תשת רשע עד).

Rava argues for future disqualification because the law of conspiring witnesses is a novelty (חידוש), since both sets of witnesses are equally credible, so we only apply the penalty from the time of the novelty onward.
An alternative version states that Rava actually agrees with Abaye regarding retroactive disqualification, and the dispute is about a different matter.

items.text: Clarifying the dispute between Rava and Abaye
items.text_en: Clarifying the dispute between Rava and Abaye
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between Rava's view (disqualification is a novelty) and Abaye's view (disqualification is due to loss to buyers). It answers that the difference lies in a case where two witnesses testified about one matter and two about another, or where the witnesses are disqualified as robbers.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the reason for Abaye's view: disqualification is due to loss to buyers (פְּסֵידָא דְלָקוֹחוֹת).

The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between Rava's view (disqualification is a novelty) and Abaye's view (disqualification is due to loss to buyers), and answers that the difference lies in cases where two witnesses testified about one matter and two about another, or where the witnesses are disqualified as robbers.

The Gemara resolves that according to the version that disqualification is a novelty (חִידּוּשׁ), there is no difference in these cases, but according to the version that it is due to loss to buyers (פְּסֵידָא דְלָקוֹחוֹת), there is a difference.

items.text: Ruling in practice
items.text_en: Ruling in practice
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya from Difti reports that Rav Pappa acted in accordance with Rava, while Rav Ashi says the halakha follows Abaye, and the general rule is that the halakha follows Abaye in six specific cases (יע"ל קג"ם).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya from Difti reports that Rav Pappa ruled in practice according to Rava's position.
Rav Ashi states that the halakha follows Abaye's position.
The gemara concludes that the halakha follows Abaye in the six specific cases enumerated by the acronym יע"ל קג"ם.

items.text: Challenge from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Challenge from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah where witnesses testified about both theft and slaughter, were found to be conspiring regarding the theft, and then regarding the slaughter. If disqualification is retroactive, why should they pay for the slaughter? This challenges Abaye's view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah where witnesses testified about theft and slaughter, were found to be conspiring, and must pay everything.
The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah refers to a case where witnesses testified about theft and slaughter separately, and were found conspiring about both.

The Gemara objects: if disqualification is retroactive, once the witnesses were found conspiring about the theft, their testimony about slaughter was retroactively invalid, so why should they pay for slaughter?

items.text: Resolution: they were disqualified for slaughter first
items.text_en: Resolution: they were disqualified for slaughter first
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the case is where they were found to be conspiring regarding the slaughter first. But even so, when they are later found to be conspiring regarding the theft, they become retroactively disqualified. The Gemara concludes that the case is where they testified simultaneously and were then found to be conspiring.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the case is where they were found to be conspiring regarding the slaughter first.
The Gemara objects that even so, when they are later found to be conspiring regarding the theft, they become retroactively disqualified, so why should they pay for the slaughter?
The Gemara concludes that the case is where they testified simultaneously and were then found to be conspiring.

items.text: Tannaitic dispute about partial disqualification
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute about partial disqualification
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Tannaitic source: if two witnesses testified about theft and two about slaughter, and they were found to be conspiring regarding the theft, the entire testimony is void. If regarding the slaughter, the thief pays double and the witnesses pay threefold. Rabbi Yosei distinguishes between two testimonies and one testimony.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes to resolve the dispute by citing a Tannaitic source: if two witnesses testified about theft and two about slaughter, and they were found conspiring regarding the theft, the entire testimony is void.
The Tanna Kamma states: if the witnesses were found conspiring regarding the slaughter, the thief pays double payment and the witnesses pay threefold payment.
Rabbi Yosei distinguishes: the leniency applies only when there are two separate testimonies, but in a single testimony, partial disqualification voids the entire testimony.

items.text: Interpreting 'two testimonies' and 'one testimony'
items.text_en: Interpreting 'two testimonies' and 'one testimony'
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially explains that 'two testimonies' means two separate groups of witnesses, and 'one testimony' means one group testifying sequentially. But this leads to a contradiction regarding Rabbi Yosei's view. The Gemara reinterprets: 'two testimonies' means one testimony that is like two testimonies, i.e., one group testifying sequentially, but not one group testifying simultaneously.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'two testimonies' and 'one testimony' mean, proposing that 'two testimonies' means two separate groups and 'one testimony' means one group testifying sequentially.

The Gemara objects that according to Rabbi Yosei's view, if one group testifies sequentially and is disqualified on the sale, the entire testimony should be void, so how could the theft testimony still stand?

The Gemara resolves the difficulty by reinterpreting: 'two testimonies' means one testimony that is like two testimonies, i.e., one group testifying sequentially, but not one group testifying simultaneously.

items.text: Dispute about 'within the time of speech'
items.text_en: Dispute about 'within the time of speech'
items.desc_en: The Gemara assumes that everyone agrees that 'within the time of speech' is considered as speech. It then suggests that the dispute between the Rabbis and Rabbi Yosei is about whether disqualification is from that point forward or retroactive. The Rabbis hold it is from that point forward, so only the slaughter testimony is void; Rabbi Yosei holds it is retroactive, so both are void because the theft testimony was within the time of speech.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara establishes the shared assumption that 'within the time of speech' (תוך כדי דיבור) is considered as speech.

The Gemara proposes that the dispute is about whether disqualification is from that point forward (מכאן ולהבא) or retroactive (למפרע), explaining the Rabbis' position that only the slaughter testimony is void.
Rabbi Yosei holds that disqualification is retroactive (למפרע), so since the theft testimony was within the time of speech, both testimonies are void.

items.text: Alternative explanation: dispute about 'within the time of speech'
items.text_en: Alternative explanation: dispute about 'within the time of speech'
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative: everyone agrees that disqualification is retroactive, but they dispute whether 'within the time of speech' is considered as speech. The Rabbis hold it is not, while Rabbi Yosei holds it is.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes an alternative: if תוך כדי דיבור (within the time of speech) is considered as speech, then everyone agrees disqualification is retroactive.
The Gemara resolves that the dispute is about whether תוך כדי דיבור (within the time of speech) is considered as speech: the Rabbis hold it is not, while Rabbi Yosei holds it is.

items.text: Opening statement: Rabbi Yosei's position on 'toch kedei dibur'
items.text_en: Opening statement: Rabbi Yosei's position on 'toch kedei dibur'
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that Rabbi Yosei holds that retraction within 'toch kedei dibur' is considered retraction, unlike Rabbi Meir.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that Rabbi Yosei holds that retraction within 'toch kedei dibur' is considered retraction, unlike Rabbi Meir.

items.text: Challenge to Rabbi Yosei from a baraita and resolution
items.text_en: Challenge to Rabbi Yosei from a baraita and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Yosei's position from a baraita about a substitute offering, where Rabbi Yosei distinguishes between initial intent and retraction. Rav Pappa explains that the case involves retraction within 'toch kedei dibur', and the Gemara distinguishes between two types of 'toch kedei dibur'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Yosei's position by citing a baraita about a substitute offering where Rabbi Meir rules that the animal is a substitute for the first designation, implying Rabbi Yosei disagrees.
The baraita presents Rabbi Yosei's position: if he intended both from the start, his words stand; if he retracted, only the first designation is valid.
The Gemara questions why the baraita needs to mention retraction, as it seems obvious that retraction invalidates the second designation.
Rav Pappa explains that the baraita refers to retraction within 'תוך כדי דיבור' (the time it takes to speak a short phrase), which is not obvious.

The Gemara resolves the challenge by distinguishing two types of 'תוך כדי דיבור': Rabbi Yosei rejects the longer student-to-rabbit greeting time but accepts the shorter rabbi-to-student greeting time.

items.text: Rava's ruling: witnesses who were contradicted and then conspired are executed
items.text_en: Rava's ruling: witnesses who were contradicted and then conspired are executed
items.desc_en: Rava states that witnesses who were first contradicted (hukhreshu) and later found to be conspiring (huzammu) are executed, because contradiction is the beginning of conspiracy.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that witnesses who were contradicted and later found conspiring are executed, because contradiction is the beginning of conspiracy.

items.text: Rava's proof from a baraita about witnesses for a slave's injury
items.text_en: Rava's proof from a baraita about witnesses for a slave's injury
items.desc_en: Rava brings a baraita about witnesses who testified that a master blinded his slave's eye and knocked out his tooth, and were found to be conspiring. The Gemara analyzes the case, concluding that it involves two sets of witnesses, and the second set was contradicted by the first and then conspired. This proves that contradiction is the beginning of conspiracy.

sub.desc_en: Rava introduces a baraita about witnesses who testified that a master blinded his slave's eye and knocked out his tooth, and were found to be conspiring, concluding that they pay the value of the eye to the slave.

The Gemara questions the baraita's scenario, arguing that if there is only one set of witnesses, the payment of the eye's value is problematic because the slave is already freed and the master would not be satisfied.

The Gemara explains that the case involves two sets of witnesses: the first set testifies that the master knocked out the tooth first, then blinded the eye; the second set contradicts them, and the master prefers the second version.
The Gemara cites the baraita's conclusion that the second set of witnesses, found to be conspiring, pays the value of the eye to the slave.
The Gemara concludes from the baraita that contradiction (הכחשה) is the beginning of conspiracy (הזמה), supporting Rava's earlier ruling.

items.text: Abaye's objection and the Gemara's question
items.text_en: Abaye's objection and the Gemara's question
items.desc_en: Abaye objects that the baraita might refer to a case where the witnesses were reversed and then conspired, not simply contradicted. The Gemara asks for the source of this distinction.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects that the baraita does not prove the principle, because it may refer to a case where the witnesses were reversed and then conspired (הוכחשו והוזמו), not simply contradicted.
The Gemara asks: from where does Abaye derive this distinction between contradiction and reversal?

items.text: Gemara's initial deduction from the Mishnah's structure
items.text_en: Gemara's initial deduction from the Mishnah's structure
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the seifa (which involves flipping and hazamah) that the reisha also involves flipping and hazamah. It explains that the seifa's case is where the later witnesses admit to the wounding but are flipped and found zomemin, and the slave testifies accordingly.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the seifa (which involves flipping and hazamah) that the reisha also involves flipping and hazamah.
The Gemara explains that the seifa's case is where the later witnesses admit to the wounding but are flipped and found zomemin, and the slave testifies accordingly.

items.text: Clarifying the timing of the later witnesses' testimony
items.text_en: Clarifying the timing of the later witnesses' testimony
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the later witnesses came after or before the court's ruling. If they came after the ruling, the defendant is not yet liable; if before, the master would still owe the full value of the slave unless the case had already been adjudicated. It concludes that the case must be where the court had already ruled.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the case is set up: if the later witnesses came after the court's ruling, the defendant is not yet liable, so the master would still claim the full value of the slave.
The Gemara answers that the later witnesses must have come before the court's ruling, so the defendant is not yet liable for the full value.
The Gemara further questions: if the case had not yet been adjudicated, the master would still claim the full value of the slave, since the defendant is not yet liable.
The Gemara concludes that the case must be where the court had already ruled, so the defendant is already liable for the full value.

items.text: Rav Acha's challenge to Rava's proof
items.text_en: Rav Acha's challenge to Rava's proof
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika asks Rav Ashi: From where does Rava derive his proof? If from the reisha, the middle witnesses are not disproven because their testimony aligns with the court's ruling, so only the first witnesses are disproven.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika's question to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika's question to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika asks Rav Ashi: From where does Rava derive his proof?

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika's objection
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika's objection
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha argues that if Rava's proof is from the reisha (first clause), the middle witnesses are not disproven because their testimony aligns with the court's ruling, so only the first witnesses are disproven.

items.text: Rava's reasoning from the seifa and the principle of hakhashah
items.text_en: Rava's reasoning from the seifa and the principle of hakhashah
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that Rava holds both reisha and seifa involve three sets of witnesses. He deduces from the seifa that hakhashah (disproof) is the beginning of hazamah, because otherwise the first witnesses would not pay damages after being disproven.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that Rava holds both the reisha and seifa involve three sets of witnesses, and he deduces from the seifa.
Rava illustrates a case where two sets of witnesses contradict each other about the order of the slave's injuries, and the first set is found to be zomemim, paying damages to the master.
The gemara concludes that if הַכְחָשָׁה (disproof) were not the beginning of הֲזָמָה (perjury), the first witnesses would not pay damages; therefore, it must be.

items.text: Abaye's objection and Rabbi Zeira's counter
items.text_en: Abaye's objection and Rabbi Zeira's counter
items.desc_en: Abaye argues that the reisha requires three sets because the master testifies, but the seifa does not need three sets since the slave's testimony is self-serving (he wants freedom). Rabbi Zeira challenges this, suggesting the case might be about blinding the eye alone.

sub.desc_en: Abaye explains that the reisha (first clause) necessarily requires three sets because the master testifies, creating a dispute that needs a third set to resolve.
Abaye questions why the seifa (latter clause) would need three sets, since the slave's testimony is inherently self-serving.
Abaye explains that the slave will say anything to gain freedom, so his testimony is unreliable and does not create a genuine dispute requiring three sets.
Rabbi Zeira challenges Abaye, suggesting the case might be about blinding the eye alone, implying a different analysis.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Partial injury and payment
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Partial injury and payment
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one injures another's eye and knocks out a tooth, the payment is only for the eye or the tooth, not both, based on the verse 'under the eye' and 'under the tooth'.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule of payment for injury to eye or tooth, and the case of both.

items.text: Abaye's derivation from the verse
items.text_en: Abaye's derivation from the verse
items.desc_en: Abaye explains that the verse 'under the eye' excludes payment for both eye and tooth, and similarly 'under the tooth' excludes payment for both.

sub.desc_en: Abaye explains that the verse 'תַּחַת עֵינוֹ' (under his eye) excludes payment for both eye and tooth, and 'תַּחַת שִׁינּוֹ' (under his tooth) excludes payment for both tooth and eye.

items.text: Rav Idi bar Avin's support from a Mishnah on perjured witnesses
items.text_en: Rav Idi bar Avin's support from a Mishnah on perjured witnesses
items.desc_en: Rav Idi bar Avin brings a Mishnah where witnesses testified about theft and slaughter, were found perjured, and pay everything. The Gemara infers that contradiction (hachra'ah) is considered the beginning of perjury (hazamah), otherwise they would not pay for slaughter after being contradicted on theft.

sub.desc_en: Rav Idi bar Avin cites a Mishnah where witnesses who testified about theft and slaughter and were found perjured pay everything.
The Gemara infers that the witnesses testified on theft and slaughter, and were found perjured on both.
The Gemara objects that once perjured on theft, they are contradicted regarding slaughter, yet the Mishnah says they pay everything.
The Gemara concludes that contradiction (הכחשה) is considered the beginning of perjury (הזמה), otherwise they would not pay for slaughter.

items.text: Resolution: The case where witnesses were perjured on slaughter first, and the dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar
items.text_en: Resolution: The case where witnesses were perjured on slaughter first, and the dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the case is where witnesses were perjured on slaughter first, and it involves a dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar about whether witnesses who were contradicted and later perjured are executed. The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Elazar holds they are not executed, based on his statement that such witnesses receive lashes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the case is where the witnesses were perjured on the slaughter first.
The Gemara frames the dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar regarding witnesses who were contradicted and later perjured.
The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Elazar holds they are not executed, citing his statement that such witnesses receive lashes.
The Gemara objects that if Rabbi Elazar held they are executed, why would they receive lashes, since a negative commandment that carries a court-imposed death penalty does not incur lashes.
The Gemara concludes definitively that Rabbi Elazar holds they are not executed.

items.text: Objection to Rabbi Elazar's reasoning and Abaye's resolution
items.text_en: Objection to Rabbi Elazar's reasoning and Abaye's resolution
items.desc_en: An objection is raised: why would they receive lashes if they are two witnesses? Abaye answers that the case is where the victim came with the witnesses on his own (i.e., the witnesses were not a pair but one witness and the victim).

sub.desc_en: The gemara objects: why would they receive lashes (לוקין)? They are two pairs of witnesses (תרי ותרי נינהו), so why rely on one pair over the other?
Abaye answers that the case is where the victim came on his own (בא הרוג ברגליו), i.e., the witnesses were not a full pair but one witness and the victim himself.

items.text: Mishnah: Theft and slaughter on the testimony of one witness or self-admission
items.text_en: Mishnah: Theft and slaughter on the testimony of one witness or self-admission
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if one steals and slaughters or sells based on one witness or his own admission, he pays double but not four or five. It also lists other cases where only double is paid, and Rabbi Shimon distinguishes between consecrated property for which one is liable and that for which he is not.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that if one steals on the testimony of two witnesses but slaughters or sells on the testimony of one witness or his own admission, he pays double payment but not the fourfold or fivefold penalty.
The Mishnah lists additional cases where only double payment applies: slaughtering on Shabbat, for idolatry, after inheriting from the father, or after consecration.
Rabbi Shimon distinguishes between consecrated property for which one bears responsibility, where the fourfold or fivefold penalty applies, and that for which one does not, where he is exempt.

items.text: Gemara: Clarification of the Mishnah's novelty regarding self-admission
items.text_en: Gemara: Clarification of the Mishnah's novelty regarding self-admission
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah needs to state the case of one witness, and explains that it teaches that self-admission is analogous to one witness: just as one witness can join with another to obligate, so too self-admission can be joined by later witnesses, excluding Rav Huna's rule that one who admits to a fine before witnesses is exempt.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah needs to state the case of one witness, as it seems obvious.

The Gemara explains that the Mishnah teaches that self-admission is analogous to one witness: just as one witness can join with another to obligate, so too self-admission can be joined by later witnesses.
The Gemara concludes that the Mishnah's ruling excludes Rav Huna's rule that one who admits to a fine before witnesses is exempt.

items.text: Rav Huna's statement and the challenge from Rabban Gamliel's case
items.text_en: Rav Huna's statement and the challenge from Rabban Gamliel's case
items.desc_en: Rav Huna states that one who admits to a fine and then witnesses come is exempt. Rav Chisda challenges this from the story of Rabban Gamliel, who blinded his slave Tavi and was told by Rabbi Yehoshua that he is exempt only because there are no witnesses, implying that if there were witnesses he would be liable. Rav Huna distinguishes that Rabban Gamliel admitted not in court, but Rabbi Yehoshua was the head of the court.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna states in the name of Rav that one who admits to a fine (קנס) and then witnesses come is exempt.
Rav Chisda challenges Rav Huna from the case of Rabban Gamliel, who blinded his slave Tavi and was told by Rabbi Yehoshua that he is exempt only because there are no witnesses.
The Gemara infers from the story that if there were witnesses, Rabban Gamliel would be liable, implying that one who admits to a fine and then witnesses come is liable, contradicting Rav Huna.
Rav Huna distinguishes that Rabban Gamliel admitted not in court, but Rabbi Yehoshua was the head of the court, so the admission was not formal.

items.text: Resolving the contradiction between two baraitot
items.text_en: Resolving the contradiction between two baraitot
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction between two baraitot: one says 'you have no witnesses' and the other says 'you have already admitted.' It first suggests they dispute whether one who admits to a fine and then witnesses come is liable or exempt, but then resolves that both agree he is exempt; they dispute whether the admission was outside court or in court.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the scenario: the admission occurred outside court.
The Gemara cites a baraita where the judge says 'you have no witnesses' and another baraita where the judge says 'you have already admitted,' raising a contradiction.
The Gemara suggests the baraitot are a dispute: one Tanna holds that one who admits to a fine and then witnesses come is liable, the other holds he is exempt.
The Gemara rejects the suggestion, stating that all agree the admitter is exempt; the dispute is whether the admission was outside court (exempt) or in court (liable).

items.text: Rav and Shmuel dispute the law of one who admits to a fine
items.text_en: Rav and Shmuel dispute the law of one who admits to a fine
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel explicitly dispute the case: Rav says one who admits to a fine and then witnesses come is exempt, Shmuel says he is liable. Rava bar Ahilai explains Rav's reasoning from the verse 'if he is found' – referring to witnesses – 'he shall be found' – referring to judges, excluding one who incriminates himself. The Gemara questions why this verse is needed, as another verse already teaches this, and concludes that Rav's position is correct.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where the court tells the thief 'you have already admitted,' and questions whether this reflects a dispute about the law of one who admits to a fine.
The Gemara suggests that the baraita reflects a Tannaic dispute: one Tanna holds that one who admits to a fine and then witnesses come is liable, the other holds he is exempt.
The Gemara rejects this: all agree that one who admits to a fine and then witnesses come is exempt; the dispute is about whether the admission was outside court or in court.
The Gemara states the explicit dispute: Rav says one who admits to a fine and then witnesses come is exempt, Shmuel says he is liable.
Rava bar Ahilai explains Rav's reasoning: the verse 'אִם הִמָּצֵא תִמָּצֵא' (if he is found, he shall be found) refers to witnesses and judges, excluding one who incriminates himself.

The Gemara questions why this verse is needed, since the principle that one cannot incriminate oneself is already derived from 'אֲשֶׁר יַרְשִׁיעֻן' (whom they shall condemn), and concludes that Rav's position is correct.

items.text: Shmuel's alternative interpretation of the verse
items.text_en: Shmuel's alternative interpretation of the verse
items.desc_en: Shmuel explains that the verse is needed for the case of a thief who admits himself, as taught by the school of Hezekiah, not for the case of one who admits to a fine.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel responds that the verse 'אֲשֶׁר יַרְשִׁיעֻן' is needed for the case of a thief who incriminates himself, as taught in the school of Chizkiyah.

items.text: Rav's challenge to Shmuel from a baraita and Shmuel's response
items.text_en: Rav's challenge to Shmuel from a baraita and Shmuel's response
items.desc_en: Rav challenges Shmuel from a baraita where one who sees witnesses coming and admits to theft but not slaughter is only liable for the principal. Shmuel deflects by saying the case is where the witnesses retracted. The Gemara notes that the later clause of the baraita, where Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon says 'let witnesses come and testify,' implies the first Tanna disagrees. Shmuel then aligns himself with Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon.

sub.desc_en: Rav challenges Shmuel from a baraita where one who admits to theft but not slaughter upon seeing approaching witnesses pays only the principal.
Shmuel deflects by explaining the baraita deals with a case where the witnesses retracted.
The Gemara objects that the later clause, where Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon says 'let witnesses come and testify,' implies the first Tanna disagrees with Shmuel's interpretation.
Shmuel resolves the objection by aligning himself with Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon, who holds that witnesses can still testify even after an admission.

items.text: Rav's position even according to Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Rav's position even according to Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that for Shmuel the dispute is between Tannaim, but for Rav it is not necessarily so. Rav explains that even Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon would agree in a case where one admits voluntarily, as opposed to admitting out of fear of witnesses.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: For Shmuel the dispute is certainly between Tannaim, but for Rav, is it necessarily between Tannaim?
Rav explains that even Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon would agree in a case where one admits voluntarily, as opposed to admitting out of fear of witnesses.

items.text: Rav Hamnuna's distinction between admitting to theft and denying theft
items.text_en: Rav Hamnuna's distinction between admitting to theft and denying theft
items.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna clarifies Rav's ruling: if one says 'I stole' and witnesses come that he stole, he is exempt because he already obligated himself in the principal. But if he said 'I did not steal' and witnesses come that he stole, and then he says 'I slaughtered and sold' and witnesses come that he slaughtered and sold, he is liable because he had exempted himself entirely.

sub.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna states that Rav's ruling applies when one says 'I stole' and witnesses come that he stole, exempting him because he already obligated himself in the principal.
Rav Hamnuna distinguishes a case where one initially denied theft, then witnesses came, and later he admitted to slaughtering and selling, making him liable because he had exempted himself entirely.

items.text: Rava's challenge and support from Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Rava's challenge and support from Rabbi Yochanan
