items.desc_en: Rava challenges Rav Hamnuna's distinction by citing the case of Rabban Gamliel, who exempted himself entirely and yet was not held liable. The Gemara then cites Rabbi Yochanan who explicitly rules in accordance with Rav Hamnuna's distinction.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects to Rav Hamnuna's distinction by citing the case of Rabban Gamliel, who exempted himself entirely and yet was not held liable, and notes that Rav Chisda did not refute this to Rav Huna.

The Gemara cites Rabbi Yochanan who explicitly rules in accordance with Rav Hamnuna's distinction, supporting the position that one who initially denies the theft is liable for the additional penalty.

items.text: Rav Ashi's proof from the Mishnah and baraita
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's proof from the Mishnah and baraita
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi proves Rav's position from the Mishnah, which states that one who steals based on two witnesses and slaughters based on one witness or his own admission pays double but not four or five. The Gemara questions why the Mishnah specifies 'stole based on two witnesses' – it could have simply said 'stole and slaughtered based on one witness or his own admission, he pays only the principal.' This implies that if he admitted to theft, he is exempt from the fine even if witnesses later come.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi asserts that both the Mishnah and a baraita support Rav's position, citing the Mishnah's ruling that one who steals based on two witnesses and slaughters based on one witness or his own admission pays double but not four or five.

The Gemara questions why the Mishnah specifies 'stole based on two witnesses,' arguing it could have simply stated that one who steals and slaughters based on one witness or his own admission pays only the principal, implying that admission of theft exempts from the fine even if witnesses later come.

items.text: Distinction between admitting to theft alone vs. theft and slaughter
items.text_en: Distinction between admitting to theft alone vs. theft and slaughter
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that if one admits to theft before witnesses but not to slaughter, he is liable for the principal but exempt from the fourfold/fivefold penalty. However, if he admits to both theft and slaughter, the admission regarding slaughter is not comparable to that of a single witness.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that if one admits to theft before witnesses but not to slaughter, the admission is comparable to a single witness, and later witnesses join to obligate him.
The Gemara concludes that if one admits to both theft and slaughter, the admission regarding slaughter is not comparable to a single witness.

items.text: Baraita about admission in the presence of approaching witnesses
items.text_en: Baraita about admission in the presence of approaching witnesses
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where one says 'I stole but did not slaughter or sell' in the presence of approaching witnesses, and he pays only the principal. The Gemara infers that if he had denied the theft entirely and then admitted to slaughter after witnesses came, he would be liable for the fourfold/fivefold penalty, proving that an admission of slaughter alone is not effective.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where one admits to theft but denies slaughter in the presence of approaching witnesses, and pays only the principal.
The Gemara questions why the baraita specifies the admission of theft with denial of slaughter, rather than a simpler formulation of 'I stole or I slaughtered and sold'.

The Gemara explains that the baraita teaches that if one denied the theft entirely and later admitted to slaughter after witnesses came, he would be liable for the fourfold/fivefold penalty, proving that an admission of slaughter alone is not effective.

items.text: Alternative explanation: the baraita teaches a different principle
items.text_en: Alternative explanation: the baraita teaches a different principle
items.desc_en: Some say the baraita itself teaches that if one admits to theft but denies slaughter, even if witnesses later testify to slaughter, he is exempt. The reason is that the Torah requires payment of four or five, not four or three.

sub.desc_en: Some say the baraita itself teaches that if one admits to theft but denies slaughter, even if witnesses later testify to slaughter, he is exempt.
The reason is that the Torah requires payment of four or five, not four or three.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbis and Sumchos regarding contradictory testimony
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbis and Sumchos regarding contradictory testimony
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a case where two witnesses testify to theft and two to slaughter, and then one set is disqualified. The Rabbis and Sumchos disagree about the payments: the Rabbis say the thief pays double and the witnesses pay threefold, while Sumchos says the witnesses pay double and the thief pays threefold for an ox and twofold for a sheep. The Gemara questions Sumchos' position.

sub.text: Gemara's presentation of the Tannaic dispute
sub.text_en: Gemara's presentation of the Tannaic dispute
sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a Tannaic dispute: two witnesses testify to theft and two to slaughter; when the theft witnesses are disqualified, the Rabbis rule the thief pays double and the witnesses pay threefold.
Sumchos rules that the witnesses pay double and the thief pays threefold for an ox and twofold for a sheep.
The Gemara questions on which part of the baraita Sumchos disagrees: if on the first clause, does Sumchos reject the principle that testimony partially invalidated is entirely invalid?
The Gemara objects that if Sumchos disagrees on the latter clause, the Rabbis' position that the thief pays double and the witnesses pay threefold seems correct.

items.text: Sumchos' actual dispute: admission of slaughter under duress
items.text_en: Sumchos' actual dispute: admission of slaughter under duress
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the real dispute is about a case where witnesses say 'you stole,' and the thief admits to theft and slaughter but claims it was not in their presence. He then brings witnesses to disqualify them, and the owner brings witnesses to testify. The Rabbis hold that the admission of slaughter is valid and exempts him, while Sumchos holds it is not a valid admission.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the actual dispute between the Rabbis and Sumchos: a case where two witnesses say 'you stole,' the thief admits to theft and slaughter but claims it was not in their presence, then brings witnesses to disqualify them, and the owner brings witnesses to testify.
The Gemara states that the dispute revolves around the admission of slaughter (הודאת טביחה).
The Rabbis hold that even though the admission of theft is due to the witnesses, the admission of slaughter is valid and exempts him from the fourfold/fivefold payment.
Sumchos holds that since the admission of theft is due to the witnesses, the admission of slaughter is not a valid admission, so he is liable.
The Gemara concludes that the first witnesses who were disqualified pay the double payment (תשלומי כפל), and the thief pays three for the ox and two for the sheep.

items.text: Rav Acha's alternative: dispute about testimony that cannot be disqualified
items.text_en: Rav Acha's alternative: dispute about testimony that cannot be disqualified
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika says that everyone agrees that an admission of slaughter is not valid; rather, the dispute is about testimony that cannot be disqualified. The Rabbis hold such testimony is invalid, while Sumchos holds it is valid. The Gemara clarifies that this applies only when the witnesses do not know the exact time, but here they are merely supporting the thief's claim.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika rejects the previous interpretation and asserts that everyone agrees that an admission of slaughter is not valid.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika's alternative
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika's alternative
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika proposes that the dispute is about testimony that cannot be disqualified, describing a case where witnesses testify about a theft that occurred in front of others.
The Rabbis hold that such testimony, which cannot be disqualified, is invalid.
Sumchos holds that testimony which cannot be disqualified is valid.

The Gemara clarifies that the principle that testimony which cannot be disqualified is invalid applies only when the witnesses do not know the exact time, but here they are merely supporting the thief's claim.

items.text: Question about the witnesses paying double
items.text_en: Question about the witnesses paying double
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the witnesses can pay double when the thief already admitted to the theft and owes the principal. Rabbi Elazar cites a teaching from Rav that resolves this.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the witnesses can pay double (תשלומי כפל) when the thief already admitted to the theft and thus owes the principal (קרן).
Rabbi Elazar cites a teaching from Rav that resolves the difficulty, implying a baraita is to be taught.

items.text: Gemara's question on consecration
items.text_en: Gemara's question on consecration
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling that one who consecrates after stealing but before slaughtering is exempt from the four- or five-fold payment. It argues that while slaughtering consecrated property is not liable, consecration itself should be considered a sale to Heaven and thus liable.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah exempts one who consecrates after stealing but before slaughtering, noting that slaughtering consecrated property is not liable, but consecration itself should be considered a sale to Heaven.
The Gemara argues that consecration should be liable, comparing it to selling to a layperson, and asks why it is not treated the same.

items.text: First answer: Rabbi Shimon's view
items.text_en: First answer: Rabbi Shimon's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests the Mishnah follows Rabbi Shimon, who holds that consecrated animals for which the owner is liable for their upkeep remain in the owner's domain. However, it objects that the latter clause of the Mishnah is explicitly Rabbi Shimon, implying the first clause is not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Shimon, who holds that consecrated animals for which the owner is liable for their upkeep remain in the owner's domain.
The Gemara objects that since the latter clause of the Mishnah is explicitly Rabbi Shimon, the first clause cannot be Rabbi Shimon.

items.text: Second answer: Rabbi Yosei HaGelili and the distinction between sacrifices
items.text_en: Second answer: Rabbi Yosei HaGelili and the distinction between sacrifices
items.desc_en: The Gemara proposes the Mishnah deals with lesser sanctities (קדשים קלים) according to Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, who considers them the owner's property. It then questions why the Mishnah didn't explicitly distinguish between lesser and most holy sacrifices, as the latter would still be liable.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the Mishnah deals with lesser sanctities (קדשים קלים) according to Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, who holds they are the owner's property.
The Gemara objects that if the Mishnah only applies to lesser sanctities, it should have explicitly distinguished between lesser and most holy sacrifices, since the latter would still be liable.

items.text: Resolution: Distinction between sale to a person and to Heaven
items.text_en: Resolution: Distinction between sale to a person and to Heaven
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that in all cases of consecration, the animal remains the owner's property, so consecration is not a sale. The difference is that selling to a person transfers ownership, while consecrating does not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that consecration is not a sale because selling to a person transfers ownership from Reuben to Shimon, while consecrating leaves the animal in Reuben's ownership.

items.text: Reversal of Rabbi Shimon's ruling
items.text_en: Reversal of Rabbi Shimon's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Shimon's statement in the Mishnah seems reversed: he should have exempted when the owner is liable for upkeep (since the animal is still in his domain) and obligated when not liable.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Rabbi Shimon's ruling in the Mishnah appears reversed: he should have exempted when the owner is liable for upkeep and obligated when not.
The Gemara objects that for sacred animals whose upkeep the owner bears, he should be exempt because they have not left his domain.
The Gemara objects that for sacred animals whose upkeep the owner does not bear, he should be liable because they have left his domain.

items.text: Reinterpretation of Rabbi Shimon's statement
items.text_en: Reinterpretation of Rabbi Shimon's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Shimon is actually addressing a different matter: the liability of a second thief who steals from a thief. He rules that one who steals consecrated property from the owner is exempt, but if the owner is liable for upkeep, the thief is liable because the animal is still considered in the owner's house.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that Rabbi Shimon's statement is actually addressing a different matter.

The Gemara explains that the Mishnah actually teaches: one who steals from a thief does not pay the fourfold or fivefold penalty, and similarly one who steals consecrated property from the owner is exempt.
The Gemara explains the reason: the verse says 'and it is stolen from the house of the man' (וְגֻנַּב מִבֵּית הָאִישׁ), excluding consecrated property from the house of the Temple.

Rabbi Shimon rules: for consecrated property that the owner is liable for upkeep, the thief is liable because the verse 'from the house of the man' applies; for property not under the owner's liability, the thief is exempt.

items.text: Challenge from Rabbi Shimon's principle and resolution
items.text_en: Challenge from Rabbi Shimon's principle and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that Rabbi Shimon holds slaughter that is not fit (e.g., of consecrated animals) is not considered slaughter, so why would he obligate payment? Rav Dimi and Ravin cite Rabbi Yochanan: the case involves slaughtering unblemished animals inside the Temple for the owners (or not for the owners), where the blood was spilled, so the slaughter is valid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that since Rabbi Shimon holds that slaughter which is not fit (שחיטה שאינה ראויה) is not considered slaughter, slaughtering consecrated animals should also be unfit, so why would he obligate payment?
Rav Dimi reports that Rabbi Yochanan answers: the case involves slaughtering unblemished animals inside the Temple for the owners (לשם בעלים), making the slaughter fit.
The Gemara objects: but then the principal (קרן) would return to the owners, so the slaughter would not be a theft.
Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avin answers: the case is where the blood was spilled (נשפך הדם), so the animal was not returned to the owners.

Ravin reports that Rabbi Yochanan gives an alternative answer: the case involves slaughtering unblemished animals inside the Temple not for the owners (שלא לשם בעלים), so the slaughter is valid and the animal does not revert to the owners.

items.text: Reish Lakish's statement
items.text_en: Reish Lakish's statement
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish states that the liability for slaughtering blemished animals outside the Temple applies specifically to slaughtering them outside.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish states that the liability for slaughtering blemished animals outside the Temple applies specifically to slaughtering them outside.
Rabbi Elazar challenges Reish Lakish's statement by asking: according to Rabbi Yochanan, does slaughter permit the animal? Surely the sprinkling of blood permits it.
Rabbi Elazar further challenges: according to Reish Lakish, does slaughter permit the animal? Surely redemption permits it.

The Gemara resolves the challenge by citing Rabbi Shimon's principle: anything designated for sprinkling is considered as already sprinkled, and anything designated for redemption is considered as already redeemed.

sub.text: Supporting baraita for Rabbi Shimon's principle
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita for Rabbi Shimon's principle
sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita where Rabbi Shimon teaches that leftover sacrificial meat (נותר) before sprinkling does not convey food impurity, illustrating that what is designated for sprinkling is considered as already sprinkled.
The baraita explains: if the meat remained overnight before sprinkling, it does not convey food impurity; after sprinkling, it does convey food impurity.
The Gemara clarifies: 'before sprinkling' means before the animal was eligible for sprinkling; 'after sprinkling' means after it became eligible for sprinkling.
The Gemara explains: if the meat remained before eligibility for sprinkling, e.g., the animal was slaughtered close to sunset and there was no time to sprinkle, it does not convey food impurity.

The Gemara explains: if the meat remained after eligibility for sprinkling, i.e., there was time to sprinkle, it conveys food impurity, proving that what is designated for sprinkling is considered as already sprinkled.
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Shimon teaches that anything designated for redemption is considered as already redeemed, completing the support for Reish Lakish's position.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's challenge
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's challenge
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar challenges both Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish: for Rabbi Yochanan, slaughter cannot permit the animal since sprinkling the blood permits it; for Reish Lakish, slaughter cannot permit it since redemption permits it.

sub.text: Rabbi Elazar's challenge to Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's challenge to Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar challenges Rabbi Yochanan: slaughter cannot permit the animal, since sprinkling the blood (זריקה) is what permits it.

sub.text: Rabbi Elazar's challenge to Reish Lakish
sub.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's challenge to Reish Lakish
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar challenges Reish Lakish: slaughter cannot permit the animal, since redemption (פדייה) is what permits it.

items.text: Introduction of Rabbi Shimon's principle
items.text_en: Introduction of Rabbi Shimon's principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Elazar overlooked Rabbi Shimon's principle that anything designated for sprinkling or redemption is considered as if already performed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves Rabbi Elazar's difficulty by noting that he overlooked Rabbi Shimon's principle that anything designated for sprinkling or redemption is considered as if already performed.

items.text: Proof for the principle regarding sprinkling
items.text_en: Proof for the principle regarding sprinkling
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita where Rabbi Shimon distinguishes between leftover meat that became impure before it was eligible for sprinkling (not impure as food) and after it was eligible (impure as food), proving that something designated for sprinkling is considered as already sprinkled.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the principle that anything designated for sprinkling is considered as already sprinkled, citing a baraita of Rabbi Shimon.
Rabbi Shimon states that there is leftover meat (נותר) that imparts טומאת אוכלין (food impurity) and leftover meat that does not.
The Gemara asks how this works: meat that remained overnight before sprinkling does not impart food impurity, but after sprinkling it does.
The Gemara clarifies that 'before sprinkling' means before the meat became eligible for sprinkling, and 'after sprinkling' means after it became eligible.

The Gemara explains that meat that remained overnight before eligibility (e.g., slaughtered close to sunset) does not impart impurity, while meat that remained after eligibility does, proving the principle that what is designated for sprinkling is considered as already sprinkled.

items.text: Proof for the principle regarding redemption
items.text_en: Proof for the principle regarding redemption
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to cite a similar baraita for the principle that something designated for redemption is considered as already redeemed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara begins to cite a baraita of Rabbi Shimon to prove the principle that something designated for redemption is considered as already redeemed.

items.text: Opening statement about the cow
items.text_en: Opening statement about the cow
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that a cow imparts food impurity, since it had a moment of fitness (i.e., when it was slaughtered and permitted for consumption).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that a cow imparts food impurity (טומאת אוכלין) because it had a moment of fitness (שעת הכושר) when it was slaughtered and permitted for consumption.

items.text: Reish Lakish's statement about Rabbi Shimon's view
items.text_en: Reish Lakish's statement about Rabbi Shimon's view
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish states that Rabbi Shimon holds that a cow can be redeemed while on the altar pyre, implying that anything designated for redemption is considered already redeemed.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish states that Rabbi Shimon holds that a cow can be redeemed while on the altar pyre, implying that anything designated for redemption is considered already redeemed.

items.text: Gemara's question and Reish Lakish's reasoning
items.text_en: Gemara's question and Reish Lakish's reasoning
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Reish Lakish does not adopt Rabbi Yochanan's view. Reish Lakish explains that the verse 'and slaughtered it or sold it' implies that only items subject to sale are subject to slaughter; consecrated animals, which cannot be sold, are exempt from the payment for slaughter.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Reish Lakish does not adopt Rabbi Yochanan's view, given that Rabbi Yochanan's position is understandable.

Reish Lakish explains that the verse 'and slaughtered it or sold it' links slaughter to sale: only items subject to sale are subject to the payment for slaughter, and consecrated animals cannot be sold, so they are exempt.

items.text: The dispute about selling a tereifah
items.text_en: The dispute about selling a tereifah
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the same principle underlies a dispute: Rabbi Yochanan holds one liable for selling a tereifah, while Reish Lakish exempts. Rabbi Yochanan argues that even if not subject to slaughter, it is subject to sale; Reish Lakish argues that since it is not subject to slaughter, it is also not subject to sale.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish regarding selling a tereifah (טריפה, a mortally wounded animal) according to Rabbi Shimon's opinion.
Rabbi Yochanan holds the seller liable because even though the tereifah is not subject to slaughter (טביחה), it is subject to sale (מכירה).
Reish Lakish exempts the seller because since the tereifah is not subject to slaughter, it is also not subject to sale.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's challenge from a baraita
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's challenge from a baraita
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan challenges Reish Lakish with a baraita: one who steals a kil'ayim and slaughters it, or a tereifah and sells it, pays four or five. He suggests this follows Rabbi Shimon, showing that even without slaughter liability, sale liability exists.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan challenges Reish Lakish with a baraita: one who steals a kil'ayim and slaughters it, or a tereifah and sells it, pays four or five, implying that even without slaughter liability, sale liability exists.

items.text: Reish Lakish's response and the Gemara's analysis
items.text_en: Reish Lakish's response and the Gemara's analysis
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish deflects by saying the baraita follows the Rabbis, not Rabbi Shimon. The Gemara objects that for the Rabbis, a tereifah is subject to sale but not slaughter, while kil'ayim is subject to slaughter but not sale. The Gemara resolves that the baraita teaches one case and the other is analogous, or vice versa.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish responds that the baraita follows the Rabbis, not Rabbi Shimon.
The Gemara objects that for the Rabbis, a tereifah is subject to sale but not slaughter, while the baraita pairs kil'ayim with slaughter and tereifah with sale.
The Gemara further objects that if the baraita follows Rabbi Shimon, kil'ayim is subject to slaughter but not sale, yet the baraita pairs kil'ayim with slaughter and tereifah with sale.

The Gemara resolves that the baraita teaches one case explicitly and the other is analogous: for Rabbi Shimon, it teaches slaughter and the same applies to sale; for the Rabbis, it teaches sale and the same applies to slaughter.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's counter-argument
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's counter-argument
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan argues that if the baraita follows Rabbi Shimon, it makes sense to list tereifah and kil'ayim separately, but if it follows the Rabbis, they should have been combined. This creates a difficulty.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan argues that if the baraita follows Rabbi Shimon, it makes sense to list tereifah and kil'ayim separately, but if it follows the Rabbis, they should have been combined.
Rabbi Yochanan objects that if the baraita follows the Rabbis, the cases of tereifah and kil'ayim should have been combined into a single clause, creating a difficulty.

items.text: Discussion of kil'ayim and the word 'seh'
items.text_en: Discussion of kil'ayim and the word 'seh'
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the exclusion of kil'ayim from the term 'seh', but notes that here the word 'or' includes it. Rava distinguishes between contexts: in theft, 'or' includes kil'ayim; in consecrated animals, 'or' excludes it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by noting that the word 'seh' (שֶׂה) excludes kil'ayim (כלאים), citing Rava's principle that wherever 'seh' appears, it excludes kil'ayim.
The Gemara answers that here the word 'or' (אוֹ) includes kil'ayim, distinguishing this context from the general rule.
The Gemara objects by citing a baraita where 'or' (אוֹ) excludes kil'ayim and a nidmeh (נדמה), questioning whether 'or' always includes.

Rava resolves the contradiction by distinguishing contexts: in theft (גניבה), 'or' includes kil'ayim because the verse cannot exclude them; in consecrated animals (קדשים), 'or' excludes them because the verse can.

items.text: Gemara's challenge to Rava's principle
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge to Rava's principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the phrase 'shor o kesev' in consecrated animals is meant to exclude kil'ayim or to include it, and argues that two exclusions are needed (for kil'ayim and nidmeh) whereas two inclusions would be superfluous.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rava's principle by noting that in consecrated animals the phrase 'שׁוֹר אוֹ כֶשֶׂב' could be interpreted either to exclude kil'ayim or to include it, and argues that the two occurrences could be read consistently either as exclusions or inclusions.

The Gemara objects that if the phrase is meant to exclude, two exclusions are needed (for kil'ayim and nidmeh), but if meant to include, two inclusions would be superfluous since once kil'ayim is included, nidmeh would certainly be included.

items.text: Rava's principle applied to various contexts
items.text_en: Rava's principle applied to various contexts
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rava's statement that 'seh' excludes kil'ayim is not needed for consecrated animals (where it is explicit), for tithes (derived via gezerah shavah), or for firstborns (derived via gezerah shavah), and that nidmeh is excluded by a different verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces Rava's principle that wherever 'שה' (a sheep) is stated, it excludes kil'ayim (a hybrid animal).

The Gemara asks for what halachic context Rava's principle is needed, noting that for consecrated animals (קדשים) the exclusion of kil'ayim is already explicit in the verse 'שור או כשב' (a bull or a sheep).

The Gemara answers that for tithes (מעשר), the exclusion is derived via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the word 'תחת' (under) used in both contexts, so Rava's principle is not needed there either.

The Gemara further answers that for firstborns (בכור), the exclusion is derived via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the word 'העברה' (passing over) used in both contexts, so Rava's principle is not needed there either.

The Gemara concludes that for nidmeh (a firstborn that resembles another species), it is excluded by the verse 'אך בכור שור' (only a firstborn bull), so Rava's principle is not needed for that either, leaving the question of why Rava's principle is necessary.

items.text: Rava's principle applied to petter chamor
items.text_en: Rava's principle applied to petter chamor
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that Rava's statement was actually said regarding the redemption of a firstborn donkey, citing a mishnah that lists items not valid for redemption, including kil'ayim.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that Rava's principle was actually stated regarding the redemption of a firstborn donkey (פטר חמור), citing a mishnah that lists invalid redemption items including kil'ayim (mixed-breed animals).

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's dispute and Rava's principle for a pure animal from an impure one
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's dispute and Rava's principle for a pure animal from an impure one
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Elazar permits kil'ayim for petter chamor, and explains that Rava's principle applies to a pure animal born from an impure one, disagreeing with Rabbi Yehoshua who derives the law from 'seh kesavim ve-seh izim'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: for Rabbi Elazar who permits kil'ayim (a hybrid animal) for redeeming a firstborn donkey (פטר חמור), what practical halachic purpose does Rava's principle serve?
Rabbi Elazar answers that Rava's principle applies to an impure animal born from a pure mother but conceived from an impure father.

The Gemara clarifies that this answer disagrees with Rabbi Yehoshua, who derives from the verse 'שֵׂה כְשָׂבִים וְשֵׂה עִזִּים' (a sheep of rams and a sheep of goats) that both parents must be sheep for the offspring to be called a 'שֶׂה' (sheep).

items.text: Clarification: can a pure animal become pregnant from an impure one?
items.text_en: Clarification: can a pure animal become pregnant from an impure one?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a pure animal can become pregnant from an impure one, and answers in the affirmative, citing a known principle.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a pure (טהורה) animal can become pregnant from an impure (טמאה) one.
The Gemara answers in the affirmative, citing a known principle that such pregnancy is possible.

items.text: Rava's question about a stolen animal designated for a vow
items.text_en: Rava's question about a stolen animal designated for a vow
items.desc_en: Rava asks whether a thief who stole an animal that was set aside for a burnt-offering can fulfill his obligation with a cheaper animal, depending on whether the vow is tied to the specific animal or to the value. The Gemara resolves the question by stating that the thief can pay with a lamb according to the Rabbis, or with a bird according to Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks whether a thief who stole an animal designated for a burnt-offering can fulfill his obligation with a cheaper animal, depending on whether the vow is tied to the specific animal or to the value.
The Gemara clarifies the two sides of the doubt: whether the vow is tied to the specific animal or to the value.
The Gemara resolves the question: the thief can pay with a lamb according to the Rabbis, or with a bird according to Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya.

sub.text: Rav Acha brei d'Rav Ika's alternative version
sub.text_en: Rav Acha brei d'Rav Ika's alternative version
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha brei d'Rav Ika transmits the resolution explicitly as a direct statement from Rava.

items.text: Mishnah: Selling an animal except for a part
items.text_en: Mishnah: Selling an animal except for a part
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one sells an animal except for one part in a hundred, or if there was partnership, or if the animal was slaughtered improperly, the thief pays double payment but not fourfold or fivefold payment.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that selling an animal except for one part in a hundred, or partnership, or improper slaughter exempts from fourfold or fivefold payment.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah and dispute between Rav and Levi
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah and dispute between Rav and Levi
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the Mishnah's phrase 'except for one part in a hundred' with a dispute between Rav (who says it refers to something that must be slaughtered with the animal) and Levi (who says it refers to its wool). A baraita supports Levi. The Gemara then reconciles Rav's view with a Tanna, and explains the underlying principles of the Tannaitic dispute regarding what constitutes a valid sale for the fourfold/fivefold payment.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah means by 'except for one part in a hundred'.
Rav explains that it refers to something that must be slaughtered with the animal.
Levi explains that it refers to its wool.
A baraita supports Levi's interpretation.
The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita listing various excluded parts and their payment implications.
The Gemara asks: Levi aligns with the first Tanna, but with whom does Rav align?
The Gemara answers that Rav aligns with the Tanna who holds that limbs requiring slaughter are excluded, but wool is not.
The Gemara asks: What is the underlying dispute between the Tannaim?
The first Tanna holds that the verse requires the entire animal to be slaughtered or sold.
Rabbi holds that slaughter applies only to what requires slaughter, and sale is analogous.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar holds that a horn, which is not meant to be cut, is a reservation, but wool, which is meant to be cut, is not.
Another Tanna holds that limbs requiring slaughter are a reservation, but horn and wool are not.
The Gemara resolves the apparent contradiction between the two statements of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar by attributing them to two different Tannaim.

items.text: Dispute about partners who steal
items.text_en: Dispute about partners who steal
items.desc_en: A baraita states that a thief who steals a lame, blind, or partnership animal is liable, but partners who steal are exempt. Another baraita contradicts this, saying partners who steal are liable. Rav Nachman resolves the contradiction: one refers to a partner stealing from his fellow, the other to a partner stealing from outsiders. Rava objects, citing a verse requiring the entire animal to be sold, so Rav Nachman offers a different resolution: one case is where the partner slaughters with the other's consent, the other without consent.

sub.desc_en: A baraita rules that a thief who steals a lame, blind, or partnership animal is liable, but partners who steal are exempt.
The gemara raises a contradiction by citing another baraita that states partners who steal are liable.
Rav Nachman resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a partner stealing from his fellow (exempt) and a partner stealing from outsiders (liable).
Rava objects, citing a verse that requires the entire animal to be sold, which is impossible when a partner steals from his fellow.
Rav Nachman offers a different resolution: one case is where the partner slaughters with the other's consent (exempt), the other without consent (liable).

items.text: Rabbi Yirmeya's question about selling an animal except for its fetus
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's question about selling an animal except for its fetus
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks whether selling an animal except for its thirty days, its labor, or its fetus constitutes a valid sale for the fourfold/fivefold payment. The Gemara distinguishes between the opinion that the fetus is considered a limb of the mother (in which case it is a valid reservation) and the opinion that it is not. The question remains unresolved (Teiku).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks whether selling an animal except for its thirty days, its labor, or its fetus constitutes a valid sale for the fourfold/fivefold payment.
The Gemara clarifies that according to the opinion that the fetus is considered a limb of the mother, the question is unnecessary because the reservation is valid.
The Gemara reframes the question according to the opinion that the fetus is not a limb of the mother.
The Gemara presents two possibilities: since the fetus is attached to the mother, it is considered a reservation; or since it is destined to separate, it is not.
An alternative formulation: since the fetus is not a limb, it is not a reservation; or since it requires slaughter together with the mother, it is considered a reservation in the body.
The question remains unresolved (Teiku).

items.text: Rav Pappa's question about cutting off a limb and selling
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's question about cutting off a limb and selling
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks: if one stole an animal, cut off a limb, and then sold it, is he liable for fourfold/fivefold payment? The question is whether the sale is considered a sale of what was stolen (which is incomplete) or whether the reservation is not significant. The question remains unresolved (Teiku).

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks whether one who stole an animal, cut off a limb, and then sold it is liable for fourfold/fivefold payment, and the question remains unresolved (Teiku).

items.text: Baraita: Thief gives to another to slaughter or sell
items.text_en: Baraita: Thief gives to another to slaughter or sell
items.desc_en: A baraita begins discussing cases where a thief gives the stolen animal to another person to slaughter or sell, implying further discussion of liability.

sub.desc_en: The baraita introduces cases where a thief gives the stolen animal to another person to slaughter or sell, setting up the discussion of liability.

items.text: Opening Mishnah and Gemara's explanation
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and Gemara's explanation
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists cases where a thief consecrates, exchanges, or gives away the stolen animal and still pays the fourfold or fivefold penalty. The Gemara explains that the first clause teaches that there is a shaliach for a transgression here, unlike elsewhere, and the latter clause teaches that selling to Heaven (consecration) is like selling to a commoner.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists cases where a thief consecrates, exchanges, or gives away the stolen animal and still pays the fourfold or fivefold penalty.
The Gemara asks what novel point the Mishnah teaches.
The Gemara explains that the first clause teaches that there is a shaliach for a transgression here, unlike elsewhere, based on the analogy of 'וּטְבָחוֹ' and 'וּמְכָרוֹ'.
The Gemara explains that the latter clause teaches that selling to Heaven (consecration) is like selling to a commoner.

items.text: Second Mishnah: liability based on location of theft and slaughter
items.text_en: Second Mishnah: liability based on location of theft and slaughter
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if the theft occurred in the owner's domain and the slaughter or sale outside, or vice versa, or both outside, the thief pays the fourfold or fivefold penalty. But if both theft and slaughter/sale occurred in the owner's domain, he is exempt. It also discusses cases of pulling the animal out and death.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the liability for the fourfold or fivefold penalty depends on whether the theft and slaughter/sale occurred inside or outside the owner's domain.
The Mishnah adds that if the thief was pulling the animal out and it died in the owner's domain he is exempt, but if he lifted it or took it out he is liable.

items.text: Gemara's inquiry: Did the Sages institute meshikhah for bailees?
items.text_en: Gemara's inquiry: Did the Sages institute meshikhah for bailees?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Sages instituted meshikhah (acquisition by pulling) for bailees. Rav Yemar attempts to prove from the Mishnah's case of giving the animal to a bailee that meshikhah was instituted, but is initially rebutted that the case refers to a thief. Rav Ashi rejects the rebuttal and concludes that indeed meshikhah was instituted for bailees, and Rabbi Elazar and a baraisa support this.

sub.desc_en: Amemar asks whether the Sages instituted meshikhah (acquisition by pulling) for bailees.
Rav Yemar attempts to prove from the Mishnah's case of giving the animal to a bailee that meshikhah was instituted.
An anonymous rebuttal rejects Rav Yemar's proof, claiming the Mishnah's case refers to a thief, not a bailee.
Rav Yemar objects that the Mishnah already taught the case of a thief, so the later clause must refer to a bailee.
Rav Ashi rejects the rebuttal, arguing that there is no difference between a thief who stole from a bailee and one who stole from the owner.
Rav Ashi concludes that the Mishnah indeed refers to a bailee, proving that meshikhah was instituted for bailees.
Rabbi Elazar explicitly states that meshikhah was instituted for bailees just as for buyers.
A baraita supports the ruling, adding that land is acquired by money, document, or chazakah, and rental is similarly acquired.

items.text: Baraisa on acquisition methods and question about rental
items.text_en: Baraisa on acquisition methods and question about rental
items.desc_en: A baraisa states that just as meshikhah was instituted for buyers, so too for bailees, and land is acquired by money, document, or hazakah, so too rental is acquired by these means. The Gemara then asks: what type of rental?

sub.desc_en: A baraisa supports the previous ruling by stating that just as meshikhah was instituted for buyers, so too for bailees, and land is acquired by money, document, or hazakah, so too rental is acquired by these means.
The Gemara asks: what type of rental is being referred to in the baraisa?

items.text: Clarification of 'hiring' in the Mishnah
items.text_en: Clarification of 'hiring' in the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's reference to 'hiring' applies to movable property, since movables are acquired by a document. Rav Chisda explains that it refers to hiring of land.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: since movables are acquired by a document, how can the Mishnah refer to 'hiring' of movables?
Rav Chisda answers that the Mishnah's 'hiring' refers to hiring of land, not movables.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's case of a thief hiding in the woods
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's case of a thief hiding in the woods
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar rules that if witnesses saw a thief hide in the woods, then slaughter and sell the animal, he pays the fourfold or fivefold penalty. The Gemara questions how he acquired the animal without a meshichah. Rav Chisda answers that he struck it with a stick, effecting acquisition.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar rules that if witnesses saw a thief hide in the woods, then slaughter and sell the animal, he pays the fourfold or fivefold penalty.
The Gemara questions how the thief acquired the animal without performing מְשִׁיכָה (pulling) to effect acquisition.
Rav Chisda answers that the thief struck the animal with a stick, effecting acquisition through a valid act of קניין (acquisition).

items.text: Distinction between a thief and a robber
items.text_en: Distinction between a thief and a robber
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that since witnesses saw the thief, he is a robber, but since he hides from them, he is a thief. It then defines a robber: Rabbi Abahu cites the example of Benaiah ben Yehoyada, and Rabbi Yochanan cites the example of the people of Shechem. The Gemara explains why each rejects the other's proof.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the thief can be considered a thief if witnesses saw him, and resolves that since he hides from them, he is a thief.
Rabbi Abahu defines a robber by citing the example of Benaiah ben Yehoyada, who openly took the spear from the Egyptian.
Rabbi Yochanan defines a robber by citing the example of the people of Shechem, who ambushed and robbed passersby.

The Gemara explains why Rabbi Abahu rejects Rabbi Yochanan's proof (the Shechemites hid, so they are not robbers) and why Rabbi Yochanan rejects Rabbi Abahu's proof (Benaiah's victim was a single person, not a general case).

items.text: Why the Torah is stricter with a thief than a robber
items.text_en: Why the Torah is stricter with a thief than a robber
items.desc_en: Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai explains that a thief equates the honor of the servant (man) to the honor of his Master (God), as if God does not see or hear. The Gemara supports this with verses from Isaiah and Psalms.

sub.desc_en: The students ask Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai why the Torah is stricter with a thief than with a robber.
Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai answers that the thief equates the honor of the servant (man) to the honor of his Master (God), while the robber does not.
The Gemara supports the answer with verses from Isaiah and Psalms, showing that the thief acts as if God does not see or hear.

items.text: Parable of the two banquets and the reason for the difference in penalties
items.text_en: Parable of the two banquets and the reason for the difference in penalties
items.desc_en: Rabbi Meir relates a parable from Rabban Gamliel comparing a thief to a robber. Rabbi Meir and Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai offer different reasons for why the penalty for stealing an ox (fivefold) is greater than for a sheep (fourfold).

sub.text: Baraita citing Rabbi Meir in the name of Rabban Gamliel
sub.text_en: Baraita citing Rabbi Meir in the name of Rabban Gamliel
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Meir introduces a parable from Rabban Gamliel comparing two banquet hosts, one who invited townspeople but not the king's children, and asks which is more severely punished.
Rabbi Meir explains that the ox's greater penalty (fivefold) is because it is taken from work, while the sheep (fourfold) is not taken from work.

sub.text: Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's alternative explanation
sub.text_en: Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's alternative explanation
sub.desc_en: Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai offers a different reason: the ox's greater penalty is because it walks on its own (less degrading to carry), while the sheep is carried on the shoulder (more degrading), so the penalty is lower.

items.text: Mishnah: Prohibition of raising small cattle and other restrictions
items.text_en: Mishnah: Prohibition of raising small cattle and other restrictions
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not raise small cattle in the Land of Israel, but may do so in Syria and deserts of Israel. It also prohibits raising chickens in Jerusalem due to sacrifices, and priests raising them in Israel due to purity. Pigs are prohibited everywhere, dogs must be chained, and traps for pigeons must be thirty ris from a settlement.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating the prohibition of raising small cattle in the Land of Israel, with exceptions for Syria and the deserts of Israel.
The Mishnah adds the prohibition of raising chickens in Jerusalem due to sacrifices, and for priests in Israel due to purity.
The Mishnah concludes with prohibitions on pigs everywhere, dogs without chains, and pigeon traps within thirty ris of a settlement.

items.text: Gemara: Exceptions and details of the prohibition of small cattle
items.text_en: Gemara: Exceptions and details of the prohibition of small cattle
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites baraitot that allow raising small cattle in forests of Israel and in Syria even in settled areas. It explains that the prohibition is because small cattle can be imported from outside the land, unlike large cattle. It also permits keeping a small animal for thirty days before a festival or a son's wedding, but not beyond that if the festival has passed.

sub.desc_en: The first baraita states the prohibition of raising small cattle in settled areas of Eretz Yisrael, but permits it in forests and in Syria even in settled areas.

A second baraita adds that small cattle may be raised in the desert of Yehuda and the desert near Akko, and explains that the sages did not decree on large cattle because most of the community could not bear it.
The Gemara explains the rationale: small cattle can be imported from outside the land, so the prohibition applies, whereas large cattle cannot be imported, so they are permitted.
A third baraita permits keeping a small animal for thirty days before a festival or a son's wedding, but forbids keeping the last one beyond thirty days if the festival has passed.

The Gemara resolves a potential misunderstanding: one might think that if the festival passed and thirty days have not yet elapsed, keeping the animal is still permitted, but the baraita clarifies that once the festival has passed, one may not keep it any longer.

items.text: The Mishnah and the students' question to Rabban Gamliel
items.text_en: The Mishnah and the students' question to Rabban Gamliel
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a butcher may buy and slaughter, but may not delay the sale of the animal for more than thirty days. The students ask Rabban Gamliel about raising small cattle, and he permits it, but the Gemara notes a contradiction with a previous ruling. The Gemara clarifies that the students actually asked about delaying the sale, and Rabban Gamliel permits it as long as the animal is tied up and not allowed to graze with the herd.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a butcher may buy and slaughter, but may not delay selling the animal for more than thirty days.
The students ask Rabban Gamliel whether one may raise small cattle, and he permits it.
The Gemara objects that a previous ruling forbids raising small cattle, contradicting Rabban Gamliel's permission.
The Gemara clarifies that the students actually asked about delaying the sale, and Rabban Gamliel permits it only if the animal is tied up and not allowed to graze with the herd.

items.text: The story of the pious man and the goat
items.text_en: The story of the pious man and the goat
items.desc_en: The Gemara relates a story of a pious man who was ill and needed to drink hot goat's milk daily. His friends saw the goat tied to his bed and refused to enter, calling him a robber. They investigated and found no sin except that he had violated the prohibition against raising small cattle. On his deathbed, he admitted this was his only sin.

sub.desc_en: The baraita introduces a story of a pious man who was ill and needed to drink hot goat's milk daily, so they brought a goat and tied it to his bed.
The pious man's friends saw the goat tied to his bed and refused to enter, calling him a robber.
The friends investigated and found no sin except the goat; on his deathbed, the pious man admitted this was his only transgression.

items.text: Rabbi Yishmael's explanation for the destruction of his family
items.text_en: Rabbi Yishmael's explanation for the destruction of his family
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael explains that his family in the Upper Galilee was destroyed because they grazed their cattle in forests and judged monetary cases alone, even though they had forests near their homes.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael states that his family in the Upper Galilee was destroyed because they grazed cattle in forests and judged monetary cases alone, despite having forests near their homes.

items.text: Laws of selling inherited animals and vows
items.text_en: Laws of selling inherited animals and vows
items.desc_en: The Gemara teaches that a shepherd who repents is not required to sell his animals immediately, but may sell them gradually. Similarly, a convert who inherits dogs and pigs may sell them gradually. A person who vows to buy a house or marry a woman in the Land of Israel is not required to do so immediately. A story is told of a woman who vowed to accept any suitor, and the Sages ruled that she only intended a suitable one.

sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches that a repentant shepherd is not forced to sell his animals immediately, but sells them gradually.
The baraita extends the same gradual sale rule to a convert who inherits dogs and pigs.
The baraita adds that one who vows to buy a house or marry a woman in the Land of Israel is not required to do so immediately, but only when finding a suitable match.
A story is told of a woman who vowed to accept any suitor, and the Sages ruled that she only intended a suitable one.

items.text: Prohibition of raising small animals and exceptions
items.text_en: Prohibition of raising small animals and exceptions
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that just as one may not raise small cattle, one may not raise small wild animals. Rabbi Yishmael permits raising certain animals like dogs, cats, monkeys, and certain rodents because they help clean the house. The Gemara explains the types of rodents mentioned.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma states that just as one may not raise small cattle, one may not raise small wild animals.
Rabbi Yishmael permits raising certain animals like dogs, cats, monkeys, and certain rodents because they help clean the house.
The Gemara asks what are the specific rodents mentioned by Rabbi Yishmael.
Rav Yehuda identifies the rodents as 'שרצא חרצא' (a type of small rodent).
An alternative opinion identifies the rodent as 'חרזא' (a type of weasel) with thin legs that grazes among roses.
The Gemara asks what is the meaning of the term 'שרצא'.
The Gemara explains that 'שרצא' refers to a rodent whose legs are short (low to the ground).

items.text: The status of Babylonia regarding small cattle
items.text_en: The status of Babylonia regarding small cattle
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says in the name of Rav that they considered Babylonia like the Land of Israel regarding the prohibition of raising small cattle. Rav Adda bar Ahavah asks Rav Huna about his own animals, and Rav Huna says they are guarded by a dog. Rav Adda bar Ahavah curses the dog, and it is said that Rav Huna had no children from that dog. Another version says Rav said this after he came to Babylonia.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says in the name of Rav that they considered Babylonia like the Land of Israel regarding the prohibition of raising small cattle.

sub.text: Rav Adda bar Ahavah to Rav Huna
sub.text_en: Rav Adda bar Ahavah to Rav Huna
sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahavah asks Rav Huna about the status of his own animals.
Rav Huna answers that his animals are guarded by a dog.
Rav Adda bar Ahavah curses the dog, saying it should bury its children.
The gemara reports that throughout Rav Adda bar Ahavah's life, Rav Huna had no children from that dog.
An alternative version attributes the statement to Rav Huna in the name of Rav, adding that Rav said this after he came to Babylonia.

items.text: Rav's refusal to enter before Shmuel
items.text_en: Rav's refusal to enter before Shmuel
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins a story about Rav, Shmuel, and Rav Assi who went to the house of Shevu'a the son, and Rav did not enter before Shmuel.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that Rav, Shmuel, and Rav Assi went to the house of Shevu'a the son, and Rav did not enter before Shmuel.

items.text: Background: Samuel's avoidance of Rav Asi and Rav
items.text_en: Background: Samuel's avoidance of Rav Asi and Rav
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why Samuel did not appear before Rav Asi, and Rav Asi did not appear before Rav, due to a prior incident where Rav cursed Samuel. It is suggested that Samuel should be the one to go to them.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that Samuel did not appear before Rav Asi, and Rav Asi did not appear before Rav, and proposes that Samuel should be the one to go to them.
The Gemara questions why Rav or Rav Asi should not be the ones to go to Samuel.
The Gemara answers that Rav only did a minor thing to Samuel, but because of the incident where Rav cursed him, Rav gained authority over him.

items.text: Rav's ruling about a cat that bit a child
items.text_en: Rav's ruling about a cat that bit a child
items.desc_en: A cat cuts off a child's hand, and Rav rules that a cat may be killed, it is forbidden to keep it, there is no prohibition of theft, and no obligation to return lost property. The Gemara clarifies the redundancy in the ruling: the latter clauses teach that even though it is permitted to kill, there is still a prohibition to keep it, and regarding the skin, there is no obligation to return it.

sub.desc_en: A cat cuts off a child's hand, and Rav issues a ruling: the cat may be killed, it is forbidden to keep it, there is no prohibition of theft, and no obligation to return lost property.
The Gemara asks: since Rav already said the cat may be killed, what additional point does the prohibition to keep it teach?
The Gemara answers: one might have thought that since killing is permitted, there is no prohibition to keep it; Rav teaches that the prohibition remains.
The Gemara further asks: since Rav said there is no prohibition of theft, what additional point does the exemption from returning lost property teach?
Ravina answers: the latter clause refers to the cat's skin, teaching that there is no obligation to return the skin to the owner.

items.text: Challenge from Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar and resolution
items.text_en: Challenge from Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar and resolution
items.desc_en: A baraita states that one may raise certain animals, including cats, because they clean the house. The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between black cats (dangerous) and white cats (safe). Rav's case involved a black cat that was like a white one, and Ravina's query about a black cat born from a white one is addressed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita where Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar permits raising cats because they clean the house, contradicting Rav's ruling.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between black cats (dangerous, forbidden) and white cats (safe, permitted).
The Gemara objects that Rav's case involved a black cat, yet he still forbade raising it, contradicting the resolution.
The Gemara resolves that Rav's cat was a black cat born from a white one, which is still dangerous.
The Gemara objects that Ravina's query about a black cat born from a white one remains unanswered.

The Gemara clarifies that Ravina's query was about a black cat born from a white cat that was itself born from a black cat, whereas Rav's cat was a black cat born from a white cat that was born from a white cat, thus the query remains unresolved.

items.text: Three halakhic statements: itching, locked door, buying a house
items.text_en: Three halakhic statements: itching, locked door, buying a house
items.desc_en: Rabbi Acha bar Pappa transmits in the name of several sages three rulings: one may sound the alarm on Shabbat for an itch, a locked door does not open quickly, and one who buys a house in Israel may write a deed of ownership even on Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Acha bar Pappa transmits a tradition in the name of several sages, introducing three halakhic statements.

The tradition states three rulings: one may sound the alarm on Shabbat for an itch, a locked door does not open quickly, and one who buys a house in Israel may write a deed of ownership even on Shabbat.

items.text: Challenge and resolution regarding sounding the alarm for an itch
items.text_en: Challenge and resolution regarding sounding the alarm for an itch
items.desc_en: A baraita states that for other calamities like an itch, one does not sound the alarm but merely cries out. The Gemara resolves this by distinguishing between a moist itch (which is dangerous and warrants alarm) and a dry itch (which does not). Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi supports this with a verse about the plague of boils in Egypt.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that lists an itch among other calamities for which one does not sound the alarm but merely cries out.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a moist itch (dangerous, warrants alarm) and a dry itch (not dangerous), and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi supports this with a verse about the plague of boils in Egypt.

items.text: Interpretations of 'a locked door does not open quickly'
items.text_en: Interpretations of 'a locked door does not open quickly'
items.desc_en: Mar Zutra explains it refers to ordination (semikha), Rav Ashi says it means one who is prayed for does not quickly receive good, and Rav Acha of Difti says they never receive good, but this is his own opinion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the verse 'a locked door does not open quickly' refers to.
Mar Zutra explains that the verse refers to ordination (סמיכה).
Rav Ashi says the verse means that one who is prayed for does not quickly receive good.
Rav Acha of Difti says that such a person never receives good.
The Gemara rejects Rav Acha of Difti's statement, noting that it is his own personal opinion, not a tradition.

items.text: Clarification: writing a deed on Shabbat
items.text_en: Clarification: writing a deed on Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how one can write on Shabbat, and explains that one tells a gentile to write, which is a rabbinic prohibition but permitted for the settlement of the Land of Israel.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how one can write a deed on Shabbat, expressing astonishment at the idea.
Rava explains that one tells a gentile to write, which is a rabbinic prohibition (שבות) but was not decreed due to the settlement of the Land of Israel.

items.text: Additional ruling: buying a city in Israel
items.text_en: Additional ruling: buying a city in Israel
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan rules that one who buys a city in Israel is compelled to purchase a road on all four sides for the settlement of the Land of Israel.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani citing Rabbi Yonatan rules that one who buys a city in Israel is compelled to purchase a road on all four sides for the settlement of the Land of Israel.

items.text: Introduction: Ten conditions of Joshua
items.text_en: Introduction: Ten conditions of Joshua
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins a new topic: the ten conditions that Joshua stipulated for the settlement of the land.

sub.desc_en: The baraita introduces the ten conditions that Joshua stipulated for the settlement of the land.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Ten stipulations
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Ten stipulations
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the ten conditions that Yehoshua instituted for the public benefit, including grazing in forests, gathering wood and herbs, cutting branches, using a spring, fishing in the Sea of Tiberias, relieving oneself behind a fence, walking on paths, moving aside for road repairs, navigating between vineyards, and the law of a met mitzvah.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah begins listing the ten stipulations of Yehoshua, starting with grazing in forests and gathering wood, herbs, and branches, and including fishing in the Sea of Tiberias.

The Mishnah concludes the list with the remaining stipulations: relieving oneself behind a fence, walking on paths, moving aside for road repairs, navigating between vineyards, and the law of a met mitzvah (an unattended corpse) acquiring its place.

items.text: Gemara: Limitation on grazing
items.text_en: Gemara: Limitation on grazing
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa qualifies the Mishnah's allowance of grazing in forests: it applies only when small cattle graze among large cattle, but not when small graze among small or large among large, and certainly not large among small.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa limits the permission to graze in forests to small cattle among large cattle, excluding small among small, large among large, and certainly large among small.

items.text: Gemara: Limitations on gathering wood
items.text_en: Gemara: Limitations on gathering wood
items.desc_en: The Gemara restricts the Mishnah's allowance of gathering wood: only thorns and thistles are permitted, not other wood; only attached wood, not detached; only moist wood, not dry; and one may not uproot the plant.

sub.desc_en: The gemara limits the permission to gather wood to thornbushes and brambles that are attached and moist, and only as long as one does not uproot them.
The Gemara further restricts that only attached (מחוברין) thorns and thistles are permitted, not detached ones.
The Gemara restricts that only moist (לחין) attached thorns and thistles are permitted, not dry ones.
The Gemara adds that one may not uproot the plant entirely.

items.text: Gemara: Contradiction about herbs in fenugreek
items.text_en: Gemara: Contradiction about herbs in fenugreek
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: the Mishnah says herbs are gathered everywhere except a fenugreek field, implying herbs harm fenugreek, but a baraita says if fenugreek grows with herbs one need not uproot them. Rav Yirmeya resolves: for seed, herbs harm; for fodder, they help. An alternative answer distinguishes between human and animal consumption, with Rav Pappa's practical test.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: the Mishnah forbids gathering herbs in a fenugreek field, implying herbs harm fenugreek, but a baraita says if fenugreek grows with herbs one need not uproot them, implying they are beneficial.
Rav Yirmeya resolves: for seed (זֶרַע) herbs harm the fenugreek by weakening it; for fodder (זִירִין) herbs help because the fenugreek grows better among them.

sub.text: Alternative answer and Rav Pappa's test
sub.text_en: Alternative answer and Rav Pappa's test
sub.desc_en: An alternative answer distinguishes between fenugreek for human consumption (herbs harmful) and for animal fodder (herbs beneficial), and Rav Pappa provides a practical test: if the fenugreek is tied in bundles it is for humans, if loose it is for animals.

items.text: Gemara: Limits on cutting branches
items.text_en: Gemara: Limits on cutting branches
items.desc_en: The Mishnah prohibits cutting from olive branches used for grafting. Rabbi Tanchum and Rabbi Biryais explain the limits: for olives, up to an egg-sized piece; for reeds and vines, from the knot upward; for other trees, from the trunk's base, not the tip; from new growth that does not bear fruit, not old growth that does; from a place not facing the sun.

sub.text: Rabbi Tanchum and Rabbi Biryais citing an elder
sub.text_en: Rabbi Tanchum and Rabbi Biryais citing an elder
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Tanchum and Rabbi Biryais explain the limits of cutting branches: for olives, an egg-sized branch; for vines and reeds, above the knot; for other trees, from the trunk's thick part, not the tip, and from new growth that does not bear fruit, from a shaded spot.

sub.text: Rabbi Tanchum and Rabbi Biryais citing an elder
sub.text_en: Rabbi Tanchum and Rabbi Biryais citing an elder
sub.desc_en: For reeds and vines, cutting is permitted only from the knot upward.

sub.text: Rabbi Tanchum and Rabbi Biryais citing an elder
sub.text_en: Rabbi Tanchum and Rabbi Biryais citing an elder
sub.desc_en: For all other trees, cutting is permitted from the trunk's base, not from the tip.

sub.text: Rabbi Tanchum and Rabbi Biryais citing an elder
sub.text_en: Rabbi Tanchum and Rabbi Biryais citing an elder
sub.desc_en: Cutting is permitted from new growth that does not bear fruit, not from old growth that does.

sub.text: Rabbi Tanchum and Rabbi Biryais citing an elder
sub.text_en: Rabbi Tanchum and Rabbi Biryais citing an elder
sub.desc_en: Cutting is permitted only from a place not facing the sun.

items.text: Stipulation: gathering wood from any place
items.text_en: Stipulation: gathering wood from any place
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may gather wood from any place, even from a field whose owner does not see the sun, citing a verse. This is the first of Joshua's stipulations.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the first stipulation of Joshua: one may gather wood from any place, even from a field whose owner does not see the sun, citing a verse.

items.text: Stipulation: spring water and Rabba bar Rav Huna's ruling
items.text_en: Stipulation: spring water and Rabba bar Rav Huna's ruling
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a newly emerging spring provides water for the townspeople. Rabba bar Rav Huna adds that the owner must be paid, but the Gemara notes the halakha is not like him.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a newly emerging spring provides water for the townspeople.
Rabba bar Rav Huna adds that the owner must be paid for the water.
The Gemara concludes that the halakha (הלכה) is not like Rabba bar Rav Huna.

items.text: Stipulation: fishing in the Sea of Tiberias and its tribal allocation
items.text_en: Stipulation: fishing in the Sea of Tiberias and its tribal allocation
items.desc_en: The Mishnah permits fishing in the Sea of Tiberias with nets but not with a sail that blocks the boat. A baraita explains that the tribes stipulated this, and another baraita notes that the sea was in Naphtali's portion, fulfilling a verse.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah permits fishing in the Sea of Tiberias with nets but prohibits spreading a sail that blocks the boat.
A baraita confirms that the tribes originally stipulated this arrangement among themselves.
Another baraita notes that the Sea of Tiberias was in Naphtali's portion, fulfilling the verse 'יָם וְדָרוֹם יְרָשָׁה' (sea and south he inherited).

items.text: Stipulation: detached and attached produce on mountains
items.text_en: Stipulation: detached and attached produce on mountains
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar teaches that detached produce on mountains is available to all tribes, while attached produce belongs to the specific tribe. A baraita adds that every tribe had land in all topographical regions, as per the verse.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar states that detached produce on mountains is presumed to belong to all tribes, while attached produce is presumed to belong to the specific tribe.
A baraita adds that every tribe had land in all topographical regions, citing a verse to show that each tribe had neighbors in all areas.

items.text: Stipulation: relieving oneself behind a fence and taking a pebble
items.text_en: Stipulation: relieving oneself behind a fence and taking a pebble
items.desc_en: The Mishnah permits relieving oneself behind a fence even in a saffron field. Rav Acha bar Yaakov limits this to taking a pebble, and Rav Chisda permits it even on Shabbat. Mar Zutra the Pious would take a pebble and tell his attendant to remove it the next day.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the stipulation that one may relieve oneself behind a fence, even in a field full of saffron.
Rav Acha bar Yaakov limits the permission to taking a pebble from the fence.
Rav Chisda adds that this permission applies even on Shabbat.
Mar Zutra the Pious would take a pebble and then tell his attendant to remove it the next day.

items.text: Stipulation: walking on paths until the second rain
items.text_en: Stipulation: walking on paths until the second rain
items.desc_en: The Mishnah permits walking on private paths until the second rain. Rav Pappa adds that for our paths, even dew is harmful.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the stipulation that people may walk on private paths until the second rain.
Rav Pappa adds that for our paths (in Babylonia), even dew is harmful, so the permission applies even before the second rain.

items.text: Stipulation: clearing roadsides and the story of Shmuel and Rav Yehuda
items.text_en: Stipulation: clearing roadsides and the story of Shmuel and Rav Yehuda
items.desc_en: The Mishnah permits clearing to the sides of roads due to road stakes. Shmuel and Rav Yehuda walk; Shmuel clears to the side. Rav Yehuda questions if Joshua's stipulation applies even in Babylonia. Shmuel answers it applies even outside the Land. A similar story with Rabbi and Rabbi Chiya involves Rabbi Yehuda ben Nekosa, whom Rabbi threatens to curse if not a worthy student.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the stipulation that one may clear debris to the sides of roads because of road stakes.
Shmuel and Rav Yehuda walk; Shmuel clears to the side; Rav Yehuda questions whether Joshua's stipulation applies even in Babylonia, and Shmuel answers it applies even outside the Land.
Rabbi and Rabbi Chiya walk; Rabbi Yehuda ben Nekosa passes them; Rabbi threatens to curse him if he is not a worthy student, and Rabbi Chiya defends him.

items.text: Stipulation: one lost among vineyards and the source from Torah
items.text_en: Stipulation: one lost among vineyards and the source from Torah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah allows one lost among vineyards to step over vines to find the way. A baraita extends this to helping a friend. The Gemara clarifies that the baraita teaches that even the lost person himself may step over. The Gemara notes that returning a lost body is from the Torah ("and you shall return it"), but Joshua's stipulation allows stepping over boundaries.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who is lost among vineyards may step over the vines to find his way.
A baraita extends the rule: one who sees a friend lost among vineyards may also step over vines to guide him back.
The Gemara asks why the baraita adds 'and likewise' — what new teaching does it convey beyond the Mishnah?
The Gemara explains: one might think only a friend who knows the way may step over, but the baraita teaches that even the lost person himself may step over.
The Gemara questions whether returning a lost person is a Torah obligation, citing the verse 'והשבתו' (and you shall return it).
The Gemara resolves: the Torah requires returning a lost person who is within the boundaries, but Joshua's stipulation allows stepping over boundaries to reach him.

items.text: Stipulation: met mitzvah acquires its place and the contradiction
items.text_en: Stipulation: met mitzvah acquires its place and the contradiction
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a met mitzvah (unclaimed corpse) acquires its place. A baraita contradicts this, saying one must move it to the side of the road or to a fallow field. Rav Beivai resolves: the case is where the corpse lies on the boundary, and since it may be moved, one may move it anywhere.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a met mitzvah (unclaimed corpse) acquires its place, meaning it may be buried where found.
The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita that says one must move the corpse to the side of the road or to a fallow field, implying it does not acquire its place.
Rav Beivai resolves: the case is where the corpse lies on the boundary (מיצר), and since it may be moved, one may move it anywhere.

items.text: Counting the stipulations: the eleventh and the source of 'walking on paths'
items.text_en: Counting the stipulations: the eleventh and the source of 'walking on paths'
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the list seems to have eleven stipulations, not ten. It explains that 'walking on paths' was instituted by Solomon, not Joshua, citing a baraita about not preventing people from entering one's field after harvest, with a verse from Proverbs.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the count of ten stipulations, noting that the list actually contains eleven.
The Gemara resolves that the stipulation of 'walking on paths' was instituted by Solomon, not Joshua, so it is not counted among Joshua's ten.
A baraita is cited to support that Solomon instituted the rule of allowing passage through fields after harvest, quoting a verse from Proverbs.

items.text: Additional stipulations: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yishmael's rulings
items.text_en: Additional stipulations: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yishmael's rulings
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks if there are more stipulations, citing Rabbi Yehuda's ruling about depositing manure in the public domain for thirty days, and Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka's rulings about cutting a friend's branch to save one's swarm, pouring out wine to save honey, and unloading wood to load flax, all as court stipulations. The Gemara concludes that these are individual opinions, not the ten.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks if there are additional stipulations beyond the ten, citing Rabbi Yehuda's ruling about depositing manure in the public domain for thirty days.

sub.text: Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka's first ruling
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka's first ruling
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka's ruling that a court stipulation allows one to enter a friend's field and cut his branch to save one's swarm, paying for the branch.

sub.text: Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka's second and third rulings
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka's second and third rulings
sub.desc_en: The Gemara continues citing Rabbi Yishmael's rulings: a court stipulation allows one to pour out his wine to save a friend's honey, and to unload his wood to load a friend's flax, receiving compensation.
The Gemara concludes that these are individual opinions (of Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yishmael) and are not included in the ten stipulations of Joshua.

items.text: Introduction: Joshua's conditions and the Tanna
items.text_en: Introduction: Joshua's conditions and the Tanna
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that Rabbi Yochanan's statement about a tree leaning into a neighbor's field is one of Joshua's conditions. It then identifies Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi as the Tanna who taught the ten conditions, citing a tradition from Rabbi Tanchum and Rabbi Beryais.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that when Rabbi Avin came, he reported Rabbi Yochanan's statement that both a tree leaning into a neighbor's field and one near the border are brought and recited over, because Joshua conditioned the land accordingly.

The Gemara identifies Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi as the Tanna who taught the ten conditions, citing a tradition from Rav Geviha of Bei Ktil, and from Rabbi Tanchum and Rabbi Beryais in the name of an elder, namely Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi.

items.text: List of Ezra's ten enactments
items.text_en: List of Ezra's ten enactments
items.desc_en: The Gemara lists the ten enactments instituted by Ezra, including reading Torah at Mincha on Shabbat, reading on Monday and Thursday, holding court on those days, laundering on Thursday, eating garlic on Shabbat eve, and various women's practices.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara lists the ten enactments instituted by Ezra, including reading Torah at Mincha on Shabbat, reading on Monday and Thursday, holding court on those days, laundering on Thursday, eating garlic on Shabbat eve, and various women's practices.

items.text: Reason for reading at Mincha on Shabbat
items.text_en: Reason for reading at Mincha on Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the enactment to read at Mincha on Shabbat was for the sake of shopkeepers who are idle at that time.
