sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the enactment to read at Mincha on Shabbat was for the sake of shopkeepers who are idle at that time.

items.text: Discussion on reading Monday and Thursday
items.text_en: Discussion on reading Monday and Thursday
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Ezra instituted reading on Monday and Thursday, citing a baraita that prophets already established this practice after three days without Torah. It explains that the prophets set the schedule, and Ezra later increased the number of readers and verses to correspond to the ten idle men.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Ezra truly instituted the reading on Monday and Thursday, implying it was already established.
A baraita is cited, showing that the prophets already instituted reading on Monday and Thursday after the people went three days without Torah.
The Gemara resolves that the prophets set the schedule, and Ezra later increased the number of readers and verses to correspond to the ten idle men.

items.text: Reason for court sessions on Monday and Thursday
items.text_en: Reason for court sessions on Monday and Thursday
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that court sessions were set on Monday and Thursday because people are available then, as they come to read the Torah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that court sessions were set on Monday and Thursday because people are available then, as they come to read the Torah.

items.text: Reason for laundering on Thursday
items.text_en: Reason for laundering on Thursday
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that laundering on Thursday is for the honor of Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the enactment to launder on Thursday is for the honor of Shabbat (כבוד שבת).

items.text: Reason for eating garlic on Shabbat eve and its benefits
items.text_en: Reason for eating garlic on Shabbat eve and its benefits
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that eating garlic on Shabbat eve is for marital relations, citing a verse about fruit in its time. It then lists five benefits of garlic, including satiating, warming, brightening the face, increasing semen, and killing intestinal lice.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that eating garlic on Shabbat eve is for marital relations (עונה), citing a verse about fruit in its time and attributing the practice to Rabbi Yehuda or others.

A baraita lists five benefits of garlic—satiating, warming, brightening the face, increasing semen, and killing intestinal lice—with an additional opinion that it also brings love and removes jealousy.

items.text: Reason for women baking early
items.text_en: Reason for women baking early
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the enactment for women to bake early is so that bread will be available for the poor.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the enactment for women to bake early is so that bread will be available for the poor.

items.text: Reason for women wearing a girdle
items.text_en: Reason for women wearing a girdle
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that the enactment for women to wear a girdle is for modesty.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the enactment for a woman to wear a girdle (סינר) is for the sake of modesty (צניעותא).

items.text: Discussion on women examining hair before immersion
items.text_en: Discussion on women examining hair before immersion
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the enactment for women to examine their hair before immersion is from the Torah, citing a baraita that the Torah requires no interposition. It concludes that the enactment is to check for knots or dirt that might constitute an interposition.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the enactment for a woman to examine her hair before immersion seems to be from the Torah, not a rabbinic ordinance.
A baraita is cited, deriving from the verse 'וְרָחַץ אֶת בְּשָׂרוֹ בַּמַּיִם' that no interposition may exist between the body and the water, and that hair is included as part of the body.
The Gemara resolves that the Torah requires only that no interposition exist, but the enactment is to check for knots or dirt that might constitute an interposition.

items.text: Completion of Ezra's enactments
items.text_en: Completion of Ezra's enactments
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the list of Ezra's enactments: the requirement for women to perform a preparatory washing before immersion, the permission for peddlers to circulate in towns to provide women with cosmetics, and the extension of the requirement for a seminal emission immersion to include even study of Torah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that Ezra enacted the requirement for women to perform a preparatory washing (חפיפה) before immersion, and that peddlers should circulate in towns to provide women with cosmetics so they would not become repulsive to their husbands.
The Gemara questions how Ezra could have enacted the requirement for a seminal emission immersion (טבילה לבעלי קריין), since this is already a Torah law.
The Gemara answers that the Torah law applies only to eating תרומה (priestly portion) and קדשים (sacred offerings), but Ezra extended it even to studying Torah words.

items.text: The ten special laws of Jerusalem
items.text_en: The ten special laws of Jerusalem
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists ten unique laws that apply to Jerusalem: a house with leprosy is not declared permanently unclean, the city does not bring the heifer whose neck is broken, it cannot become an apostate city, it does not become impure through leprosy, no projections or balconies are built, no refuse heaps, no kilns, no gardens or orchards (except rose gardens from the early prophets), no chickens are raised, and no corpse is left overnight. The Gemara provides scriptural sources for the first four and practical reasons for the rest.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the ten special laws of Jerusalem.
The Gemara provides the scriptural source for the first law: a house with leprosy is not declared permanently unclean because Jerusalem was not divided among the tribes.
The Gemara provides the scriptural source for the second law: Jerusalem does not bring the heifer whose neck is broken because it was not divided among the tribes.
The Gemara provides the scriptural source for the third law: Jerusalem cannot become an apostate city because it was not divided among the tribes.
The Gemara provides the scriptural source for the fourth law: Jerusalem does not become impure through leprosy because it was not divided among the tribes.
The Gemara explains the practical reason for the fifth law: no projections or balconies are built because of the tent of impurity and to prevent harm to pilgrims.
The Gemara explains the practical reason for the sixth law: no refuse heaps are made because of vermin.
The Gemara explains the practical reason for the seventh law: no kilns are made because of smoke.
The Gemara explains the practical reason for the eighth law: no gardens or orchards are made because of the stench of fertilizer.
The Gemara explains the practical reason for the ninth law: no chickens are raised because of the sanctity of the offerings.
The Gemara notes that the tenth law, that no corpse is left overnight, is a tradition (גמרא).

items.text: The story of the Hasmonean siege and the ban on pigs and Greek wisdom
items.text_en: The story of the Hasmonean siege and the ban on pigs and Greek wisdom
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts a historical incident during a Hasmonean civil war where the besieged party sent up a pig instead of the daily sacrifice, causing the land to quake. In response, the Sages declared a curse on anyone who raises pigs or teaches his son Greek wisdom. The story is linked to a Mishnah about the location of the omer and two loaves.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not raise pigs anywhere.
The baraita recounts the Hasmonean siege where the besieged party would lower coins and receive daily offerings.
An elder versed in Greek wisdom advised the besiegers to send up a pig instead of the sacrifice, which they did.
The pig's claws caused the land to quake, and the Sages then cursed pig-raising and Greek wisdom, linking this to the Mishnah about the omer and two loaves.

items.text: Question on the permissibility of Greek wisdom
items.text_en: Question on the permissibility of Greek wisdom
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Greek wisdom is actually forbidden, citing a baraita where Rabbi permits it in the Land of Israel.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Greek wisdom (חכמת יוונית) is actually forbidden, given that a baraita records Rabbi permitting it in the Land of Israel.

items.text: The debate on Greek wisdom
items.text_en: The debate on Greek wisdom
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the earlier statement that Greek language is forbidden, citing a baraita that permits Greek wisdom. It resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between Greek language and Greek wisdom, and by noting that the house of Rabban Gamliel was permitted to study Greek wisdom because they were close to the government.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah forbids Greek language, citing a baraita that permits Greek wisdom, and Rabbi Yosei's statement about Aramaic.
The Gemara objects that Greek wisdom cannot be forbidden, citing Rav Yehuda's tradition that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's house had 500 children study Greek wisdom.
The Gemara resolves that the house of Rabban Gamliel was an exception because they were close to the government, as illustrated by the parallel case of Avtolmos bar Reuven.

items.text: The law of dog breeding
items.text_en: The law of dog breeding
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may only raise a dog if it is chained. A baraita adds that one may raise a dog in a border town, chaining it by day and releasing it at night. Rabbi Eliezer HaGadol equates raising dogs to raising pigs, and the Gemara explains that this is for the purpose of placing a curse on the owner.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may only raise a dog if it is chained.
A baraita adds that one may raise a dog in a border town, chaining it by day and releasing it at night.
Rabbi Eliezer HaGadol equates raising dogs to raising pigs.
The Gemara asks what practical difference this comparison makes.
The Gemara explains that the comparison is for the purpose of placing a curse on the owner.

items.text: Babylon as a border town
items.text_en: Babylon as a border town
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef bar Minyumi quoting Rav Nachman states that Babylon is considered like a border town, and the Gemara specifies that this refers to Nehardea.

sub.text: Rav Yosef bar Minyumi quoting Rav Nachman
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef bar Minyumi quoting Rav Nachman
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman states that Babylonia is like a border town, and the Gemara specifies that this refers to Nehardea.
The Gemara clarifies that the reference to Babylon as a border town specifically means Nehardea.

items.text: The dog that caused the Divine Presence to depart
items.text_en: The dog that caused the Divine Presence to depart
items.desc_en: Rabbi Dostai of Biri expounds a verse to teach that the Divine Presence rests on no fewer than 22,000 Israelites. If one is missing, a pregnant woman could complete the count, but if a dog barks at her and causes her to miscarry, the dog's owner causes the Divine Presence to depart. A story illustrates this: a woman entered a house, a dog barked, the owner said not to fear as its teeth were removed, but she replied that the benefit was already thrown away and she had miscarried.

sub.desc_en: A story illustrates the principle: a woman entered a house, a dog barked, the owner said not to fear as its teeth were removed, but she replied that the benefit was already thrown away and she had miscarried.

items.text: The distance for setting traps for doves
items.text_en: The distance for setting traps for doves
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not set traps for doves if they are more than four mil from the dovecote, but the Gemara questions this because a dovecote must be fifty amos from the city. Abaye explains that doves fly far but their stomachs fill within fifty amos. The Gemara then questions whether they fly only thirty ris, citing a baraita that in a settled area one may not set traps even a hundred mil away. Rav Yosef and Rabbah offer different interpretations, and the Gemara resolves the contradiction by suggesting the traps are for non-Jewish, ownerless, or the trapper's own doves.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not set traps for doves if the traps are more than four mil from the dovecote.
The Gemara questions whether doves really fly that far, citing a Mishnah that a dovecote must be fifty amos from the city.
Abaye explains that doves fly far in flight but their stomachs fill within fifty amos.
The Gemara questions whether doves fly only thirty ris, citing a baraita that in a settled area one may not set traps even a hundred mil away.
Rav Yosef interprets the baraita as referring to a settled area of vineyards.
Rabbah interprets the baraita as referring to a settled area of dovecotes.
The Gemara objects that even according to Rabbah, the trapper would still be taking doves from the dovecotes themselves.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by suggesting the traps are for non-Jewish, ownerless, or the trapper's own doves.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Five payments for injury
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Five payments for injury
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who injures another is liable for five payments: damage, pain, healing, lost time, and shame. It then defines each: damage is assessed by comparing the victim's value as a slave before and after injury; pain is evaluated by what a person would pay to avoid such pain; healing covers medical costs; lost time is compensated as if the victim were a watchman of cucumbers; shame depends on the status of both parties.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that one who injures another is liable for five payments.
The Mishnah defines the payment for damage (נזק) by comparing the victim's value as a slave before and after injury.
The Mishnah defines the payment for pain (צער) by assessing what a person would pay to avoid such suffering.
The Mishnah defines the payment for healing (ריפוי) covering medical costs, with conditions for liability.
The Mishnah defines the payment for lost time (שבת) as if the victim were a watchman of cucumbers.
The Mishnah defines the payment for shame (בושת) as depending on the status of both the one who shames and the one shamed.

items.text: Gemara's first question: Why not literal eye?
items.text_en: Gemara's first question: Why not literal eye?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Why does the Mishnah interpret 'eye for an eye' as monetary compensation? The Torah says 'eye for an eye' – perhaps it means a literal eye?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah interprets 'eye for an eye' as monetary compensation, suggesting it might mean a literal eye.

items.text: First answer: Derivation from 'striker' analogy and verse about ransom
items.text_en: First answer: Derivation from 'striker' analogy and verse about ransom
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that it cannot be literal, citing a baraita that compares 'striker of man' to 'striker of beast' – just as the latter is for payment, so too the former. Additionally, the verse 'Do not take ransom for the life of a murderer' implies that for limbs that do not heal, ransom is taken.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the literal interpretation by citing a baraita that compares 'striker of man' to 'striker of beast' to derive monetary payment.
The baraita adds a second proof from the verse 'Do not take ransom for the life of a murderer,' implying that for non-healing limbs ransom is taken.

items.text: Clarification of the 'striker' analogy and objection
items.text_en: Clarification of the 'striker' analogy and objection
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies which verse is used for the analogy, rejecting one that deals with capital punishment and settling on a verse about giving a blemish. It then raises an objection: another verse says 'one who strikes a man shall be put to death' – perhaps that means literal death? The Gemara answers that it cannot, because it is juxtaposed to 'striker of beast' and followed by 'as he gives a blemish, so shall be given to him', indicating monetary payment.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which verse of 'striker' is used for the analogy, and rejects one that deals with capital punishment.
The Gemara settles on a verse about giving a blemish, using a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) of 'הכאה' (striking) to derive monetary payment.
The Gemara objects that another verse says 'one who strikes a man shall be put to death' – perhaps that means literal death, not monetary payment.
The Gemara resolves that it cannot be literal death, because it is juxtaposed to 'striker of beast' and followed by 'as he gives a blemish, so shall be given to him', indicating monetary payment.

items.text: The 'if you wish to say' argument: Why not learn from man's death?
items.text_en: The 'if you wish to say' argument: Why not learn from man's death?
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the baraita's phrase 'if you wish to say': the Tanna had a difficulty – why learn from beast rather than from man? The answer: we derive damages from damages, not from death. But one could counter: derive man from man, not from beast! Hence the additional verse about ransom for limbs.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the baraita's phrase 'if you wish to say' means, explaining that the Tanna had a difficulty: why derive from 'one who strikes a beast' rather than from 'one who strikes a man'?
The Gemara proposes an answer: we derive damages from damages, not from death, but the counter-argument is that we should derive man from man, not from beast.

The Gemara resolves that this is why the baraita says 'if you wish to say' and cites the verse 'do not take ransom for a murderer's soul' to teach that ransom is taken for limbs that do not regenerate.

items.text: Refining the ransom verse and its necessity
items.text_en: Refining the ransom verse and its necessity
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the ransom verse is needed for limbs, as it might be needed to teach that one cannot take money and then kill the murderer. It is shown that this is derived from 'according to his wickedness', so the verse indeed teaches about limbs. Then the Gemara asks: if we have the ransom verse, why do we need the 'striker' analogy? The answer: to prevent the option of giving a literal limb instead of money.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the verse 'לֹא תִקְחוּ כֹפֶר לְנֶפֶשׁ רֹצֵחַ' (do not take ransom for the life of a murderer) is indeed needed to exclude limbs, suggesting it might be needed for another purpose.
The Gemara objects that the verse is needed to teach that one cannot take money and then kill the murderer (not to do two things to him).
The Gemara rejects this, arguing that the principle of 'כְּדֵי רִשְׁעָתוֹ' (according to his wickedness) already teaches that one cannot impose two punishments, so the verse is not needed for that.
The Gemara further questions whether the verse is needed to teach that one cannot take money and then exempt the murderer from punishment.

The Gemara resolves that if the verse were only for that purpose, it would have said 'לַאֲשֶׁר הוּא רָשָׁע לָמוּת' (for one who is wicked to die); the extra phrase 'לְנֶפֶשׁ רֹצֵחַ' (for the life of a murderer) teaches that ransom is not taken for a murderer but is taken for limbs that do not heal.
The Gemara asks: since we have the verse 'לֹא תִקְּחוּ כֹפֶר' (do not take ransom), why do we need the analogy of 'מַכֵּה' (striker) from the animal case?

The Gemara answers that without the analogy, one might think the offender could choose to give his literal eye or its monetary value; the analogy from the animal case teaches that only monetary payment is allowed.

items.text: Rabbi Dosteai's argument: Inequality of eyes
items.text_en: Rabbi Dosteai's argument: Inequality of eyes
items.desc_en: A baraita of Rabbi Dosteai ben Yehuda argues that 'eye for an eye' must be monetary, because if one person's eye is large and the other's small, literal talion is impossible, and the Torah demands equal justice. The Gemara objects: perhaps the Torah means taking the light (vision) equally? But this is rejected because the verse says 'eye', not 'light'.

sub.text: Baraita of Rabbi Dosteai ben Yehuda
sub.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Dosteai ben Yehuda
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Dosteai ben Yehuda opens by asserting that 'עין תחת עין' (an eye for an eye) means monetary compensation, and poses the rhetorical alternative that it might mean a literal eye.
He argues that literal talion is impossible if one person's eye is large and the other's small, because the Torah demands equal justice.
He adds that even if one suggests taking money in such a case, the Torah requires 'משפט אחד' (one law) equal for all, implying monetary compensation in all cases.
The Gemara objects: perhaps the Torah means taking the light (vision) equally, not the physical eye, so the inequality of eye size is irrelevant.

items.text: Opening challenge: literal retaliation for killing a minor or adult
items.text_en: Opening challenge: literal retaliation for killing a minor or adult
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a difficulty: if a minor kills an adult or vice versa, how can we execute them literally? The Torah says 'one judgment for you'—a judgment equal for all. Rather, the Torah demands taking a life; similarly here, it demands taking 'light' (sight), so it must be monetary.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: if a minor kills an adult or vice versa, how can we execute them literally? The Torah says 'one judgment for you'—a judgment equal for all. Rather, the Torah demands taking a life; similarly here, it demands taking 'light' (sight), so it must be monetary.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai's argument and a counter-challenge
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai's argument and a counter-challenge
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai says 'an eye for an eye' means monetary compensation. He argues: if a blind man blinds someone, or a cripple cripples someone, how can we fulfill literal retaliation? The Torah demands a judgment equal for all. The Gemara objects: perhaps where possible it is literal, where impossible we exempt? This is supported by the case of a treifa killing a healthy person.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai argues that 'עַיִן תַּחַת עַיִן' means monetary compensation, challenging literal retaliation with cases of a blind man blinding another or a cripple crippling another, and citing the Torah's demand for a uniform judgment.

The Gemara objects: perhaps where literal retaliation is possible it is applied, and where impossible (as with a blind man) we exempt the perpetrator, supported by the case of a טריפה (a mortally wounded person) killing a healthy person.

items.text: Derivation from the school of Rabbi Yishmael: 'כֵּן יִנָּתֶן בּוֹ'
items.text_en: Derivation from the school of Rabbi Yishmael: 'כֵּן יִנָּתֶן בּוֹ'
items.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Yishmael taught that the verse 'כֵּן יִנָּתֶן בּוֹ' (so shall be given in him) indicates monetary payment, as 'giving' refers to money. A challenge is raised: the phrase 'כַּאֲשֶׁר יִתֵּן מוּם בָּאָדָם' (as he gives a blemish in a person) would then also imply money? The Gemara answers: they derive from an extra verse—since 'כֵּן יִנָּתֶן בּוֹ' is superfluous, it teaches monetary compensation; the other phrase is just stylistic.

sub.text: Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.text_en: Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Yishmael teaches: the verse 'כֵּן יִנָּתֶן בּוֹ' (so shall be given in him) indicates monetary payment, and the extra phrase 'כַּאֲשֶׁר יִתֵּן מוּם בָּאָדָם' (as he gives a blemish in a person) is written only because of the style of the verse.
The school of Rabbi Yishmael taught that the verse 'כֵּן יִנָּתֶן בּוֹ' (so shall be given in him) indicates monetary payment, as 'giving' refers to money.
A challenge is raised: the phrase 'כַּאֲשֶׁר יִתֵּן מוּם בָּאָדָם' (as he gives a blemish in a person) would then also imply money?
The Gemara answers: they derive from an extra verse—since 'כֵּן יִנָּתֶן בּוֹ' is superfluous, it teaches monetary compensation; the other phrase is just stylistic.

items.text: Derivation from the school of Rabbi Chiyya: 'יָד בְּיָד'
items.text_en: Derivation from the school of Rabbi Chiyya: 'יָד בְּיָד'
items.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Chiyya taught that 'יָד בְּיָד' (hand for hand) refers to something given from hand to hand, i.e., money. A challenge: 'רֶגֶל בְּרָגֶל' (foot for foot) would then also imply money? The Gemara answers: they derive from an extra verse—since 'יָד בְּיָד' is superfluous given the general principle, it teaches monetary compensation; 'רֶגֶל בְּרָגֶל' is just parallel phrasing.

sub.text: Tanna of the school of Rabbi Chiyya
sub.text_en: Tanna of the school of Rabbi Chiyya
sub.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Chiyya teaches: the verse 'יָד בְּיָד' (hand for hand) refers to something given from hand to hand, i.e., money; the extra phrase 'רֶגֶל בְּרָגֶל' (foot for foot) is written only because of the style.
The Gemara objects: if 'יָד בְּיָד' means money, then 'רֶגֶל בְּרָגֶל' (foot for foot) should also mean money, which is absurd.

The Gemara answers: the school of Rabbi Chiyya derives from an extra verse—since 'יָד בְּיָד' is superfluous given the general principle, it teaches monetary compensation; 'רֶגֶל בְּרָגֶל' is merely parallel phrasing.

items.text: Abaye's derivation from the school of Chizkiya: 'נֶפֶשׁ תַּחַת נָפֶשׁ'
items.text_en: Abaye's derivation from the school of Chizkiya: 'נֶפֶשׁ תַּחַת נָפֶשׁ'
items.desc_en: Abaye says: derive from the school of Chizkiya, which taught that 'עַיִן תַּחַת עַיִן' and 'נֶפֶשׁ תַּחַת נָפֶשׁ' imply not a life and an eye for an eye. If literal, sometimes blinding could cause death, taking both life and eye. The Gemara objects: perhaps we assess whether the offender can endure it; if he can, we do it, and if he dies, he dies—just as in lashes, if assessed and he dies, the court is exempt.

sub.desc_en: Abaye introduces a derivation from the school of Chizkiya: the verse 'עַיִן תַּחַת עַיִן' and 'נֶפֶשׁ תַּחַת נָפֶשׁ' imply monetary compensation, because if taken literally, blinding could accidentally kill the offender, taking both eye and life.

The Gemara objects: perhaps we assess the offender's capacity to endure the punishment; if he can endure, we proceed, and if he dies in the process, the court is exempt, just as in lashes where assessment is made and death under the court's hand results in exemption.

items.text: Rav Zevid's derivation from 'פֶּצַע תַּחַת פָּצַע'
items.text_en: Rav Zevid's derivation from 'פֶּצַע תַּחַת פָּצַע'
items.desc_en: Rav Zevid in the name of Rabbah says: the verse 'פֶּצַע תַּחַת פָּצַע' (wound for wound) teaches to give compensation for pain in place of injury. If literal, both suffer equal pain. The Gemara objects: some are more sensitive and feel more pain; the compensation is for the average pain between them.

sub.text: Rav Zevid in the name of Rabbah
sub.text_en: Rav Zevid in the name of Rabbah
sub.desc_en: Rav Zevid cites the verse 'פֶּצַע תַּחַת פָּצַע' to argue that compensation for pain (צער) is given in place of actual injury (נזק).
The Gemara objects: if the verse were taken literally (ממש), both parties would suffer equal pain, which is impossible.
The Gemara rejects the objection: some people are more sensitive (מפנק) and feel more pain, others less, so equal pain is not assumed.
The Gemara resolves: compensation is given according to the average pain (היאך דביני ביני) between the two parties.

items.text: Rav Pappa's derivation from 'וְרַפֹּא יְרַפֵּא'
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's derivation from 'וְרַפֹּא יְרַפֵּא'
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa in the name of Rava says: the verse 'וְרַפֹּא יְרַפֵּא' (and he shall surely heal) teaches to give medical costs in place of injury. If literal, both would need a doctor. The Gemara objects: some heal quickly, others slowly; compensation is for the average healing time.

sub.text: Rav Pappa in the name of Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Pappa in the name of Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa in the name of Rava derives from the verse 'וְרַפֹּא יְרַפֵּא' (and he shall surely heal) that one must pay medical costs instead of literal injury, because if literal, both parties would need a doctor.
The Gemara objects that the derivation is unnecessary, since differences in healing speed are handled by paying the average cost (הַיְאךְ דְּבֵינֵי בֵּינֵי).

items.text: Rav Ashi's gezerah shavah from 'תַּחַת' in ox and resolution
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's gezerah shavah from 'תַּחַת' in ox and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi says: derive 'תַּחַת'–'תַּחַת' from the ox case, where 'שׁוֹר תַּחַת הַשּׁוֹר' means monetary payment. A challenge: derive from the human case 'נֶפֶשׁ תַּחַת נֶפֶשׁ' which is literal? The Gemara answers: we derive damages from damages, not from capital cases. Counter: derive human from human, not animal from animal? Rav Ashi concludes: derive from 'תַּחַת אֲשֶׁר עִנָּהּ'—human from human and damages from damages.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi proposes a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the ox case: just as 'שׁוֹר תַּחַת הַשּׁוֹר' means monetary payment, so too 'עַיִן תַּחַת עַיִן' means monetary payment.
The Gemara objects: why derive from the ox case? Derive instead from the human case 'נֶפֶשׁ תַּחַת נֶפֶשׁ', which is literal (capital punishment).
The Gemara answers: we derive damages from damages, not from capital cases; but the counter-objection is that we should derive human from human, not animal from animal.
Rav Ashi resolves: derive from the verse 'תַּחַת אֲשֶׁר עִנָּהּ' (Deuteronomy 22:29), which involves both human and damages, thus satisfying both conditions.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's literal view and reinterpretation
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's literal view and reinterpretation
items.desc_en: A baraita states Rabbi Eliezer says 'an eye for an eye' is literal. The Gemara objects: does Rabbi Eliezer reject all these derivations? Rabbah says: it means we do not assess him as a slave (but as a free person). Abaye asks: as a free person has no fixed value? Rav Ashi says: it means we assess based on the injurer, not the injured.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that Rabbi Eliezer interprets 'an eye for an eye' literally.
The Gemara objects: does Rabbi Eliezer reject all the derivations of the other Tannaim?
Rabbah explains that Rabbi Eliezer's literal view means we do not assess the injurer as a slave.
Abaye asks: if not as a slave, then as a free person? But a free person has no fixed monetary value.
Rav Ashi resolves: Rabbi Eliezer's literal view means we assess based on the injurer's value, not the injured party's.

items.text: Practical cases and Rava's ruling on assessing damages in Babylonia
items.text_en: Practical cases and Rava's ruling on assessing damages in Babylonia
items.desc_en: A case: a donkey severed a child's hand. Rav Pappa bar Shmuel ordered assessment of four items (excluding damage). Rava said we assess five. Abaye noted a donkey only pays for damage. They assessed as a slave. The father refused, saying it's degrading. Another case: an ox gored a child's hand. Rava ordered assessment as a slave, but was told that such assessments are not collected in Babylonia. Rava said: only if he seizes property. Rava's principle: damages of ox on ox or ox on man are collected in Babylonia; damages of man on man or man on ox are not, because they require a court of 'Elohim' (experts).

sub.desc_en: A case is brought: a donkey severed a child's hand, and Rav Pappa bar Shmuel ordered assessment of four items (excluding damage).
Rava objects that the Mishnah lists five items, not four; Rav Pappa bar Shmuel clarifies he meant excluding damage.
Abaye objects that a donkey only pays for damage, so the assessment should be only for damage.
Rav Pappa bar Shmuel instructs to assess the damage, but notes that it must be assessed as a slave.

sub.text: Rav Pappa bar Shmuel's final instruction
sub.text_en: Rav Pappa bar Shmuel's final instruction
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa bar Shmuel instructs to assess the child's value as a slave.
The child's father refuses the assessment, saying it is degrading.
The sages object that the father is obligating the child; the father responds he will appease the child when grown.
A second case: an ox gored a child's hand; Rava orders assessment as a slave.
The sages object that Rava himself said such assessments are not collected in Babylonia.
Rava responds that it is only if he seizes property.
Rava's principle is stated: damages of ox on ox or ox on man are collected in Babylonia; damages of man on man or man on ox are not.
The Gemara asks why damages of man on man or man on ox are not collected in Babylonia, answering that they require a court of 'Elohim' (experts).

items.text: Gemara's initial objection: 'We need judges, and there are none!'
items.text_en: Gemara's initial objection: 'We need judges, and there are none!'
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the earlier distinction between cases involving oxen and those involving humans is flawed because Babylonian courts lack qualified judges (אלהים) to adjudicate damages at all.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the earlier distinction between cases involving oxen and those involving humans is flawed because Babylonian courts lack qualified judges (אלהים) to adjudicate damages at all.

items.text: First attempted distinction: Agency in admissions and loans
items.text_en: First attempted distinction: Agency in admissions and loans
items.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that Babylonian courts act as agents for litigants only in matters of admissions and loans, not in damages. But this is rejected because human vs. human and human vs. ox cases also involve admissions and loans.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if the court acts as agents (שליחותייהו) for matters of admissions and loans, why not also for human damages?
The Gemara rejects the distinction, noting that human-human and human-ox cases also involve admissions and loans.

items.text: Refinement: Agency only in matters we are certain of
items.text_en: Refinement: Agency only in matters we are certain of
items.desc_en: The Gemara refines: Babylonian courts act as agents only in matters where the facts are known (קים לן בגויה), not in uncertain matters.

sub.desc_en: The court answers that they act as agents only for matters whose value is known (קים לן בגויה), not for unknown amounts.

items.text: Objection: Ox vs. ox is also uncertain, and fixed penalties
items.text_en: Objection: Ox vs. ox is also uncertain, and fixed penalties
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that ox vs. ox cases are also uncertain (market price varies), and fixed penalties like double payment (כפל) and four/five payment are certain, so agency should apply there too.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that in ox vs. ox cases the market price is also uncertain, and fixed penalties like double payment (כפל) and four/five payment are certain, so agency should apply there too.

items.text: Second refinement: Agency only in monetary matters, not penalties
items.text_en: Second refinement: Agency only in monetary matters, not penalties
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that agency applies only to monetary matters (ממונא), not to penalties (קנסא).

sub.desc_en: The court answers that they act as agents only for monetary compensation (ממונא), not for fines (קנסא).

items.text: Objection: Human vs. human is monetary, so why not?
items.text_en: Objection: Human vs. human is monetary, so why not?
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that human vs. human damages are monetary, so agency should apply. The answer: agency applies only to frequent matters (שכיחא), and human vs. human is infrequent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that human damages are monetary, but the court answers that they only act for common (שכיחא) matters, and human damages are uncommon.
The Gemara answers that agency is performed only for frequent matters (שכיחא), and human vs. human damages are infrequent.

items.text: Objection: Embarrassment and depreciation are frequent
items.text_en: Objection: Embarrassment and depreciation are frequent
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that embarrassment (בושת) and depreciation (פגם) are frequent, so agency should apply. The Gemara initially agrees, citing Rav Papa's collection of 400 zuz for embarrassment, but then notes that Rav Chisda objected that this is a penalty (קנסא) and cannot be collected in Babylonia.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that embarrassment and degradation (בושת ופגם) are common, citing Rav Pappa's collection of 400 zuz for embarrassment, but Rav Chisda's letter to Rav Nachman rejects this as a fine (קנסא).
The Gemara initially agrees, citing Rav Papa's collection of 400 zuz for embarrassment.
Rav Chisda objects that this is a penalty (קנסא) and cannot be collected in Babylonia.

items.text: Final resolution: Agency requires frequency and financial loss
items.text_en: Final resolution: Agency requires frequency and financial loss
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that agency applies only to matters that are both frequent (שכיחא) and involve financial loss (חסרון כיס). Human vs. human is infrequent, and embarrassment has no financial loss, so neither is adjudicated in Babylonia.

sub.desc_en: The court resolves that they act as agents only for common matters involving financial loss (חסרון כיס), excluding uncommon matters or common ones without loss.

items.text: Challenge: Rava's ruling on ox that gored in Babylonia
items.text_en: Challenge: Rava's ruling on ox that gored in Babylonia
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the earlier distinction by citing Rava's ruling that an ox that gored is not collected in Babylonia. The Gemara clarifies that this applies to a tam (innocent ox), not a mu'ad (forewarned ox), but then notes that there is no mu'ad in Babylonia unless it was forewarned elsewhere. The Gemara resolves that Rava's ruling refers to tooth and foot (שן ורגל), which are mu'ad from the start.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the earlier ruling by citing Rava's statement that an ox that gored is not collected in Babylonia, questioning how the court can collect for ox goring ox.

The Gemara initially distinguishes that Rava's ruling applies to a tam (innocent ox), while the collection here is for a mu'ad (forewarned ox), and then addresses the objection that there is no mu'ad in Babylonia by saying the ox was forewarned elsewhere and brought there.
The Gemara objects that this scenario is uncommon (מִילְּתָא דְלָא שְׁכִיחָא), and the earlier principle established that the court does not act as agents for uncommon matters.
The Gemara resolves that Rava's ruling refers to damage by tooth and foot (שן ורגל), which are mu'ad (forewarned) from the outset, thus reconciling the apparent contradiction.

items.text: New topic: Pain (צער) without a wound – who is the Tanna?
items.text_en: New topic: Pain (צער) without a wound – who is the Tanna?
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the Mishnah's ruling that pain is compensated even without a wound (e.g., by a spit or nail). Rava identifies the Tanna as Ben Azzai, citing a dispute between Rabbi and Ben Azzai about whether the Torah first mentions 'burn' (כויה) or 'wound' (חבורה).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who is the Tanna behind the rule that pain (צער) without wound is compensated, and Rava identifies it as Ben Azzai, citing a dispute with Rabbi about the order of the terms 'כויה' (burn) and 'חבורה' (wound).
Rava identifies the Tanna as Ben Azzai, citing a dispute between Rabbi and Ben Azzai about whether the Torah first mentions 'burn' (כויה) or 'wound' (חבורה).

items.text: Explanation of the dispute: Rabbi vs. Ben Azzai
items.text_en: Explanation of the dispute: Rabbi vs. Ben Azzai
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the dispute: Rabbi holds that 'burn' implies no wound, so the Torah added 'wound' to require a wound for liability. Ben Azzai holds that 'burn' implies a wound, so the Torah added 'wound' to exclude liability without a wound.

sub.desc_en: The Stam explains that Rabbi holds 'כויה' implies no wound, so the Torah added 'חבורה' to require a wound for compensation.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi holds the word 'כויה' (burn) implies no wound, so the Torah added 'חבורה' (wound) to require a wound for liability.
The Gemara explains that Ben Azzai holds the word 'כויה' (burn) implies a wound, so the Torah added 'חבורה' (wound) to exclude liability without a wound.

items.text: Rav Papa's challenge: Reversing the interpretations
items.text_en: Rav Papa's challenge: Reversing the interpretations
items.desc_en: Rav Papa challenges the explanation, arguing that the opposite interpretation is more plausible: Rabbi holds that 'burn' implies a wound, so 'wound' excludes liability without a wound; Ben Azzai holds that 'burn' implies no wound, so 'wound' requires a wound. The Gemara concludes that the dispute remains unresolved (אמסקנא קיימי).

sub.desc_en: Rav Papa objects that the opposite interpretation is more plausible: since Rabbi holds that 'כויה' (burn) implies a wound, the word 'חבורה' (wound) was written to exclude liability without a wound; Ben Azzai holds that 'כויה' implies no wound, so 'חבורה' requires a wound.

sub.text: Rav Papa's alternative interpretation for Rabbi
sub.text_en: Rav Papa's alternative interpretation for Rabbi
sub.desc_en: Rav Papa explains that according to his reversal, Rabbi holds that 'כויה' implies a wound, so 'חבורה' was written to exclude liability without a wound.

sub.text: Rav Papa's alternative interpretation for Ben Azzai
sub.text_en: Rav Papa's alternative interpretation for Ben Azzai
sub.desc_en: Rav Papa explains that according to his reversal, Ben Azzai holds that 'כויה' implies no wound, so 'חבורה' was written to require a wound.
The Gemara concludes that the dispute between Rabbi and Ben Azzai remains unresolved (קיימי אמסקנא).

items.text: Alternative explanation: Both agree 'burn' is ambiguous
items.text_en: Alternative explanation: Both agree 'burn' is ambiguous
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative: both agree that 'burn' can mean either with or without a wound, and the dispute is about the purpose of the additional word 'wound'.

sub.desc_en: The Stam offers an alternative explanation that all agree 'כויה' is ambiguous, and the dispute is about something else.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi and Ben Azzai on the principle of כלל ופרט
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi and Ben Azzai on the principle of כלל ופרט
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi and Ben Azzai disagree about whether the verse is interpreted using the principle of כלל ופרט. Rabbi holds that it is not, and the word 'חבורה' is needed for additional blood payments.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that Rabbi and Ben Azzai disagree about whether the verse is interpreted using the principle of כלל ופרט (general followed by specific) when the general and specific are distant from each other.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi holds the verse is not interpreted by כלל ופרט, so the word 'חבורה' is needed for additional blood payments; Ben Azzai holds it is interpreted by כלל ופרט.

items.text: How to assess pain (צער) in the place of injury
items.text_en: How to assess pain (צער) in the place of injury
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how to evaluate pain when it accompanies injury. Abba of Shmuel suggests assessing how much a person would take to have his hand cut off, but this is rejected because it includes all five payments. The Gemara refines the scenario to a hand already condemned by the government, and Rav Huna bar Yehoshua clarifies the wording.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how to assess pain (צער) when it occurs in the same place as the injury (נזק).
Abba of Shmuel proposes assessing how much a person would take to have his hand cut off.
The Gemara objects that cutting off a hand includes all five payments, not just pain alone.
The Gemara further objects that the scenario involves judges (שופטני), not a standard assessment.
The Gemara refines the scenario to cutting off an already severed hand, but objects that this still includes pain and embarrassment (בושת).
The Gemara refines to a hand condemned by the government, between poison and sword, but an objection is raised that the person would not take money and cause himself pain.
The Gemara resolves by assessing how much a person would pay to have his condemned hand cut off between sword and poison.
The Gemara objects that the mishna's wording 'ליטול' (to take) should be 'ליתן' (to give).
Rav Huna bar Yehoshua resolves that 'ליטול' means 'this one takes from that one what that one gave'.

items.text: Baraita on healing and lost labor when wounds grow over
items.text_en: Baraita on healing and lost labor when wounds grow over
items.desc_en: A baraita states that if a wound grows over due to the injury, the assailant must pay for healing and lost labor; if not due to the injury, he is exempt. Rabbi Yehuda says even if due to the injury, he pays for healing but not lost labor. The Sages say that whoever is liable for lost labor is liable for healing.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with the Tanna Kamma's ruling: if the wound grows over due to the injury, the assailant pays for healing and lost labor; if not due to the injury, he is exempt.
Rabbi Yehuda states that even if the wound grows over due to the injury, the assailant pays for healing but not for lost labor.
The Sages rule that whoever is liable for lost labor is liable for healing, and whoever is exempt from lost labor is exempt from healing.

items.text: Rabbah's analysis of the dispute: wound given to heal or not
items.text_en: Rabbah's analysis of the dispute: wound given to heal or not
items.desc_en: Rabbah reports that the Sages in the school of Rav say the dispute is about whether a wound is given to heal (ניתנה לאגד). He refines this: all agree it is given to heal, but not to an excessive bandage. Rabbi Yehuda holds that since it is not given to an excessive bandage, only healing is obligated, while the Sages derive lost labor from the juxtaposition to healing. Rabbi Yehuda uses the word 'רק' to exclude lost labor.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: On what basis do Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages dispute the obligation of lost labor (שבת) in the case of healing?
Rabbah reports that the Sages in the school of Rav say the dispute is about whether a wound is given to heal (ניתנה לאגד).
Rabbah objects: If the wound is not given to heal, even healing should not be obligated; therefore all agree it is given to heal, but not to an excessive bandage.
Rabbah resolves: Rabbi Yehuda holds that since it is not given to an excessive bandage, only healing is obligated, while the Sages derive lost labor from the juxtaposition (היקש) to healing.
Rabbah adds: Rabbi Yehuda uses the word 'רַק' (only) to exclude lost labor, while the Sages interpret 'רַק' as excluding only cases not caused by the wound.

items.text: Why the verse mentions healing according to the later Sages
items.text_en: Why the verse mentions healing according to the later Sages
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the verse mentions healing if the later Sages say liability for healing follows liability for lost labor. It answers that the verse is needed for the teaching of the school of Rabbi Yishmael, that a doctor is permitted to heal.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the verse mentions healing (ריפוי) if the later Sages (רבנן בתראי) hold that liability for healing follows liability for lost labor (שבת).
The Gemara answers that the verse is needed for the teaching of the school of Rabbi Yishmael (דבי רבי ישמעאל), that a doctor is permitted to heal.

items.text: Baraita on wounds growing over and the interpretation of 'רק'
items.text_en: Baraita on wounds growing over and the interpretation of 'רק'
items.desc_en: A baraita derives from 'רק שבתו יתן ורפא ירפא' that if the wound grows over due to the injury, the assailant pays for healing and lost labor; 'רק' excludes cases not due to the injury. Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda says even due to the injury he is exempt. The Gemara explains two versions of this opinion and clarifies the case of 'שלא מחמת המכה' with a story about eating sweets against doctor's orders.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites a verse to derive that if a wound grows over due to the injury, the assailant pays for healing and lost labor, and 'רק' excludes cases not due to the injury.
Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda states that even if the wound grows over due to the injury, he is exempt, citing the same word 'רק'.
One version says Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda exempts completely, like the later rabbis.
Another version says he is exempt only from lost labor but liable for healing, like his father.
The Gemara questions why the baraita needs a verse to exclude cases not due to the injury, as that seems obvious.
The Gemara explains that 'שלא מחמת המכה' refers to a case where the victim disobeyed the doctor's dietary instructions, and the verse excludes liability for that.

items.text: Dialogue between the injured party and the assailant about medical care
items.text_en: Dialogue between the injured party and the assailant about medical care
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a series of exchanges where the injured party rejects the assailant's offers of medical care, each time with a proverbial response. The assailant offers to treat him himself, bring a free doctor, a distant doctor, or give money for self-treatment, but the injured party refuses.

sub.desc_en: The injured party rejects the assailant's offer to treat him personally, saying the assailant is like a lurking lion.
The injured party rejects the assailant's offer to bring a free doctor, saying a free doctor is worth nothing.
The injured party rejects the assailant's offer to bring a distant doctor, saying a distant doctor blinds the eye.
The injured party rejects the assailant's offer to give him money for self-treatment, saying he will neglect himself and take too much.
The injured party rejects the assailant's offer to set a fixed payment, saying he will certainly neglect himself and be called a damaging ox.

items.text: Source that all payments are made in the place of injury
items.text_en: Source that all payments are made in the place of injury
items.desc_en: A baraita states that all payments are made in the place of injury. Rav Zevid in the name of Rava derives this from the verse 'פצע תחת פצע', meaning that pain is given in the place of injury. The Gemara questions this derivation.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that all payments are made in the place of injury.

sub.text: Rav Zevid in the name of Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Zevid in the name of Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Zevid in the name of Rava derives this from the verse 'פֶּצַע תַּחַת פָּצַע', meaning that pain is given in the place of injury.
The Gemara objects that this verse is needed for another purpose, questioning the derivation.

items.text: Derivation of refu'ah as part of nezek
items.text_en: Derivation of refu'ah as part of nezek
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from the verse 'וְרַפֹּא יְרַפֵּא' that the injurer must pay for medical expenses as part of the damage payment (nezek). It rejects alternative interpretations that the verse merely permits doctors to heal or teaches about healing itself, concluding that the extra wording teaches that refu'ah is included in nezek.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the verse 'פֶּצַע תַּחַת פָּצַע' teaches that an unintentional injurer is like an intentional one, and concludes that the extra wording teaches two things.

sub.text: Rav Pappa in the name of Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Pappa in the name of Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa in the name of Rava states that the verse 'וְרַפֹּא יְרַפֵּא' teaches that medical expenses (refu'ah) are included in the damage payment (nezek).

The Gemara objects that the verse is needed for the teaching of Tanna debei Rabbi Yishmael that a doctor is permitted to heal, but then rejects this by noting the extra wording, concluding that refu'ah is included in nezek.

items.text: Examples of tza'ar, ripui, shevet, and boshet without nezek
items.text_en: Examples of tza'ar, ripui, shevet, and boshet without nezek
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the five components of damages (nezek, tza'ar, ripui, shevet, boshet) can occur independently. It gives examples: tza'ar without a wound (e.g., branding with a spit), ripui without nezek (e.g., applying a harsh medicine that reddens the skin), shevet without nezek (e.g., locking someone in a cell), and boshet without nezek (e.g., spitting in someone's face).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the previous derivation that the five components can occur without nezek (monetary damage), and asks how that is possible.
The Gemara gives the first example: tza'ar (pain) without nezek occurs when one burns another with a spit or nail, even on the fingernail where no wound is made.
The Gemara gives the second example: ripui (healing costs) without nezek occurs when one applies a harsh medicine that reddens the skin, requiring further treatment to restore its color.
The Gemara gives the third example: shevet (lost labor) without nezek occurs when one locks another in a cell and idles him.
The Gemara gives the fourth example: boshet (humiliation) without nezek occurs when one spits in another's face.

items.text: Shevet calculated as a cucumber guard
items.text_en: Shevet calculated as a cucumber guard
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the calculation of shevet (lost labor): the injured person is evaluated as if he were a cucumber guard, not according to his actual profession. It addresses the objection that this seems unfair, since a skilled worker would earn more, and answers that the payment for the limb itself (nezek) already compensates for the loss of his higher earning potential.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states the rule for shevet (lost labor): the injured person is evaluated as if he were a cucumber guard.
The Gemara raises an objection: this seems unfair because the injured person would have earned more in his actual skilled profession, not as a lowly cucumber guard.
The Gemara answers that justice is not compromised, because the payment for the limb itself (nezek) already compensates for the loss of his higher earning potential.

items.text: Rava's rulings on shevet for specific injuries
items.text_en: Rava's rulings on shevet for specific injuries
items.desc_en: Rava provides specific rulings for calculating shevet in cases of severed hand, broken leg, blinded eye, and deafening. For each, he states the payment for the limb (nezek) and the shevet evaluation as a different type of worker (e.g., cucumber guard, gate guard, mill operator). For deafening, he rules that the injurer pays the full value of the person (demei kulo).

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that for cutting off a hand, the injurer pays the value of the hand and shevet (lost labor) evaluated as if the victim were a cucumber guard.
Rava rules that for breaking a leg, the injurer pays the value of the leg and shevet evaluated as if the victim were a gate guard.
Rava rules that for blinding an eye, the injurer pays the value of the eye and shevet evaluated as if the victim were a mill operator.
Rava rules that for deafening a person, the injurer pays the full value of the victim (demei kulo), as the victim is rendered entirely unemployable.

items.text: Rava's query: sequential injuries without assessment
items.text_en: Rava's query: sequential injuries without assessment
items.desc_en: Rava raises a question: if someone successively cuts off a hand, breaks a leg, blinds an eye, and then deafens the victim, but none of the earlier injuries were assessed for payment, does the injurer pay the full value (demei kulo) for all together, or are each assessed separately? The Gemara explores the practical difference regarding tza'ar and boshet, and then asks a follow-up: if they were assessed, does that change the outcome? The question remains unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: Rava asks whether sequential injuries without interim assessment are compensated as a single lump sum (דמי כולו) or each injury is assessed separately.

The Gemara clarifies the practical difference: even if the lump sum covers נזק (damage), רפוי (healing), and שבת (lost labor), the injurer must still pay separate צער (pain) and בושת (humiliation) for each injury.

The Gemara raises a second scenario: if the injuries were assessed but not yet paid, does the injurer still pay the full value (דמי כולו) or must he pay each assessment separately? The question remains unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Rabba's query: shevet for temporary disability
items.text_en: Rabba's query: shevet for temporary disability
items.desc_en: Rabba asks about shevet for a temporary injury that reduces the victim's value (e.g., a hand injury that will heal). Does the injurer pay nothing because it will heal, or does he pay for the current loss? The Gemara begins to bring a proof from a baraita about one who strikes his parents without causing a wound or who injures another on Yom Kippur.

sub.desc_en: Rabba asks about shevet for a temporary injury that reduces the victim's market value: does the injurer pay nothing because it will heal, or does he pay for the current loss?
The Gemara proposes to resolve Rabba's query by citing a baraita about one who strikes his parents without causing a wound or who injures another on Yom Kippur.

items.text: Opening Mishnah excerpt
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah excerpt
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who strikes another is liable for all five payments.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who strikes another is liable for all five payments.

items.text: Gemara's question and resolution about 'without wound'
items.text_en: Gemara's question and resolution about 'without wound'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what case of striking without a wound is meant, initially suggesting a temporary injury, but then resolves it refers to shaving or anointing with a depilatory that does not heal, addressing Rava's earlier statement about deafening.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what case of striking without a wound is meant, initially suggesting a temporary injury, and notes that the Mishnah still imposes all five payments.
The Gemara suggests the case is deafening without a wound, but objects that Rava said deafening necessarily involves a drop of blood.
The Gemara suggests the case is shaving, but objects that hair grows back, which was precisely the unresolved question.
The Gemara resolves that the case is anointing with a depilatory that does not heal, so the injury is permanent.

items.text: Application of the five payments to the shaving case
items.text_en: Application of the five payments to the shaving case
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains how each of the five payments applies to the case of shaving: pain from the stubble, healing costs, lost work time, and great shame.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains how each of the five payments applies to the case of shaving: pain from the stubble, healing costs, lost work time, and great shame.

items.text: Dispute between Abaye and Rava on lost work time
items.text_en: Dispute between Abaye and Rava on lost work time
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute between Abaye and Rava regarding payment for lost work time when a temporary injury occurs, and extends the dispute to a case of injuring a Hebrew slave.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces that a matter which was a question for Rava was obvious to Abaye, and vice versa.
The Gemara cites the explicit dispute: Abaye rules that the injurer pays both a large and small compensation for lost work time, while Rava rules he pays only the daily lost value.

The Gemara cites a parallel dispute regarding cutting off a Hebrew slave's hand: Abaye says the large compensation goes to the slave and the small to the master, while Rava says all goes to the slave to buy land whose produce the master eats.

items.text: Clarification of the dispute regarding a slave's injury
items.text_en: Clarification of the dispute regarding a slave's injury
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that if the injury is to a non-visible part of the slave, the payment goes entirely to the slave, but if it diminishes the slave's value to the master, the dispute between Abaye and Rava applies.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what is the case where the slave's value diminished only for himself but not for his master?
The Gemara answers: if he cut off the tip of his ear or the tip of his nose, the entire payment goes to the slave.
The Gemara concludes: if the injury diminishes the slave's value to his master, the dispute between Abaye and Rava applies.

items.text: Identifying the Tanna of the Mishnah on shame
items.text_en: Identifying the Tanna of the Mishnah on shame
items.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes the Mishnah's statement that shame is assessed according to the insulter and the insulted, and concludes it follows Rabbi Shimon, not Rabbi Meir or Rabbi Judah, despite a potential defense for Rabbi Judah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by quoting the Mishnah's rule on shame and asks which Tanna authored it.
The Gemara cites a baraita recording the positions of Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Judah, and Rabbi Shimon on assessing shame.
The Gemara argues that the Mishnah cannot be Rabbi Meir (who assesses all equally) nor Rabbi Judah (who exempts a blind person from shame), so it must be Rabbi Shimon.
The Gemara raises a possible defense: Rabbi Judah's statement that a blind person has no shame means he does not receive shame payments, but we still give him payment when he is the victim.

The Gemara rejects the defense, noting that the Mishnah's continuation lists a sleeping person as exempt when shaming others but does not mention a blind person, proving the Mishnah is definitively Rabbi Shimon.

items.text: Resolving a baraita on unintended shame
items.text_en: Resolving a baraita on unintended shame
items.desc_en: The Gemara addresses a baraita about one who intended to shame a small person but shamed a large one, and resolves it by reinterpreting 'small' and 'large' as literal age, not wealth, and defending it as consistent with Rabbi Judah or Rabbi Meir.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a baraita about unintended shame and asks which Tanna authored it, noting it does not align with Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Judah, or Rabbi Shimon.
The Gemara assumes 'small' and 'large' refer to wealth, and explains why each Tanna's view would reject the baraita.
The Gemara explains Rabbi Shimon's position by comparing shame to murder, requiring specific intent, citing verses.
The Gemara suggests the baraita follows Rabbi Judah, who holds that slaves have no shame for payment but their shame can be assessed for the perpetrator's liability.
The Gemara alternatively suggests the baraita follows Rabbi Meir, reinterpreting 'small' and 'large' as literal age rather than wealth.
The Gemara objects that a minor has no shame, and resolves by citing Rav Pappa that a minor can be embarrassed and feel shame.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who embarrasses a naked person, a blind person, or a sleeping person is liable. However, a sleeping person who embarrasses another is exempt. If one falls from a roof and causes damage and embarrassment, he is liable for damages but exempt for embarrassment unless he intended it.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the laws of embarrassment: one who embarrasses a naked, blind, or sleeping person is liable; a sleeping person who embarrasses is exempt; one who falls from a roof and causes damage and embarrassment is liable for damages but exempt for embarrassment unless he intended it.

items.text: Gemara's clarification of the Mishnah's cases
items.text_en: Gemara's clarification of the Mishnah's cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that one who embarrasses a naked person is liable, but it is not comparable to embarrassing a clothed person. Similarly, embarrassing someone in a bathhouse is not comparable to the street. Rav Pappa explains that 'naked' means his clothes were blown off by wind and he lifted them too much, causing embarrassment; 'bathhouse' refers to embarrassing him by the river.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited stating that one who embarrasses a naked person is liable, but it is not comparable to embarrassing a clothed person, and similarly for a bathhouse versus the street.
The Gemara questions how a naked person can be embarrassed, since he is already exposed.
Rav Pappa explains that 'naked' refers to a case where wind blew off his clothes and he lifted them too much, causing embarrassment.
The Gemara questions how a bathhouse can be a place of embarrassment, since people expect to be seen there.
Rav Pappa explains that 'bathhouse' refers to embarrassing him by the river, where he is not expected to be seen.

items.text: Rabbi Abba bar Memel's question about embarrassing a deceased person
items.text_en: Rabbi Abba bar Memel's question about embarrassing a deceased person
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba bar Memel asks: if one embarrasses a sleeping person who then dies, what is the law? Rav Zevid explains the dilemma: is the liability due to the victim's personal shame (which no longer exists after death) or due to the degradation caused? The Gemara attempts to resolve this from a baraita about a deaf-mute and a minor having embarrassment, but a fool does not. The Gemara concludes that the basis is degradation, not shame, as a minor can be shamed (as Rav Pappa said, they can be shamed and feel shame).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba bar Memel asks: if one embarrasses a sleeping person who then dies, what is the law?
Rav Zevid explains the dilemma: is the liability due to the victim's personal shame (כיסופא) which no longer exists after death, or due to the degradation (זילותא) caused?

sub.text: Gemara's attempted resolution from a baraita
sub.text_en: Gemara's attempted resolution from a baraita
sub.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to resolve the dilemma from a baraita where Rabbi Meir states that a deaf-mute and a minor have embarrassment, but a fool does not, arguing that if liability were due to shame, a minor would not be included.
The Gemara objects: if liability is due to degradation, even a fool should be included, but the baraita excludes him.

sub.text: Gemara's conclusion with Rav Pappa's explanation
sub.text_en: Gemara's conclusion with Rav Pappa's explanation
sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the basis is degradation (זילותא), not shame, as Rav Pappa explains that a minor can be shamed (דמכלמו ליה ומכלם).

items.text: Rav Pappa's alternative formulation of the question
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's alternative formulation of the question
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa rephrases the question: is the liability due to the victim's own shame (which ends at death) or due to the family's disgrace? The Gemara attempts to resolve this from the same baraita, concluding that it is due to family disgrace, as a minor can cause family disgrace. Rav Pappa affirms that a minor can be shamed and feel shame.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa rephrases the question: is the liability for shaming a sleeping person who dies due to the victim's own shame (which ends at death) or due to the family's disgrace?

The Gemara cites the baraita about a deaf-mute and a minor having shame, and argues that if the liability were due to the victim's own shame, a minor would not be included since a minor is not capable of shame.

The Gemara objects: if the liability is due to family disgrace, then even a fool should have shame, yet the baraita says a fool has no shame; the Gemara answers that a fool suffers the greatest disgrace of all.

sub.text: Gemara's conclusion and Rav Pappa's affirmation
sub.text_en: Gemara's conclusion and Rav Pappa's affirmation
sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the liability is due to family disgrace, and Rav Pappa affirms that a minor can be shamed and feel shame, resolving the objection.

items.text: Rabbi's baraita on embarrassment of a deaf-mute, fool, and minor
items.text_en: Rabbi's baraita on embarrassment of a deaf-mute, fool, and minor
items.desc_en: A baraita of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi states: a deaf-mute has embarrassment, a fool does not, and a minor sometimes has it (when he can be shamed and feels shame) and sometimes not (when he cannot).

sub.desc_en: A baraita of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi is cited, stating that a deaf-mute has embarrassment, a fool does not, and a minor sometimes has it (when shamed and feels shame) and sometimes not (when shamed but does not feel shame).

items.text: The Mishnah's ruling on a blind person vs. Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: The Mishnah's ruling on a blind person vs. Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's ruling that embarrassing a blind person is liable contradicts Rabbi Yehuda, who holds a blind person has no embarrassment. The Gemara explains Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning via a verbal analogy from false witnesses, and extends this to exemptions from exile, lashes, and court-imposed death penalties. The Gemara details the scriptural derivations for each exemption.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's ruling that embarrassing a blind person is liable contradicts Rabbi Yehuda's position.
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda rules that a blind person has no embarrassment, and extends this to exemptions from exile, lashes, and court-imposed death penalties.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's exemption of a blind person from all Torah laws
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's exemption of a blind person from all Torah laws
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning for exempting a blind person from all Torah laws, based on a scriptural analogy between the laws of murder and other judgments, and between judgments and commandments. A baraita extends this exemption to include the law of embarrassment and all commandments.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by citing Rabbi Yehuda's position that a blind person is exempt from all Torah judgments, and explains his reasoning through a scriptural analogy between the laws of murder and other judgments.
A baraita extends Rabbi Yehuda's exemption to include the law of embarrassment and all commandments, and Rav Shisha brei d'Rav Idi provides the scriptural basis linking judgments to commandments.

items.text: Rav Yosef's reflection on the reward for mitzvot
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's reflection on the reward for mitzvot
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef reflects on his earlier view that following Rabbi Yehuda's opinion (that a blind person is exempt from commandments) would be beneficial, as he would perform mitzvot without being commanded. However, after hearing Rabbi Chanina's statement that one who is commanded and performs is greater, he now prefers the opposite ruling, as being commanded yields greater reward.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef states that he used to think that following Rabbi Yehuda's opinion (that a blind person is exempt from commandments) would be beneficial, because he would perform mitzvot without being commanded.
Rav Yosef now prefers the opposite ruling after hearing Rabbi Chanina's statement that one who is commanded and performs is greater, because being commanded yields greater reward.

items.text: Mishnah: Laws of damages for humans and animals
items.text_en: Mishnah: Laws of damages for humans and animals
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a series of laws comparing damages to humans and animals, specifying the five payments (nezek, tza'ar, ripui, shevet, boshet) and the payment for offspring. It details cases of striking parents, injuring on Yom Kippur or Shabbat, injuring Hebrew and Canaanite slaves, and the liability of deaf-mutes, imbeciles, minors, slaves, and women. Rabbi Yehuda exempts slaves from embarrassment.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating the stringency of humans over animals regarding the five payments (nezek, tza'ar, ripui, shevet, boshet) and payment for offspring, while an ox pays only for damage.
The Mishnah rules that one who strikes a parent without causing a wound, or injures another on Yom Kippur, is liable for all payments.
The Mishnah details liability for injuring a Hebrew slave (exempt from shevet if the slave is his own) and a Canaanite slave of others, with Rabbi Yehuda exempting slaves from boshet.
The Mishnah states that a deaf-mute, imbecile, or minor has a bad encounter: one who injures them is liable, but if they injure others, they are exempt.
The Mishnah rules that a slave and a woman have a bad encounter: one who injures them is liable, but they are exempt if they injure others, though they pay after being freed or divorced.
The Mishnah concludes that one who strikes a parent causing a wound, or injures another on Shabbat, is exempt from all payments because he is judged for his life.

items.text: Gemara inquiry: Compensation for injuring a minor daughter
items.text_en: Gemara inquiry: Compensation for injuring a minor daughter
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar asks Rav whether compensation for injuring a minor daughter belongs to her father. The Gemara considers two possibilities: since the father is granted the benefit of her youth (e.g., for marriage), perhaps the injury compensation is also his because it reduces her value; or, since he cannot injure her himself, perhaps he does not acquire this right.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar asks Rav: when one injures a minor daughter belonging to others, to whom does the compensation for injury (חבלה) belong?

The Gemara raises the possibility that since the Torah granted the father the benefit of his daughter's youth (שבח נעורים), the injury compensation also belongs to him, because the injury reduces her monetary value.

The Gemara raises the alternative possibility: perhaps the father only acquires the benefit of her youth (שבח נעורים) because he can marry her off even to a leprous man, but injury compensation is not his, since he cannot injure her himself, so the Torah did not grant him this right.

items.text: Rav's limitation on father's rights
items.text_en: Rav's limitation on father's rights
items.desc_en: Rav states that the Torah only granted a father the right to the 'beauty of youth' (shevach ne'urim) damages. Abaye clarifies that Rav concedes regarding shevet (loss of work) because the daughter's earnings belong to her father until she reaches majority.

sub.desc_en: Rav states that the Torah only granted a father the right to the 'beauty of youth' (שבח נעורים) damages for his daughter.
The gemara raises an objection from a baraita stating that one who injures a Hebrew slave is liable for all five payments, including שבת (loss of work), when the slave's time belongs to himself.
Abaye explains that Rav concedes regarding שבת (loss of work) because the daughter's earnings belong to her father until she reaches majority.

items.text: Challenge from baraita about daughter
items.text_en: Challenge from baraita about daughter
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited: one who injures his adult son pays him immediately; for a minor son, he sets aside a fund; for his minor daughter, he is exempt, but others who injure her must pay her father. The Gemara explains that this too refers to shevet.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: one who injures his adult son pays him immediately; for a minor son, he sets aside a fund; for his minor daughter, he is exempt, but others who injure her must pay her father.
The Gemara explains that this baraita too refers to שבת (compensation for lost labor), not to the other four payments.

items.text: Contradiction regarding adult sons
items.text_en: Contradiction regarding adult sons
items.desc_en: A contradiction is raised: another baraita states that one who injures his own adult children is exempt. The resolution is that the first baraita refers to children who are not dependent on their father's table, while the second refers to those who are dependent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: the first baraita says one who injures his adult son pays him immediately, but another baraita says one who injures his own sons and daughters is exempt.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: the first baraita deals with sons who are not dependent on their father's table, while the second deals with those who are dependent.

items.text: Challenge from the daughter case
items.text_en: Challenge from the daughter case
items.desc_en: If the first baraita is about non-dependent children, why does the father receive payment for his daughter's injury? She needs support. The Gemara answers that even according to the view that a master can say 'work for me and I will not feed you' for a Canaanite slave, for a Hebrew slave the Torah requires support, and certainly for his daughter. Rava bar Rav Ulla adds that this applies only to the surplus (ha'adafah) beyond her needs.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: if the first baraita is about children not dependent on their father, why does the father receive payment for his daughter's injury? She needs support!

The Gemara answers: even according to the view that a master can say 'work for me and I will not feed you' for a Canaanite slave, for a Hebrew slave the Torah requires support, and certainly for his daughter.
Rava bar Rav Ulla adds that this applies only to the surplus (העדפה) beyond her needs.

items.text: Challenge from the second baraita
items.text_en: Challenge from the second baraita
items.desc_en: If the second baraita is about dependent children, why do adult children receive payment directly? They should give to the father. The Gemara explains that the father only cares about losses from his own pocket, not windfalls. Further challenges from found objects and the daughter's case are resolved by distinguishing between a stingy father (non-dependent) and a non-stingy father (dependent).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: if the second baraita is about dependent children (סמוכים על שולחנו), why do adult children receive payment directly? They should give to the father.
The Gemara answers: the father only cares about losses from his own pocket, not about windfalls that come from outside.

items.text: Definition of 'segullah'
items.text_en: Definition of 'segullah'
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda and Rabbah bar Rav Huna debate the meaning of 'segullah' (the fund set aside for a minor): one says a Torah scroll, the other says a date palm that produces fruit.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the term 'segullah' (the fund set aside for a minor) means.
Rav Chisda answers that 'segullah' means a Torah scroll.
Rabbah bar Rav Huna answers that 'segullah' means a date palm from which he eats dates.

items.text: Dispute between Resh Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Dispute between Resh Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish agrees with Rav that only shevach ne'urim is granted to the father. Rabbi Yochanan adds even petzi'ah (a small wound). The Gemara objects that petzi'ah is trivial, but clarifies that even Rabbi Elazar only questioned about chavalah (a significant injury), not petzi'ah.

sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish states that the Torah granted the father only the earnings of his daughter's youth (שבח נעורים).
Rabbi Yochanan adds that the father also receives compensation for a small wound (פציעה).
The Gemara objects: can it enter your mind that a trivial wound (פציעה) is included?
