The Gemara clarifies that even Rabbi Elazar only questioned about a significant injury (חבלה), not a trivial wound (פציעה), so Rabbi Yochanan's statement is not problematic.

items.text: Clarifying the case of p'tziah (wounding without depreciation)
items.text_en: Clarifying the case of p'tziah (wounding without depreciation)
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially assumed that p'tziah (wounding) does not reduce the slave's value, so it was not included in the Mishnah's list. Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina explains that the case is where he wounded her in the face, which did reduce her value.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara initially assumes that p'tziah (wounding) does not reduce the slave's value, so it was not included in the Mishnah's list.
Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina explains that the case is where he wounded her in the face, which did reduce her value.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's reason for exempting one who wounds a slave
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's reason for exempting one who wounds a slave
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who wounds a Canaanite slave of others is liable, except according to Rabbi Yehuda. The Gemara explains Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning: the verse says 'a man and his brother,' excluding a slave who has no brotherhood (in lineage). The Rabbis counter that a slave is a brother in mitzvot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the reason behind Rabbi Yehuda's position in the Mishnah.
Rabbi Yehuda derives from the verse 'איש ואחיו' (a man and his brother) that one who wounds a slave is exempt, because a slave lacks brotherhood (lineage).
The Rabbis counter that a slave is considered a brother in terms of מצוות (commandments), so the exemption does not apply.

items.text: Challenge: false witnesses against a slave
items.text_en: Challenge: false witnesses against a slave
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Yehuda: if a slave has no brotherhood, then false witnesses against a slave should not be executed, as the verse says 'as he plotted to do to his brother.' Rava in the name of Rav Sheishet answers that another verse, 'you shall purge the evil from your midst,' applies in all cases.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Yehuda: if a slave has no brotherhood, then false witnesses against a slave should not be executed, as the verse says 'as he plotted to do to his brother.'

sub.text: Rava in the name of Rav Sheishet
sub.text_en: Rava in the name of Rav Sheishet
sub.desc_en: Rava in the name of Rav Sheishet answers that another verse, 'you shall purge the evil from your midst,' applies in all cases, overriding the limitation.

items.text: Challenge: slave's fitness for kingship
items.text_en: Challenge: slave's fitness for kingship
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the Rabbis: if a slave is considered a brother in mitzvot, then a slave should be fit for kingship. The response is that the verse 'from among your brothers' means from the choicest of your brothers, excluding slaves and converts.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the Rabbis: if a slave is considered a brother in mitzvot, then a slave should be fit for kingship.

The Gemara responds by noting that the same objection applies to a convert, and resolves both by citing the verse 'מִקֶּרֶב אַחֶיךָ' (from among your brothers), which means from the choicest of your brothers, excluding slaves and converts.

items.text: Deriving a slave's disqualification from testimony
items.text_en: Deriving a slave's disqualification from testimony
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that according to the Rabbis, a slave should be fit for testimony since the verse says 'false witness against his brother.' Ulla attempts to derive disqualification via a kal vachomer from a woman, but the argument is refuted. After several attempts, Mar bar Ravina derives from the verse 'fathers shall not be put to death for sons' that a slave, who has no lineage, is disqualified. The Gemara then distinguishes a slave from a convert, who has lineage downward.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that according to the Rabbis, a slave should be fit for testimony since the verse says 'false witness against his brother.'
Ulla attempts to derive a slave's disqualification from testimony via a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument) from a woman.
The Gemara refutes Ulla's argument by noting that a woman lacks circumcision, but a slave has it; a minor, who has circumcision, is also disqualified, but the comparison fails.
The Gemara refutes further: a minor lacks מצוות (commandments), but a slave has them; a woman, who has מצוות, is also disqualified, so the argument is circular.

sub.text: Gemara's attempted resolution via common element
sub.text_en: Gemara's attempted resolution via common element
sub.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to derive disqualification from the common element (צד השווה) of woman and minor—both are not in all מצוות—and applies it to a slave.
The Gemara refutes the common element: woman and minor are not 'איש' (a man), but a slave is, so the analogy fails.

sub.text: Gemara's alternative derivation from a robber
sub.text_en: Gemara's alternative derivation from a robber
sub.desc_en: The Gemara tries to derive disqualification from a robber (גזלן), but refutes it because a robber's own actions cause his disqualification, unlike a slave.

sub.text: Gemara's attempt from robber and one of the others
sub.text_en: Gemara's attempt from robber and one of the others
sub.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to derive disqualification from a robber combined with one of the previous cases (woman or minor), but does not elaborate.

Mar bar Ravina derives a slave's disqualification from the verse 'לֹא יוּמְתוּ אָבוֹת עַל בָּנִים' (fathers shall not be put to death for sons), interpreting it to mean fathers are not put to death based on testimony of those who have no lineage (חַיִיס) of sons, i.e., a slave.
The Gemara objects: if the same logic applies to the parallel verse 'וּבָנִים לֹא יוּמְתוּ עַל אָבוֹת', then a convert, who has no lineage upward, would also be disqualified from testimony.
The Gemara answers: a convert has lineage downward (children), unlike a slave who has no lineage either upward or downward.
The Gemara supports this by noting that if a convert were disqualified, the verse would have been written differently to teach both disqualifications.

sub.text: Gemara's alternative derivation via kal vachomer
sub.text_en: Gemara's alternative derivation via kal vachomer
sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that a slave's disqualification can be derived via a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument) from a convert: if a convert, who has lineage downward, is disqualified, then a slave with no lineage at all is certainly disqualified.
The Gemara concludes: the verse itself implies that a slave, with no lineage at all, is disqualified, while a convert, who has lineage downward, is fit for testimony.

sub.text: Gemara's digression on the parallel verse
sub.text_en: Gemara's digression on the parallel verse
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the verse 'וּבָנִים לֹא יוּמְתוּ עַל אָבוֹת' was written: it is parallel to the first verse and does not imply a convert's disqualification.

items.text: Story of the deaf-mute, imbecile, and minor's harmful contact
items.text_en: Story of the deaf-mute, imbecile, and minor's harmful contact
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the contact of a deaf-mute, imbecile, and minor is harmful. The Gemara begins a story about the mother of Rav Shmuel bar Abba from Hagronya, who was married to Rabbi Abba and wrote her property to her son.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the contact of a deaf-mute, imbecile, and minor is harmful.
The Gemara begins a story about the mother of Rav Shmuel bar Abba from Hagronya, who was married to Rabbi Abba and wrote her property to her son.

items.text: Opening incident and Shmuel's ruling
items.text_en: Opening incident and Shmuel's ruling
items.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar Abba brings a case before Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba, who establishes him in property. Rabbi Abba then reports the matter to Rav Hoshaya, who brings it to Rav Yehuda. Rav Yehuda reports Shmuel's ruling: a woman who sold her melog property during her husband's lifetime and then died – the husband takes it from the buyers.

sub.desc_en: The gemara recounts the chain of transmission: Rav Shmuel bar Abba brings a case before Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba, who establishes him in property; the matter reaches Rav Yehuda, who reports Shmuel's ruling that a woman who sold her melog property during her husband's lifetime and then died – the husband takes it from the buyers.

items.text: Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba's objection from the Mishnah and the dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba's objection from the Mishnah and the dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba cites a Mishnah about one who writes property to his son after his death, where the son cannot sell because the property is in the father's domain, and the father cannot sell because it is written for the son. He argues that if the father dies, the buyer acquires, even if the son died in the father's lifetime, aligning with Reish Lakish's view. The Gemara then cites the dispute: if the son sold in the father's lifetime and died, Rabbi Yochanan says the buyer does not acquire, while Reish Lakish says he does.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba cites a Mishnah about one who writes property to his son after his death, where neither father nor son can sell during the father's lifetime.
Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba infers from the Mishnah that when the father dies, the buyer acquires even if the son died in the father's lifetime, since the property never came into the son's possession.
The Gemara identifies that Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba's position aligns with Reish Lakish, who holds that the buyer acquires regardless of whether the son died in the father's lifetime.
The Gemara cites the explicit dispute: if the son sold in the father's lifetime and died, Rabbi Yochanan says the buyer does not acquire, while Reish Lakish says he does.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's reasoning: kinyan peirot is like kinyan haguf
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's reasoning: kinyan peirot is like kinyan haguf
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that the Mishnah's ruling that the buyer acquires only after the father's death applies only when the son did not die in the father's lifetime, because the property came into the son's possession. But if the son died in the father's lifetime, the buyer does not acquire even after the father's death. This shows that Rabbi Yochanan holds that kinyan peirot (right to usufruct) is like kinyan haguf (ownership of the body), so when the son sold, he sold what was not his.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that the Mishnah's ruling that the buyer acquires only after the father's death applies only when the son did not die in the father's lifetime, because the property came into the son's possession; but if the son died in the father's lifetime, the buyer does not acquire even after the father's death.
The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Yochanan holds that קִנְיַן פֵּירוֹת (right to usufruct) is like קִנְיַן הַגּוּף (ownership of the body), so when the son sold, he sold what was not his.

items.text: Reish Lakish's reasoning: kinyan peirot is not like kinyan haguf
items.text_en: Reish Lakish's reasoning: kinyan peirot is not like kinyan haguf
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish explains that the Mishnah's ruling that the buyer acquires after the father's death applies whether or not the son died in the father's lifetime, because the son had ownership rights. This shows that Reish Lakish holds that kinyan peirot is not like kinyan haguf, so when the son sold, he sold what was his.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish states that the buyer acquires the property even if the son died in the father's lifetime.

sub.text: Reish Lakish's reasoning from the Mishnah
sub.text_en: Reish Lakish's reasoning from the Mishnah
sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish explains that the Mishnah's ruling that the buyer acquires after the father's death applies whether or not the son died in the father's lifetime.
The Gemara concludes that Reish Lakish holds that קִנְיַן פֵּירוֹת (ownership of produce) is not like קִנְיַן הַגּוּף (ownership of the body), so when the son sold, he sold what was his.

items.text: Conclusion that both Rabbi Yirmeya and Rav Yehuda follow Reish Lakish
items.text_en: Conclusion that both Rabbi Yirmeya and Rav Yehuda follow Reish Lakish
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that both Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba and Rav Yehuda hold like Reish Lakish. Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba argues: if kinyan peirot were like kinyan haguf, then when the father dies and the son died in the father's lifetime, why would the buyer acquire? The seller sold what was not his! Therefore, it must be that kinyan peirot is not like kinyan haguf.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that both Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba and Rav Yehuda hold like Reish Lakish.

Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba argues: if קִנְיַן פֵּירוֹת (the right to usufruct) were like קִנְיַן הַגּוּף (ownership of the body), then when the father dies and the son died in the father's lifetime, why would the buyer acquire? The seller sold what was not his!
The Gemara concludes: must we not learn from this that קִנְיַן פֵּירוֹת (the right to usufruct) is not like קִנְיַן הַגּוּף (ownership of the body)?

items.text: Rav Yehuda's response: Shmuel says this case is not comparable to our Mishnah
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's response: Shmuel says this case is not comparable to our Mishnah
items.desc_en: The case is brought back to Rav Yehuda, who says that Shmuel stated: this case is not comparable to our Mishnah. Rav Yosef explains: if the Mishnah had said 'one who writes his property to his father,' one could derive that kinyan peirot is not like kinyan haguf. But since it says 'to his son,' it is because the son is his heir.

sub.desc_en: The case is brought back to Rav Yehuda, who reports Shmuel's statement that this case is not comparable to our Mishnah.

Rav Yosef explains that if the Mishnah had said 'one who writes his property to his father,' one could derive that קִנְיַן פֵּירוֹת (the right to usufruct) is not like קִנְיַן הַגּוּף (ownership of the corpus).
Rav Yosef concludes that since the Mishnah says 'to his son,' the ruling is because the son is his heir, not because of the principle of קִנְיַן פֵּירוֹת.

items.text: Abaye's objection and the resolution: the enactment of Usha
items.text_en: Abaye's objection and the resolution: the enactment of Usha
items.desc_en: Abaye objects: does a son inherit from a father but a father not inherit from a son? The father comes to exempt the property from the son; here too, the husband comes to exempt the property from the brother. The Gemara explains that Shmuel's statement 'not comparable to our Mishnah' refers to the enactment of Usha, as Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina taught: in Usha they enacted that a woman who sold her melog property during her husband's lifetime and died – the husband takes it from the buyers.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects: just as a son inherits from a father but a father does not inherit from a son, yet the father comes to exempt the property from the son, so too here the husband comes to exempt the property from the brother.

sub.text: Gemara's resolution via the enactment of Usha
sub.text_en: Gemara's resolution via the enactment of Usha
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Shmuel's statement 'not comparable to our Mishnah' refers to the enactment of Usha, as Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina taught: in Usha they enacted that a woman who sold her melog property during her husband's lifetime and died – the husband takes it from the buyers.

items.text: Support from a baraita
items.text_en: Support from a baraita
items.desc_en: Rav Idi bar Avin adds that we also learn in a baraita: 'We testify about so-and-so that he divorced his wife and paid her ketubah.' This supports the enactment.

sub.desc_en: Rav Idi bar Avin cites a baraita that witnesses testify about a man who divorced his wife and paid her ketubah, supporting the enactment that the husband can reclaim melog property sold by his wife.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: טובת הנאה defined
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: טובת הנאה defined
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if witnesses are found to be conspiring (zomemin) against a woman who is still married, they do not pay the full ketubah but only the טובת הנאה (right of benefit). This is assessed by how much a person would pay for the right to inherit her ketubah if she is widowed or divorced, or if she dies, her husband inherits it.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah defines טובת הנאה (right of benefit) as the assessed value a person would pay for the right to inherit the ketubah if the woman is widowed or divorced, or if she dies her husband inherits it.

items.text: Gemara's question: Why not sell the entire ketubah?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Why not sell the entire ketubah?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions: If the Takkanat Usha (which prevents a wife from selling her ketubah outright) does not apply, why does the husband inherit? She should be able to sell her entire ketubah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions: If the Takkanat Usha does not apply, why does the husband inherit? She should be able to sell her entire ketubah.

items.text: Abaye's first answer: Distinction between types of property
items.text_en: Abaye's first answer: Distinction between types of property
items.desc_en: Abaye responds: If the Sages said this about melog property (usufruct property), would they say it about iron-sheep property (principal property)? The distinction implies that the Takkanat Usha applies only to certain property.

sub.desc_en: Abaye answers: If they said so regarding נכסי מלוג (usufruct property), would they say so regarding נכסי צאן ברזל (iron-sheep property)?

items.text: Abaye's statement: טובת הנאה belongs to the wife
items.text_en: Abaye's statement: טובת הנאה belongs to the wife
items.desc_en: Abaye asserts that טובת הנאה belongs to the wife. If it belonged to the husband, the witnesses could argue: What did we cause you to lose? If you had sold the right of benefit, the husband would have taken it from you. Rav Shalman adds: Because there is profit for the household (the husband benefits indirectly).

sub.desc_en: Abaye digresses: Since the concept of טובת הנאה (benefit of sale) has come before us, let us say something about it: טובת הנאה belongs to the wife, for if it belonged to the husband, the witnesses could argue that she suffered no loss.
Rav Shalman objects: The reason is that there is a household profit (the husband benefits from the property during marriage).
Rav Shalman adds that the husband indirectly benefits from the wife's right of benefit because it brings profit to the household.

items.text: Rava's ruling: טובת הנאה is the wife's, husband does not eat its produce
items.text_en: Rava's ruling: טובת הנאה is the wife's, husband does not eat its produce
items.desc_en: Rava rules: טובת הנאה belongs to the wife, and the husband does not eat its produce (i.e., he does not benefit from the right). The reason: The Sages instituted produce (peirot) for him, but not the produce of produce (peira de-peira).

sub.desc_en: Rava rules: The benefit of sale (טובת הנאה) belongs to the wife, and the husband does not consume its produce, because the Sages instituted for him only primary produce (פירי), not secondary produce (פירי דפירי).
Rava explains the reason: the Sages instituted for the husband the produce (פירות) of the wife's property, but not the produce of produce (פירי דפירי).

items.text: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna's proof from a baraita
items.text_en: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna's proof from a baraita
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua cite a baraita: A slave and a woman have a bad impact; one who injures them is liable, but if they injure others, they are exempt. If the Takkanat Usha did not apply, she could sell melog property and pay. The Gemara counters: Even with the Takkanat Usha, she could sell melog property with טובת הנאה and pay, but she has none (i.e., no melog property).

sub.text: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua
sub.text_en: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua cite a baraita stating that a slave and a woman have a bad impact: one who injures them is liable, but if they injure others, they are exempt.

sub.text: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua's question
sub.text_en: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua's question
sub.desc_en: They argue: if the Takkanat Usha (תקנת אושא) did not apply, the woman could sell her melog property (נכסי מלוג) and pay the injured party.
The Gemara objects: even with the Takkanat Usha (תקנת אושא), she could sell melog property (נכסי מלוג) with טובת הנאה (benefit of the right) and pay, but she has none (i.e., no melog property).

items.text: Discussion: Why not sell the ketubah with טובת הנאה?
items.text_en: Discussion: Why not sell the ketubah with טובת הנאה?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Why not sell her ketubah with טובת הנאה and pay? It answers: This follows Rabbi Meir, who says a man may not delay his wife without a ketubah even for an hour. The reason is so that divorce is not easy for him; here he does not divorce her, because if he does, the buyers would collect her ketubah from him. But טובת הנאה is merely rights (mili), and rights are not subject to lien (i.e., cannot be collected).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Why not sell her ketubah with טובת הנאה (the right to benefit from its collection) and give the proceeds to the injured party?
The Gemara answers: This follows Rabbi Meir, who says a man may not delay his wife without a ketubah even for an hour.
The Gemara explains the reason: so that divorce is not easy for him; here he does not divorce her, because if he does, the buyers would collect her ketubah from him.
The Gemara resolves: But טובת הנאה (the right to benefit) is merely rights (מילי), and rights are not subject to lien (cannot be collected from the husband).

items.text: Objection and resolution: The problem of Shmuel's law
items.text_en: Objection and resolution: The problem of Shmuel's law
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: Why not? These rights are sold for money! Rather, it is because of Shmuel's law: One who sells a promissory note to another and then forgives it, it is forgiven; even an heir can forgive. So if she sells the right and then forgives the husband, she loses the buyer's money. The Gemara responds: They say: Let her sell and give him, and if she forgives the husband, she forgives. They say: Certainly she forgives him (i.e., she will inevitably forgive).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: Why can't she sell the right of טובת הנאה (benefit of the marriage contract)? These rights are sold for money! Rather, the reason is Shmuel's law: one who sells a promissory note and then forgives it, it is forgiven, and even an heir can forgive.
The Gemara responds: Let her sell and give him, and if she forgives the husband, she forgives.
The Gemara resolves: Certainly she forgives him regarding the husband, and she would not lose the buyer's money by her own hand.

items.text: Final suggestion: Sell to the one who injured her
items.text_en: Final suggestion: Sell to the one who injured her
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests: If you say, let her sell the right of benefit to the one who injured her (the witness who caused the loss), so that he can collect from the husband.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests: Perhaps she should sell the benefit of sale (טובת הנאה) to the one who injured her.

items.text: Clarification of the previous case
items.text_en: Clarification of the previous case
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why a wife who forgives her husband's debt does not lose her ketubah: she is not causing a loss since she would not have received anything anyway. The court is not troubled unnecessarily.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that a wife who forgives her husband's debt does not lose her ketubah because she is not causing a loss (she would not receive anything anyway), and the court is not troubled unnecessarily.

items.text: Challenge from the baraita about a wife who injured her husband
items.text_en: Challenge from the baraita about a wife who injured her husband
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions a baraita that states a wife who injured her husband does not lose her ketubah. Why can't she sell her ketubah to her husband for the benefit of the injury? The Gemara answers that this case involves injury, where if she forgives, there is no loss.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the baraita that says a wife who injured her husband does not lose her ketubah, asking why she cannot sell her ketubah to her husband for the benefit of the injury.
The Gemara answers that this case involves injury (חבלה), where if the wife forgives the debt to her husband, there is no loss to the husband's creditors.

items.text: Attribution to Rabbi Meir and objection
items.text_en: Attribution to Rabbi Meir and objection
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the baraita as following Rabbi Meir, who forbids a man from living with his wife without a ketubah. The reason is to prevent easy divorce. The Gemara objects: even so, he could divorce her and collect from her injury payment.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the baraita as following Rabbi Meir, who forbids a man from living with his wife even one hour without a ketubah.
The Gemara objects: even with Rabbi Meir's reason to prevent easy divorce, the husband could still divorce her and collect from her injury payment.

items.text: Resolution: her ketubah is larger
items.text_en: Resolution: her ketubah is larger
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the case is where her ketubah is large, so he would not lose much for the sake of the small injury payment.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the difficulty by explaining that the case involves a large ketubah, so the husband would not lose much for the sake of the small injury payment.

items.text: Further refinement of the case
items.text_en: Further refinement of the case
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if her ketubah is larger than the biblical ketubah, let her collect from the biblical portion and sell the rest for the injury. The answer is that her ketubah is not larger than the biblical ketubah, so the injury is only four zuz, and he would not lose twenty-five for four zuz.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions: if her ketubah exceeds the biblical ketubah, why not let her collect the biblical portion and sell the rest for the injury?
The Gemara answers: the case is where her ketubah is not larger than the biblical ketubah, so the injury is only four zuz, and he would not lose twenty-five for four zuz.

items.text: Challenge from another baraita
items.text_en: Challenge from another baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that says just as she cannot sell her ketubah while married, she cannot lose it. But sometimes she does lose it, e.g., when her ketubah is larger than the biblical ketubah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the previous resolution by citing a baraita that states a wife cannot lose her ketubah while married, yet there are cases where she does lose it, such as when her ketubah exceeds the biblical ketubah.

items.text: Rava's resolution: the baraita refers to the ketubah of sons
items.text_en: Rava's resolution: the baraita refers to the ketubah of sons
items.desc_en: Rava explains that the baraita's end refers to the ketubah of sons (benin dichrin). Just as a woman who sells her ketubah to others does not lose the ketubah of sons, so too when she sells to her husband, she does not lose it, because she was coerced by money.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves the baraita by explaining that its end refers to the ketubah of sons (כתובת בנין דכרין), and just as a woman who sells her ketubah to others does not lose that right, so too when she sells to her husband she does not lose it, because she was coerced by money.

items.text: Discussion of the Usha enactment and conflicting baraitot
items.text_en: Discussion of the Usha enactment and conflicting baraitot
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers whether the dispute about melog slaves leaving for tooth or eye reflects a disagreement about the Usha enactment. It suggests two resolutions: one before and after the enactment, or both after, with the reason following Rava's logic.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the dispute about melog slaves reflects a disagreement about the Usha enactment, citing two conflicting baraitot.
The Gemara initially suggests that the dispute is about whether the Usha enactment applies: one Tanna rejects it, the other accepts it.
The Gemara rejects this, asserting that both Tannaim accept the Usha enactment, and the baraitot reflect different time periods: one before and one after the enactment.
The Gemara offers an alternative resolution: both baraitot are after the enactment, and the dispute follows Rava's logic regarding the husband's rights.

items.text: Introduction of Rava's principle and initial question
items.text_en: Introduction of Rava's principle and initial question
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that hekdesh, chametz, and shichrur nullify liens. It questions whether this is a dispute among Tannaim regarding Rava's principle, but concludes that everyone agrees with Rava, and the case here is where the rabbis weakened the husband's lien.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that hekdesh (consecration), chametz (leaven on Passover), and shichrur (manumission of a slave) nullify liens.
The Gemara asks whether this principle is a dispute among Tannaim regarding Rava's rule.
The Gemara answers that everyone agrees with Rava, and the case here is where the rabbis weakened the husband's lien.

items.text: Alternative explanation: Dispute about the ordinance of Usha
items.text_en: Alternative explanation: Dispute about the ordinance of Usha
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative explanation: everyone agrees that these Tannaim do not accept the ordinance of Usha, and the dispute here is about whether the acquisition of produce is like the acquisition of the body.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative explanation: everyone agrees that these Tannaim do not accept the ordinance of Usha, and the dispute here is about whether the acquisition of produce is like the acquisition of the body.

items.text: Dispute among Tannaim regarding the sale of a slave with a condition
items.text_en: Dispute among Tannaim regarding the sale of a slave with a condition
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita where a master sells his slave with a condition that the slave will serve him for thirty days. Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Yosei, and Rabbi Eliezer dispute which master is subject to the law of 'day or two days' (Exodus 21:21) regarding the slave's death, based on whether the acquisition of produce (the right to use the slave) is considered like the acquisition of the body.

sub.desc_en: The baraita introduces a case: a master sells his slave to another, stipulating that the slave will serve the seller for thirty days.
Rabbi Meir rules that the first master is subject to the law of 'day or two days' because he holds that acquisition of produce (the right to use the slave) is like acquisition of the body.
Rabbi Yehuda rules that the second master is subject to the law because he holds that acquisition of produce is not like acquisition of the body.

Rabbi Yosei rules that both masters are subject to the law because he is uncertain whether acquisition of produce is like acquisition of the body, and in cases of doubt regarding capital law, he is lenient.
Rabbi Eliezer rules that neither master is subject to the law because neither has full ownership of the slave as his own 'silver' (property).

items.text: Rava explains Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning
items.text_en: Rava explains Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning
items.desc_en: Rava explains Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning: the verse 'for he is his money' (Exodus 21:21) implies money that is exclusively his, not shared.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks what is Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning for his position.
Rava explains that Rabbi Eliezer derives from the verse 'כי כספו הוא' (for he is his money) that the slave must be money exclusively belonging to the master, not shared.

items.text: Application of Rabbi Eliezer's view to Amemar's ruling
items.text_en: Application of Rabbi Eliezer's view to Amemar's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Amemar's ruling that a husband and wife who sold melog property have done nothing is in accordance with Rabbi Eliezer's view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that Amemar's ruling that a husband and wife who sold melog property have done nothing aligns with Rabbi Eliezer's view.

items.text: Attribution of a baraita about a half-slave to Rabbi Eliezer
items.text_en: Attribution of a baraita about a half-slave to Rabbi Eliezer
items.desc_en: Rav Mordechai tells Rav Ashi that a baraita stating that a half-slave or a slave of two partners does not go free through loss of non-reverting limbs is in accordance with Rabbi Eliezer, who requires the slave to be exclusively his master's money.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who is the Tanna of the baraita that a half-slave or a slave of two partners does not go free through loss of non-reverting limbs.
Rav Mordechai tells Rav Ashi that they say in the name of Rava that the baraita is in accordance with Rabbi Eliezer.

Rav Mordechai explains that just as Rabbi Eliezer requires the slave to be exclusively his master's money (כַּסְפּוֹ – הַמְיוּחָד לוֹ), so too here the verse 'עַבְדּוֹ' requires the slave to be exclusively his.

items.text: Mishnah: Laws of compensation for striking and insulting
items.text_en: Mishnah: Laws of compensation for striking and insulting
items.desc_en: The mishnah lists the payments for various acts of assault and humiliation: a sela for striking, a maneh for slapping, two hundred zuz for backhanding, and four hundred zuz for more severe insults like tearing hair or spitting.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah opens by listing the compensation for striking a fellow: a sela, with Rabbi Yehuda citing Rabbi Yosei HaGelili who says a maneh.
The mishnah continues: for slapping (סְטָרוֹ) one pays two hundred zuz, and for backhanding (לְאַחַר יָדוֹ) four hundred zuz.

The mishnah lists additional insults—tearing the ear, pulling hair, spitting that reaches the victim, removing his cloak, or uncovering a woman's head in the market—each carrying a penalty of four hundred zuz.

items.text: Mishnah: shame damages and the story of the woman and the jug
items.text_en: Mishnah: shame damages and the story of the woman and the jug
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states the principle that shame compensation is assessed according to the victim's status. Rabbi Akiva adds that even the poor are treated as if they were nobles who lost their wealth, being children of the Patriarchs. A story follows: a man uncovered a woman's head in the market; Rabbi Akiva obligated him to pay 400 zuz. The man asked for time, then deliberately provoked the woman into uncovering her head again by breaking a jug of oil in front of her. He brought witnesses and argued he should not pay. Rabbi Akiva rejected his argument, stating that one who injures himself, though forbidden, is exempt, but others who injure him are liable.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the general rule that shame compensation is assessed according to the victim's status.
Rabbi Akiva adds that even poor Israelites are treated as if they were nobles who lost their wealth, being children of the Patriarchs.

sub.text: Story: the incident and initial ruling
sub.text_en: Story: the incident and initial ruling
sub.desc_en: A story is told: a man uncovered a woman's head in the market; Rabbi Akiva obligated him to pay 400 zuz, and granted the man's request for time.
The man watched the woman at her courtyard entrance, broke a jug of oil in front of her, causing her to uncover her head and wipe her hand on it.
The man brought witnesses and argued before Rabbi Akiva that he should not pay 400 zuz for the woman who uncovered her own head.
Rabbi Akiva rejects the argument, stating that one who injures himself, though forbidden, is exempt, but others who injure him are liable.

items.text: Gemara: Tyrian or provincial maneh?
items.text_en: Gemara: Tyrian or provincial maneh?
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: does the Mishnah's stated amount of 400 zuz refer to a Tyrian maneh (the standard coinage) or a provincial maneh (of lesser value)? It attempts to resolve the matter from a case where Rabbi Yehuda Nasi, citing Rabbi Yose HaGelili, ordered a man who struck his friend to pay a Tyrian maneh. The Gemara concludes that the Mishnah also refers to a Tyrian maneh.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: does the Mishnah's stated amount of 400 zuz refer to a Tyrian maneh (the standard coinage) or a provincial maneh (of lesser value)?
The Gemara brings a case where Rabbi Yehuda Nasi, citing Rabbi Yose HaGelili, ordered a man who struck his friend to pay a Tyrian maneh.
The Gemara concludes that the Mishnah also refers to a Tyrian maneh.

items.text: Can a witness serve as judge?
items.text_en: Can a witness serve as judge?
items.desc_en: The Gemara examines the phrase 'Here I am, here is Rabbi Yose HaGelili' from the previous case. It first proposes that Rabbi Yehuda Nasi meant he himself saw the blow, so he acted as a witness and also as judge. The Gemara objects, citing a dispute between Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva on whether an eyewitness can become a judge. A resolution is offered: the baraita where Rabbi Tarfon allows it applies when they saw the act at night, when they were unfit to judge. Alternatively, the Gemara reinterprets the statement: Rabbi Yehuda Nasi merely stated his own opinion (like Rabbi Yose HaGelili) and that there were witnesses who testified, so he was not acting as both witness and judge.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Rabbi Yehuda Nasi meant by saying 'Here I am, here is Rabbi Yose HaGelili'.
The Gemara proposes that Rabbi Yehuda Nasi meant he himself saw the blow, acting as both witness and judge, and ruled that the defendant must pay a Tyrian maneh.
The Gemara objects: does this imply that a witness can become a judge?
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Tarfon allows some witnesses to become judges, but Rabbi Akiva forbids it entirely.
The Gemara objects that even Rabbi Tarfon only allows some witnesses to become judges, not a single witness becoming a judge.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita applies when they saw the act at night, when they were unfit to judge, so the case is different.
The Gemara offers an alternative: Rabbi Yehuda Nasi merely stated his own opinion like Rabbi Yose HaGelili, and there were witnesses who testified, so he was not acting as both witness and judge.

items.text: Does Rabbi Akiva hold that a witness cannot become a judge?
items.text_en: Does Rabbi Akiva hold that a witness cannot become a judge?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Akiva indeed maintains that a witness cannot become a judge, citing a baraita where Shimon HaTimni deduces from a verse that all injuries are subject to witnesses, excluding those that occur before the court. Rabbi Akiva challenges him: if the blow happened before the court, would the judges know the exact details? He then argues that the court cannot inspect a falling building or rebuild it. Ultimately, the Gemara explains that Rabbi Akiva was only speaking in terms of Shimon HaTimni's logic, not his own view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Akiva holds that a witness cannot become a judge.
The Gemara cites a baraita where Shimon HaTimni deduces from a verse that all injuries are subject to witnesses, excluding those that occurred before the court.

sub.text: Rabbi Akiva's challenge to Shimon HaTimni
sub.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's challenge to Shimon HaTimni
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva challenges Shimon HaTimni: if the blow happened before the court, would the judges know the exact details of the injury?
Rabbi Akiva argues that the court cannot inspect a falling building or rebuild it, showing the absurdity of Shimon HaTimni's position.
Shimon HaTimni revises his position: the exclusion is for a case where the stone left the striker's hand without witnesses.
The Gemara infers from the baraita that Rabbi Akiva implies that if the blow occurred before the court, a witness could become a judge.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Akiva was only speaking in terms of Shimon HaTimni's logic, not his own view.

items.text: A baraita on judging a tam and a mu'ad ox for capital and monetary cases
items.text_en: A baraita on judging a tam and a mu'ad ox for capital and monetary cases
items.desc_en: A baraita states: for a tam ox that killed and caused damage, one judges it according to capital cases and not monetary cases; for a mu'ad, one judges monetary cases first, then capital cases. If they adjudicated the capital case first, they do not go back for the monetary case. The Gemara questions this: why can't they go back? Rava reports that he found the Rabbis of the school of Rav sitting and saying that this baraita follows Shimon HaTimni, who held that the ox is subject to witnesses and thus the case is like capital matters, preventing re-litigation for money.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that a tam ox that killed and caused damage is judged by capital-case rules, not monetary-case rules.
The baraita continues: for a mu'ad ox, one judges monetary cases first, then capital cases; if they adjudicated the capital case first, they do not go back for the monetary case.
The Gemara questions: why can't they go back and judge the monetary case after having judged the capital case first?

Rava reports that the Rabbis of the school of Rav explained that this baraita follows Rabbi Shimon HaTimni, who held that the ox is subject to witnesses like capital cases, preventing re-litigation for money.

items.text: Clarification of the earlier ruling about assessment for capital cases
items.text_en: Clarification of the earlier ruling about assessment for capital cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the earlier assumption that court assessment is needed, noting that once a capital case is concluded, no delay is allowed. The answer is that the case involves a defendant who fled, so the court assesses damages first, then later tries the capital case. Rav Mari bar Rav Kahana states that this shows that the property (רידיא) belongs to the owner.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the need for court assessment in capital cases, since once the verdict is reached no delay is permitted.
The Gemara answers that the case involves a defendant who fled, so assessment is done before the capital trial.
The Gemara objects that if the defendant fled, how can the court adjudicate monetary claims without the defendant present.
The Gemara answers that the court assesses damages first from the defendant's property (רידיא), then later tries the capital case.
Rav Mari bar Rav Kahana concludes that this ruling demonstrates that the property (רידיא) belongs to the owner.

items.text: The question: Is there assessment for damages?
items.text_en: The question: Is there assessment for damages?
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises the question of whether there is assessment for damages (יש אומד לנזקין) or not. It attempts to resolve this from the Mishnah about a pit: if the pit is less than ten handbreadths, the owner is exempt for death but liable for damages. One interpretation suggests that any depth can cause damage, implying no assessment; another interpretation says the Mishnah counts from top to bottom, implying that assessment is needed for each specific damage.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises the question of whether there is assessment for damages (יש אומד לנזקין) or not, contrasting it with capital cases where assessment is done for life-and-death.

The Gemara cites a baraita about a pit: less than ten handbreadths exempts from death but imposes liability for damages, and interprets it as counting from bottom to top, implying no assessment for damages.

The Gemara rejects the interpretation, arguing that the baraita counts from top to bottom, implying that assessment is needed for each specific damage, thus supporting the possibility of assessment for damages.

items.text: Attempt to resolve from the case of a slave's injury
items.text_en: Attempt to resolve from the case of a slave's injury
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita: if one strikes a slave on the eye and blinds him, or on the ear and deafens him, the slave goes free; but if he strikes near the eye without blinding, or near the ear without deafening, the slave does not go free. This might imply that assessment is needed for damages. However, the Gemara rejects this: the reason is that the slave brought it upon himself by startling, as taught in another baraita.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about a slave's injury to suggest that assessment (אומדנא) is needed for damages, implying that there is assessment for damages.
The Gemara rejects the proof, explaining that the slave's freedom is not due to assessment but because he startled himself, as taught in a supporting baraita.

items.text: Resolution from the Mishnah about assessing recovery time
items.text_en: Resolution from the Mishnah about assessing recovery time
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a Mishnah: five things are assessed and given immediately, including healing and lost time. If the victim recovers after assessment, he receives the full amount. This seems to prove that there is assessment for damages. However, the Gemara clarifies that this assessment is about the person (how long he will be laid up), not about the object (whether a particular object causes damage). The question remains unresolved until Shimon HaTimni's statement about a fist being unique, which proves that there is assessment for damages.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah that lists five things assessed and given immediately, including healing and lost time, and states that if the victim recovers after assessment, he receives the full amount.
The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that there is assessment for damages (יש אומד לנזקין).
The Gemara clarifies that this assessment is about the person (how long he will be laid up), not about the object (whether a particular object causes damage), so the question remains.
The Gemara restates the unresolved question: whether we assess the object itself to determine if it causes damage.

The Gemara brings Shimon HaTimni's statement that a fist is unique because it is entrusted to the court and witnesses, proving that there is assessment for damages (יש אומד לנזקין), and the matter is resolved.

items.text: Support for Rava's ruling on partial recovery
items.text_en: Support for Rava's ruling on partial recovery
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's ruling that if the victim recovers after assessment he receives the full amount supports Rava's statement: if one was assessed for a full day but recovered halfway through and worked, he is paid for the full day, because Heaven had mercy on him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Marei's statement that if the victim was assessed and then recovered, he receives the full assessment, and notes that this supports Rava's ruling that one assessed for a full day who recovers halfway and works is paid for the full day because Heaven had mercy on him.

items.text: Discussion of spitting and embarrassment
items.text_en: Discussion of spitting and embarrassment
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the Mishnah's case of spitting that reaches the victim. Rav Pappa says this applies only if the spit hits the victim's body, not his garment. The Gemara asks: why not treat it like embarrassment by words? The answer from the West in the name of Rabbi Yosei bar Avin is that embarrassment by words is exempt from any payment.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the case of spitting that reaches the victim.
Rav Pappa limits the Mishnah's case to spitting that hits the victim's body, not his garment.
The Gemara asks why spitting on the garment is not treated like embarrassment by words, which would still require payment.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Avin's answer (from the West)
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Avin's answer (from the West)
sub.desc_en: The answer from the West in the name of Rabbi Yosei bar Avin is that embarrassment by words is exempt from any payment, so spitting on the garment is also exempt.

items.text: Debate: Is the Tanna Kamma lenient or stringent?
items.text_en: Debate: Is the Tanna Kamma lenient or stringent?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Tanna Kamma's statement that everything is according to the victim's honor is lenient (allowing a poor person to receive less) or stringent (requiring a rich person to pay more). It resolves from Rabbi Akiva's statement that even the poor are treated as free people who lost their property, proving that the Tanna Kamma is lenient.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question about the Tanna Kamma's statement: whether it is lenient (allowing a poor person to receive less) or stringent (requiring a rich person to pay more).
The Gemara resolves the question by citing Rabbi Akiva's statement that even the poor are treated as free people who lost their property, proving that the Tanna Kamma is lenient.

items.text: Time for payment of embarrassment vs. damages
items.text_en: Time for payment of embarrassment vs. damages
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's story where time was given for payment, citing Rabbi Chanina's rule that no time is given for damages (חבלות). The answer distinguishes: for damages that cause monetary loss, no time is given; for embarrassment, which does not cause monetary loss, time is given. The Gemara then resolves a contradiction between the Mishnah and a baraita about a woman standing at the door: the Mishnah deals with embarrassment, while the baraita deals with damages.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's story where time was given for payment, citing Rabbi Chanina's rule that no time is given for damages (חבלות).
The Gemara answers that for damages that cause monetary loss, no time is given; for embarrassment, which does not cause monetary loss, time is given.
The Gemara raises a contradiction between the Mishnah and a baraita about a woman standing at the door, where Rabbi Akiva says a person is permitted to injure himself.
Rava resolves the contradiction: the Mishnah deals with embarrassment, while the baraita deals with damages.

items.text: Opening challenge: contradiction from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening challenge: contradiction from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah that one who injures himself is exempt, but others who injure him are liable. This implies that one is not permitted to injure oneself, which is then challenged by a baraita about oaths.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah that one who injures himself is exempt, but others who injure him are liable, implying that one is not permitted to injure oneself.

items.text: Gemara's question and resolution via baraita about oaths
items.text_en: Gemara's question and resolution via baraita about oaths
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether one is indeed not permitted to injure oneself, citing a baraita that implies one can swear to harm oneself. Shmuel explains the baraita refers to fasting, and the Gemara clarifies that harming others through fasting is possible by pressuring them. Another baraita defines harming others as physical assault, leading to the conclusion that the dispute is between Tannaim.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the premise that one is not permitted to injure oneself, citing a baraita that implies one can swear to harm oneself.
Shmuel explains that the baraita refers to fasting, not physical injury.
The Gemara objects that one cannot force others to fast.
The Gemara answers that one can pressure others through a vow to fast.
The Gemara cites another baraita that defines harming others as physical assault, not fasting.
The Gemara concludes that the dispute is between Tannaim regarding whether one is permitted to injure oneself.

items.text: Conclusion: dispute between Tannaim
items.text_en: Conclusion: dispute between Tannaim
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the disagreement about whether one may injure oneself is a dispute between Tannaitic sources, with some permitting and others forbidding.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by declaring that the dispute about self-injury is a disagreement between Tannaitic sources, with one Tanna permitting and another forbidding.

items.text: Identifying the Tanna who forbids self-injury
items.text_en: Identifying the Tanna who forbids self-injury
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to identify which Tanna holds that one may not injure oneself. It considers Rabbi Elazar's derivation from a verse about blood, but rejects it because murder is different. It then considers Rabbi Elazar's statement about tearing garments excessively, but rejects it because garments are different. Finally, it cites Rabbi Elazar HaKappar's kal vachomer from the Nazirite who abstains from wine, concluding that one who causes himself pain is called a sinner.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which Tanna holds that one may not injure oneself.
The Gemara suggests it is Rabbi Elazar, who derives from the verse 'וְאַךְ אֶת דִּמְכֶם לְנַפְשֹׁתֵיכֶם אֶדְרֹשׁ' that one may not shed one's own blood.
The Gemara rejects this, arguing that murder (קטלא) is different from mere injury.

The Gemara suggests it is Rabbi Elazar, who rules that one who tears garments excessively for a mourner is liable for בל תשחית (the prohibition against destruction), and all the more so for one's own body.

The Gemara rejects this, arguing that garments are different because their damage is irreversible, citing Rabbi Yochanan who called his garments 'my honors' and Rav Chisda who lifted his garments to avoid thorns.
The Gemara concludes that the Tanna is Rabbi Elazar HaKappar, who derives from the Nazirite's verse that one who causes himself pain is called a sinner, using a קל וחומר (a fortiori) argument.

items.text: Discussion of cutting down trees: Rabba bar bar Chana's teaching
items.text_en: Discussion of cutting down trees: Rabba bar bar Chana's teaching
items.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana taught before Rav that if one claims 'You killed my ox' or 'You cut down my saplings' and the other responds 'You told me to do so', the latter is exempt. Rav objects that this would leave no room for life. Rav then suggests the teaching be interpreted as referring to an ox standing to be slaughtered or a tree standing to be cut down.

sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana teaches before Rav that if one claims 'You killed my ox' or 'You cut down my saplings' and the other responds 'You told me to do so', the latter is exempt.
Rav objects that this ruling would leave no room for life, as anyone could claim they were told to act.
Rav suggests that the teaching be interpreted as referring to an ox standing to be slaughtered or a tree standing to be cut down, thus limiting the exemption.

items.text: Clarification of the claim: performing a mitzvah
items.text_en: Clarification of the claim: performing a mitzvah
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that in such a case, the claimant could argue that he wanted to perform the mitzvah himself, as illustrated by a story where Rabban Gamliel required payment to one who covered the blood before the slaughterer.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if the animal was already designated for slaughter, what claim does the plaintiff have against the one who slaughtered it?
The Gemara answers: the plaintiff can claim that he wanted to perform the mitzvah of covering the blood himself.

A baraita is cited: the verse 'ושפך וכסה' (and he shall pour out and cover) teaches that the one who slaughters should cover the blood, and a story is told where Rabban Gamliel obligated a person who covered the blood before the slaughterer to pay ten gold coins.

items.text: Laws of cutting down fruit trees
items.text_en: Laws of cutting down fruit trees
items.desc_en: Rav states that a date palm that produces a kav is forbidden to cut down. The Gemara challenges this with a baraita about olive trees, but distinguishes because olives are valuable. Rabbi Chanina says his son died only because he cut down a fig tree before its time, but Ravina permits it if the tree is worth more for wood. A baraita from the Torah about fruit trees and non-fruit trees is cited, emphasizing that non-fruit trees may be cut down first.

sub.desc_en: Rav rules that a date palm producing a kav of fruit is forbidden to cut down.
The Gemara challenges Rav with a baraita that sets a minimum measure of a quarter-log for an olive tree before it may not be cut down.
The Gemara distinguishes olives as more valuable, so the baraita's measure does not apply to date palms.
Rabbi Chanina testifies that his son died only because he cut down a fig tree before its time.
Ravina permits cutting down a fruit tree if its wood is worth more than its fruit.
A baraita from the Torah distinguishes between fruit trees and non-fruit trees, emphasizing that non-fruit trees may be cut down first.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: The limitation of monetary compensation
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: The limitation of monetary compensation
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that even if one pays compensation, he is not forgiven until he requests forgiveness from the victim, as shown by Abraham's prayer for Abimelech.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by asking whether one who pays compensation is forgiven, and answers with a limiting verse.

items.text: Stories of Shmuel and Rav Chisda about produce and vines
items.text_en: Stories of Shmuel and Rav Chisda about produce and vines
items.desc_en: Shmuel tastes dates that have a wine flavor and learns they are from between vines; Rav Chisda orders his tenant to uproot vines planted among date palms, noting that vines acquire the taste of dates but not vice versa.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel tastes dates with a wine flavor and learns from his tenant that they come from between vines, then asks for more from the source.
Rav Chisda sees vines among date palms and orders them uprooted, explaining that vines acquire the taste of dates but not vice versa.

items.text: Mishnah: Forgiveness requires personal request
items.text_en: Mishnah: Forgiveness requires personal request
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that even after paying damages, the offender is not forgiven until he asks for forgiveness, citing the verse about Abraham and Abimelech. It also asks how we know that one who does not forgive is cruel.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that even after paying damages, the offender is not forgiven until he personally requests forgiveness.
The Mishnah cites the verse about Abraham and Abimelech as a prooftext for the requirement of personal forgiveness.
The Mishnah asks how we know that one who refuses to forgive is cruel.
The Mishnah answers by citing the verse that Abraham prayed for Abimelech, implying that forgiveness is expected.

items.text: Mishnah: Cases of liability for damage to body and property
items.text_en: Mishnah: Cases of liability for damage to body and property
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists cases where one says 'blind my eye' or 'break my jug' – the perpetrator is liable even if the victim says 'on condition of exemption'. For property damage, saying 'on condition of exemption' exempts, but if he says 'do so to so-and-so on condition of exemption', he is liable.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists cases of liability for damage to body and property, distinguishing when a condition of exemption is effective.

items.text: Gemara: The requirement for forgiveness and the lesson from Abimelech
items.text_en: Gemara: The requirement for forgiveness and the lesson from Abimelech
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraisa that monetary compensation covers shame but not pain; forgiveness requires a personal request. It questions why Abraham had to pray for Abimelech's wife to be returned, and answers that a prophet's wife requires restoration, but another's does not. Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani explains that Abraham taught Abimelech a lesson about hospitality, and from here we learn that a Noahide who could have learned but did not is liable.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that monetary compensation covers shame but not pain; forgiveness requires a personal request, as derived from the verse about Abraham and Abimelech.
The Gemara questions why the verse specifies that Abraham prayed for Abimelech's wife to be returned, implying that only a prophet's wife requires restoration.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani explains that the verse 'return the man's wife' applies in any case, and Abraham taught Abimelech a lesson about hospitality: one should ask about food and drink, not about the wife.
From this incident, the Gemara derives that a Noahide (בן נח) who could have learned proper conduct but did not is liable for punishment.

items.text: Interpretations of the double 'עָצֹר' and the plague on Abimelech's household
items.text_en: Interpretations of the double 'עָצֹר' and the plague on Abimelech's household
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar explains the two 'עָצֹר's: one for men (loss of semen) and two for women (semen and childbirth). A baraisa adds a second for men (children) and a third for women (children). Ravina adds a third for men (the opening of the womb) and a fourth for women. The school of Rabbi Yannai says even Abimelech's hen did not lay an egg.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar asks why the verse uses the double expression 'עָצֹר עָצַר' (surely restrained).
Rabbi Elazar answers: one restraint on men (loss of semen) and two on women (semen and childbirth).
A baraita adds a second restraint on men (children) and a third on women (children).
Ravina adds a third restraint on men (opening of the womb) and a fourth on women.
The school of Rabbi Yannai adds that even Abimelech's hen did not lay an egg, illustrating the extreme restraint.

items.text: Rava and Rabbah bar Mari: The one who prays for another is answered first
items.text_en: Rava and Rabbah bar Mari: The one who prays for another is answered first
items.desc_en: Rava asks Rabbah bar Mari for the source that one who prays for his friend while needing the same thing is answered first. Rabbah bar Mari cites Job, and Rava adds a proof from Abraham's prayer for Abimelech, after which Sarah was remembered.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks Rabbah bar Mari for the scriptural source of the rabbinic principle that one who prays for his friend while needing the same thing himself is answered first.
Rabbah bar Mari cites the verse about Job, where Job's captivity was returned when he prayed for his friends, implying he was answered first.
Rava adds a proof from Abraham's prayer for Abimelech, after which Sarah was remembered, showing that the one who prays for another is answered first.

items.text: Rava and Rabbah bar Mari: The proverb about suffering with the thorn
items.text_en: Rava and Rabbah bar Mari: The proverb about suffering with the thorn
items.desc_en: Rava asks about the folk saying 'with the thorn, the cabbage is stricken'. Rabbah bar Mari cites a verse from Jeremiah, and Rava adds another from the same prophet.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks Rabbah bar Mari about the source of the folk saying 'with the thorn, the cabbage is stricken' (the innocent suffer with the guilty).
Rabbah bar Mari cites a verse from Jeremiah (2:29) where God says 'Why do you contend with Me? All of you have transgressed against Me' — implying collective guilt.
Rava adds another verse from Jeremiah (44:23) — 'Until when will you refuse to keep My commandments and My laws' — as an alternative source for the same principle.

items.text: Rava and Rabbah bar Mari: The five men taken by Joseph and the story of Judah's bones
items.text_en: Rava and Rabbah bar Mari: The five men taken by Joseph and the story of Judah's bones
items.desc_en: Rava asks about the five men Joseph took from his brothers. Rabbah bar Mari says they were those whose names were doubled (e.g., Judah). When Rava objects that Judah's name is also doubled, he explains it was doubled in meaning. Rabbi Yonatan explains that for 40 years Judah's bones were rolling in the ark until Moses prayed, citing Judah's role in Reuben's confession.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks Rabbah bar Mari who were the five men Joseph took from his brothers.
Rabbah bar Mari answers in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that they were those whose names were doubled (e.g., Judah).
Rava objects that Judah's name is also doubled (יהודה), so he should have been among the five.
Rabbah bar Mari explains that Judah's name was doubled in meaning, not in form, and cites Rabbi Yonatan's question about the verse.
Rabbi Yonatan explains that for 40 years Judah's bones were rolling in the ark until Moses prayed, citing Judah's role in causing Reuben to confess.
The prayer is answered: Judah's bones are restored, he joins the heavenly academy, understands the rabbis' discussions, and receives divine assistance.

items.text: Rava and Rabbah bar Mari: The proverb about poverty following the poor
items.text_en: Rava and Rabbah bar Mari: The proverb about poverty following the poor
items.desc_en: Rava asks about the folk saying 'poverty follows the poor'. Rabbah bar Mari cites a Mishnah about rich and poor bringing first fruits in different baskets, and the poor's baskets are given to the priests.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks Rabbah bar Mari for the source of the folk saying 'poverty follows the poor'.

Rabbah bar Mari cites a Mishnah where rich bring first fruits in gold/silver baskets and poor in wicker baskets, and the poor's baskets are given to the priests, illustrating how poverty follows the poor.
Rava offers an alternative scriptural source for the proverb, but the text cuts off before citing it.

items.text: Source for the saying about eating early to avoid heat and cold
items.text_en: Source for the saying about eating early to avoid heat and cold
items.desc_en: Rava asks Rabbah bar Mari for the source of the rabbinic saying to eat early in summer due to heat and in winter due to cold, and the folk saying that sixty runners cannot catch a man who eats in the morning. Rabbah bar Mari cites the verse 'They shall not hunger nor thirst, neither shall the heat nor sun smite them' (Isaiah 49:10). Rava then offers an alternative source from Exodus 23:25-26, which is interpreted to mean that reciting Shema and prayer, along with bread and salt and water, remove illness, and a baraita identifies this illness as the gall-bladder, which causes 83 ailments that are nullified by this practice.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a verse about the leper who must cry 'Unclean, unclean,' introducing the theme that poverty follows the poor.

Rava asks Rabbah bar Mari for the source of the rabbinic saying to eat early in summer due to heat and in winter due to cold, and the folk saying that sixty runners cannot catch a man who eats in the morning; Rabbah bar Mari cites the verse 'They shall not hunger nor thirst, neither shall the heat nor sun smite them' (Isaiah 49:10).
Rava offers an alternative source from Exodus 23:25-26, interpreting it to mean that reciting Shema and prayer, along with bread and salt and water, remove illness.
A baraita identifies the illness as the gall-bladder, which causes 83 ailments that are nullified by eating bread with salt and drinking water in the morning.

items.text: Source for the saying about a friend calling you a donkey
items.text_en: Source for the saying about a friend calling you a donkey
items.desc_en: Rava asks Rabbah bar Mari for the source of the folk saying that if your friend calls you a donkey, you should put a saddle on your back. Rabbah bar Mari cites the verse where the angel asks Hagar 'Where have you come from and where are you going?' and she responds 'I am fleeing from my mistress Sarai' (Genesis 16:8), implying she accepted the label.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks Rabbah bar Mari for the source of the rabbinic saying that if your friend calls you a donkey, you should prepare a saddle for your back.
Rabbah bar Mari cites the verse where the angel calls Hagar 'maidservant of Sarai' and she accepts that label in her response (Genesis 16:8).

items.text: Source for the saying to admit your own fault first
items.text_en: Source for the saying to admit your own fault first
items.desc_en: Rava asks Rabbah bar Mari for the source of the folk saying that if you have a bad trait, you should mention it first. Rabbah bar Mari cites the verse where Eliezer says 'I am the servant of Abraham' (Genesis 24:34), immediately identifying himself as a servant.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks Rabbah bar Mari for the source of the folk saying that if you have a bad trait, you should mention it first.
Rabbah bar Mari cites the verse where Eliezer says 'I am the servant of Abraham' (Genesis 24:34), immediately identifying himself as a servant.

items.text: Source for the saying about the lowly goose with drooping eyes
items.text_en: Source for the saying about the lowly goose with drooping eyes
items.desc_en: Rava asks Rabbah bar Mari for the source of the folk saying that the goose walks low and its eyes droop (i.e., the humble are overlooked). Rabbah bar Mari cites the verse where Ruth says to Boaz 'May the Lord reward you, and may you be blessed... for you have shown kindness to your maidservant' (Ruth 2:20), implying her lowly status.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks Rabbah bar Mari for the source of the folk saying that the goose walks low and its eyes droop.
Rabbah bar Mari cites the verse where Ruth says to Boaz 'May the Lord reward you... remember your maidservant' as the source.

items.text: Source for the saying about not being invited despite hearing the call
items.text_en: Source for the saying about not being invited despite hearing the call
items.desc_en: Rava asks Rabbah bar Mari for the source of the folk saying that sixty pains come upon one who hears his friend's call but does not eat (i.e., does not respond). Rabbah bar Mari cites the verse where Adonijah invited many but did not invite Solomon (1 Kings 1:10). Rava offers an alternative source from Genesis 24:67 and 25:1, where after Isaac married Rebecca and was comforted, Abraham immediately took another wife, implying that one who does not respond is replaced.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks Rabbah bar Mari for the source of the folk saying that sixty pains come upon one who hears his friend's call but does not eat.
Rabbah bar Mari cites the verse from 1 Kings 1:25-26 where Nathan complains that Adonijah did not invite him, Zadok, Benaiah, and Solomon.

Rava offers an alternative source from Genesis 24:67 and 25:1, where after Isaac married Rebecca and was comforted, Abraham immediately took another wife, implying that one who does not respond is replaced.

items.text: Source for the saying about wine to the owner and gratitude to the server
items.text_en: Source for the saying about wine to the owner and gratitude to the server
items.desc_en: Rava asks Rabbah bar Mari for the source of the folk saying that wine belongs to the owner but gratitude goes to the server. Rabbah bar Mari cites the verses where Moses laid his hands on Joshua so that the people would listen to him (Numbers 27:18-20), implying that the honor goes to the one who facilitates.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks Rabbah bar Mari for the source of the folk saying that wine belongs to the owner but gratitude goes to the server.
Rabbah bar Mari cites the verses where Moses laid his hands on Joshua so that the people would listen to him (Numbers 27:18-20), implying that the honor goes to the one who facilitates.

items.text: Source for the saying about a hungry dog swallowing dung
items.text_en: Source for the saying about a hungry dog swallowing dung
items.desc_en: Rava asks Rabbah bar Mari for the source of the folk saying that when a dog is hungry, it swallows its own excrement. Rabbah bar Mari cites the verse 'A sated soul despises honey, but a hungry soul finds even bitter things sweet' (Proverbs 27:7), implying that hunger makes one accept anything.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks Rabbah bar Mari for the source of the folk saying that a hungry dog swallows its own excrement.
Rabbah bar Mari cites the verse 'A sated soul despises honey, but a hungry soul finds even bitter things sweet' (Proverbs 27:7) as the source, implying that hunger makes one accept anything.

items.text: Source for the saying about a bad palm tree joining a grove of thorns
items.text_en: Source for the saying about a bad palm tree joining a grove of thorns
items.desc_en: Rava asks Rabbah bar Mari for the source of the folk saying that a bad palm tree goes and joins a grove of thorns (i.e., like attracts like). Rabbah bar Mari responds that this principle is written in the Torah, repeated in the Prophets, tripled in the Writings, taught in the Mishnah, and stated in a baraita. He cites verses: Esau went to Ishmael (Genesis 28:9), worthless men gathered to Jephthah (Judges 11:3), and 'every bird dwells with its kind' (Ben Sira 13:16). The Mishnah states that anything attached to an impure item is impure, and the baraita says Rabbi Eliezer taught that the pig goes to the raven because they are of the same kind.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks Rabbah bar Mari for the source of the folk saying that a bad palm tree goes and joins a grove of thorns (i.e., like attracts like).
Rabbah bar Mari responds that this principle is written in the Torah, repeated in the Prophets, tripled in the Writings, taught in the Mishnah, and stated in a baraita.
Rabbah bar Mari cites the verse 'And Esau went to Ishmael' (Genesis 28:9) as the Torah source.
Rabbah bar Mari cites the verse 'And there were gathered vain fellows to Yiftah' (Judges 11:3) as the Prophets source.
Rabbah bar Mari cites the verse 'Every bird dwells with its kind, and man with those like him' (Ben Sira 13:16) as the Writings source.
Rabbah bar Mari cites the Mishnah (Kelim 12:2) that anything attached to an impure item is impure, and anything attached to a pure item is pure.
Rabbah bar Mari cites the baraita where Rabbi Eliezer says that not for naught did the starling go to the raven, but because it is its kind (both non-kosher birds).

items.text: Source for the saying about throwing a big beam at one who doesn't respond
items.text_en: Source for the saying about throwing a big beam at one who doesn't respond
items.desc_en: Rava asks Rabbah bar Mari for the source of the folk saying that if you call your friend and he does not answer, you should throw a big beam at him (i.e., rebuke him harshly). Rabbah bar Mari cites the verse 'Because I have purified you and you were not purified, you shall not be purified again' (Ezekiel 24:13), implying that ignoring a call leads to severe consequences.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks Rabbah bar Mari for the source of the folk saying that if one calls his friend and he does not answer, one should throw a large beam at him.

Rabbah bar Mari cites the verse 'Because I have purified you and you were not purified, you shall not be purified again' (Ezekiel 24:13) as the source, implying that ignoring a call leads to severe consequences.

items.text: Source for the saying about not throwing a stone into a well you drank from
items.text_en: Source for the saying about not throwing a stone into a well you drank from
items.desc_en: Rava asks Rabbah bar Mari for the source of the folk saying that you should not throw a stone into a well from which you have drunk. Rabbah bar Mari cites the verse 'You shall not abhor an Edomite, for he is your brother; you shall not abhor an Egyptian, for you were a stranger in his land' (Deuteronomy 23:8), implying gratitude for past benefit.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks Rabbah bar Mari for the biblical source of the folk saying that one should not throw a stone into a well from which one has drunk.

Rabbah bar Mari cites the verse 'You shall not abhor an Edomite, for he is your brother; you shall not abhor an Egyptian, for you were a stranger in his land' (Deuteronomy 23:8) as the source, implying gratitude for past benefit.

items.text: Source for the saying about lifting a burden only if it is light
items.text_en: Source for the saying about lifting a burden only if it is light
items.desc_en: Rava asks Rabbah bar Mari for the source of the folk saying that if there is no burden, I will lift it, but if not, I will not lift it (i.e., one only takes on a task if it is easy). Rabbah bar Mari cites the verse where Barak says to Deborah 'If you go with me, I will go; if not, I will not go' (Judges 4:8), implying conditional willingness.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks Rabbah bar Mari for the source of the folk saying that one lifts a burden only if it is light.
Rabbah bar Mari cites the verse where Barak says to Deborah 'If you go with me, I will go; if not, I will not go' (Judges 4:8) as the source.

items.text: Source for the saying about the young respecting elders and the old respecting children
items.text_en: Source for the saying about the young respecting elders and the old respecting children
items.desc_en: Rava asks Rabbah bar Mari for the source of the folk saying that when we were young, we were respected by men, but now that we are old, we are respected by children (i.e., status changes with age). Rabbah bar Mari cites the verse where initially God went before them in a pillar of cloud by day and fire by night (Exodus 13:21), but later the text changes, implying a shift in leadership or guidance.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks Rabbah bar Mari for the source of the folk saying that when we were young we were considered men, but now that we are old we are considered children.

Rabbah bar Mari cites the verse from Exodus 13:21 where initially God went before them in a pillar of cloud by day and fire by night, and then notes that later the text changes, implying a shift in leadership or guidance.

items.text: Opening verse and Rava's question
items.text_en: Opening verse and Rava's question
items.desc_en: Rava asks Rabba bar Mari about the folk saying 'after the wealthy, drag the wood' (i.e., one's fortune follows one's patron). Rabba bar Mari answers with a verse about Lot's prosperity while accompanying Abraham.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse 'Behold, I send an angel before you, to keep you by the way' (Exodus 23:20).

sub.text: Rava's question to Rabba bar Mari
sub.text_en: Rava's question to Rabba bar Mari
sub.desc_en: Rava asks Rabba bar Mari about the source of the folk saying 'after the wealthy, drag the wood' (i.e., one's fortune follows one's patron).
Rabba bar Mari answers by citing the verse about Lot's prosperity while accompanying Abraham (Genesis 13:5).

items.text: Punishment for one who judges another
items.text_en: Punishment for one who judges another
items.desc_en: Rav Chanan teaches that one who brings a lawsuit against another is punished first, citing Sarah's complaint against Abraham and Abraham's subsequent mourning. This applies only when the accuser has a valid claim in earthly courts.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chanan states that one who brings a judgment against another is punished first.
Rav Chanan cites the verse where Sarah complains to Abraham and the verse where Abraham mourns for Sarah as proof.
