Rav Chanan limits the rule to cases where the accuser has a valid claim in earthly courts.

items.text: The power of curses and being pursued
items.text_en: The power of curses and being pursued
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak warns against being the one who cries out more than the one cried against, and teaches that a commoner's curse should not be taken lightly, as Avimelech's curse on Sarah was fulfilled in her descendants (Isaac's blindness). Rabbi Abahu advises always being among the pursued, not the pursuers, as doves and pigeons are pursued and yet are fit for the altar.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak warns that woe to one who cries out more than the one cried against, citing a baraita that both are heard but the cryer is answered more quickly.
Rabbi Yitzchak teaches that a commoner's curse should not be taken lightly, as Avimelech's curse on Sarah was fulfilled in Isaac's blindness.
Rabbi Abahu advises always being among the pursued rather than the pursuers, as doves and pigeons are pursued yet fit for the altar.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the Mishnah's case of one who says 'blind my eye' and asks why the first clause (blinding an eye) is treated differently from the latter clause (cutting off a hand).

sub.text: Rav Asi bar Chama to Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Asi bar Chama to Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Asi bar Chama asks Rava why the Mishnah's first clause (blinding an eye) is treated differently from the latter clause (cutting off a hand).
Rava answers that the first clause is different because a person does not waive compensation for major limbs (ראשי איברים).
Rav Asi bar Chama objects that a person can waive compensation for pain (צער), citing a baraita that one who says 'hit me, wound me on condition of exemption' is exempt, and Rava is silent.
Rava asks if Rav Asi bar Chama has heard anything on this matter, and Rav Asi bar Chama reports that Rav Sheshet said the reason is due to family blemish (פגם משפחה).
The Gemara records two opinions: Rabbi Oshaya says the reason is family blemish (פגם משפחה), and Rava says it is because a person does not waive compensation for major limbs (ראשי איברים).

items.text: First answer and objection
items.text_en: First answer and objection
items.desc_en: Rava answers that one cannot forgive the loss of major limbs. Rav Asi objects with a baraita that one can forgive pain (hitting or wounding) and be exempt. Rava is silent, then asks if Rav Asi has heard anything on this. Rav Asi cites Rav Sheshet that the reason is due to family blemish (פגם משפחה).

sub.desc_en: Rava answers that the first clause (blinding) is different because one does not forgive the loss of major limbs.
Rav Asi objects by citing a baraita that one who says 'hit me, wound me on condition of exemption' is exempt, showing one can forgive pain; Rava is silent.

sub.text: Rav Asi bar Chama citing Rav Sheshet
sub.text_en: Rav Asi bar Chama citing Rav Sheshet
sub.desc_en: Rava asks if Rav Asi has heard anything on this; Rav Asi cites Rav Sheshet that the reason is due to family blemish (פגם משפחה).

items.text: Debate over the reason
items.text_en: Debate over the reason
items.desc_en: The Gemara records a dispute: Rabbi Oshaya says the reason is family blemish, while Rava says it is because one cannot forgive the loss of major limbs. Rabbi Yochanan adds that sometimes 'yes' means 'no' and 'no' means 'yes', as illustrated by a baraita.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara records a dispute: Rabbi Oshaya says the reason is family blemish, while Rava says it is because one cannot forgive the loss of major limbs.
Rabbi Yochanan adds that sometimes 'yes' means 'no' and 'no' means 'yes', as illustrated by a baraita.

items.text: Baraita on 'yes' and 'no'
items.text_en: Baraita on 'yes' and 'no'
items.desc_en: A baraita supports Rabbi Yochanan: if one says 'hit me' and the other says 'yes' to exemption, it is not valid (yes is like no). If one says 'tear my garment' and the other says 'no' to exemption, he is liable (no is like yes).

sub.desc_en: A baraita supports Rabbi Yochanan's principle: if one says 'hit me' and the other says 'yes' to exemption, it is not valid (yes is like no); if one says 'tear my garment' and the other says 'no' to exemption, he is liable (no is like yes).

items.text: Contradiction and resolution regarding 'to guard'
items.text_en: Contradiction and resolution regarding 'to guard'
items.desc_en: The Mishnah says one who breaks a jug or tears a garment is liable, but a baraita says 'to guard' implies not to destroy. Rav Huna resolves: one case is where the item came to him for safekeeping, the other not. Rabba objects that 'to guard' implies it came for safekeeping. Rabba then resolves: both cases are where it came for safekeeping, but one where it came for safekeeping, the other where it came for tearing (i.e., the owner instructed him to tear it).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who breaks a jug or tears a garment is liable.
The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita that interprets 'to guard' as excluding destruction, tearing, or distributing to the poor.
Rav Huna resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a case where the item came into the person's possession and one where it did not.
Rabba objects that the phrase 'to guard' itself implies the item came into the person's possession for safekeeping.
Rabba resolves that both cases involve the item coming into possession, but one is for safekeeping and the other for tearing (i.e., the owner instructed him to tear it).

items.text: Practical application: charity chest
items.text_en: Practical application: charity chest
items.desc_en: A charity chest was deposited with a man in Pumpedita, who was negligent and it was stolen. Rav Yosef held him liable. Abaye objected based on the baraita 'to guard – not to distribute to the poor'. Rav Yosef answered that the poor of Pumpedita are allotted fixed portions, so it is considered 'to guard'.

sub.desc_en: A charity chest was deposited with a man in Pumpedita; he was negligent and it was stolen, and Rav Yosef held him liable.
Abaye objects, citing the baraita that 'to guard' excludes distribution to the poor, so the guardian is not liable for theft.
Rav Yosef answers that the poor of Pumpedita receive fixed portions, so the deposit is considered 'to guard' and he is liable.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one steals wood and makes it into vessels, or wool and makes it into garments, he pays according to the value at the time of the theft. It also discusses cases of a pregnant cow or a fleece-bearing sheep, and concludes with the general rule that all robbers pay according to the value at the time of the theft.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the rule that one who steals wood and makes it into vessels, or wool and makes it into garments, pays according to the value at the time of the theft.
The Mishnah presents the case of a pregnant cow or a fleece-bearing sheep that were stolen and then gave birth or were shorn, requiring payment based on the value at the time of theft.
The Mishnah concludes with the general rule that all robbers pay according to the value at the time of the theft.

items.text: Gemara's initial question and contradiction
items.text_en: Gemara's initial question and contradiction
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that only a change like making vessels (עשאן כלים) counts, but smoothing (שיפן) does not. It then raises a contradiction from a baraita that states smoothing wood or stone, or whitening wool, also requires payment at the time of theft.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that only a change like making vessels (עשאן כלים) counts as a change, but smoothing (שיפן) or whitening (ליבנן) does not.
The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita that states smoothing wood, chiseling stones, or whitening wool also requires payment at the time of theft.

items.text: Abaye's resolution: two types of change
items.text_en: Abaye's resolution: two types of change
items.desc_en: Abaye explains that our Tanna teaches about a reversible rabbinic change (שינוי דרבנן), and all the more so an irreversible Torah change (שינוי דאורייתא). He specifies that the Mishnah's cases involve planed wood (נסרים) and spun wool (צמר טווי), which are reversible. The baraita, however, teaches only about Torah-level changes.

sub.desc_en: Abaye resolves the contradiction by stating that our Tanna teaches about a reversible rabbinic change (שינוי דרבנן), and all the more so an irreversible Torah change (שינוי דאורייתא).
Abaye specifies that the Mishnah's cases involve planed wood (נסרים) and spun wool (צמר טווי), which are reversible changes.
Abaye concludes that the baraita teaches only about Torah-level changes, not rabbinic ones.

items.text: Rav Ashi's alternative resolution
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's alternative resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi argues that our Tanna also teaches about Torah-level changes: the wood is made into beams (בוכאני), which is smoothing, and the wool into cloaks (נמטי), which is an irreversible change.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi resolves the contradiction by arguing that our Tanna also teaches about Torah-level changes: the wood is made into beams (בוכאני), which is smoothing, and the wool into cloaks (נמטי), which is an irreversible change.

items.text: Debate on whitening as a change
items.text_en: Debate on whitening as a change
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether whitening (ליבון) constitutes a change, citing a contradiction about dyeing. Abaye resolves it by attributing the views to Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis. Rava distinguishes between beating (נפוצי) and combing (סרוקי). Rabbi Chiya bar Avin distinguishes between whitening (חוורי) and sifting (כברויי).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether whitening (ליבון) constitutes a change, citing a contradiction from a baraita where whitening without dyeing makes one liable.
Abaye resolves the contradiction by attributing the view that whitening is a change to Rabbi Shimon and the opposing view to the Rabbis, citing a baraita about wool processing.
Rava distinguishes between beating (נפוצי) and combing (סרוקי), explaining that both views can be attributed to Rabbi Shimon depending on the processing stage.
Rabbi Chiya bar Avin distinguishes between whitening (חוורי) and sifting (כברויי), offering another resolution to the contradiction.

items.text: Dyeing vs. whitening for Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Dyeing vs. whitening for Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that if dyeing is not a change for Rabbi Shimon, surely whitening is not. It cites a baraita where Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda says in Rabbi Shimon's name that dyeing does constitute a change. Abaye resolves that the first baraita reflects the Rabbis' view of Rabbi Shimon, while the second is Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda's own view. Rava says the Rabbis never disagreed with Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda, and dyeing is different because it can be removed with soap; the earlier case involved a permanent dye like indigo.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if dyeing (צֶבַע) is not considered a change (שִׁינּוּי) for Rabbi Shimon, can whitening (לִיבּוּן) possibly be considered a change?
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda says in Rabbi Shimon's name that dyeing does constitute a change (מִצְטָרֵף), contradicting the earlier assumption.
Abaye resolves the contradiction: the first baraita reflects the Rabbis' understanding of Rabbi Shimon's view, while the second is Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda's own understanding of Rabbi Shimon's view.

Rava says the Rabbis never disagreed with Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda, and dyeing is different because it can be removed with soap (צָפוֹן); the earlier case involved a permanent dye like indigo (קָלָא אִילָן).

items.text: List of Tannaim who hold that change stands in place
items.text_en: List of Tannaim who hold that change stands in place
items.desc_en: Abaye lists five Tannaim (Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda, Beit Shammai, Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, and Rabbi Yishmael) who all hold that a change (שינוי) stands in its place (i.e., the object is acquired by the change). The Gemara begins to elaborate on Beit Shammai's view regarding a harlot's hire.

sub.desc_en: Abaye lists five Tannaim who all hold that a change (שינוי) stands in its place, i.e., the object is acquired by the change.
The Gemara asks: What is the source for Beit Shammai's position?
A baraita is cited: If one gave wheat as a harlot's hire and made it into fine flour, olives into oil, or grapes into wine, one teaching says it is forbidden, another says it is permitted.
Rav Yosef says that the teaching of Gurion resolves the contradiction.

items.text: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel on change in stolen objects
items.text_en: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel on change in stolen objects
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel regarding whether a change in a stolen object (e.g., from אספורק) effects acquisition. Beit Shammai derives from 'גם שניהם' that the change acquires, while Beit Hillel derives from 'הם' that it does not. The Gemara clarifies the scriptural derivations and notes that Beit Hillel also learns from 'הם' that offspring are not acquired.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel regarding whether a change in a stolen object (e.g., from אספורק) effects acquisition, with Beit Shammai deriving from 'גם שניהם' that the change acquires and Beit Hillel deriving from 'הם' that it does not.

The Gemara questions Beit Shammai about the verse 'הם' and explains that Beit Shammai uses it to exclude offspring, while Beit Hillel derives both exclusion of change and exclusion of offspring from it.
The Gemara questions Beit Hillel about the verse 'גם' and notes that the word 'גם' remains problematic for Beit Hillel.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's statement
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks about Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's position, citing a baraita where he says that one who steals wheat, grinds, kneads, and bakes it, and then separates challah, does not bless but rather blasphemes, as per the verse 'בוצע ברך נאץ ה׳'. This implies that the change does not effect acquisition, aligning with Beit Shammai.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the statement of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov is, referring to his position on change of ownership.
A baraita is cited where Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov rules that one who steals wheat, processes it, and separates חלה (challah) does not bless but rather blasphemes, citing the verse 'בוצע ברך נאץ ה׳'.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's ruling and its explanation
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's ruling and its explanation
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's principle: a thief who improves a stolen object has the upper hand—he can either take the improvement or say 'your property is before you'. Rav Sheshet explains that this applies only when the improvement is reversible (הכחשה דהדר), but for irreversible change, the thief says 'your property is before you'. The Gemara questions why the thief cannot do the same for improvement, and answers: due to the enactment for penitents.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the source of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's ruling.
A baraita cites Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's principle: a thief who improves a stolen object has the upper hand—he can either take the improvement or say 'your property is before you'.
The Gemara asks what the baraita means.
Rav Sheshet explains that the principle applies only when the improvement is reversible (הכחשה דהדר), but for irreversible change, the thief says 'your property is before you'.
The Gemara objects: if so, even for improvement the thief should be able to say 'your property is before you'.
The Gemara answers that the thief cannot do so for improvement due to the enactment for penitents (תקנת השבים).

items.text: Rabbi Yishmael's ruling on pe'ah
items.text_en: Rabbi Yishmael's ruling on pe'ah
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about the mitzvah of pe'ah: one separates from the standing grain, or from sheaves, or from the pile before smoothing. After smoothing, he tithes and gives. In the name of Rabbi Yishmael, they said he may even separate from the dough and give. This suggests that change does not effect acquisition, as the dough is considered the owner's.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the source is for Rabbi Yishmael's position, and introduces a baraita about the mitzvah of pe'ah.
The baraita details the sequence for separating pe'ah, and in the name of Rabbi Yishmael it adds that one may even separate from the dough, implying that change does not effect acquisition.

items.text: Rava's rejection of the proof that all Tannaim follow Beit Shammai
items.text_en: Rava's rejection of the proof that all Tannaim follow Beit Shammai
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks Abaye if all these Tannaim support Beit Shammai. Abaye says they did not disagree with Beit Shammai on this matter. Rava challenges this, arguing that each Tanna's ruling is limited to a specific context: Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda to color that can be removed, Beit Shammai to a case of prohibition, Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov to a blessing on a mitzvah through transgression, Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar to reversible deterioration, and Rabbi Yishmael to pe'ah due to an extra verse 'תעזב'. He concludes that gifts to the poor are different.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks Abaye whether all these Tannaim are being cited to support Beit Shammai's position.
Abaye answers that the Tannaim are not supporting Beit Shammai; rather, Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel did not disagree on this matter.
Rava objects that each Tanna's ruling is limited to a specific context, beginning with Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda who only spoke about dye that can be removed.
Rava continues that Beit Shammai only spoke about a case of prohibition (איסור).
Rava continues that Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov only spoke about a blessing on a mitzvah that comes through transgression (מצוה הבאה בעבירה).
Rava continues that Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar only spoke about reversible deterioration (הכחשה דהדר).
Rava concludes that Rabbi Yishmael only spoke about pe'ah due to an extra verse 'תעזב', and gifts to the poor are different.

items.text: Rabbi Yonatan's inquiry about Rabbi Yishmael's reasoning
items.text_en: Rabbi Yonatan's inquiry about Rabbi Yishmael's reasoning
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yonatan asks whether Rabbi Yishmael's ruling is because he holds that change does not effect acquisition, or because of the extra verse 'תעזב'. The Gemara then considers: if change does not effect acquisition, why is the extra verse needed? And for the Rabbis, what is the extra verse for? It answers that the verse teaches about one who abandons his vineyard and then harvests it—he is liable for pe'ah but exempt from tithes.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yonatan asks whether Rabbi Yishmael's ruling is because he holds that change does not effect acquisition (שינוי אינו קונה), or because of the extra verse 'תעזב' (you shall leave).
The Gemara asks: if Rabbi Yishmael's reasoning is that change does not effect acquisition, why is the extra verse 'תעזב' needed? And for the Rabbis, what is the extra verse for?
The Gemara answers that the verse 'תעזב' teaches about one who abandons his vineyard and then harvests it—he is liable for pe'ah (פאה) but exempt from tithes (מעשר).

items.text: Reconciling Shmuel's rulings with Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
items.text_en: Reconciling Shmuel's rulings with Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda said in Shmuel's name that the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar. The Gemara notes a contradiction: Shmuel also said that we do not assess improvement for a thief or robber, only for a victim. For Rava, who limits Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar to reversible deterioration, there is no contradiction. For Abaye, who applies it to irreversible deterioration, the Gemara explains that Abaye taught the tradition differently, with Shmuel's ruling on assessment applying to irreversible deterioration.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports in Shmuel's name that the binding law (הלכה) follows Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar.
The Gemara objects: Did Shmuel really say that? He elsewhere ruled that we do not assess improvement for a thief or robber, only for a victim (נזקין).

The Gemara explains that according to Rava, who limits Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's ruling to reversible deterioration (הכחשה דהדר), there is no contradiction: Shmuel's ruling on assessment applies to irreversible deterioration (הכחשה דלא הדר).
The Gemara asks: But according to Abaye, who applies Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's ruling to irreversible deterioration, what can be said to resolve the contradiction?

The Gemara resolves that Abaye transmitted the tradition differently: Rav Yehuda said in Shmuel's name that the ruling on assessment applies to irreversible deterioration, thus reconciling the two statements.

items.text: Opening ruling and question
items.text_en: Opening ruling and question
items.desc_en: The Mishnah's ruling is stated as following Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, but the Gemara questions whether the anonymous editor actually holds this view.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the halacha follows Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, but the Gemara questions whether the anonymous editor actually holds this view.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's principle on changed stolen property
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's principle on changed stolen property
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that by Torah law, a stolen object that has changed returns in its original state, citing the verse 'and he shall return the stolen object which he stole.' The Mishnah's different ruling is explained as a rabbinic enactment for the sake of repentant sinners.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that by Torah law a stolen object that has changed returns in its original state, citing the verse 'וְהֵשִׁיב אֶת הַגְּזֵלָה אֲשֶׁר גָּזָל' (and he shall return the stolen object which he stole), and explains that the Mishnah's different ruling is a rabbinic enactment for repentant sinners.

items.text: Contradiction from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Contradiction from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yochanan elsewhere rules that the halakha follows an anonymous Mishnah, which states that if one dyed the stolen object before returning it, he is exempt—contradicting his own statement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yochanan elsewhere rules that the halakha follows an anonymous Mishnah, which states that if one dyed the stolen object before returning it, he is exempt—contradicting his own statement.

items.text: Resolution via Rabbi Yaakov
items.text_en: Resolution via Rabbi Yaakov
items.desc_en: A certain rabbi named Rabbi Yaakov clarifies that Rabbi Yochanan's statement applies only to a change that reverts to its original state, such as planed wood made into vessels, not to dyeing which is irreversible.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov resolves the contradiction by explaining that Rabbi Yochanan's statement applies only to a reversible change, like planed wood made into vessels, not to dyeing which is irreversible.

items.text: Baraita on robbers and usurers
items.text_en: Baraita on robbers and usurers
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that robbers and usurers who wish to return ill-gotten gains are not accepted, and those who accept from them are frowned upon. Rabbi Yochanan explains this was enacted in Rabbi's days due to a story where a man's wife prevented his repentance by noting even his belt was stolen.

sub.desc_en: The baraita rules that robbers and usurers who return ill-gotten gains are not accepted, and those who accept are frowned upon.

Rabbi Yochanan explains that this baraita was taught in the days of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, citing a story where a man's wife prevented his repentance by noting even his belt was stolen, leading to the enactment.

items.text: Challenge from a baraita on inherited usury
items.text_en: Challenge from a baraita on inherited usury
items.desc_en: A baraita states that children who inherit usury money are not required to return it, implying the father would be. The Gemara explains the baraita's structure: it teaches about the children to contrast with the case of a marked item, where they must return for their father's honor.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita: children who inherit usury money are not required to return it, implying the father would be obligated to return it.

The Gemara answers that by right the father would also not be obligated; the baraita teaches about the children only to contrast with the latter clause about a marked item, where they must return for their father's honor.

items.text: Objection and resolution regarding father's honor
items.text_en: Objection and resolution regarding father's honor
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that returning for father's honor violates the verse 'do not curse a prince among your people'—applied to a sinner. It resolves with Rav Pinchas's principle: the father had repented but died before returning the item.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that returning for father's honor violates the verse 'do not curse a prince among your people'—applied to a sinner.
The Gemara resolves with Rav Pinchas's principle: the father had repented but died before returning the item.

items.text: Another baraita: robbers and usurers return
items.text_en: Another baraita: robbers and usurers return
items.desc_en: A baraita states that robbers and usurers, even if they collected, must return. The Gemara clarifies that this refers to usurers, and explains that they return but are not accepted, doing so only to fulfill their heavenly obligation.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited stating that robbers and usurers, even if they collected, must return the money.
The Gemara questions the phrase 'even if they collected' regarding robbers, and clarifies that the baraita actually refers to usurers.
The Gemara explains that they return the money but it is not accepted from them, and they do so only to fulfill their heavenly obligation.

items.text: Baraita on shepherds, tax collectors, and repentance
items.text_en: Baraita on shepherds, tax collectors, and repentance
items.desc_en: A baraita says shepherds, tax collectors, and customs officials have a difficult repentance and return only to those they recognize. The Gemara reconciles this with the previous baraita by distinguishing between before and after the enactment.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita stating that shepherds, tax collectors, and customs officials have a difficult repentance and return only to those they recognize.
The Gemara questions why the baraita says their repentance is difficult, given that they return the stolen items even though recipients do not accept them.
Rav Chisda resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between before the enactment (when repentance is difficult) and after the enactment (when recipients accept the return).

items.text: Rav Nachman's resolution
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman resolves the contradiction by stating that when the stolen object is no longer extant, both cases are after the enactment and there is no difficulty.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman resolves the contradiction by stating that when the stolen object is no longer extant, both cases are after the enactment and there is no difficulty.

items.text: Distinguishing cases of extant vs. non-extant stolen object
items.text_en: Distinguishing cases of extant vs. non-extant stolen object
items.desc_en: The Gemara distinguishes between cases where the stolen object still exists and where it does not, then questions why the belt (avnet) is treated as extant, answering that it refers to its value. It then challenges that even when extant, the rabbis made a tikun for returnees, citing the case of a stolen beam built into a building, and distinguishes due to the loss of the building.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara distinguishes between a case where the stolen object still exists and one where it does not.
The Gemara questions why the belt (avnet) is treated as if the stolen object is extant.
The Gemara answers that 'avnet' refers to its value, not the physical belt.
The Gemara objects that even when the stolen object is extant, the rabbis made a tikun (remedy) for returnees, citing the case of a stolen beam built into a building.
The Gemara resolves that the case of the beam is different because of the loss of the building, so the rabbis treated it as if the beam does not exist.

items.text: Baraita on stolen pregnant cow or shorn ewe
items.text_en: Baraita on stolen pregnant cow or shorn ewe
items.desc_en: A baraita presents the dispute: Rabbi Meir requires returning the animal with its offspring or wool, Rabbi Yehuda says the stolen object returns as is, and Rabbi Shimon says it is assessed as if valued in money.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with the Tanna Kamma's position: one who steals a shorn ewe or pregnant cow must return the animal along with its wool or offspring.
Rabbi Yehuda states that the stolen object returns as is, without compensation for offspring or wool.
Rabbi Shimon says the stolen object is assessed as if it were valued in money at the time of theft.

items.text: Inquiry into Rabbi Meir's reasoning
items.text_en: Inquiry into Rabbi Meir's reasoning
items.desc_en: The Gemara inquires whether Rabbi Meir holds that change in place suffices (shinui bimkomo omed) or that change acquires (shinui koneh) and he penalizes. The practical difference is a case where the animal lost weight.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an inquiry: what is Rabbi Meir's reasoning — does he hold that change in place suffices (שינוי במקומו עומד) or that change acquires (שינוי קונה) and he penalizes?
The Gemara clarifies the practical difference between the two possibilities: a case where the animal lost weight after the theft.

items.text: Proof from a baraita on aged animals and slaves
items.text_en: Proof from a baraita on aged animals and slaves
items.desc_en: A baraita states that for a stolen animal that aged, Rabbi Meir requires payment at the time of theft, but for slaves he says 'here is yours before you.' The Gemara argues: if Rabbi Meir held shinui bimkomo omed, he would say the same for animals; thus he must hold shinui koneh and penalizes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita: for a stolen animal or slave that aged, Rabbi Meir requires payment at the time of theft for animals, but for slaves he says 'here is yours before you.'

The Gemara argues: if Rabbi Meir held that shinui bimkomo omed (change in place stands), he would say the same for animals; thus he must hold shinui koneh (change acquires) and penalizes here as a קנס (penalty).

items.text: Alternative explanation: Rabbi Meir addressing the Sages
items.text_en: Alternative explanation: Rabbi Meir addressing the Sages
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative: Rabbi Meir was speaking to the Sages according to their own view that shinui koneh, but he himself holds shinui does not acquire; he only asks them to concede regarding slaves as land. The Sages respond that slaves are movable property.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that Rabbi Meir was speaking to the Sages according to their own view that שינוי קונה (change of ownership through alteration) applies, while he himself holds that שינוי does not acquire; he only asks them to concede regarding slaves as land.
The Sages respond that slaves are movable property (מטלטלי), not land, so the principle that land cannot be stolen does not apply.

items.text: Proof from dyeing wool
items.text_en: Proof from dyeing wool
items.desc_en: A baraita: if one gave wool to dye red and it was dyed black, Rabbi Meir says he pays only the wool's value, not the improvement. The Gemara argues: if Rabbi Meir held shinui does not acquire, he would require paying for the improvement; thus he must hold shinui koneh and penalizes. Conclusion: indeed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita: if one gave wool to dye red and it was dyed black, Rabbi Meir says he pays only the wool's value, not the improvement.
The Gemara argues: if Rabbi Meir held that shinui does not acquire, he would require paying for the improvement.
The Gemara concludes: Rabbi Meir holds shinui koneh, and the baraita penalizes him for the change.

items.text: Refined inquiry: intentional vs. unintentional
items.text_en: Refined inquiry: intentional vs. unintentional
items.desc_en: Some say the earlier inquiry was unnecessary because Rav reversed the baraita, proving Rabbi Meir holds shinui koneh and penalizes. The real inquiry is whether the penalty applies only to intentional acts or also to unintentional ones.

sub.desc_en: Some say the earlier inquiry was unnecessary because Rav reversed the baraita, proving Rabbi Meir holds shinui koneh and penalizes.
The real inquiry is whether the penalty applies only to intentional acts or also to unintentional ones.

items.text: Proof from five who collect from encumbered property
items.text_en: Proof from five who collect from encumbered property
items.desc_en: A mishnah lists five who collect from encumbered property, including fruits and improvement of fruits. The Gemara identifies Rabbi Meir as the authority who holds that 'achrayut' is not a scribal error, and explains improvement of fruits as a case of a stolen field sold and improved, where the original owner collects the improvement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a mishnah listing five who collect from encumbered property, as a proof for the dispute about Rabbi Meir's view on change of ownership.

The mishnah enumerates the five categories: fruits, improvement of fruits, a stepfather's support obligation, a debt document without אחריות (encumbrance clause), and a marriage contract without אחריות.
The Gemara asks: Who is the authority who holds that אחריות (encumbrance) is not a scribal error? It answers: Rabbi Meir.
The Gemara explains the case of 'improvement of fruits': a stolen field sold to another who improved it, and the original owner collects the improvement when the field leaves the buyer's possession.

items.text: Gemara's first question: Does the robber pay the improvement even when unintentional?
items.text_en: Gemara's first question: Does the robber pay the improvement even when unintentional?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's ruling that the robber pays the principal from encumbered property and the improvement from free property applies even when the robber was unaware that land is not subject to theft (a shoegag). It suggests this would imply that the court penalizes even an unintentional robber, but the Gemara rejects this, explaining the case involves a learned purchaser who knows the law.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's ruling that the robber pays the principal from encumbered property and the improvement from free property applies even when the robber was unaware that land is subject to theft (a shoegag), implying that the court penalizes even an unintentional robber.
The Gemara rejects the implication, explaining that the case involves a learned purchaser (תלמיד חכם) who knows the law, not an unintentional robber.

items.text: Proof from the dyer's case: No penalty for unintentional acts
items.text_en: Proof from the dyer's case: No penalty for unintentional acts
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about a dyer who dyes wool the wrong color: Rabbi Meir says he pays only the value of the wool, not the improvement. If the court penalized even unintentional acts, the dyer would have to pay the improvement. Since he does not, the Gemara concludes that the court penalizes only intentional acts, not unintentional ones.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about a dyer who dyes wool the wrong color, where Rabbi Meir rules he pays only the value of the wool, not the improvement.
The Gemara argues that if the court penalized even unintentional acts, the dyer would have to pay the improvement.
The Gemara concludes that the court penalizes only intentional acts, not unintentional ones.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon on improvement
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon on improvement
items.desc_en: The Mishnah records Rabbi Yehuda's view that the stolen object returns as is (with improvement going to the robber) and Rabbi Shimon's view that it is appraised as if it were a deposit of money. Rav Zevid explains they dispute who receives the improvement that is physically attached to the stolen object: Rabbi Yehuda says it belongs to the victim, Rabbi Shimon says it belongs to the robber.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the dispute: Rabbi Yehuda says the stolen object returns as is (with improvement going to the robber), and Rabbi Shimon says it is appraised as if it were a deposit of money.
The Gemara asks what is the practical difference between the two opinions.

Rav Zevid explains that they dispute who receives the improvement that is physically attached to the stolen object: Rabbi Yehuda says it belongs to the victim, Rabbi Shimon says it belongs to the robber.

items.text: Rav Pappa's alternative explanation: Dispute over the robber's share
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's alternative explanation: Dispute over the robber's share
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa argues that all agree the improvement belongs to the robber; the dispute is about whether the robber takes all the improvement (Rabbi Yehuda) or only a half, third, or quarter (Rabbi Shimon).

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa argues that all agree the improvement belongs to the robber; the dispute is about whether the robber takes all the improvement (Rabbi Yehuda) or only a half, third, or quarter (Rabbi Shimon).

items.text: Challenge to Rav Pappa from the Mishnah of the pregnant cow
items.text_en: Challenge to Rav Pappa from the Mishnah of the pregnant cow
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a robber stole a cow and it gave birth, he pays the value at the time of theft. This supports Rav Zevid (who attributes the improvement to the victim according to Rabbi Yehuda) but challenges Rav Pappa, who says the improvement always belongs to the robber. Rav Pappa responds that the Mishnah's mention of birth is incidental; even without birth, he pays the original value.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah is cited: if one stole a cow and it became pregnant and gave birth, he pays the value at the time of the theft.

The Gemara challenges Rav Pappa: according to Rav Zevid the Mishnah aligns with Rabbi Yehuda, but according to Rav Pappa (who holds the improvement always belongs to the robber), the Mishnah fits neither Rabbi Yehuda nor Rabbi Shimon.
Rav Pappa responds that the same rule applies even without birth; the mention of birth is incidental, carried over from the first clause.

items.text: Baraita supports Rav Pappa
items.text_en: Baraita supports Rav Pappa
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that explicitly supports Rav Pappa's interpretation: Rabbi Shimon says the object is appraised as if it were a deposit of money, and the robber takes a half, third, or quarter.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited that explicitly supports Rav Pappa's interpretation: Rabbi Shimon says the object is appraised as if it were a deposit of money, and the robber takes a half, third, or quarter.

items.text: Question about Rabbi Shimon's method: Payment in money or in kind?
items.text_en: Question about Rabbi Shimon's method: Payment in money or in kind?
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi reports a question from the study of Rav Kahana: According to Rabbi Shimon, when the robber is paid his share of the improvement, is he paid in money or does he take a portion of the meat? They resolve this from a statement of Shmuel about three cases where improvement is appraised and paid in money. Ravina challenges Shmuel's consistency, and the Gemara distinguishes between improvement that is portable and that which is not.

sub.text: Rav Ashi's report of the study of Rav Kahana
sub.text_en: Rav Ashi's report of the study of Rav Kahana
sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi reports that in the study of Rav Kahana they asked: According to Rabbi Shimon, when the robber is paid his share of the improvement, is he paid in money or does he take a portion of the meat?

They resolved the question from Rav Nachman's citation of Shmuel: three cases where improvement is appraised and paid in money — firstborn to a commoner, creditor to a purchaser, and creditor to orphans.

Ravina challenges Rav Ashi: Does Shmuel really say the creditor pays the purchaser the improvement? Shmuel elsewhere says the creditor collects the improvement! Rav Ashi distinguishes: here the improvement is portable (מגיע לכתפיים), there it is not.

sub.text: Ravina's further objection from daily practice
sub.text_en: Ravina's further objection from daily practice
sub.desc_en: Ravina objects further: But daily practice shows that Shmuel collects even portable improvement! Rav Ashi responds: It is not difficult (the distinction still holds).

items.text: Gemara's question about the Mishnah's ruling on a stolen field with improvements
items.text_en: Gemara's question about the Mishnah's ruling on a stolen field with improvements
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's distinction between a creditor who collects a field with its improvements and one who collects only the field. It raises an objection based on the view that a purchaser can redeem the field from the creditor, and resolves it by explaining that the field was made an apphoteki (collateral) so the creditor collects only from this field.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question about the Mishnah's distinction between a creditor who collects a field with its improvements and one who collects only the field.
The Gemara objects that according to the view that a purchaser can redeem the field from the creditor, the purchaser could demand compensation for his improvements.
The Gemara resolves that the case involves a field made an אפותיקי (collateral), so the creditor collects only from this field.

items.text: Rava's ruling on a thief who improves and then sells or bequeaths
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on a thief who improves and then sells or bequeaths
items.desc_en: Rava states that if a thief stole an object, improved it, and then sold or bequeathed it, the improvement is transferred with the sale or inheritance.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that if a thief stole an object, improved it, and then sold or bequeathed it, the improvement is transferred with the sale or inheritance.

items.text: Rava's query about a purchaser who improves
items.text_en: Rava's query about a purchaser who improves
items.desc_en: Rava raises a question about a purchaser who improves the stolen property after buying it from the thief. He resolves it by stating that the first seller (the thief) sells all rights that will come to him, so the improvement belongs to the purchaser.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks what the law is regarding a purchaser who improves stolen property after buying it from the thief.
The Gemara resolves that the first seller (the thief) sells all rights that will come to him, so the improvement belongs to the purchaser.

items.text: Rava's query about a gentile who improves, and the case of a gentile in the middle
items.text_en: Rava's query about a gentile who improves, and the case of a gentile in the middle
items.desc_en: Rava asks about a gentile who improves stolen property. Rav Acha from Difti objects that we do not institute a takkanah for a gentile. Rava clarifies the case: a Jew stole, sold to a gentile who improved it, and then the gentile sold it back to a Jew. The question is whether the rabbis instituted a takkanah for the improvement since the chain involves a gentile in the middle. The Gemara concludes with teiku (undecided).

sub.desc_en: Rava asks: what is the law regarding a gentile who improves stolen property?
Rav Acha from Difti objects to Ravina: would we institute a takkanah (rabbinic enactment) for a gentile?
Ravina responds: the query is unnecessary in that case; rather, it is where the gentile sold the property to a Jew.
The Gemara objects: ultimately, one who acquires from a gentile is considered like a gentile, so the same problem applies.
The Gemara clarifies: the case is where a Jew stole, sold to a gentile who improved it, and then the gentile sold it back to a Jew.
The Gemara poses the dilemma: since the chain begins and ends with a Jew, do the rabbis institute a takkanah for the improvement, or because a gentile is in the middle, do they not?
The Gemara concludes with תיקו (teiku — the question stands unresolved).

items.text: Rav Papa's ruling on a stolen palm tree that is cut down or altered
items.text_en: Rav Papa's ruling on a stolen palm tree that is cut down or altered
items.desc_en: Rav Papa rules that if one steals a palm tree and cuts it down, even if he moves it to his own land, he does not acquire it because it is still called a palm tree. If he makes it into beams, he does not acquire it because it is still called palm beams. But if he makes the beams into small sticks, he acquires it. Similarly, if he makes large beams into small beams, he does not acquire; if he makes them into cut pieces, he acquires.

sub.desc_en: Rav Papa rules that if one steals a palm tree and cuts it down, even if he moves it to his own land, he does not acquire it because it is still called a palm tree.
If he makes the tree into beams, he does not acquire it because they are still called palm beams.
If he makes the beams into small sticks, he acquires them; similarly, if he makes large beams into small beams he does not acquire, but if he makes them into cut pieces he acquires.

items.text: Rava's ruling on a stolen lulav that is transformed
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on a stolen lulav that is transformed
items.desc_en: Rava rules that if one steals a lulav (palm branch) and makes it into hutzim (palm leaves), he acquires it because the name changes. If he makes the hutzim into a chufya (broom), he acquires it. But if he makes the chufya into a sharshura (rope), he does not acquire it because it can be undone and revert to a chufya.

sub.desc_en: Rava opens the section with a ruling that if one steals a לולב (lulav, palm branch) and turns it into הוצי (hutzim, palm leaves), he acquires it because the name changes from 'lulav' to 'hutzim'.
Rava adds that if the thief turns the hutzim into a חופיא (chufya, broom), he acquires it because the name changes again from 'hutzim' to 'chufya'.

Rava concludes that if the thief turns the chufya into a שרשורא (sharshura, rope), he does not acquire it, because the rope can be undone and reverted to a chufya, so the transformation is not permanent.

items.text: Rav Papa's query about a split spine of a lulav
items.text_en: Rav Papa's query about a split spine of a lulav
items.desc_en: Rav Papa asks about a lulav whose spine (the central rib) has split. He brings a proof from Rabbi Matun citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that if the spine is removed, the lulav is invalid, implying that splitting is similar to removal and thus invalidates.

sub.desc_en: Rav Papa asks whether a lulav whose spine (the central rib) has split is valid for the mitzvah.

sub.text: Proof from Rabbi Matun citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.text_en: Proof from Rabbi Matun citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.desc_en: Rav Papa brings a supporting baraita from Rabbi Matun citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that if the spine is removed, the lulav is invalid, implying that splitting is similar to removal and thus invalidates.

items.text: Gemara's question on the distinction between 'torn' and 'split'
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the distinction between 'torn' and 'split'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the law for a torn animal is the same as for a split one, and answers that a torn animal is different because it is lacking.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the law for a torn animal (ניטלה) applies equally to a split one (נחלקה).
The Gemara answers that a torn animal is different because it is lacking (חסר), unlike a split one.

items.text: Alternative version: proof from Rabbi Matun
items.text_en: Alternative version: proof from Rabbi Matun
items.desc_en: Some say that Rabbi Matun reported Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's ruling that a split twin is considered as if torn and is invalid, providing proof.

sub.desc_en: The alternative version cites Rabbi Matun quoting Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that a split twin is considered as if torn and invalid, providing proof.

items.text: Rav Pappa's principles on change and new faces
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's principles on change and new faces
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa states that if one steals earth and makes it into a brick, he does not acquire it because it can revert; but if he steals a brick and makes it into earth, he acquires it because new matter has come. Similarly for a coin made into a vessel and vice versa, and for old garments made new and vice versa.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa states the principle: stealing earth and making it into a brick does not effect acquisition because it can revert, but stealing a brick and making it into earth does effect acquisition because new matter has come.
Rav Pappa extends the principle to a coin made into a vessel and vice versa, applying the same logic of new faces.
Rav Pappa extends the principle to old garments made new and vice versa, explaining that oldness is inherently recognizable.

items.text: The general rule and Rabbi Ila'a's teaching
items.text_en: The general rule and Rabbi Ila'a's teaching
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that all robbers pay according to the time of the theft. The Gemara asks what 'this is the rule' comes to include, and answers that it includes Rabbi Ila'a's teaching that if one steals a lamb and it becomes a ram, or a calf and it becomes an ox, a change has occurred in his hand and he acquires it.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the general rule that all robbers pay according to the value at the time of the theft.
The Gemara asks what the phrase 'this is the rule' comes to include beyond the explicit cases.

The Gemara answers that it includes Rabbi Ila'a's teaching that if one steals a lamb and it becomes a ram, or a calf and it becomes an ox, a change (שינוי) has occurred in his hand and he acquires it, so if he then slaughters or sells it, it is his own animal.

items.text: Case of stolen oxen and Rav Nachman's ruling
items.text_en: Case of stolen oxen and Rav Nachman's ruling
items.desc_en: A man stole a yoke of oxen, plowed and sowed with them, then returned them. Rav Nachman ordered an appraisal of the improvement. Rava objected that the land also improved, but Rav Nachman said he meant half. Rava argued that since the oxen returned intact, the robber should only pay as at the time of theft. Rav Nachman revealed he wanted to penalize the robber because he was a habitual thief.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a case: a man stole a yoke of oxen, plowed and sowed with them, then returned them and came before Rav Nachman.
Rav Nachman orders an appraisal of the improvement the oxen caused.
Rava objects: the oxen improved, but the land also improved — why not appraise the land's improvement too?
Rav Nachman clarifies he meant only half the improvement — the oxen's contribution, not the land's.
Rava objects further: since the oxen returned intact, the robber should pay only their value at the time of theft, per the Mishnah's rule.
Rav Nachman rebukes Rava for interrupting his court, citing Huna the colleague's saying about judicial authority, and reveals he intended to penalize the robber because he was a habitual thief.

items.text: Mishnah: payment for aged or deteriorated objects
items.text_en: Mishnah: payment for aged or deteriorated objects
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if one steals an animal and it ages, or slaves and they age, he pays as at the time of theft. Rabbi Meir says regarding slaves he can say 'yours is before you.' Similarly for coins that cracked, produce that rotted, or wine that soured, he pays as at the time of theft. But for coins that became invalid, terumah that became impure, chametz that passed Passover, or an animal that became unfit for the altar, he says 'yours is before you.'

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the rule that if one steals an animal or slaves and they age, he pays as at the time of theft.
Rabbi Meir adds that regarding slaves, the thief can say 'yours is before you' and return them as-is.
The Mishnah continues: for coins that cracked, produce that rotted, or wine that soured, he pays as at the time of theft.
The Mishnah concludes: for coins that became invalid, terumah that became impure, chametz that passed Passover, or an animal that became unfit for the altar, he says 'yours is before you'.

items.text: Gemara: clarification of 'aged' and attribution of Rabbi Ila'a's teaching
items.text_en: Gemara: clarification of 'aged' and attribution of Rabbi Ila'a's teaching
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa explains that 'aged' includes even emaciation that does not recover. Mar Kashisha then reports that Rabbi Yochanan said the same as Rabbi Ila'a about a lamb becoming a ram, but Rav Ashi corrects him that it was said in the name of Rabbi Ila'a.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa clarifies that the Mishnah's term 'הזקינה' (aged) includes even emaciation (כחשה) that does not recover, not only literal aging.

Mar Kashisha reports to Rav Ashi that Rabbi Yochanan said the same ruling as Rabbi Ila'a regarding a stolen lamb becoming a ram, but Rav Ashi corrects him that it was said in the name of Rabbi Ila'a, not Rabbi Yochanan.

items.text: Debate on Rabbi Meir's ruling and the halakha
items.text_en: Debate on Rabbi Meir's ruling and the halakha
items.desc_en: Rav ruled that the halakha follows Rabbi Meir regarding slaves. The Gemara questions why Rav abandons the Sages for Rabbi Meir, and explains that the Mishnah was taught in reverse. A baraita is cited about a cow and a donkey, and the Gemara concludes that Rav's ruling is consistent with his version of the Mishnah.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah cites Rabbi Meir's position that regarding slaves, the robber says 'That which is yours is before you.'

sub.text: Rav Chanina bar Abdimi citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Chanina bar Abdimi citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Chanina bar Abdimi reports that Rav ruled the halakha follows Rabbi Meir.
The Gemara questions why Rav abandons the Sages and follows Rabbi Meir.
The Gemara answers that a baraita teaches the opposite, with the Sages holding Rabbi Meir's position.
The Gemara further questions why Rav abandons the Mishnah for a baraita.
The Gemara answers that Rav's version of the Mishnah also taught the opposite.
The Gemara asks why Rav reversed the Mishnah in light of the baraita rather than the opposite.
The Gemara answers that Rav's Mishnah was already taught in the opposite version.
The Gemara offers an alternative explanation: one mishna is not reversed for one baraita, but one mishna is reversed for two baraitot.

A baraita is cited about exchanging a cow for a donkey or selling a maidservant, where if one claims the birth was in his possession and the other is silent, the claimant acquires the offspring; if both are uncertain, they divide.
The baraita continues: if both claim possession, the seller swears, as per Rabbi Meir's principle that all Torah oaths are taken without payment.
The Sages say that no oath is taken regarding slaves or land, indicating slaves have the status of land.
The Gemara questions why Rav said 'the halakha follows Rabbi Meir' if according to Rav the Mishnah attributes that position to the Sages.
The Gemara resolves that Rav meant: according to the version you (the Gemara) reversed and taught, the halakha follows Rabbi Meir.

items.text: Gemara's question on Rav's ruling about seizing a slave
items.text_en: Gemara's question on Rav's ruling about seizing a slave
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rav Avda's view that a slave is like land, citing Rav Daniel bar Rav Katina's statement that one who seizes another's slave and works him is exempt. If a slave were like land, why would he be exempt?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rav Avda's view that a slave is like land, citing Rav Daniel bar Rav Katina's statement that one who seizes another's slave and works him is exempt, and argues that if a slave were like land, the seizure would be a trespass in the owner's domain.

items.text: Distinction: not during work time, and the case of dwelling in a courtyard
items.text_en: Distinction: not during work time, and the case of dwelling in a courtyard
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the case is when the slave is not working for his master. It cites a story where Rabbi Abba asked Rav Huna about one who dwells in another's courtyard without permission, and the answer was that no rent is required. The Gemara then questions whether the owner is pleased with the slave's weakening, and answers that he is pleased to avoid the slave becoming idle.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by stating that the case of Rav's ruling is when the slave is not working for his master.

sub.text: Story of Rabbi Abba and Rav Huna
sub.text_en: Story of Rabbi Abba and Rav Huna
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a story where Rabbi Abba asked Rav Huna about one who dwells in another's courtyard without permission, and the answer was that no rent is required.
The Gemara objects that the analogy to a courtyard dweller is not apt, because in that case the owner benefits from the dwelling, but here the slave's weakening is a loss.
The Gemara answers that the owner is indeed pleased with the slave's weakening, because it prevents the slave from becoming idle and rebellious.

items.text: מעשה רב יוסף בר חמא בעבדי בעלי חוב
items.text_en: Story of Rav Yosef bar Chama and his son Rabba
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef bar Chama would seize slaves of debtors and work them. His son Rabba questioned this, citing Rav Nachman that a slave is worthless. Rabba distinguished between a slave who dances in winepresses and all slaves. Rav Yosef then cited Rav Daniel's ruling that one is exempt, as the owner is pleased. Rabba countered that this applies only when the creditor does not have a debt claim, but here it appears as interest. Rav Yosef conceded.
items.desc: רב יוסף בר חמא היה תוקף עבדים של חייביו ועושה בהם מלאכה, בטענה שאינם שווים את מזונם. בנו רבה חלק עליו, והראה שהדבר נראה כריבית. רב יוסף חזר בו.

sub.desc_en: The narrator describes Rav Yosef bar Chama's practice of seizing debtors' slaves and working them.
sub.desc: מציג את מעשה רב יוסף בר חמא שתוקף עבדי חייביו ועובד בהם, ואת שאלת רבה בנו על טעם הדבר.

sub.desc_en: Rabba asks his father Rav Yosef bar Chama why he works the slaves.
sub.desc: רב יוסף בר חמא משיב שהוא סובר כרב דניאל, שהתוקף עבד חברו ועשה בו מלאכה פטור, כי נוח לבעל העבד שלא יתבטלו הרגלי העבודה שלו.

sub.text_en: Rav Yosef bar Chama's first answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef bar Chama cites Rav Nachman's ruling that a slave is worthless, justifying his practice.
sub.desc: רבה משיג שדברי רב דניאל אמורים רק כשאינו נושה בחברו, אבל כאן שנושה בו הדבר נראה כריבית, ומביא ראיה מרב יוסף בר מיניומי בשם רב נחמן.

sub.desc_en: Rabba objects that Rav Nachman's statement applies only to a worthless slave who dances in winepresses, not to all slaves who do real work.
sub.desc: מציג את מעשה רב יוסף בר חמא שתוקף עבדי חייביו ועובד בהם, ואת שאלת רבה בנו על טעם הדבר.

sub.text_en: Rav Yosef bar Chama's second answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef bar Chama cites Rav Daniel bar Rav Katina's ruling that one who seizes another's slave and works him is exempt, because the owner is pleased that his slave is not idle.
sub.desc: רב יוסף בר חמא משיב שהוא סובר כרב דניאל, שהתוקף עבד חברו ועשה בו מלאכה פטור, כי נוח לבעל העבד שלא יתבטלו הרגלי העבודה שלו.

sub.desc_en: Rabba counters that Rav Daniel's exemption applies only when the creditor has no debt claim, but here Rav Yosef bar Chama is a creditor, so it appears as interest (ריבית), citing Rav Yosef bar Minyomi's ruling.
sub.desc: רבה משיג שדברי רב דניאל אמורים רק כשאינו נושה בחברו, אבל כאן שנושה בו הדבר נראה כריבית, ומביא ראיה מרב יוסף בר מיניומי בשם רב נחמן.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef bar Chama concedes to Rabba's argument, saying 'I retract.'
sub.desc: רבה משיג שדברי רב דניאל אמורים רק כשאינו נושה בחברו, אבל כאן שנושה בו הדבר נראה כריבית, ומביא ראיה מרב יוסף בר מיניומי בשם רב נחמן.

items.text: מחלוקת רב ושמואל בתוקף ספינת חברו
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on seizing a boat
items.desc_en: It was stated: One who seizes another's boat and works it – Rav says the owner can choose to take the hire or the depreciation; Shmuel says he only takes the depreciation. Rav Pappa resolves that they do not disagree: one case is a boat hired out, the other is not; alternatively, both are hired out but one case the seizer intended to hire, the other to steal.
items.desc: נאמרה מחלוקת: התוקף ספינת חברו ועשה בה מלאכה – רב אומר יכול לתבוע שכר או פחת, שמואל אומר רק פחת. רב פפא מיישב שאין מחלוקת, וההבדל תלוי אם הספינה עשויה להשכיר או לא, או בכוונת התוקף.

sub.desc_en: The gemara states a dispute: Rav says the seizer of a boat may choose to take its hire or its depreciation, while Shmuel says he only takes the depreciation.
sub.desc: פותח במחלוקת בין רב לשמואל: רב מתיר לתובע לבחור בין שכר לפחת, ושמואל מגביל לפחת בלבד.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa resolves the dispute by distinguishing between a boat that is hired out and one that is not, or between a seizer who intended to hire and one who intended to steal.
sub.desc: רב פפא מיישב שאין מחלוקת: ההבדל תלוי אם הספינה עשויה להשכיר או לא, או בכוונת התוקף – לשכור או לגזול.

items.text: פירושי 'נסדק' ו'נפסל' במטבע גזול
items.text_en: Interpretations of 'cracked' and 'invalidated' coin
items.desc_en: Rav Huna says 'cracked' means literally cracked, 'invalidated' means the government invalidated it. Rav Yehuda says government invalidation is also cracking; 'invalidated' means one city invalidated it but it circulates elsewhere. Rav Chisda challenges Rav Huna with the case of rotted produce or soured wine, where the robber pays as at the time of theft. Rav Huna distinguishes because the taste and smell changed. Rava challenges Rav Yehuda with the case of terumah that became impure, where the robber says 'here it is before you'. Rav Yehuda distinguishes because the loss is not recognizable.
items.desc: רב הונא ורב יהודה נחלקו בפירוש המשנה: לרב הונא 'נפסל' הוא פסלתו מלכות, ולרב יהודה גם זה נסדק, ו'נפסל' הוא מטבע שיוצא במדינה אחרת. הגמרא מקשה על כל אחד מהם ממשניות אחרות, והם מתרצים לפי ההבדל בין שינוי הטעם והריח לבין שינוי הנראה לעין.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna defines 'cracked' as literally cracked and 'invalidated' as invalidated by the government.
sub.desc: רב הונא מפרש את המשנה: 'נסדק' – סדק ממש, 'נפסל' – פסלתו מלכות.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda argues that government invalidation is also a form of cracking, and 'invalidated' refers to a coin invalidated in one city but circulating elsewhere.
sub.desc: רב יהודה חולק: גם פסלתו מלכות הרי הוא כנסדק, ו'נפסל' האמור במשנה הוא מטבע שפסלתו מדינה זו ויוצא במדינה אחרת.

sub.text_en: Rav Chisda's challenge to Rav Huna
sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda challenges Rav Huna by comparing government invalidation to rotted produce or soured wine, where the robber pays as at the time of theft.
sub.desc: רב חסדא מקשה על רב הונא: הרי פירות שהרקיבו ויין שהחמיץ דומים לפסלתו מלכות, ובמשנה אמרו שמשלם כשעת הגזילה – ואילו כאן אתה אומר שאינו משלם?

sub.text_en: Rav Huna's response to Rav Chisda
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna distinguishes because in the produce case the taste and smell changed, whereas the coin's physical properties did not change.
sub.desc: רב הונא מתרץ: בפירות ויין השתנה טעמם וריחם, אבל במטבע לא השתנה גופו.

sub.desc_en: Rava challenges Rav Yehuda by comparing government invalidation to תרומה (priestly portion) that became impure, where the robber says 'here it is before you'.
sub.desc: רבא מקשה על רב יהודה: הרי תרומה שנטמאה דומה לפסלתו מלכות, ובמשנה אמרו שאומר 'הרי שלך לפניך' – ואילו אתה אומר שפסלתו מלכות הרי הוא כנסדק ומשלם?

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda distinguishes because in the תרומה case the loss is not recognizable, whereas the coin's invalidation is recognizable.
sub.desc: רב יהודה מתרץ: בתרומה הנזק אינו ניכר לעין, אבל במטבע פסול הנזק ניכר.

items.text: פתיחת מחלוקת במלוה על המטבע ונפסל
items.text_en: Beginning of a new statement about a loan on a coin that becomes invalid
items.desc_en: It was stated: One who lends to another on a coin, and the coin becomes invalid – Rav said... (the text breaks off).
items.desc: נאמרה מחלוקת בין רב ושמואל לגבי המלווה את חברו על המטבע ונפסל המטבע – רב אמר... (הקטע נקטע).

sub.desc_en: A dispute is introduced about a lender who lends on a coin that is later invalidated, with Rav's opinion beginning.
sub.desc: פותח במחלוקת בין רב ושמואל לגבי דין מלווה שהלווה על מטבע מסוים ונפסל המטבע.

items.text: Shmuel's ruling on paying with obsolete coins
items.text_en: Shmuel's ruling on paying with obsolete coins
items.desc_en: Shmuel rules that a debtor can pay with coins that are no longer current, telling the creditor to spend them in Meishan. Rav Nachman qualifies this: it applies only if the creditor regularly goes to Meishan.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one pays with the coin current at the time of payment.
Shmuel rules that the debtor can tell the creditor to spend the obsolete coin in Meishan.
Rav Nachman qualifies Shmuel's ruling: it applies only if the creditor regularly travels to Meishan.

items.text: Rava's objection from the Mishnah of maaser sheni
items.text_en: Rava's objection from the Mishnah of maaser sheni
items.desc_en: Rava challenges Rav Nachman from a baraita: one may not redeem maaser sheni with non-current coins, but later coins similar to earlier ones are valid. Rav Nachman deflects by saying the baraita deals with kingdoms that do not prohibit each other's currency.

sub.desc_en: Rava challenges Rav Nachman by citing a baraita that prohibits redeeming maaser sheni with non-current coins, but implies that later coins similar to earlier ones are valid.
Rav Nachman deflects by explaining that the baraita deals with kingdoms that do not prohibit each other's currency.

items.text: Shmuel's ruling applies when kingdoms are strict
items.text_en: Shmuel's ruling applies when kingdoms are strict
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that Shmuel's ruling applies when kingdoms prohibit foreign currency, and the debtor can only deliver the coins under duress, where the authorities do not investigate but would confiscate if found.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that Shmuel's ruling applies specifically when kingdoms are strict about foreign currency, and the debtor can only deliver the coins under duress (בדחק), where authorities do not investigate but would confiscate if found.

items.text: Second objection: coins from different locations
items.text_en: Second objection: coins from different locations
items.desc_en: A baraita states that one cannot redeem maaser sheni with coins from one location when they are in another, even if the creditor will eventually go there. The Gemara resolves this by saying it applies when kingdoms are strict, and the coins are usable for buying animals to bring to Jerusalem.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a baraita as an objection: one cannot redeem maaser sheni with coins from one location when they are in another, even though the creditor will eventually go there.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita applies when kingdoms are strict about coinage, and the coins are usable for buying animals to bring to Jerusalem.

items.text: Reconciling with the enactment of Jerusalem currency
items.text_en: Reconciling with the enactment of Jerusalem currency
items.desc_en: A baraita says the Sages enacted that coins should circulate in Jerusalem. Rabbi Zeira resolves the contradiction: when Israel is dominant, the enactment applies; when the nations are dominant, the earlier ruling applies.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited that the Sages enacted that coins should circulate in Jerusalem, contradicting the earlier ruling that coins not in circulation cannot be used for חילול (redemption of second tithe).

Rabbi Zeira resolves the contradiction: when Israel is dominant over the nations, the enactment applies and Jerusalem coins circulate; when the nations are dominant over themselves, the earlier ruling that non-circulating coins are invalid applies.

items.text: תיאור מטבע ירושלים ומטבע אברהם אבינו
items.text_en: Description of ancient Jewish coins
items.desc_en: A baraita describes the designs of the Jerusalem coin (David and Solomon on one side, Jerusalem on the other) and the coin of Abraham (an old man and woman on one side, a young man and virgin on the other).
items.desc: ברייתא מתארת את צורת המטבעות: מטבע ירושלים – דוד ושלמה מצד אחד וירושלים עיר הקודש מצד שני; מטבע אברהם אבינו – זקן וזקנה מצד אחד ובחור ובתולה מצד שני.

sub.desc_en: The baraita describes the designs of the Jerusalem coin (David and Solomon on one side, Jerusalem on the other) and the coin of Abraham (an old man and woman on one side, a young man and virgin on the other).
sub.desc: ברייתא מתארת את צורת המטבעות: מטבע ירושלים – דוד ושלמה מצד אחד וירושלים עיר הקודש מצד שני; מטבע אברהם אבינו – זקן וזקנה מצד אחד ובחור ובתולה מצד שני.

items.text: דין המלווה על המטבע והוסיפו עליו
items.text_en: Rava's inquiry about a loan when currency is devalued
items.desc_en: Rava asks Rav Chisda: if one lent a specific coin and the currency was later devalued (by adding weight or alloy), what is the law? Rav Chisda says the debtor pays with the current coin, even if it is lighter or debased. Rav Ashi adds that if the devaluation is due to the coin's quality, we deduct accordingly.
items.desc: רבא שואל את רב חסדא: המלווה את חבירו על המטבע והוסיפו עליו – מהו? רב חסדא עונה: נותן לו מטבע היוצא באותה שעה, אפילו אם הוא גדול כנפה או כתרטיא. רבא מקשה שהרי הפירות זוללים, ורב אשי מתרץ: אם הזול מחמת הטיבעא – מנכין לו.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks Rav Chisda: if one lent a specific coin and the currency was later devalued (by adding weight or alloy), what is the law?
sub.desc: רבא שואל את רב חסדא: מה הדין במלווה את חבירו על המטבע והוסיפו עליו?

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda answers that the debtor pays with the current coin, even if it is lighter or debased, and confirms this for both a lighter coin (נפיא) and a heavier coin (תריטא).
sub.desc: רבא שואל את רב חסדא: מה הדין במלווה את חבירו על המטבע והוסיפו עליו?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: but the value of goods has dropped (due to the devaluation), so the creditor suffers a loss.
sub.desc: רבא מקשה: הרי הפירות זוללים, ויש כאן ריבית.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi resolves: we examine the cause; if the devaluation is due to the coin's quality (not market fluctuation), we deduct accordingly from the repayment.
sub.desc: רבא מקשה: הרי הפירות זוללים, ויש כאן ריבית.

items.text: דין הפחתת שווי מטבעות ישנים
items.text_en: Introduction: The case of the agardemim coins
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether depreciation due to the door's value should be deducted, and then presents the case of Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua who dealt with agardemim coins at a rate of ten for eight.
items.desc: הגמרא דנה במקרה שבו מטבעות ישנים ירדו בערכם, וקובעת שאין להפחית את החוב בשל ירידת שווי השוק. עם זאת, אם המטבעות השתבחו לצורך התכה, יש להתייחס לכך כריבית. מובאת דוגמה ממעשה של רב פפא ורב הונא שהחליפו עשרה מטבעות ישנים בשמונה חדשים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether depreciation due to the door's value should be deducted from the payment.
sub.desc: קובע שאם המטבעות ירדו בגלל שער השוק, אין להפחית את החוב.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers by citing the case of Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua who dealt with agardemim coins at a rate of ten for eight, showing that depreciation is not deducted.
sub.desc: מקשה שהמטבעות השתבחו לצורך התכה, ולכן יש בזה ריבית.

items.text: Rabbah's ruling: Throwing a coin into the sea
items.text_en: Rabbah's ruling: Throwing a coin into the sea
items.desc_en: Rabbah rules that one who throws another's coin into the deep sea is exempt because he can say 'it is before you, take it.' However, if the water is murky or he took it by hand, he is liable.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah rules that one who throws another's coin into the deep sea is exempt because he can say 'it is before you, take it.'
Rabbah qualifies that the exemption applies only in clear water where the coin is visible, but not in murky water.
Rabbah further qualifies that the exemption applies only if he threw the coin, but if he took it by hand, he is liable as a robber and must return it.

items.text: Rava's objection and Rabbah's answer regarding maaser
items.text_en: Rava's objection and Rabbah's answer regarding maaser
items.desc_en: Rava objects from a mishnah that one cannot redeem maaser sheni coins that fell into the sea. Rabbah distinguishes because maaser requires the money to be 'in your hand' as per the verse.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects from a mishnah that one cannot redeem maaser sheni coins that are not in one's possession, such as a purse that fell into the sea.
Rabbah distinguishes that maaser sheni requires the money to be 'in your hand' (מצוי בידך) as per the verse 'וצרת הכסף בידך', and here it is not.

items.text: Rabbah's ruling: Filing down a coin
items.text_en: Rabbah's ruling: Filing down a coin
items.desc_en: Rabbah rules that one who files down another's coin is exempt because he did nothing, but only if he struck it with a hammer and flattened it; if he filed it with a file, he caused a loss and is liable.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah rules that one who files down another's coin is exempt from liability.
Rabbah explains the reason: the filer did nothing actionable because the coin remains intact.
Rabbah distinguishes: if he struck it with a hammer and flattened it, he is exempt; but if he filed it with a file, he caused a loss and is liable.

items.text: Rava's objection from a baraita about a slave and Rabbah's reasoning
items.text_en: Rava's objection from a baraita about a slave and Rabbah's reasoning
items.desc_en: Rava objects from a baraita that a slave goes free if his master blinds his eye, but not if he strikes near the eye without blinding. Rabbah explains his consistent view: deafening necessarily involves a wound, so it is different.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects from a baraita: if a master blinds a slave's eye or deafens his ear, the slave goes free, but if he strikes near the eye without blinding or near the ear without deafening, the slave does not go free.
Rabbah explains his consistent view: deafening necessarily involves a wound (a drop of blood falls into the ear), so it is different from striking near the ear without deafening.

items.text: דין הצורם אוזן פרת חברו
items.text_en: Rabbah's ruling: Cutting the ear of another's cow and Rava's objection
items.desc_en: Rabbah rules that one who cuts the ear of another's cow is exempt because the cow remains as is and not all cows are for sacrifice. Rava objects from a mishnah about performing work with the red heifer, which is exempt from human law but liable in heaven; the Gemara resolves that even cutting is exempt, and the mishnah teaches that even non-obvious damage is liable in heaven.
items.desc: רבה פוטר את מי שצורם אוזן פרת חברו, מכיוון שהפרה עדיין ראויה לשימושים אחרים, ורוב השוורים אינם עומדים להקרבה. רבא מקשה מברייתא על העושה מלאכה במי חטאת ובפרת חטאת, שם הפגיעה אינה ניכרת אך חייב בדיני שמים. הגמרא מתרצת שגם בצורם פטור מדיני אדם, והברייתא באה להשמיע שאף בפגיעה לא ניכרת חייב בדיני שמים.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah rules that one who slits the ear of another's cow is exempt from liability, reasoning that the cow remains usable and most cows are not destined for sacrifice.
sub.desc: רבה פוטר את הצורם אוזן פרת חברו, בטענה שהפרה לא ניזוקה בשימושיה הרגילים ורוב השוורים אינם מיועדים להקרבה.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects from a baraita about performing work with the red heifer: since non-obvious damage is exempt from human law but obvious damage (like slitting an ear) should be liable, Rabbah's exemption is challenged.
sub.desc: רבא מקשה מברייתא: בעושה מלאכה במי חטאת ובפרת חטאת, שהנזק אינו ניכר, פטור מדיני אדם; אבל בצורם, שהנזק ניכר, חייב מדיני אדם – בניגוד לדברי רבה.

sub.desc_en: The Sages resolve that even slitting the ear is exempt from human law, and the baraita teaches that even non-obvious damage is liable under the laws of Heaven.

items.text: דין השורף שטר חברו
items.text_en: Rabbah's ruling: Burning another's document and Rami bar Chama's challenge
items.desc_en: Rabbah rules that one who burns another's document is exempt because he can say 'I burned paper from you.' Rami bar Chama challenges this, asking how the case is possible.
items.desc: רבה פוטר את מי ששורף שטר של חברו, בטענה ששרף רק את הנייר. רמי בר חמא מקשה על כך ושואל באילו נסיבות מדובר.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah rules that one who burns another's promissory note is exempt, because he can say 'I burned only your paper.'
sub.desc: רבה פוטר את השורף שטר חברו, בטענה ששרף רק את הנייר ואינו חייב על אובדן הראיה.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama challenges Rabbah's ruling, asking under what circumstances the case could occur.
sub.desc: רבה פוטר את השורף שטר חברו, בטענה ששרף רק את הנייר ואינו חייב על אובדן הראיה.

items.text: Rava's ruling on damaging a document and Rav Dimi's attribution to a Tannaitic dispute
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on damaging a document and Rav Dimi's attribution to a Tannaitic dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how to assess damages when a document is destroyed without witnesses knowing its content. Rava rules that the court relies on the plaintiff's credibility. Rav Dimi bar Chanina asserts that this ruling reflects a dispute between Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis regarding whether 'davar hagram lemamon' (a cause of money) is considered like money.

items.text: Rav Huna's objection: limiting Rabbi Shimon's principle to cases where the item itself is monetary
items.text_en: Rav Huna's objection: limiting Rabbi Shimon's principle to cases where the item itself is monetary
items.desc_en: Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua objects, arguing that Rabbi Shimon's principle applies only when the item itself is fundamentally monetary, as in Rabba's case of chametz before Pesach. After Pesach, when the chametz becomes prohibited, the dispute between Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis applies, but not for a document which is not inherently monetary.

items.text: הלכה למעשה בדין שורף שטר
items.text_en: Amemar's ruling on the practice of judges regarding 'garme'
items.desc_en: Amemar states that a judge who rules according to the principle of 'garme' (indirect causation) collects the value of a valid document, while one who does not rule by 'garme' collects only the value of the paper. A practical case occurred where Rafram compelled Rav Ashi to collect like a beam for a date palm.
items.desc: אמימר פוסק שהדן בדיני גרמי מגבה דמי שטר מעליא, והדן בדיני דגרמי מגבה דמי ניירא. מסופר שרפרם כפה את רב אשי וגבה ממנו כשורא לצלמא.

items.text: איסורי הנאה והחזרתם: מחלוקת רבי יעקב ורבנן
items.text_en: The principle of 'harei shelcha lefanecha' for forbidden benefit items and the dispute about completing a bull's verdict in its absence
