items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that for chametz after Pesach, one says 'harei shelcha lefanecha'. Rav Chisda identifies the Tanna as Rabbi Yaakov, based on a beraita about a goring bull. Rabba rejects this, arguing that all agree on the principle for forbidden benefit items; rather, the dispute is about completing the bull's verdict in its absence, with the Rabbis requiring the owner's presence and Rabbi Yaakov allowing it.
items.desc: הגמרא דנה במשנה האומרת בחמץ שעבר עליו הפסח 'הרי שלך לפניך'. רב חסדא תולה זאת בדעת רבי יעקב, אך רבא דוחה וטוען שהמחלוקת היא בגומרין דינו של שור שלא בפניו.

items.text: ברייתא על החזרת גזילה באיסורי הנאה
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's inquiry and the beraita listing cases of 'harei shelcha lefanecha'
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda asks Rabba bar Shmuel if he has a tradition about forbidden benefit items. Rabba bar Shmuel cites a beraita from the verse 'veheshiv et hagezeilah' teaching that one returns the object as it was when stolen, listing cases like coins that became invalid, produce that rotted, wine that soured, etc., where one says 'harei shelcha lefanecha'. The Gemara notes that this beraita follows the Rabbis' view, and Rabba bar Shmuel advises not to reveal this to the Rabbis.
items.desc: רב חסדא מוצא את רבה בר שמואל ושואל על איסורי הנאה. רבה בר שמואל מביא ברייתא הדורשת 'והשיב את הגזילה אשר גזל' – יחזיר כעין שגזל, וממנה לומדים שגם בחמץ שעבר עליו הפסח אומרים 'הרי שלך לפניך'. רב חסדא מודה בטעותו.

items.text: הרקיבו כולן מול הרקיבו מקצתן
items.text_en: Reconciling the beraita with the Mishnah on rotted produce
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: the beraita says for rotted produce one says 'harei shelcha lefanecha', but a Mishnah states one pays as at the time of the theft. Rav Pappa resolves that the beraita refers to produce that completely rotted, while the Mishnah refers to produce that partially rotted.
items.desc: רב פפא מיישב סתירה בין המשנה (משלם כשעת הגזילה) לברייתא (הרי שלך לפניך) בפירות שהרקיבו: ברייתא מדברת בהרקיבו מקצתן, משנה בהרקיבו כולן.

items.text: Mishnah on craftsmen's liability and the Gemara's discussion on 'uman koneh bishvach kli'
items.text_en: Mishnah on craftsmen's liability and the Gemara's discussion on 'uman koneh bishvach kli'
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that craftsmen who receive items to repair and damage them are liable to pay. The Gemara cites Rav Asi distinguishing between giving a finished chest to nail and breaking it (liable) versus giving wood to make a chest and breaking it (exempt, because the craftsman acquires the improvement). The Gemara analyzes whether the Mishnah's first clause refers to wood or finished items, concluding that the Mishnah explains itself with the example of a chest, and supports this by noting that if the first clause were about wood, the second clause would be redundant.

items.text: Opening question from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening question from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a dyer ruined the wool, he pays only the value of the wool, not the enhancement. The Gemara infers that this applies after the wool fell, implying the artisan acquires the enhancement, challenging the principle that an artisan does not acquire the enhancement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah's phrasing that the dyer ruined the wool after it fell into the vat, implying the artisan acquires the enhancement (שבח כלי), challenging the principle that an artisan does not acquire the enhancement.

items.text: Shmuel's first answer and rejection
items.text_en: Shmuel's first answer and rejection
items.desc_en: Shmuel explains that the Mishnah refers to the dyer ruining the wool at the moment it fell, so there is no enhancement. The Gemara objects that if so, the Mishnah should mention the value of the dye, not just the wool. The Gemara concludes that Shmuel was merely deflecting.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel answers that the Mishnah deals with a case where the dyer ruined the wool at the moment it fell, so there is no enhancement (שבחא).
Shmuel gives a second answer: the wool and dye belong to the owner, and the dyer only receives his wage (אגר ידיה).
The Gemara objects that if so, the Mishnah should have said 'pays him the value of the wool and the dye' (דמי צמרו וסמנין), not just the wool.
The Gemara concludes that Shmuel was merely deflecting (דחויי) and not giving a genuine answer.

items.text: Challenge from the law of bal talin
items.text_en: Challenge from the law of bal talin
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita: if a craftsman finishes a garment and the owner is informed, the owner does not violate bal talin until the end of the day. If the garment was given at midday, once the sun sets, he violates bal talin. This challenges the idea that the artisan acquires the enhancement, because if he did, the garment would be partly his and the wage would not be a loan.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about a craftsman finishing a garment, showing that the owner violates בל תלין (the prohibition against delaying wages) after sunset, which challenges the idea that the artisan acquires the enhancement.
The Gemara asks: if the artisan acquires the enhancement, why would the owner violate בל תלין (the prohibition against delaying wages)?

items.text: Rav Mari's resolution and refinement
items.text_en: Rav Mari's resolution and refinement
items.desc_en: Rav Mari bar Rav Kahana answers that the case involves a garment that needed only scraping (גירדא דסרבלא), which has no enhancement. The Gemara objects that even scraping is an enhancement. The Gemara refines: the craftsman was hired per stroke (ביטשי), which is pure labor, not enhancement.

sub.desc_en: Rav Mari bar Rav Kahana answers that the case involves a garment that needed only scraping (גירדא דסרבלא), which has no enhancement.
The Gemara objects that even scraping is an enhancement, since the purpose is to soften the garment.
The Gemara refines that the craftsman was hired per stroke (ביטשי), which is pure labor, not enhancement.

items.text: Support from Rav Sheshet and a distinction
items.text_en: Support from Rav Sheshet and a distinction
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the initial assumption supports Rav Sheshet, who ruled that a contractor (קבלנות) violates bal talin. The Gemara asks if this contradicts Rav Asi. Shmuel bar Acha answers that the case involves a messenger (שליחא דאיגרתא), not a craftsman who acquires enhancement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the initial assumption (that the craftsman was hired for the whole job, not per beat) supports Rav Sheshet's ruling that a contractor (קבלנות) violates בל תלין (the prohibition against delaying wages).
The Gemara cites the question posed to Rav Sheshet about whether a contractor violates בל תלין, and his affirmative answer.
The Gemara asks whether Rav Sheshet's ruling contradicts Rav Asi's position that a craftsman does not acquire the enhancement (שבח כלי).
Shmuel bar Acha answers that Rav Sheshet's case involves a messenger (שליחא דאיגרתא), not a craftsman who acquires enhancement, so there is no contradiction.

items.text: Debate among Tannaim and alternative explanations
items.text_en: Debate among Tannaim and alternative explanations
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages about betrothal through work: Rabbi Meir says she is betrothed immediately upon completion, while the Sages say only when money reaches her hand. The Gemara analyzes whether this dispute hinges on whether an artisan acquires the enhancement, or on other factors like whether wages exist from the beginning or whether one can betroth with a loan. Three alternative explanations are offered.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Tannaitic dispute: Rabbi Meir says a woman is betrothed immediately when the artisan completes the jewelry, while the Sages say she is not betrothed until money reaches her hand.

The Gemara asks what 'money' means in the Sages' statement, rejecting the possibility that it refers to the same jewelry (since Rabbi Meir would then have no basis for betrothal) and concluding it must mean other money.
The Gemara establishes a shared assumption: all agree that wages exist from beginning to end, and that betrothal with a loan is invalid.
The Gemara proposes that the dispute is about whether an artisan acquires the enhancement of the vessel: Rabbi Meir says yes, the Sages say no.

The Gemara rejects the first explanation, asserting that all agree the artisan does not acquire the enhancement; instead, the dispute is about whether wages exist only at the end (Rabbi Meir) or from beginning to end (Sages).
The Gemara completes the second explanation: the Sages hold that wages exist from beginning to end.
The Gemara offers a third explanation: all agree wages exist from beginning to end, but the dispute is about betrothal with a loan — Rabbi Meir says it is valid, the Sages say it is not.

items.text: Rava's principle and the case of adding a gem
items.text_en: Rava's principle and the case of adding a gem
items.desc_en: Rava establishes that everyone agrees on three principles: rental is from beginning to end, one cannot betroth with a loan, and a craftsman does not acquire the improvement of the vessel. The dispute here is about a case where the craftsman added a gem of his own; Rabbi Meir holds that the woman's mind is on the coin (the present), while the Rabbis hold it is on the loan.

sub.desc_en: Rava establishes three universal principles: rental is from beginning to end, one cannot betroth with a loan, and a craftsman does not acquire the improvement of the vessel.
The Gemara asks: what then is the dispute about? It answers: a case where the craftsman added a gem of his own.
The Gemara explains: Rabbi Meir holds that the woman's mind is on the coin (the present), while the Rabbis hold it is on the loan.

items.text: Tannaitic dispute on betrothal with wages
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute on betrothal with wages
items.desc_en: A baraita presents a dispute among Tannaim about betrothal with wages: the first Tanna distinguishes between past and future work, Rabbi Nathan holds that even future work does not effect betrothal, and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi says that only adding a gem of his own makes it valid. The Gemara clarifies the differences between these opinions: the first Tanna and Rabbi Nathan differ regarding rental, while Rabbi Nathan and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi differ regarding a loan plus a coin.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a baraita presenting a dispute among Tannaim about betrothal with wages.
The first Tanna rules that betrothal with wages for past work is invalid, but with wages for future work is valid.
Rabbi Nathan holds that even betrothal with wages for future work is invalid, and certainly for past work.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi rules that betrothal with wages for either past or future work is invalid, but if he added a gem of his own, it is valid.
The Gemara clarifies the differences between the opinions: the first Tanna and Rabbi Nathan differ regarding rental, while Rabbi Nathan and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi differ regarding a loan plus a coin.

items.text: Shmuel's ruling on a skilled butcher who damages
items.text_en: Shmuel's ruling on a skilled butcher who damages
items.desc_en: Shmuel rules that a skilled butcher who damages the animal is liable to pay, because he is a damager and a negligent party, and it is as if he was told to slaughter from one place and did so from another. The Gemara explains why both terms are needed: 'damager' alone might imply only when paid, so 'negligent' teaches that even when unpaid he is liable.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel rules that a skilled butcher who damages the animal is liable to pay, because he is a damager and a negligent party, analogous to one who was told to slaughter from one place and did so from another.
The Gemara asks why Shmuel needed to state both that the butcher is a damager and that he is a negligent party.
The Gemara explains that 'damager' alone might imply liability only when paid, so 'negligent' teaches that even when unpaid he is liable.

items.text: Objection from a baraita and Shmuel's response
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita and Shmuel's response
items.desc_en: Rav Chama bar Guria objects to Shmuel from a baraita that says a skilled butcher is exempt when unpaid, but Shmuel dismisses him. Another scholar objects, and Shmuel explains that he was speaking according to Rabbi Meir's opinion, who holds that one must be cautious, and the baraita follows the Rabbis.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chama bar Gurya objects to Shmuel by citing a baraita that distinguishes between a skilled butcher (פטור) and an amateur (חייב) when unpaid, but both are חייב when paid.
Shmuel dismisses the objection with a curse, telling Rav Chama bar Gurya to 'stir his brain'.
Another scholar comes and objects to Shmuel with the same baraita.
Shmuel explains that he was speaking according to Rabbi Meir's opinion, who holds that one must be cautious, and the baraita follows the Rabbis.

items.text: Identifying which Rabbi Meir is meant
items.text_en: Identifying which Rabbi Meir is meant
items.desc_en: The Gemara seeks to identify which ruling of Rabbi Meir Shmuel refers to. It considers three possibilities: the case of an animal tied and locked (where the dispute is about verses), the case of a dyer who changes the color (where the dispute is about direct action), and the case of a broken jug (where the dispute is about negligence). The last is accepted as the source.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which specific ruling of Rabbi Meir is being referenced, proposing a mnemonic 'קל״ן' to organize the possibilities.
The Gemara cites the first possibility: a Mishnah where Rabbi Meir holds an owner liable for damage caused by an animal that was tied and locked, even if the owner took precautions.
The Gemara rejects this possibility, noting that the dispute there is about interpreting verses, not about the principle of negligence.
The Gemara cites the second possibility: a Mishnah where Rabbi Meir rules that a dyer who changes the color of wool must pay only the value of the wool, not the enhanced value.
The Gemara rejects this possibility, noting that the dispute there is about direct action (the dyer actively changed the color), not about negligence.

The Gemara identifies the correct source: a Mishnah where Rabbi Meir holds one liable for damage caused by a broken jug or fallen camel that was not cleared, and it is established that the dispute there is about whether one who stumbles is considered negligent (פושע).

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling and the distinction between paid and unpaid
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling and the distinction between paid and unpaid
items.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana reports that Rabbi Yochanan ruled a skilled butcher is liable even if he is as expert as the butchers of Tzippori. An apparent contradiction is raised from another incident where Rabbi Yochanan required proof of expertise to exempt. The Gemara resolves that one case is unpaid and the other is paid, as Rabbi Zeira advises advancing a dinar to make the butcher liable.

sub.text: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana reports that Rabbi Yochanan ruled a skilled butcher who damages is liable, even if as expert as the butchers of Tzippori.
The Gemara objects by citing a contradictory incident where Rabbi Yochanan required proof of expertise to exempt a butcher.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing unpaid work (חנם) from paid work (שכר), citing Rabbi Zeira's advice to advance a dinar to make the butcher liable.

items.text: Supporting baraita for paid liability
items.text_en: Supporting baraita for paid liability
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited: one who takes wheat to a miller, flour to a baker, or an animal to a butcher and they ruin it, they are liable because they are like a paid bailee. The Gemara corrects the text to say 'because he is a paid bailee'.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: one who takes wheat to a miller, flour to a baker, or an animal to a butcher and they ruin it, they are liable because they are like a paid bailee.
The Gemara corrects the baraita's text from 'כנושא שכר' (like a paid bailee) to 'נושא שכר' (a paid bailee).

items.text: Rav's ruling on a defective animal and the meaning of 'two things'
items.text_en: Rav's ruling on a defective animal and the meaning of 'two things'
items.desc_en: A case of a treifa animal came before Rav; he declared it treifa and exempted the butcher from paying. Rav Kahana and Rav Asi met the owner and said Rav did two things to you. The Gemara explores whether this was for the worse (ruling like the minority and exempting) or for the better (preventing a doubtful prohibition and theft). It concludes it was for the better.

sub.desc_en: A case of a treifa animal came before Rav; he declared it treifa and exempted the butcher from paying.

The Gemara asks what 'two things' Rav did to the owner, suggesting it might have been for the worse (ruling like the minority and exempting the butcher), and questions whether it is permitted to speak that way.
A baraita is cited that a judge must not say 'I acquit and my colleagues convict, but what can I do since they outnumber me,' as this is talebearing.
The Gemara concludes that Rav's 'two things' were for the better: preventing the owner from eating a doubtful prohibition (ספק איסור) and preventing him from a doubtful theft (ספק גזילה).

items.text: Dispute about a money changer who evaluates a coin
items.text_en: Dispute about a money changer who evaluates a coin
items.desc_en: A dispute is presented: one baraita says a skilled money changer is exempt if he errs, while another says both skilled and unskilled are liable. Rav Pappa explains that the exemption applies to coins like a darkon and an issar that need no expertise, and the error was due to a new die. The Gemara then discusses Rabbi Chiya's case where he replaced a coin he had approved, acting beyond the letter of the law.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute between two baraitot: one exempts a skilled money changer who errs in evaluating a coin, while the other holds both skilled and unskilled liable.
Rav Pappa explains that the exemption applies only to coins like a darkon and an issar that require no expertise, and the error was due to a new die that had just been minted.
A story is told: a woman showed a coin to Rabbi Chiya who approved it, but later others said it was bad; Rabbi Chiya instructed Rav to replace it and record it as a bad transaction.
The Gemara asks: if the exemption is because no expertise is needed, why did Rabbi Chiya, who also needed no expertise, replace the coin?
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Chiya acted לפנים משורת הדין (beyond the letter of the law), as taught by Rav Yosef from the verse 'וְהוֹדַעְתָּ לָהֶם'.

items.text: Opening exposition of biblical verses
items.text_en: Opening exposition of biblical verses
items.desc_en: The Gemara interprets the verse 'the way' as acts of kindness, 'they shall walk' as visiting the sick, 'in it' as burial, 'the deed' as judgment, and 'which they shall do' as acting beyond the letter of the law.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara interprets the verse 'the way' as acts of kindness, 'they shall walk' as visiting the sick, 'in it' as burial, 'the deed' as judgment, and 'which they shall do' as acting beyond the letter of the law.

items.text: Resh Lakish's coin and the principle of garmi
items.text_en: Resh Lakish's coin and the principle of garmi
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish shows a dinar to Rabbi Elazar, who declares it good. Resh Lakish says he relies on him, and Rabbi Elazar questions whether he would be liable to replace it if found bad, citing that Rabbi Meir holds one liable for indirect damage (garmi), but the Gemara does not accept that view. Resh Lakish responds that they do accept Rabbi Meir's view.

sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish shows a dinar to Rabbi Elazar, who declares it good, and Resh Lakish says he relies on him.

Rabbi Elazar questions whether Resh Lakish would hold him liable to replace the coin if found bad, citing that Rabbi Meir holds one liable for indirect damage (גרמי) but the Gemara does not accept that view.
Resh Lakish responds that they do accept Rabbi Meir's view of liability for indirect damage.

items.text: First attempt: Rabbi Meir's ruling on a judge who errs
items.text_en: First attempt: Rabbi Meir's ruling on a judge who errs
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks which ruling of Rabbi Meir is meant, and suggests the mishnah where a judge who errs in judgment must pay from his own pocket. However, Rabbi Ila'a said in the name of Rav that this applies only if he physically handled the money, so it is direct action, not indirect causation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which specific ruling of Rabbi Meir is being referenced, and proposes the mishnah about a judge who errs in judgment.
The Gemara cites the mishnah where a judge who errs in judgment must pay from his own pocket, as a possible source for Rabbi Meir's position.

sub.text: Rabbi Ila'a in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rabbi Ila'a in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ila'a said in the name of Rav that the mishnah's ruling applies only if the judge physically handled the money, making it direct action rather than indirect causation, so it cannot be the source for Rabbi Meir's view on indirect causation.

items.text: Second attempt: Rabbi Meir on a dyer who changes color
items.text_en: Second attempt: Rabbi Meir on a dyer who changes color
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests another case: a dyer who is given wool to dye red but dyes it black, or vice versa, where Rabbi Meir says he pays the value of the wool. But there too, he acts directly with his hands.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes a second case from a Mishnah: a dyer who changes the color of wool from red to black or vice versa, where Rabbi Meir rules he pays the value of the wool.
The Gemara rejects this case because the dyer acts directly with his hands, so it does not prove liability for indirect causation (גרמא).

items.text: Third attempt: Rabbi Meir on vines over a neighbor's grain
items.text_en: Third attempt: Rabbi Meir on vines over a neighbor's grain
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests another case: one who trellises his vine over a neighbor's grain, which renders the grain forbidden and he is liable. But there too, he acts directly with his hands.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes a third case: Rabbi Meir's ruling that one who trellises his vine over a neighbor's grain renders the grain forbidden (קידש) and is liable, suggesting this is a case of indirect causation (גרמא).
The Gemara objects that even here the person acts directly with his hands (בידים), so it is not a case of pure indirect causation.

items.text: Fourth attempt: Rabbi Meir on a breached vineyard partition
items.text_en: Fourth attempt: Rabbi Meir on a breached vineyard partition
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins a fourth example from a baraita about a vineyard partition that was breached, but the segment cuts off before completion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a fourth attempt to find a case where Rabbi Meir holds one liable for indirect damage (גרמא), citing a baraita about a breached vineyard partition, but the segment cuts off before the baraita is completed.

items.text: Opening Tosefta-style statement
items.text_en: Opening Tosefta-style statement
items.desc_en: A general principle about responsibility for a breached fence: the owner is repeatedly warned to repair it, and if he despairs and does not, he is liable.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna states a general principle: one who is warned to repair a fence and despairs of doing so is liable for its consequences.

items.text: Mishnah: Dyer who ruins wool
items.text_en: Mishnah: Dyer who ruins wool
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the case of a dyer who burns the wool in the vat: he pays the wool's value. If he dyes it 'ka'ur', payment is based on the lesser of the improvement or the expense.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the law of a dyer who burns the wool in the vat or dyes it 'ka'ur', specifying payment based on the lesser of the improvement or the expense.

items.text: Mishnah: Dyeing the wrong color
items.text_en: Mishnah: Dyeing the wrong color
items.desc_en: If the dyer dyes the wool the wrong color (red instead of black or vice versa), Rabbi Meir says he pays the wool's value; Rabbi Yehuda says payment is based on the lesser of improvement or expense.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the case of a dyer who dyes the wool the wrong color.
Rabbi Meir rules that the dyer pays the full value of the wool.
Rabbi Yehuda rules that payment is based on the lesser of the improvement or the expense.

items.text: Gemara: Clarifying 'ka'ur'
items.text_en: Gemara: Clarifying 'ka'ur'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'ka'ur' means. Rav Nachman quoting Rabbah bar bar Chanah explains it as 'kalbos', and then Rabbah bar Shmuel begins to define 'kalbos'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the term 'ka'ur' in the Mishnah means.

sub.text: Rav Nachman quoting Rabbah bar bar Chanah
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman quoting Rabbah bar bar Chanah
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar bar Chanah explains that 'ka'ur' means 'kalbos' (a type of dye).
The Gemara then asks what 'kalbos' itself means.
Rabbah bar Shmuel begins to define 'kalbos', but his statement is cut off at the end of the section.

items.text: Opening Baraita on Changing the Vessel
items.text_en: Opening Baraita on Changing the Vessel
items.desc_en: The baraita presents a dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda about a craftsman who changes the type of vessel (e.g., wood for a chair used for a bench). Rabbi Meir says the owner pays only the value of the wood; Rabbi Yehuda says the craftsman receives the lesser of the improvement or the expense. Rabbi Meir concedes that if the vessel is made ugly, the craftsman receives the lesser of the improvement or the expense.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with a dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda about a craftsman who changes the vessel type: Rabbi Meir says the owner pays only the value of the wood; Rabbi Yehuda says the craftsman receives the lesser of the improvement or the expense.
The baraita adds that Rabbi Meir concedes in a case where the vessel is made ugly, the craftsman receives the lesser of the improvement or the expense.

items.text: Gemara's Question on Dye's Enhancement
items.text_en: Gemara's Question on Dye's Enhancement
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: does dye add value to wool (שבח סממנין על הצמר) or not? It considers a case where one stole dye and used it to dye wool, but rejects that because of the change (שינוי). The real case is where the dye was already dissolved (סממנין שרויין). The question is whether the dyer must return the dye's value or can say 'you have nothing against me.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: does the dye add value to the wool (יש שבח סממנין על הצמר) or not?
The Gemara considers a case where one stole dye and ground and dissolved it, but rejects it because the change (שינוי) already gives the thief ownership.
The Gemara refines the case to where the dye was already dissolved (סממנין שרויין), and the question is whether the dyer must return the dye's value or can say 'you have nothing against me.'

items.text: Refining the Question: Dye's Value vs. Return of Dye
items.text_en: Refining the Question: Dye's Value vs. Return of Dye
items.desc_en: The Gemara refines the question: if there is no enhancement, the dyer must still pay for the dye he destroyed. So the real question is whether the dyer can return the dyed wool and say 'take your dye' (since it is visible) or must pay for the dye. The Gemara objects that the dye cannot be physically returned because it is absorbed, and removing it would destroy the wool.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that even if the dye has no enhancement value, the dyer must still pay for the dye he destroyed, so the question is not about the dye's value.
The Gemara objects that the dye cannot be physically returned because it is absorbed, and removing it would destroy the wool.

items.text: Case of Stolen Wool and Dye from One Owner
items.text_en: Case of Stolen Wool and Dye from One Owner
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a case where one stole both wool and dye from the same person, dyed the wool, and returns the wool. The question is whether the dye's value is added to the wool (so he returns both) or not (so he returns only the wool). The Gemara suggests that if the wool appreciated in value, the thief benefits, but if dye prices fell, the question remains. Alternatively, if a monkey dyed the wool, the question is whether the dye's value is added.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reframes the case as one where a thief stole both wool and dye from the same owner, dyed the wool, and now returns the wool.
The Gemara poses the question: does the dye's value attach to the wool, requiring the thief to return both, or not, so he returns only the wool?
The Gemara suggests that if the wool appreciated in value, the thief benefits, but the question remains if dye prices fell.
Alternatively, the Gemara posits a case where a monkey dyed the wool, leaving the question of whether the dye's value is added.

items.text: Ravina's Case: Wool and Dye from Different Owners
items.text_en: Ravina's Case: Wool and Dye from Different Owners
items.desc_en: Ravina presents a case where the wool belongs to one person and the dye to another, and a monkey dyed the wool. The question is whether the dye's value is added to the wool (so the dyer must return the dye's value) or not (so he says 'you have nothing against me').

sub.desc_en: Ravina presents a case where wool belongs to one person and dye to another, and a monkey dyed the wool, posing the question whether the dye's value is added to the wool or not.

items.text: Proof from Orlah and Shevi'it: Dye is a Significant Entity
items.text_en: Proof from Orlah and Shevi'it: Dye is a Significant Entity
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a proof: a garment dyed with orlah peels must be burned, showing that the dye is a significant entity (חזותא מילתא היא). Rava explains that the Torah forbids benefit from orlah, including dyeing. Similarly, a garment dyed with shevi'it peels must be burned, but there the verse 'תהיה' teaches that it must remain in its original state.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita: a garment dyed with orlah peels must be burned, proving that the dye is a significant entity (חזותא מילתא היא).
Rava explains that the Torah forbids benefit that is visually apparent, citing a baraita that extends the prohibition of orlah from eating to all forms of benefit, including dyeing.
The Gemara brings another baraita: a garment dyed with shevi'it peels must be burned, but distinguishes it by citing the verse 'תהיה' which requires the produce to remain in its original state.

items.text: Rava's first contradiction: garment dyed with orlah peels vs. blood absorbed in a house
items.text_en: Rava's first contradiction: garment dyed with orlah peels vs. blood absorbed in a house
items.desc_en: Rava raises a contradiction: a garment dyed with orlah peels must be burned, implying that the appearance (חזותא) is significant. Yet a house that absorbed a quarter-log of blood is considered pure if the blood was absorbed in vessels that were there initially, but impure if in vessels added later. This shows that appearance is not always significant.

sub.desc_en: Rava raises a contradiction: a garment dyed with orlah peels must be burned, implying that appearance (חזותא) is significant.

Rava contrasts with the case of a quarter-log of blood absorbed in a house, where the ruling depends on whether the absorbing vessels were present initially or added later, showing that appearance is not always decisive.

items.text: Clarification: blood absorbed in a garment
items.text_en: Clarification: blood absorbed in a garment
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that if blood is absorbed in a garment, we examine whether the garment can be washed and yield a quarter-log of blood; if so, it is impure, otherwise pure.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the case of blood absorbed in a garment by stating that we examine whether washing the garment yields a quarter-log of blood; if so, it is impure, otherwise pure.

items.text: Rav Kahana's resolution: leniency of quarter-log measures
items.text_en: Rav Kahana's resolution: leniency of quarter-log measures
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana answers that the case of blood absorbed in a garment is a leniency of rabbinic quarter-log measures, referring to blood of trampling (דם תבוסה) which is rabbinic, so the rule is lenient.

sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana resolves the contradiction by explaining that the lenient ruling about blood absorbed in a garment applies only to the rabbinic category of דם תבוסה (blood of trampling), where quarter-log measures are treated leniently.

items.text: Rava's second contradiction: wood of shevi'it vs. wood not subject to shevi'it
items.text_en: Rava's second contradiction: wood of shevi'it vs. wood not subject to shevi'it
items.desc_en: Rava raises another contradiction: a mishnah states that certain dyeing plants have shevi'it sanctity for both themselves and their monetary value, implying wood has shevi'it sanctity. Yet another source says that leaves gathered for wood have no shevi'it sanctity.

sub.desc_en: Rava raises a contradiction: a mishnah states that certain dyeing plants have shevi'it sanctity for both themselves and their monetary value, implying wood has shevi'it sanctity.
Rava cites a contradictory source: leaves gathered for wood have no shevi'it sanctity, implying wood lacks shevi'it sanctity.

The gemara resolves the contradiction by citing the verse 'לאכלה' (for eating), which limits shevi'it sanctity to items whose benefit and removal occur simultaneously, excluding wood whose benefit comes after removal.
The gemara objects: there are wood chips (for fuel) whose benefit and removal are simultaneous, so they should have shevi'it sanctity.
Rava begins his answer to the objection (the continuation of his answer is implied but not fully quoted in the given source).

items.text: The contradictory source: leaves for wood have no shevi'it sanctity
items.text_en: The contradictory source: leaves for wood have no shevi'it sanctity
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the contradictory source: leaves of reeds and vines gathered for wood have no shevi'it sanctity, unlike those gathered for food.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita: leaves of reeds and vines gathered for wood have no shevi'it sanctity, unlike those gathered for food.

items.text: Resolution: the verse 'for food' excludes wood
items.text_en: Resolution: the verse 'for food' excludes wood
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves: the verse says 'for food' (לאכלה), meaning only items whose benefit and removal are simultaneous are subject to shevi'it sanctity; wood, whose benefit comes after removal, is excluded.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by citing the verse 'for food' (לאכלה), which limits shevi'it sanctity to items whose benefit and removal are simultaneous, excluding wood whose benefit comes after removal.

items.text: Objection: wood for burning has simultaneous benefit and removal
items.text_en: Objection: wood for burning has simultaneous benefit and removal
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: there is wood used for burning (e.g., for light or heat) where the benefit and removal are simultaneous, so it should be subject to shevi'it sanctity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that there is wood used for burning (e.g., for light or heat) where the benefit and removal are simultaneous, so it should be subject to shevi'it sanctity.

items.text: Rava's response (unfinished)
items.text_en: Rava's response (unfinished)
items.desc_en: Rava begins to respond, but the text cuts off, leaving the resolution incomplete.

sub.desc_en: Rava begins to respond, but the text cuts off, leaving the resolution incomplete.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that unspecified wood is presumed to be for heating.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that unspecified wood is presumed to be designated for heating.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's ruling
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's ruling
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana suggests that the Mishnah's ruling is a matter of Tannaic dispute regarding the use of shemittah produce. The Gemara explores the positions of the Rabbis and Rabbi Yosei, and concludes that the baraita prohibiting melugma aligns with Rabbi Yosei.

sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana asserts that the Mishnah's ruling about wood for heating is a Tannaic dispute, citing a baraita where the Rabbis prohibit using shemittah produce for soaking or laundering, while Rabbi Yosei permits it.

The Gemara asks for the reasoning of the Rabbis and Rabbi Yosei, and each cites a verse: the Rabbis derive from 'לאכלה' (for eating) that produce is not for soaking or laundering, while Rabbi Yosei derives from 'לכם' (for you) that it is for all needs.

The Gemara objects that the Rabbis also have the verse 'לכם', and explains that they interpret it as limited to items whose benefit and removal are simultaneous, excluding soaking and laundering where benefit comes after removal.

The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yosei also has the verse 'לאכלה', and explains that he uses it to exclude melugma (a cosmetic compress), as taught in a baraita that distinguishes between soaking/laundering (permitted via 'לכם') and melugma (forbidden via 'לאכלה').
The Gemara asks why the baraita includes laundering but excludes melugma, and answers that laundering is common to all people, while melugma is not.
The Gemara concludes that the baraita prohibiting melugma and other uses aligns with Rabbi Yosei, because if it were the Rabbis, they would also prohibit soaking and laundering.

items.text: Mishnah citation
items.text_en: Mishnah citation
items.desc_en: The Mishnah of Rabbi Yehuda regarding the craftsman's deviation is cited.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah cites Rabbi Yehuda's ruling regarding the craftsman's deviation, where the craftsman pays the lesser of the improvement or the expense.

items.text: Discussion of the principle of 'machloket v'achar kach satam'
items.text_en: Discussion of the principle of 'machloket v'achar kach satam'
items.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that the halakha follows Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha and Rabbi Yehuda. Rav Yosef questions the need for the ruling regarding Rabbi Yehuda, as the Mishnah appears to be a dispute followed by an anonymous ruling. The Gemara resolves the issue by discussing the order of tractates and the possibility of 'ein seder laMishnah'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that the halakha follows Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha and Rabbi Yehuda.

Rav Yosef questions why Rav Huna needed to rule regarding Rabbi Yehuda, since the Mishnah appears to be a dispute followed by an anonymous ruling, and explains why the ruling regarding Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha was necessary.

Rav Yosef objects that the ruling regarding Rabbi Yehuda is unnecessary because the Mishnah in Bava Kamma is a dispute followed by an anonymous ruling in Bava Metzia, and the principle is that the halakha follows the anonymous ruling.

Rav Huna answers that the ruling was necessary because one might think 'אין סדר למשנה' (the Mishnah has no fixed order) applies across tractates, but within one tractate it does not apply, and Nezikin is considered one tractate.
An alternative resolution is offered: the anonymous ruling in Bava Metzia is stated as a definitive halakha (הלכתא פסיקתא), so it is not treated as a standard anonymous ruling that follows a dispute.

items.text: Beginning of a new baraita
items.text_en: Beginning of a new baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a baraita about one who gives money to his agent.

sub.desc_en: The baraita begins by presenting a case of one who gives money to his agent.

items.text: Conflicting baraitot on the shaliach's profit or loss
items.text_en: Conflicting baraitot on the shaliach's profit or loss
items.desc_en: Two baraitot are cited: one says any change in price (profit or loss) goes to the shaliach; the other says profit goes to the middle (the owner) and loss to the shaliach. This sets up the Gemara's question.

sub.desc_en: Two conflicting baraitot are cited: one says profit or loss goes to the agent; the other says profit goes to the middle and loss to the agent.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's resolution: Rabbi Meir vs. Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's resolution: Rabbi Meir vs. Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan resolves the contradiction by attributing the first baraita to Rabbi Meir, who holds that shinui koneh (a change in the item effects acquisition), and the second to Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that shinui does not acquire.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan resolves the contradiction by attributing the first baraita to Rabbi Meir and the second to Rabbi Yehuda.
Rabbi Yochanan explains that Rabbi Meir holds shinui koneh (change acquires) and Rabbi Yehuda holds shinui does not acquire.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's objection and alternative resolution
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's objection and alternative resolution
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar objects: perhaps Rabbi Meir only holds shinui koneh for items fit for personal use, not for commerce. He then resolves the baraitot differently: both are Rabbi Meir, but one case is for eating and the other for trade.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar objects to Rabbi Yochanan's explanation, suggesting that Rabbi Meir's principle of shinui koneh may only apply to items fit for personal use, not for merchandise.
Rabbi Elazar resolves the baraitot by attributing both to Rabbi Meir, distinguishing between grain for eating (where the agent acquires it) and grain for trade (where the profit is split).

items.text: Challenge from the West and Rav Shemuel bar Sartari's response
items.text_en: Challenge from the West and Rav Shemuel bar Sartari's response
items.desc_en: The sages in the West challenge Rabbi Yochanan's view according to Rabbi Yehuda: how does the wheat owner know to acquire the wheat for the money owner? Rav Shemuel bar Sartari objects that even with wheat for wheat the same problem arises. Rabbi Avahu distinguishes: in the wheat-for-wheat case, the agent acts as the householder's agent.

sub.desc_en: The sages in the West challenge Rabbi Yochanan's view according to Rabbi Yehuda: how does the wheat owner know to acquire the wheat for the money owner?
Rav Shemuel bar Sartari objects that if the challenge stands, even in the wheat-for-wheat case the same problem would arise.
Rabbi Avahu distinguishes: in the wheat-for-wheat case, the agent acts as the householder's agent, so the acquisition is valid.

items.text: Proof from the Mishnah of one who consecrates property
items.text_en: Proof from the Mishnah of one who consecrates property
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu brings a proof from a Mishnah: one who consecrates his property does not include his wife's clothing, etc. The Gemara asks why not say 'who told the dyer to acquire the dye for the woman?' The answer is that the dyer acts as the woman's agent, just as here the agent acts for the householder.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu cites a Mishnah that one who consecrates his property does not include his wife's clothing, etc.
The Gemara asks why not say 'who informed the dyer to acquire the dye for the woman?'
The Gemara answers that the dyer acts as the woman's agent, just as here the agent acts for the householder.

items.text: Rabbi Abba's objection and Abaye's resolution
items.text_en: Rabbi Abba's objection and Abaye's resolution
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba objects: one who consecrates property does not intend to include his wife's clothing. Rabbi Zeira challenges with tefillin, which are included. Abaye explains: one intends to include tefillin because it is a mitzvah, but not his wife's clothing due to enmity.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba rejects the previous explanation, stating that one who consecrates property does not intend to include his wife's and children's clothing.
Rabbi Zeira objects, citing a mishna that one's phylacteries are consecrated even though one might not intend to include them.
Abaye explains that one does intend to include phylacteries because it is a mitzvah, but not his wife's clothing due to the enmity it would cause.

items.text: Rav Oshaya's challenge and Rabbi Abba's final answer
items.text_en: Rav Oshaya's challenge and Rabbi Abba's final answer
items.desc_en: Rav Oshaya challenges from the case of those liable for valuations, who are distrained: does one intend to be distrained? Rabbi Abba then revises: one who consecrates property is considered as if he originally granted his wife's clothing to them.

sub.desc_en: Rav Oshaya objects that the mishna about those liable for valuations (ערכין) is taught here, and it states that the Temple treasury distrains them, implying that intention is not required for consecration.
Rav Oshaya asks rhetorically whether a person intends to be distrained, challenging the idea that lack of intent prevents consecration.
Rabbi Abba resolves that one who consecrates his property is considered as if he originally granted his wife's and children's clothing to them, so it was never his to consecrate.

items.text: Case of buying a field in another's name
items.text_en: Case of buying a field in another's name
items.desc_en: A baraita states: one who buys a field in a friend's name is not forced to sell; if he says 'on condition,' he is forced. Rav Sheshet explains it refers to buying in the name of the Exilarch. The Gemara questions whether this implies acquisition, linking to the earlier challenge. Abaye clarifies the baraita's meaning.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states the rule: one who buys a field in a friend's name is not forced to sell, but if he said 'on condition,' he is forced.
The Gemara asks what the baraita means.
Rav Sheshet explains the baraita refers to buying a field in the name of the Exilarch.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Compelling a seller to sell again
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Compelling a seller to sell again
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a seller is not compelled to sell a second time, but if the buyer stipulated 'on condition,' the seller is compelled.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a seller is not compelled to sell a second time, but if the buyer stipulated 'על מנת (on condition),' the seller is compelled.

items.text: Gemara's question on the first clause: Purchasing in another's name
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the first clause: Purchasing in another's name
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah needed to state that a buyer who purchases land in another's name cannot compel the seller to write a second deed, and explains that it teaches the seller can claim he arranged the transaction with the named buyer.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's first clause: one who purchases land in another's name cannot compel the seller to sell again.
The Gemara asks why this is obvious, suggesting a possible objection: the buyer might claim he intended to purchase for himself and merely named a proxy, expecting a separate deed.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah teaches the seller can respond: I arranged the transaction with the person in whose name you bought, so he should write you a deed.

items.text: Gemara's question on the second clause: Stipulation 'on condition'
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the second clause: Stipulation 'on condition'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah needed to state that if the buyer stipulated 'on condition,' the seller is compelled, and explains it teaches that even if the buyer told witnesses he wants a second deed, the seller cannot claim he misunderstood.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah's second clause is necessary, since it seems obvious that if the buyer stipulates 'on condition' the seller is compelled.

The Gemara explains that the clause is needed for a case where the buyer told witnesses in the seller's presence that he wants a second deed, and the seller cannot claim he thought the buyer meant the original deed.

items.text: Story of Rav Kahana's flax purchase
items.text_en: Story of Rav Kahana's flax purchase
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana gave money for flax, the flax appreciated, and the owners sold it. He asked Rav whether he could take his money back; Rav ruled that if the sellers say 'this is Kahana's flax,' he may take it, otherwise not.

sub.desc_en: The narrator sets the scene: Rav Kahana gave money for flax, and later the owners sold the appreciated flax.
Rav Kahana comes before Rav and asks whether he can retrieve his money.
Rav rules that if the sellers say 'this is Kahana's flax,' Rav Kahana may take it; otherwise, he may not.

items.text: Attribution to the Westerners' principle
items.text_en: Attribution to the Westerners' principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whose opinion Rav follows, and answers that it is like the Westerners who say: Who informed the wheat owner that he should acquire wheat for the money owner?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whose opinion Rav follows in the story of Rav Kahana.
The Gemara answers that Rav follows the Westerners (בני מערבא), who hold that the seller is not obligated to sell again unless the buyer explicitly stated 'on condition'.

items.text: Objection: Rav Kahana gave four and would take eight?
items.text_en: Objection: Rav Kahana gave four and would take eight?
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rav Kahana gave four and would take eight due to appreciation, which seems like robbery; but it answers that the flax appreciated on its own, and the rule is that robbers pay at the time of robbery.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rav Kahana gave four and would take eight due to appreciation, which seems like robbery.
The Gemara answers that the flax appreciated on its own, and the rule is that robbers pay at the time of robbery (כִּשְׁעַת הַגְּזֵלָה).

items.text: Alternative explanation: It was a loan, not a purchase
items.text_en: Alternative explanation: It was a loan, not a purchase
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers another answer: Rav Kahana's money was a loan, not a purchase, so he never acquired the flax; Rav's ruling follows his own view that one can make a loan on produce but not on money.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative explanation: Rav Kahana's money was a loan (אמנה), not a purchase, so he never acquired the flax; Rav's ruling follows his own view that one can make a loan on produce but not on money.

items.text: Mishnah: Returning a stolen object after a false oath
items.text_en: Mishnah: Returning a stolen object after a false oath
items.desc_en: The Mishnah details the laws of a robber who swore falsely about a stolen object worth at least a perutah: he must return it even to Media, cannot give it to the victim's son or agent but may give it to a court agent, and if the victim dies, to his heirs. It then discusses cases where the principal or the fifth was paid or forgiven.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the law of a robber who swore falsely about a stolen object worth at least a perutah: he must return it even to Media, cannot give it to the victim's son or agent but may give it to a court agent, and if the victim dies, to his heirs.
The Mishnah lists cases where the principal or the fifth was paid or forgiven, and whether the robber must still travel to the victim.
The Mishnah begins a case where the robber paid the principal but swore falsely about the fifth.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who swears falsely about a deposit must pay the principal, a fifth, and a guilt-offering. It implies that the obligation applies only when a false oath was taken.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who swears falsely about a deposit pays principal, a fifth, and a guilt-offering, citing the verse about a deposit and false oath.

items.text: Gemara's initial question
items.text_en: Gemara's initial question
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's implication that only one who swore is liable, and asks whose opinion this follows—neither Rabbi Tarfon nor Rabbi Akiva, as a baraita shows they disagree about a case where one stole from five people and does not know which one.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's implication that only one who swore is liable, and notes that neither Rabbi Tarfon nor Rabbi Akiva would agree, as a baraita shows their disagreement about a case where one stole from five people and does not know which one.
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Tarfon says the thief places the stolen item between them and withdraws, while Rabbi Akiva says he must pay each one until he repays every victim.

items.text: Analysis of the difficulty
items.text_en: Analysis of the difficulty
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the problem: if the Mishnah follows Rabbi Tarfon, even with an oath he allows leaving the stolen item; if it follows Rabbi Akiva, even without an oath he requires payment to each.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: whose view does the Mishnah follow? If Rabbi Tarfon, even with an oath he allows leaving the stolen item; if Rabbi Akiva, even without an oath he requires payment to each.

items.text: First resolution: Mishnah follows Rabbi Akiva
items.text_en: First resolution: Mishnah follows Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests the Mishnah follows Rabbi Akiva, who requires payment to each only when an oath was taken, citing the verse 'to whom it belongs he shall give it on the day of his guilt'. Rabbi Tarfon, however, instituted a rabbinic enactment even with an oath, as per Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok. Rabbi Akiva only applies the enactment when the robber knows the victim, not when he stole from one of five.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Akiva, who requires payment to each only when an oath was taken, citing the verse 'to whom it belongs he shall give it on the day of his guilt'.

sub.text: Supporting baraita of Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita of Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok
sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Tarfon instituted a rabbinic enactment even with an oath, as per the baraita of Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Akiva only applies the rabbinic enactment when the robber knows the victim, not when he stole from one of five.

items.text: Objection from baraitot
items.text_en: Objection from baraitot
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Yehuda and Rava cite baraitot where Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva disagree about a case of theft from one of five without any mention of an oath, and a story about a pious man who bought from one of two people without swearing. This disproves the previous resolution, as the pious man would not swear falsely.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Yehuda cites a baraita where Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva disagree about a case of theft from one of five without any mention of an oath, disproving the previous resolution that the Mishnah requires an oath.
The Gemara objects: if the Mishnah requires an oath, why would the baraita distinguish between buying and stealing without mentioning an oath?
Rava cites a story about a pious man who bought from one of two people without swearing, and the pious man would not swear falsely, disproving the oath requirement.

sub.text: Gemara's rejection of a possible answer
sub.text_en: Gemara's rejection of a possible answer
sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the possible answer that the pious man swore and then became pious, because the pious men mentioned in such stories were pious from the outset.

items.text: Second resolution: Mishnah follows Rabbi Tarfon
items.text_en: Second resolution: Mishnah follows Rabbi Tarfon
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Tarfon, who agrees that when an oath was taken, the robber must pay each one, based on the verse. Rabbi Akiva penalizes even without an oath. The Gemara then questions why the Mishnah specifically mentions an oath, since Rabbi Tarfon would require payment even without an oath when the robber admits, as shown in a baraita.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Tarfon, who agrees that when an oath was taken, the robber must pay each one, based on the verse.
The Gemara questions why the Mishnah specifically mentions an oath, since Rabbi Tarfon would require payment even without an oath when the robber admits.
A baraita is cited showing that Rabbi Tarfon requires payment to each claimant even without an oath when the robber admits.

items.text: Rava's distinction regarding the thief's admission
items.text_en: Rava's distinction regarding the thief's admission
items.desc_en: Rava explains that the Mishnah's case is different because the thief knows the victim and admitted the theft; since the money can be returned, it is like a deposit. Therefore, if the thief swore, he must bring the money to the owner; if he did not swear, it remains a deposit until the owner comes to take it.

items.text: Dispute about a messenger appointed in front of witnesses
items.text_en: Dispute about a messenger appointed in front of witnesses
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda and Rabbah argue about the status of a messenger appointed in front of witnesses. Rav Chisda holds he is a valid messenger, because the effort to appoint him with witnesses shows intent to authorize him. Rabbah holds he is not a valid messenger, because the appointment implies only that the person is trustworthy, not that he is an agent.

items.text: Challenge to Rav Chisda from a baraita
items.text_en: Challenge to Rav Chisda from a baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about a borrower who sends a cow via his son, slave, or messenger, and is exempt if it dies. The Gemara asks: if the messenger was not appointed with witnesses, how do we know? If he was, the baraita says he is exempt, which challenges Rav Chisda. Rav Chisda resolves that the baraita refers to a hired worker or daily laborer, not a formal messenger.

items.text: Challenge from the Mishnah and resolution
items.text_en: Challenge from the Mishnah and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Chisda from the Mishnah: 'He shall not give to his son or his messenger.' If the messenger was not appointed with witnesses, how do we know? If he was, the Mishnah forbids it. Rav Chisda explains that the Mishnah refers to a hired worker. The Gemara then asks: but for a messenger appointed with witnesses, would he be valid? The Mishnah's later clause about a court messenger implies that a messenger appointed with witnesses is valid. The Gemara answers that the Mishnah does not teach a definitive rule for a messenger appointed with witnesses, because it depends on who appointed him.

items.text: Support from a Tanna
items.text_en: Support from a Tanna
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar that supports the distinction: a court messenger appointed by the victim is valid, but if appointed by the thief, he is not.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar's ruling
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar's ruling
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar both rule that a messenger appointed in front of witnesses is valid. They explain that the Mishnah's prohibition refers to a case where the victim is merely finding a messenger for the thief, or as Rav Chisda said, to a hired worker.

items.text: Introduction of Rav Yehuda's statement
items.text_en: Introduction of Rav Yehuda's statement
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says in the name of Shmuel, beginning a new statement.

items.text: Dispute about sending money with a signed document
items.text_en: Dispute about sending money with a signed document
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not send money via a document (דיוקני) even if witnesses are signed on it. Rabbi Yochanan disagrees and permits it if witnesses are signed.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not send money via a document (דיוקני) even if witnesses are signed on it.
Rabbi Yochanan disagrees and permits sending money if witnesses are signed on the document.

items.text: Practical solution for sending money: acquisition through land
items.text_en: Practical solution for sending money: acquisition through land
items.desc_en: The Gemara relates a story where Rava advises Rabbi Safra to first obtain a receipt (התקבלתי) before collecting money. Later, Rava retracts, explaining that if the debtor dies, the receipt is useless against heirs. The solution is to acquire the money through land (אגב ארעא) and then write a receipt.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the practical solution is for sending money safely, and introduces the story of Rabbi Abba who owed money to Rav Yosef bar Chama and instructed Rabbi Safra to collect it.
Rava initially advises Rabbi Safra to first obtain a receipt (התקבלתי) from Rabbi Abba before collecting the money.

Rava retracts, explaining that if Rabbi Abba dies before the money is collected, the receipt is useless against heirs, and proposes instead to acquire the money through land (אגב ארעא) and then write a receipt.

The Gemara brings a supporting story where Rav Papa transferred a debt of twelve thousand zuz to Rav Shmuel bar Abba by acquiring it through the threshold of his house (אגב אסיפא דביתיה), and Rav Shmuel bar Abba went out to greet him.

items.text: Evidence that the fifth (חומש) is monetary
items.text_en: Evidence that the fifth (חומש) is monetary
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings three proofs that the additional fifth paid by a thief is considered monetary (ממונא) and not a fine: from the Mishnah, from a baraita, and from another source. This implies that heirs must pay it if the thief dies.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's ruling that a thief pays the principal and a fifth, inferring that the fifth is monetary (ממונא) and thus heirs must pay it if the thief dies.
The Gemara brings a baraita where one who pays the principal and swears about the fifth adds a fifth on the fifth, proving the fifth is monetary.
A baraita explicitly states that heirs pay the principal and the fifth but are exempt from the guilt-offering, confirming the fifth is monetary.

items.text: Contradiction: heirs exempt from fifth in certain cases
items.text_en: Contradiction: heirs exempt from fifth in certain cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: a baraita states that heirs do not pay the fifth for their father's theft unless both the father and son swore. The verse excludes the son from liability when he did not steal.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: a baraita states that heirs pay the fifth (חומש) of their father's theft, implying the fifth is monetary property, yet another source exempts them.

The baraita specifies that a son is exempt from the fifth (חומש) for his father's theft only when neither he nor his father swore, citing the verse 'אֲשֶׁר גָּזָל וַאֲשֶׁר עָשָׁק' to exclude the son who did not steal.

items.text: Rav Nachman's resolution: admitted vs. not admitted
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's resolution: admitted vs. not admitted
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman resolves the contradiction: one case is where the father admitted (הודה), the other where he did not admit.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a case where the father admitted (הודה) and where he did not admit.

items.text: Objection and further clarification: 'did not admit' means the father
items.text_en: Objection and further clarification: 'did not admit' means the father
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if the father did not admit, why would the son pay even the principal? A baraita shows that the son pays principal only when both swore. Rav Huna explains that the phrase 'יש תלמוד' in the baraita means there is a verse to derive the law.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if the father did not admit, why would the son pay even the principal? And the baraita's focus on the חומש (fifth) implies the principal is paid.
A baraita is cited: the son pays principal only when both he and his father swore; otherwise, the verse 'יש תלמוד' (there is a teaching) derives the law.
Rav Huna explains that 'יש תלמוד' means there is a verse to derive the law, and Rabbah clarifies the reading.

items.text: Final resolution: father did not admit, son admitted, but theft not extant
items.text_en: Final resolution: father did not admit, son admitted, but theft not extant
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes: 'did not admit' refers to the father not admitting, while the son admitted. The son is liable for the fifth due to his own oath, but only if the stolen object is not extant (אין גזילה קיימת) and there is אחריות (liability of assets). The Gemara questions whether such a loan can be collected from heirs, and leaves the issue unresolved.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that 'did not admit' refers to the father not admitting, while the son admitted.
The Gemara questions how the son can be liable for the fifth (חומש) due to his own oath, and the answer is given that it applies when the stolen object is not extant (אין גזילה קיימת).
The Gemara objects that if the stolen object is not extant, even the principal (קרן) should not be paid, and the answer is that there is liability of assets (אחריות).
The Gemara questions the value of liability of assets, noting that an oral loan (מלוה על פה) cannot be collected from heirs or purchasers.
The Gemara leaves the issue unresolved, indicated by the word 'אמרי' (they say).

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's exemption from the fifth
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's exemption from the fifth
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling that one who swears falsely about a deposit and then confesses pays the principal but not the fifth when the deposit was land. Rav Huna bar Yehoshua explains that the fifth is not paid for denial of a lien on land, and Rava presents a case where the deposit was a document of the father held by others, so the thief did not know it was a deposit.

items.text: Rav Pappa's dispute on whether to follow the stolen object's location
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's dispute on whether to follow the stolen object's location
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa presents two versions of a ruling: in the first, if the stolen object still exists, the thief must go after it to return it, fearing it may appreciate; in the second, even if it exists, he need not go after it, as we do not fear appreciation.

items.text: Rava's case of three bundles that depreciated
items.text_en: Rava's case of three bundles that depreciated
items.desc_en: Rava rules that if one stole three bundles worth three perutot and they depreciated to two perutot, and he returned two bundles, he must return the third. The Gemara compares this to the case of stolen chametz that became forbidden after Passover, where the thief says 'your property is before you' only if the chametz still exists; otherwise, he must pay, since it was originally valuable.

items.text: Rava's query on partial return of stolen bundles
items.text_en: Rava's query on partial return of stolen bundles
items.desc_en: Rava asks: if one stole two bundles worth one perutah and returned one, what is the law? The Gemara initially resolves that there is no stolen object and no return, but then clarifies: even though the stolen object is gone, the mitzvah of return is not fulfilled.

items.text: Rava's query on nazirite shaving with one hair remaining
items.text_en: Rava's query on nazirite shaving with one hair remaining
items.desc_en: Rava asks about a nazirite who shaved and left two hairs, then one fell out and he shaved the other: is it valid? The Gemara resolves that since there is no hair and no shaving, the mitzvah of shaving is not fulfilled.

items.text: Rava's query on a barrel sealed halfway with lees
items.text_en: Rava's query on a barrel sealed halfway with lees
items.desc_en: Rava asks about a barrel that was punctured and sealed with lees: if one sealed half of it, what is the law? Rav Yemar cites a mishnah requiring smearing for a reed seal, but the Gemara distinguishes: without smearing the reed does not hold, whereas sealing halfway with a substance that holds is effective.

items.text: Rava's query on stolen chametz after Passover
items.text_en: Rava's query on stolen chametz after Passover
items.desc_en: Rava begins a new query about the case of stolen chametz that became forbidden after Passover, but the text cuts off.

items.text: Rava's question about a deposit turned to dust
items.text_en: Rava's question about a deposit turned to dust
items.desc_en: Rava raises a question: if a deposit has turned to dust and the bailee swears falsely about it, is he liable for theft? The question hinges on whether the bailee's denial is considered a denial of money, since he would have to pay if it were stolen.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks whether a bailee who swore falsely about a deposit that turned to dust is liable for theft, given that he would have to pay if it were stolen, or whether the denial is not considered a denial of money since the deposit is now mere dust.

items.text: Rabbah's precedent and resolution
items.text_en: Rabbah's precedent and resolution
items.desc_en: Rabbah had already resolved this question: in cases where the bailee denies theft and claims a different status (unpaid watchman, paid watchman, borrower), he is liable because he denies money. The Gemara applies this logic to the case of dust: since he would have to pay if stolen, his denial is a denial of money.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces that Rabbah had already resolved Rava's question by citing a precedent where a bailee who denies theft and claims a different status is liable.
Rabbah rules that a bailee who denies theft and claims to be an unpaid watchman, paid watchman, or borrower is liable because he exempts himself from liability.
The Gemara concludes that even though the dust is currently worthless, since the bailee would have to pay if stolen, his denial is a denial of money.

items.text: Amram's objection and Rava's resolution
items.text_en: Amram's objection and Rava's resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Amram objects to Rava's ruling based on a baraita that exempts one who admits to the principal (modeh ba'ikar) from the added payment. Rava distinguishes: the baraita refers to a case where the bailee says 'take it' (i.e., the deposit is still intact), while Rava's case is where the deposit is in a marsh (i.e., destroyed).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports that Rava was teaching the ruling about a deposit in a marsh, and Rav Amram raised an objection.
Rav Amram cites a baraita that exempts one who admits to the principal (מודה בעיקר) from the added payment, implying that Rava's ruling is inconsistent.
Rava distinguishes: the baraita refers to a case where the bailee says 'take it' (הלך) and the deposit is intact, while his ruling applies when the deposit is in a marsh (אגם) and destroyed.

items.text: Clarifying the baraita's cases
items.text_en: Clarifying the baraita's cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains each case in the baraita: 'you sold it to me' means he claims he didn't pay; 'you gave it to me' or 'your father gave it to me' means he claims the gift was conditional and not fulfilled; 'I found it lost' means he claims he didn't know it was yours. In all these, he admits the principal but denies the obligation to return.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the claim 'you sold it to me' constitutes an admission of the principal (מודה בעיקר), since the defendant admits the ox is the plaintiff's but claims he bought it.
The Gemara explains that the defendant admits the ox is the plaintiff's but claims he never paid, so the admission is that the principal (the ox) belongs to the plaintiff.
The Gemara questions how the claims 'you gave it to me' or 'your father gave it to me' constitute an admission of the principal.
The Gemara explains that the defendant admits the ox is the plaintiff's but claims the gift was conditional on providing a service that was not performed, so the principal is admitted.
The Gemara questions how the claim 'I found it lost' constitutes an admission of the principal, since the finder should have returned it.

Avuh deShmuel explains that the defendant admits the object is the plaintiff's but claims he did not know it belonged to him, so he is מודה בעיקר (admitting the principal) but denying the obligation to return.

items.text: Ben Azzai's three oaths and the dispute about a single witness
items.text_en: Ben Azzai's three oaths and the dispute about a single witness
items.desc_en: Ben Azzai lists three types of oaths regarding a lost object: knowing the object but not the finder, knowing the finder but not the object, and knowing neither. The Gemara corrects the last to 'knowing both'. The dispute between Rav Ami and Shmuel about whether this oath exempts or obligates is linked to a Tannaitic dispute about whether one who swears a single witness is liable.

sub.desc_en: Ben Azzai lists three types of oaths regarding a lost object: knowing the object but not the finder, knowing the finder but not the object, and knowing neither.
The Gemara objects that if one knows neither the object nor the finder, the oath is truthful and thus irrelevant.
The Gemara corrects the third case to 'knowing both the object and the finder'.
The Gemara asks what practical halachic difference this classification serves.
Rav Ami citing Rabbi Chanina says the oath exempts the defendant, while Shmuel says it obligates him.
The Gemara links the dispute between Rav Ami and Shmuel to a Tannaitic dispute about whether one who swears a single witness is liable or exempt.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of the dispute's basis
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the dispute's basis
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains the dispute: one Sage holds that a thing that causes monetary loss (דבר הגורם לממון) is considered like money itself, while the other holds it is not considered like money.

items.text: The liability of a denier of a deposit
items.text_en: The liability of a denier of a deposit
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet rules that one who denies a deposit becomes a robber and is liable for accidents. The Gemara questions whether the verse 'lo techachashu' refers to monetary penalty or oath penalty, and resolves that when witnesses come he is liable for accidents, and when he confesses he pays principal, fifth, and guilt-offering.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet rules that one who denies a deposit becomes a robber and is liable for accidents.
A baraita is cited, deriving from the verse 'וכחש בה' the penalty for denial, and from 'לא תכחשו' the warning.
The Gemara asks whether the penalty derived from 'וכחש בה' refers to a monetary penalty.
The Gemara answers that the penalty is for the oath, not monetary, based on the structure of the baraita where the latter clause discusses an oath.
The Gemara resolves that both cases involve an oath: when witnesses come he is liable for accidents, and when he confesses he pays principal, fifth, and guilt-offering.

items.text: Disqualification from testimony and the case of a marsh
items.text_en: Disqualification from testimony and the case of a marsh
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama objects: if a denier is disqualified from testimony, why does the Mishnah list one who is suspected of false oaths as still valid? The Gemara answers that the case is where the deposit is in a marsh and the bailee intends to delay, not to deny. Rav Idi bar Avin adds that one who denies a loan is still valid for testimony.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama objects from the Mishnah: if a denier of a deposit is disqualified from testimony, why does the Mishnah list one who is suspected of false oaths as still valid, implying the denier is not disqualified?
The Gemara infers: if the earlier ruling were true, the denier would be disqualified by the act of denial itself, contradicting the Mishnah.
The Gemara answers: the case in the Mishnah is where the deposit is in a marsh (אגם), so the bailee intends only to delay until he can retrieve it, not to deny ownership — thus no disqualification.

sub.text: Rav Idi bar Avin's supporting statement
sub.text_en: Rav Idi bar Avin's supporting statement
sub.desc_en: Rav Idi bar Avin adds supporting evidence: one who denies a loan (not a deposit) is still valid for testimony, showing that denial alone does not disqualify.

items.text: Opening statement: a depositee is disqualified from testimony
items.text_en: Opening statement: a depositee is disqualified from testimony
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins with a brief statement that one who denies a deposit is disqualified from serving as a witness.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a brief statement that one who denies a deposit is disqualified from testimony.

items.text: Challenge from Ilfa and resolution via Rav Huna
items.text_en: Challenge from Ilfa and resolution via Rav Huna
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the opening statement with Ilfa's principle that an oath acquires but denial does not, and resolves by explaining that the case involves a deposit lying in a marsh, or by citing Rav Huna's ruling that once the owner accepted the oath, the bailee is exempt even if witnesses come.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the opening statement by citing Ilfa's principle that a שבועה (oath) acquires (i.e., effects exemption), but a denial (כפירה) does not acquire.
The Gemara offers a first resolution: the case involves a deposit lying in a marsh (אגם), where the bailee cannot return it, so the oath is the only means of exemption.

The Gemara provides an alternative resolution: the phrase 'שבועה קונה' is interpreted according to Rav Huna's ruling that once the owner accepts the bailee's oath, the bailee is exempt even if witnesses later come.

items.text: Rav Huna's ruling and Rava's distinction
items.text_en: Rav Huna's ruling and Rava's distinction
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents Rav Huna's ruling in full, and Rava distinguishes between a loan (where the money was given for spending) and a deposit (which remains the owner's property), though Rav applies the ruling even to deposits.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna cites Rav's ruling that if someone claims 'you owe me a maneh' and the other denies, swears, and then witnesses come, he is exempt, based on the verse 'ולקח בעליו ולא ישלם' (the owner has accepted the oath and no payment is made).

Rava explains that Rav's ruling applies logically to a loan (מלוה), given for spending, but for a deposit (פקדון) which remains the owner's property, one might think otherwise; however, Rav applies it even to a deposit because the verse is written regarding a deposit.

items.text: Rav Nachman's teaching and the objection from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's teaching and the objection from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman teaches Rav Huna's ruling, and Rav Acha bar Minyomi objects with a Mishnah where a bailee who swore and witnesses testified he ate the deposit must pay the principal. Rav Nachman answers that the oath was outside court, but the objection continues with a case of theft where double payment applies, forcing Rav Nachman to give a strained answer distinguishing between jumping and not jumping to swear.
