sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman sits and teaches Rav Huna's ruling that a bailee who swore falsely is exempt from payment.
Rav Acha bar Minyomi objects by citing a Mishnah where a bailee who swore and witnesses testified he ate the deposit must pay the principal.
Rav Nachman answers that the Mishnah deals with a case where the bailee swore outside court, not in court.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Minyomi's further objection
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Minyomi's further objection
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Minyomi objects further by citing the continuation of the Mishnah where a bailee who claimed theft and witnesses testified he stole must pay double, which does not apply outside court.
Rav Nachman gives a strained answer, distinguishing between the first clause (outside court) and the second clause (in court), and then between jumping to swear and not jumping.

items.text: Rami bar Chama's challenge and the explanation of Rav's source
items.text_en: Rami bar Chama's challenge and the explanation of Rav's source
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks why Rav Nachman argues with Rav if he accepts his view, and Rav Nachman explains he is only explaining Rav's position. The Gemara then clarifies that Rav's verse refers to all who swear in the Torah and pay nothing.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama challenges Rav Nachman: if you do not accept Rav's view, why do you involve yourself in explaining it?
Rav Nachman explains that he is only clarifying Rav's position, as Rav himself would resolve the Mishnah this way.
The Gemara objects: Rav himself cited a verse, implying he derived his ruling from Scripture, not from the Mishnah.

The Gemara resolves that Rav's verse 'וְלָקַח בְּעָלָיו וְלֹא יְשַׁלֵּם' (the owner shall take and he shall not pay) comes to teach the general principle that all who swear in the Torah swear and do not pay.

items.text: Rav Hamnuna's objection and resolution
items.text_en: Rav Hamnuna's objection and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna objects with a Mishnah that one who swore five times and denied is liable for each, which seems to contradict Rav. The Gemara resolves by saying the Mishnah refers to an oath outside court or one who jumped to swear, thus not conflicting with Rav's ruling.

sub.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna objects by citing a Mishnah where one who swore five times and denied is liable for each, with Rabbi Shimon's reason that he could have retracted and confessed, which seems to contradict Rav's ruling.

The Gemara questions how Rav's resolution (that the Mishnah refers to a case where the defendant jumped to swear or swore outside court) can apply here, since the Mishnah explicitly says 'he swore upon him' and 'in front of the court'.

The Gemara resolves that Rav Hamnuna himself both raised and answered the objection: the Mishnah is read in two directions — 'he swore upon him' refers to outside court, and 'in front of the court' refers to one who jumped to swear.

items.text: Rava's objection and final resolution
items.text_en: Rava's objection and final resolution
items.desc_en: Rava objects with a Mishnah about a bailee who claimed theft and swore, then admitted or witnesses came, which includes double payment. Rava concludes that Rav's ruling applies only to a case where the bailee claimed loss, swore, did not admit, and witnesses came, not to cases of admission or theft claims.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects by citing a Mishnah where a bailee who claimed theft, swore, and then admitted or had witnesses come, must pay double payment and an asham, contradicting Rav's ruling.
The Gemara notes that one cannot answer that this case involves an oath outside court or a leap (קפץ), because the Mishnah explicitly mentions double payment (כפל), which only applies in court.

Rava explains that Rav's ruling does not apply to any case involving admission (הודאה), whether the bailee claimed loss or theft, because the verse 'והתוודה' (and he shall confess) requires payment of principal and a fifth.

Rava further clarifies that Rav's ruling also does not apply when the bailee claimed theft and witnesses came, because the Torah mandates double payment (תשלומי כפל); Rav's ruling only applies when the bailee claimed loss, swore, did not admit, and witnesses came.

items.text: Rav Gammada's report and Rav Ashi's challenge
items.text_en: Rav Gammada's report and Rav Ashi's challenge
items.desc_en: Rav Gammada reports Rava's teaching before Rav Ashi, who challenges that Rav Hamnuna knew Rav said 'admitted' and still objected, so how can Rava claim Rav did not say 'admitted'? Rav Acha Saba explains that Rav Hamnuna's difficulty was different.

sub.desc_en: Rav Gammada goes and reports Rava's teaching before Rav Ashi.
Rav Ashi challenges: Rav Hamnuna, a student of Rav, knew Rav said 'admitted' and still objected, so how can Rava claim Rav did not say 'admitted'?
Rav Acha Saba explains to Rav Ashi that Rav Hamnuna's difficulty was different from what Rava assumed.

items.text: Gemara's objection to the previous assumption
items.text_en: Gemara's objection to the previous assumption
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues that if one who swears falsely is liable when witnesses come, then we can obligate him in a sacrifice for the later oath because he could have confessed. But if he is exempt when witnesses come, then why would we obligate him in a sacrifice for an oath when he could have confessed, since he hasn't confessed yet?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a conditional argument: if one who swears falsely is liable when witnesses come, then obligating him in a sacrifice for the later oath is justified because he could have confessed.
The Gemara objects: if he is exempt when witnesses come, then why obligate him in a sacrifice for the oath when he could have confessed, since he hasn't confessed yet?

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on the bailee who claims theft
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on the bailee who claims theft
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that one who falsely claims theft of a deposit pays double payment, and if he slaughters or sells the animal, he pays four or five-fold payment. This is derived from a comparison to an actual thief. The Gemara raises an objection that a thief pays double without an oath, but the bailee only pays double after an oath, but the Gemara dismisses this because it is a hekesh (analogy) and one does not respond to a hekesh.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that a bailee who falsely claims theft pays double payment, and if he slaughters or sells the animal, he pays four or five-fold payment.
The Gemara explains the reasoning: just as a thief pays double and then four or five-fold for slaughter or sale, so too the bailee who claims theft pays double and then four or five-fold.
The Gemara objects: a thief pays double without an oath, but the bailee only pays double after an oath, so the analogy is imperfect.
The Gemara dismisses the objection because the derivation is a הֶיקֵּשׁ (verbal analogy), and one does not respond to a הֶיקֵּשׁ.

items.text: Support for the derivation from the verses
items.text_en: Support for the derivation from the verses
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that this works well for the opinion that one verse refers to a thief and one to a bailee who claims theft. But for the opinion that both verses refer to the bailee, the Gemara explains that the derivation is from the repetition of the word 'gannav' (thief) in the verses.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the derivation works well for the opinion that one verse refers to a thief and one to a bailee who claims theft, but asks what can be said for the opinion that both verses refer to the bailee.
The Gemara answers that the derivation is from the repetition of the word 'גנב' (thief) in the verses.

items.text: Challenge from a baraita and resolutions
items.text_en: Challenge from a baraita and resolutions
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba challenges Rabbi Yochanan from a baraita where witnesses testify that the bailee ate the animal, and he pays double payment but not four or five-fold. The Gemara resolves that the case is where he ate it as neveila (carrion), or as tereifa according to Rabbi Meir, or a ben peku'a according to Rabbi Meir, or after a court ruling of 'go pay him' which makes him a robber. The Gemara concludes that the baraita holds one of these possibilities.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba's challenge to Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba's challenge to Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba challenges Rabbi Yochanan by citing a baraita where witnesses testify that the bailee ate the animal, and he pays double payment but not four or five-fold, implying that eating does not trigger the higher payment.
The Gemara answers that the case is where he ate it as נְבֵילָה (carrion), which is not a valid act of slaughter, so the four or five-fold payment does not apply.
The Gemara objects that the baraita could be explained as eating a טְרֵיפָה (terefa animal), following Rabbi Meir who holds that an invalid slaughter is still considered slaughter.

The Gemara objects that the baraita could be explained as a בֶּן פְּקוּעָה (a fetus found alive in a slaughtered animal), which according to Rabbi Meir requires slaughter, so eating it without slaughter would not trigger the higher payment.

The Gemara objects that the baraita could be explained as a case where the court ruled 'צֵא תֵּן לוֹ' (go pay him), after which the bailee becomes a robber (גַּזְלָן) and is exempt from the four or five-fold payment, as per Rava's ruling.

The Gemara clarifies Rava's distinction: if the court said 'חַיָּיב אַתָּה לִיתֵּן לוֹ' (you are obligated to give him), the bailee remains a thief and is liable for the four or five-fold payment, because the matter is not yet settled.

The Gemara concludes that the baraita holds one of these possibilities (neveila, tereifa, ben peku'a, or after a court ruling), and the objection about a partner who slaughters without knowledge is not raised because the baraita only states one of several possible cases.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on lost property
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on lost property
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that one who falsely claims theft of a lost article pays double payment, derived from the verse 'on all lost property'. Rabbi Abba bar Memel challenges this from a baraita about a minor's deposit, and the Gemara distinguishes that the lost property comes from a competent person, while the minor's deposit does not.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that one who falsely claims theft of a lost article pays double payment, derived from the verse 'עַל כׇּל אֲבֵדָה אֲשֶׁר יֹאמַר' (on all lost property).

Rabbi Abba bar Memel challenges from a baraita that a deposit given by a minor is invalid, requiring the deposit and claim to be equal, implying lost property from a minor would not trigger double payment.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba's first answer
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba's first answer
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba answers that the case involves a minor who ate the deposit while still a minor, so the lost property analogy does not apply.
The Gemara objects that if the answer is correct, the baraita should have said 'until the eating and claim are equal' rather than 'the giving and claim are equal'.
Rav Ashi resolves that lost property comes from a competent person (בן דעת), while the minor's deposit does not, so the cases are distinct.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's requirement for partial admission
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's requirement for partial admission
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that one who falsely claims theft of a deposit is not liable unless he denies part and admits part, based on the verse 'ki hu zeh'. This disagrees with Rabbi Chiyya bar Yosef.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that one who falsely claims theft of a deposit is not liable unless he denies part and admits part, citing the verse 'כי הוא זה' (for it is this).
The gemara notes that this ruling of Rabbi Yochanan disagrees with the position of Rabbi Chiyya bar Yosef, who is about to be cited.

items.text: Gemara's question on the juxtaposition of parshiyot
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the juxtaposition of parshiyot
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the verse 'כי הוא זה' is written in the context of a loan, and asks what distinguishes a loan from other cases.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the verse 'כי הוא זה' is written in the context of a loan, and asks what distinguishes a loan from other cases.

items.text: Rabbah's explanation for the oath on partial admission
items.text_en: Rabbah's explanation for the oath on partial admission
items.desc_en: Rabbah explains that the Torah requires an oath for one who admits to part of a claim because a person is not brazen enough to deny a debt entirely in front of his creditor, but may try to evade payment temporarily by denying part.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah introduces the principle that a person is not brazen enough to deny a debt entirely in front of his creditor, explaining why the Torah requires an oath for partial admission.
Rabbah explains that the debtor admits to part to evade payment temporarily, and the Torah imposes an oath to compel full admission.

items.text: Distinction between loan and deposit
items.text_en: Distinction between loan and deposit
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbah's reasoning applies only to a loan, where the borrower is not brazen, but regarding a deposit, the bailee is brazen and would deny entirely, so the oath on partial admission does not apply.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that Rabbah's reasoning applies only to a loan, where the borrower is not brazen, but regarding a deposit, the bailee is brazen and would deny entirely, so the oath on partial admission does not apply.

items.text: Introduction of the four bailees by Rami bar Chama
items.text_en: Introduction of the four bailees by Rami bar Chama
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama teaches a baraita listing the four categories of bailees, setting the stage for further discussion.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama teaches a baraita introducing the four categories of bailees.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Bailees requiring partial admission
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Bailees requiring partial admission
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that bailees who swear an oath of deposit must have partially admitted and partially denied the claim. The four types of bailees are listed: unpaid guardian, borrower, paid guardian, and renter.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that bailees who swear an oath of deposit must have partially admitted and partially denied the claim, and lists the four types of bailees: unpaid guardian, borrower, paid guardian, and renter.

items.text: Rava explains Rami bar Hama's reasoning
items.text_en: Rava explains Rami bar Hama's reasoning
items.desc_en: Rava explains the scriptural sources for each bailee's inclusion in the oath of deposit. For an unpaid guardian, the verse 'כי הוא זה' is explicit; for a paid guardian, a verbal analogy of 'נתינה' is used; for a borrower, the extra 'ו' in 'וכי ישאל' connects it; and for a renter, it depends on whether one holds him like a paid guardian or an unpaid guardian.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks: what is Rami bar Hama's reasoning for including each bailee in the oath of deposit? He then explains each source: for an unpaid guardian the verse 'כי הוא זה' is explicit; for a paid guardian a verbal analogy of 'נתינה' is used.
Rava continues: for a borrower the extra 'ו' in 'וכי ישאל' connects it; for a renter the law depends on whether one holds him like a paid guardian or an unpaid guardian.

items.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Yosef: Theft claim requires laying hands
items.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Yosef: Theft claim requires laying hands
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Yosef teaches that one who claims a theft of a deposit is not liable for an oath until he has laid hands on it, as derived from the verse 'אם לא שלח ידו במלאכת רעהו'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Yosef states that one who claims a theft of a deposit is not liable for an oath until he has laid hands on it.
The Gemara explains the reasoning: the verse 'וְנִקְרַב בַּעַל הַבַּיִת... אִם לֹא שָׁלַח יָדוֹ' implies that the case deals with one who has laid hands on the deposit.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's qualification: Standing at its trough
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's qualification: Standing at its trough
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that the Mishnah was taught regarding an animal standing at its trough. Rabbi Zeira asks whether this means that laying hands acquires it and the oath is ineffective, or whether even standing at its trough is sufficient.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba reports Rabbi Yochanan's statement that the Mishnah was taught regarding an animal standing at its trough.

sub.text: Rabbi Zeira's question to Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba
sub.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's question to Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira asks whether Rabbi Yochanan meant precisely that only when standing at its trough does laying hands not acquire it, or whether even standing at its trough is sufficient to exempt from the oath.

items.text: Rabbi Assi's parallel case: Claim of loss then theft
items.text_en: Rabbi Assi's parallel case: Claim of loss then theft
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba responds that he did not hear this, but heard a similar case: Rabbi Assi said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that one who first claims loss and swears, then claims theft and swears, and witnesses come, is exempt. Rabbi Zeira suggests this is because the first oath acquired it, but Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba explains it is because he already discharged his obligation to the owner. This is supported by Rabbi Avin in the name of Rabbi Ila'a.

sub.desc_en: רבי חייא בר אבא (Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba) responds to רבי זירא (Rabbi Zeira) that he did not hear the specific ruling about an animal standing at its trough, but he heard a similar case.
רבי אסי (Rabbi Assi) reports in the name of רבי יוחנן (Rabbi Yochanan) that one who first claims loss and swears, then claims theft and swears, and witnesses come, is exempt from double payment.
רבי זירא (Rabbi Zeira) asks whether the reason for the exemption is that the bailee acquired the deposit through the first oath.
רבי חייא בר אבא (Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba) rejects this inference, explaining that the exemption is because the bailee already discharged his obligation to the owner with the first oath.

sub.text: Rabbi Avin citing Rabbi Ila'a citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Avin citing Rabbi Ila'a citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: רבי אבין (Rabbi Avin) reports in the name of רבי אילעא (Rabbi Ila'a) in the name of רבי יוחנן (Rabbi Yochanan) the same ruling: one who claims loss and swears, then claims theft and swears, and witnesses come, is exempt because he already discharged his obligation to the owner with the first oath.

items.text: Rav Sheshet and Rav Nachman debate liability after laying hands
items.text_en: Rav Sheshet and Rav Nachman debate liability after laying hands
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet rules that one who claims theft and laid hands is exempt from the oath, as the verse implies 'if he did not lay hands, he is liable; if he did, he is exempt.' Rav Nachman objects based on the three oaths administered: that he did not mishandle, did not lay hands, and it is not in his possession. He argues that the oath about laying hands should be like the oath about possession, where if revealed to be false, he is liable. Rav Sheshet responds that it is like the oath about mishandling, where if revealed to be false, he is exempt from double payment.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet rules that a bailee who falsely claims theft and misappropriated the deposit is exempt from double payment, citing the verse that implies liability only if he did not misappropriate.

Rav Nachman objects by noting the three oaths administered to a bailee, arguing that the oath about not misappropriating should be like the oath about possession, where if revealed false, he is liable.
Rav Sheshet rejects the objection, arguing that the oath about not misappropriating is like the oath about not being negligent, where if revealed false, he is exempt from double payment.

items.text: Rami bar Hama's dilemma: Money or oath triggers exemption from fifth
items.text_en: Rami bar Hama's dilemma: Money or oath triggers exemption from fifth
items.desc_en: Rami bar Hama raises a question: Does the money that obligates double payment exempt from the fifth, or does the oath that obligates double payment exempt from the fifth? The case is where one first claimed theft and swore, then claimed loss and swore.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Hama raises a dilemma: Does the money that obligates double payment exempt from the fifth, or does the oath that obligates double payment exempt from the fifth?
The Gemara clarifies the case: one who first claimed theft and swore, then claimed loss and swore.

items.text: Gemara's question: keifel vs. chomesh
items.text_en: Gemara's question: keifel vs. chomesh
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the obligation to pay double (keifel) exempts one from the added fifth (chomesh) when witnesses come first and the defendant admits later, or whether the oath that would have obligated keifel is what exempts chomesh.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if witnesses came regarding the first claim and the defendant admitted regarding the second claim, what is the halakha regarding the added fifth?
The Gemara presents two possibilities: either the monetary obligation of double payment exempts from the added fifth, or the oath that obligates double payment exempts from the added fifth.

items.text: Rava's proof from a baraita
items.text_en: Rava's proof from a baraita
items.desc_en: Rava brings a baraita where a person accuses another of stealing his ox, the defendant swears, and witnesses testify; the defendant pays double. If he admits on his own, he pays principal, chomesh, and asham. The Gemara infers that admission after witnesses does not exempt chomesh, proving that the monetary obligation of keifel (not the oath) exempts chomesh.

sub.desc_en: Rava cites a baraita about a person accused of stealing who swears and is convicted by witnesses, paying double; if he admits on his own, he pays principal, chomesh, and asham.
The Gemara notes that in the baraita, witnesses render the defendant liable for double payment, and admission after witnesses does not obligate chomesh.
The Gemara objects: if the oath that renders double payment exempts chomesh, then why does admission after witnesses not require chomesh, since the oath does not render double payment?
The Gemara concludes that the monetary obligation of keifel, not the oath, exempts from chomesh.

items.text: Ravina's query: chomesh and keifel on two people
items.text_en: Ravina's query: chomesh and keifel on two people
items.desc_en: Ravina asks about a case where one ox is entrusted to two people; one admits after swearing (liable for chomesh) and the other has witnesses come (liable for keifel). The question is whether the Torah's prohibition of paying both chomesh and keifel applies per person or per item of property. The Gemara concludes with 'teiku' (undecided).

sub.desc_en: Ravina raises a dilemma: if the additional one-fifth payment and the double payment are split between two people (one admits after swearing, the other has witnesses testify), what is the halakha?

The Gemara presents two possibilities: either the Torah is particular about one person not paying both penalties, allowing each person to pay his own, or the Torah is particular about one monetary obligation not incurring both penalties, and since it is one ox, the penalties cannot be split; the dilemma remains unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Rav Papa's query: two chomesh or two keifel on one person
items.text_en: Rav Papa's query: two chomesh or two keifel on one person
items.desc_en: Rav Papa asks about a person who twice admits after swearing (liable for two chomesh) or twice has witnesses come after swearing (liable for two keifel) regarding the same property. The question is whether the Torah forbids multiple payments of the same type on one item. Rava's statement that the Torah added many fifths to one principal resolves it: multiple payments are allowed.

sub.desc_en: Rav Papa asks whether a person who twice admits after swearing (liable for two חומש (additional one-fifth) payments) or twice has witnesses come after swearing (liable for two כפל (double) payments) regarding the same property must pay both.

Rav Papa clarifies the two possibilities: either the Torah forbids two different types of payment on one item, so here only one type applies and multiple payments are allowed; or the Torah forbids two payments of any type on one item, so here multiple payments are forbidden.

The Gemara resolves the dilemma by citing Rava's statement that the verse 'וחמישיתיו יוסף עליו' (and he shall add its fifths to it) teaches that the Torah added many fifths to one principal, proving multiple payments of the same type are allowed.

items.text: Dispute between Abaye and Rava: who gets the double payment?
items.text_en: Dispute between Abaye and Rava: who gets the double payment?
items.desc_en: When a bailee is sued, swears, pays, and then the thief is caught, Abaye says the double payment goes to the owner (since the bailee was troubled by the oath and does not acquire the double), while Rava says it goes to the bailee (since he paid, he acquires the double). They derive their positions from different clauses of a Mishnah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: When a bailee is sued, swears, pays, and then the thief is caught, to whom does the double payment go?
Abaye says the double payment goes to the owner of the deposit.
Rava says the double payment goes to the bailee, the one in whose possession the deposit was when it was stolen.
Abaye explains his reasoning: since the bailee troubled the owner with an oath, the owner does not grant acquisition of the double payment to the bailee.
Rava explains his reasoning: since the bailee paid, the owner grants acquisition of the double payment to the bailee.

sub.text: Gemara's citation of the Mishnah's first clause
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of the Mishnah's first clause
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the first clause of the Mishnah: if the bailee paid and did not wish to take an oath, the thief pays the double payment to the bailee.

sub.text: Gemara's citation of the Mishnah's latter clause
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of the Mishnah's latter clause
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the latter clause of the Mishnah: if the bailee took an oath and did not wish to pay, the thief pays the double payment to the owner.

The Gemara explains that Abaye infers from the first clause and Rava from the latter clause: Abaye notes that the first clause specifies 'did not wish to take an oath' as the reason the bailee gets the double payment.

items.text: Dispute between Rava and Abaye on the Mishnah's wording
items.text_en: Dispute between Rava and Abaye on the Mishnah's wording
items.desc_en: Rava and Abaye debate the correct reading of the Mishnah regarding a bailee who swore and then paid: to whom does he pay? Rava infers from the latter clause that if he paid, he pays the one with whom the deposit is found; Abaye reads the Mishnah differently, explaining that the bailee paid after the oath to the original owner.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if a bailee took an oath and then paid, the thief pays double to the owner of the deposit.
Rava infers from the latter clause that if the bailee paid (instead of not wanting to pay), the thief pays the one in whose possession the deposit was.
The Gemara notes that the latter clause is difficult for Abaye; Abaye explains that the Mishnah means the bailee paid after the oath, so the thief pays the owner.
The Gemara notes that the first clause is difficult for Rava; Rava explains that the Mishnah means the bailee paid to nullify his oath, so the thief pays the one with whom the deposit was.

items.text: Rava's ruling on the thief's liability after the bailee's oath
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on the thief's liability after the bailee's oath
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers a case where the bailee was sued, swore, and the thief was identified. Rava rules that if the bailee swore truthfully, the thief is exempt by the bailee's admission; if he swore falsely, the thief is not exempt. Rava then raises a query about a bailee who attempted to swear falsely but was prevented, left unresolved.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: if the bailee was sued, swore, the thief was identified, and the thief admitted to the bailee but denied to the owners who brought witnesses, is the thief exempt from double payment through his admission to the bailee?
Rava rules: if the bailee swore truthfully, the thief is exempt by the bailee's admission; if he swore falsely, the thief is not exempt.
Rava raises an unresolved query: if the bailee rose to swear falsely but was prevented, what is the halakha?

The Gemara notes that Rav Kahana and Rav Tavyomei transmit different versions of Rava's query: Rav Kahana's version is as above, while Rav Tavyomei's version asks about a bailee who actually swore falsely, also left unresolved.

items.text: Query: Thief's exemption after the bailee paid the owners
items.text_en: Query: Thief's exemption after the bailee paid the owners
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a new case: the bailee paid the owners, the thief was identified, the owners admitted, and the bailee denied with witnesses. The question is whether the thief is exempt by the owners' admission. The Gemara presents two possible arguments: the bailee can say the owners are removed, or the owners can say they will pursue the thief for the bailee's benefit. The issue remains unresolved.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a new case: the bailee paid the owners, the thief was identified, the owners admitted, and the bailee denied with witnesses; the question is whether the thief is exempt by the owners' admission.
The Gemara presents two possible arguments: the bailee can say the owners are removed, or the owners can say they will pursue the thief for the bailee's benefit; the issue remains unresolved.

items.text: Abaye and Rava on the bailee's options when theft was by force
items.text_en: Abaye and Rava on the bailee's options when theft was by force
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses a case where the deposit was stolen by force and the thief was identified. Abaye distinguishes between an unpaid bailee (who may choose to sue or swear) and a paid bailee (who must sue). Rava holds that both must sue and cannot swear. The Gemara reconciles Rava's view with a teaching of Rav Huna bar Avin, explaining that Rava's case is where the bailee already swore.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the case and presents Abaye's ruling: an unpaid bailee may choose to sue or swear, but a paid bailee must sue and cannot swear.
Rava rules that both an unpaid and a paid bailee must sue the thief and cannot take an oath.
The Gemara asks whether Rava's ruling contradicts the teaching of Rav Huna bar Avin, who distinguishes between an unpaid and a paid bailee.
Rava explains that his case deals with a bailee who already took an oath before the thief was recognized.
The Gemara objects that Rav Huna bar Avin's wording implies the bailee has not yet taken an oath.
Rava reinterprets Rav Huna bar Avin's statement: after taking an oath, an unpaid bailee may choose to stand by his oath or to sue the thief.

items.text: Rabbah Zuti's query on the return of the stolen animal
items.text_en: Rabbah Zuti's query on the return of the stolen animal
items.desc_en: Rabbah Zuti asks: if the animal was stolen by force, the thief returned it to the bailee's house, and then it died through negligence, does the bailee's liability resume? The question is left unresolved.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah Zuti asks whether the bailee's liability resumes after a stolen animal is returned to his house and then dies through negligence; the question is left unresolved.

items.text: Mishnah: Oaths and payments for lost or stolen deposits
items.text_en: Mishnah: Oaths and payments for lost or stolen deposits
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents cases: if a bailee swore that the deposit was lost but witnesses say he consumed it, he pays the principal; if he admitted on his own, he pays principal, fifth, and guilt-offering. If he swore it was stolen but witnesses say he stole it, he pays double; if he admitted, he pays principal, fifth, and guilt-offering. It also discusses a robber of his father who swears and dies, and a father who forbids his son by vow from his property.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the case of a bailee who claimed the deposit was lost, swore falsely, and witnesses testified he consumed it — he pays the principal.
The Mishnah adds that if the bailee admitted on his own, he pays principal, a fifth, and a guilt-offering.
The Mishnah presents a second case: the bailee claimed theft, swore falsely, and witnesses testified he stole it — he pays double.
The Mishnah adds that if he admitted on his own, he pays principal, a fifth, and a guilt-offering.
The Mishnah discusses a robber of his father who swore and died — he pays principal, fifth, and guilt-offering to his brothers or sons, and if he has no funds, he borrows and creditors collect.
The Mishnah concludes with a father who forbids his son by vow from his property — if the father dies, the son inherits.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a thief who stole from a convert dies, his heirs do not inherit the stolen object; instead, it is returned to the convert's heirs or brothers. If the convert has no relatives, the thief must borrow and creditors collect.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the law regarding a thief who stole from a convert and died, specifying that the stolen item is returned to the convert's heirs or brothers, and if there are no relatives, the thief must borrow and creditors collect.

items.text: Gemara's initial statement
items.text_en: Gemara's initial statement
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef extends the Mishnah's rule even to a charity purse. Rav Pappa adds that the thief must explicitly say 'This is the stolen object of my father.'

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef extends the Mishnah's rule even to a charity purse.
Rav Pappa adds that the thief must explicitly say 'This is the stolen object of my father.'

items.text: Gemara's question
items.text_en: Gemara's question
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Why must he say that? Can't he simply forgive the debt to himself? It cites a Mishnah that one can forgive the principal but not the added fifth, implying forgiveness is valid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Why must he say that? Can't he simply forgive the debt to himself? It cites a Mishnah that one can forgive the principal but not the added fifth, implying forgiveness is valid.

items.text: Resolution via Rabbi Yochanan and the Baraita
items.text_en: Resolution via Rabbi Yochanan and the Baraita
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan resolves the contradiction by attributing the two positions to different Tannaim: Rabbi Yosei HaGelili holds that forgiveness is effective (even for oneself), while Rabbi Akiva holds it is not. The Gemara explains the Baraita and notes that Rabbi Yosei's case involves a loan (zikefo), which teaches Rabbi Akiva's stringency.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan resolves the contradiction by attributing the two positions to different Tannaim: Rabbi Yosei HaGelili and Rabbi Akiva.
The Gemara cites a baraita about robbery of a convert, where Rabbi Yosei HaGelili and Rabbi Akiva dispute whether the robber can keep the money if the convert established it as a loan.
The Gemara explains the general positions: Rabbi Yosei HaGelili holds that forgiveness is effective for both oneself and others, while Rabbi Akiva holds it is not effective in either case.
The Gemara notes that according to Rabbi Yosei HaGelili the loan detail is unnecessary, but it is included to highlight Rabbi Akiva's stringency that even a loan does not remedy the situation.

items.text: Rav Sheshet's objection
items.text_en: Rav Sheshet's objection
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet objects: If the distinction is between oneself and others, the Baraita should have stated the more lenient case (for oneself) and the stricter case (for others) would follow a fortiori. The current formulation is redundant.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet objects that if Rabbi Yoḥanan's distinction between oneself and others were correct, the baraita should have taught the more lenient case (for oneself) and the stricter case (for others) would follow a fortiori, making the current formulation redundant.

items.text: Rav Sheshet's alternative resolution
items.text_en: Rav Sheshet's alternative resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet reinterprets: Both opinions are Rabbi Yosei HaGelili; he permits forgiveness for others but not for oneself. The case in the Baraita (zikefo) is why the thief keeps the money—because it was a loan, not forgiveness.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet resolves that both mishnayot follow Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, who permits forgiveness for others but not for oneself, and explains that in the Baraita the thief keeps the money because the convert had made it a loan.

items.text: Rava's alternative resolution
items.text_en: Rava's alternative resolution
items.desc_en: Rava argues both opinions are Rabbi Akiva; he forbids forgiveness for oneself but permits it for others. Thus the Baraita's case (zikefo) is consistent with Rabbi Akiva's view.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves the contradiction by attributing both the mishna and the baraita to Rabbi Akiva, who forbids forgiveness for oneself but permits it for others.

items.text: קושיית הגמרא על שיטת רבי יוסי הגלילי ותירוץ רבא
items.text_en: Resolving the case of גזל הגר
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Rabbi Yosei HaGelili can hold that a thief can forgive the debt even to himself, and then explains the case: the thief stole from a convert, swore falsely, and the convert died; after death, the thief confessed, and the property is given to the priests.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה על הסברו של רבא: אם הגזלן יכול למחול לעצמו, כיצד ניתן למצוא מקרה שבו התשלום ניתן לכהנים? רבא מתרץ שמדובר במקרה שבו הגזלן נשבע לשקר והגר מת, ואז הגזלן מודה לאחר מיתת הגר, כך שהשם קנה את התשלום ונתנו לכהנים.

sub.desc_en: The gemara questions how the case of גזל הגר (robbery of a convert) can be found if Rabbi Yosei HaGlili holds that even the robber himself can forgo the debt.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה על הסברו של רבא: אם הגזלן יכול למחול לעצמו, כיצד ניתן למצוא מקרה שבו התשלום ניתן לכהנים?

sub.desc_en: Rava answers that the case involves a robber who swore falsely to a convert, the convert died, and the robber confessed after death, at which point the property is acquired by Heaven and given to the priests.
sub.desc: רבא מתרץ שמדובר במקרה שבו הגזלן נשבע לשקר והגר מת, ואז הגזלן מודה לאחר מיתת הגר, כך שהשם קנה את התשלום ונתנו לכהנים.

items.text: דין גזל הגיורת
items.text_en: Inquiry about a female convert
items.desc_en: Ravina asks whether the law of גזל הגר applies to a female convert (גיורת). The Gemara brings a baraita that derives from the word 'איש' that a male convert is specified, but a female is included via 'המושב', and the word 'איש' teaches that one must search for relatives of a male but not of a minor.
items.desc: רבינא שואל האם דין גזל הגר חל גם על גיורת. רב אהרן מביא ברייתא המלמדת שהכתוב 'איש' בא למעט קטן, אך גיורת בכלל הדין, כפי שנלמד מכפילות הלשון 'המושב'.

sub.desc_en: Ravina asks whether the law of גזל הגר (robbery of a convert) applies to a female convert, questioning if the word 'איש' (man) excludes women or is just the biblical style.
sub.desc: רבינא שואל האם דין גזל הגר חל גם על גיורת, או שמא הכתוב 'איש' ממעט אשה.

sub.desc_en: Rav Aharon cites a baraita that derives from the word 'איש' that a man is included, and from 'המושב' (the returned) that a woman is also included.
sub.desc: רב אהרן מביא ברייתא המלמדת מכפילות הלשון 'המושב' שגיורת בכלל הדין.

sub.desc_en: The baraita explains that the word 'איש' teaches that one must search for a male convert's redeemers, but not for a minor, as it is known he has no redeemers.
sub.desc: הברייתא מבארת ש'איש' בא למעט קטן, לא אשה, ולגבי קטן אין צורך לחזור אחר גואלים.

items.text: למי ניתן התשלום – כהן שבאותו משמר
items.text_en: The priest of the watch
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that the property given to the priests goes to the priest of the watch (משמר), as derived from the verse 'לַה׳ לַכֹּהֵן' and the comparison to the ram of atonement.
items.desc: ברייתא דורשת את הפסוק 'לה' לכהן' ומלמדת שהתשלום ניתן לכהן שבאותו משמר, כמו איל הכפורים.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that the phrase 'לה' לכהן' (to God, to the priest) indicates the property is given to the priest of that watch, not any priest, as derived from the verse about the ram of atonement.
sub.desc: ברייתא דורשת את הפסוק 'לה' לכהן' ומלמדת שהתשלום ניתן לכהן שבאותו משמר, כמו איל הכפורים.

items.text: דין כהן שגזל גר – אינו יכול לומר 'שלי'
items.text_en: A priest who stole from another priest
items.desc_en: A baraita discusses a case where a priest stole from another priest, and one might think the thief can keep it since it will go to priests anyway. Rabbi Natan offers a kal vachomer argument, but the Gemara refutes it, concluding that the stolen item is distributed among all the priests.
items.desc: ברייתא דנה במקרה שבו הגזלן הוא כהן. נאמר שאינו יכול לטעון שהתשלום שייך לו, שכן גם לכהנים אחרים יש חלק בו. התשלום יוצא מתחת ידו ומתחלק לכל אחיו הכהנים.

sub.desc_en: A baraita presents a case where a robber stole from a priest and argues that since the stolen item goes to priests anyway, the robber might think it should be his, but a kal vachomer (a fortiori) argument shows otherwise.
sub.desc: ברייתא פותחת בשאלה: מניין שכהן שגזל גר אינו יכול לטעון שהתשלום שייך לו, שהרי הוא זוכה בשל אחרים.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Natan presents a different kal vachomer: if for something in which the priest has no share until it enters his domain, he cannot remove it from the robber's hand, then for something in which he already has a share, certainly no one can remove it.
sub.desc: רבי נתן מביא קל וחומר: בדבר שאין לכהן חלק בו עד שיכנס לרשותו, משנכנס אין מוציאים; בדבר שיש לו חלק בו מלכתחילה, כל שכן שאין מוציאים.

sub.desc_en: The gemara rejects the kal vachomer, arguing that in the case of no share, others also have no share, but in robbery, since the priest has a share, others also have a share, so the stolen item leaves his hand and is divided among all priests.
sub.desc: דוחה את הקל וחומר: בדבר שאין לכהן חלק בו גם לאחרים אין חלק, אבל בגזל יש חלק גם לכהנים אחרים, ולכן הגזל יוצא מתחת ידו ומתחלק לכל אחיו הכהנים.

items.text: Resolution via the field of inheritance
items.text_en: Resolution via the field of inheritance
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the previous conclusion with a verse, and resolves it by comparing to the law of a field that goes to priests in the Jubilee year, using a gezeirah shava of 'לכהן'–'לכהן'. A baraita teaches that such a field is not kept by the priest who redeemed it but is distributed among all priests.

items.text: זכויות כהן בקרבנותיו
items.text_en: A priest's own offerings
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that a priest may bring his own offerings at any time, and the labor and hide are his, as derived from the verse 'וְאִישׁ אֶת קֳדָשָׁיו לוֹ יִהְיוּ'. If the priest is a ba'al mum, he gives the offering to the priest of the watch, but the labor and hide remain his.
items.desc: ברייתא מלמדת שכהן יכול להקריב קרבנותיו בכל עת, ועבודת הקרבן ועורו שייכים לו. אם הכהן בעל מום, הוא נותן את הקרבן לכהן אחר שבאותו משמר, אך העבודה והעור שייכים לו.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that a priest may bring his offerings at any time, derived from the verse 'ובא בכל אות נפשו ושרת' (and he shall come with all his soul's desire and serve).
sub.desc: הברייתא פותחת בשאלה: מניין שכהן רשאי להקריב קרבנותיו בכל עת שירצה, ומשיבה בפסוק.

sub.desc_en: The baraita derives from 'ואיש את קדשיו לו יהיו' that the service and hide of the offering belong to the priest, and if he is a בעל מום (blemished priest), he gives it to the priest of that watch, but the service and hide are his.
sub.desc: הברייתא שואלת מניין שעבודת הקרבן ועורו שייכים לכהן המקריב, ומשיבה בפסוק.

items.text: Case of an old or sick priest
items.text_en: Case of an old or sick priest
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if the owner is old or sick, he gives the animal to any priest he wishes, but its service and hide go to the men of the watch. The Gemara questions how this is possible: if he can perform service, he should get the hide; if not, how can he appoint an agent? Rav Papa resolves that he can perform service with difficulty, but eating with difficulty is considered gluttonous eating and is insignificant, so the hide goes to the watch.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if the owner is old or sick, he gives the animal to any priest he wishes, but its service and hide go to the men of the watch.
The Gemara questions how the Mishnah's case is possible: if the priest can perform service, he should get the hide; if not, how can he appoint an agent?
Rav Papa resolves that the priest can perform service with difficulty, but eating with difficulty is considered gluttonous eating and is insignificant, so the hide goes to the watch.

items.text: Case of a tamei priest in a communal offering
items.text_en: Case of a tamei priest in a communal offering
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet raises a similar case: a tamei priest in a communal offering gives the animal to any priest he wishes, but its service and hide go to the men of the watch. The Gemara questions: if there are tahor priests, can tamei ones serve? If not, why do the watch get the hide? Rava explains that it refers to balei mumim tehorim (blemished but pure priests) of that watch.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet presents a case of a priest who is impure regarding a communal offering, and the Gemara questions how it is possible.
Rava resolves the difficulty by explaining that the case refers to priests with blemishes who are pure within that watch.
Rava resolves the difficulty by explaining that the case refers to balei mumim tehorim (blemished but pure priests) of that watch.

items.text: Case of a Kohen Gadol who is an onen
items.text_en: Case of a Kohen Gadol who is an onen
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi raises a case of a Kohen Gadol who is an onen (mourner before burial). The Mishnah already teaches that a Kohen Gadol may sacrifice while an onen but does not eat or receive a portion. The Gemara explains that one might think the Torah only allows him to sacrifice himself, but not to appoint an agent; Rav Ashi teaches that he can.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi states that a High Priest who is an acute mourner gives his offering to any priest he wishes, with the service and hide going to the priestly watch.
The Gemara asks what novelty Rav Ashi teaches, citing the known baraita that a High Priest sacrifices while an onen but does not eat or receive a portion.
The Gemara explains that one might have thought the High Priest can only sacrifice himself but not appoint an agent; Rav Ashi teaches that he can appoint an agent.

items.text: Mishnah: Laws of the ger's stolen property
items.text_en: Mishnah: Laws of the ger's stolen property
items.desc_en: The Mishnah details the laws of one who robs a ger and swears falsely, then the ger dies. The robber pays the principal and the fifth to the priests, and brings an asham to the altar. Various scenarios are given: if he dies after bringing the money and the asham, the money goes to his sons and the asham is left to pasture; if he gave the money to the watch and died, the heirs cannot retrieve it; if he gave the money to one priestly watch and the asham to another, the asham is sacrificed by the second watch; and the fifth does not delay the atonement.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the law of one who robs a ger and swears falsely, then the ger dies: the robber pays the principal and the fifth to the priests, and brings an asham to the altar, citing the verse.

The Mishnah states that if the robber died while bringing the money and the asham, the money goes to his sons and the asham is left to pasture and sold for communal offerings; if he gave the money to the watch and died, the heirs cannot retrieve it.

The Mishnah rules that if the robber gave the money to one watch and the asham to another, he fulfills his obligation; but if he gave the asham first and then the money, he must bring another asham if the first was already sacrificed.
The Mishnah concludes that if the robber gave the principal but not the fifth, the lack of the fifth does not delay the atonement.

items.text: First baraita: Interpretation of "asham"
items.text_en: First baraita: Interpretation of "asham"
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that interprets "asham" as the principal and "hamushav" as the fifth. It questions whether "asham" might refer to the ram. The practical difference is to exclude Rava's ruling that returning the stolen property at night or in halves is invalid, because the Torah calls it "asham" (implying it must be like a sacrifice). The verse "milvad eil hakipurim" confirms that "asham" means the principal.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that 'asham' refers to the principal and 'hamushav' to the fifth, or perhaps 'asham' refers to the ram.
The Gemara asks the practical difference, and explains it is to exclude Rava's ruling that returning the stolen object at night or in halves is invalid.
The Gemara concludes from the verse 'besides the ram of atonement' that 'asham' refers to the principal.
The Gemara resolves the interpretation by citing the verse 'מלבד איל הכפורים' to confirm that 'אשם' means the principal.

items.text: Second baraita: Excluding the fifth as a delay
items.text_en: Second baraita: Excluding the fifth as a delay
items.desc_en: Another baraita interprets "asham" as the principal and "hamushav" as the fifth, questioning if "asham" might be the fifth. The practical difference is to exclude the Mishnah's ruling that the fifth does not delay, implying it might. The verse "veheshiv et ashamo berosho vachamishito" confirms that "asham" is the principal.

sub.desc_en: Another baraita teaches that 'asham' is the principal and 'hamushav' the fifth, or perhaps 'asham' is the fifth.
The Gemara asks the practical difference, and explains it is to counter the Mishnah's ruling that the fifth does not delay, suggesting it might delay.
The Gemara concludes from the verse 'and he shall return his asham in its head and its fifth' that 'asham' refers to the principal.
The practical difference is to exclude the Mishnah's ruling that the fifth does not delay, implying that if "asham" were the fifth, it would delay.
The gemara objects that, on the contrary, the fifth should delay, contradicting the Mishnah.
The gemara resolves by citing the verse "veheshiv et ashamo berosho vachamishito" to confirm that "asham" is the principal, not the fifth.

items.text: Third baraita and Rava's rulings
items.text_en: Third baraita and Rava's rulings
items.desc_en: A third baraita interprets "asham" as the principal and "hamushav" as the fifth, specifying that it speaks of gezel hager. It questions if "hamushav" might mean double payment for theft. The verse "veheshiv et ashamo" confirms it speaks of property returned in full. The Gemara then cites Rava's rulings: returning at night or in halves is invalid because the Torah calls it "asham"; and if the stolen property does not have a perutah's worth for each priest, the robber has not fulfilled his obligation, as the verse requires "ha'asham hamushav" to be returnable to each priest.

sub.desc_en: The baraita interprets 'asham' as the principal and 'hamushav' as the fifth, specifying it speaks of gezel hager, and rejects the possibility that 'hamushav' means double payment by citing the verse 'veheshiv et ashamo' which confirms it refers to property returned in full.
Rava rules that returning the stolen property at night or in halves is invalid because the Torah calls it 'asham' (a sacrificial term requiring proper handling).

Rava rules that if the stolen property does not have a perutah's worth for each priest, the robber has not fulfilled his obligation, as the verse 'ha'asham hamushav' requires returnability to each priest.

items.text: Rava's query about insufficient for a watch
items.text_en: Rava's query about insufficient for a watch
items.desc_en: Rava asks: if the stolen property does not have enough for the watch of Yehoyariv but does have enough for another watch, what is the law? The segment ends mid-query.

sub.desc_en: Rava inquires about a case where the stolen object does not have enough for the watch of Yehoyariv but does have enough for another watch.

items.text: שאלת רבא לגבי נתינה למשמרת ידעיה בזמן משמרת יהויריב
items.text_en: Question about a gift to a priest of the wrong watch
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks about a case where one gave a convert's stolen property to a priest of the watch of Yedayah, but the priest belongs to the watch of Jehoiarib. The question is whether the gift is valid because it was given to the right person, or invalid because it was not given to his own watch. The Gemara concludes with תיקו (undecided).
items.desc: רבא מעלה ספק: אם נתן פרוטה למשמרת ידעיה בזמן משמרת יהויריב, האם זה נחשב כהשבה או לא? הספק נותר בתיקו.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what is the halakha regarding a gift given to the priestly watch of Jedaiah when the value is insufficient for each priest?
sub.desc: רבא שואל מה הדין בנתינת פרוטה למשמרת ידעיה בזמן משמרת יהויריב.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies: if the money was given during Jedaiah's own watch, there is no dilemma because the value suffices.
sub.desc: הגמרא מבהירה שאם נתן בזמן המשמרת המתאימה, אין ספק.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises the real dilemma: if the money was given during Joiarib's watch, is it valid or not? The question remains unresolved (תיקו).
sub.desc: הגמרא מעמידה את הספק בנתינה בזמן משמרת אחרת, ומסיימת בתיקו.

items.text: שאלת רבא: האם כהנים מחלקים גזל הגר כנגד גזל הגר?
items.text_en: Rava's question: Can priests exchange one convert's stolen property for another?
items.desc_en: Rava asks whether priests may divide the stolen property of one convert against that of another. The Gemara initially considers whether the Torah's term 'אשם' (guilt offering) implies that, just as guilt offerings cannot be exchanged, so too convert's stolen property cannot be exchanged. Rava then resolves that it is indeed called 'אשם', so they cannot exchange them.
items.desc: רבא שואל אם כהנים יכולים לחלק ביניהם גזל הגר, כמו שמחלקים אשם. הוא פושט שהתורה קראה לזה 'אשם', ולכן אסור לחלקו כנגד גזל אחר.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks whether priests may divide the stolen property of one convert against that of another.
sub.desc: רבא שואל אם כהנים רשאים לחלק ביניהם גזל הגר זה כנגד זה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that since the Torah calls it 'אשם' (guilt offering), just as guilt offerings cannot be exchanged, so too convert's stolen property cannot be exchanged.
sub.desc: רבא מציג צד אפשרי: כשם שאין מחלקים אשם כנגד אשם, כך אין לחלק גזל הגר כנגד גזל הגר.

sub.desc_en: Alternatively, the Gemara suggests that convert's stolen property is monetary, not a sacrifice, so it may be divided.
sub.desc: רבא מציג צד אפשרי: כשם שאין מחלקים אשם כנגד אשם, כך אין לחלק גזל הגר כנגד גזל הגר.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves that the Torah calls it 'אשם', so priests may not divide convert's stolen property against another.
sub.desc: רבא פושט את הספק: התורה קראה לגזל הגר 'אשם', ולכן אין לחלקו כנגד גזל אחר.

items.text: Rava's question: Are priests heirs or recipients of gifts regarding convert's property?
items.text_en: Rava's question: Are priests heirs or recipients of gifts regarding convert's property?
items.desc_en: Rava asks whether priests are considered heirs of the convert or recipients of a gift when receiving the stolen property. The practical difference is illustrated with a case of leavened bread that was stolen and became forbidden after Passover: if they are heirs, they inherit it as is; if they are gift recipients, the gift is worthless since the bread is now mere dust.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks whether priests are considered heirs of the convert or recipients of a gift when receiving the stolen property.

The Gemara explains the practical difference: if the priests are heirs, they inherit the leavened bread as is after Passover; if they are gift recipients, the gift is worthless since the bread is now mere dust.

items.text: Rav Zeira's question and resolution: Priests as gift recipients regarding animal tithes
items.text_en: Rav Zeira's question and resolution: Priests as gift recipients regarding animal tithes
items.desc_en: Rav Zeira raises a further question: even if priests are gift recipients, the practical difference is whether they must separate animal tithes from ten animals that fell to them from convert's property. The Gemara brings a proof from a baraita listing the twenty-four priestly gifts, which includes 'גזל הגר' (convert's stolen property) as a gift, concluding that priests are indeed recipients of gifts, not heirs.

sub.desc_en: Rav Zeira reframes the dilemma: even if priests are gift recipients, the earlier question about leavened bread is not our dilemma, since the Torah explicitly commands giving that gift.
Rav Zeira specifies the practical difference: if ten animals come to the priest from the convert's stolen property, must he separate animal tithe from them?

The Gemara presents two possibilities: if priests are heirs, they are obligated in animal tithe; if they are gift recipients, they are exempt, as per the mishna that one who receives a gift is exempt from animal tithe.
The Gemara cites a baraita listing the twenty-four priestly gifts, given with a generalization-detail-generalization and a covenant of salt.
The baraita teaches that fulfilling these gifts is equivalent to fulfilling the entire Torah, and violating them is equivalent to violating the entire Torah.

The baraita lists the ten gifts consumed in the Temple: animal sin-offering, bird sin-offering, definite guilt-offering, provisional guilt-offering, communal peace-offerings, log of oil for the leper, surplus of the omer, two loaves, shewbread, and leftovers of grain-offerings.
The baraita lists the four gifts consumed in Jerusalem: firstborn, first fruits, portions from the thanks-offering and nazirite's ram, and hides of consecrated animals.

The baraita lists the ten gifts consumed in the boundaries: teruma, teruma of the tithe, challah, first of the sheared wool, the gifts of slaughtered animals, redemption of the firstborn son, redemption of the firstborn donkey, ancestral field, dedicated field, and convert's stolen property.
The Gemara concludes from the baraita that convert's stolen property is called a gift, proving that priests are recipients of gifts, not heirs.

items.text: דין כסף מכפר מחצה וקושיות על כך
items.text_en: Abaye's proof that money atones partially for a guilt offering
items.desc_en: Abaye learns from the Mishnah that if one gave the money for a guilt offering to the priests of the watch and then died, the money does not return to the heirs, proving that money atones partially. The Gemara challenges this with cases of a sin-offering whose owners died, a guilt-offering whose owners died, and a yevamah who fell to a blemished man, but distinguishes each based on halakhic traditions or circumstances.
items.desc: אביי לומד מהמשנה שכסף מכפר מחצה, אחרת היה חוזר ליורשים. הגמרא מקשה מחטאת ואשם שמתו בעליהם, ומתרצת בהלכה למשה מסיני. קושיה נוספת מיבמה מול מוכה שחין.

sub.desc_en: Abaye learns from the Mishnah that money given for a guilt-offering atones partially, because otherwise it would return to the robber's heirs since he did not intend to give it without full atonement.
sub.desc: אביי לומד מהמשנה שכסף מכפר מחצה, שאם לא היה מכפר היה הכסף חוזר ליורשים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if the robber's intention matters, then a sin-offering whose owners died should be released to non-sacred status, since the owner did not separate it with the intention of it dying.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: אם כן, חטאת שמתו בעליה תיפוק לחולין, ומתרצת שזו הלכה למשה מסיני שהולכת למיתה.

sub.desc_en: The Sages answer that a sin-offering whose owners died is a halakhic tradition that it goes to death, overriding the owner's presumed intention.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: אם כן, חטאת שמתו בעליה תיפוק לחולין, ומתרצת שזו הלכה למשה מסיני שהולכת למיתה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects similarly: a guilt-offering whose owner died should be released to non-sacred status, since the owner did not intend it to die.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: גם אשם שמתו בעליו יפוק לחולין, ומתרצת שזו הלכה למשה מסיני שהאשם רועה.

sub.desc_en: The Sages answer that for a guilt-offering the tradition is: whatever causes a sin-offering to die, in a guilt-offering the animal grazes until blemished.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: גם אשם שמתו בעליו יפוק לחולין, ומתרצת שזו הלכה למשה מסיני שהאשם רועה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects further: a yevamah who fell to a brother afflicted with boils should go free without חליצה (ḥalitza), since she did not betroth herself with that intention.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: יבמה שנפלה לפני מוכה שחין תיפוק בלא חליצה, ומתרצת ששם אנו עדים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara begins to answer that there we are witnesses (the text is cut off, but the answer distinguishes the yevamah case based on witnesses or circumstances).
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: יבמה שנפלה לפני מוכה שחין תיפוק בלא חליצה, ומתרצת ששם אנו עדים.

items.text: Opening statement about Resh Lakish's view
items.text_en: Opening statement about Resh Lakish's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins with a statement by Resh Lakish about preferring to sit as a pair rather than as a widow, which is a general principle about companionship.

sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish states a general principle that it is better to sit as a pair than as a widow, implying that any companionship is preferable to solitude.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages about returning money or asham
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages about returning money or asham
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one gave the money to Yehoiariv and the asham to Yedayah, the money must be returned to the asham according to Rabbi Yehuda, while the Sages say the asham must be returned to the money. Rava explains the case: the asham was given to Yehoiariv during Yehoiariv's watch, but the money was given to Yedayah during Yehoiariv's watch. Rabbi Yehuda penalizes Yedayah, while the Sages penalize the sons of Yehoiariv for accepting the asham before the money.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the dispute: if one gave the money to Yehoiariv and the asham to Yedayah, Rabbi Yehuda says the money returns to the asham, while the Sages say the asham returns to the money.
The Gemara asks: what are the circumstances? If each priest received the gift during his own watch, each has acquired his own — so why would either need to return anything?

Rava explains: the asham was given to Yehoiariv during Yehoiariv's watch, but the money was given to Yedayah during Yehoiariv's watch; Rabbi Yehuda penalizes Yedayah for receiving money outside his watch, while the Sages penalize the sons of Yehoiariv for accepting the asham before the money.

items.text: Rabbi's statement: if the asham was already sacrificed
items.text_en: Rabbi's statement: if the asham was already sacrificed
items.desc_en: Rabbi says that according to Rabbi Yehuda, if the sons of Yehoiariv already sacrificed the asham, another asham must be brought and sacrificed by the sons of Yedayah, and the first asham's hide is used. The Gemara questions what the first asham is good for, and Rava answers: for its hide.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi states that according to Rabbi Yehuda, if the sons of Yehoiariv already sacrificed the asham, another asham must be brought and sacrificed by the sons of Yedayah, and the first asham's hide is retained by the sons of Yehoiariv.
The Gemara asks: what is the first asham good for, since it is a disqualified offering?
Rava answers: the first asham is used for its hide.

items.text: Rabbi's second statement: if the asham still exists
items.text_en: Rabbi's second statement: if the asham still exists
items.desc_en: Rabbi says that according to Rabbi Yehuda, if the asham still exists, it should be returned to the money. The Gemara questions this because Rabbi Yehuda holds that the money should be returned to the asham. The answer is that this case is where the watch of Yehoiariv has ended and they did not claim the asham, implying they waived their rights.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi cites a baraita stating that according to Rabbi Yehuda, if the asham still exists, it should be returned to the money.
The Gemara questions how Rabbi Yehuda could say to return the asham to the money, since he holds the opposite: money should be returned to the asham.
The Gemara answers that this case is where the watch of Yehoiariv has ended and they did not claim the asham.
The Gemara concludes that the baraita teaches that the priests waived their rights to the asham, so the money is returned to the asham.

items.text: Rabbi's third statement: if both watches ended
items.text_en: Rabbi's third statement: if both watches ended
items.desc_en: Rabbi says that according to Rabbi Yehuda, if the asham still exists, the money should be returned to the asham. The Gemara questions why this is not obvious. The answer is that this case is where both watches have ended and neither claimed, so one might think they waived rights to each other; the teaching is that since they did not claim, the original rule applies.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi states that according to Rabbi Yehuda, if the asham still exists, the money should be returned to the asham.
The Gemara asks why this ruling is not obvious, since Rabbi Yehuda already holds that money follows the asham.

The Gemara explains that the case is where both watches have ended and neither claimed, so one might think they waived rights to each other; the teaching is that since they did not claim, the original rule applies.

items.text: Source for the rule that the asham precedes the money
items.text_en: Source for the rule that the asham precedes the money
items.desc_en: Rava derives from the verse "the asham that is returned to the Lord, to the priest, besides the ram of atonement" that the money comes first. A rabbi objects by comparing to the verse "besides the morning burnt-offering" which does not imply that the additional offerings come first. Rava responds that he derives from "which he will atone with" that atonement has not yet occurred.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural source of the mishnah's rule that the asham precedes the money.
Rava derives from the verse 'האשם המושב לה׳ לכהן, מלבד איל הכפורים אשר יכפר בו' that the money comes first.
A certain rabbi objects by comparing to the verse 'מלבד עולת הבקר', which would imply that additional offerings precede the daily morning offering, contradicting the known rule.
The Gemara cites a baraita that nothing precedes the daily morning offering, and Rava's interpretation that 'העולה' means the first offering, refuting the objection.
Rava responds that he derives the rule from the phrase 'אשר יכפר בו', indicating that atonement has not yet occurred, so the money must come first.

items.text: Tosefta: requirements for atonement and the role of the ram and asham
items.text_en: Tosefta: requirements for atonement and the role of the ram and asham
items.desc_en: The Tosefta teaches that if one brought the guilt-offering but not the ram, or the ram but not the guilt-offering, he has not fulfilled his obligation. The ram and asham are indispensable, but the fifth (additional payment) is not. The Gemara then discusses whether one can learn from the case of a common person to the case of consecrated property and vice versa, concluding that the ram and asham are indispensable in both cases, but the fifth is not.

sub.desc_en: The Tosefta opens by citing a verse to prove that if one brought the principal (קרן) without the guilt-offering (אשם), or the guilt-offering without the principal, he has not fulfilled his obligation.
The Tosefta adds a second proof: if one brought the guilt-offering before the principal, he also has not fulfilled his obligation, as the verse implies the guilt-offering must come first.

The Tosefta raises the possibility that the fifth (חומש) might also be indispensable, but rejects it by citing the same verse, showing that only the ram and guilt-offering are indispensable for consecrated property, not the fifth.

The Gemara concludes by drawing a reciprocal analogy: from the case of a common person (הדיוט) we learn that the guilt-offering includes the principal, and from consecrated property (הקדש) we learn that the fifth is not indispensable in either case.

items.text: משנת הפתיחה: גזלן שהאכיל בניו או השאיר גזילה
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a robber feeds his children stolen food or leaves it before them, the children are exempt from repayment. However, if the stolen item has a lien (אחריות), they are liable.
items.desc: המשנה קובעת שאם גזלן האכיל את בניו בגזילה או השאיר להם גזילה בירושה, הבנים פטורים מלשלם. אולם אם הגזילה היא דבר שיש בו אחריות (כגון קרקע), הבנים חייבים לשלם.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the law: a robber who feeds his children stolen food or leaves it to them exempts the children from repayment, but if the item has a lien (אחריות) they are liable.
sub.desc: המשנה פותחת בדין גזלן שהאכיל בניו או השאיר להם גזילה, ומבדילה בין גזילה רגילה (הבנים פטורים) לבין דבר שיש בו אחריות (הבנים חייבים).

items.text: Rav Chisda's ruling
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's ruling
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda rules that if a robber stole an item before the owners despaired (יאוש), and another person ate it, the victim can collect from either the robber or the eater, because the item remains in the owner's domain.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda rules that if a robber stole an item before the owners despaired (יאוש), and another person ate it, the victim can collect from either the robber or the eater, because the item remains in the owner's domain.

items.text: Challenge to Rav Chisda from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Challenge to Rav Chisda from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Chisda from the Mishnah, which exempts children who ate stolen food left by their father. Rav Chisda deflects by saying the Mishnah refers to after despair (יאוש).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Chisda by citing the Mishnah, which exempts children who ate stolen food left by their father, implying a contradiction to Rav Chisda's ruling.
Rav Chisda deflects the challenge by explaining that the Mishnah refers to a case after the owners had despaired (יאוש) of retrieving the stolen item, whereas his ruling applies before despair.

items.text: Rami bar Chama's inference
items.text_en: Rami bar Chama's inference
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama infers from the Mishnah's exemption that the heir's status is like that of a purchaser (רשות יורש כרשות לוקח), meaning they are not liable for the original theft.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama infers from the Mishnah's exemption that the heir's status is like that of a purchaser (רשות יורש כרשות לוקח), meaning they are not liable for the original theft.

items.text: Rava's first explanation
items.text_en: Rava's first explanation
items.desc_en: Rava rejects Rami bar Chama's inference, arguing that the heir's status is not like a purchaser. He explains the Mishnah as dealing with a case where the children ate the stolen item. When challenged that the Mishnah's second clause implies the first deals with the stolen item still extant, Rava reinterprets 'אחריות' as 'other property' left by the father.

sub.desc_en: Rava rejects Rami bar Chama's inference, arguing that the heir's domain is not like a purchaser's, and explains the Mishnah as dealing with a case where the children consumed the stolen item.
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah's second clause implies the first clause deals with a stolen item that is still extant, contradicting Rava's explanation.
Rava answers by reinterpreting 'אחריות' in the Mishnah as referring to other property left by the father, not the stolen item itself.

items.text: Rabbi's teaching to his son
items.text_en: Rabbi's teaching to his son
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi taught his son Shimon that 'אחריות' does not mean a literal lien but even a cow or donkey used for work, requiring return due to the honor of their father.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects to Rava's explanation by citing that Rabbi taught his son Rabbi Shimon that 'אחריות' in the mishna does not mean a literal lien but even a cow or donkey used for work, which the heirs must return due to the honor of their father.

items.text: שיטת רבי אושעיא ורבא
items.text_en: Rava's revised explanation via Rabbi Oshaya
items.desc_en: Rava praises Rabbi Oshaya for resolving the Mishnah: if the stolen item is extant, heirs are liable; if not, they are exempt; if the father left other property, they are liable.
items.desc: רבא מאמץ את שיטת רבי אושעיא: אם הגזילה קיימת – היורשים חייבים להחזיר; אם אינה קיימת – פטורים; ואם האב השאיר אחריות נכסים – חייבים לשלם. רבא רואה בכך תירוץ למשנה.

sub.desc_en: Rava declares that when he dies, Rabbi Oshaya will come to greet him because Rava explains the Mishnah in accordance with Rabbi Oshaya's opinion.
sub.desc: רבא פותח בהצהרה כי הוא מיישב את המשנה לפי שיטת רבי אושעיא.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Oshaya's baraita is cited: if the stolen item is extant, heirs are liable; if not, they are exempt; if the father left other property, they are liable.
sub.desc: רבא פותח בהצהרה כי הוא מיישב את המשנה לפי שיטת רבי אושעיא.

items.text: בחינת הברייתא מול רב חסדא ורמי בר חמא
items.text_en: Final challenges and resolutions
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Chisda from the case where the stolen item is not extant (exempt), and Rami bar Chama from the case where it is extant (liable). Both deflect by saying their respective rulings apply after despair (יאוש).
items.desc: הגמרא בוחנת את הברייתא של רבי אושעיא: הסעיף הפוטר כשאין גזילה קיימת – לכאורה קשה על רב חסדא, אך מתרצים שמדובר לאחר יאוש. הסעיף המחייב כשיש גזילה קיימת – לכאורה קשה על רמי בר חמא, אך מתרצים שמדובר קודם יאוש.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Chisda from the baraita's ruling that when the stolen item is not extant the heirs are exempt, which contradicts Rav Chisda's position.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: סעיף הברייתא הפוטר כשאין גזילה קיימת – לכאורה סותר את שיטת רב חסדא המחייב.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda deflects the challenge by explaining that the baraita refers to a case after the owners' despair (יאוש), whereas his ruling applies before despair.
sub.desc: רב חסדא מתרץ: הברייתא עוסקת לאחר יאוש, ואילו דבריו נאמרו קודם יאוש.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rami bar Chama from the baraita's ruling that when the stolen item is extant the heirs are liable, which contradicts Rami bar Chama's position that the domain of an heir is like that of a purchaser.
sub.desc: רב חסדא מתרץ: הברייתא עוסקת לאחר יאוש, ואילו דבריו נאמרו קודם יאוש.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama begins to deflect the challenge, presumably by distinguishing the baraita's context (the text is cut off).
sub.desc: רב חסדא מתרץ: הברייתא עוסקת לאחר יאוש, ואילו דבריו נאמרו קודם יאוש.

items.text: Dispute over heirs' liability for usury money
items.text_en: Dispute over heirs' liability for usury money
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama infers from a baraita that an heir's status is like a purchaser's, so they are exempt from returning usury money left by their father. Rava disagrees, arguing that the verse 'Do not take usury' only warns the father, not his son, so the heir is not obligated.

items.text: Two versions of the teaching
items.text_en: Two versions of the teaching
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the dispute between Rami bar Chama and Rava is taught in two versions: one applies it to the baraita, and the other to the Mishnah. The version that applies it to the Mishnah holds that Rami bar Chama agrees with Rava regarding the baraita.

items.text: Baraita on stolen property left to heirs
items.text_en: Baraita on stolen property left to heirs
items.desc_en: A baraita states that if a robber feeds his children stolen food, they are exempt from repayment. If he leaves the stolen item to them, adult heirs are liable, but minors are exempt. If adults claim ignorance of their father's accounts, they are exempt. Rava clarifies that this exemption applies only if they claim they know the accounts and nothing is owed.

items.text: Another baraita: liability when heirs consume the stolen item
items.text_en: Another baraita: liability when heirs consume the stolen item
items.desc_en: Another baraita states that if a robber leaves stolen property to his heirs and they consume it, both adults and minors are liable. The Gemara questions how minors can be liable, and Rav Papa explains that the baraita refers to a case where the property is left but not yet consumed, so they are liable to return it.

items.text: Rava's case of a borrowed cow left to heirs
items.text_en: Rava's case of a borrowed cow left to heirs
items.desc_en: Rava discusses a case where a father left a borrowed cow to his heirs. They may use it during the loan period, but if it dies, they are not liable for its accidental loss. If they mistakenly slaughter and eat it, they pay the cheap meat price. If the father left collateral, they must pay. The Gemara notes two versions of this teaching, one of which conflicts with Rav Papa's earlier statement.

items.text: Rav Papa's principle on concurrent prohibitions
items.text_en: Rav Papa's principle on concurrent prohibitions
items.desc_en: Rav Papa states that if one steals a cow and slaughters it on Shabbat, he is liable because the prohibition of theft preceded Shabbat. But if the cow was borrowed, he is exempt because the prohibitions of theft and Shabbat arise simultaneously.

items.text: Derivation from verse and dispute with Sumchus
items.text_en: Derivation from verse and dispute with Sumchus
items.desc_en: A baraita derives from the verse 'and he shall return the stolen item which he stole' that one must return the exact object stolen. From this, the rule is stated: if a robber feeds his children, they are exempt; if he leaves it to them, both adults and minors are liable. Sumchus argues that adults are liable but minors are exempt.

items.text: Case of Rabbi Yirmeya's brother-in-law
items.text_en: Case of Rabbi Yirmeya's brother-in-law
items.desc_en: The brother-in-law of Rabbi Yirmeya struck him, and the case came before Rabbi Avin. The brother-in-law claimed he was seeking his own property. Rabbi Yirmeya said he had witnesses that the father had possession, but Rabbi Avin questioned whether witnesses are accepted in such a case.

items.text: Gemara's initial objection and exchange
