items.text_en: Gemara's initial objection and exchange
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects to the idea of accepting testimony without the defendant, citing a mishnah that implies liability even for minors. A speaker suggests that Sumchus holds a dissenting view, and another expresses concern that this would undermine his own position.

items.text: Rabbi Avahu's citation and distinction
items.text_en: Rabbi Avahu's citation and distinction
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu cites a ruling of Rav Yosef bar Chama quoting Rabbi Oshaya about a minor who seizes a field, where the court acts immediately. The Gemara distinguishes this case from one where the defendant has a presumptive right from his father.

items.text: קבלת עדים שלא בפני בעל דין – דעת רבי יוחנן
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's statement and Rabbi Yochanan's astonishment
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi quotes Rabbi Shabtai that testimony is accepted without the defendant. Rabbi Yochanan is astonished, but Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina qualifies the ruling to cases of illness or travel needs.
items.desc: רב אשי בשם רבי שבתי אומר שמקבלים עדים שלא בפני בעל דין, ורבי יוחנן תמה על כך. רבי יוסי בר חנינא מקבל מרבי יוחנן שמותר רק במקרים מיוחדים: כשהתובע חולה, עדיו חולים, או שעדיו מבקשים לצאת לים, ושלחו לנתבע ולא בא.

items.text: קבלת עדים שלא בפני בעל דין – דעת שמואל
items.text_en: Shmuel's ruling and Mar Ukva's clarification
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quotes Shmuel that testimony is accepted without the defendant. Mar Ukva clarifies that this applies only if the court has already begun the case and summoned him; otherwise, the defendant can claim he wants to go to the Great Court. Ravina adds that this applies when he holds a document from the Great Court.
items.desc: רב יהודה בשם שמואל אומר שמקבלים עדים שלא בפני בעל דין. מר עוקבא מפרש ששמואל התכוון למקרה שפתחו לו בדין ושלחו לו ולא בא, אבל אם לא פתחו לו יכול לומר 'לבית דין הגדול אני הולך'. רבינא מוסיף שזה בתנאי שיש דיסקא מבית דין הגדול.

items.text: קיום שטר שלא בפני בעל דין – מחלוקת רב ורבי יוחנן
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Rabbi Yochanan on document ratification
items.desc_en: Rav holds that documents may be ratified without the defendant, while Rabbi Yochanan disagrees, citing a verse requiring the owner to be present. Rav Sheishet explains Rabbi Yochanan's reasoning.
items.desc: רב אומר שמקיימים שטר שלא בפני בעל דין, ורבי יוחנן אוסר. רב ששת מסביר את טעמו של רבי יוחנן בגזירה שווה מפסוק 'והועד בבעליו' – בעל השור צריך לעמוד על שורו, ובעל השטר צריך לעמוד על שטרו.

items.text: הלכות קיום שטר והוצאה לפועל – דעת רבא
items.text_en: Rava's halakhic ruling and detailed procedures
items.desc_en: Rava rules that documents are ratified even if the defendant protests, but if he requests time to bring witnesses, the court grants it. The Gemara details the process: waiting periods, writing a proclamation, and the conditions for issuing an attachment order, including distinctions between loans and deposits, and movable versus immovable property.
items.desc: רבא פוסק שמקיימים שטר שלא בפני בעל דין, אפילו אם הוא צועק. אם מבקש זמן להביא עדים, נותנים לו. לאחר מכן מפרטת הגמרא את סדר ההתראה: שלושה ימי בית דין, תשעים יום של פתיחה, ולבסוף אדרכתא. דינים מיוחדים למלווה לעומת פקדון, ולקרקע לעומת מטלטלין. כמו כן דנים בהודעה לנתבע בהתאם למרחקו, ובמקרה של רבינא שהמתין שנים עשר חודש לנתבע מרוחק.

items.text: מהימנות שלוחא דרבנן ומסירת זימון
items.text_en: Ravina's rulings on court messengers and timing
items.desc_en: Ravina rules that a court messenger is believed like two witnesses for excommunication, but not for a proclamation that costs money. He also states that time is granted based on the word of a woman or neighbors, and only if the defendant is not in town.
items.desc: רבינא אומר ששלוחא דרבנן נאמן כשני עדים לעניין שמתא, אך לא לפתיחא כי זה כרוך בהוצאה כספית. עוד אומר רבינא שנותנים זימון על פי אשה או שכנים כשהנתבע לא בעיר.

items.text: Conditions for issuing a court summons
items.text_en: Conditions for issuing a court summons
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies when a summons (פתיחא) is valid. If the defendant is in the city, the summons is not issued because the court's messenger might have found him. Similarly, if the defendant passed by the courthouse, the summons is invalid because the court itself could have notified him. If the defendant came to court on the same day, the summons is not needed; otherwise, it is assumed he forgot.

items.text: Rava's ruling on tearing the summons
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on tearing the summons
items.desc_en: Rava rules that a summons written for failure to appear in court cannot be torn until the defendant actually comes. A summons for failure to obey the court cannot be torn until the defendant obeys. However, once the defendant says 'I will obey,' the summons is torn immediately.

items.text: Setting court dates and the case of the woman
items.text_en: Setting court dates and the case of the woman
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda states that court dates are set on Monday, Thursday, and the following Monday. Rav Asi challenges Rav Kahana for issuing a summons to a woman the morning after summoning her the previous evening, citing Rav Chisda's rule. Rav Kahana responds that the rule applies only to a man who is busy and not in the city, but a woman who is in the city and does not come is considered rebellious.

items.text: Times when court dates are not set
items.text_en: Times when court dates are not set
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda rules that court dates are not set during Nisan, Tishrei, the eve of a festival, or the eve of Shabbat. However, dates can be set after these periods, except after the eve of Shabbat because people are busy with Shabbat preparations. Rav Nachman adds that dates are not set for wedding parties during the wedding week or for festival pilgrims during the festival. In his time, due to deceivers, they became concerned.

items.text: Returning items for the sake of parental honor
items.text_en: Returning items for the sake of parental honor
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a lost item has a mark of ownership (אחריות), the finder must return it. Rabbi taught his son Shimon that this includes even a cow used for plowing or a donkey used for working, which must be returned out of respect for their father. Rav Kahana asks Rav about a bed used for reclining or a table used for eating, and Rav responds with a verse implying that the answer is obvious.

items.text: Mishnah: Prohibition on exchanging money with tax collectors
items.text_en: Mishnah: Prohibition on exchanging money with tax collectors
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one may not exchange large coins for small ones from the treasury of tax collectors or from the purse of customs collectors, nor may one accept charity from them. However, one may take from their home or from the market. The Gemara adds a Tosefta that one may give a dinar and receive the change.

items.text: Reconciling the Mishnah with the principle of 'dina d'malchuta dina'
items.text_en: Reconciling the Mishnah with the principle of 'dina d'malchuta dina'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's prohibition on dealing with tax collectors, given Shmuel's principle that 'the law of the land is law.' Rabbi Chanina bar Kahana in the name of Shmuel answers that the Mishnah refers to a tax collector who has no fixed rate. The school of Rabbi Yannai says it refers to a tax collector who sets himself up independently. This explanation is applied to three different contexts: the Mishnah, the prohibition of wearing shatnez to evade customs, and the permission to vow to tax collectors.

items.text: Rav Ashi's distinction: a gentile tax collector
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's distinction: a gentile tax collector
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that the permission to evade customs applies only to a gentile tax collector, as derived from a baraita about judging a case between a Jew and a gentile. Rabbi Yishmael allows using subterfuge to favor the Jew, while Rabbi Akiva prohibits it due to desecration of God's name. The Gemara then questions whether robbing a gentile is permitted, citing Rabbi Shimon's teaching from Rabbi Akiva that it is forbidden, based on a verse about redemption.

items.text: Opening exposition on the verse
items.text_en: Opening exposition on the verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara interprets the verse 'and he shall reckon with his purchaser' to mean that the seller must be precise with the buyer, implying that one should not overcharge or deceive.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara interprets the verse 'וְחִשַּׁב עִם קֹנֵהוּ' to mean that the seller must be precise with the buyer, not overcharge or deceive.

items.text: Rav Yosef's distinction between a gentile and a ger toshav
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's distinction between a gentile and a ger toshav
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef resolves a contradiction by distinguishing between a gentile and a ger toshav (resident alien). Abaye challenges this, arguing that the verse explicitly refers to a ger toshav, not a gentile, and further explains the terms.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a gentile (גוי) and a ger toshav (resident alien).
Abaye objects that both cases are written together in the same verse, and the verse explicitly says 'לְגֵר תּוֹשָׁב' (to a resident alien), not to a gentile.
Abaye explains that the phrase 'מִשְׁפַּחַת גֵּר' (family of a ger) refers to a gentile, and 'אוֹ לְעֵקֶר' (or to the root) refers to one sold to idolatry.

items.text: Rava's distinction between robbery and cancellation of a loan
items.text_en: Rava's distinction between robbery and cancellation of a loan
items.desc_en: Rava offers a different resolution: the prohibition applies to robbery itself, but not to canceling a loan. Abaye objects that a Hebrew slave involves cancellation of a loan, but Rava holds that the slave's body is acquired.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between the prohibition of robbery itself (גזל) and the cancellation of a loan (הפקעת הלוואתו).
Abaye objects that a Hebrew slave involves cancellation of a loan, yet Rava's earlier position prohibits it.
The gemara explains that Rava consistently holds that a Hebrew slave's body is acquired (גופו קנוי), so the transaction is not merely a loan cancellation.

items.text: איסור גזל גוי והיתר אבידתו
items.text_en: Rav Bibi bar Giddel's ruling on robbery and lost property of a gentile
items.desc_en: Rav Bibi bar Giddel states that robbing a gentile is forbidden, but returning lost property is permitted. The Gemara questions whether this applies even when the item comes into one's possession, and Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair adds that in a place of Chillul Hashem, even lost property is forbidden.
items.desc: רב ביבי בר גידל בשם רבי שמעון חסידא קובע שגזל גוי אסור, אך אבידתו מותרת. הגמרא מביאה מקורות לכך, ומגבילה את ההיתר במקום שיש חילול השם.

sub.text: רב ביבי בר גידל בשם רבי שמעון חסידא
sub.text_en: Rav Bibi bar Giddel citing Rabbi Shimon Chasida
sub.desc_en: Rav Bibi bar Giddel in the name of Rabbi Shimon Chasida states the principle: robbing a gentile is forbidden, but returning lost property is permitted.
sub.desc: פותח בקביעה שגזל גוי אסור ואבידתו מותרת.

sub.text: רב ביבי בר גידל בשם רבי שמעון חסידא
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna provides a scriptural proof that robbing a gentile is forbidden, citing the verse about eating the nations only when they are subjugated.
sub.desc: פותח בקביעה שגזל גוי אסור ואבידתו מותרת.

sub.text: רב חמא בר גוריא אמר רב
sub.text_en: Rav Chama bar Gurya citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Chama bar Gurya in the name of Rav provides a scriptural proof that returning lost property to a gentile is permitted, citing the verse 'to every lost thing of your brother'.
sub.desc: מביא מקרא להיתר אבידת גוי: 'לכל אבדת אחיך' – רק לאחיך אתה מחזיר.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the permission to keep lost property applies only when it has not yet come into one's possession, but once it has, perhaps one must return it.
sub.desc: מקשה: שמא ההיתר דווקא כשלא באה האבידה לידו, אבל אם באה לידו – יחזיר.

sub.desc_en: Ravina answers that the verse 'and you find it' implies even when it has come into one's possession, so the permission still applies.
sub.desc: מקשה: שמא ההיתר דווקא כשלא באה האבידה לידו, אבל אם באה לידו – יחזיר.

sub.text_en: Supporting baraita of Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair
sub.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair who adds that in a place of Chillul Hashem (desecration of God's name), even returning lost property to a gentile is forbidden.
sub.desc: מקשה: שמא ההיתר דווקא כשלא באה האבידה לידו, אבל אם באה לידו – יחזיר.

items.text: היתר טעות גוי ומעשים של אמוראים
items.text_en: Shmuel's ruling on a gentile's error and practical examples
items.desc_en: Shmuel rules that benefiting from a gentile's mistake is permitted. The Gemara brings several stories of Amoraim who took advantage of a gentile's error in pricing, with some cautionary measures to avoid Chillul Hashem.
items.desc: שמואל מתיר להנות מטעות גוי. מובאים מעשים של שמואל, רב כהנא, רבינא ורב אשי שהתנהלו כך, תוך הקפדה על היתר ההטעיה.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel rules that benefiting from a gentile's mistake is permitted.
sub.desc: שמואל פוסק שמותר להנות מטעותו של גוי במסחר.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a story where Shmuel bought a gold basin from a gentile and included an extra zuz to avoid Chillul Hashem.
sub.desc: שמואל פוסק שמותר להנות מטעותו של גוי במסחר.

sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana bought 120 barrels from a gentile and added an extra zuz, telling the gentile he relies on him to avoid Chillul Hashem.
sub.desc: מביא מעשה שבו רב כהנא קנה מאה ועשרים חביות במחיר מאה והעלים דינר, ואמר לגוי שיסמוך עליו.

sub.desc_en: Ravina bought a palm tree with a gentile and instructed his servant to take the roots first because the gentile knows the count, to avoid Chillul Hashem.
sub.desc: מביא מעשה שבו רב כהנא קנה מאה ועשרים חביות במחיר מאה והעלים דינר, ואמר לגוי שיסמוך עליו.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi, seeing grapes in a vineyard, instructed his servant to check if they belong to a gentile, and when challenged, explained that a gentile takes money but a Jew does not, thus avoiding Chillul Hashem.
sub.desc: מביא מעשה שבו רב אשי ראה אשכולות ענבים בכרם, ציווה לשמשו לקחת רק אם הם של גוי, וכשהגוי תמה השיב שגוי לוקח דמים וישראל לא.

items.text: דינא דמלכותא דינא
items.text_en: The principle that the law of the land is binding
items.desc_en: Shmuel states that the law of the land is binding. Rava supports this by noting that people use roads built by the king's decree. Abaye questions whether this is due to the owners' despair, but Rava argues that without the king's law, despair would not occur. The Gemara addresses a case where the king's agents deviate from his orders.
items.desc: שמואל קובע שדין המלכות הוא דין מחייב. רבא מביא ראיה מכך שמשתמשים בגשרים שנבנו מעצים שנעקרו ללא רשות, ודוחה את הסבר הייאוש.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel states the principle that the law of the land is binding (דינא דמלכותא דינא).
sub.desc: שמואל פותח וקובע את הכלל שדין המלכות הוא דין מחייב.

sub.desc_en: Rava supports Shmuel's principle by noting that people use roads built by the king's decree, implying acceptance of the king's authority.
sub.desc: שמואל פותח וקובע את הכלל שדין המלכות הוא דין מחייב.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects that perhaps the use of the roads is due to the owners' despair (יאוש) of recovering their property, not because of the king's law.
sub.desc: אביי מקשה: שמא הטעם הוא ייאוש הבעלים, ולא דין המלכות.

sub.desc_en: Rava rejects the objection, arguing that without the king's law, the owners would not despair, because they would expect the return of their property.
sub.desc: אביי מקשה: שמא הטעם הוא ייאוש הבעלים, ולא דין המלכות.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions a case where the king's agents deviate from his orders, e.g., he said to take from all districts but they took from only one.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: הרי שליחי המלך לא פעלו לפי הוראתו, אלא כרתו מחבל אחד בלבד.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the king's agent is like the king himself and did not trouble to take from all districts; the agents caused their own loss by not taking from all and collecting payment.
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת: שליח המלך נחשב כמלך ואינו טורח, והבעלים הפסידו לעצמם שהיה להם לקחת מכל הבאגים ולגבות דמים.

items.text: Rava's rulings on taxes and boundaries
items.text_en: Rava's rulings on taxes and boundaries
items.desc_en: Rava rules that a partner in a field must pay the king's tax, but a sharecropper does not. He also states that a resident of a city can compel another resident to pay taxes. Regarding buying from shepherds, it is forbidden within the city's boundary due to mixing of animals, but permitted outside; Ravina adds that if owners pursue, it is forbidden even outside.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that a partner in a field pays the king's tax, but a sharecropper does not because he only takes his sharecropping fee.
Rava rules that a city resident can compel another resident to pay taxes, but only for the current year's land and head tax, not for past years since the king has already been appeased.
Rava rules that buying from shepherds within the city's boundary is forbidden because their animals mix with the city's livestock.
Ravina adds that buying from shepherds outside the boundary is permitted, but if the owners are pursuing the animals, it is forbidden even outside the boundary.

items.text: איסור העדת עדות בערכאות של גויים
items.text_en: Rava's decree against testifying in gentile courts
items.desc_en: Rava (or Rav Huna) decrees that a Jew who testifies in a gentile court against another Jew is excommunicated, because gentile courts extract money improperly.
items.desc: רבא או רב הונא מכריזים שמשמתים יהודי שמעיד בערכאות של גויים נגד ישראל, משום שהגויים מוציאים ממון שלא כדין.

sub.desc_en: Rava (or Rav Huna) decrees that a Jew who testifies in a gentile court against another Jew is excommunicated.
sub.desc: פותח בהכרזה כי יהודי המעיד בערכאות גויים נגד ישראל משמתים אותו.

sub.desc_en: The gemara explains the reason: gentile courts extract money improperly, unlike Jewish courts.
sub.desc: פותח בהכרזה כי יהודי המעיד בערכאות גויים נגד ישראל משמתים אותו.

items.text: Gemara's question about a prominent person as a witness
items.text_en: Gemara's question about a prominent person as a witness
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses whether a prominent person, who is relied upon like two witnesses, can be compelled to testify or can avoid testifying. Rav Ashi recounts a question raised in Rav Huna's study: does such a person have the power to extract money based on his word, or since he is prominent, he cannot evade and must testify? The question remains unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a distinction: the rule that one witness suffices applies only to a single witness in certain courts, but in other courts even a single witness is treated as unreliable.

Rav Ashi reports a question raised in Rav Huna's study: whether a prominent person relied upon like two witnesses can extract money on his word without testifying, or whether he cannot evade and must testify.
The question remains unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Selling land to a non-Jew adjacent to a Jewish neighbor
items.text_en: Selling land to a non-Jew adjacent to a Jewish neighbor
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi rules that a Jew who sells land to a non-Jew adjacent to a Jewish neighbor's field is excommunicated. The reason is not due to the law of the neighbor (bar metzra), which does not apply when buying from or selling to a non-Jew, but because we tell him: 'You have placed a lion on the border.' He remains excommunicated until he accepts responsibility for any damage caused.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi rules that a Jew who sells land to a non-Jew adjacent to a Jewish neighbor's field is excommunicated.
The Gemara questions the reason for the excommunication, noting that the law of the neighbor (bar metzra) does not apply when buying from or selling to a non-Jew.
The Gemara explains that the excommunication is because the seller has placed a lion on the border, and he remains excommunicated until he accepts responsibility for any damage caused.

items.text: Mishnah: Items taken by tax collectors or robbers become the owner's after despair
items.text_en: Mishnah: Items taken by tax collectors or robbers become the owner's after despair
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if tax collectors took a donkey and gave another, or robbers took a garment and gave another, these belong to the recipient because the owners have despaired. Similarly, one who rescues items from a river, a band of soldiers, or robbers acquires them if the owners have despaired. Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka adds that a woman or minor is believed to testify about a bee swarm's origin, and one may enter a neighbor's field to retrieve his swarm, paying for any damage, but may not cut branches with intent to pay. Rabbi Yishmael permits cutting and paying.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that items taken by tax collectors or robbers and replaced with others belong to the recipient due to the owners' despair (יֵאוּשׁ).
The Mishnah adds that one who rescues items from a river, a band of soldiers, or robbers acquires them if the owners have despaired.
The Mishnah extends the rule to a bee swarm, stating that if the owners have despaired, the finder acquires it.

Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka rules that a woman or minor is believed to testify about a bee swarm's origin, and one may enter a neighbor's field to retrieve his swarm, paying for damage, but may not cut branches with intent to pay.
Rabbi Yishmael permits cutting the branches and paying the damages.

items.text: Gemara: Dispute about returning items after despair
items.text_en: Gemara: Dispute about returning items after despair
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents two versions of a baraita. One holds that if one took such items, he must return them to the original owners, because despair without a change of possession (ye'ush shelo mida'at) does not acquire, and the item came into his possession through prohibition. The other version says that if he wishes to return, he returns to the original owners, because despair does acquire, but if he says he does not want property not his own, he returns them.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that if one took such items, he returns them to the original owners, because יאוש (despair) without a change of possession does not acquire, and the item came into his possession through prohibition.
The alternative version holds that יאוש (despair) does acquire, but if the finder says he does not want property not his own, he returns them to the original owners.

items.text: Rav Ashi and Rav Yosef debate despair regarding Jewish vs. non-Jewish robbers
items.text_en: Rav Ashi and Rav Yosef debate despair regarding Jewish vs. non-Jewish robbers
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi says the Mishnah's ruling that the item belongs to the recipient applies only to non-Jewish robbers, because Jewish robbers can be taken to court, so the owner does not despair. Rav Yosef objects, arguing the opposite: non-Jews judge with beatings, so the owner does not despair; Jews, who can be sued, do despair. The Gemara concludes that the dispute was actually about the latter clause of the Mishnah: one who rescues from non-Jews or robbers acquires only if the owners explicitly despaired, but not by default. For non-Jews, the owner does not despair because they judge with beatings; for Jewish robbers, the owner despairs because they can be sued.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's ruling that items taken by tax collectors or robbers belong to the recipient because the owners despair.
Rav Ashi limits the Mishnah's leniency to non-Jewish robbers, because a Jewish robber can be taken to court the next day, so the owner does not despair.
Rav Yosef objects, arguing the opposite: non-Jews judge with beatings (גיתי), so the owner does not despair; Jews can be sued in court, so the owner does despair.

The Gemara resolves that the dispute was actually about the latter clause of the Mishnah: one who rescues from non-Jews or robbers acquires only if the owners explicitly despaired, but not by default.
The Gemara concludes that for non-Jewish robbers, the owner does not despair because they judge with beatings; for Jewish robbers, the owner despairs because they can be sued.

items.text: Dispute between Ulla and Rabbah about known despair
items.text_en: Dispute between Ulla and Rabbah about known despair
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah about hides: those of a householder become susceptible to impurity through thought; those of a tanner do not; those of a robber do not; those of a thief do. Rabbi Shimon reverses: a robber's hides become susceptible, a thief's do not, because the owners have not despaired. Ulla says the dispute is only in a case of unspecified despair, but when despair is known, all agree that despair acquires. Rabbah argues that even with known despair, they dispute. Abaye supports Ulla from the Mishnah's phrase 'because the owners have not despaired,' implying that if they had, it would be his. Rabbah counters that he reads the text as 'because there is no despair for the owners.'

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the rule that hides of a householder become susceptible to impurity through thought, but those of a tanner do not.
The Mishnah states that a robber's hides do not become susceptible through thought, but a thief's hides do.
Rabbi Shimon reverses the ruling: a robber's hides become susceptible, a thief's do not, because the owners have not despaired.
Ulla states that the dispute between Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Shimon is only in a case of unspecified despair, but when despair is known, all agree that יאוש (despair) acquires.
Rabbah argues that even with known despair, the dispute between Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Shimon continues.
Abaye challenges Rabbah, citing the Mishnah's phrase 'because the owners have not despaired,' implying that if they had despaired, the hides would belong to the robber.
Rabbah counters that he reads the Mishnah's text as 'because there is no despair for the owners,' not as Abaye reads it.

items.text: Reconciling the Mishnah with the dispute about despair
items.text_en: Reconciling the Mishnah with the dispute about despair
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks who authored the Mishnah about tax collectors and robbers. If it is the Rabbis, the case of a robber is difficult; if Rabbi Shimon, the case of a thief is difficult. According to Ulla, who holds that known despair is agreed upon, the Mishnah deals with a known case, and all agree. According to Rabbah, who holds that even known despair is disputed, the Mishnah cannot be either the Rabbis or Rabbi Shimon. The Gemara answers that it deals with armed robbers, and it follows Rabbi Shimon. The objection that this is the same as a robber is dismissed: there are two types of robbers.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who authored the Mishnah about tax collectors and robbers.
The Gemara objects that if the Mishnah follows the Rabbis, the case of a robber is difficult; if it follows Rabbi Shimon, the case of a thief is difficult.
The Gemara explains that according to Ulla, who holds that known despair is agreed upon, the Mishnah deals with a known case and all agree.
The Gemara asks that according to Rabbah, who holds that even known despair is disputed, the Mishnah cannot be either the Rabbis or Rabbi Shimon.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah deals with armed robbers and follows Rabbi Shimon.
The Gemara objects that this is the same as a robber, and the answer dismisses it by noting there are two types of robbers.

items.text: Further support and resolution from another Mishnah
items.text_en: Further support and resolution from another Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites another Mishnah stating that the consecrations, terumot, and ma'aserot of a thief, robber, and extortionist are valid. Again, the same question arises: who authored it? According to Ulla, it deals with known despair, and all agree. According to Rabbah, it must be about armed robbers and follows Rabbi Shimon. The objection that this is the same as a robber is again answered: there are two types. Alternatively, the Gemara suggests that the Mishnah follows Rabbi, who equates a thief with a robber.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah stating that the consecrations, terumot, and ma'aserot of a thief, robber, and extortionist are valid.
The Gemara asks who authored this Mishnah, noting that if it follows the Rabbis, the inclusion of a robber is problematic, and if it follows Rabbi Shimon, the inclusion of a thief is problematic.
According to Ulla, who holds that in a case of known despair all agree that despair acquires, this Mishnah deals with known despair and is acceptable to all.
The Gemara objects that according to Rabbah, who holds that even in known despair there is a dispute, this Mishnah cannot be attributed to either the Rabbis or Rabbi Shimon.
The Gemara answers that this Mishnah also deals with armed robbers and follows Rabbi Shimon.
The Gemara objects that an armed robber is the same as a robber, and the answer is that there are two types of robber.
Alternatively, the Gemara suggests that the Mishnah follows Rabbi, who equates a thief with a robber.

items.text: The dispute over Rabbi's statement: thief like which robber?
items.text_en: The dispute over Rabbi's statement: thief like which robber?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi's statement that a thief is like a robber refers to the Rabbis' view (no acquisition) or Rabbi Shimon's view (acquisition). It attempts to resolve this from a mishna about tax collectors taking a donkey, concluding that the mishna must follow Rabbi Shimon and refer to armed bandits, distinguishing two types of robbers.

items.text: Second attempt: a baraita on consecration by thieves
items.text_en: Second attempt: a baraita on consecration by thieves
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita stating that a thief, robber, and extortionist's consecrations are valid. It again questions the identity of the authority, and resolves similarly that it refers to armed bandits and Rabbi Shimon, with two types of robbers.

items.text: הוכחה מדברי רבי לבנו: גזלן דרבי שמעון
items.text_en: Proof from Rabbi's teaching to his son
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi brings a teaching where Rabbi told his son that items without intrinsic value must be returned due to their father's honor. The Gemara infers that without this reason, they would not be returned, proving Rabbi holds the thief acquires like Rabbi Shimon's robber.
items.desc: רב אשי מביא ראיה מדברי רבי לבנו רבי שמעון, שממשנת 'לא דבר שיש בו אחריות' משמע שרק משום כבוד אביהן חייבים להחזיר, הא לאו הכי לא – ומכאן שרבי סובר כגזלן דרבי שמעון.

items.text: דין נחיל של דבורים – יאוש בעלים
items.text_en: The swarm of bees and despair
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the mishna's phrase 'and similarly a swarm of bees,' teaching that even though a swarm is acquired by rabbinic law, one does not assume the owner despairs unless they actually do.
items.desc: הגמרא מבארת מדוע המשנה מוסיפה 'וכן נחיל של דבורים': ללמד שאף שקניין דבורים הוא דרבנן, אין יאוש בלא ידיעה, ורק אם נתייאשו הבעלים – קנה המוצא.

items.text: נאמנות אשה וקטן במסיח לפי תומו
items.text_en: Testimony of a woman or minor by casual conversation
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the mishna's ruling that a woman or minor is believed about a swarm. Rav Yehuda explains it refers to when owners are chasing and the woman/minor speak casually. Rav Ashi limits this to testimony about a woman. The Gemara questions this with cases of a minor's testimony about immersion and a captive woman, resolving that rabbinic leniencies apply.
items.desc: דיון בנאמנות אשה וקטן האומרים 'מכאן יצא נחיל זה'. הגמרא מבררת שזהו מסיח לפי תומו, ומקשה מסיפורים על תרומה ושבויה שמוכיחים שנאמנות זו חלה גם בדאורייתא. מתרצים שבתרומה ובשבויה הקלו.

items.text: תנאי בית דין להצלת נכסי חברו
items.text_en: Court condition for cutting branches and pouring wine
items.desc_en: A baraita from Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka states that a court condition allows one to enter a neighbor's field to cut branches to save his swarm, and to pour out wine to save honey, with compensation from the saved property, as Joshua conditioned the land.
items.desc: ברייתא בשם רבי ישמעאל בן רבי יוחנן בן ברוקה קובעת תנאי בית דין: מותר להיכנס לשדה חברו ולקצוץ סוכו כדי להציל נחילו, וכן לשפוך יינו ולהציל דובשנו, ולפרוק עציו ולטעון פשתנו – על מנת לשלם מן המוצלח.

items.text: המכיר כליו וספריו ביד אחר ויצא שם גניבה
items.text_en: Identifying stolen vessels and books
items.desc_en: The mishna states that if one recognizes his vessels in another's possession and there is a rumor of theft, the buyer swears what he paid and takes them. The Gemara questions the rumor's validity, and Rav Yehuda and Rav Kahana describe scenarios. Further concerns about specific items are addressed by Rabbi Yochanan, Rabbi Yossi bar Chanina, and Rav. Rava limits the ruling to one who usually sells his vessels.
items.desc: המשנה דנה במקרה שהתובע מזהה כליו וספריו אצל אחר ויצא שם גניבה בעיר – הלוקח נשבע כמה נתן ונוטל. הגמרא מבררת מתי שם הגניבה נחשב ראיה, ודנה במקרים שונים של גנבים ולסטים.

items.text: Initial question and answer about the buyer's obligation
items.text_en: Initial question and answer about the buyer's obligation
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the buyer must go to such lengths to return the stolen item, and suggests that if the thief needed money he might have sold it. Rav Ashi answers that the thief is known as a thief in the city, implying the buyer is not liable.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the buyer must go to such lengths to return the stolen item, suggesting the thief might have sold it because he needed money.
Rav Ashi answers that the thief is known as a thief in the city, implying the buyer is not liable.

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Rabbi Yochanan about the buyer's recourse
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Rabbi Yochanan about the buyer's recourse
items.desc_en: An explicit dispute is recorded: Rav (citing Rabbi Chiyya) says the buyer's claim is against the first (the thief), while Rabbi Yochanan (citing Rabbi Yannai) says it is against the second (the original owner). Rav Yosef reconciles them by distinguishing before and after יאוש.

sub.desc_en: An explicit dispute is introduced: Rav (citing Rabbi Chiyya) says the buyer's claim is against the first (the thief), while Rabbi Yochanan (citing Rabbi Yannai) says it is against the second (the original owner).
Rav Yosef reconciles the dispute by distinguishing before יאוש (despair of recovery) — where the buyer claims against the original owner — and after יאוש — where the buyer claims against the thief.
The gemara notes that both Rav and Rabbi Yochanan accept the principle of Rav Chisda (that the buyer's claim depends on יאוש).

items.text: Abaye's challenge from the Mishnah of מתנות כהונה
items.text_en: Abaye's challenge from the Mishnah of מתנות כהונה
items.desc_en: Abaye challenges Rav Yosef's reconciliation, citing a Mishnah about priestly gifts that is like before יאוש, yet the Sages dispute whether the buyer deducts from the price. Rav adds that if the butcher weighed for him, the claim is against the butcher, implying a dispute even before יאוש.

sub.desc_en: Abaye challenges Rav Yosef's reconciliation by citing a Mishnah about priestly gifts (מתנות כהונה) that are like before יאוש (despair), yet the Sages dispute whether the buyer deducts from the price.

Abaye cites the Mishnah that distinguishes between buying the cow's innards without specification (priestly gifts given to the priest, no deduction) and buying by weight (the buyer deducts from the price).
Rav adds that the Mishnah's ruling applies only when the buyer weighed for himself, but if the butcher weighed for him, the claim is against the butcher, implying a dispute even before יאוש.

The Gemara clarifies that Rav's statement should be read as 'even the claim is against the butcher,' teaching that priestly gifts are not subject to the law of stolen property (אין מתנות כהונה נגזלות).

items.text: Rav Zevid's explanation of the dispute based on יאוש
items.text_en: Rav Zevid's explanation of the dispute based on יאוש
items.desc_en: Rav Zevid explains that the dispute is when the owners despaired in the buyer's hands but not in the thief's. One holds that יאוש followed by שינוי רשות acquires, but not the reverse; the other holds there is no difference.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: According to Abaye who said they dispute, what is the basis of their dispute? It answers: In the principle of Rav Chisda.
Rav Zevid explains: The case is where the owners despaired in the buyer's hands but not in the thief's hands.

sub.text: Rav Zevid's resolution of the dispute
sub.text_en: Rav Zevid's resolution of the dispute
sub.desc_en: Rav Zevid resolves: One opinion holds that יאוש (despair) followed by שינוי רשות (change of ownership) acquires, but not the reverse; the other holds there is no difference.

items.text: Rav Pappa's explanation based on תקנת השוק
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's explanation based on תקנת השוק
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa explains the dispute is about a cloak, where all agree it returns to its owner, but they argue about תקנת השוק. Rav says the buyer takes from the thief and no תקנת השוק applies; Rabbi Yochanan says the buyer takes from the owner and תקנת השוק applies. The Gemara questions Rav's view from Rav Huna's ruling about חנן בישא, and distinguishes because the thief was notorious. Rava adds that if the thief is well-known, no תקנת השוק applies.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa introduces the dispute as being about a cloak (גלימא), where all agree it returns to its owner, and the argument is about תקנת השוק (market adjustment).
Rav, citing Rabbi Chiyya, rules that the buyer takes from the thief (הדין עם הראשון) and no תקנת השוק applies.
Rabbi Yochanan, citing Rabbi Yannai, rules that the buyer takes from the owner (הדין עם השני) and תקנת השוק applies.

The Gemara objects: does Rav really hold that no תקנת השוק applies? Citing Rav Huna's ruling about חנן בישא (a notorious thief), where the buyer was told to pay the owner, implying תקנת השוק was applied.
The Gemara distinguishes: the case of חנן בישא is different because the thief cannot be made to pay, so it is treated as if the thief was not identified.
Rava rules: if the thief is well-known (מפורסם), no תקנת השוק applies; the Gemara clarifies that חנן בישא was notorious for wickedness but not for theft.

items.text: Cases where תקנת השוק does or does not apply
items.text_en: Cases where תקנת השוק does or does not apply
items.desc_en: The Gemara lists cases: if the thief paid a debt or credit, no תקנת השוק; if he mortgaged for double value, there is a dispute; if he sold at equal value, there is a dispute. The halakha is that תקנת השוק applies in all cases except paying a debt or credit.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that if a thief paid a debt or credit with stolen goods, תקנת השוק (the market ordinance) does not apply, because people assume the thief was repaying a prior obligation.
The Gemara lists the case of a mortgage: if the thief mortgaged an item worth 200 for 100, תקנת השוק applies; if he mortgaged equal value, Ameimar and Mar Zutra dispute whether it applies.
The Gemara rules that in the mortgage case, תקנת השוק applies.
The Gemara lists the case of a sale: if the thief sold equal value, תקנת השוק applies; if he sold 100-value for 200, Rav Sheshet and Rava dispute whether it applies.
The Gemara rules that תקנת השוק applies in all cases except paying a debt or credit.

items.text: Case of Avimi bar Nazi and the ruling of Rav Kohen
items.text_en: Case of Avimi bar Nazi and the ruling of Rav Kohen
items.desc_en: Avimi bar Nazi stole a cloak and gave it to a creditor for a debt, then borrowed more. When the thief was caught, Ravina ruled the first part is 'stole and paid a debt' (no תקנת השוק), and for the second, the buyer takes his money and returns the cloak. Rav Kohen challenges that the cloak might have been given for the first debt, and the later money was a loan; the halakha follows Rav Kohen.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces the case of Avimi bar Nazi, who was owed four zuz by a man; the man stole a cloak and gave it to Avimi, then borrowed another four zuz; later the thief was caught and the case came before Ravina.
Ravina rules that the first part is 'stole and paid a debt' (no תקנת השוק), and for the second part the buyer takes his money and returns the cloak.

Rav Kohen objects that the cloak might have been given for the first debt, making it 'stole and paid a debt', and the later money was a loan; the matter was brought before Rabbi Avahu, who ruled the halakha follows Rav Kohen.

items.text: Case of the stolen book and the dispute between Abaye and Rava
items.text_en: Case of the stolen book and the dispute between Abaye and Rava
items.desc_en: A thief stole a book and sold it for 80 zuz; the buyer sold it for 120. When the thief was caught, Abaye ruled the owner pays 80 to the second buyer and takes the book, then the second buyer collects 40 from the first buyer. Rava objects that if a buyer from a thief gets תקנת השוק, certainly a buyer from a buyer does. Rava rules the owner pays 120 to the second buyer, takes the book, and then collects 40 from the first buyer and 80 from the thief.

sub.desc_en: The gemara presents a case: a thief named Narsha stole a book, sold it to a Papunaite for 80 zuz, who then sold it to a Bar-Mahozite for 120 zuz; eventually the thief was caught.
Abaye rules that the owner pays 80 zuz to the second buyer (Bar-Mahozite) and takes the book, then the second buyer collects 40 zuz from the first buyer (Papunaite).
Rava objects: if a buyer from a thief receives תקנת השוק (market overt protection), certainly a buyer from a buyer should receive it, so Abaye's ruling is inconsistent.
Rava rules that the owner pays 120 zuz to the second buyer and takes the book, then collects 40 zuz from the first buyer and 80 zuz from the thief.

items.text: Opening Mishnah about saving honey with wine
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah about saving honey with wine
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where one person's wine barrel and another's honey jug are involved; the wine owner pours his wine to save the honey. This introduces a new topic about property damage and rescue.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where one person's wine barrel and another's honey jug are involved; the wine owner pours his wine to save the honey.

items.text: משנת הפתיחה: דיני מציל נכסי חברו
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents two cases: one where a person saves another's property without stipulation, receiving only his wages; and one where he stipulates that the owner must pay for his lost property, in which case the owner must pay.
items.desc: המשנה קובעת כי מי שמציל את נכסי חברו תוך אובדן נכסיו שלו, זכאי רק לשכרו, אלא אם התנה במפורש שישלם לו דמי נכסיו. שתי דוגמאות מובאות: יין ודבש, וחמור יקר לעומת חמור זול.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents two cases: one who saves another's property without stipulation receives only his wages, but if he stipulates payment for his own lost property, the owner must pay.
sub.desc: המשנה פותחת בדין מציל נכסי חברו: זכאי רק לשכרו, אלא אם התנה במפורש שישלם דמי נכסיו.

items.text: קושיית הגמרא: מדוע לא יטען 'מהפקירא קא זכינא'?
items.text_en: Gemara's first question and answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the rescuer cannot claim the saved property as ownerless (hefker), citing a baraita about a person carrying jugs of wine and oil who cannot declare them as terumah. Rabbi Yirmeya answers that the case is where the olive press beam is still attached, meaning the oil is not yet fully ownerless.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה: מדוע המציל אינו יכול לטעון שזכה בנכסים מהפקר, שהרי הנכסים האבודים נחשבים להפקר? היא מביאה ברייתא האוסרת להפריש תרומה ומעשר על פירות הנשפכים, ומתרצת בשם רבי ירמיה שהדין חל רק כשהחבית עדיין שלמה בחלקה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the rescuer cannot claim he acquired the property from ownerless status, citing a baraita that one cannot retroactively designate wine as terumah when it is breaking.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: מדוע המציל אינו יכול לטעון שזכה בדבש מהפקר, שהרי הנכסים האבודים נחשבים להפקר? היא מביאה ברייתא האוסרת להפריש תרומה ומעשר על פירות הנשפכים.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya explains that the case is where the olive press beam is still attached, so the wine is not yet ownerless.
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת בשם רבי ירמיה שהדין חל רק כשהחבית עדיין שלמה בחלקה, ולכן אינה נחשבת להפקר.

items.text: קושיה מברייתא אחרת: מעשר שני על מטבעות
items.text_en: Contradiction from another baraita and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita where a person can declare his produce redeemed onto money in his hand. It resolves that the case is where he can save the property, but only with difficulty (by pressing), so initially he should not make such a declaration.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה מברייתא אחרת המתירה להחלל מעשר שני על מטבעות גם במצב סכנה, ומתרצת שמדובר במקרה שבו יכול להציל את המטבעות בדוחק, ולכן לכתחילה לא יאמר, אך בדיעבד דבריו קיימים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects by citing a baraita where one can retroactively designate produce as tithes when facing danger, contradicting the earlier baraita.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה מברייתא המתירה לחלל מעשר שני על מטבעות בדיעבד, בניגוד לברייתא הקודמת האוסרת להפריש תרומה על פירות הנשברים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the first baraita deals with a case where one can save the items, but only with difficulty, so retroactive designation is not allowed.
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת שהברייתא הראשונה עוסקת במקרה שאינו יכול להציל כלל, ואילו הברייתא השנייה עוסקת במקרה שיכול להציל בדוחק, ולכן לכתחילה לא יאמר אך בדיעבד דבריו קיימים.

items.text: קושיה מברייתא על חביות טבל טמא
items.text_en: Another contradiction regarding loss and Rabbi Yirmeya's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether one may not declare in a case of loss, citing a baraita about ten barrels of tevel where one can declare a broken barrel as terumah. Rabbi Yirmeya again answers that the case is where the olive press beam is attached. The Gemara then questions the case of a barrel that was uncovered.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה מברייתא המתירה להפריש תרומת מעשר מחבית שנשברה על חברותיה, ומתרצת בשם רבי ירמיה שהדין חל רק כשהחבית עדיין שלמה בחלקה. נשאלת שאלה לגבי חבית שנתגלתה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether one may not make such a declaration even when there is loss, citing a baraita that allows designating a broken barrel of טבל (untithed produce) as terumah for others.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה מברייתא המתירה להפריש תרומת מעשר מחבית טבל טמא שנשברה או נתגלתה על חברותיה, ומדייקת שבשמן לא יעשה כן מפני הפסד כהן.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya again explains that the case is where the beam is attached, and the Gemara questions the use of a barrel that was uncovered.
sub.desc: רבי ירמיה מתרץ שהברייתא עוסקת במקרה שהחבית עדיין שלמה בחלקה, והגמרא שואלת: לגבי חבית שנתגלתה – למה היא ראויה?

items.text: דיון בכשרות יין שנתגלה
items.text_en: Discussion on uncovered liquids and Rabbi Nehemya's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers if uncovered liquid is usable for sprinkling, citing a baraita about uncovered water. It suggests using a strainer, per Rabbi Nehemya's opinion. A further discussion notes that if the strainer's bottom is covered, the poison does not rise, and Rabbi Simon quotes Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that the ruling applies only if the strainer was not shaken.
items.desc: הגמרא דנה האם יין שנתגלה ראוי לזילוף, ומביאה ברייתא האוסרת שימוש במים מגולים. מתרצת שניתן לסנן את היין, ומביאה את דעת רבי נחמיה המתיר סינון בתנאים מסוימים. דוחה קושיה משם רבי שמעון בשם רבי יהושע בן לוי, ומתרצת שאפשר להניח דבר על פי החבית.

items.text: דין תרומה מטמא על טמא
items.text_en: Rabbi Nehemya's ruling on terumah from impure
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether one can separate terumah from impure produce, citing a baraita that permits it from impure on impure, but Rabbi Nehemya restricts it to demai produce. The Gemara concludes that the case here is also demai.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה על דברי רבי נחמיה, שהרי ברייתא אחרת אוסרת לתרום מטמא על טמא, ומתרצת שהברייתא עוסקת בדמאי.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Nechemya allows terumah from טמא (impure) produce onto טמא, citing a baraita that limits such designation.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה על שיטת רבי נחמיה: האם מותר לתרום מטמא על טמא?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that Rabbi Nechemya's restriction applies only to ודאי (certain) produce, but here it is דמאי (doubtfully tithed produce), so it is permitted.
sub.desc: הגמרא מביאה ברייתא המפרטת את דיני התרומה מטמא על טמא, ובה רבי נחמיה מגביל היתר זה לדמאי בלבד.

items.text: הבחנה בין יין לשמן: הפסד כהן
items.text_en: Distinction between wine and oil for sprinkling
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why oil is singled out due to loss to the priest, since wine is also usable for sprinkling. It answers that the case is with new wine, which could lead to sin if aged. For oil, one might put it in a disgusting vessel, but wine for sprinkling would not be placed in such a vessel. The Gemara notes that the concern for sin is a dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel.
items.desc: הגמרא דנה בהבחנה בין יין לשמן בברייתא, ומסבירה ששמן ראוי להדלקה ואילו יין חדש אינו ראוי לזילוף. דוחה קושיה שניתן ליישנו, ומתרצת שמא יבוא לידי תקלה. דן באפשרות להניח בכלי מאוס, ומסיים בציון מחלוקת תנאים בעניין.

items.text: מחלוקת בית שמאי ובית הלל בזילוף יין טמא
items.text_en: Dispute about spilled wine: Beit Hillel vs. Beit Shammai and Rabbi Yishmael's compromise
items.desc_en: Beit Hillel says spilled wine should be used for sprinkling, Beit Shammai says it should all be spilled. Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei attempts to mediate, distinguishing between house and field, or old and new wine, but is told there is no third compromise.
items.desc: בית שמאי אומרים שיש לשפוך את היין הטמא כולו, ובית הלל אומרים שניתן לזלף. רבי ישמעאל ברבי יוסי מציע הכרעה: בבית יזלף, בשדה ישפוך. יש אומרים שהכרעתו הייתה בין יין ישן לחדש, אך נדחתה בטענה שאין הכרעה שלישית מכרעת.

items.text: Gemara's question: Why can't the owner claim deception?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Why can't the owner claim deception?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why, if someone says 'I will save your property,' he cannot claim he was joking, citing a parallel case of a fugitive hiring a ferryman where the hirer can claim deception. The Gemara initially suggests the same logic should apply here.

items.text: Distinction between the cases: Rami bar Chama's explanation
items.text_en: Distinction between the cases: Rami bar Chama's explanation
items.desc_en: The Gemara distinguishes the cases: the first case (fugitive) is like a fisherman who lost fish worth a zuz, so the hirer can claim deception. But the second case (saving property) is different because the rescuer actually saved something, so he is entitled to full payment.

items.text: הצלת חמור שנשטף בנהר
items.text_en: Mishnah: River swept away donkeys; need for both clauses
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses a case where a river swept away one's donkey and another's, and the owner saved the other's. The Gemara explains why both clauses are necessary: the first teaches that if he explicitly said he would save, he gets full value; the second teaches that in a standard case he only gets wages.
items.desc: המשנה מביאה מקרה של חמורים שנשטפו בנהר, והגמרא מסבירה ששני המקרים (יין ודבש, חמורים) נצרכים: במקרה של יין, שבו האובדן נעשה בידיים, התנאי מחייב גם בסתמא; במקרה של חמורים, שהאובדן בא מעצמו, בסתמא מקבל רק שכר טרחה.

items.text: Rav Kahana's question: If the saved donkey returns on its own
items.text_en: Rav Kahana's question: If the saved donkey returns on its own
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana asks Rav: if one went down to save a donkey and it came up on its own, what is the law? Rav answers that Heaven had mercy on him, implying he gets nothing beyond his wages.

items.text: Story of Rav Safra and the lion: Acquiring the donkey
items.text_en: Story of Rav Safra and the lion: Acquiring the donkey
items.desc_en: A story about Rav Safra traveling with a caravan where a lion was given a donkey each night. When it was Rav Safra's turn, the lion didn't eat the donkey, and Rav Safra took it. Rav Acha from Difti questions whether he could acquire it since it was abandoned only for the lion, but Rav Safra acted for convenience.

items.text: ירד להציל ולא הציל
items.text_en: Rav's question: If one went down to save but didn't succeed
items.desc_en: Rav asks Rabbi: if one went down to save but did not succeed, what is the law? Rabbi responds that this is a simple question: he only gets his wages.
items.desc: רב שואל את רבי יהודה הנשיא: אם ירד להציל חמור חברו ולא הצליח, מה דינו? רבי עונה שזו שאלה פשוטה: אין לו אלא שכרו, ואינו מקבל תשלום על חמורו שאבד.

items.text: התחלת ברייתא על שוכר פועל
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita about hiring a worker
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita about hiring a worker, which seems to contradict the previous ruling.
items.desc: רב מקשה על דברי רבי מברייתא העוסקת בשוכר פועל, אך הקטע נקטע.

items.text: דין שכר שליח שהביא אוכל לחולה ומצאו שמת או הבריא
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's ruling about hiring porters
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling that if one hires porters to bring items for a sick person and finds the person dead or recovered, he pays full wages. The Gemara distinguishes this from the case of a robber, arguing that in the Mishnah the agent fulfilled his mission, whereas in the robber's case he did not.
items.desc: הגמרא דנה במקרה של שליח שנשלח להביא אוכל לחולה, ומצאו שמת או הבריא. רבי יהודה הנשיא מבחין בין מקרה זה, בו השליח ביצע את שליחותו, לבין מקרה החמורים, בו לא הצליח להציל.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's ruling that one who hires porters to bring produce for a sick person and finds the person dead or recovered must pay full wages.
sub.desc: הברייתא מביאה דין שליח שהביא אוכל לחולה ומצאו שמת או הבריא, שהשליח מקבל שכרו משלם.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the cases are different: in the Mishnah the agent fulfilled his mission, whereas in the robber's case he did not.
sub.desc: רבי יהודה הנשיא דוחה את הדמיון בין המקרים: שם השליח ביצע שליחותו, כאן לא הצליח להציל.

items.text: Baraita on caravan in the desert and porters' agreements
items.text_en: Baraita on caravan in the desert and porters' agreements
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that if a caravan is threatened by a troop, they assess losses based on money, not lives. If they hired a guide, they assess based on lives as well. Porters may stipulate that if one loses his donkey, another will be provided, but not if lost in a place of danger. If the porter says 'give me and I will guard', they do not listen.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with the rule for a caravan threatened by a troop: they assess losses based on money, not lives.
The baraita adds that if they hired a guide, they assess based on lives as well, and they may not deviate from the porters' custom.
The baraita concludes with the rule that porters may stipulate replacement of a lost donkey, except in a place of danger, and if a porter says 'give me and I will guard', they do not listen.

items.text: Gemara's clarification on the porter's stipulation
items.text_en: Gemara's clarification on the porter's stipulation
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the ruling about not listening to the porter who wants to guard his own donkey is necessary even if he has another donkey, because one might think he is reliable, but the Gemara teaches that guarding by one person is different from guarding by two.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the ruling is necessary, since it seems obvious, and answers that it is needed in a case where the porter has another donkey.
The Gemara explains that one might think the porter is reliable because he guards his own donkey, but the Gemara teaches that guarding by one person is different from guarding by two.

items.text: Baraita on ship in the sea and sailors' agreements
items.text_en: Baraita on ship in the sea and sailors' agreements
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that if a ship is threatened by a wave and they lighten its load, they assess based on weight, not value. Sailors may stipulate that if one loses his ship, another will be provided, but not if lost in a place of danger. If he deviates to a place where ships do not go, they do not provide.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that if a ship is threatened by a wave and they lighten its load, they assess based on weight, not value, and they must not deviate from the sailors' custom.

The baraita continues: sailors may stipulate that if one loses his ship, another will be provided, but not if lost in a place of danger, and if he deviates to a place where ships do not go, they do not provide.

items.text: Gemara's clarification on the ship's deviation
items.text_en: Gemara's clarification on the ship's deviation
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the ruling about deviation is necessary when one travels in Nissan (when ships go one parasang) to a place that is like Tishrei (when ships go two parasangs), because one might think he is following the usual route, but the Gemara teaches that he is not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the ruling about deviation is necessary, implying it is obvious.

The Gemara explains that the ruling is needed when one travels in Nissan (when ships go one parasang) to a place that is like Tishrei (when ships go two parasangs), because one might think he is following the usual route, but the Gemara teaches that he is not.

items.text: ברייתא: דין המציל משיירה – לעצמו או לאמצע
items.text_en: Baraita on one who saves property from a troop and the dispute among Amoraim
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that if a caravan is attacked and one member saves property, it goes to the middle (shared). If he says 'I will save for myself', it is his. The Gemara questions this, and Rami bar Chama, Rava, and Rav Ashi offer different explanations: partners, workers, or saving with difficulty.
items.desc: ברייתא קובעת כי אם אחד מהשיירה הציל את הרכוש, ההצלה היא לאמצע, אלא אם כן אמר בפירוש שהוא מציל לעצמו. הגמרא דנה במקרים שונים ומציעה מספר הסברים: רמי בר חמא (שותפין), רבא (פועלים), ורב אשי (הצלה בדחק).

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that if a caravan is attacked and one member saves property, the saved property goes to the middle (shared), but if he explicitly says 'I will save for myself', it is his.
sub.desc: ברייתא פותחת בדין המציל משיירה: אם הציל סתם – ההצלה לאמצע, ואם אמר בפירוש 'אני מציל לעצמי' – ההצלה לעצמו.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the baraita: if the saver can save alone, even the second clause should go to the middle; if he cannot save alone, even the first clause should be his own.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: מה הנסיבות? אם יכול להציל – אפילו בסיפא ההצלה לאמצע; אם אינו יכול – אפילו ברישא ההצלה לעצמו.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama explains that the case involves partners, and the rule follows the principle of a partner dividing without the other's knowledge: if he declared his intent, he separates; if not, he does not.
sub.desc: רמי בר חמא מתרץ: מדובר בשותפין; אמירה 'לעצמי' נחשבת חלוקת שותפות, ואם לא אמר – לא חלק.

sub.desc_en: Rava explains that the case involves hired workers, following Rav's principle that a worker can retract even mid-day, and as long as he hasn't retracted, the property is in the employer's domain.
sub.desc: רבא מתרץ: מדובר בפועלים; כל עוד לא חזר בו – המציל ברשות בעל הבית, וכשחזר בו – המציל לעצמו, משום שישראל אינם עבדים לעבדים.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that the case is when he can save only with difficulty; if he revealed his intent (to save for himself), it is his; if not, it goes to the middle.
sub.desc: רב אשי מתרץ: מדובר כשיכול להציל בדחק; גילוי דעת 'לעצמי' מוכיח ייאוש השותפים, ואם לא גילה – ההצלה לאמצע.

items.text: Mishnah on one who robs a field and the Gemara's discussion
items.text_en: Mishnah on one who robs a field and the Gemara's discussion
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that if one robs a field and it is taken by tax collectors, if it is a general decree, he says 'yours is before you'; if due to the robber, he must provide another field. The Gemara discusses the correct term (מסיקין or מציקין), defines when it is due to the robber (e.g., if he informed), and relates a case where Rav Nachman ruled against an informer, with Rav Yosef questioning whether it is a law or a penalty.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the law: if one robs a field and tax collectors take it, if it is a general decree he says 'yours is before you'; if due to the robber, he must provide another field.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak justifies both variant readings of the Mishnah's term (מסיקין or מציקין) by citing biblical verses.
The Gemara asks what case the Mishnah's second clause refers to, rejecting the obvious scenario that the robber's own land was singled out for seizure.
The Gemara answers that the case is where the robber informed (אחוי אחוויי) on the owner's field, causing it to be seized along with others.
A story is related: an informer came before Rav Nachman, who obligated him to pay; Rav Huna bar Chiya asked Rav Nachman whether this is a law (דינא) or a penalty (קנסא).

sub.text: Rav Nachman's answer and Rav Yosef's question
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman's answer and Rav Yosef's question
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman answers that it is a law based on the Mishnah; after they left, Rav Yosef asks Rav Huna bar Chiya what practical difference the question makes.

items.text: Opening question: Is it a monetary judgment or a fine?
items.text_en: Opening question: Is it a monetary judgment or a fine?
items.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a question about whether a certain case involves a monetary judgment (דינא) or a fine (קנסא), and notes that if it is a fine, we cannot derive laws from it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the case involves a monetary judgment (דינא) or a fine (קנסא), and notes that if it is a fine, we cannot derive laws from it.

items.text: Proof from the tannaitic tradition about fines
items.text_en: Proof from the tannaitic tradition about fines
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove that fines cannot be used for derivation from a baraita about the laws of one who renders wine libation (מנסך) and one who mixes terumah (מדמע). The initial assumption is that the change in ruling is due to the fine status, but the Gemara rejects this, offering an alternative explanation based on the extent of loss.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that fines cannot be used for derivation.
The Gemara cites a baraita about the evolution of rulings on one who renders wine libation (מנסך) and one who mixes terumah (מדמע).
The Gemara objects that the change in ruling must be because the case involves a fine (קנס), and fines cannot be used for derivation.
The Gemara rejects the objection, explaining that the change was due to a shift in concern about the extent of loss, not the fine status.

items.text: ברייתא הפוכה והסבר מחודש: שיטת רבי אבין ורבי ירמיה
items.text_en: Contradictory baraita and resolution via Rabbi Avin and Rabbi Yirmeya
items.desc_en: A contradictory baraita is presented where the order of rulings is reversed. The Gemara resolves the contradiction by explaining that the initial and final opinions follow different Tannaitic views: Rabbi Avin's opinion regarding liability for murder and property, and Rabbi Yirmeya's opinion that acquisition occurs at the time of lifting.
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה ברייתא הפוכה (של אביו של רבי אבין) שבה דימוע קודם לניסוך, ומסבירה שהשינוי נובע ממחלוקת בין רבי אבין לרבי ירמיה: האם החיוב מיתה וקנס חלים בו-זמנית או בנפרד.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the previous explanation by citing a contradictory baraita from Rabbi Avin's father, which reverses the order of rulings.
The Gemara infers that the reason for the change is that we do not derive rulings from a קנס (penalty) case.
The Gemara rejects the inference and explains that the initial and final opinions follow different Tannaitic views: Rabbi Avin and Rabbi Yirmeya.

The Gemara cites Rabbi Avin's opinion that one who shoots an arrow from the beginning of four cubits to the end of four cubits, tearing silk in its path, is exempt from property liability because the lifting is for the sake of placing, and he is liable for his life.
The Gemara cites Rabbi Yirmeya's opinion that acquisition occurs at the time of lifting, so property liability begins then, but liability for one's life does not occur until the time of libation.

items.text: דין ישראל שאנסוהו גויים והראה ממון חברו
items.text_en: Case of a Jew forced to reveal a friend's property
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Yehuda encountered a case where a Jew, forced by gentiles, revealed his friend's money. He ruled that the revealer is liable. Rava objects, citing a baraita that distinguishes between merely pointing and physically handing over. Rabbah adds that if the revealer acted on his own initiative, it is like handing over.
items.desc: רב הונא בר יהודה מספר לרבא שפסק שחייב ישראל שאנסוהו גויים והראה ממון חברו. רבא מורה לו להחזיר את הדין, על פי ברייתא הפוטרת אותו אלא אם נטל ונתן ביד. רבה מוסיף שאם הראה מרצונו – חייב כנוטל ונותן ביד.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Yehuda visits the house of the poor, and when Rava asks if a case came before him, he reports that he ruled a Jew liable for revealing a friend's money under coercion.
sub.desc: רב הונא בר יהודה סיפר לרבא שפסק שחייב לשלם במקרה של יהודי שאנסוהו גויים והראה ממון חברו.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects, citing a baraita that distinguishes between merely pointing (פטור) and physically handing over (חייב), and tells Rav Huna to reverse his ruling.
sub.desc: רבא הורה להחזיר את הדין, כי הברייתא פוטרת אלא אם נטל ונתן ביד.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah adds that if the Jew revealed the property on his own initiative (without being forced), it is considered like physically handing over and he is liable.
sub.desc: רבא מוסיף שאם הראה מרצונו, דינו כנטל ונתן ביד.

items.text: מעשה ביין של רב מרי ופטורו של המוסר
items.text_en: Case of a man forced to carry wine and Rav Ashi's ruling
items.desc_en: A man forced by gentiles to carry Rav Mari's wine was exempted by Rav Ashi, who distinguishes between being forced to carry from the start (where the gentile is the primary actor) and later involvement. Rabbi Avahu challenges this with a baraita about handing over a bundle, but Rav Ashi limits the baraita to cases where the parties are on opposite sides of a river.
items.desc: מסופר על אדם שאנסוהו גויים להראות יין של רב מרי, ולאחר מכן נשא ונתן ביד. רב אשי פוטרו בטענה שכבר הראה להם את היין מתחילה, ולכן מעשה הנשיאה אינו מחייבו. רבי אבא מקשה מברייתא על 'הושט לי', ורב אשי מתרץ שמדובר בצדדי נהר.

sub.desc_en: The narrator introduces a case where a man forced by gentiles to carry Rav Mari's wine was exempted by Rav Ashi.
sub.desc: מביא מעשה ביהודי שהראה יין של רב מרי לגויים, נשא ונתן ביד, ורב אשי פטר אותו.

sub.desc_en: The rabbis challenge Rav Ashi by citing a baraita that says if one took and gave with his own hand, he is liable.
sub.desc: הרבנן מקשים על רב אשי מברייתא האומרת שאם נשא ונתן ביד – חייב.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi distinguishes: the baraita applies only when the gentile did not initially force him to carry, but here the gentile forced him from the start, so the gentile is the primary actor.
sub.desc: הרבנן מקשים על רב אשי מברייתא האומרת שאם נשא ונתן ביד – חייב.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu challenges Rav Ashi with a baraita about handing over a bundle of sheaves or a cluster of grapes to an extortionist, which holds the person liable.
sub.desc: רבי אבהו מקשה מברייתא שבה אנס אמר 'הושט לי' והמושיט חייב, אף שהאנס כבר עומד שם.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi resolves the objection by limiting the baraita to a case where the parties are on opposite sides of a river, so the person is the primary actor, unlike the forced carrier.
sub.desc: רבי אבהו מקשה מברייתא שבה אנס אמר 'הושט לי' והמושיט חייב, אף שהאנס כבר עומד שם.

items.text: דין המוסר רשת במחלוקת לשר המלך
items.text_en: Case of a disputed property handed to a royal officer
items.desc_en: Two people disputed ownership of a field; one handed it to a royal officer. Abaye says he can claim he handed over his own property, but Rava disagrees and rules that we excommunicate him until he brings the matter to court.
items.desc: מסופר על רשת ששני אנשים רבו עליה, ואחד מהם מסרה לשר המלך. אביי פוטרו בטענה שיכול לומר 'שלי מסרתי', ורבא מחייבו ומציע לנדותו עד שיביא את הרשת לדין.

sub.desc_en: The gemara presents a case where two people disputed ownership of a field, and one handed it over to a royal officer.
sub.desc: פתיחה לתיאור מקרה של סכסוך על רשת דגים ומסירתה לשר המלך.

sub.desc_en: Abaye rules that the one who handed over the field can claim he handed over his own property, thus exempting himself from liability.
sub.desc: פתיחה לתיאור מקרה של סכסוך על רשת דגים ומסירתה לשר המלך.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects, arguing that Abaye's reasoning cannot stand because it would allow anyone to evade justice by claiming ownership.
sub.desc: פתיחה לתיאור מקרה של סכסוך על רשת דגים ומסירתה לשר המלך.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that we excommunicate the one who handed over the field until he brings the matter to court.
sub.desc: פתיחה לתיאור מקרה של סכסוך על רשת דגים ומסירתה לשר המלך.

items.text: Rav Kahana's action against a man threatening to reveal a friend's straw
items.text_en: Rav Kahana's action against a man threatening to reveal a friend's straw
items.desc_en: A man wanted to reveal his friend's straw to gentiles. Rav told him not to, but he persisted. Rav Kahana removed his hat (a symbolic act). Rav then cited a verse comparing Jewish property to a trapped deer, and advised Rav Kahana to flee to Eretz Yisrael due to the danger from Persian authorities.

sub.desc_en: A man wanted to reveal his friend's straw to gentiles; Rav told him not to, but the man persisted.
Rav Kahana, sitting before Rav, removed the man's hat as a symbolic act of protest.
Rav cited a verse comparing Jewish property to a trapped deer, implying that once in gentile hands, it is hopeless.
Rav advised Rav Kahana to flee to Eretz Yisrael due to the danger from Persian authorities who now care about bloodshed.

items.text: Rav Kahana's arrival in Eretz Yisrael and his debate with Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Rav Kahana's arrival in Eretz Yisrael and his debate with Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana went to Eretz Yisrael, found Reish Lakish, and arranged to study before Rabbi Yochanan. Initially, he refrained from challenging Rabbi Yochanan, causing him to be moved back seven rows. Rabbi Yochanan mocked him as a fox. Rav Kahana then prayed and began to challenge Rabbi Yochanan, who was impressed. During a debate, Rabbi Yochanan's cushions were removed, and he asked to see Rav Kahana. Seeing his lips moving, Rabbi Yochanan thought he was mocking him, became upset, and Rav Kahana died. The next day, Rabbi Yochanan learned that this was Rav Kahana's manner, and he went to the cave where Rav Kahana was buried.

sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana goes to Eretz Yisrael, finds Reish Lakish concluding the day's study session, and demonstrates his sharpness by analyzing the material.
The next day, Rav Kahana is seated in the first row before Rabbi Yochanan but refrains from challenging him, causing him to be moved back seven rows, and Rabbi Yochanan mocks him as a fox.

Rav Kahana prays that the seven rows be an exchange for the seven years he was told not to challenge Rabbi Yochanan, then stands and begins to challenge Rabbi Yochanan, who is impressed and moves him back to the first row.
During the debate, Rabbi Yochanan's seven cushions are removed one by one as Rav Kahana challenges him, until Rabbi Yochanan sits on the ground.

Rabbi Yochanan, an old man with drooping eyelids, asks to see Rav Kahana; seeing his lips moving, he mistakenly thinks Rav Kahana is mocking him, becomes upset, and Rav Kahana dies; the next day, Rabbi Yochanan learns this was Rav Kahana's manner and goes to his burial cave.

items.text: תחיית רב כהנא על ידי רבי יוחנן
items.text_en: The story of Rabbi Elazar and the snake
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar, who had been avoiding Rabbi Yochanan, is miraculously brought back by a snake. Rabbi Yochanan convinces him to return, and Rabbi Elazar resolves all of Rabbi Yochanan's doubts.
items.desc: רבי יוחנן מקים את רב כהנא מן המתים באמצעות תפילה, לאחר שזה נפטר בצער על עלבונו. רב כהנא מסכים לשוב רק אם יובטח לו שלא ימות שוב, והזמן שחלף כבר חלף. לאחר מכן רב כהנא פותר לרבי יוחנן את כל ספקותיו, ורבי יוחנן מודה שתלמידי בבל גדולים משל ארץ ישראל.

sub.desc_en: A snake miraculously appears and Rabbi Yochanan commands it to open its mouth for Rabbi Elazar to enter; the snake only opens when called 'תלמיד אצל הרב' (student before the master), and Rabbi Yochanan prays to restore the snake.
sub.desc: רבי יוחנן פונה לנחש הכורך את המערה, מבקש שיפתח את פיו, ולאחר שהנחש נענה לקריאה 'תלמיד אצל הרב', הוא מתפלל ומקים את רב כהנא לתחייה.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar apologizes for avoiding Rabbi Yochanan and agrees to return only if Rabbi Yochanan can pray that he will not die again, otherwise he refuses because the opportunity has passed.
sub.desc: רבי יוחנן מביע צער שלא ידע על דרכו של רב כהנא, ורב כהנא מתנה את שובו בכך שלא ימות שוב; הגמרא מעירה שזמנו כבר חלף.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan restores Rabbi Elazar, who then resolves all of Rabbi Yochanan's doubts, prompting Rabbi Yochanan to remark that the students' teachings are actually the master's.
sub.desc: רבי יוחנן מקים את רב כהנא לגמרי, שואל את כל ספקותיו ורב כהנא פותרם; מכאן אומר רבי יוחנן שמה שאמר 'שלכם' הוא למעשה 'שלהם'.

items.text: דין מוסר שהראה נכסי חברו לגויים
items.text_en: Case of pointing to Rabbi Abba's cloak
items.desc_en: A man pointed to Rabbi Abba's cloak, leading to its theft. The rabbis initially considered liability based on a mishnah about a judge's error, but Rabbi Ila cited Rav's ruling that liability only applies if the person physically handled the item. They then sent him to Rabbi Shimon ben Elyakim and Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat, who held him liable based on a baraita about indirect damage.
items.desc: אדם הראה לגויים משי של רבי אבא, והם תפסו אותו. הדיינים חשבו לחייבו על פי משנת 'דן את הדין', אך רבי אילעא אמר שרב מפרש שהמשנה עוסקת במי שנשא ונתן ביד. רבי אבא נשלח לרבי שמעון בן אליקים ורבי אלעזר בן פדת, שחייבו את המוסר על פי משנת 'אם מחמת הגזלן' העוסקת בהראה.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a case where a man pointed to Rabbi Abba's cloak, and Rabbi Avahu, Rabbi Chanina bar Papi, Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha, and Rabbi Ila were sitting together.
sub.desc: פותח בסיפור המעשה: אדם הראה לגויים את המשי של רבי אבא, והדיינים ישבו לדון.

sub.desc_en: The rabbis initially considered holding the man liable based on the mishnah about a judge who errs, where the judge must pay from his own pocket.
sub.desc: הדיינים סברו לחייב את המוסר על פי משנת 'דן את הדין', המחייבת דיין שטעה לשלם מביתו.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ila objects, citing Rav's ruling that liability for indirect damage only applies if the person physically handled the item.
sub.desc: רבי אילעא דוחה את הראיה בשם רב: המשנה עוסקת רק במי שנשא ונתן ביד, ולא במוסר בעלמא.

sub.desc_en: The rabbis tell Rabbi Ila to go to Rabbi Shimon ben Elyakim and Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat, who adjudicate cases of indirect damage (גרמא).
sub.desc: רבי אילעא דוחה את הראיה בשם רב: המשנה עוסקת רק במי שנשא ונתן ביד, ולא במוסר בעלמא.

sub.text: רבי שמעון בן אליקים ורבי אלעזר בן פדת
sub.desc_en: He went to them, and they held the man liable based on a baraita about a robber whose field is swept away, and the gemara establishes that the case involved mere pointing (אחוי אחוויי).
sub.desc: הם חייבו את המוסר על פי משנת 'אם מחמת הגזלן', והוכיחו שהמשנה עוסקת בהראה בעלמא.

items.text: Case of the silver cup and the principle of saving oneself with another's property
items.text_en: Case of the silver cup and the principle of saving oneself with another's property
items.desc_en: A bailee gave away a deposited silver cup to thieves to save himself. Raba exempted him, but Abaye objected that this is saving oneself with another's property. Rav Ashi distinguishes: if the bailee was a prominent person, the thieves came for him; otherwise, they came for the cup.

sub.desc_en: The gemara presents a case: a bailee gave a deposited silver cup to thieves to save himself, and Raba exempted him from liability.
Abaye objects that this is a case of saving oneself with another's property, which is forbidden.
Rav Ashi resolves the objection by distinguishing: if the bailee was a prominent person, the thieves came for him, so he is exempt; otherwise, they came for the cup, and he is liable.

items.text: Case of the redemption of captives fund
items.text_en: Case of the redemption of captives fund
items.desc_en: A bailee gave away a purse designated for redeeming captives to thieves to save himself. Rava exempted him, and when Abaye objected, Rava ruled that there is no greater redemption of captives than this.

sub.desc_en: A man had a purse designated for redeeming captives deposited with him, and when thieves came, he gave it to them.
Rava exempted the bailee from liability.
Abaye objected that the bailee was saving himself at the expense of another's money.
Rava responded that there is no greater redemption of captives than this, justifying the exemption.

items.text: דין רודף והצלה בנכסי הזולת
items.text_en: Case of the donkey and the pursuer
items.desc_en: A man sank another's donkey to save people on a ferry. Raba exempted him, and Abaye objected. Raba explained that the donkey's owner was a pursuer (rodef), and then elaborated the laws of a pursuer: a pursuer who breaks objects is exempt, the pursued who breaks the pursuer's objects is exempt, but breaking others' objects is prohibited. A rescuer who breaks objects is exempt by rabbinic enactment.
items.desc: אדם הטביע חמורו של אחר שהסכן את הספינה. רבה פוטר משום שבעל החמור היה רודף. רבה מבאר: רודף ששבר כלים – פטור; נרדף ששבר כלי רודף – פטור, אבל כלי אחר – חייב; מציל ששבר כלים – פטור, לא מן הדין אלא כדי שאנשים יצילו.

sub.desc_en: A man sank another's donkey to save people on a ferry, and the case came before Raba.
sub.desc: מעשה באדם שהקדים והעלה חמורו למעבורת לפני אחרים, החמור סיכן להטביע את הספינה, ואדם אחר דחף את החמור לנהר והטביעו; רבה פטר את המציל.

sub.desc_en: Raba exempted the man who sank the donkey.
sub.desc: מעשה באדם שהקדים והעלה חמורו למעבורת לפני אחרים, החמור סיכן להטביע את הספינה, ואדם אחר דחף את החמור לנהר והטביעו; רבה פטר את המציל.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objected that the man was saving himself with another's property, which is prohibited.
sub.desc: מעשה באדם שהקדים והעלה חמורו למעבורת לפני אחרים, החמור סיכן להטביע את הספינה, ואדם אחר דחף את החמור לנהר והטביעו; רבה פטר את המציל.

sub.desc_en: Raba explained that the donkey's owner was a pursuer (rodef) from the start, so the rescuer is exempt.
sub.desc: מעשה באדם שהקדים והעלה חמורו למעבורת לפני אחרים, החמור סיכן להטביע את הספינה, ואדם אחר דחף את החמור לנהר והטביעו; רבה פטר את המציל.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Raba's general rule: a pursuer who breaks objects while chasing is exempt, whether the objects belong to the pursued or anyone else, because he is already liable for his life.
sub.desc: רבה מבאר את שיטתו: רודף שהיה רודף אחר חברו להורגו ושבר כלים – פטור, שהרי מתחייב בנפשו.

sub.desc_en: The pursued who breaks the pursuer's objects is exempt, but breaking others' objects is prohibited.
sub.desc: רבה ממשיך: נרדף ששבר כלי רודף – פטור, אבל כלי של כל אדם – חייב, שאסור להציל עצמו בממון חברו.

sub.desc_en: A rescuer who breaks objects is exempt by rabbinic enactment, not by strict law, to encourage rescue.
