sub.desc: רבה פוסק: מציל ששבר כלים – פטור, לא מן הדין אלא כדי שאנשים יצילו.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara: The river swept away the field
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara: The river swept away the field
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a river swept away a stolen field, the thief says 'yours is before you.' The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Elazar holds the thief liable to provide another field, while the Sages exempt him. The dispute is based on different hermeneutical methods: Rabbi Elazar uses ribbui u'miut (amplification and limitation) to include all items except documents, while the Sages use klal u'prat (general and specific) to limit liability to movable property with intrinsic value, excluding land, slaves, and documents.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a river swept away a stolen field, the thief says 'yours is before you' and is exempt.
A baraita presents the dispute: Rabbi Elazar holds the thief liable to provide another field, while the Sages exempt him.
The Gemara asks: what is the basis of their dispute? It explains that Rabbi Elazar uses the hermeneutical method of ribbui u'miut (amplification and limitation) on the verse.
The Gemara explains that the pattern of amplification-limitation-amplification includes everything, so Rabbi Elazar includes land and excludes only documents.
The Gemara specifies that the limitation excludes only documents (שטרות) from liability.
The Gemara explains that the Sages use the method of klal u'prat (general and specific), which limits liability to items similar to the specific case.

sub.text: Gemara's conclusion of the Sages' position
sub.text_en: Gemara's conclusion of the Sages' position
sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the Sages limit liability to movable property with intrinsic value, excluding land, slaves, and documents.

items.text: Baraita about a cow and the dispute's application
items.text_en: Baraita about a cow and the dispute's application
items.desc_en: A baraita similarly records a dispute between Rabbi Elazar and the Sages regarding a stolen cow swept away by a river. Rav Pappa explains that the case involves a field that was stolen and then the thief planted it, leading to a different analysis.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited recording a dispute between Rabbi Elazar and the Sages regarding a stolen cow swept away by a river, mirroring the earlier dispute about a field.
The Gemara asks: In that case (of the cow), what is the basis of their dispute?
Rav Pappa answers that the case involves a field that was stolen and then the thief planted it, leading to a different analysis.

items.text: Opening statement linking to previous discussion
items.text_en: Opening statement linking to previous discussion
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the dispute between Rabbi Elazar and the Rabbis about a cow lying in a field and swept away by a river follows their respective reasoning.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the dispute between Rabbi Elazar and the Rabbis about a cow lying in a field and swept away by a river follows their respective reasoning.

items.text: Mishnah: Returning in settled area vs. desert
items.text_en: Mishnah: Returning in settled area vs. desert
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who robbed, borrowed, or received a deposit from another may not return it in the desert if the transaction occurred in a settled area, but if it was agreed to return in the desert, he may.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one who robbed, borrowed, or received a deposit from another in a settled area may not return it in the desert, but if it was agreed to return in the desert, he may.

items.text: Gemara's question and Abaye's resolution
items.text_en: Gemara's question and Abaye's resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita about repayment location for loans vs. lost items and deposits. Abaye resolves that a loan can be claimed anywhere, but a lost item or deposit can only be claimed in its place.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita: a loan can be repaid anywhere, but a lost item or deposit can only be repaid in its place.
Abaye resolves: a loan can be claimed anywhere, but a lost item or deposit can only be claimed in its place.

items.text: Clarifying the case of 'on condition to go to the desert'
items.text_en: Clarifying the case of 'on condition to go to the desert'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's case is necessary when the depositor said he is going to the desert and the bailee agreed to return it there.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: the Mishnah's case of 'on condition to go out to the desert' is obvious.
The Gemara explains: the case is necessary where the depositor said 'this deposit is with you because I am going to the desert' and the bailee agreed to return it there.

items.text: Mishnah: Certainty vs. uncertainty in claims
items.text_en: Mishnah: Certainty vs. uncertainty in claims
items.desc_en: The Mishnah distinguishes between one who says 'I robbed you' but is unsure if he returned it (liable) and one who says 'I don't know if I robbed you' (exempt).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule: one who admits to a past wrong but is uncertain about restitution is liable, while one who is uncertain about the wrong itself is exempt.

items.text: Dispute between Rav Huna/Rav Yehuda and Rav Nachman/Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav Huna/Rav Yehuda and Rav Nachman/Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute about a case where one claims 'you have a maneh of mine' and the other says 'I don't know'. Rav Huna and Rav Yehuda hold he is liable because a definite claim overrides uncertainty, while Rav Nachman and Rabbi Yochanan hold he is exempt because money remains in its owner's presumptive status.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute: if one claims 'you have a maneh of mine' and the other says 'I don't know', Rav Huna and Rav Yehuda say he is liable, while Rav Nachman and Rabbi Yochanan say he is exempt.

The Gemara explains the reasoning: Rav Huna and Rav Yehuda hold that a definite claim (ברי) overrides uncertainty (שמא), while Rav Nachman and Rabbi Yochanan hold that money remains in its owner's presumptive status (אוקי ממונא בחזקת מריה).

items.text: Reconciling the Mishnah with the dispute
items.text_en: Reconciling the Mishnah with the dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the Mishnah's exemption in the second clause fits with the dispute, and resolves that the Mishnah deals with a case where the claimant did not demand payment, and the first clause refers to one who wishes to fulfill a heavenly obligation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the Mishnah's second clause (exemption for 'I don't know if I borrowed') can be reconciled with the dispute, arguing that if the first clause (obligation) refers to a case where the claimant demands payment, the second clause contradicts it by exempting the defendant.

The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah's first clause refers to a case where the claimant did not demand payment, and the obligation applies only to one who wishes to fulfill a heavenly obligation (יְדֵי שָׁמַיִם).

items.text: Support from Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Support from Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba quotes Rabbi Yochanan that one who says 'a maneh is in your hand' and the other says 'I don't know' is liable when he seeks to fulfill a heavenly obligation.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: It was also stated: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba said Rabbi Yochanan ruled that one who says 'I don't know' is liable when coming to fulfill a heavenly obligation.

items.text: Mishnah: Returning a stolen lamb without owner's knowledge
items.text_en: Mishnah: Returning a stolen lamb without owner's knowledge
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses a case where one steals a lamb from the flock, returns it, and it dies or is stolen again. If the owners counted the flock and it was complete, the thief is exempt from liability.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one steals a lamb, returns it, and it dies or is stolen again without the owner's knowledge, but the owner counted the flock and found it complete, the thief is exempt from liability.

items.text: Dispute about the need for the owner's knowledge
items.text_en: Dispute about the need for the owner's knowledge
items.desc_en: Rav, Shmuel, Rabbi Yochanan, and Rav Chisda debate whether the owner's knowledge (da'at) is required for the return to be effective, and how the Mishnah's counting clause applies to the first or second part of the Mishnah.

sub.desc_en: Rav states that when the owner knows of the return, the owner's knowledge (דעת) is required; when the owner does not know, a count (מנין) exempts, and the Mishnah's counting clause applies to the latter part (סיפא).
Shmuel argues that whether the owner knows or not, a count exempts, and the Mishnah's counting clause applies to the entire Mishnah (כולה).
Rabbi Yochanan holds that when the owner knows, a count exempts; when the owner does not know, even a count is unnecessary, and the Mishnah's counting clause applies to the first part (רישא).

Rav Chisda asserts that when the owner knows, a count exempts; when the owner does not know, the owner's knowledge (דעת) is required, and the Mishnah's counting clause applies to the first part (רישא).

items.text: Rava's statement (incomplete)
items.text_en: Rava's statement (incomplete)
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to cite Rava's opinion, but the text is cut off.

sub.desc_en: Rava begins to speak (the continuation is cut off in the source).

items.text: Gemara's challenge to Rav Chisda and Rava's position
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge to Rav Chisda and Rava's position
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rav Chisda's reasoning and cites a case where Rava holds a person liable for a lamb taken from a flock even if he returned it, unless he counted it. The Gemara clarifies that Rava's case is where the owner did not count the flock.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Rav Chisda's reasoning is, suggesting it is because the shepherd is armed with external dogs (so he is not afraid to steal).
The Gemara objects that Rava seems to contradict Rav Chisda, citing a case where Rava holds a person liable for a lamb taken from a flock even if he returned it, unless he counted it.
The Gemara resolves that Rava's case is specifically where the owner did not count the flock, so there is no contradiction.

items.text: Rav's position and Rav Chanan bar Abba's qualification
items.text_en: Rav's position and Rav Chanan bar Abba's qualification
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav's statement that returning an animal to a desert flock exempts the thief, but Rav Chanan bar Abba qualifies that Rav agrees liability applies in the case of a marsh (where the owner can find it).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav's statement by citing that Rav himself said returning a stolen animal to a desert flock exempts the thief.
Rav Chanan bar Abba qualifies that Rav agrees liability applies in the case of a marsh (where the owner can find it).

items.text: Tannaitic dispute between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a baraita where Rabbi Yishmael says a thief must return the stolen item to the place he stole it, while Rabbi Akiva requires the owner's knowledge. The Gemara initially assumes the dispute is about a coin (where Rabbi Yitzchak's principle applies) and relates it to Rav and Shmuel, but then reinterprets it as about a lamb without the owner's knowledge, relating to Rav Chisda and Rabbi Yochanan.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a baraita where Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva dispute whether a thief must return the stolen item to its original place or needs the owner's knowledge.

The Gemara assumes both Tannaim accept Rabbi Yitzchak's principle that one constantly checks his coin purse, and suggests the dispute is about a coin with the owner's knowledge, aligning with the dispute between Rav and Shmuel.
The Gemara rejects the initial assumption and reinterprets the dispute as about a lamb taken without the owner's knowledge, aligning with the dispute between Rav Chisda and Rabbi Yochanan.

items.text: Rav Zevid's resolution regarding a guardian who stole
items.text_en: Rav Zevid's resolution regarding a guardian who stole
items.desc_en: Rav Zevid in the name of Rava explains that all agree a guardian who steals from the owner's property is liable like Rav Chisda, but the dispute is about a guardian who steals from his own domain: Rabbi Akiva holds his guardianship ends, Rabbi Yishmael holds it does not.

sub.text: Rav Zevid in the name of Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Zevid in the name of Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Zevid resolves the dispute between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yishmael by distinguishing between a guardian who steals from the owner's property (all agree liable) and one who steals from his own domain (Rabbi Akiva holds guardianship ends, Rabbi Yishmael holds it does not).

items.text: Dispute about counting as exemption
items.text_en: Dispute about counting as exemption
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a Tannaitic dispute about whether a robber is exempt if he includes the stolen item in a calculation. It initially assumes both sides accept Rabbi Yitzchak's principle and disagree about whether counting exempts, but then reinterprets that they disagree about Rabbi Yitzchak's principle itself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the dispute about whether counting exempts is a Tannaitic dispute.
The Gemara cites a baraita where one Tanna says the robber is exempt if he includes the stolen item in a calculation, and another says he is not exempt.
The Gemara initially assumes both sides accept Rabbi Yitzchak's principle and asks whether they disagree about whether counting exempts.
The Gemara resolves that if they accept Rabbi Yitzchak's principle, all agree counting exempts; the dispute is actually about Rabbi Yitzchak's principle itself.

items.text: Two alternative resolutions for the counting dispute
items.text_en: Two alternative resolutions for the counting dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers two alternative explanations: one distinguishes between placing the item in the owner's purse versus his hand, and the other distinguishes between whether the owner has other coins in his purse or not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers a first alternative resolution: everyone accepts Rabbi Yitzchak's principle, and the dispute is between placing the coins in the owner's purse versus his hand.
The Gemara offers a second alternative resolution: both cases involve counting and placing in the purse, but the dispute is whether the owner has other coins in his purse or not.

items.text: Mishnah: Restrictions on buying from shepherds and watchmen
items.text_en: Mishnah: Restrictions on buying from shepherds and watchmen
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not buy wool, milk, or kids from shepherds, nor wood or fruit from fruit watchmen, but may buy certain items from women and in specific places. If they say to hide the purchase, it is forbidden. Eggs and chickens may be bought anywhere.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by listing items one may not buy from shepherds and fruit watchmen.
The Mishnah lists permitted purchases from women and in specific places, and concludes with a general rule about eggs and chickens.

items.text: Baraita elaborating on the Mishnah
items.text_en: Baraita elaborating on the Mishnah
items.desc_en: A baraita details what may and may not be bought from shepherds: not goats, kids, or fleece, but sewn garments (since they are theirs), milk and cheese in the desert but not in settled areas, and four or five sheep or fleeces but not two. Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes between domesticated and desert animals.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by listing items that may not be bought from shepherds (goats, kids, fleece, plucked wool) and items that may be bought (sewn garments, milk and cheese in the desert, four or five sheep or fleeces but not two).
Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes between domesticated animals (בַּיָּיתוֹת) and desert animals (מִדְבָּרִיּוֹת), stating that one may buy from shepherds only when the owner would notice the sale.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the baraita's numbers
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the baraita's numbers
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the baraita says four or five sheep but not three, and resolves the contradiction with the later statement that three may be bought, by distinguishing between healthy and emaciated animals.

sub.desc_en: Mar states the baraita's rule that one buys four or five sheep, and the Gemara questions why four is mentioned when five is more restrictive.
Rav Chisda explains that 'four' means four out of five, or alternatively four from a small flock and five from a large flock.
The Gemara points out an internal contradiction in the baraita: the first clause permits only four or five, but the later clause implies that three is also permitted.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between healthy animals (בָּרְיָיתָא), where only four or five are bought, and emaciated animals (כְּחִישָׁתָא), where even three may be bought.

items.text: Uncertainty about Rabbi Yehuda's position
items.text_en: Uncertainty about Rabbi Yehuda's position
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an uncertainty whether Rabbi Yehuda's statement about domesticated and desert animals refers to the first part (limiting purchases to four or five only for domesticated) or the last part (allowing even two for domesticated). A baraita resolves that Rabbi Yehuda allows buying four or five from any flock, but only domesticated ones.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an uncertainty whether Rabbi Yehuda's statement in the baraita refers to the first part (domesticated animals) for a stricter ruling, or to the last part (desert animals) for a lenient ruling.

The Gemara elaborates both possible interpretations: if Rabbi Yehuda refers to the first part, he restricts even four or five to domesticated animals; if to the last part, he permits even two domesticated animals.

A baraita is cited to resolve the uncertainty: Rabbi Yehuda rules that domesticated animals may be purchased from shepherds, but desert animals may not, and in any case one may buy four or five sheep from any flock.

items.text: Rava buys from a sharecropper; Abaye objects
items.text_en: Rava buys from a sharecropper; Abaye objects
items.desc_en: Rava purchases produce from a sharecropper. Abaye objects based on the Mishnah that one may not buy from guardians of produce. Rava distinguishes: a guardian has no share in the land, but a sharecropper does, so he is selling his own portion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the phrase 'in every place' that the mishnah refers to the latter clause and rules leniently.
Abaye objects to Rava's purchase from a sharecropper, citing the mishnah that one may not buy from guardians of produce.
Rava distinguishes: a guardian has no share in the land, but a sharecropper does, so he is selling his own portion.

items.text: Baraita on buying from fruit guardians
items.text_en: Baraita on buying from fruit guardians
items.desc_en: A baraita details when one may buy from fruit guardians: when they sit and sell with baskets before them, but if they say 'hide it' it is forbidden. One may buy from the garden entrance but not from behind.

sub.desc_en: The baraita rules that one may buy from fruit guardians when they sit selling with baskets before them, but not if they say 'hide it' or from behind the garden.

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on buying from a robber
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on buying from a robber
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel dispute when one may buy from a robber: Rav requires a majority of the goods to be his own, Shmuel allows even if only a minority is his. Rav Yehudah rules like Shmuel.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks from what point it is permitted to buy from a robber.
Rav rules that one may buy only when the majority of the goods belong to the robber.
Shmuel permits buying even when only a minority of the goods belong to the robber.
Rav Yehudah instructs the judge Adda to rule in accordance with Shmuel's lenient position.

items.text: Dispute about lost property (ממון מסור)
items.text_en: Dispute about lost property (ממון מסור)
items.desc_en: Rav Huna and Rav Yehudah dispute whether one may actively destroy property that has been handed over to a non-Jewish authority. One permits it, reasoning that the property is no worse than the person's life; the other forbids it, lest the wicked man have worthy descendants, citing the verse 'The wicked prepares and the righteous wears.'

sub.desc_en: The gemara presents a dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Yehudah regarding whether one may actively destroy ממון מסור (property handed over to a non-Jewish authority).

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of the first opinion
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the first opinion
sub.desc_en: The gemara explains the first opinion: destroying the property is permitted because the property is no worse than the person's life (which is forfeit).

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of the second opinion
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the second opinion
sub.desc_en: The gemara explains the second opinion: destroying is forbidden because the wicked man may have worthy descendants, citing the verse 'יָכִין רָשָׁע וְצַדִּיק יִלְבַּשׁ' (the wicked prepares and the righteous wears).

items.text: Rav Chisda dismisses a dishonest sharecropper
items.text_en: Rav Chisda dismisses a dishonest sharecropper
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda had a sharecropper who would weigh and give, weigh and take (cheating). He dismissed him, applying to himself the verse 'The wealth of the sinner is stored up for the righteous.'

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda dismisses a dishonest sharecropper who cheated by weighing and taking extra, applying the verse 'The wealth of the sinner is stored up for the righteous' to himself.

items.text: Dispute on the verse 'What is the hope of the profane'
items.text_en: Dispute on the verse 'What is the hope of the profane'
items.desc_en: Rav Huna and Rav Chisda dispute the meaning of 'his soul' in the verse: one says it refers to the soul of the victim, the other to the soul of the robber. Each brings proof texts, and the Gemara resolves the apparent contradictions between the verses.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Chisda over the meaning of 'his soul' in the verse about the profane.
Rav Huna argues that 'his soul' refers to the victim's soul, citing the verse 'he takes the soul of its owners'.
Rav Chisda argues that 'his soul' refers to the robber's soul, citing the verse 'He will take the soul of those who take them'.
The Gemara objects to Rav Huna: the verse says 'owners', which implies the current owner (the robber), not the original victim.
The Gemara objects to Rav Chisda: the verse 'He will take the soul of those who take them' is explained as 'because they take the soul' (of the victim), supporting Rav Huna.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan: robbing a perutah is like taking a life
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan: robbing a perutah is like taking a life
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan teaches that one who robs another of a perutah is as if taking his soul, citing verses. The Gemara extends this: even the souls of his children, even if he pays, and even if he only causes indirect loss, as in the case of Saul and the Gibeonites.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan opens by teaching that one who robs another of a perutah is as if taking his soul, citing verses.
The Gemara adds additional verses to support the severity of robbery.
The Gemara asks why additional verses are needed, and answers that the first verse only implies the robber's own soul, but the second verse extends to the souls of his children.
The Gemara raises a possible limitation: perhaps the severity applies only when the robber does not pay, but if he pays it is less severe; the third verse refutes this.

The Gemara raises another limitation: perhaps the severity applies only to direct robbery, not indirect causation; the fourth verse about Saul and the Gibeonites refutes this, showing that indirect harm is also considered as killing.

items.text: Buying from women, slaves, and minors; charity collectors
items.text_en: Buying from women, slaves, and minors; charity collectors
items.desc_en: A baraita permits buying woolen and linen vessels from women in certain regions, but not wine, oil, or flour. Abba Shaul adds that a woman may sell for a head-covering. Charity collectors may accept a small amount but not a large one. The Gemara relates that Ravina accepted items from women in Mechoza, and Rabba Tosfa'ah objected, but Ravina considered them a small amount.

sub.desc_en: A baraita permits buying woolen and linen vessels from women in certain regions, but not wine, oil, or flour; Abba Shaul adds that a woman may sell for a head-covering, and all who say 'hide it' are forbidden.
The baraita adds that charity collectors may accept a small amount from women, but not a large amount.

The baraita further rules that one may buy olives or oil from olive-press workers by measure, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel permits buying small amounts of olives from women in the Upper Galilee due to embarrassment.
Rabba Tosfa'ah objects to Ravina accepting items from women in Mechoza, citing the baraita that charity collectors may only accept a small amount.
Ravina answers that for the wealthy people of Mechoza, these items are considered a small amount.

items.text: Mishnah and baraita on what a craftsman may keep
items.text_en: Mishnah and baraita on what a craftsman may keep
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that lint from a launderer belongs to him, but from a comber to the owner. A tailor may keep a thread sufficient for sewing, and a patch 3x3 handbreadths belongs to the owner. A carpenter's shavings from an adze are his, from an axe belong to the owner. The Gemara cites a baraita that one may buy lint from a launderer, and a launderer may take two upper threads.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that lint from a launderer belongs to him, but from a comber to the owner; a launderer may keep three upper threads, and if black on white he takes all.

The Mishnah continues: a tailor may keep a thread sufficient for sewing, a patch 3x3 handbreadths belongs to the owner; a carpenter's shavings from an adze are his, from an axe belong to the owner, and if working at the owner's house even the boards belong to the owner.
A baraita supports the Mishnah: one may buy lint from a launderer because it is his, and a launderer may take two upper threads as his own.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Limits on the weaver's work
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Limits on the weaver's work
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a weaver may not add more than three threads to the cloth, nor comb the fabric for the warp but only for the woof, and may only straighten it lengthwise, not widthwise, unless it is up to a handbreadth.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the limits on a weaver's work: no more than three threads added, combing only for the woof, and straightening only lengthwise unless up to a handbreadth.

items.text: Gemara's resolution of the thread count contradiction
items.text_en: Gemara's resolution of the thread count contradiction
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: the Mishnah says three threads, but a previous source said two. It resolves by distinguishing between thick threads (two) and thin threads (three).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the master said 'two threads' but the Mishnah says 'three', raising a contradiction.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between thick threads (two) and thin threads (three).

items.text: Gemara's resolution of the combing contradiction
items.text_en: Gemara's resolution of the combing contradiction
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction between the Mishnah (comb only for the woof) and a baraita (comb only for the warp). It resolves by distinguishing between a cloak (woof) and a shirt (warp).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: the Mishnah says comb only for the woof, but a baraita says the opposite.
The Gemara resolves by distinguishing between a cloak (glima) and a coat (sarbala).

items.text: Rabbi Yirmeya's question on the thread count
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's question on the thread count
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks whether the three threads include the one used for bringing and returning (the needle thread) or not. The question remains unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks whether the three threads refer to bringing and taking as one or two, and the question remains unresolved (teiku).

items.text: Gemara's resolution of the straightening contradiction
items.text_en: Gemara's resolution of the straightening contradiction
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction between the Mishnah (straighten lengthwise but not widthwise) and a baraita (straighten widthwise but not lengthwise). It resolves by distinguishing between a cloak (lengthwise) and a himation (widthwise).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: the Mishnah says straighten only lengthwise, but a baraita says the opposite.
The Gemara resolves by distinguishing between a cloak (glima) and a linen garment (hemyoni).

items.text: Baraita on buying from a wool-comber
items.text_en: Baraita on buying from a wool-comber
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that one may not buy wool scraps from a wool-comber because they are stolen from the customer, but where custom allows it, one may. In any case, one may buy a full pillow or cushion of wool scraps because the change in form acquires ownership.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that one may not buy combed wool from a comber because it is not his, but in places where it is his custom, one may buy; and one may always buy a full pillow or cushion of combed wool because the change in form acquires it.
The baraita adds an exception: where local custom grants the scraps to the worker, one may buy them.
The baraita states that in any case, one may buy a full pillow or cushion of wool scraps because the change in form acquires ownership.
The gemara explains the rationale: the worker acquires ownership through the change (שינוי) in the form of the wool.

items.text: Baraita on buying from a weaver
items.text_en: Baraita on buying from a weaver
items.desc_en: A baraita lists items one may not buy from a weaver (e.g., threads, warp threads, etc.) but one may buy a finished garment, woof, warp, spun, and woven. The Gemara clarifies that 'woven' refers to pieces of cloth.

sub.desc_en: The baraita lists items one may not buy from a weaver: threads, warp threads, spools, and remnants of skeins.
The baraita lists items one may buy from a weaver: a finished garment, woof, warp, spun, and woven.
The Gemara questions why the baraita lists 'woven' separately, since if one may buy spun thread, certainly one may buy woven cloth.
The Gemara answers that 'woven' here refers to pieces of cloth (patches), not fully woven garments.

items.text: Baraita on buying from a dyer
items.text_en: Baraita on buying from a dyer
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that one may not buy certain items from a dyer (e.g., samples, plucked wool), but one may buy a dyed garment, spun wool, and garments. The Gemara clarifies that 'garments' refers to felt cloaks.

sub.desc_en: A baraita lists items one may not buy from a dyer (samples, etc.) and items one may buy (dyed garment, spun, garments).
The Gemara questions why the baraita lists both 'garments' and 'spun' when the latter implies the former.
The Gemara explains that 'garments' (בגדים) here means a specific type of garment (namtei).

items.text: Baraita on leather worker's leftovers
items.text_en: Baraita on leather worker's leftovers
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that when one gives hides to a tanner, the cuttings and plucked wool belong to the owner, but the wool that rises and washes away belongs to the tanner.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that when one gives hides to a tanner, the clippings and pluckings belong to the owner, but the residue that floats up in water belongs to the tanner.

items.text: Rav Yehuda on the dyer's leftover and tekhelet
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda on the dyer's leftover and tekhelet
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda explains that the dyer's leftover is called 'katzra' and the dyer takes it. He also says that all such leftovers count toward the minimum of tekhelet threads, but his son Yitzchak is particular about them.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda identifies the black residue as 'katzra' and says the dyer takes it, and that all such residues count toward the techelet (blue wool) count, but his son Yitzchak is strict about them.
Rav Yehuda rules that all such leftovers count toward the minimum of tekhelet threads, but notes that his son Yitzchak is particular about them.

items.text: Dispute on the measure of leftover thread for a tailor
items.text_en: Dispute on the measure of leftover thread for a tailor
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses how much thread a tailor may keep as leftover. Rav Asi says a full needle's length beyond the needle. The Gemara questions whether 'beyond the needle' means another full needle's length or just a little, and resolves from a baraita that it is a full needle's length.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the case of a tailor who left leftover thread, and the Gemara asks how much thread is considered leftover for sewing.
Rav Asi answers that the leftover thread is a full needle's length beyond the needle.
The Gemara raises a doubt: does 'beyond the needle' mean another full needle's length or just a little?
The Gemara cites a baraita that discusses leftover thread and a patch, distinguishing between when the owner is particular and when not.
The Gemara argues that if the leftover is a full needle's length beyond, then less than that is useful for a plug; but if only a little, less than that has no use.
The Gemara concludes that the correct interpretation is a full needle's length beyond the needle.

items.text: Contradiction on the carpenter's leftovers and Rava's resolution
items.text_en: Contradiction on the carpenter's leftovers and Rava's resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction between two sources about what belongs to the carpenter and what to the owner. Rava resolves it by explaining that in the Tanna's locale there are two types of axes (a large one called 'kashil' and a small one called 'ma'atzad'), while in the baraita's locale there is only one called 'ma'atzad'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction between the Mishnah's ruling about the carpenter's leftovers and a baraita that assigns the chips from a ma'atzad (adze) to the owner and those from a magera (saw) to the carpenter.

Rava resolves the contradiction by explaining that in the Tanna's locale there are two types of axes (a large one called 'kashil' and a small one called 'ma'atzad'), while in the baraita's locale there is only one called 'ma'atzad'.

items.text: Baraita on stonecutters and gardeners, and Rav Yehuda's ruling
items.text_en: Baraita on stonecutters and gardeners, and Rav Yehuda's ruling
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that stonecutters' chips are not considered stolen, but for gardeners (pruning trees, vines, etc.), if the owner is particular, they are stolen; otherwise, they belong to the worker. Rav Yehuda adds that reeds and shoots are not stolen unless the owner is particular, and Ravina notes that Mata Mechasya is a place where they are particular.

sub.desc_en: The baraita lists various workers (stonecutters, gardeners, etc.) and rules that their leftover materials are not considered stolen unless the owner is particular about them.
Rav Yehuda adds that reeds and shoots are not stolen unless the owner is particular about them.
Ravina notes that in Mata Mechasya, the owners are particular about such items, so they are considered stolen.
